en: Homage to Vāgīśvara!
Having prostrated before the omniscient one, the teacher of the world who is the source of all, this definition of words is now being stated— concise, clear, and complete.

Now, for what purpose is the instruction of the phonemes? It is for the sake of the *pratyāhāra* (abbreviated syllable). For the *pratyāhāra* serves to facilitate the operation of the grammatical treatise with brevity.
The *pratyāhāra* sūtra is: *aiuṇ*. 0.1.

Having taught the phonemes in this sequence—*a*, *i*, *u*—he places the letter *ṇ* at the end as an *it* for the purpose of *pratyāhāra*. Its pronunciation occurs by means of a single [vowel], namely the letter *a*, according to the rule *ṛko ’ṇo ralau* (Pāṇini 1.1.15). Furthermore, this is a reference to the genus (*jāti*). *ṛḷk*, 0.2.

Having taught these two phonemes, *ṛ* and *ḷ*, he places the letter *k* at the end of the preceding [vowels] for the purpose of forming a *pratyāhāra*. Its pronunciation occurs by means of four [rules]: by the vowel *a* in *ako 'ki dīrghaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.106), by the vowel *i* in *iko yaṇ aci* (Pāṇini 6.1.77), by the vowel *u* in *ugitaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.6), and by the vowel *ṛ* in *ṛko 'ṇo ralau* (Pāṇini 1.1.15). Since the phonemes beginning with *a* are the domain of frequent usage, the purpose of their instruction is easily understood.

The phoneme *ḷ* is employed only in the context of the root *kḷp*. Since the substitution of *l* for *ṛ*—by the rule "that which is previously established is not valid" (6.3.27)—is not considered valid, the operations dependent on *a*-sounds (*ackāryāṇi*) would apply to the *ṛ*-sound alone. Why, then, is *ḷ* taught? It is so that those subsequent operations dependent on *a*-sounds which result from the prescription of *l* should also apply to *ḷ*. What, then, are these? They are protracted vowels (*pluta*), circumflex accent (*svarita*), and reduplication (*dvirvacana*): e.g., *kḷ3ptaśikha*, *prakḷptaḥ*, and *kḷpttavān*.

Furthermore, even for an imitation of an incorrect word-form that arises from incapacity, correctness is desired; therefore, the letter *ḷ* is taught even when situated therein, so that the grammatical operations (*ackārya*) applicable to vowels may be understood. When a girl, instead of saying "ṛtaka," pronounces "ḷtaka" due to a deficiency in her vocal power, another person imitates her, saying, "This girl said, 'ḷtaka'.

Having taught the two sounds *e* and *o* in the rule *eoṅ*, he places the letter *ṇ* at the end to form a *pratyāhāra*. Its pronunciation is performed by a single sound: by the vowel *e* in the rule *iko 'deṅ guṇavṛddhī* (Pāṇini 1.1.3).

Having taught the two phonemes *a* and *au* as *ai* and *au*, he places the letter *c* at the end of the preceding [group] for the purpose of forming a *pratyāhāra*. Its pronunciation occurs by means of four [phonemes]: by the letter *a* in Pāṇini 5.2.36 (*aca ādaij hetur araktavikāre*), by the letter *i* in 5.2.4 (*khitīca ekāco 'm*), by the letter *e* in 5.1.75 (*eco 'yavāyāvaḥ*), and by the letter *ai* in 6.1.3 (*ajāgṛṇiśvīnāṃ sicy ataṅy ādaij*). How is it that, in the *pratyāhāra*, the *anubandhas* are not included in the references to *ac*?

"Because it is an indicator (*jñāpaka*), because it is not primary, and because elision (*lopa*) is stronger. Regarding those parts of phonemes that resemble other phonemes, the grammatical operation pertaining to those [other phonemes] does not apply to them; for they merely imitate their shadow, and are not those very [phonemes] themselves. Indeed, the teachers maintain that a phoneme is produced by a distinct effort. An exception must be made regarding the phoneme *ṛ* in the rules concerning the suffix *nuk*, the substitution of *l* for *r*, and the substitution of *ṇ*. [The rule *hayavaralaṇ* (Pāṇini 1.1.69)]... [Note: The provided text fragment ends with "hayavaralaṇ". The full rule is *hayavaralaṇam ajjhalau* (Pāṇini 1.1.69), which defines the consonants.]

Having taught these letters—ha, ya, va, ra, and la—he places the letter *ṇ* at the end of the preceding ones for the purpose of forming a *pratyāhāra*. Its pronunciation occurs by means of two [rules]: by the letter *i* in *iṇaḥ ṣaḥ* (P. 8.3.39), and by the letter *ya* in *iko yaṇ aci* (P. 6.1.77). All references to *iṇ* are made with this [final] *ṇ*, whereas all references to *aṇ* are made with the preceding *ṇ*. Furthermore, this is a reference to the genus (*jāti*). This letter *r* is taught after the letter *y*.

In the case of *tasya yarupādāne yayupādāne yamupādāne copādāne sati prātar nayati*, the substitution of *ñam* would apply by the rule *yato ñami ñam vā* (Pāṇini 6.4.140). In *nadīhradaḥ*, reduplication would apply by the rule *aco rahād dve* (Pāṇini 6.4.141). In *naraṃ rathena*, the substitution of *yam* would apply by the rule *anusvārasya yayi yam* (Pāṇini 6.4.151). This is not a fault.

In the view that a grammatical rule (*lakṣaṇa*) operates only once upon its object—whether that object be a form, a word-meaning, or a collection—it is the case that in the rule *yaro ñami ñam vā*, the substitute *ñam* becomes more proximate [to the original]. Thus, by this [rule], all those [sounds] such as *ṅa* and so forth, which belong respectively to the *ga*-sounds and others by virtue of their place of articulation (*sthāna*) or their quality (*guṇa*), are excluded; both by place alone and by quality alone. Consequently, the *ṇa*-sound is not the most proximate to the *ra*-sound by way of place alone.

Even though the *repha* (the sound *r*) is included within the *yar* group and thus would have attained the status of being an element subject to grammatical operation (*kāryitva*) even in the case of reduplication, that status is set aside by its being directly taught as a cause (*nimittabhāva*); therefore, the *repha* is not reduplicated. Furthermore, the rule *anusvārasya yayi yam* prescribes a *yama* only once for the *anusvāra*, because the *anusvāra* is more closely proximate to its own cause. Since there is no nasal sound (*anunāsika*) more closely proximate to the cause—the *repha*—there will be no *yama* in the case of *naraṃ rathena*.

In this context, the vowel *a* in *ha-kāra* and so forth is for the purpose of pronunciation, because it serves no other purpose elsewhere; furthermore, even for the consonants (*hal*), the reference is made by way of their general class (*jāti*). (0.6) *ña-ma-ṅa-ṇa-na-m*.

Having taught these letters—*ña*, *ma*, *ṅa*, *ṇa*, and *na*—he places the letter *m* at the end of the preceding group for the purpose of forming a *pratyāhāra*. Its pronunciation occurs by means of five [letters]: by the letter *a* in *śaś cho ’m* (Pāṇini 6.4.157); by the letter *ya* in *anusvārasya yayi yam* (6.4.151); by the letter *ña* in *yaro ñami ñam vā* (6.4.140); by the letter *ma* in *vinmator mam* (?); and by the letter *ṅa* in *ṅamo hrasvād dve* (6.4.17).

Some, however, reject the *anubandha* *m*, asserting that all these *pratyāhāra*s may be formed with the letter *ñ*. If that were the case, since there would be no occurrence of *jhabh* capable of undergoing doubling by the rule *ṅamo hrasvād dve*, one would have to understand the absence of doubling through a cumbersome process of comprehension.

[The author] teaches the two phonemes *jha* and *bha* as *jhabhañ*, and places the letter *ñ* at the end of the preceding group for the sake of forming a *pratyāhāra*. Its pronunciation occurs with a single [effort], namely by the letter *y* according to the rule *ād yañi* (Pāṇini 6.2.39).

Having taught the letters *gha*, *ḍha*, and *dha* [in the rule *ghaḍhadhaṣ*], he places the letter *ṣ* at the end of those preceding sounds for the purpose of forming a *pratyāhāra*. Its pronunciation occurs by means of two [letters]: by *jha* and *bha*, as in the rule *jhaṣa ekācaḥ sdhvor baśo bhaṣ* (Pāṇini 6.1.6). [Then follows] *jabagaḍadaś*.

Having taught these letters—ja, ba, ga, ḍa, and da—and having placed the letter śa, which has been modified by *it*, at the end of the preceding [group], he does so for the purpose of forming a *pratyāhāra* (abbreviation). Its pronunciation occurs through five [letters]: by the letter *a* in the rule *bho-bhago-aghobhyo 'si lopaḥ* (6.4.24); by the letter *ha* in the rule *haśi ca ato ror* (6.1.119); by the letter *va* in the rule *vaśi* (6.1.128); by the letter *ja* in the rule *jhalo jaś* (6.3.67); and by the letter *ba* in the rule *jhaṣa ekācaḥ sdhvor baśo bhaṣ* (6.3.69). [The remaining letters are] *kha, pha, cha, ṭha, tha, ca, ṭa, ta, va*.

Having taught these letters—kha, pha, cha, ṭha, tha, ca, ṭa, and ta—he places the letter *va* at the end for the purpose of forming a *pratyāhāra*. Its pronunciation is by means of a single [phoneme], namely the *eh* sound in the rule *naś chavy apraśān* (Pāṇini 6.4.3). The inclusion of *kha* and *pha* is for the sake of subsequent purposes. *kapay* (0.11).

Having taught these two phonemes *ka* and *pa*, he places the letter *ya* at the end of the preceding [group] for the purpose of forming a *pratyāhāra*. Its pronunciation occurs by means of five [letters]: by *ya* in *anusvārasya yayi yam* (P. 8.3.23); by *ma* in *maya uño 'ci va* (P. 8.3.32); by *jha* in *jhayo ho jhay* (P. 8.4.62); by *kha* in *pumaḥ khayy am-par-e* (P. 8.3.6); and by *ca* in *cayaḥ śari dvitīyaḥ* (P. 8.4.47). [The remaining letters are] *śa*, *ṣa*, *sa*, and *ra*.

Having taught these letters—*śa*, *ṣa*, and *sa*—he places the letter *r* at the end of the preceding group for the purpose of forming a *pratyāhāra*. Its pronunciation occurs by means of five [letters]: by the letter *y* in the rule *yaro ñami ñam vā* (Pāṇini 6.4.140); by the letter *jha* in the rule *halo jharāṃ jhari saṃsthāne lopo vā* (Pāṇini 6.4.155); by the letters *kha* and *ca* in the rule *khari ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.148); and by the letter *śa* in the rule *ṅṇoḥ kukṭukau śari* (Pāṇini 6.4.12). [The *pratyāhāra* is] *hal* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.1.70).

Having taught the single phoneme *ha*, he places the letter *la* at the end of the preceding [group] for the purpose of forming a *pratyāhāra*. Its pronunciation occurs by means of six [phonemes]: by the vowel *a* according to Pāṇini 1.1.12 (*śidanekāl sarvasya*); by the *ha* according to 6.2.30 (*hali pity uta auṅ*); by the *va* according to 6.3.51 (*supi vali tadvat*); by the *ra* according to 6.2.21 (*ralo halāder idutoḥ sani ca*); by the *jha* according to 6.3.55 (*jhalo jhali*); and by the *k* according to 7.2.43 (*śala igupāntād adṛśo 'niṭaḥ ksa*).

[This is] by means of the letter *ś*. Now, for what purpose is this letter *h* taught again, even though it has already been taught? It is so that the rules for the optional substitution of *adeṅ*, the rule for *ksa*, and the rules for *iṭ* may apply. In that regard, in the forms *snihitvā* and *snehitvā*, the optional substitution of *adeṅ* [for the final vowel and following consonant] may occur according to Pāṇini 6.2.21 (*ralo halāder idutoḥ sani ca*). Furthermore, in the form *alikṣat* from the root *lih*, the suffix *ksa* may occur according to Pāṇini 1.2.65 (*śala igupāntād adṛśo 'niṭaḥ ksa*). And in the forms *rudihi* and *svapihi*, the augment *iṭ* may occur according to the rule concerning suffixes beginning with a consonant (*valādi*).

In rules involving the term *jhal*, the inclusion of the letter *ha* [in the *haś* class] is intended so that *ha* may be included as well. But then, for what purpose is *ha* taught in the rule *hayavaralaṇ*? It is so that *ha* may be included in rules involving the term *aś* and in rules involving the term *haś*.
The suffixes *ṇa*, *ṅa*, *ña*, and *va* are known to follow from one [letter]; *ka* and *ca* from four; *ṇa* and *ṣa* from two; *rśi* from five; and *la* is prescribed after six.

This *pratyāhāra* was already established even in the earlier grammatical treatises (*vyākaraṇa*). However, this is the distinction: that which was [previously] *ai-au-ṣ* has been made *ai-au-j*. For instance, it is recited [in the *Phiṭ-sūtras*]: "In a word ending in a light syllable, as well as in words of two syllables having many vowels, the penultimate vowel is heavy; and also in the case of grasses and grains that have two vowels" (*phiṭsūtra* 2.19.4). [Furthermore, regarding the technical rule: "The first [letter], together with the last [indicatory letter], includes those in between" (*ādir antyena sahetā*, Pāṇini 1.1.71).

A [group of letters] indicated by the first [letter] and the final [indicatory] *it* is to be understood as including the letters in between when it is employed. [Examples of vowel sandhi (*saṃdhi*) according to *ako 'ki dīrghaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.102): *daṇḍāgram* (staff-tip), *dadhīndraḥ* (Indra of yogurt), *madhūṣṭraḥ* (camel of honey). [Examples of compound formation (*samāsa*) according to *sup supā* (Pāṇini 2.1.4): *rājapuruṣaḥ* (king's man), *nīlotpalam* (blue lotus).
And *savarga*: (1.1.2) that which is indicated by the letter *u* is to be understood together with its class (*varga*). By the rule *coḥ kuḥ* (6.3.59), there is the substitution of *k*.
*Tā tatkālaḥ*: (1.1.3) [The vowel *t* denotes a sound] having the same duration as itself.

The time [of pronunciation] indicated by the letter *takāra* is to be understood as the relevant period. Therefore, by the rule *bhisa ais* (Pāṇini 7.1.9), we have *vṛkṣaiḥ*, *plakṣaiḥ*. Here it does not apply: *mālābhiḥ*.

Regarding the mention of *do* in *do 'paḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.4), it should be understood that only that which has the vowel *a* as its penultimate (*apakāraka*) is included. By the rule *do dat* (Pāṇini 6.2.96), we have *dattam*. Here it does not apply: *dātaṃ barhiḥ* (cut grass), *avadātaṃ mukham* (a bright face).

"Anaṃśacihnam" (1.1.5): That which is a "sign" (*cihna*) that has not become a constituent part (*anaṃśabhūta*) should be understood as non-existent (*asad*). [Example: *iṭa īṭi* (6.3.57), as in *akoṣīt*. Why is the mention of "non-constituent part" (*anaṃśagrahaṇa*) necessary? [Counter-example: *ekāco halādeḥ kriyārthād bhṛśābhīkṣṇye yaṅ* (1.1.40), as in *pāpacyate*. *er ac* (1.3.45), as in *cayaḥ*, *jayaḥ*. From the root *iṇ* with the suffix *kvip* and the augment *tuk*: *eti iti it*. It goes; it does not stay; the meaning is that it perishes. "A rule [applies] to that which ends in a qualifier" (1.1.6).

It should be understood that a grammatical rule applies to that which ends with a qualifying element (*viśeṣaṇa*). For example, by *ata iñ* (Pāṇini 4.1.95), we have *dākṣiḥ* and *plākṣiḥ*. However, where there is no qualifying element, there is no application of the rule to that which ends with it. For example, by *naḍādibhyaḥ phak* (Pāṇini 4.1.99), we have *nāḍāyanaḥ* and *cārāyaṇaḥ*; but here [the suffix] does not apply, as in *sautranāḍiḥ*. This is because of the principle *saptamyāṃ pūrvasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.66).

In the case of an instruction involving the seventh case (*saptamī*), it should be understood that the grammatical operation applies to the preceding element alone. As in *iko yaṇ aci* (Pāṇini 6.1.77): *dadhy udakam*. Why does [the substitution] not occur in *samit atra*? Because in the rule *aci*, the locative denotes a proximity-based substratum (*aupaśleṣika ādhāra*). In that context, it is stated only this much: the operation applies to the preceding element, not to the subsequent one. For the fifth case, however, the rule is *pañcamyāṃ parasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.67).

In an instruction involving the fifth case (*pañcamī*), it should be understood that the grammatical operation applies only to what follows. Therefore, by the rule *bhisa ais* (Pāṇini 7.1.9), we have *vṛkṣaiḥ*. It does not apply here, as in *mālābhir atra*. Why does it not apply here in the case of *dṛṣadbhiḥ*? Because the operation has already been fulfilled for the immediately preceding element, it does not apply to a separated one. According to the rule *ādeḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.54), when an operation is prescribed for "the following," it is to be understood as applying to the first letter of that following element. Thus, by the rule *dvay-anta-prāder anād apa īt* (Pāṇini 5.2.113), we have *dvīpaḥ*, *antarīpaḥ*, *samīpaḥ*, and *nīpaḥ*.

(1.1.10) *ṣaṣṭhyāntyasya*: An operation prescribed for that which is designated by the genitive case should be understood to apply to the final [element] thereof. (5.4.52) *aṣṭano vā supy āt*: [The substitution of] *āt* optionally [occurs] for *aṣṭan* before a case-ending (*sup*). [Examples: *aṣṭābhiḥ*, *aṣṭabhiḥ*. (1.1.11) *ṅit*.

That which has *ṅ* as its *it* (indicatory letter) applies to the final [phoneme]. [The rule] *anaṅ sau* (Pāṇini 7.1.93) [is an example]: *sakhā*. [The word] *ṣaṣṭhī* [in the sūtra 1.1.49] is understood [to mean "of that which is in the genitive case"]; thus [the substitute does not apply] to *viśnaḥ*. [The rule] *śidanekāl sarvasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.55): that substitute which has *ś* as its *it*, being *anekāl* (having more than one phoneme), should be understood to replace the whole [original element]. [The rule] *jasaḥ śī* (Pāṇini 7.1.17): *sarve*. [The rule] *bhrasjo bharj vā* (Pāṇini 6.1.16): *bhraṣṭā*, *bharṣṭā*.

(1.1.13) *ṭakitāv ādyantau*: It should be understood that when a suffix marked with *ṭ* or *k* is prescribed by means of a genitive case ending, those marked with *ṭ* and *k* are respectively the initial and final elements [of the base]. (6.2.34) *bruva iṭ*: [The augment] *iṭ* is added after the root *brū*. Example: *bravīti*. (3.3.108) *trapujatunoḥ ṣuk*: [The suffix] *ṣuk* is added after the words *trapu* and *jatun*. Examples: *trāpuṣam*, *jātuṣam*. (1.1.14) *mid aco 'ntyāt paraḥ*: An augment marked with *m* is placed after the final vowel of the base.

That which has the letter *m* as its augment (*makāra*) should be understood as following the final vowel (*antyād acaḥ*). [As in] *vaca um* (P. 6.2.69): *avocat*. The governing rule for *parasmaipada* extends up to the suffix *kap*. Regarding *ṛko ’ṇo ralau* (P. 1.1.15):
it should be understood that the letters *r* and *l* take the place of the *aṇ* vowels that follow the sounds *ṛ* and *ḷ*. [Examples: *kartā*, *kalptā*. [These refer to] the vowels *ṛ* and *ḷ*.

(1.1.16) *Vipratiṣedhe* (in case of conflict): when two rules, each having its own scope, apply to the same instance, that which is subsequent takes effect. For example, the substitution of *e* takes precedence over the substitution of *ā*, as in *vṛkṣebhyaḥ*. Furthermore, this word *para* signifies "desired" (*iṣṭa*). Consequently, terms such as *pūrvavipratiṣedha* (prior conflict) need not be explicitly mentioned. (1.1.17) *Tijaḥ kṣāntau san*: the desiderative suffix *san* is applied after the root *tij* in the sense of forbearance.

The suffix *san* follows the root *tij* when it occurs in the sense of "patience" (*kṣamā*). Example: *titikṣate*. Why specify "in the sense of patience"? [Otherwise: *tejanam*, *tejaḥ*, *tejayati*. The letter *n* is for the purpose of marking that this applies to the rules concerning *san* and *yaṅ* (Pāṇini 6.1.9).

The suffix *san* follows the root *kit* when it occurs in the senses of "doubt" (*saṃśaya*) and "medical treatment" (*cikitsā*) (Pāṇini 3.1.5). Examples: *vicikitsati*, *cikitsati*. In other senses: *niketaḥ*, *saṃketaḥ*, *ketanam*, *ketaḥ*, *ketayati*.
*gup* in the sense of censure (1.1.19): when *gup* occurs in the sense of censure, the suffix *san* follows it. Example: *jugupsate*. In other senses: *gopitā*, *gopanam*, *gopāyati*.
*badh* [takes *san*] and *ī* is substituted for its vowel (1.1.20).
The suffix *san* follows the root *badh*, when it signifies censure, and the vowel *i* is replaced by *ī*. Thus, *bībhatsate*. In other cases, it is *badhakaḥ*.
[The rule] *śāndānmānaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.21).

The root *śā* [from *śo*] and *dā* [from *do*], when followed by the suffix *san*, become *śi* and *dī* respectively; and the vowel *i* becomes *ī*. Thus: *śīśāṃsati*, *śīśāṃsate*; *dīdāṃsati*, *dīdāṃsate*; *mīmāṃsati*, *mimāṃsate*. How is it that forms such as *niśānam* and *avadānam* are established? They are established by the addition of the suffix *lyuṭ* to the roots *śyai* and *dyai*. How is it that *mānanam*, *mānaḥ*, and *mānayati* are established? They are established by the root belonging to the *curādi* class. Furthermore, the optional presence of the causative suffix *ṇic* is indicated by the rule *ghuṣer aviśabdane* (Pāṇini 7.2.23). Here, due to its association with *śā* and *dān*, the root *mān* belonging to the *bhūvādi* class is intended. And the elision of the infinitive suffix *tumun* occurs when the sense is "desire" (*icchāyām*), according to Pāṇini 6.4.106.

The suffix *saN* occurs after an infinitive (*tumun*) in the sense of desire, and there is elision (*luk*) of the infinitive because it is explicitly stated [in the rule]. For example: *cikīrṣati* ("he wishes to do"). Why does it not occur here: *kartum icchati* ("he wishes to do")? Because it is expressed by separate words. What is the purpose of the requirement "after an infinitive"? [Consider: *bhojanam icchati* ("he wishes for food"). What is the purpose of the requirement "in the sense of desire"? [Consider: *bhoktum gacchati* ("he goes to eat"). In the case of *icchati cikīrṣitum* ("he wishes to wish to do"), a further *saN* does not occur after the one ending in *saN*. Why? Because of the contradiction of an action acting upon itself (*svātmani kriyāvirodhāt*).

For at the time of the prescription of *saN* after a desire (*icchā*), there is no base (*prakṛti*) ending in *icchā-saN*. But here it certainly occurs, as in *jugupsiṣate*. How is it that one says *kūlaṃ pipatiṣati*? Just as the sentence "the bank desires to fall" (*kūlaṃ patitum icchati*) is indeed possible, so too will the compound form (*vṛtti*) be possible. [Objection: But how then is the sentence itself possible? [Response: Because people have such an intention to speak (*vivakṣā*); [this is taught by] Pāṇini 3.1.9: *vyāpyāt kāmyac*.

The affix *kāmyac* follows the root *iṣ* (to desire) when it has the sense of "desiring" provided that it is preceded by an object (*vyāpya*). For example: *putram icchati* ("he desires a son") becomes *putrakāmyati*; *vastrakāmyati* ("he desires a garment"). Why is it said "provided that it is preceded by an object"? Consider: *dātreṇecchati* ("he desires [to act] with a sickle"). Why does it not occur here in the case of *rājñaḥ putram icchati* ("he desires the king's son")? Because of its dependency (*sāpekṣatvāt*). Indeed, something that depends on another cannot enter into a state of semantic unification (*ekārthībhāva*) with yet another word. If that is so, then it should also not occur here: *ātmanaḥ putram icchati* ("he desires his own son"). It should certainly not occur there either.

For it is not the case that one "desires a son for oneself" (*putrakāmyati*). How, then, is the son understood as being one's own? Because no other [object] is heard [in the context], and because the desire has that [son] as its object. The particle *ca* is for the purpose of subverting the accent prescribed by *satiśiṣṭa* [rules], as in *putrakāmyiṣyati*.
[The rule] *sasaṃkhyād amaḥ kyaj vā* (Pāṇini 3.1.8) applies.

The suffix *kyac* is optionally applied after the root *iṣ* (to desire), provided it is preceded by an object (*vyāpya*) that possesses a number and ends in the suffix *am*, in the sense of "desiring. Examples: *putram icchati* → *putrīyati*, *putrakāmyati* (he desires a son). *vastram icchati* → *vastrīyati*, *vastrakāmyati* (he desires a garment). Why is it said "provided it possesses a number"? Consider: *svar icchati* (he desires heaven); *pṛthag icchati* (he desires separately). Why is it said "ending in *am*"? Consider: *idam icchati* (he desires this); *kim icchati* (he desires what?). [In the rule *kakāraḥ kyasya vā* (Pāṇini 5.3.66),] the letter *ka* is for the purpose of including the general term *ky*, and the letter *ca* is for the purpose of preventing the obstruction of that general inclusion. [Next: *upamānād ācāre* (Pāṇini 3.1.10; cf. 1.1.25). "After a word denoting a standard of comparison, [the suffix *kvip* is applied] in the sense of behaving like that."

The suffix *kyac* follows after an object of comparison (*upamāna*) when the sense of "behaving like" (*ācāra*) is intended. For example: *putram ivācarati* ("he behaves as if toward a son") becomes *putrīyati māṇavakam* ("he treats the boy as a son"). Why is it said "after an object of comparison"? [Consider: *putram ācarati* ("he behaves toward a son [as a son]"). From a substratum (*ādhāra*):

the suffix *kyac* follows after a substratum that serves as an object of comparison when the sense of "behaving like" is intended. For example: *kuṭyām ivācarati* ("he behaves as if in a hut") becomes *kuṭīyati prāsāde* ("he treats the palace as a hut"); *prāsādīyati kuṭyām* ("he treats the hut as a palace").

*kartur vip* (1.1.27): After a word denoting the agent (*kartṛ*) used as a standard of comparison (*upamāna*), the suffix *vip* occurs in the sense of behaving like that. For example: "he behaves like a horse" (*aśva ivācarati*) becomes *aśvati*; [similarly] *gardabhati*.
[The suffix *vip*] is marked with the indicator *ṅ* after the words *galbha*, *klība*, and *hoḍa* (1.1.28).

The suffix *vip* occurs after words such as *galbha* when they function as the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) in the sense of "behaving like"; and this suffix is treated as having the marker *ṅ*. Thus: *galbhate*, *klībate*, *hoḍate*; *galbhāṃcakre*. The letter *ṅ* is for the purpose of [triggering] the *taṅ* (middle voice) and *āna* (periphrastic perfect) affixes. How is it that one says *galbhāyate*? Because intermediate exceptions (*apavāda*) supersede preceding rules, but not subsequent ones. [This refers to the rule for] *kyaṅ* (Pāṇini 3.1.11).

The suffix *kyaṅ* occurs after a word denoting the agent of comparison when the sense is "behaving like. Examples: *aśvāyate*, *gardabhāyate*, *śyenāyate*; *payāyate*, *payasyate*. By the rule *kyaṅi vā* (Pāṇini 6.4.102), there is optionally the elision of the suffixal *s*. Examples: *ojāyate*, *apsarāyate*. By the rule *ojopsarasor* (Pāṇini 6.4.103), there is obligatory elision of the suffixal *s* due to its being restated here. In the sense of the suffix *cvī*—that is, when expressing the transformation of something into what it was not before (*abhūtatadbhāva*)—*kyaṅ* occurs after words such as *bhṛśa* etc., and there is the elision of the final *s* and *t*. Example: that which was not intense (*abhṛśa*) becomes intense (*bhṛśa*), [expressed as] *bhṛśāyate*. *śīghrāyate*.

*bhṛśa*, *śīghra*, *capala*, *paṇḍita*, *utsuka*, *unmanas*—[the suffix *kyaṅ* is applied after these]: *unmanāyate*; *abhimanas*, *abhimanāyate*; *durmanas*, *durmanāyate*; *sumanas*, *sumanāyate*; *rehat*, *rehāyate*; *vehat*, *vehāyate*; *saṃścat*, *saṃścāyate*; *tṛpat*, *tṛpāyate*; *śucivarcas*, *aṇḍara*, *ojas*, *nīla*, *madra*, *phena*, *harita*, *manda*. The rule applies only when the agent (*kartṛ*) is the subject; for example: *abhṛśaṃ bhṛśaṃ karoti* ("he makes what was not intense into something intense"). Why does [the suffix] not apply here in the case of *bhṛśībhavati*? Because the meaning has already been expressed [by the suffix *-bhū-*]. (1.1.31) *ḍāj-lohitādibhyaḥ kyaṣ* ("after words ending in the suffix *ḍāc* and after *lohita* etc., the suffix *kyaṣ* is applied").

The suffix *kyaṣ* occurs after words ending in the suffix *ḍāc* and after words such as *lohita*, when they are used in the sense of the suffix *cvī*. This is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open class of words). [The suffix *kyac* occurs] after the words *kaṣṭa*, *kakṣa*, *sattra*, and *gahana* when there is the sense of "exerting oneself toward" (*kramaṇa*) evil. (Pāṇini 3.1.14–15; 1.4.142; 3.1.17).

The suffix *kyaṅ* occurs after words such as *śabda*, ending in the accusative case, in the sense of "he performs that [action]. He makes a sound: *śabdāyate*. — *vairāyate* — *kalahāyate* — *abhrāyate* — *kaṇvāyate* — *meghāyate* — *aṭṭāyate* — *aṭāyate*. Others, however, read *aṭāṭeti*; for them, this is the form derived from the root *aṭ* with the suffix *yaṅ*, followed by the feminine suffix *ā*. — *śikāyate* — *soṭāyate* — *koṭāyate* — *poṭāyate* — *pruṣṭāyate* — *sudināyate* — *durdināyate* — *nīhārāyate*.
Pāṇini 3.1.19: *namas-tapas-tapasaḥ kyac* (The suffix *kyac* occurs after *namas*, *tapas*, and *varivas*).

The suffix *kyac* follows words such as *namas* ending in the second case when the sense is "he performs" (*karoti*). Examples: *namaskaroti*, *namasyati devān* ("he pays homage to the gods"); *tapasyati śatrūn* ("he exerts himself against his enemies"); *varivasyati gurūn* ("he honors his teachers"). Regarding the rule *citraṅ āścarye* (Pāṇini 3.1.38): the suffix *kyac* follows the word *citraṅ*—which ends in the second case and denotes something wonderful—when the sense is "he performs. Examples: *citraṃ karoti*, *citrīyate*. The marker *ṅ* is for the purpose of introducing the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) terminations. Why "wonderful"? [Counter-example: *citraṃ karoti* ("he paints a picture").

*Kaṇḍvādibhyo yak* (Pāṇini 3.1.27): The suffix *yak* occurs after the roots *kaṇḍū* and others when they end in the accusative case and have the meaning "he performs" (*karoti*). He performs scratching: *kaṇḍūyati*, *kaṇḍūyate*. *kaṇḍūñ*, *mantuñ*: *mantūyati*, *mantūyate*. *valgu*: *valgūyati*. *asuñ*: *asūyati*, *asūyate*. *hṛṇiṅ*: *hṛṇīyate*. *mahiṅ*: *mahīyate*. *veṅ*: *veyate*. *lāṅ*: *lāyate*. Some read [the root] as *veḍlāṭ*; others as *veṭ lāṭ*. According to them, [the forms are] *veḍlāṭyati*, *veṭyati*, *lāṭyati*. *tiras*: *tirasyati*. *iyas*: [forms *iyasyati*].

*iyasyati*—*iras*; *iras-yati*—*uras*; *uras-yati*—*uṣas*; *uṣas-yati*—*kusubha*, *magadha*; by [Pāṇini 7.3.64], *yaki*, there is elision of the final vowel (*alopa*)—*godhā*, *medhā*, *tantas*, *pampas*, *bhiṣaj*, *arara*, *sapara*, *iṣudha*, *curaṇa*, *turaṇa*, *bhuraṇa*, *duvas*, *gadgada*, *elā*, *kelā*, *khelā*, *leṭ*, *loṭ*, *sukha*, *duḥkha*.

[The suffix] *yaṅ* is applied after a root consisting of a single vowel, beginning with a consonant, and having an action as its meaning, when expressing intensity (*bhṛśa*) or repetition (*abhīkṣṇya*). (Pāṇini 3.1.22).

The suffix *yaṅ* occurs after a single-vowel (*ekāc*) root that begins with a consonant (*halādi*), provided that the root has a verbal action as its meaning and denotes intensity (*bhṛśa*) or repetition (*paunaḥpunya*). Intensity means "very," while repetition means "frequently. For example: *atyartham* or *punaḥ* *pacati* ("he cooks excessively" or "he cooks repeatedly") becomes *pāpacyate*. Why does it say "single-vowel"? [Consider: *jāgarti abhīkṣṇam* ("he wakes up repeatedly"). Why does it say "beginning with a consonant"? [Consider: *abhīkṣṇam īhate* ("he strives repeatedly"). Why does it say "having a verbal action as its meaning"? [Consider: *prātti bhṛśam* ("he obtains intensely"). For prefixes (*prādayaḥ*) do not denote the action; rather, they are indicators of specific qualities (*viśeṣadyotaka*). Why does it say "intensity and repetition"? [Consider: *pacati* ("he cooks"). The governing rule (*adhikāra*) "having a verbal action as its meaning" applies until the section on the formation of nominal stems (*sup-vidhi*).

From the roots *ṛ*, *sūtri*, *mūtri*, *sūci*, *aṭ*, *śūrṇu*, and others (Pāṇini 3.1.24), the suffix *yaṅ* occurs to express intensity (*bhṛśa*) or frequency (*abhīkṣṇya*). Examples: *arāryate*, *sosūtryate*, *momūtryate*, *sosūcyate*, *aṭāṭyate*, *aśāśyate*, *proṇonūyate*.
According to Pāṇini 3.1.23, the suffix *yaṅ* occurs after a root meaning "motion" (*gatyartha*) specifically to express crookedness (*kauṭilya*).

The suffix *yaṅ* occurs after verbal roots meaning "motion" (*gatyartha*) only when expressing crookedness (*kauṭilya*), and not merely intensity (*bhṛśa*) or repetition (*abhīkṣṇya*). Examples: *caṅkramyate*, *dandramyate*, *jaṅgmyate*. In other cases, it means "he goes repeatedly. [Pāṇini 3.1.24:
"After the roots *lup*, *sad*, *car*, *gṛ*, *jap*, *jabh*, *dah*, and *daś*, when they denote something censurable (*garhya*). (1.1.43)

The suffix *yaṅ* occurs after the roots *lup* and others when they convey a sense of censure (*garhita*). Examples: *lolupyate* (he censures by tearing up), *sāsadyate*, *cañcūryate*, *nijegilyate*, *jañjapyate*, *jañjabhyate*, *dandahyate*, *dandaśyate*. Why "when conveying a sense of censure"? [Consider: *lumpati* (he tears up). Because of the continued application of the word "only" (*eva*), the suffix *yaṅ* occurs after these roots only when they convey a sense of censure, not when they convey other meanings. Example: *punaḥ punar lumpati* (he tears up again and again). Why is it a qualifier of the root? [Consider: *japati vṛṣalaḥ* (the low-born man mutters). (1.1.44) *na śubharucaḥ*: The suffix *yaṅ* does not occur after the roots *śubh* and *ruc*. Examples: *abhīkṣṇaṃ śobhate* (he shines repeatedly), *bhṛśaṃ rocate* (it shines intensely).

*cur-ādibhyo ṇic* (Pāṇini 3.1.25): after the roots *cur* and others, the suffix *ṇic* occurs in the sense of the root itself (*svārthe*). Examples: *corayati*, *nāṭayati*. The letter *ṇ* is for the sake of introducing the suffixes *ātaḥ* and *aiC*; the letter *c* is for the sake of preventing the obstruction of general reference. It is recited among the *cur*-class roots [in the Dhātupāṭha] with the rule: *supo dhātvarthe bahulam iṣṭhavac ca* (Dhātupāṭha 10.103). By this, the operations characteristic of the superlative suffix *iṣṭhan* occur and do not occur. For example: from *paṭu* (clever), *paṭuṃ karoti* becomes *paṭayati*; from *laghu* (light), *laghayati*. Due to the state of being like *iṣṭhan*, there is the elision of the final vowel and following consonant (*antyājādilopa*), as well as the absence of the augment *āT*.

Likewise, one says "he speaks of something as large," *sthavayati*, *davayati*, and so forth. One says "he speaks the truth," *satyāpayati*. [One says] *arthāpayati* (he speaks the meaning) and *vedāpayati* (he makes known). Regarding these, the suffix *-āpuk* will be taught. He releases a noose, *vipāśayati*. He perceives a form, *nirūpayati*. He sings along with a lute, *upavīṇayati*. He shaves with cotton, *anutūlayati*. He praises with verses, *upaślokayati*. He marches out with an army, *abhiṣeṇayati*. He strokes the body hairs in the direction of growth, *anulomayati*.

He takes the skin; *tvacayati*. There is no elision [of the penultimate vowel] because of the rule *naikāca* (Pāṇini 6.4.165). He arms himself with armor; *saṃvarmayati*. He adopts a color; *varṇayati*. He scatters with powder; *avacūrṇayati*. He makes a thread; *sūtrayati*. Likewise: *muṇḍayati*, *miśrayati*, *ślakṣṇayati*, *lavaṇayati*, *vratayati*. He completely covers with a garment; *saṃvastrayati*. He takes up a plow; *halayati*. He takes up strife; *kalayati*.

Due to the application of the *iṣṭhavad-bhāva* (the treatment as if it were the superlative suffix), there is the absence of *āT*, *aiC*, and *auC*. Consequently, because it lacks a penultimate vowel (*aglopin*), the *sanvadbhāva* does not apply. Thus, we have *ajahalat*, *acakalat*, and *apīpaṭat*; the long *ī* occurs here by virtue of the rule of *bahula* (diversity). Similarly, we have *kṛtayati*, *tūstayati*, and so forth. The root *ṇiṅ* is listed in that very same [Dhātupāṭha] under the meaning "to shake off" (*aṅganirasane*) [Dhātupāṭha 10.104]. From *hastaṃ nirasyati*, we derive *hastayate*. Likewise, *pādayate*. From *utpucchayate*, *nipucchayate*, and *paripucchayate*. Why specify "shaking off"? [To exclude cases like: *pucchaṃ ācaṣṭe*, *pucchayati*.

In that very same [work], it is recited under *śvetāśva-aśvatara-gāloḍita-āhvaraka* as "there is the elision of *aśva*, *tara*, and *taka*" (*dhātupāṭha* 10.105). One explains a white horse, or one approaches with it, thus: *śvetayate*; *aśvayate*; *gāloḍayate*; *āhvarayate*. One collects goods together: *saṃbhāṇḍayate*. One gathers or puts on a robe: *saṃcīvarayate*. The *taṅ* (ātmanepada) ending is applied by the rule *phalavati* (Pāṇini 1.4.124). Accordingly, the author of the *Dhātupāṭha* also says: "In the case of *puccha* and so forth, it is established simply by the meaning of the verbal root itself" (*pāṇinīyadhātupāṭha* 10.395).

Regarding *prayojakavyāpāre* (Pāṇini 1.4.55): when one prompts an agent, the suffix *ṇic* follows a verbal root whose action is for the sake of that [prompting] activity. For example: *kārayati* ("he causes to do"), *hārayati* ("he causes to take away"). Now, an objection is raised: since an agent is also the prompter of instruments (*karaṇa*) and so forth, the suffix *ṇic* would also apply to their activity. [Response: This will not occur because of the force of the explicit mention of "the prompter" (*prayojaka*). Furthermore, it is because of the force of the separate statement regarding the roots of the *cur*-class (*curādi*). How then is it that one says, "The storyteller has Kaṃsa killed" (*kaṃsaṃ ghātayati kathakaḥ*) or "He has Bali bound" (*baliṃ bandhayati*)? [In these cases, the meaning is: "Go, Kaṃsa is being killed! What is the use of your going? That Kaṃsa is already dead! [Thus, the *ṇic* here does not denote the actual prompting of the agent.]

In this way, one *ācaṣṭe* (announces) the passing of the night; [thus] he causes the night to pass (*rātriṃ vivāsayati*). Having set out from Kauśāmbī, he causes the sun to rise at Māhiṣmatī. One *ācaṣṭe* the conjunction with Puṣya; [thus] one joins the moon with Puṣya (*puṣyeṇa candraṃ yojayati*). *gupū-dhūpa-vichi-pani-pana āyo vā* (Pāṇini 1.3.47): after the roots *gup* and the others, the suffix *āya* optionally follows in the sense of the root itself (*svārthe*). Thus: *gopāyitā*, *goptā*; *dhūpāyitā*, *dhūpitā*; *vicchāyitā*, *vicchitā*; *paṇāyitā*, *paṇitā*; *panāyitā*, *panitā*. Because of its association with *pani* (in the sense of praise), it is the *paṇi* meaning "to praise" that is understood here. In this case, it does not apply: *śatasya paṇitā* ("one who bargains for a hundred").
*ṛta īyaṅ* (1.1.48): After the vowel *ṛ*, the substitute *īyaṅ* optionally occurs. [Examples: *ṛtīyitā*, *artitā*. *kamo ṇiṅ* (1.1.49).
The suffix *kam* optionally becomes *niṅ*. [Thus we have] *kāmayitā* and *kamitā*.

According to the rule *śity āyādayaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.50), when a suffix beginning with *ś* follows, the suffixes *āya* and others necessarily occur after roots such as *gup* and others, because of their re-enunciation [in this specific context]. [Examples are: *gopāyati*, *dhūpāyati*, *vicchāyati*, *paṇāyati*, *panāyati*, *ṛtīyate*, and *kāmayate*.
Aṣṭādhyāyī 3.1.36: *anekāco liṭa ām kṛbhvastiliṭ cānu* (1.1.51).

For a root consisting of more than one vowel (*anekāc*) used in the sense of action, the substitute *ām* is applied in place of the *liṭ* [perfect] suffix; furthermore, the *liṭ* prescribed after the roots *kṛ*, *bhū*, and *as* is employed as an auxiliary. Examples: *culumpāñcakāra*, *cikīrṣāñcakāra*, *kārayāmbabhūva*, *pācayāmāsa*. By virtue of the force of the separate mention [of *kṛ*, *bhū*, and *as*], the substitution of *bhū* for *as* does not occur [in this context]. Why specify "more than one vowel"? Consider: *papāca*. Aṣṭādhyāyī 3.1.37: *ijāder gurumato ’nṛcchūrṇoḥ* (1.1.52). [The substitute *ām* is applied] after a root beginning with the vowel *i* or *ī* (*ijādi*), which contains a heavy syllable (*gurumat*), excluding the roots *ṛcch* and *ūrṇu*.

The *ām* suffix is substituted for the *liṭ* (perfect tense) following a root that begins with *ij*, is heavy (*gurumān*), and expresses an action, provided it excludes the roots *ṛcchi* and *ūrṇu*. Furthermore, the roots *kṛ*, *bhū*, or *as* are subsequently employed (*anuprayujyate*). Examples: *īhāṃcakre*, *vyucchāṃcakāra*. Why "beginning with *ij*"? Consider *tatakṣa*. Why "heavy"? Consider *iyeṣa*; this root is not heavy at the time the *liṭ* suffix is prescribed. However, in the case of *ucch*, because it is heavy precisely at the time the *liṭ* suffix is prescribed, *ām* occurs; this is indicated by the prohibition of *ṛcchi*. For this very reason, even when followed by a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*), it possesses heaviness. Why "excluding *ṛcchi* and *ūrṇu*"? Consider *ānarcha* and *prorṇunāva*. *Kāsayadayāsaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.53).

The suffix *ām* is substituted for the *liṭ* [perfect] following the roots *kāsa*, *udaya*, and *ās*, and the *liṭ* of the roots *kṛ*, *bhū*, or *as* is subsequently applied. Examples: *kāsāṃcakre*, *palāyāṃcakre*, *uddayāṃcakre*, *āsāṃcakre*.
(1.1.54) *jāgruṣo vā*:

The suffix *ām* is optionally substituted for the *liṭ* following the root *jāgṛ* and the root *uṣ*, and the *liṭ* of the roots *kṛ*, *bhū*, or *as* is subsequently applied. Examples: *jāgarāṃcakāra*, *jajāgāra*; *oṣāṃcakāra*, *uvoṣa*.

*bhī-hrī-hūnāṃ dve ca* (Pāṇini 1.1.55): For these roots *bhī*, *hrī*, and *hū*, the suffix *ām* optionally occurs after the *liṭ* [perfect tense marker], and by virtue of its association with that, reduplication (*dvitva*) also occurs; furthermore, the root *kṛ*, *bhū*, or *as* is subsequently applied (*anuprayujyate*). Examples: *bibhayāñcakāra*, *bibhāya*; *jihrayāñcakāra*, *jihrāya*; *juhavāñcakāra*, *juhāva*. Since the reduplication is already established by the rule *liṭi* (5.1.2), the statement *dve ca* is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtham*), meaning that reduplication occurs with *ām* only for these [roots] and not for others. Thus it has been illustrated. *bibharām* (1.1.56).

The *ām* suffix is optionally substituted for the *liṭ* [perfect] of the root *bhṛ*; there is reduplication and the substitution of *i* for the radical vowel; and the *liṭ* of the roots *kṛ*, *bhū*, or *as* is subsequently employed. Thus: *bibharāṃcakāra* or *babhāra*. Regarding *vidām* (Pāṇini 3.1.41): the *ām* suffix is optionally substituted for the *liṭ* of the root *vid*; there is the substitution of *e* for the radical vowel; and the *liṭ* of the roots *kṛ*, *bhū*, or *as* is subsequently employed. Thus: *vidāṃcakāra* or *viveda*.

*Loṭaḥ kṛloṭ* (Pāṇini 1.1.58): For the *loṭ* [imperative] ending of the root *vid*, the form *vidām* is optionally substituted; furthermore, the *loṭ* [imperative] following the root *kṛ* is employed as an auxiliary. [Examples: *vidāṃ karotu*, *vidāṃ kurutām*, *vidāṃ kurvantu*; [or] *vettu*, *vittām*, *vidantu*. *Syatāsī lṛluṭoḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.59).

When *lṛṭ* or *lṛṅ* follows, *sya* is added after a verbal root used in the sense of an action; when *luṭ* follows, *tās* is added. [Examples: *kariṣyati* (he will do), *akariṣyat* (he would have done), *śvaḥ kartā* (he will do tomorrow).

When *luṅ* follows, *sic* is added after a verbal root used in the sense of an action (Pāṇini 3.1.43; 1.1.60). [Example: *akārṣīt* (he did). The vowel *i* in *sic* serves as a marker for the rule *ataṅy ādaij* (Pāṇini 6.1.3); the letter *c* is for the purpose of preventing the *anudātta* accent of the augment (*āgama*).

*Spṛśa-mṛśa-kṛṣa-tṛpa-dṛpo vā* (Pāṇini 1.2.61): After the roots *spṛś* and others, the *sic* suffix optionally occurs in the *luṅ* (aorist). Thus: *asprākṣīt*, *aspārkṣīt*, *aspṛkṣat*; *amrākṣīt*, *amārkṣīt*, *amṛkṣat*; *akrākṣīt*, *akārkṣīt*, *akṛkṣat*; *atrāpsīt*, *atārpsīt*, *atṛpat*; *adrāpsīt*, *adārpsīt*, *adṛpat*. *Dādhā-gāti-sthā-bhū-pō ’taṅi luk* (Pāṇini 1.1.62): In place of the roots *dā* and *dhā*, the root *gā* (from *iṇ*), and the roots *sthā*, *bhū*, and *pā* (to drink), there is elision (*luk*) [of the root] when followed by an affix marked with *ṅ* that does not belong to the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) set.

After these [roots], there is elision (*luk*) of the *sic* affix when it does not belong to the *ataṅ* (non-*ātmanepada*) voice. Examples: *adāt*, *adhāt*, *agāt*, *asthāt*, *abhūt*, *apāt*. Why "when not *ataṅ*"? Consider: *adiṣātāṃ grāmau devadattena* ("the two villages were eaten by Devadatta"). Because of the specific mention of the roots *gā* and *pā* and their association [with the rule for elision], this elision does not occur here: *agāsīd gāyanaḥ* ("the singer sang") and *apāsīn nṛpaḥ* ("the king drank"). [The rule] *ghrādheśāchāso vā* (Pāṇini 1.1.63) applies.

The *sic* affix following roots beginning with *ghrā* optionally undergoes elision (*lug*). Examples: *aghrāt*, *aghāsīt*; *adhāt*, *adhāsīt*; *aśāt*, *aśāsīt*; *acchāt*, *acchāsīt*; *asāt*, *asāsīt*. This applies only when not in the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) voice; for example: *sumanasau devadattena aghrāsātām* ("the two Sumanas flowers were smelled by Devadatta").
[This is governed by Pāṇini 1.2.64: *tanādibhyas tathāsoḥ*].

The *sic* suffix following roots such as *tan* and others is optionally elided (*luk*) when followed by *tathāsu*. Thus: *atata*, *atathāḥ*; *ataniṣṭa*, *ataniṣṭhāḥ*; *asata*, *asathāḥ*; *asaniṣṭa*, *asaniṣṭhāḥ*. Why specify "when followed by *tathāsu"? [To exclude cases where it is not followed by these]. Because the word *ta* is understood here as being accompanied by *thās*, this rule does not apply here: *ataniṣṭa yūyam*. Even in the alternative where there is no elision (*aluk*), the *s* is dropped according to Pāṇini 6.4.101 (*hrasvād aṅgāt*). Thus: *akṛta*, *akṛthāḥ*.

According to Pāṇini 3.1.45 (*śala igupadhād aniṭaḥ ksaḥ*), the *ksa* suffix is applied after roots ending in *śal* with a penultimate *i*, *u*, or *ṛ*, provided they are not marked with *ṅ* or *ṇ* (i.e., are *aniṭ*).

The suffix *kṣa* occurs after a root ending in *śal*, having *i* or *u* as its penultimate letter (*igupadha*), excluding the root *dṛś*, provided it is used in the sense of an action (*kriyārtha*) and is *aniṭ* (lacking the augment *iṭ*) in the *luṅ* tense. Examples: *alikṣat*, *adhukṣat*. Why "ending in *śal*"? Consider *abhaitsīt*. Why "having *i* or *u* as its penultimate letter"? Consider *adhākṣīt*. Why "excluding *dṛś*"? Consider *adarśat* and *adrākṣīt*. Why "*aniṭ*"? Consider *akoṣīt*. [The rule] *śliṣaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.66) [is also applied].

In the *luṅ* tense, the suffix *ksa* occurs after the root *śliṣ* because of its re-mention [in this rule]. This supersedes the *aṅ* suffix prescribed for roots such as *puṣ*. Thus: *upāślikṣat kanyāṃ devadattaḥ* ("Devadatta embraced the girl"). In that case, would the *ciṇ* suffix also not be superseded? As in: *upāśleṣi kanyā devadattena* ("The girl was embraced by Devadatta")? [No,] for "exceptions stated earlier supersede the immediately following rules, not those further removed. [The rule applies] only when the root is *aniṭ* (lacking the *iṭ* augment). Thus: *aśleṣīt*, meaning "he embraced" (*adhākṣīt*). [This concludes the discussion on] *sattvāśleṣe* (Pāṇini 1.4.67).

The suffix *ksa* occurs after the root *śliṣ* in the *luṅ* tense when it means "to adhere" with reference to living beings, but not otherwise. For example: *upāśliṣaj jatu ca kāṣṭhaṃ ca* ("the lac and the wood adhered together") and *vyatyaśliṣṭa jatu ca kāṣṭhaṃ ca* ("the lac and the wood adhered to each other").

Regarding the rule *ṇiśridrusrukamaḥ kartari caṅ* (Pāṇini 1.3.68): the suffix *caṅ* occurs in the *luṅ* tense after roots ending in *ṇi* and after the roots *śri*, *dru*, *sru*, *kram*, when the agent (*kartṛ*) is expressed. Examples: *acīkarat* ("he caused to do"), *aśiśriyat* ("he resorted to"), *adudruvat* ("he ran"), *asusruvat* ("he flowed"), *acakamata* ("he desired"). Why specify "when the agent is expressed"? Consider: *akārayiṣātāṃ kaṭau devadattena* ("the two mats were caused to be made by Devadatta"). The letter *c* in *caṅ* serves as a marker (*cihna*) for the rule *cakāraś caṅi* (Pāṇini 5.1.24). The letter *ṅ* is for the purpose of prohibiting the substitution of *eṅ* (i.e., it prevents the *guṇa* substitution).

*dheśver vā* (1.1.69): After the roots *dheṭ* and *śvi*, the *caṅ* substitute optionally occurs in the *luṅ* tense. Examples: *adadhat*, *adhāsīt*, *adhāt*; *aśiśviyat*, *aśvayīt*, *aśvat*. The restriction "in the sense of the agent" (*kartari*) applies here; thus [the *caṅ* does not apply in the passive], as in *adhiṣātāṃ gāvau vatsena* ("the two cows were made to swell by the calf"). *ṛsṛśāsasukhyāvaco ’ṅ* (1.1.70): After the roots *ṛ*, *sṛ*, *śās*, *su*, *khyā*, and *vac*, the suffix *aṅ* is applied in the *luṅ* tense.

The suffix *aṅ* is applied after these [roots] in the *luṅ* tense: *ārat*, *samārata*; *asarat*; *aśiṣat*; *āsthat*, *paryāsthata*; *ākhyat*; *avocat*. Due to its association with *śās*, the first two roots (*ṛ* and *sṛ*) are understood here as having their *śap* dropped; therefore, it does not apply here: *ārṣīt*, *asārṣīt*. Regarding *hvā-lip-sicaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.71):
the suffix *aṅ* is applied to the roots *hve* (to call), *lip* (to smear), and *sic* (to sprinkle) in the *luṅ* tense. Examples: *ahvat*, *alipat*, *asicat*.
After roots beginning with *hve*, the suffix *aṅ* optionally occurs when *taṅ* follows. Examples: *āhvata*, *āhvāsta*; *alipata*, *alipta*; *asicata*, *asikta*.
(1.1.73) *lṛdidyutādipuṣyatyādibhyo ’taṅi*: [The suffix *aṅ* is applied] after roots ending in *ḷ*, those beginning with *dyut*, and those beginning with *puṣ*, provided that *taṅ* does not follow.

After roots beginning with *dyut* and those beginning with *puṣ*, the suffix *aṅ* is used in place of *luṅ* when it does not belong to the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) voice. Examples: *agamat*, *asṛpat*; *vyadyutat*, *aśvitat*; *apuṣat*, *aśuṣat*. Why "when not belonging to the *taṅ*"? Consider *vyadyotiṣṭa*, *vyaloṭiṣṭa*. Because of the specific mention of the *śyan* affix (*puṣyati*), the rule does not apply to *puṣṇāti*: *apoṣīt*. (1.1.74) *irito vā*:

After a root marked with the indicatory letter *iṛ*, the suffix *aṅ* optionally occurs in place of *luṅ* when it refers to an action for the sake of another action (*kriyārtha*) and does not belong to the *taṅ* voice. Examples: *arudhat*, *arautsīt*. Only "when not belonging to the *taṅ*" applies here: *aruddha*.

Regarding *jṝ-śvi-stambhu-mrucu-mlucu-glucuḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.75): after these roots, when the *luṅ* suffix follows and it does not have the *ātmanepada* marker (*taṅ*), the *aṅ* augment optionally occurs. Thus: *ajarat*, *ajārīt*; *aśvat*, *aśvayīt*; *aśiśviyat*. *Astabhat*, *astambhīt*. *Amrucat*, *amrocīt*. *Amlucat*, *amlocīt*. *Nyaglucat*, *nyaglocīt*. The form *nyagluñcīt* is the form of the root *gluñci*. Now, one might object: surely the form *nyaglucat* is also accepted as a form of *gluñci*, and in that case, its meaning of "motion" is understood. Since verbal roots have multiple meanings, *gluci* will also possess the sense of motion.
Regarding *ciṇ te padaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.76): [the *ciṇ* augment is applied] after the root *pad* when the *taṅ* markers follow.

In the *luṅ* [aorist] tense, when *tabhūta* follows, the suffix *ciṇ* occurs. [Examples: *udapādi*. Why "when *tabhūta*"? [Counter-example: *udapatsātām*. The letter *c* in *ciṇ* (Pāṇini 1.1.85) is for the purpose of marking the *ciṇ* suffix. The letter *ṇ* is for the purpose of [indicating] the *ādaic* vowels. According to Pāṇini 1.1.77, *ciṇ* optionally occurs after the roots *dīp*, *jan*, *budh*, *pūr*, *tāy*, and *pyāy* when *luṅ* in the *tabhūta* form follows. [Examples: *adīpi*, *adīpiṣṭa*; *ajani*, *ajaniṣṭa*; *abodhi*, *abuddha*; *apūri*, *apūriṣṭa*; *atāyi*, *atāyiṣṭa*; *apyāyi*, *apyāyiṣṭa*.
Regarding *bhāvāpyayoḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.78):

when the *luṅ* suffix follows a verbal root used in the sense of "becoming" (*bhāva*) or "being acted upon" (*apya*), the *ciṇ* affix occurs after that which has the purpose of an action (*kriyārtha*). Examples: *āsi bhavatā* ("you were [made to sit]") and *akāri kaṭo bhavatā* ("a mat was made by you"). In the case of *akāri kaṭaḥ svayam eva*, the agent is understood from the word *svayam*; however, the *ciṇ* affix occurs only when there is an object (*vyāpya*). But when the *lakāra* suffix denotes the agent, then it is: *akṛta kaṭaḥ svayam eva*. Likewise: *adohi gauḥ svayam eva* and *adugdha gauḥ svayam eva*. Even for the root *rudh*, the *ciṇ* affix is indeed desired when there is an intention to express the object: *aruddhi gauḥ svayam eva*.

"The cow was obstructed by Devadatta. But when the cow itself is the agent, then it indeed becomes: "The cow obstructed herself. And the meaning of "herself" (*ātmanā*) is exactly the same as the meaning of "by herself" (*svayam eva*). When "was obstructed" (*arodhi*) is stated, the agency is not understood unless another word expressing the agent is heard. Therefore, here too, when there is a desire to express the object (*vyāpyavivakṣā*), the *ciṇ* suffix must occur. But when the *l*-suffix denotes the agent, then it is: "The cow obstructed herself."

Even then, pervasion (*vyāpyatā*) is understood either from the other word *ātmānam* or from the expression *svayam eva*. In the example *atapta tapas tāpasaḥ*, the *lakāra* suffix denotes the agent alone; the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) ending occurs by rule 1.4.75, *tapa-āpye*. Furthermore, the root *tap-* here functions in the sense of "to perform" (*karoti*). The meaning is: "The ascetic did not perform penance. By rule 1.1.79, *nānoḥ tapaḥ*, the *ciṇ* affix does not occur after the root *tap-* when preceded by the prefix *anu*, provided that *anu* is a qualifier (*viśeṣya*). Example: *anvavātapta pāpena karmaṇā* ("He was tormented by evil karma"). Why say "after *anu*"? Observe: *atāpi pṛthivī rājñā* ("The earth was heated by the king").
*Tiṅ-śit-yag-aliḍ-āśīr-liṅ-i* (Pāṇini 1.3.90):

The suffix *yag* occurs after a verbal root when expressing a state (*bhāva*) or a passive action (*apya*), provided it is followed by a *tiṅ* or a *śit* suffix, excluding the *liṭ* and the *āśīr-liṅ*. Examples: *āsyate devadattena* (is being sat by Devadatta). *āsyamānam* (being sat). *gamyate grāmaḥ* (the village is being gone to). *gamyamānaḥ* (being gone to). Why "excluding *liṭ* and *āśīr-liṅ*"? *babhūve devadattena* (Devadatta has become). *bibhide kusūlaḥ* (the granary burst open). *bhaviṣīṣṭa* (may he become). *pakṣīṣṭa odanaḥ* (may the rice be cooked). In the case of *bhidyate kusūlaḥ svayam eva* ("the granary bursts open by itself"), the fact that it is the object (*vyāpyatā*) is understood from the hearing of the word *bhidyate*, while its status as the agent (*kartṛtva*) is understood from the hearing of the words *svayam eva*.

But when there is an intention to express agency (*kartṛtva*), as in "the granary splits itself" (*bhinatti kusūla ātmānam*), it is understood that "the cow milks" means "it releases milk. Likewise, [in the cases] "the cow milked by herself," "the cow flows by herself," and "the staff bends by itself," the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) ending is applied according to the rule *snunamaḥ svayam* (Pāṇini 1.3.67).

"The elephant scatters [flowers] by itself," "the garland strings itself," "the garland weaves itself," and "the mat desires to be made by itself"—in these cases, the *ātmanepada* ending (*taṅ*) is applied according to Pāṇini 1.3.74 (*kirādisranthagranthasanām āpye*), because the object is intended to be the agent. Therefore, in the case of "the *udumbara* tree ripens its red fruit," it is precisely the state of being the object (*vyāpyatā*) that is intended to be qualified by the action. However, when the agency is intended, one says "the self cooks itself" (*pacaty ātmānam*).

In the case of *parivārayante kaṇṭakā vṛkṣam* ("the thorns surround the tree"), the suffix *taṅ* (the middle voice ending) applies by rule 1.4.124, *phalavati*. However, when connected with another word (*padāntara*), it is understood that the fruit of the action does not accrue to the agent. Likewise, in *kārayate kaṭaḥ svayam eva*, *corayate gauḥ svayam eva*, *bhūṣayate kanyā svayam eva*, *maṇḍayate kanyā svayam eva*, *śrayate daṇḍaḥ svayam eva*, *brūte kathā svayam eva*, and *āhate gauḥ svayam eva*, the status of the agent alone is understood. In these cases, *taṅ* applies by rule 1.4.73, *āṅo yamahanaḥ*. Furthermore, [the suffix *niṣ* is applied] by rule 1.1.81, *tapas-tapa-āpyāt*.

The suffix *ya* occurs after the root *tapa-* when it means "to obtain through austerity. From this [root], *tāpasaḥ* ("an ascetic") is formed: he performs austerity (*tapyate tapas*). By [Pāṇini 1.4.75] *tapa-āpyāt*, the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) endings are applied. Why say "when meaning to obtain through austerity"? [Consider: *suvarṇakāra uttapati suvarṇam* ("the goldsmith heats the gold"). This rule is begun for the sake of the agent.

By [Pāṇini 3.1.68] *kartari śap*, when a *tiṅ* or a *śit* suffix follows, the *śap* augment occurs in the sense of the agent. Examples: *tarati*, *nayati*, *dhārayaḥ*, *pārayaḥ*. It is only in the case of non-aorist (*aliṭ*) and benedictive (*āśīrliṅ*) that [this applies]; thus: *babhūva*, *bhūyāt*. The letter *ś* is for the purpose of indicating [the application of Pāṇini 6.1.49] *eco 'śity ād*; the letter *p* is for the purpose of indicating [the application of Pāṇini 5.4.35] *śap-śyan*.
*adādibhyo luk* (1.1.83): There is elision (*luk*) of *śap* following [roots] beginning with *ad*. [Examples: *atti*, *hanti*. *hūnāṃ dve ca* (1.1.84).
The *śap* affix of roots such as *hu* is elided, and there is reduplication. *juhoti*. *bibheti*. [Pāṇini 6.4.104] *ciṇaḥ*:
the *ta* suffix following *ciṇ* is elided. *udapādi*. This applies only when [the suffix] is marked with *tiṅ* or *śit*: *akāritarām*.

*yaṅo bahulam* (1.1.86): After the *yaṅ* suffix, elision (*luk*) occurs diversely. For example, *roravīti* and *rorūyate*. However, in some cases it occurs invariably: *loluvaḥ*, *popuvaḥ*. In other cases it does not occur: *lolūyā*. *divādibhyaḥ śyan* (1.1.87).

The affix *śyan* occurs in place of *śap* after roots beginning with *div*, provided that *śap* would otherwise apply. Thus: *dīvyati*, *sīvyati*. Regarding Pāṇini 1.3.68 (*bhrāśabhlāśabhramukramuklamutrasitruṭilaṣo vā*): *śyan* optionally occurs after the roots beginning with *bhrāś*. Thus: *bhrāśyate* or *bhrāśate*; *bhlāśyate* or *bhlāśate*; *bhramyati* or *bhramati*. Because these belong to the *bhūvādi* class, there is no lengthening of the vowel. *krāmyati* or *krāmati*; *klāmyati* or *klāmati*; *trasyati*; *truṭyati* or *truṭati*; *laṣyati* or *laṣati*.
(1.1.89) *yasaḥ*: After the root *yas*, the affix *śyan* optionally occurs. Thus, one says either *yasyati* or *yasati*. (1.1.90) *samaḥ*...

The suffix *śyan* occurs after the root *yama* when it means "to restrain" (*saṃyasyati*) or "to fasten" (*samyasati*). Why "when it means 'to restrain' (*sama*)"? [Because otherwise it would be] *āyasyati*. Regarding the rule *kuṣirañjor āpye* (Pāṇini 1.3.91):

the suffix *śyan* occurs after the roots *kuṣ* and *rañj* only when the agent is that which is being acted upon (*āpya*). [Examples: *kuṣyati pādaḥ svayam eva* ("the foot festers of its own accord"); *rajyati vastraṃ svayam eva* ("the cloth colors of its own accord"). Why "when the agent is that which is being acted upon (*āpya*)"? [Because otherwise it would be] *kuṣṇāti* and *rañjati*.
*Tu-dādi-bhyaḥ śaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.77): The suffix *śa* follows roots belonging to the *tud-ādi* group. For example: *tudati*, *nudati*.
*Rudh-ādīnāṃ śnam* (Pāṇini 3.1.78): The suffix *śnam* follows roots belonging to the *rudh-ādi* group.

The augment *śnam* follows the final vowel of the roots beginning with *rudh*. [Examples: *ruṇaddhi*, *bhinatti*. According to Pāṇini 1.1.94, the suffix *u* follows the roots beginning with *tan*. [Examples:
*tanoti*, *sanoti*, *karoti*.

*svādibhyaḥ śnuḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.73): After roots beginning with *su*, the suffix *śnu* follows. [Examples: *sunoti*, *sinoti*. *śrukṛvdhivāṃ śṛkṛdhi ca* (Pāṇini 3.1.74): For the roots *kṛ* and *vṛdh*, *śru* is substituted by *śṛ*, and for *kṛ*, it is substituted by *kṛdhi*.
For the roots *śru*, *kṛ*, *dhī*, and *vī*, the suffix *śnu* occurs, and *śṛ*, *kṛ*, and *dhi* become their respective substitutes. Thus: *śṛṇoti*, *kṛṇoti*, *dhinoti*.
Alternatively, the suffix *śnu* may optionally follow the root *akṣ*:
*nirakṣṇoti* or *nirakṣati*.

(98) *Takṣ* [is used] in the sense of making thin (*tanūkṛti*). In the sense of making thin, the root *takṣ* optionally takes the suffix *śnu*. Examples: *nistakṣṇoti*, *nistakṣati*. Why say "in the sense of making thin"? [Observe: *saṃtakṣati vāgbhiḥ* ("he refines with words"). (Pāṇini 1.1.99) *stambhu-stumbhu-skambhu-skumbhu-skubhyaḥ*.
The suffix *śnu* follows these [roots]: *stabhnóti*, *stubhnóti*, *skabhnóti*, *skubhnóti*, *skunóti*.
Regarding the suffix *śnā*:
(Pāṇini 3.1.81) *śnā* follows these very same [roots]: *stabhnāti*, *stubhnāti*, *skabhnāti*, *skubhnāti*, *skunāti*.

(1.1.101) *kryādibhyaḥ*: after roots beginning with *krī*, the suffix *śnā* follows. [Examples: *krīṇāti*, *prīṇāti*. (1.1.102) *halo hau śānac*: after a root ending in a consonant, the suffix *śānac* occurs before the ending *hi*.

After a verbal root ending in a consonant (*hal*), when followed by the second person singular imperative suffix *dhv* (which is not the domain of *śnā*), the suffix *śānac* occurs. Examples: *puṣāṇa*, *gṛhāṇa*. Why "after a consonant" (*hala*)? [Consider: *krīṇīhi*. Why "when followed by *dhv*" (*hau*)? [Consider: *aśnāti*.
Regarding *bahulam* (Pāṇini 1.4.103): it should be understood that this term *bahulam* is the governing heading (*adhikṛta*).
Regarding *bhāvāpyayoḥ* (Pāṇini 3.4.69):
it should be understood that this [sūtra] is governed by the rule *kriyāyāṃ kriyāvyāpye ca* (Pāṇini 3.4.70).
*Tavyānīyarkelimaraḥ* (Pāṇini 3.4.70).

The suffixes *tavya* and others occur frequently after a verbal root when used in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāva*) or the object (*karman*). Examples: *kartavyam*, *karaṇīyam* (that which is to be done); *kartavyaḥ kaṭaḥ*, *karaṇīyaḥ kaṭaḥ* (the mat that is to be made). In the sense of the object, we have *bhidelimā māṣāḥ* (beans that are easily split). Because of the rule regarding "frequently" (*bahula*), these suffixes also occur in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*) and so forth: *snānīyaṃ cūrṇam* (powder for bathing), *dānīyo brāhmaṇaḥ* (a Brahmin worthy of gifts), *samāvartanīyo guruḥ* (a teacher from whom one may return [after studies]), *pravacanīya upādhyāyaḥ* (a teacher who is to be taught), *upasthānīyaḥ śiṣyaḥ* (a pupil who is to be attended upon). We shall explain elsewhere that the suffix *tavya* may optionally have the *svarita* accent. Regarding *vāstavyaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.106):

the suffix *tavya* is applied to the root *vas* in the sense of the agent, and the lengthening of the vowel is prescribed as an irregularity (*nipātana*). Thus, "he dwells" (*vasati*) is called *vāstavyaḥ*.

By the rule *yat* (Pāṇini 3.1.97), the suffix *yat* frequently occurs after a verbal root when it has the sense of another action (*kriyārtha*), as well as in the senses of "becoming" (*bhāva*) and "attainment" (*āpya*). Examples: *ceyam*, *jeyam*, *bhavyam*. In the sense of attainment: *bhavyaḥ puruṣaḥ* ("a person capable [of being]"); *geyāni brāhmaṇena sāmāni* ("the Sāman hymns are to be sung by the Brāhmaṇa"). In the sense of becoming: *geyo brāhmaṇaḥ sāmnām* ("a Brāhmaṇa who is fit for the Sāmans"). [The author] will state the suffix *ṇyat* after roots ending in *ṛ* or *hal* (consonants). [The rule continues: *puṣa-kita-kati-cati-yati-śasi-sahi-yajaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.108).

After verbal roots ending in the *pavarga* (labials) and after those beginning with *śak*, the suffix *ya* occurs diversely (*bahulam*) in the sense of the action (*bhāva*) or the object (*āpya*). Examples: *japyam*, *labhyam*; *śakyam*, *takyam*, *catyam*, *yatyam*, *śasyam*, *sahyam*, *yajyam*. We shall state that for roots ending in *jan*, *vadh*, and those having *i* or *u* as their penultimate vowel, the accent falls on the first syllable (*svaritam vakṣyāmaḥ*).
[The rule] *gadamadayamo 'prādeḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.109) applies.

The suffix *ya* occurs after the words *gada*, etc., when they are not preceded by a *prādi* prefix. Examples: *gadyam*, *madyam*, *yamyam*. Why "not preceded by a *prādi*" (*aprādeḥ*)? [Counter-examples: *pragādyam*, *pramādyam*, *āyāmyam*. The *prādi* prefixes are: *pra*, *parā*, *apa*, *sam*, *anu*, *ava*, *nir*, *dur*, *vi*, *āṅ*, *adhi*, *api*, *ni*, *ati*, *su*, *ud*, *abhi*, *prati*, *pari*, *upa*. The mention of *yama* is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtham*). Regarding the rule *caraḥ* (Pāṇini 3.3.16): the suffix *ya* occurs after the root *car* in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāva*) or a product (*āpyaya*). Example: *caryam*. The restriction "not preceded by a *prādi*" applies here as well: [counter-example] *abhicāryam*.

(1.1.111) *āṅo ’gurau*: That which follows the prefix *āṅ* [becomes a single substitute] when it does not refer to a heavy syllable (*aguru*). Example: *ācarya-deśaḥ*. Why "not a heavy syllable"? Example: *ācāryaḥ*.

(1.1.112) *avadyapaṇyavaryā garhyavikreyānirodeṣu*: [The suffix *yat* is applied after the root *vṛ* with the prefix *ava* to form] *avadya*, *paṇya*, and *varya* in the senses of "blameworthy," "marketable for sale," and "unobstructed" respectively.

The word *avadya* is an irregularly formed (nipātita) term when it has the sense of "blameworthy"; otherwise, it is *anadya*. The word *paṇya* is an irregularly formed term when it has the sense of "that which is for sale"; otherwise, it is *pāṇya*. The word *varyā* is used when "non-restraint" is understood; otherwise, it is *vṛtyā*. Because of the feminine gender specification here, it does not apply in this case: *vāryā ṛtvijaḥ* ("the priests are to be chosen"). The word *vahya* is an irregularly formed term when it denotes an instrument (*karaṇa*). That by which one carries is *vahya*, such as a cart (*śakaṭa*); otherwise, it is *vāhya*.
(1.1.114) *Aryaḥ* is irregularly formed (*nipātyate*) when meaning "master" or "vaiśya. In other senses, it is *āryaḥ*. (1.1.115) *Ṛtumatī* [is called] *upasaryā*.
The form *upasaryā* is an irregularly formed (*nipātita*) word when it means "a woman in her fertile period. Otherwise, it is *upasāryā*. Regarding *ajaryam saṃgatam* (Pāṇini 6.1.116):

the form *ajaryam* is an irregularly formed word in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*), provided it refers to a "meeting" (*saṃgata*). An example is *ajaryam āryasaṃgatam* ("an unaging meeting of noble persons"). Why is "meeting" (*saṃgata*) specified? [To exclude cases such as: *ajaritā kambalaḥ* ("the woolen blanket has not aged").

*vadaḥ supaḥ kyap ca* (Pāṇini 3.1.106): After a verbal root meaning "to speak" (*vad*), when preceded by a *sup*-ending word, the suffix *kyap* occurs, as well as *yat*. Examples: *brahmodyam*, *brahmavadyam*. Why "after a *sup*-ending word"? [Counter-example: *vādyam*. [The rule applies] only when not preceded by a prefix: *abhivādyam*. *bhuvaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.107).

The suffix *kyap* occurs after a nominal stem (*sup*) following the root *bhū*. Example: *brahmabhūyam gataḥ* ("he has attained the state of Brahman"). Only after a nominal stem: *bhavyam*. Only when not preceded by *pra* and other such prefixes: *prabhavyam*. Regarding the rule *hanas ta ca* (Pāṇini 3.3.76): the suffix *kyap* occurs after the root *han* following a nominal stem in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāve*), and the letter *t* is substituted for the final [n] of the root. Example: *brahmahatyā* ("the killing of a Brahmin"). Why "in the sense of an abstract action"? Consider: *śvaghātyaḥ* ("one who kills dogs"). Why "after a nominal stem"? Consider: *ghāto vartate* ("the act of killing occurs"). Why "not preceded by *pra* and others"? Consider: *upaghātaḥ* ("an injury"). Due to the presence of the term *bahulam* ("variously"), the suffix *ṇyat* does not occur here either.

Pāṇini 3.1.109 (*iṇ-stu-śāsu-vṛñ-dṛ-juṣaḥ*): The suffix *kyap* occurs after the roots *iṇ* and others. Examples: *ityaḥ*, *stutyaḥ*, *śiṣyaḥ*, *vṛtyaḥ*. However, from the root *vṛñ*: *vāryā ṛtvijaḥ* ("the officiating priests are to be chosen"). Also: *ādṛtyaḥ*, *juṣyaḥ*. How is it that we have *upeyaḥ*, *avaśyastutyaḥ*, *āśāsyam* (where the suffix appears to be *yat*), and *anivāryo gajair anyaiḥ svabhāva iva dehinām*? [The answer is: Because of the rule of "diversity" (*bahulādhikāra*). Pāṇini 3.1.110 (*ṛdupāntād akḷpicṛtaḥ*): [The suffix *kyap* occurs] after a root ending in *ṛ* or having *ṛ* as its penultimate letter, except for *kḷp* and *cṛt*.

The suffix *kyap* occurs after a verbal root ending in the vowel *ṛ*, provided it is used in the sense of an action (*kriyārtha*), with the exception of the roots *kḷp* and *cṛt*. [Examples: *vṛtyam*. Why is it said "with the exception of *kḷp* and *cṛt*"? [Counter-examples: *saṃkalpyam*; *vicartyam*. Regarding *kheyam*: after the root *khan*, *kyap* is applied and the form *kheyam* is thus prescribed as an irregularity (*nipātyate*).

(1.1.123) *bhṛño 'saṃjñāyām*: After the root *bhṛ*, when not forming a name (*asaṃjñā*), the suffix *kyap* occurs. Example: *bhṛtyaḥ*. Why "when not forming a name"? Consider *bhāryā*. But surely, even when forming a name, there is *kyap* in the feminine? No; because that [suffix] is prescribed for the abstract state (*bhāva*). (1.1.124) *samo vā*: [The suffix *kyap* occurs after *bhṛ*] optionally after the prefix *sam*.
The suffix *kyap* optionally occurs after the root *bhṛ* when preceded by the prefix *sam*. Thus: *saṃbhṛtyaḥ*, *saṃbhāryaḥ*.

According to Pāṇini 3.1.125 (*kṛvṛṣimṛjiśaṃsiduhiguhaḥ*), the suffix *kyap* optionally occurs after the roots *kṛ*, *vṛṣ*, *mṛj*, *śaṃs*, *duh*, and *guh*. Thus: *kṛtyam*, *kāryam*; *vṛṣyam*, *varṣyam*; *mṛjyam*, *mārgyam*; *śasyam*, *śaṃsyam*; *duhyam*, *dohyam*; *guhyam*, *gohyam*.

*rājasūya-rucya-kṛṣṭapacya-avyathyāḥ* (1.1.126): these words are formed as irregular derivations (*nipātana*). *Rājasūya*: that which is to be pressed (*sotavya*) by a king (*rājan*). How is *sūrya* [formed]? From the word *sura*, the suffix *ṇyat* is added in its own sense (*svārthika*). Alternatively, it is due to the irregular derivation (*nipātana*) in Pāṇini 5.3.153: *sūryāgastyayoḥ*. The formation of *mṛṣodyam*—from *vad* preceded by *mṛṣā* with the suffix *kyap*—is already established; however, in other cases it will not occur because of the rule of diversity (*bahulādhikāra*). *Rucya*: that which shines (*rocate*). *Kṛṣṭapacyāḥ*: rice plants that ripen in ploughed soil (*kṛṣṭe pacyante*). *Avyathya*: that which does not waver (*na vyathate*). *kupyājyabhidyoddhyasidhyayugyāni nāmni* (1.1.127): [The following forms are used] when they denote a name.

These verbal forms are irregularly formed (*nipātyante*) as proper names (*saṃjñā*). *Kupyam* means wealth (*dhanam*). *Ājyam* means clarified butter (*ghṛtam*). There is a river named *Bhidyaḥ*. Likewise, *Uddhyaḥ* and *Sidhyaḥ*. How is *Puṣyaḥ* [formed]? It is due to the irregular formation (*nipātana*) prescribed by the rule *tiṣyapuṣyayor* (Pāṇini 5.3.154). *Yugyam* means a vehicle (*yānam*). In other cases: *gopyam*, *ājyam*, *bhedham*, *ujjhyam*, *sedhanam* or *sedhyam*, and *yogyam*. [The rule] *jityā-vipūya-vinīya-halimuñja-kalk-eṣu* (Pāṇini 1.1.128) [applies].

The words *jitya*, etc., are irregularly formed (*nipātita*) in the senses of *hali* and so forth. *Jityā haliḥ*; anything else is *jeya*. *Vipūyo muñjaḥ*; anything else is *vipāvya*. *Vinīyaḥ kalkaḥ*; anything else is *vineya*. Regarding *padāsvairipakṣyabāhyāsu grahaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.129):

the suffix *kyap* is applied to the root *grah* in the senses of "word" (*pada*) and so forth. *Pragṛhyaṃ padaṃ*: a word that is not euphonically combined (*saṃdhi*) with a following vowel. *Avagṛhyaṃ padaṃ*: a word for which a pause (*avagraha*) is made. In the sense of "not independent" (*asvairiṣu*): *gṛhyakā ime*; the meaning is "those who are confined. In the sense of "belonging to a party" (*pakṣyeṣu*): *arjunagṛhyaḥ*. In the sense of "external" (*bāhyāyām*): *grāmagṛhyā strī*. Anything else [formed from *grah*] is *grāhya*.
Pāṇini 3.1.124: *ṛhalo ṇyat*.
The suffix *ṇyat* is applied after verbal roots ending in an *ṛ*-vowel or a consonant (*hal*) when they signify an action. Examples: *kāryam*, *hāryam*; *pākyam*, *vākyam*. Pāṇini 3.1.125:
*pāṇisamavābhyāṃ sṛjaḥ*. The suffix *ṇyat* is applied after the root *sṛj* when preceded by the words *pāṇi* and *samava*.

The suffix *ṇyat* occurs after the root *sṛj* when preceded by *pāṇi* or *sam-ava*. For example: *pāṇisargyā rajjuḥ* (“a rope for releasing with the hand”) and *samavasargyā* (“for releasing together”). Why specify “after *pāṇi* and *sam-ava*”? [Consider: *sṛjyam* (“to be emitted”).

By the rule *or āvaśyake* (Pāṇini 3.1.125), the suffix *ṇyat* occurs after a verbal root ending in *u* when necessity (*avaśya-bhāva*) is understood. For example: *lāvyam* (“must be reaped”) and *avaśya-lāvyam* (“necessarily to be reaped”). Other than that, it is *lavyam* (“to be reaped”).

(1.1.133) After the roots *ās*, *yu*, *pi*, *rapi*, *lap*, *trap*, *cam*, *id*, and *dabh*, as well as after *su* preceded by *āṅ*, the suffix *ṇyat* occurs. Thus: *āsāvyam*, *yāvyam*, *vāpyam*, *rāpyam*, *abhilāpyam*, *apatrāpyam*, *ācāmyam*, *avadābhyam*.
(1.1.134) Or [the suffix *ṇyat* occurs] after *amāvasu*.

The suffix *ṇyat* optionally occurs after the root *vas* preceded by *amā*. Because the moon and sun dwell together (*saha vasataḥ*) in this [lunar day], it is called *amāvāsyā* or *amāvasyā*. When the suffix *ṇyat* is not applied, the suffix *yat* occurs. Because of the prohibition "one does not dwell in fire" (*anau vasa*), the initial acute accent (*ādyudāttatva*) does not take effect. (1.1.135) *praṇāyya* is an irregularly formed word (*nipātana*) when it means "disapproved. Thus, *praṇāyyaś cauraḥ* ("the thief is disapproved"). Why "when it means disapproved"? [Because otherwise] *praṇeyaḥ sādhuḥ* ("the virtuous man is to be led"). How then is this [Vedic passage] to be explained: *jyeṣṭhāya putrāya pitā brahma brūyāt praṇāyyāyāntevāsine ca* ("A father should impart the Veda to his eldest son and to a pupil who is worthy of being led")? [It is explained] because of the rule of "diversity" (*bahulādhikāra*).

*dhāyyā-pāyya-nayya-sāṃnāyya-nikāyyāḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.136): the words *dhāyyā* and so forth are irregularly formed (*nipātita*) when they function as proper names (*saṃjñā*). *Dhāyyā* refers to a *sāmidhenī* verse; it is used in this sense by convention even outside that context: "they recite the *dhāyyās*. In other cases, it means something else that is to be placed (*dheya*). *Pāyya* means a measure; in other cases, it means something else that is to be drunk (*peya*). *Ānāyya* refers to the *dakṣiṇāgni* (southern sacrificial fire), for it is brought forward and established from the *gārhapatya* fire. In other cases, it means something else that is to be brought (*āneya*). *Sāṃnāyya* refers specifically to a particular kind of oblation (*havis*); in other cases, it means something else that is to be brought together (*saṃneya*). *Nikāyya* means a dwelling; in other cases, it means something else that is to be deposited (*niceya*).
Regarding the sacrifice (*kratu*), the words *kuṇḍapāyya* and *saṃcāyya* are irregularly formed (*nipātita*).

When the sacrifice is the meaning to be expressed, these two words are derived as follows: in this [sacrifice], Soma is drunk from cups (*kuṇḍa*); thus it is the *kuṇḍapāyya* sacrifice. Due to the irregular formation (*nipātana*), it has the acute accent on the first syllable. In this [sacrifice], Soma is collected together; thus it is the *saṃcāyya* sacrifice.
Regarding the fire-altar (*agni*), the words *citya*, *upacāyya*, and *paricāyya* [are irregularly formed]. (Pāṇini 1.1.137–138)

The words *cityā* and others are irregularly formed (*nipātyante*) in the sense of "fire" (*agni*). *Cityo 'gniḥ*: "A fire that is piled up. [This is derived from] the root *ci* ("to pile") with the suffix *kyap*, and there is also the acute accent on the final syllable. *Agneś cityā* becomes *agnicityā*. *Upacāyyo 'gniḥ*: "A fire that is piled up near. [This is derived from] *upa-ci*. *Paricāyyaḥ*: "A fire that is piled around. [The form] *samūhya* is established by means of the suffix *ūhin*; for that too is used in some instances in the sense of the root *vah* ("to carry"). And *saṃvāhya* indeed occurs in the sense of "fire" as well. [These forms are explained by] Pāṇini 3.1.139: *kartari ṇvultṛcau* ("the suffixes *ṇvul* and *tṛc* occur in the sense of the agent").

The suffixes *ṇvul*, *tṛc*, and *ac* occur after a verbal root when it signifies an agent (*kartṛ*) and follows another word intended for the sake of the action (*kriyārtha*). Examples: *pācakaḥ* (one who cooks), *paktā* (one who cooks), *pacaḥ* (one who cooks). By the rule "in various ways" (*bahulam*), we have: *pādābhyāṃ hriyate* (carried by the feet), *pādahārakaḥ*; *gale cupyate* (squeezed at the throat), *galecopakaḥ*. Because of the governing principle of "in various ways," the suffix *ac* occurs even in cases where *aṇ* would otherwise be expected, as in *śvapacaḥ* (dog-cooker) and *jārabharaḥ* (supporter of a paramour). How is it that there are forms such as *nadī-carī*, *bhaṣī*, *plavī*, *corī*, *gāhī*, *sūdī*, and *devī*? They should be listed among the *gaurādi* group [of feminine nouns]. The governing heading "when signifying an agent" (*kartari*) applies prior to the rules for case endings (*sup-vidhi*). [The specific rule is: *nandigrahādibhyo lyuṇiniḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.134).

The suffixes *lyu* (ana), *ṇini*, and *niṅ* occur after the roots beginning with *nandi* and those beginning with *graha* when used in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*). From the causative forms of *nandi*, *vāsi*, *madi*, *dūṣi*, *sādhi*, *śobhi*, *vardhi*, and *roci*, when used as proper names (*saṃjñāyām*): from *nandayati* comes *nandanaḥ*; likewise, *vāsanaḥ*, *madanaḥ*, *dūṣaṇaḥ*, *sādhanaḥ*, *śobhanaḥ*, *vardhanaḥ*, and *rocanaḥ*. From *sahi*, *tapi*, and *dami* in the sense of a proper name, even without the causative marker (*aṇyantāt*): *sahanaḥ*, *tapanaḥ*, and *damanaḥ*.

*jalpanaḥ*, *darpaṇaḥ*, *ramaṇaḥ*, *saṃkrandanaḥ*, *saṃharṣaṇaḥ*, *saṃkarṣaṇaḥ*, *durdharṣaṇaḥ*, *janārdanaḥ*, *madhusūdanaḥ*, *pavanaḥ*, *lavaṇaḥ*. [In these cases,] the substitution of *ṇ* occurs by virtue of the rule for the suffix *nipātanāṇ*. *vibhīṣaṇaḥ*, *cittavināśanaḥ*, *kuladamanaḥ*. The suffix occurs even in the absence of the scope for *aṇ* when preceded by an object of pervasion (*vyāpyapūrva*). Examples: one who seizes is *grāhī*; *sthāyī*; *nirakṣī*; *niśrāvī*. For the roots *yāci*, *vraj*, *vad*, and *vas*, when preceded by the negative particle *nañ*, [the suffix *ini* is applied]: *ayācī*, *avrājī*, *avādī*, *avāsī*.

Regarding *ac* suffixes which do not have a conscious agent (*acittakartṛka*): *gharmasya bālātapaḥ akārī* ("the morning sun has made the heat"). In the sense of "one who experiences" (*viṣayī*), we have *viṣayī*; in the sense of "one who overcomes" (*abhibhavī*), we have *abhibhāvī*; and in the sense of "one who subdues" (*paribhavī*), we have *paribhāvī*—where the short vowel occurs by way of irregular derivation (*nipātana*). How is it that [the forms] *utsāhī*, *uddāsī*, *udbhāsī*, *saṃmardī*, and *niveśī* are formed? They are established by means of the suffix *-in*. Similarly, *avyāhārī*, *aparādhī*, and *uparodhī*. [The rule] *jñā-kṛ-prī-jū-ṣāntāt kaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.141) [applies].

The suffix *ka* occurs after the roots *jñā*, *kṛ*, and *prī*, as well as after roots ending in a short *i* vowel (*igupadha*), when used in the agentive sense (*kartari*). Thus: from *jānāti* comes *jña*; *utkiraḥ*; *priyaḥ*; *vikṣipaḥ*. Because the rule states "in various ways" (*bahulam*), we also have: *vikṣeptā* and *vikṣepakaḥ*. Furthermore, *devaḥ*, *prasevaḥ*, and *meṣaḥ* [are formed with *ka*]. Regarding the rule *ātaḥ prādibhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.3):

the suffix *ka* occurs after verbal roots ending in long *ā*, provided they follow prefixes (*prādi*) that indicate purpose of action (*kriyārtha*). Thus: *prasthaḥ*. The root *traiṅ* meaning "to protect" (Dhātupāṭha 1.484) forms *sutraḥ*. Similarly, *suglaḥ*.
