Pāghrādhmādheṭdṛśaḥ śaḥ (1.1.143): The suffix *śa* occurs after the roots *pā* and others. *utpibaḥ*. Because of its association with *ghrā* and the others, the root *pibati* is understood here. *ujjighraḥ*. By virtue of the rule of diversity (*bahulādhikāra*), the form *vyāghraḥ* occurs with the suffix *ka*. *vidhamaḥ*, *uddhayaḥ*, *paśyaḥ*, *vipaśyaḥ*, *utpaśyaḥ*.
Dhāripārivedyudejicetisātisahivindo 'prādeḥ (1.1.144).

The suffix *śa* occurs after the roots *dhṛ*, *pṛ*, *vid*, and *uj*, provided they are not preceded by an upasarga (*prādi*). Examples: *dhārayaḥ*, *pārayaḥ*, *vedayaḥ*, *udejayaḥ*, *cetayaḥ*, *sātayaḥ*, *sāhayaḥ*; [after *vid*: *vindaḥ*, *govindaḥ*, *aravindaḥ*. Why does it say "not preceded by an upasarga"? Consider *pravedakaḥ*. Regarding the rule *lipo neś ca* (Pāṇini 3.1.145): the suffix *śa* occurs after the root *lip* when not preceded by an upasarga, and also after the root *ni-lip*. Examples: *limpaḥ*; *nilimpā* are the name of certain gods. How is it that [the forms] *dadaḥ* and *dadhaḥ* are formed? They are established by the vowel *a* [of the root *dā*]. We shall explain the specific accentuation in the eighth [chapter].

*jvalādibhyo ṇo vā* (Pāṇini 3.1.140): after roots such as *jvala* "to blaze" (Dhātupāṭha 1.561), the suffix *ṇa* optionally occurs. Thus: *jvālaḥ*, *jvalaḥ*; *cālaḥ*, *calaḥ*. The roots beginning with *jvala* and ending with *kasa* are included because of the use of the particle *vṛt* [as a marker]. *śyādiṇvyadhaśvasatanaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.141).

The suffix *ṇa* occurs after the root *śyai*, which ends in long *ā*, and after roots beginning with *iṇ*. Examples: *avaśyāyaḥ* (dew). The mention of *śyai* is for the purpose of excluding the application of *ka*. Examples: *dāyaḥ*, *dhāyaḥ*, *pratyāyaḥ*, *vyādhaḥ*, *śvāsaḥ*, *avatānaḥ*. [In the case of] *lehaḥ* and *śleṣaḥ*, the formation is established by [the addition of] *ac*. Regarding *asamaḥ sroḥ* (Pāṇini 3.3.66): the suffix *ṇa* occurs after the root *sru* when preceded by *āṅ* and *sam*. Examples: *āsrāvaḥ*, *saṃsrāvaḥ*. How is *āsravaḥ* formed? By virtue of the rule of *bahulam* (diversity). Why say "not preceded by *sam*" (*asama*)? Consider *parisravaḥ*.

hṛ-so-'vāt (1.1.149): After the prefix *ava*, the suffix *ṇa* occurs following the roots *hṛ* and *sā*. Examples: *avahāraḥ*, *avasāyaḥ*. Why "after *ava*"? [Consider: *haraḥ*. dunyo 'prādeḥ (1.1.150).

The suffix *ṇa* occurs after the roots *du* and *nī* when they are not preceded by a *prādi* prefix. Thus: *dāvaḥ*, *nāyaḥ*. Why "not preceded by a *prādi*"? Consider: *pradavaḥ*, *praṇayaḥ*. Due to the rule of *bahulādhikāra* (diversity of application), we have *vanadavaḥ*.
[Vārttika 1.1.151: After the root *bhū*, the suffix *ṇa* optionally occurs. Thus: *bhāvaḥ*, *bhavaḥ*.
After the root *grah*, the suffix *ṇa* optionally becomes *ṇa*. Thus, *grāhaḥ* "an aquatic creature" and *grahaḥ* "the sun and so forth.
After the root *grah* with the prefix *gehe*, the suffix *ka* is applied. (Pāṇini 3.1.143–144).

What is the meaning of the term *graha* when it refers to a house? It is *gṛham*, *gṛhāḥ*. According to Pāṇini 1.1.154 (*gas thakan*), the suffix *thakan* is applied to the root *gai*; thus, *gāthakaḥ*.
The suffix *ṇyut* occurs after the root *gā* (to sing). [Thus formed are] *gāyanaḥ* (a singer) and *gāyanī* (a female singer).
The suffix *ha* occurs [after the root *gā*] when referring to rice or time. (Pāṇini 3.1.140) (Note: This is a reference to the rule governing the formation of *gāhaḥ*.)

The suffix *ṇyuT* occurs after the roots *hā* ("to abandon") and *i* ("to go") when referring to rice (*vrīhi*) or time (*kāla*). *Hāyana* refers to varieties of rice; *hāyana* refers to a year. Why specify "rice or time"? [Consider: *hātā* ("one who abandons").

By the rule *nṛtikhanirajaḥ śilpini ṣvun* (Pāṇini 3.1.145), the suffix *ṣvun* occurs after the roots *nṛt* ("to dance"), *khan* ("to dig"), and *raj* ("to dye") when the agent is a craftsman (*śilpin*). Thus: *nartakaḥ*, *khanakaḥ*, *rajakaḥ*. The nasalization (*anunāsika*) is elided due to its pronunciation [in the root list]. The letter *ṣ* is for the purpose of deriving the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ*: *nartakī*, *khanakī*, *rajakī*.

*pru-sṛ-lvo vun* (Pāṇini 3.1.140): The suffix *vun* occurs after the roots *pru*, *sṛ*, and *lū* when denoting an artisan (*śilpin*). Thus: *pravakaḥ*, *sarakaḥ*, *lavakaḥ*. However, for one whose craft this is not, he is called a *protā* (weaver). *āśiṣi* (Pāṇini 3.1.141): [The suffix *vun* occurs] in the sense of a blessing (*āśis*).

When a sense of wishing (*āśaṃsā*) is implied, the suffix *vun* occurs after a word denoting an action for the sake of another action. For example: *jīvatāt*, *jīvakaḥ*; *nandatāt*, *nandakaḥ*. The first quarter of the first chapter in the Cāndra Grammar is completed. [Sūtra 1.2.1: After a word denoting that which is pervaded (*vyāpya*), the suffix *aṇ* occurs.

The suffix *aṇ* occurs after a word denoting an action that is the object (*vyāpya*) of another action which is the purpose (*artha*) of that [first] action. For example: *kumbhaṃ karoti* (he makes a jar) → *kumbhakāraḥ* (jar-maker); *kāṇḍalāvaḥ* (reaper of stalks); *vedādhyāyaḥ* (student of the Veda). Because of the rule of "diversity" (*bahulādhikāra*), it does not occur here: *ādityaṃ paśyati* (he sees the sun), *himavantaṃ śṛṇoti* (he hears of the Himalayas), *grāmaṃ gacchati* (he goes to the village). How is it then that [the forms] *māṃsaśīlā*, *māṃsakāmā*, *māṃsabhakṣā*, *kalyāṇācārā*, *kalyāṇapratīkṣā*, and *duḥkhakṣamā* are formed? [Answer: "She whose habit (*śīla*) is with respect to meat" is *māṃsaśīlā*. This should be applied in all cases accordingly.

If this is so, then since there is an approach (*abhigama*) to water (*ambhas*) for it, the form *ambho'bhigama* would result; however, the form *ambho'bhigāmī* is intended. This will not be a problem, because even within the section on compounds (*samāsa-prakaraṇa*), there is the rule of "diversity" (*bahulādhikāra*).
[This is supported by] Pāṇini 5.2.70: *ātaḥ aprādēḥ kaḥ*.

The suffix *ka* occurs after a word ending in the vowel *ā*, provided that it is not preceded by a *pra*-type prefix (*prādi*). Examples: *godakaḥ* ("cow-giver"), *kambaladaḥ* ("wool-giver"). Why "not preceded by a *pra*-type prefix"? Consider: *vaḍavāsaṃdāyaḥ* ("one who gives a mare"). It is stated that this is "frequently" (*bahulam*) so: *svargahvāyaḥ* ("one who calls out to heaven"), *tantravāyaḥ* ("weaver"), *dhānyamāyaḥ* ("one who measures grain"), and *godāyo vrajati* ("he goes for the cow-gift"). In some cases, it occurs even when preceded by a *pra*-type prefix: *prapāpradaḥ* ("one who provides a water-shed"), *pathiprajñaḥ* ("one who knows the way"), *gosaṃkhyaḥ* ("one who counts cows"). This *ka* is the same as the previous one [discussed in Pāṇini 3.2.3]. However, it has been stated that the suffix *aṇ* does not apply everywhere. [This concludes the section on] *supaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.3).

The suffix *ka* occurs after a word ending in *ā*, provided that it is a noun denoting an action (*kriyārtha*). One drinks with the armpit (*kakṣa*); thus, *kakṣapaḥ*. One drinks with two [hands]; thus, *dvipaḥ*. A tree (*pādapaḥ*: one who stands on feet). One stands on level ground; thus, *samasthaḥ*. One stands on uneven ground; thus, *viṣamasthaḥ*. One rubs the belly (*tunda*); thus, *tundaparimṛjaḥ*. This *ka* is the same as the previous one; it refers specifically to a lazy person. Similarly, one who removes sorrow (*śoka*); thus, *śokāpanudaḥ*. When a son is born, one who causes joy (*ānanda*) is what is meant. In other cases, however, we have *tundaparimārjaḥ* (one who merely rubs his belly) and *śokāpanodaḥ* (one who merely removes sorrow).

Thus, "one who splits the roots" is a *mūlavibhuja* chariot. *Nakhamuca* refers to bows. *Kākaguhā* refers to sesame seeds. "One who takes a share" (*aṃśahara*)—like *śvapaca* and others—the suffix *ac* is applied; hence *aṃśahara*. As before, there is no application of the suffix *aṇ*. However, in the sense of "carrying," we see *bhārahāra* ("burden-carrier"). Similarly, *kavacahara* refers to a Kṣatriya prince. Likewise, in the sense of habitual action (*tācchīlya*), we have *puṣpāhara* ("flower-gatherer"). Similarly: *pūjārhā* refers to a Brāhmaṇī woman. *Stamberama* refers to an elephant. *Karṇejapa* refers to a slanderer. [In these cases], by the rule *saptamyā bahulam* (Pāṇini 5.4.11), there is no elision (*aluk*) of the locative case ending.

*śaktigrahaḥ*, *lāṅgalagrahaḥ*, *aṅkuśagrahaḥ*, *yaṣṭigrahaḥ*, *tomaragrahaḥ*, *ghaṭagrahaḥ*, *ghaṭīgrahaḥ*, and *dhanurgrahaḥ*—all these are established by the suffix *ac*. Similarly, *sūtragraha* is used in the sense of "holding" (*dhāraṇe*); elsewhere it is *sūtragrāhaḥ*. It is also used in the sense of a name (*saṃjñāyām*): one who brings welfare is *śaṃkarā*. One who sleeps in the sky is *khaśayaḥ*. One who sleeps on his side is *pārśvaśayaḥ*. One who sleeps supine is *uttānaśayaḥ*. *digdhasahaśayaḥ* is a compound of two types [of *tatpuruṣa*]. *kiṃkarā*, *yatkarā*, *tatkarā*, and *bahukarā* likewise take *ac* as before. According to Pāṇini 3.2.16, the suffix *ṭa* is applied after the root *car*.

The suffix *ṭa* is applied after a word ending in *sup* when followed by the root *car*. For example: *kuruṣu carati* (he moves among the Kurus) becomes *kurucaraḥ*; *kurucarī*. *Bhikṣāṃ carati* (he goes for alms) becomes *bhikṣācaraḥ*; *senayā carati* (he moves with the army) becomes *senācaraḥ*. *Ādāyacaraḥ*. Due to the rule of *bahulādhikāra* (diversity of application), this does not occur here: *kurūṃś carati* (he moves through the Kurus).
By the rule *puro'grato'grebhyaḥ sarteḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.19), the suffix *ṭa* is applied after the roots *sar* following the words *puras*, *agrataḥ*, and *agre*.

Thus: *puraḥsaraḥ*, *puraḥsarī*; *agrataḥsaraḥ*, *agrataḥsarī*; *agresaraḥ*, *agresarī*. Due to irregular derivation (*nipātana*), there is no elision (*aluk*) [of the case-ending], or the word *asaṃkhya* may end in *e*.
(1.2.6) *pūrvāt kartuḥ*:

After the word *pūrva* when it denotes an agent (*kartṛ*), the suffix *ṭa* is applied to the root *sṛ*. Thus: *pūrvaḥ sartā* = *pūrvasaraḥ*; *pūrvasarī*. Why "of the agent"? [Consider: *pūrvaṃ sarati* = *pūrvasāraḥ*. (1.2.7) *kṛño hetuśīlānulomeṣu*: [The suffix *ṭa* is applied] after the root *kṛ* when the meanings of cause (*hetu*), disposition (*śīla*), or compliance (*ānuloma*) are intended.

The suffix *ṭa* (forming an agentive noun) occurs after the root *kṛ* following a verbal suffix (*sup*), when the sense of "cause" (*hetu*) or "agent" (*kartṛ*) is understood, provided that the agent is either "favorable" (*anuloma*) or simply "favorable" (*anukūla*). A cause is a factor whose causal power is recognized. Examples: *vidyā yaśaskarī* ("learning brings fame"), *kanyā śokakarī* ("a daughter causes grief"), *dhanaṃ kulakaram* ("wealth sustains the family"), *śīlaṃ prakṛtiḥ* ("character is one's nature"), *śrāddhakaraḥ* ("one who performs ancestral rites"). "Favorable" means compliant. Example: *vacanakaraḥ* ("one who obeys instructions"). Likewise: *divākaraḥ*, *divasakaraḥ*, *dinakaraḥ*, *niśākaraḥ*, *rajanīkaraḥ*, *kṣapākaraḥ*, *vibhākaraḥ*, *prabhākaraḥ*.

*Bhāskaraḥ* (the maker of light); [the *s* is inserted due to the rule beginning with] *kaska-*; *kārakaraḥ*, *antakaraḥ*, *anantakaraḥ*, *ādikaraḥ*, *bahukaraḥ*, *nāndīkaraḥ*, *kiṃkaraḥ*, *lipikaraḥ*, *libikaraḥ*, *balikaraḥ*, *bhaktikaraḥ*, *kartṛkaraḥ*, *citrakaraḥ*, *kṣetrakaraḥ*, *ekakaraḥ*, *jaṅghākaraḥ*, *bāhukaraḥ*, *ahaskaraḥ*, *yatkaraḥ*, *tatkaraḥ*, *dhanuṣkaraḥ*, *aruṣkaraḥ*, *karmakaraḥ*, *ghaṭīkaraḥ*, and so forth.

In what sense is it said "in *hetu* and so forth"? [Examples are: *kumbhakāraḥ*, *karmakāraḥ*, *śabdakāraḥ*, *ślokakāraḥ*, *kalahakāraḥ*, *gāthākāraḥ*, *vairakāraḥ*, *cāṭukāraḥ*, *sūtrakāraḥ*, *mantrakāraḥ*, *padakāraḥ*, *kramakāraḥ*. However, in the case of those whose habitual activity (*śīla*) consists in making pots and so forth, [the suffix will] not apply due to the governing rule of *bahulam* (diversity).
[The next rule is: *stamba-śakṛdbhyām vrīhi-vatsayoḥ in* (Pāṇini 3.2.81).

The suffix *in* occurs after the root *kṛ* when preceded by *stamba* and *śakṛt*, in the senses of "rice" (*vrīhi*) and "calf" (*vatsa*) respectively. The letter *n* is for the purpose of making the initial syllable acute. *Stambakariḥ* means rice; *śakṛtkariḥ* means a calf. Why specify "in the senses of rice and calf"? [To show: *stambakāraḥ* (one who makes a clump), *śakṛtkāraḥ* (one who makes dung). (1.2.9) After the root *hṛ*, when preceded by *dṛti* and *nātha*, the suffix *in* occurs in the sense of an animal (*paśu*) as the agent. *Dṛtihariḥ* means an animal; *nāthahariḥ*. Why specify "an animal"? [To show: *dṛtihāraḥ* (a leather-bag carrier), *nāthahāraḥ* (a protector-carrier).
*phalegrahiḥ*, *ātmaṃbhariḥ*, and *kukṣiṃbhariḥ* (1.2.10):

these words are derived as irregular formations (*nipātana*). One who grasps fruits is *phalegrahiḥ*. One who nourishes only himself is *ātmaṃbhariḥ*. One who nourishes only his belly is *kukṣiṃbhariḥ*. Regarding 1.2.11: after the root *ej* ("to move"), the suffix *khaś* is applied.

The suffix *khaś* occurs after a nominal stem (*sup*) following the root *ejayati*. The letter *kh* in *khaś* serves the purpose of qualifying [the rule] by *khiti sasaṃkhyasya* (Pāṇini 6.1.75). Examples: *aṅgamejayaḥ*, *janamejayaḥ*. Regarding *śunīstanād dheṭaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.29):

the suffix *khaś* occurs after the root *dheṭ* (to suck) when it follows the words *śunī* and *stana*. Examples: *śunindhayaḥ*, *śunindhayī*; *stanandhayaḥ*, *stanandhayī*. Since the suffix would otherwise be redundant in its original form, the letter *ṭ* is understood to serve the purpose of introducing the feminine suffix *ṅīp*.

(1.2.13) After *nāsikā*, *nāḍī*, *muṣṭi*, *ghaṭī*, and *khārī*, the suffix *khaś* is applied to the root *dhēṭ* ("to suck"). Examples: *nāsikandhayaḥ* ("sucking through the nose"), *nāḍindhayaḥ*, *muṣṭindhayaḥ*, *ghaṭindhayaḥ*, *kharindhayaḥ*.
(1.2.14) The suffix *khaś* is also applied after words such as *pāṇi* to the root *dhmā* ("to blow").

The suffix *khaś* occurs after the root *dhmā* when preceded by words such as *nāsikā* and others, as well as *pāṇi* and others. Examples include: *nāsikandhamaḥ*, *nāḍindhamaḥ*, *muṣṭindhamaḥ*, *ghaṭindhamaḥ*, *kharindhamaḥ*; and *pāṇindhamaḥ*, *karandhamaḥ*, *vātandhamaḥ*, etc.

Regarding *kūlād udo rujivahaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.31): the suffix *khaś* occurs after the roots *ruj* and *vah* when preceded by *ud* which itself is preceded by *kūla*. Examples include: *kūlamudrujaḥ* and *kūlamudvahaḥ*.

(1.2.16) *vahābhrāl lihaḥ*: After the words *vaha* and *abhra*, the suffix *khaś* occurs before the root *lih*. [Examples: *vahaṃliho gauḥ* ("a bull that licks the yoke"); *abhraṃliho vāyuḥ* ("wind that licks the clouds"). (1.2.17) *parimāṇāt pacaḥ*: [The suffix *khaś* occurs] after a word denoting measure (*parimāṇa*) before the root *pac*.

The suffix *khaś* occurs after the root *pac* when followed by a word denoting measure. For example: *droṇapacā sthālī* ("a pot cooking a *droṇa* [measure]") and *khārīpacaḥ kaṭāhaḥ* ("a cauldron cooking a *khārī* [measure]").

Regarding *mitanakhat* (Pāṇini 3.2.34): the suffix *khaś* occurs after the root *pac* when preceded by the words *mita* and *nakha*. For example: *mitampacā brāhmaṇī* ("a Brahmin woman who cooks sparingly") and *nakhampacā yavāgūḥ* ("gruel that burns the nails").

(1.2.19) *vidhv-aruṣ-tilāt tudah*: After the words *vidhu*, *arus*, and *tila*, the suffix *khaś* is applied to the root *tud*. Examples: *vidhuntudaḥ*, *aruntudaḥ*, *tilantudaḥ*. (1.2.20) *vātamajaśardhaṃjaheraṃmadaparantapadviṣantapabhagaṃdarapurandarāḥ*: [The following are irregular formations: *vātamaja*, *śardhaṃjaha*, *heramada*, *parantapa*, *dviṣantapa*, *bhagaṃdara*, and *purandara*.

These words are formed as irregular derivatives (*nipātana*). "They run toward the wind" (*vātam ajanti*) thus they are *vātamajāḥ* (deer). They abandon their strength (*śardham jahati*), thus they are *śardhajihāḥ* (beans). He intoxicates with joy (*irayā mādyati*), thus he is *iramadaḥ*. He torments the enemy (*param tāpayati*), thus he is *parantapaḥ*. He torments one who hates him (*dviṣantam tāpayati*), thus he is *dviṣantapaḥ*. He tears open the vulva (*bhagam dārayati*), thus it is *bhagaṃdaraḥ*. He tears down the city (*puram dārayati*), thus he is *purandaraḥ*.
[The suffix *kha* is applied after the root *dṛś* when preceded by *ugra*, *asūrya*, etc. (Pāṇini 3.2.37).

The suffix *khaś* occurs after the words *ugra* and *asūrya* when they are followed by the root *dṛś*. [Examples: *ugraṃ paśyati* → *ugrapaśyaḥ* ("one who looks at something fierce"); *na sūryaṃ paśyanti* → *asūryampaśyāni mukhāni* ("faces that do not look at the sun"). This is because the negative particle (*nañ*) connected with the root *dṛś* attains a single meaning with *sūrya* through its expressive power (*gamakatvāt*).

(1.2.22) *lalāṭāt tapaḥ*: The suffix *khaś* occurs after the root *tap* when it follows the word *lalāṭa*. [Example: *lalāṭaṃ tapati* → *lalāṭantapaḥ* ("one who scorches the forehead"), such as the sun.

(1.2.23) *priyavaśād vadaḥ*: After the words *priya* and *vaśa*, the suffix *khaś* occurs before the root *vad*. [Examples: *priyaṃvadaḥ* (one who speaks kindly), *vaśaṃvadaḥ* (one who speaks according to another's will). (1.2.24) *vācaṃyamo vrate*: [The suffix *khac* occurs after the root *yam*] when preceded by *vāc* in the sense of a religious vow (*vrata*).
The form *vācaṃyama* is an irregularly formed word (*nipātyate*) when a religious vow (*vrata*) is understood; otherwise, it is simply "restraint of speech" (*vāgyāma*).
According to Pāṇini 3.2.41 (*sarvāt sahaḥ*), the suffix *khaś* occurs after the root *sah* when preceded by the word *sarva*. Thus: *sarvaṃsahaḥ* ("enduring everything").

(1.2.26) *Kūla*, *abhra*, and *karīṣa*: after these and after the word *sarva*, the suffix *khaś* is applied to the root *kaṣ*. Thus: *kūlaṃkaṣā nadī* (a river that erodes its banks), *abhraṃkaṣo giriḥ* (a mountain that scrapes the clouds), *karīṣaṃkaṣā vātyā* (a whirlwind that scatters dried cow-dung), and *sarvaṃkaṣaḥ khalaḥ* (a wicked person who ruins everything). (1.2.27) After the roots *megha*, *ṛti*, and *bhaya*, the suffix *kha* is applied to the root *kṛ*.

The suffix *kha* occurs after the root *kṛ* when preceded by *megha* and others. Thus: *meghaṃkaraḥ*, *ṛtiṃkaraḥ*, *bhayaṃkaraḥ*. How is *abhayaṃkaraḥ* formed? It is through the application of the rule for compounds ending in a word (*tadanta-vidhi*) where *bhaya* is a declined noun (*subanta*).

From the rule *kṣemapriyamadrād aṇ ca* (Pāṇini 3.2.28): the suffix *kha* and also the suffix *aṇ* occur after the root *kṛ* when preceded by *kṣema*, *priya*, and *madra*. Thus: *kṣemaṃkaraḥ* and *kṣemakāraḥ*; *priyaṃkaraḥ* and *priyakāraḥ*; *madraṃkaraḥ* and *madrakāraḥ*. The inclusion of the suffix *aṇ* is for the purpose of prohibiting the suffix *ṭa* in cases such as those governed by the rule *hetvādiṣu*.

(1.2.29) *āśitād bhuvo bhāvakaraṇayoḥ*: After the word *āśita*, the suffix *kha* is added to the root *bhū* in the sense of "state" (*bhāva*) or "instrument" (*karaṇa*). *Duḥkham āśitambhavam* ("the state of being satiated with difficulty"). *Alam āśitambhava odanaḥ* ("rice sufficient for satiety").
(1.2.30) *bhṛvṛtṝjisahitapidamo nāmni*: [The suffix *kha* is added] after the roots *bhṛ*, *vṛ*, *tṝ*, *ji*, *sahi*, *tap*, and *dam* when forming a proper name (*nāmni*).

The suffix *kha* occurs after these [words] when they function as proper names (*saṃjñā*). Examples: *viśvaṃbharā* ("the supporter of all," i.e., the earth), *vasudhā*; *patiṃvarā* ("choosing a husband," i.e., a maiden); *rathantaraṃ* ("the Rathantara," i.e., a Sāman chant); *śatruṃjayaḥ* ("conqueror of enemies"), *śatruṃsahaḥ* ("endurer of enemies"), *śatruntapaḥ* ("tormentor of enemies"), *arindamaḥ* ("tamer of foes").

(1.2.31) *dhārer dhar ca*: After a nominal stem (*sup*), the suffix *kha* occurs after the root *dhṛ*, and there is the substitution of *dhar* for it. Example: *vasundharā* ("the bearer of wealth," i.e., the earth).

*gamaḥ* (1.2.32): After a *sup*-ending word, the suffix *kha* is added to the root *gam*. Examples: *sutaṃgamaḥ*, *bhujaṃgamaḥ*, *mitaṃgamā* (a female elephant), *pūrvaṃgamāḥ* (paths leading forward), *hṛdayaṃgamāḥ* (words that reach the heart).
*vihāyaso viha ca* (1.2.33): [The suffix *kha* is added] after the word *vihāyas*, and *viha* is substituted for it.
The suffix *kha* occurs after the word *vihāyas*, and *viha* is its substitute. Thus: *vihaṅgamaḥ*.

[By rule 1.2.34] the suffix *khaṅ* occurs after a nominal ending (*sup*) followed by the root *gam*. Thus: *turaṅgaḥ*, *bhujaṅgaḥ*, *pravaṅgaḥ*, *plavaṅgaḥ*. [In the case of *vihāyas*,] *viha* is substituted for *vihāyas* as well; thus: *vihaṅgaḥ*.

The suffix *ḍa* occurs after the verb *gam* when it follows a *sup*-ending word. Examples: *bhujagaḥ*, *turagaḥ*, *pravagaḥ*, *plavagaḥ*, *patagaḥ*, *antagaḥ*, *atyantagaḥ*, *adhvagaḥ*, *dūragaḥ*, *pāragaḥ*, *sarvagaḥ*, *anantagaḥ*, *sarvatragaḥ*, *pannagaḥ*, *grāmagaḥ*, *gurutalpagaḥ*, *sugaḥ*, *durgaḥ*, *nirgo deśaḥ*. [The substitution of] *viha* for *vihāyas* occurs only in this context: *vihagaḥ*. *Uragaḥ* (1.2.36).

This word is formed as an irregular derivation (*nipātana*). One who moves by means of the chest (*uras*) is an *uraga* (serpent). According to Pāṇini 3.2.49 (*hanaḥ*), the suffix *ḍa* occurs after the root *han* when it follows a noun ending in a case-suffix (*sup*). Thus: one who removes affliction (*kleśa*) is a *kleśāpaha*; one who would kill a whale (*timi*) is a *timihā*; likewise, *tamo'paha* (dispeller of darkness), *duḥkhāpaha* (dispeller of suffering), and *paṭaha* (kettledrum). How is *dārvāghāṭa* (woodpecker) explained? It will be derived from the root *ghaṭ* (to strike). Similarly, there are *cārvāghāṭa* and *varṇasaṃghāṭa*. One who strikes what is beautiful (*cāru*) is a *cārvāghāta*; similarly, *varṇasaṃghāta*. [Objection: In that case, the form *dārvāghāta* would also result. [Response: That is indeed desired when it is not a technical name (*asaṃjñāyām*).

(1.2.38) *śīrṣa-kumārābhyāṃ ṇiniḥ*: After the words *śīrṣa* and *kumāra*, the suffix *ṇini* is applied to the root *han*. Examples: *śīrṣaghātī* ("one who strikes the head"), *kumāraghātī* ("one who kills a child"). (1.2.39) *ṭak*.

The suffix *ṭak* is frequently applied after the root *han* when it follows a word ending in a case-ending (*sup*). Examples: *jāyāghnas tilakālakaḥ* (a mole that destroys a wife), *patighnī pāṇilekhā* (a line on the hand that destroys a husband), *jāyāghno brāhmaṇaḥ* (a Brāhmaṇa who destroys his wife), *patighnī vṛṣalī* (a low-caste woman who destroys her husband), *śleṣmaghnaṃ trikaṭukam* (trikaṭu that destroys phlegm), *pittaghnaṃ ghṛtam* (ghee that destroys bile), *vātaghnaṃ tailam* (oil that destroys wind), *kṛtaghnaḥ khalaḥ* (an ungrateful rogue), *śatrughnaḥ śūraḥ* (a hero who destroys enemies). Because of the governing rule of "frequently" (*bahulādhikārāt*), it occurs even with the dative case, as in *goghno 'tithiḥ* (a guest who destroys [the merit of] cows).
[This applies also to] *hastikapāṭāt* in the sense of capability (Pāṇini 1.2.40).

When capability (*śakti*) is implied, the suffix *ṭak* is applied after the words *hastin* and *kapāṭa* following the root *han*. Examples: *hastighnaḥ* ("an elephant-killer"), *kapāṭaghnaḥ* ("a door-panel-breaker"). Why "when capability is implied"? [Counter-examples: *hastighātaḥ* ("the killing of an elephant"), *kapāṭaghātaḥ* ("the striking of a door-panel"). Why "after *hastin* and *kapāṭa*"? [Counter-example: *cauraghātaḥ* ("a thief-killer"). (1.2.41) *nagarād ahastini*:

After the word *nagara* ("city"), the suffix *ṭak* is applied after the root *han* when the agent is not an elephant. Example: *nagaraghno 'gniḥ* ("a fire that destroys a city"). Why "when not an elephant"? [Counter-example: *nagaraghāto hastī* ("an elephant that destroys a city").

*pāṇigha-tāḍagha* (Pāṇini 1.2.42): these two words are irregularly formed (*nipātita*) when the agent is a craftsman (*śilpin*). One who strikes with the hands (*pāṇibhyām hanti*) or strikes the hand (*pāṇim hanti*) is a *pāṇigha*. One who strikes with a club (*tāḍam hanti*) is a *tāḍagha*. Why "when a craftsman"? [To show that] otherwise it is *pāṇighātaḥ* and *tāḍaghātaḥ*. *rājagha* (Pāṇini 1.2.43).
This word is derived as an irregular formation (*nipātana*). One who kills a king is *rājaghaḥ*.

[The suffix] *ṭak* occurs after a nominal ending (*sup*) following the root *gai* (to sing). Thus: *vaktragaḥ*, *vaktragī*; *sāmagaḥ*, *sāmagī*. It is stated "in various ways" (*bahulam*): hence *sāmasaṃgāyaḥ*.

(1.2.45) *śīdhusurāt pibaḥ*: After the words *śīdhu* and *surā*, the suffix *ṭak* is applied to the root *pā* (meaning "to drink," Dhātupāṭha 1.274), provided that *pā* is related to the substitute *piba*. Examples: *śīdhupaḥ* (a male drinker of *śīdhu*), *śīdhupī* (a female drinker of *śīdhu*); *surāpaḥ* (a male drinker of *surā*), *surāpī* (a female drinker of *surā*). Why say *śīdhusurāt*? [Consider] *kṣīrapā* (one who drinks milk). Why say *pibaḥ*? [Consider] *surāṃ pāti* (he protects the *surā*), *surāpā* (a protector of *surā*). How is it that both *surāpā* and *surāpī* occur when it is a technical name (*saṃjñā*)? In that case, because the action is intended merely for the sake of etymological derivation, both forms will be valid. (1.2.46) *subhagāḍhyasthūlapalitanagnāndhapriyād acver bhuvaḥ khiṣṇuc-khukañau*: After the words *subhaga*, *āḍhya*, *sthūla*, *palita*, *nagna*, *andha*, and *priya*, the suffixes *khiṣṇuc* and *khukañ* are applied after the root *bhū* (meaning "to become"), provided that the word *cvi* does not follow.

After words such as *subhaga* and others ending in *a*, which denote similarity through the suffix * cvi* and function in the sense of *cvi*, the suffixes *khiṣṇuc* and *khukañ* are applied after the root *bhū* in the agentive sense (*kartari*). Examples: *subhagaṃbhaviṣṇuḥ*, *subhagaṃbhāvukaḥ*; *āḍhyaṃbhaviṣṇuḥ*, *āḍhyaṃbhāvukaḥ*; *sthūlaṃbhaviṣṇuḥ*, *sthūlaṃbhāvukaḥ*; *palitaṃbhaviṣṇuḥ*, *palitaṃbhāvukaḥ*; *nagnaṃbhaviṣṇuḥ*, *nagnaṃbhāvukaḥ*; *andhaṃbhaviṣṇuḥ*, *andhaṃbhāvukaḥ*.

*priyaṃbhaviṣṇuḥ*, *priyaṃbhāvukaḥ*. Why does [the rule] say "not ending in *ac*"? [Consider: *āḍhyībhavitā*. Forms such as *svāḍhyaṃbhaviṣṇuḥ* are established by means of the rule for extension (*tadantavidhi*). Regarding *kṛñaḥ karaṇe khyun* (Pāṇini 3.2.47): after the root *kṛ* ("to do/make"), when it occurs in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa*) as a *kāraka*, the suffix *khyun* is applied. This applies when words such as *subhaga* and others—which end in *ac*—are used in the sense of the suffix * cvi* (i.e., expressing a change of state), due to their similarity to forms with *cv*. Examples: *subhagaṃkaraṇam* ("making fortunate"), *āḍhyaṃkaraṇam* ("making wealthy"), *svāḍhyaṃkaraṇam* ("making very wealthy"), *sthūlaṃkaraṇam* ("making stout"), *palitaṃkaraṇam* ("making grey"), *nagnaṃkaraṇam* ("making naked"), *andhaṃkaraṇam* ("making blind"), *priyaṃkaraṇam* ("making dear").

*Spṛśo ’nudakāt kvin* (Pāṇini 3.2.58): The suffix *kvin* occurs after the root *spṛś* when it is not preceded by the word *udaka*. For example, one who touches clarified butter (*ghṛta*) is called *ghṛtaspṛk*; one who touches with a mantra is called *mantraspṛk*. Why "not preceded by *udaka*"? [Consider] *udakasparśaḥ*. The letter *k* is for the purpose of preventing the substitution of *eṅ* (i.e., to prevent the elision of the penultimate vowel). The letter *n* serves as a marker according to *kvinaḥ kuḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.62), and the letter *i* is for the purpose of applying *ver anacaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.67).
*Dadhṛg-uṣṇig-kruñcaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.59).

These words ending in *kvip* are treated as irregular formations (*nipātana*). From the root *dhṛṣ*, there is reduplication and the acute accent on the final syllable: *dadhṛk*. From *snih* preceded by *ut*, there is the elision of *t* and the substitution of *ṣ*: *uṣṇik*. From *kruñc*, there is the non-elision of the nasal: *kruṅ*. The forms *ṛtvij*, *sraj*, and *diś* are established through specific irregularities (*nipātana*): [the former] from *ṛtvigbhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.151), [the middle] from *srajo viniḥ* (4.2.137), and [the last] from *digādibhyaḥ* (3.3.17).
By the rule *añcuyujaḥ* (1.2.50), the suffix *kvip* occurs after the roots *añc* and *yuj*. Thus: *pratyaṅ* and *yuṅ*.
(1.2.51) *samānānyatyadāder upamānād vyāpye dṛśaḥ ksa-kañau ca*:

After the words *samāna* and *anya*, as well as after those beginning with *tyad* when used as standards of comparison (*upamāna*), the suffixes *ksa* and *kañ* are applied [to the root] *dṛś* when it denotes the object (*vyāpya*), and the suffix *kvip* is also applied. One who is seen as similar (*samāna*) is: *sadṛkṣaḥ*, *sadṛśaḥ*, *sadṛk*. One who is seen as different (*anya*) is: *anyādṛkṣaḥ*, *anyādṛśaḥ*, *anyādṛk*. One who is seen like that (*tyad*) is: *tyādṛkṣaḥ*, *tyādṛśaḥ*, *tyādṛk*. One who is seen like that (*tad*) is: *tādṛkṣaḥ*, *tādṛśaḥ*, *tādṛk*. Why say "after *samāna*, *anya*, and those beginning with *tyad*"? [Consider: *vṛkṣa iva dṛśyate* ("it is seen like a tree"). Why say "from a standard of comparison" (*upamānāt*)? [Consider: *sa dṛśyate* ("he is seen").
Why is it stated "pervading" (*vyāpya*)? It is for the purpose of qualifying [the rule] *nakāraḥ kaṅkvarapakhyun* (Pāṇini 2.3.17), which says "he sees as if he were that.

According to *bhajo ṇviḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.62), the suffix *ṇvi* follows after the verbal root *bhaj* when preceded by a noun in the accusative case (*sup*). Thus we have *ardhabhāk* ("sharing half") and *pādabhāk* ("sharing a quarter").

*kvip*, *vic*, *manin*, *kvanip*, *vanip*: these suffixes occur diversely (*bahulam*) after a verb when another action is intended [by the agent].
