*Sudhīvā*. [The suffix] *vanip* [is applied]. *Bhūridāvā*. The vowel *i* [in the rule] serves as an indicator (*cihna*) for the rule *ver anaca* (Pāṇini 5.1.64). According to *duho dughaḥ* (1.2.54), the form *dugha* comes after the verbal root *duh* when followed by a case-ending (*sup*). Thus, *kāmadughā dhenuḥ* ("the cow that milks all desires"). Because of the governing principle of *bahulam* ("diversely"), [one also finds] *kāmadhuk*.

The suffix *ṇini* is applied after a verbal root when the sense of necessity (*avaśyambhāva*) is implied. Thus, from roots meaning "to give" used for the sake of an action, *ṇini* occurs: *avaśyaṃdāyī* ("one who necessarily gives") and *śatadāyī* ("one who gives a hundred").
[Pāṇini 3.2.78] The suffix *ṇini* is applied after a verbal root not denoting a genus (*ajāti*) when expressing habit (*śīla*) or frequency (*abhīkṣṇya*). [Pāṇini 3.2.56]

The suffix *ṇini* occurs after a verbal noun ending in a case-suffix (*sup*) that does not denote a genus (*ajāti*), provided that the action is intended as a purpose and the meanings of "habit" (*śīla*) or "repetition" (*abhīkṣṇya*) are understood. Examples: *uṣṇabhojī* ("one who habitually eats hot food"); *kṣīrapāyina uśīnarāḥ* ("the Uśīnaras are those who habitually drink milk"); *udāsārī* ("one who habitually retreats"); *pratyāsārī* ("one who habitually advances"). Why say "not denoting a genus"? Consider: *brāhmaṇān āmantrayitā* ("one who addresses Brahmins").

From the word *sādhu* (Pāṇini 3.2.57), the suffix *ṇini* occurs after a verbal noun ending in a case-suffix when the action is intended as a purpose. Examples: *sādhukārī* ("one who acts well"); *sādhudāyī* ("one who gives well"). How is *brahmavādī* explained? It is derived from *brahma-vādaḥ* ("discourse on Brahman"); one who possesses such discourse is a *brahmavādī*.

(1.2.58) *kartur upamānāt*: The suffix *ṇini* occurs after a word signifying an agent that functions as a standard of comparison (*upamāna*), provided it is intended to express an action (*kriyārtha*). Example: "He cries out like a camel" (*uṣṭra iva krośati*) → *uṣṭrakrośī*. Why "of the agent"? [Counter-example: "He eats kodrava grains as if they were śāli rice. Why "from a standard of comparison"? [Counter-example: "The camel cries out. (1.2.59) *vrate*: [The suffix *ṇini* occurs] when the sense is that of a religious observance (*vrata*).

The suffix *ṇini* occurs after a nominal stem (*sup*) ending in a word denoting an action, when a religious observance (*vrata*) is implied. For example: *aśrāddhabhojī* ("one who does not eat at a funeral feast"). This restriction applies to the undertaking [of the vow] due to a specific purpose; that is, when food is available, he eats only what is not from a funeral feast (*aśrāddha*), and not what is from a funeral feast (*śrāddha*).
After the root *man* (Pāṇini 3.2.82), the suffix *ṇini* occurs after a nominal stem (*sup*) following the verb *man*. For example: *paṭumānī* ("one who considers himself clever").

*ātmani khaś ca* (Pāṇini 3.2.82): After a word ending in a *sup*-case suffix, the affix *khaś* is applied after the verb *man* when it has the self (*ātman*) as its object; the affix *ṇini* is also applied. One who considers himself learned is called *paṇḍitamanyaḥ* or *paṇḍitamānī*.
*bhūte* (Pāṇini 3.2.84): [The affixes mentioned previously are applied] when the action is completed in the past.
This is the governing heading (*adhikāra*).
[The rule] *yajaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.63) states:

after the verb root *yaj* (to sacrifice), when following a nominal suffix (*sup*), the suffix *ṇini* occurs in the sense of the past (*bhūte*). Example: one who has sacrificed with the Agniṣṭoma is called *agniṣṭomayājī*. The word "past" (*bhūta*) is specified [in the rule] precisely for this reason: [otherwise, one would also say] *agniṣṭomena yajate* (he sacrifices with the Agniṣṭoma).

*Hanaḥ kutsāyām* (Pāṇini 3.2.64): After the root *han*, when a nominal suffix (*sup*) follows and contempt (*kutsā*) is implied, the suffix *ṇini* occurs. Examples: *pitṛvyaghātī* (one who slays his paternal uncle), *mātulaghātī* (one who slays his maternal uncle). Why "when contempt is implied"? [Answer: *cauraṃ hatavān* (he has killed a thief). In the cases *brahmahā*, *bhrūṇahā*, and *vṛtrahā*, the suffix is simply *kvip* as previously mentioned. It is also seen after words other than those preceded by another [word]: *madhuhā*. Furthermore, it is also seen in other forms: *brahmaghnaḥ* (slayer of a Brahmin); this refers to the slayer of Vṛtra. It is also seen from other roots: *brahmavit* (knower of Brahman). This occurs even when the action has already taken place or will take place, because of its established usage there or due to the rule of diversity (*bahulādhikāra*).

Thus, *sukṛt*, *karmakṛt*, *pāpakṛt*, *mantrakṛt*, and *puṇyakṛt* are established by the previous rule alone. However, it is also seen after words other than those previously mentioned: *sūtrakṛt*, *śāstrakṛt*, and *bhāṣyakṛt*. It is also seen after other words: *mantravit*. Furthermore, another form is seen: *karmakāraḥ* and *mantrakāraḥ*. *Somasut* is established by the previous rule alone; however, it is also seen after words other than those previously mentioned: *surāsut*. Another form is also seen: *somaṃ sutavān*.

*agnicit*, *śyenacit*, and *kaṅkacit* are established by the preceding rule [Pāṇini 3.2.91]. *Somavikrayī*, *ghṛtavikrayī*, *tailavikrayī*, and *kṣīravikrayī*: the suffix *in* will apply after the word *vikraya*. *Devadṛśvā*, *rājayudhvā*, *rājakṛtvā*, *sahayudhvā*, and *sahakṛtvā* are established by the preceding suffix *kvanip* [Pāṇini 3.2.91]. The exclusion of the suffix *aniṣṭhan*, however, is due to the governing principle of "diversity" (*bahulādhikāra*). [The suffix] *ḍaḥ* [is applied according to Pāṇini 4.1.85].

The suffix *ḍa* is frequently applied after a word ending in a *su*-suffix (*sup*), provided that the word denotes an action and refers to the past. Born in the cow-pen: *upasarajaḥ*. Dharma born from Brahmins: *brahmaṇajaḥ*. War born from Kṣatriyas: *kṣatriyajaṃ yuddham*. Born of the Buddha: *buddhijaḥ*. Born of refinement: *saṃskārajaḥ*. Not born: *ajaḥ*. Twice-born: *dvijaḥ*. Progeny: *prajā*. Born from above: *abhijāḥ*; born around: *parijāḥ*. Born after a man: *pumanujā*. Younger brother: *anujaḥ*. Bent down: *prahvaḥ*. One who has violated the Veda: *brahmajyaḥ*. A moat: *parikhā*. One who has taken the best: *varāhaḥ*. [This applies to] the *ktavat* suffix [as well]. (Pāṇini 3.2.102)
The suffix *ktavatu* occurs after a verbal root denoting an action when it refers to a past time and expresses the agent: *gatavān* ("he has gone"), *śayitavān* ("he has lain").

The suffix *kta* occurs after a verbal root denoting an action when it refers to a past time, expressing either the abstract state (*bhāva*) or the object (*karman*) of that action (Pāṇini 3.4.70): *āsitaṃ bhavatā* ("you have sat"), *kṛtaḥ kaṭo bhavatā* ("a mat has been made by you").
(1.2.68) *kartari cārambhe*:

When there is an action at its inception, the suffix *kta* occurs with the agent (*kartṛ*), as well as in accordance with what has already been prescribed. For example: *prakṛto bhavān kaṭam* (you have begun the mat); *prakṛtaḥ kaṭo bhavatā* (the mat was begun by you). *prasupto bhavān*; *prasuptaṃ bhavatā* (you have fallen asleep; sleep was entered upon by you). (1.2.69) *śliṣa-śīṅ-sthā-āsa-vasa-jana-ruha-jṝbhyaḥ*. [The suffix *kta* occurs after these roots when used with the agent.]

The suffix *kta* occurs after the roots *śliṣ* and others in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*), as well as in its default application. You have embraced the teacher; the teacher has been embraced by you. You have lain upon the bed; the bed has been lain upon by you. You have attended upon the teacher; the teacher has been attended upon by you. You have worshipped the teacher; the teacher has been worshipped by you. You have dwelt with the teacher; the teacher has been dwelt with by you. The boy has followed after the girl; the girl has been followed after by the boy.

"You have climbed the tree"; "the tree has been climbed by you. "Devadatta has grown old following the low-caste woman"; "the low-caste woman has been aged out by Devadatta. [Pāṇini 1.4.52: "The locus of actions whose meaning is 'motion' or 'eating' is also called *karman*. (1.2.70)

The suffix *kta* occurs after a root meaning "motion" (*gatyartha*) that is not transitive (*avyāpya*), when used in the sense of an action (*kriyārtha*), to denote the locus (*ādhāra*); it also occurs in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*) as prescribed by the general rules. Examples: *idam eṣāṃ yātam* ("this is the distance they have traveled"), *iha te yātāḥ* ("here they have gone"), *iha tair yātam* ("here they have traveled [by them]"), *ayaṃ tair yātaḥ panthāḥ* ("this is the path traveled by them"). *idam eṣām āsitam* ("this is where they have sat"), *iha ta āsitāḥ* ("here they have sat"), *iha tair āsitam* ("here they have sat [by them]"). In the case of the statement, "If it has rained, the rice has ripened," the intended meaning here is the successful completion of the collection of causal factors (*kāraṇasāmagrī*). [The rule continues: "After a root meaning 'eating' (*āhāra*)," (Pāṇini 3.4.71).

The suffix *kta* occurs after a root meaning "eating" when it denotes the locus (*ādhāra*), as well as in its regular sense. For example: *idam eṣāṃ bhuktam* ("this has been eaten by them"); *idam eṣāṃ pītam* ("this has been drunk by them"). *iha tair bhuktam* ("here it was eaten by them"); *iha taiḥ pītam* ("here it was drunk by them"). *odanas tair bhuktaḥ* ("rice was eaten by them"); *pītam udakam* ("water was drunk [by them]"). The separation of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) is for the sake of excluding the agent (*kartṛ*). How is it that [the word] *pītā gāvaḥ* ("cows that have drunk") is formed? It is formed because "drinking exists in them," thus they are called *pītāḥ*; or alternatively, it is due to the rule of diversity (*bāhulaka*). The forms *sutvā*, *sutvānau*, and *sutvānaḥ* are established by means of the suffix *kvanip*. The forms *yajvā*, *yajvānau*, and *yajvānaḥ* are established by means of the suffix *vanip*. According to Pāṇini 3.2.104, *jṝṣo 'tṛn*: the suffix *atṛn* occurs after the root *jṝ* ("to grow old"). Thus: *jaran*, *jaratī*.

*śruśṛṇudṛśām liṭ vā* (1.2.73): After the roots *śru*, *śṛṇu*, and *dṛś*, the *liṭ* [perfect] tense optionally occurs in the sense of the past. Examples: *upaśuśrāva*, *upāśrauṣīt*, *upāśṛṇot*; *upasasāda*, *upāsadat*, *upāsīdat*; *anūvāsa*, *anvavātsīt*, *anvavasat*. *liṭaḥ kvasuḥ* (1.2.74): The suffix *kvasu* is substituted for the *liṭ* [perfect].
The suffix *kvasu* optionally occurs as a substitute for the *liṭ* (perfect) tense marker. Examples: *upaśuśruvān*, *upaśuśrāva*; *jagmivān*, *jagāma*.

Regarding *īyivān*, *anāśvān*, and *anūcānaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.2.75): these words ending in *liṭ* are optionally prescribed as irregular forms (*nipātana*). Examples: *īyivān*, *iyāya*; *upeyivān*, *upeyāya*; *samīyivān*, *samiyāya*. *anāśvān*, *nāśa*; *anūcānaḥ*, *anūvāca*.

*Lṛṅ* (Pāṇini 3.2.111): *Lṛṅ* occurs after a verb signifying an action that took place in the past (*bhūte*), provided it is used for the purpose of expressing another action. Example: *akārṣīt* ("he did"). How is it that one says, "I stayed there during the remainder of the night"? Having remained awake the entire night, because the night had not yet dawned, he regards the time as if it were the current day (*adyatana*). However, one who has slept even for a moment, knowing it to be indeed non-current-day time (*anadyatana*), does not say, "I stayed there. And in all cases where there is a desire to express the general past tense (*bhūtakālasāmānya*), *lṛṅ* certainly occurs, as in: "We went to the cowherd villages," "We drank milk," and "We lay down upon withered grass."

*anadyatane laṅ* (1.2.77): The suffix *laṅ* occurs after a verbal root denoting an action intended for another action, when the sense refers to the past but not the immediate day (*anadyatana*). Example: *apacat* ("he cooked [yesterday]"). Why "not the immediate day"? Example: *apākṣīt* ("he cooked [today]"). Why "for another purpose"? Example: *adya hyo vābhukṣmahi* ("we ate today or yesterday"). *smṛtyuktau lṛṭ* (1.2.78): [The suffix] *lṛṭ* occurs when there is a statement regarding memory.

When there is a statement of recollection (*smṛti-vacana*), the *lṛṭ* (future tense suffix) occurs in the sense of a past action not belonging to the current day. For example: "Do you remember, Devadatta, that we lived in Kaśmīra? or "Do you recall, Devadatta, that we lived in Kaliṅga?

However, by the rule *na yadi* (Pāṇini 3.2.113), when the word *yad* is employed in a statement of recollection, the *lṛṭ* does not occur after a verb denoting an action in the sense of a past action not belonging to the current day. For example: "Do you remember, Devadatta, that we lived in Kaśmīra? (where *yad* is used).
In the case of *vākāṅkṣāyām* (Pāṇini 3.3.135),

when there is an expectancy for another action (*kriyāntarākāṅkṣā*) while a statement from the Smṛti is being employed, the suffix *lṛṭ* optionally occurs after a verb signifying an action that refers to the past non-todays' time (*bhūtānadyatana*), provided it is used with the particle *yadi* or *cāyadi*.

"Do you remember, Devadatta, that we were in Kaśmīra, that we would eat rice there? "Do you remember, Devadatta, that we lived in Kaśmīra, that we ate rice there? "Do you remember, Devadatta, that we will live in Kaśmīra, that we will eat rice there? "Do you remember, Devadatta, that we lived in Kaśmīra, that we ate rice there? Why does [the suffix *laṭ*] not occur here: "Do you remember, Devadatta, thus indeed we lived in Kaśmīra"? Or: "We lived constantly in Kaśmīra"? [The answer is: because of the optionality established by rule (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*) or because of the inclusion of the term "frequently" (*bahula*) in the governing rule.

*parokṣe liṭ* (1.2.81): The *liṭ* [perfect] affix occurs after a verbal root denoting an action that refers to a past time not belonging to the current day (*bhūtānadyatana*), when the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) is out of sight (*parokṣa*). Examples: *jagāma* ("he went"); *supto 'haṃ kila vilalāpa* ("I, while asleep, indeed lamented"); *matto 'haṃ kila vilalāpa* ("I, while intoxicated, indeed lamented"). In cases of absolute concealment (*atyantāpahnavā*), even that which was directly perceived may be concealed; thus: *kaḥ kaliṅgaṃ jagāma?* ("Who went to Kaliṅga?"), *kaḥ kāmarūpaṃ viveśa?* ("Who entered Kāmarūpa?"). Furthermore, although the action is out of sight, if it is known by the world and within the range of the speaker's own perception—such that the "out-of-sight" status is not intended to be emphasized—the *laṅ* [imperfect] affix is used instead.

"Jarta conquered the Hūṇas"—here, even though [the action] exists, there is no desire to express it, as in the case of "the girl has no belly" (*anudarā kanyā*). Likewise: *iti hākarot*, *iti ha cakāra*; *śaśvad akarot*, *śaśvac cakāra*. [Examples of the interrogative: "Did he go to Pāṭaliputra? (*kim agacchat pāṭaliputram*); "Did he go? (*kiṃ jagāma*). How is it regarding the past other than the immediate present, whether it be remote or non-remote? [Examples: *karoti sma*; "In the past, students lived here" (*vasantīha purā chāttrāḥ*). Because the time is indicated by the words *sma* and *purā*, [the action], though occurring at that [past] time, is treated as being in the present.

"Rāghava says that it was so. In the case of "Students lived here in the past," the *liṭ* (perfect tense) indeed occurs when there is remoteness (*parokṣa*). When the state of remoteness is not intended to be expressed, one uses the *laṅ* (imperfect): "Students lived here in the past. Even when the non-recent past (*anadyatana*) is not intended to be expressed, one uses the *luṅ* (aorist): "Students lived here in the past. In response to a question, as in "Indeed, I am doing it," the present tense is used because the fruit of the action persists. Likewise: "I am indeed doing it. Even when the negation "I am not doing it" is used, the present tense is employed. This is according to the rule: *vartamāne laṭ* (Pāṇini 3.2.123).
When the sense is present, *laṭ* occurs after a verb denoting an action [in the present]. For example: *pacati*, *paṭhati*.
Regarding *videḥ śvasuḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.83): after the root *vid*, the suffix *śvas* frequently replaces *laṭ*. For example: *vidvān*, *vetti*, *vidan*.

*Śatṛ* (Pāṇini 3.2.124): The substitute *śatṛ* frequently occurs in place of the present tense marker (*laṭ*). Examples: *san brāhmaṇaḥ* ("the Brāhmaṇa exists"), *asti brāhmaṇaḥ*; *juhvat* ("sacrificing"), *juhoti*; "O you who are cooking" (*he pacan*); "see the one cooking" (*pacantaṃ paśya*); "done by the one cooking" (*pacatā kṛtam*); "those who chatter are known as scholars" (*jalpanto jñāyante paṇḍitāḥ*); "he sits while reading" (*paṭhan nāste*); "do not cook" (*mā pacan*); "holding the Upaniṣad" (*dhārayann upaniṣadam*); "hating the thief" (*caurasya dviṣan*); "hating the thief" (*cauraṃ dviṣan*); "pressing [Soma]" (*sunvantaḥ*); "one who is worthy" (*arhan*). *(Pāṇini 3.2.125): The suffix *śatṛ* is applied after the root *iṅ* when expressing capability.*

When capacity (*śakti*) is implied, the *laṭ* [present tense] undergoes the substitution of *śatṛ*. Example: *adhīyan pārāyaṇam* ("he is capable of studying the *pārāyaṇa*"). Why "when capacity"? Example: *adhīte pārāyaṇam, na ca śaknoti* ("he studies the *pārāyaṇa*, but is not able [to complete it]"). Regarding *śānac*: the *laṭ* undergoes the substitution of *śānac* diversely (*bahulam*). Examples: *pacamānaḥ* ("cooking"), *pacate* ("he cooks"); *he pacamāna* ("O you who are cooking"); *pacamānaṃ paśya* ("see him cooking"); *pacamānena kṛtam* ("done by one who is cooking"); *śayānā bhuñjate Yavanāḥ* ("the Yavanas eat while lying down"); *adhīyāna āste* ("he sits while studying"). Do not use the form *pacamānaḥ* [in this sense]. We shall state that for the roots *pū* and *yaj*, there is acute accent on the first syllable (*ādyudāttatva*) when *śānac* follows.

(1.2.87) *śaktivayaḥśīleṣu*: When capacity (*śakti*), age (*vayas*), or character (*śīla*) are implied, the suffix *śānac* is substituted for the present tense marker *laṭ*. Because it is restated here, it applies even after roots that do not take the *ātmanepada* endings. For example: "How many here are killing Kaṇva? (*katīha kaṇvaṃ nighnānāḥ?*); "How many here are prattling? (*katīha jalpamānāḥ?*); "How many here are putting on armor? (*katīha kavacaṃ paryasyamānāḥ?*); "How many here are dancing? (*katīha nṛtyamānāḥ?*). (1.2.88) *tau lṛṭaḥ*: Those two [suffixes] are substituted for the future tense marker *lṛṭ*.
The suffixes *śatṛ* and *śānac* occur diversely (*bahulam*) even after the *lṛṭ* [future] tense. Examples: *kariṣyan*, *kariṣyamāṇaḥ*; *kariṣyati*, *kariṣyate*. Regarding the rule *tṛn* 1.2.89:

after a verbal root meaning "for the sake of an action," the suffix *tṛn* occurs diversely in the sense of habit (*śīla*), being good at something (*sādhu*), or duty (*dharma*). Examples: *upādātā kumārakān* ("one who is habitually fond of taking children"); *gantā khelaḥ* ("one who is good at playing"); *muṇḍayitāraḥ śrāviṣṭhāyanā bhavanti vadhūm ūḍhām* ("the Śrāviṣṭhāyanas are those who have the habit of shaving the heads of their married daughters"). The governing heading (*adhikāra*) "in the sense of habit, etc. extends until the end of the chapter. How is it that [words like] *hotā*, *potā*, *neṣṭā*, *tvaṣṭā*, and *kṣattā* are formed? They are simply derived from the *uṇādi* suffixes.

Pāṇini 3.2.138: *nirālaṃbhyāṃ kṛṣṇuc* (1.2.90). After the roots *kṛ* preceded by *nir* and *alam*, the suffix *iṣṇuc* occurs when a habitual disposition (*śīla*) or similar quality is implied. Examples: *nirākariṣṇuḥ* (one who habitually rejects), *alaṃkariṣṇuḥ* (one who habitually adorns). Pāṇini 3.2.139: *udaḥ pacapatamadaḥ* (1.2.91). [The suffix *iṣṇuc* occurs after the root *mad* preceded by *ud* when used with the words *pac*, *pata*, or *mada*. (Note: This sūtra is cited here as part of the same grammatical context.)

The suffix *iṣṇuc* occurs after the roots *pac* and others that follow it when they are preceded by the prefix *ud*, provided that a sense such as habitual action (*śīla*) or the like is understood. Examples: *utpaciṣṇuḥ* (one who habitually cooks thoroughly), *utpatiṣṇuḥ* (one who habitually flies up), *unmadiṣṇuḥ* (one who habitually becomes insane).

By rule 1.2.92, the suffix *iṣṇuc* occurs after the following roots when a sense such as habitual action or the like is intended: *pra-jan*, *ruc*, *apa-trap*, *vṛt*, *vṛdh*, *sah*, *car*, and *bhrāj*. Examples: *prajaniṣṇuḥ* (one who habitually procreates), *rociṣṇuḥ* (one who habitually shines), *apatrapiṣṇuḥ* (one who habitually feels shame), *vartiṣṇuḥ* (one who habitually turns), *vardhiṣṇuḥ* (one who habitually grows), *sahiṣṇuḥ* (one who habitually endures), *cariṣṇuḥ* (one who habitually wanders), *bhrājiṣṇuḥ* (one who habitually blazes).
*bhuvaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.2.93): The suffix *iṣṇuc* is applied after the root *bhū*. [Example: *bhaviṣṇuḥ* ("one who is about to be").
*jiglaś ca ksnuḥ* (Pāṇini 1.2.94).

The suffix *ksnu* is applied after the roots *ji* (to conquer), *glai* (to become weary), and *bhū* (to become) when expressing habitual action (*śīla*) and so forth. Examples: *jiṣṇuḥ* (conqueror), *glāsnuḥ* (one who becomes weary), *bhūṣṇuḥ* (one who becomes).
Regarding *sthāsnuḥ*:
the absence of *it*-lengthening (*itvābhāvaḥ*) is prescribed as a formal anomaly (*nipātana*) for the form *sthāsnuḥ*.

(1.2.96) *trasigṛdhidhṛṣikṣipeḥ knuḥ*: after the roots *tras*, *gṛdh*, *dhṛṣ*, and *kṣip*, the suffix *knū* occurs in the sense of habitual disposition (*śīla*) and so forth. Thus: *trasnuḥ*, *gṛdhnuḥ*, *dhṛṣṇuḥ*, *kṣipnuḥ*. It need not be stated that the suffix *ghinuṇ* follows *śam* and others: one who possesses tranquility (*śama*) is called *śamī*. Likewise: *damī*, *tamī*, *śramī*, *bhramī*, *kṣamī*, *klamī*, *unmādī*.

Likewise: one who associates, one who complies, one who stretches, one who exerts, one who wanders about, one who clings, one who laments, one who is feverish, one who causes fever, one who casts around, one who wails, one who reviles, one who burns with grief, one who is deluded, one who finds fault, one who hates, one who seeks to harm, one who milks [the earth], one who is joined, one who sports, one who discriminates, one who renounces, one who is passionate, one who shares, one who transgresses, one who behaves improperly, one who steals, one who attacks, one who expands, one who dallys, one who boasts, one who trusts, one who longs for, one who desires, one who prattles, one who spreads out, one who runs away, one who crushes, one who disputes.

The suffix *ini* is seen after [roots] other than those already mentioned: *virodhin*, *prayāmin*, *prayāsin*, *visārin*, *visargin*, *saṃvādin*, *vivādin*, *anuvādin*, *vidāyin*, *vidāhin*, *saṃcārin*, *vyabhicārin*, *vighātin*, *vidrāvin*, *saṃvāsin*. It is also seen after others: *rogin*, *bhogin*, and so forth. The suffix *tṛn* will also apply after roots such as *śam* according to usage, by virtue of the rule of diversity (*bahulādhikāra*): *pravaditṛ*, *pravasitṛ*. Furthermore, it need not be stated that the suffix *vuñ* follows *nindā* and others.

The form *nindaka* is established by the suffix *ṇvul*; likewise are *hiṃsakaḥ*, *kleśakaḥ*, *khādakaḥ*, *vināśakaḥ*, *parikṣepakaḥ*, *parirāṭakaḥ*, *parivādakaḥ*, *vyābhāṣakaḥ*, *asūyakaḥ*, *paridevakaḥ*, and *ākrośakaḥ*. It is also seen after other roots: *ghātakaḥ*, *mārakaḥ*. Regarding the rule "after roots meaning 'to move' (*cāla*) and 'to sound' (*śabda*), provided they are not marked with the indicatory letter *ā*, the suffix *yuc* is applied" (Pāṇini 3.2.148): after roots meaning "to move" and "to sound," when they lack an object and denote habitual action (*śīla*) and so forth, the suffix *yuc* occurs. Examples: *calanaḥ*, *copanaḥ*; *ravaṇaḥ*, *śabdanaḥ*. Why say "provided they are not marked with the indicatory letter *ā*" (*anāpyāt*)? [Consider: *paṭhitā vidyām* ("he has studied the science").

(1.2.98) *taṅvato halāder aṅaḥ*: The suffix *yuc* occurs after that verbal base (*aṅga*) which ends in a consonant (*hal*), begins with a consonant (*hal-ādi*), and is marked with the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) designation, provided the meaning refers to habit (*śīla*) and so forth. Examples: *vartanaḥ*, *vardhanaḥ*, *devanaḥ*. The form *paridevakaḥ* does not occur because of the rule of "diversity" (*bahulādhikāra*). Why say "ending in a consonant" (*taṅvataḥ*)? [Otherwise,] *bhavitā*. Why say "beginning with a consonant" (*halādeḥ*)? [Otherwise,] *edhitā*. Why include the word "beginning" (*ādi*)? So that it may also apply here: *jugupsanaḥ*, *titikṣaṇaḥ*. Why say "verbal base" (*aṅaḥ*)? [Otherwise,] *śayitā*. The restriction "not after roots ending in *ā*" (*anāpyāt*) applies as well: *vasitā vastram*. (1.2.99) *ju-caṅkramya-dandramya-sṛ-gṛdhi-jvala-śuca-laṣa-pata-padaḥ*.

From these [roots], the suffix *yu* is applied to form words meaning "one who is habitually engaged in" (*śīlādi*) such actions: *javanaḥ*, *caṅkramaṇaḥ*, *dandramaṇaḥ*, *saraṇaḥ*, *gardhanaḥ*, *jvalanaḥ*, *śocanaḥ*, *abhilaṣaṇaḥ*, *prapatanaḥ*, and *prapadanaḥ*. According to some, the inclusion of roots meaning "to move" (*calanārtha*) and the mention of the root *pad* is for the sake of including those that have a pervasive sense (*vyāpyavat*). Others say that the mention of *pad* is for the purpose of re-enjoining the suffix *yuc* after it has been barred by *ukañ*. However, that is unnecessary because of the rule of "diversity" (*bahulādhikāra*). Still others maintain that it is intended to indicate that among suffixes expressing habitual action (*tācchīlika*), there is no mutual exclusion between a general rule (*utsarga*) and its exception (*apavāda*).

Nevertheless, [the rule] is useless, because we observe co-occurrence (*samāveśa*) as well. For instance, co-occurrence is observed in such cases as *gāmuka* and *gantṛ*; likewise, *vikatthī* and *vikatthana*, *bhāsuraṃ* and *bhāsvaraṃ* and *bhāsanaṃ*, *jāgaritā* and *jāgarūka*, *vardhiṣṇuḥ* and *vardhanaḥ*, and *apalāṣukaḥ* and *apalaṣaṇaḥ*. Therefore, it is established here precisely by virtue of the governing rule of "diversity" (*bahulam*). Regarding *krudhabhūṣārthāt* (Pāṇini 3.2.151): after verbal roots meaning anger and those meaning adornment, the suffix *yuc* occurs in the sense of habit (*śīla*) and so forth. Examples: *krodhanaḥ*, *kopanaḥ*; *bhūṣaṇaḥ*, *maṇḍanaḥ*.

*na yadīkṣaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.2.101): After a root ending in *yakāra*, and after *dīkṣ*, the suffix *yuc* does not occur. [Examples: *knūyitā*, *dīkṣitā*. It should be stated that there is a prohibition for *sūd* and *dīp*: [the forms] *sūditā* and *dīpitā*? It need not be stated. For here [in usage], we see *arisūdana*. As for *dīp* as well, the suffix *ra* will be its sublater. How then is *dīpitā* formed? There will be a co-occurrence (*samāveśa*) of *tṛn* with *ra*; *yuc* will not occur because of the rule of "diversity" (*bahulādhikāra*). *laṣapatapadasthābhūśṝvṛṣahanakamagama ukañ* (Pāṇini 1.2.102).

The suffix *ukañ* occurs after the roots *laṣ* and others when the meanings "habitual practice" (*śīla*) and so forth are intended. Examples: *apalāṣukaḥ*, *prapātukaḥ*, *upapādukaḥ*, *upasthāyukaḥ*, *prabhāvukaḥ*, *praśārukaḥ*, *pravarṣukaḥ*, *āghātukaḥ*, *kāmukaḥ*, *āgāmukaḥ*.
[Furthermore,] the suffix *ṣākan* occurs after the roots *jalp*, *bhikṣ*, *kuṭṭ*, *luṇṭ*, and *vṛṅ*. (Pāṇini 3.2.156)

The suffix *ṣākan* occurs after verbs such as *jalp* in the sense of [habitual] action regarding qualities such as moral conduct (*śīla*). Examples: *jalpākaḥ*, *bhikṣākaḥ*, *kuṭṭākaḥ*, *luṇṭākaḥ*, *varākaḥ*. The letter *ṣ* is for the purpose of introducing the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ*: *jalpākī*. How is *prajavī* formed? It is *prajavī* because "he possesses speed" (*prajava*)—thus it is derived by adding *in*. Similarly: *vijayī*, *darī*, *kṣayī*, *viśrayī*, *atyayī*, *vamī*, *avyathī*, *abhyamī*, *paribhavī*, *prasavī*. [The suffix] *āluc* occurs after the roots *spṛh*, *gṛh*, *pat*, and *śīṅ* (Pāṇini 3.2.158).

The suffix *āluc* occurs after these [roots] when they denote habitual disposition (*śīla*) and so forth: *spṛhayāluḥ*, *gṛhayāluḥ*, *patayāluḥ*, *śayāluḥ*. How is it that there are forms such as *dayāluḥ*, *nidrāluḥ*, *tandrāluḥ*, and *śraddhāluḥ*? We shall explain that these possess suffixes expressing the sense of "having the quality of" (*matvarthīya*). By the rule *dheṭ-śī-śada-sado ruḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.157), the suffix *ru* occurs after the roots *dhā* and others when they denote habitual disposition and so forth: *dhāruḥ*, *seruḥ*, *śadruḥ*, *sadruḥ*. How is it that there is the form *dāru*? It is due to a specific grammatical exception (*nipātana*) in the rule *aṅguleḥ saṅkhyā-de-r dāruṇi* (Pāṇini 5.4.86).
*sṛghasadaḥ kmarac* (Pāṇini 3.2.160): the suffix *kmarac* occurs after these [roots]: *sṛ*, *ghas*, and *ad*. [Examples: *sṛmaraḥ*, *ghasmaraḥ*, *admaraḥ*.
*bhañjibhāsimido ghurac* (Pāṇini 3.2.161): the suffix *ghurac* occurs after the roots *bhañj*, *bhās*, and *mid*.

The suffix *ghurac* occurs after roots such as *bhañj*. That which breaks by itself, or causes itself to break, is *bhaṅguraṃ kāṣṭham* ("brittle wood"). However, in the case of one who breaks another, the suffix does not occur, due to the rule of "frequently" (*bahula*) being in force. From *bhās* comes *bhāsuraḥ* ("shining"); from *med* comes *meduraḥ* ("fat"). After the roots *vid*, *bhid*, and *chid*, the suffix *kurac* occurs [Pāṇini 3.2.162].

The suffix *kurac* occurs after the roots *vid* and others. One who knows is a *viduraḥ*. That which splits by itself or splits itself is *bhiduraḥ*. That which is split by itself or cuts itself is *chiduraḥ*. However, when it is another that splits or cuts [it], the suffix does not occur there, because of the rule of "diversity" (*bahulādhikāra*). Even in that case, some maintain: "the destroyer of the darkness of faults" (*doṣāndhakārabhiduraḥ*) and "the cutter of the proud enemy's faction" (*dṛptāripakṣacchiduraḥ*).
By the rule *iṇ-jisṛ-naśaḥ kvarap* (Pāṇini 3.2.164), the suffix *kvarap* occurs after the roots *iṇ* and others. Thus: *itvaraḥ*, *jitvaraḥ*, *sṛtvaraḥ*, *vinaśvaraḥ*.
the form *gatvara* is established as an irregular derivation (*nipātana*).
(1.2.111) *jāgur-ūka*: [the suffix] *ūka* is applied after the root *jāgṛ*.
The suffix *ūka* follows the root *jāgarti*. Thus: *jāgarūkaḥ*.

According to Pāṇini 3.2.168 (*yajajapadahadaśo yaṅaḥ*), the suffix *ūka* follows roots such as *yaj* and others when they are in the intensive (*yaṅ*) form. Thus: *yāyajūkaḥ*, *jañjapūkaḥ*, *dandahūkaḥ*, *dandaśūkaḥ*.

*sahicalivahaḥ kikinau* (1.2.113): After the roots *sah*, *cal*, and *vah*, when they are in the intensive (*yaṅ*) form, the suffixes *kikin* and *kin* occur. Examples: *sāsahiḥ*, *cācaliḥ*, *vāvahiḥ*. *pāpatiḥ* (1.2.114): [The suffix *kikin* occurs] after the root *pat* in the intensive form. Example: *pāpatiḥ*.
In the word *pāpati*, the absence of the *nīk* augment is prescribed as a *nipātana*.

In the rule *cakrisasrijajñayaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.115), *cakra* and the others are prescribed as *nipātanas*. How is the form *dadhi* established? It is established by the *nipātana* rule *asthidadhi-* (Pāṇini 6.1.63). The word *nemi* is derived from the *uṇādi* suffixes.

*smi-aja-hiṃsa-dīpa-na-ma-kam-pa-raḥ* (1.2.116): After the roots *smi* and the others, the suffix *ra* occurs. Thus: *smeraḥ*, *ajasram*, *hiṃsraḥ*, *dīpraḥ*, *namraḥ*, *kamraḥ*, *kampraḥ*. The suffix *yuc* also indeed occurs: *kamanaḥ*, *kampana*. *san-āśaṃsa-uḥ* (1.2.117).

After [verbal roots] ending in the suffix *san*, the suffix *u* follows the word *āśaṃsa*. Thus: *cikīrṣuḥ* (desiring to do), *āśaṃsuḥ* (expecting). [The word] *bhikṣuḥ* is derived by Pāṇini 3.3.77 (*bhikṣunaṭasūtram*).
The two words *vinduḥ* and *icchuḥ* are established as irregular forms (*nipātana*) by Pāṇini 1.2.118.
In *svapna* and *tṛṣṇa* (1.2.119), the suffix *nañiṅ* is applied irregularly (*nipātyate*) to the roots *svap* and *tṛṣ*.
In *śrī* and *vandī*, the suffix *āru* is applied (1.2.120).
The suffix *āru* follows the roots *śṛṇāti* and *vandati*. [Examples: *śarāruḥ* (one who destroys), *vandāruḥ* (one who praises).
*bhiyaḥ kruḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.174):
The suffix *kru* follows the root *bhī*. [Example: *bhīruḥ* (fearful). With the suffix *kan*, it becomes *bhīrukaḥ*; with the substitution of *la* for *ra*, it becomes *bhīlukaḥ*.

*stha-ābhāsi-peski-kasibhyaś ca* (1.2.122): The suffix *varac* is applied after the roots *sthā*, *bhās*, *pes*, and *kas*. Thus: *sthāvaraḥ*; by *īśvarārthāt* (2.2.69), *īśvaraḥ*; *bhāsvaraḥ*, *pesvaraḥ*, *kasvaraḥ*.

The suffix *varac* occurs after the root *yā* when it is in the intensive (*yaṅ*) form. Thus, *yāyāvaraḥ*. How is the derivation of *bhrāṭ*, *bhāḥ*, *dhūḥ*, *vidyut*, *ūrk*, *pūḥ*, *grāvastut*, *svayaṃbhūḥ*, and *pratibhūḥ* explained? They are established by the addition of the suffix *kvip* according to the preceding rule [Pāṇini 3.2.178]. *Vāk*, *prāṭ*, *śrīḥ*, *śatadruḥ*, *kaṭaprūḥ*, *srūḥ*, and *jūḥ* are derived from the *uṇādi* suffixes. Similarly, *āyatastūḥ*, *juhūḥ*, *didyut*, *jagat*, and *dadṛt* are formed. As for *dhīḥ*, it is established by the specific grammatical exception (*nipātana*) in Pāṇini 5.3.89: *asudhiyaḥ*.

*vibhuḥ*, *prabhuḥ*, *saṃbhuḥ*, *śambhuḥ*, and *mitadruḥ* are derived from the *uṇādi* suffixes. *Dhātrī*, *dātram*, *netram*, *śastram*, *yotram*, *yoktram*, *stotram*, *tottram*, *setram*, *sektram*, *meḍḍhram*, *pattram*, *daṃṣṭrā*, and *naddhrī*—these are derived from the *uṇādi* suffixes *ṣṭran* and *an* in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇe*). Likewise: *halasya potram* (the plowshare of the plow), *sūkarasya potram* (the snout of the boar), *aritram*, *lavitram*, *dhavitram*, *savitram*, *khanitram*, *sahitram*, *caritram*, and *pavitram*.

In the case of *pavitram* [in the phrase] "the purifier in the sacrifice," *Pavitrā* as the name of a river, *Pavitra* as the name of a seer (*ṛṣi*), and *pavitra* as fire, the suffix *-kta* denotes the state of having become so (*bhūtakālatā*) in the sense of "having been purified. Similarly: *rājñāṃ mataḥ* (approved by kings), *rājñām iṣṭaḥ* (desired by kings), *rājñāṃ buddhaḥ* (understood by kings), *rājñāṃ pūjitaḥ* (honored by kings). Likewise: *śīlitaḥ*, *rakṣitaḥ*, *kṣāntaḥ*, *ākruṣṭaḥ*, *juṣṭaḥ*, *ruṣṭaḥ*, *ruṣitaḥ*, *abhivyāhṛtaḥ*, *dayitaḥ*, *hṛṣṭaḥ*, *kāntaḥ*, *saṃyataḥ*, *udyataḥ*, *amṛtaḥ*.
In the expression *kaṣṭam*, the suffix *-kta* denotes the state of having come to be (*bhūtatā*) itself, even when used in the sense of a cause; however, in this context, the result is yet to be.

The second quarter of the first [chapter] is completed. *Uṇādayaḥ* (1.3.1): After a verb used in the sense of purpose (*kriyārtha*), the *uṇādi* suffixes are applied diversely (*bahulam*). Some occur in the present tense: *kāruḥ* (artisan), *vāyuḥ* (wind). Some occur in the past: that which has been traversed is a *vartma* (path); that which has been smeared is *bhasma* (ashes). Some occur in the future: one who will go to the village is a *grāmagamī*; one who will come to the village is a *grāmāgāmī*. Also in the sense of the future periphrastic (*bhaviṣyat*) [suffix]: one who is about to happen is *bhāvī*. Even in the scope of the aorist (*luṅ*): "Tomorrow he will go to the village" (*śvo grāmagamī*). Some occur in the sense of the ablative (*apādāna*): *bhīmaḥ* (terrible), *bhīṣmaḥ* (formidable). Some occur in the sense of the dative (*saṃpradāna*): *dāśaḥ* (one who gives).
*bhaviṣyati lṛṭ* (Pāṇini 3.3.15): The suffix *lṛṭ* follows a verbal root denoting an action intended for another action, when it expresses a future sense. Example: *kariṣyati*.
*anadyatane luṭ* (Pāṇini 3.3.15): [The suffix *luṭ* follows a verbal root] when expressing a future sense that is not of today.

The suffix *luṭ* occurs after a verb expressing an action intended for another action, provided it denotes a future sense when the present time is not applicable. Example: *śvaḥ kartā* ("He will do tomorrow"). Why [is the condition] "another word-meaning" (*anyapadārtha*) stated? [To exclude cases like: *adya śvo vā gamiṣyati* ("He will go today or tomorrow"). How is it that in the expression *yāvad bhuṅkte tato vrajati* ("As soon as he eats, then he goes"), [the suffix is not *luṭ*]? Because that which is in the vicinity of the present is included by the mention of the "present. Alternatively, the state of being present is understood from one word, while the state of being future is understood from another word. Why, then, does the suffix *lṛṭ* not occur here? Because from that point onward, the present tense is what is intended to be expressed.

However, the use of the word *yāvat* would not occur when there is an intention to express the future tense. For instance, in the example "Study, O student, before the lightning flashes," only the present tense is intended, because that which is proximate to [the action] is included by the mention of that [action]. Alternatively, since the future state is understood from the word *purā*, at that time it is actually the present. But when the words *kadā* or *karhi* are employed, all three verbal suffixes (*lakāra*) occur according to what is intended within their respective domains.

When does he eat? When will he eat? When (*karhi*) will he be an eater? The *liṅ* and other [optative] suffixes also occur: when did he eat? When has he eaten? Likewise, in the employment of interrogative pronouns (*kiṃvṛtta*), when desire (*lipsā*) is implied: who among you gives alms? Who will give you alms? Who is the giver of alms to you? Likewise, when the accomplishment of what is desired is intended to be expressed: he who gives you alms goes to the heavenly world.

"Whoever shall give alms to you will go to the heavenly world; whoever is a giver of alms to you has gone to the heavenly world; whoever did not give alms to you has gone to the heavenly world. Likewise: "If the preceptor comes, then you should study the *Chandas*; if the preceptor will come, then you should study grammar; if the preceptor is to come, then you should study *Mīmāṃsā*."

Likewise: "If the teacher should come after a moment (*muhūrta*), if the teacher will come, if the teacher is to come—then you should study the *Chandas*"; or: "If the teacher should come after a moment, then you should study the *Chandas*. The optative (*liṅ*) indeed occurs in the sense of expectation (*āśaṃsā*). Therefore, the optative must necessarily occur even in cases other than those involving a period of one *muhūrta*. For example: "If the teacher should come, then you should study the *Chandas*. [And: "The aorist (*luṅ*) is used with the particle *mā*" (Pāṇini 3.3.175).

When *māṅ* is employed in the sense of the future, *luṅ* occurs after a verb ending in the present tense when it expresses an action for the sake of another action. Example: *mā kārṣīt*. Why is the letter *ṅ* [in *māṅ*] used? [To show that it does not apply to other forms: *mā karotu*; *mā kariṣyati*. Regarding *smapare laṅ ca* (Pāṇini 1.3.5): When *māṅ* is employed followed by *sma*, *laṅ* occurs, as well as *luṅ*. Examples: *mā sma karot*; *mā sma kārṣīt*.

*Tuṃun* is used in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāve*) when it expresses a future action for the sake of another action that is understood to be for that purpose (Pāṇini 3.3.10). When an action is intended for the sake of another action, *tuṃun* occurs after a verbal root expressing a future meaning. Example: *paktum vrajati* ("he goes in order to cook"). Why is "in the sense of the abstract action" (*bhāve*) specified? Consider: *pakṣyāmīti vrajati* ("he goes thinking 'I shall cook'"). [In this case, the suffix is *luṭ*, not *tuṃun*. Why is "for the sake of another action" (*kriyāyām*) specified? Consider: *bhikṣiṣya iti asya jaṭāḥ* ("his matted hair is such that he will beg"). [The matted hair is a permanent characteristic, not for the sake of an action. Why is "for the sake of that [action]" (*tadarthāyām*) specified? Consider: *gamiṣyatas te bhaviṣyaty annaṃ bhojanāya* ("food will be available for your eating when you go"). [The food exists for the purpose of eating, not for the purpose of going. The letter *n* in *tuṃun* is for the sake of the accent; the letter *u* is for the sake of pronunciation. How is it that *kārako vrajati* ("he goes as a doer") is formed? It is established by the previous rule [Pāṇini 3.3.9] using the suffix *ṇvul*.

In that case, would not the suffixes *tṛc* and so forth also apply? No, because they do not convey the sense of being for that purpose (*tādarthya*). For in the expressions "the agent goes" (*kartā vrajati*) or "the thrower goes" (*vikṣepo vrajati*), the sense of being for that purpose is not understood. If it is argued that the suffix *ṇvul* would likewise not apply—since in the expression "the doer goes" (*kārako vrajati*), the sense of being for that purpose is not understood—then [we reply]: if the sense of being for that purpose were understood from the context (*prakaraṇa*), the same would apply to the suffixes *tṛc* and so forth. Therefore, suffixes such as *ṇvul* cannot possibly occur when the sense of being for that purpose is intended; rather, that sense is understood from the context.

Nevertheless, because of the rule regarding "frequently" (*bahulādhikāra*), the suffix *ṇvul* will apply, while *tṛc* and the others will not. In such cases as *pākāya vrajati*, *paktaye vrajati*, and *pacanāya vrajati*, the dative case expressing purpose (*tādarthya*) is established from nouns ending in *ghañ* and other suffixes. As for *godāyo vrajati*, even though it falls within the domain of the *kṛt* suffixes, the suffix *aṇ* will apply due to the mention of "frequently. [Objection: In that case, would it not apply elsewhere as well? [Response: Due to the mention of "frequently," it will not apply elsewhere. [The rule] *ghañ kārake ca* (Pāṇini 3.3.19) applies.

The suffix *ghañ* is frequently applied after a verbal root to denote either an action (*bhāva*) or an agent (*kāraka*). Regarding the action (*bhāva*): *pākaḥ* (cooking), *tyāgaḥ* (renunciation). Regarding the agent (*kāraka*), first in the sense of a technical name (*saṃjñā*): that by which one goes is a *pāda* (foot); that which causes pain is a *roga* (disease); that which enters is a *veśa* (dwelling); that which touches is a *sparśa* (a specific type of disease); that which moves toward another time is a *sāra* (a firm object); that by which they move is *sāra* (strength); *atīsāra* is a disease; *visāra* is a fish; that which is thrown is a *prāsa* (javelin); those by whom things are split are *dārāḥ* (spouses).

*Jāraḥ* means "that by which one ages. Even when not forming a technical name (*asaṃjñāyām*), [the suffix *ghañ* is applied]: *dāyo dattaḥ* ("a gift has been given"), *lābho labdhaḥ* ("a gain has been obtained"). According to Pāṇini 1.3.8, *ghañ* occurs after a word denoting a number, that is, after a word whose meaning is limited by a number: *eka-staṇḍula-niścāyaḥ* ("one handful of rice"). By virtue of the rule of frequent usage (*bahulādhikārāt*), we have *eko niścayaḥ*. Also: *ekā tilocchritiḥ* ("one heap of sesame seeds").

(1.3.9) *iṅaḥ ṣid vā*: After the root *iṅ*, the suffix *ghañ* occurs, optionally with the marker *ṣit*. From this [root], one studies by approaching him: *upādhyāyaḥ* (teacher). [With feminine suffixes: *upādhyāyī*, *upādhyāyā*. (1.3.10) *śṝ vāyuvarṇanivṛteṣu*: [The suffix *ghañ* is applied after the root *śṝ* when meaning wind, color, or covering.]

The suffix *ghañ* occurs after the root *śṝ* in the senses of "wind" (*vāyu*) and so forth. Thus: *śāsaḥ* = wind; *śāraḥ* = color; *nīśāraḥ* = covering. Why say "in these [senses]"? [Otherwise,] *śaraḥ* [would also be derived here]. (1.3.11) *prādibhyo ruvaḥ*:

The suffix *ghañ* occurs after the root *ru* when preceded by *pra* and other such prefixes. Thus: *saṃrāvaḥ*. Why say "after *pra* and others"? [Otherwise,] *ravaḥ* [would also be derived here]. How then is *rāvaḥ* formed? It is due to the rule of "great diversity" (*bahulādhikāra*).

*samo yudruduvaḥ* (1.3.12). The suffix *ghañ* occurs after the root *yu* and others when preceded by the prefix *sam*. Examples: *saṃyāvaḥ*, *saṃdrāvaḥ*, *saṃdāvaḥ*. Why [is it said] "when preceded by *sam*"? [To show that otherwise the suffix does not apply: *yavaḥ*, *dravaḥ*, *davaḥ*. How then are [the forms] *yāvaḥ*, *drāvaḥ*, *dāvaḥ* derived? Because of the restriction that *ghañ* occurs only after these roots when preceded by *sam*, these [other forms] also arise due to the non-universality (*anityatva*) of that rule. *veḥ kṣuśruvaḥ* (1.3.13). [The suffix *ghañ* occurs after the roots *kṣu* and *śru* when preceded by the prefix *vi*.]

The suffix *ghañ* occurs after the roots *kṣau* and *śru* when preceded by the prefix *vi-*. Thus: *vikṣāvaḥ* and *viśrāvaḥ*. Why "preceded by *vi-"? [To show: *kṣavaḥ*, *śravaḥ*. Regarding Pāṇini 1.3.14 (*śribhuvo ’prādeḥ*): the suffix *ghañ* occurs after the roots *śri* and *bhū* when they are not preceded by a preposition (*prādi*). Thus: *śrāyaḥ*, *bhāvaḥ*. Why "not preceded by a preposition"? [To show: *praśrayaḥ*, *prabhavaḥ*. How then is it that *prabhāvaḥ*, *vibhāvaḥ*, and *anubhāvaḥ* are formed? It is due to the rule of "great diversity" (*bahulādhikāra*). Alternatively, *prabhāvaḥ* is "excellent being" (*prakṛṣṭo vā bhāvaḥ*), *vibhāvaḥ* is "dispersed being" (*vigato vā bhāvaḥ*), and *anubhāvaḥ* is "consequent being" (*anugato vā bhāvaḥ*).

*Niyaḥ* (1.3.15): The suffix *ghañ* occurs after the root *nī-* when it is not preceded by a preverb (*prādi*). Thus, *nāyaḥ*. [The rule specifies] "not preceded by a preverb" (*aprādeḥ*); therefore, *praṇayaḥ*. How is *nayaḥ* formed? It is due to the irregular derivation (*nipātana*) in the rule *nyāyo nayaḥ* (1.3.28). *Avodaḥ* (1.3.16).

The suffix *ghañ* occurs after the root *nī* preceded by *ava* and *ud*. Examples: *avanāyaḥ*, *unnāyaḥ*. How is *unnayaḥ* [justified]? By virtue of the rule of "diversity" (*bahulādhikāra*). Alternatively, *unnayaḥ* means "an upward movement" (*udgataḥ nayaḥ*). Regarding the rule *pareḥ dyūte* (Pāṇini 3.3.38):

the suffix *ghañ* occurs after the root *nī* preceded by *pari* when the context is gambling. Example: *pariṇāyena śārīn hanti* ("He strikes the dice with a throw"). Why "in gambling"? [To exclude cases like] *pariṇayaḥ* ("marriage").
(1.3.18) *prāt srudru-stuvaḥ*:

after the prefix *pra-*, the suffix *ghañ* occurs after the roots *sru*, *dru*, and *stu*. Examples: *prasrāvaḥ*, *pradrāvaḥ*, *prastāvaḥ*. Why [specify] *pra-*? [To exclude] *sravaḥ*, *dravaḥ*. How then [to derive] *srāvaḥ*? By virtue of the rule of "diversity" (*bahulādhikāra*). (1.3.19) *nirabheḥ pūlvaḥ*: [the suffix *ghañ* occurs after the root *pū* following *ni-* and *abhi-*].
The suffix *ghañ* occurs after the roots *pū* and *lū* when preceded by *ni-* and *abhi-*. Examples: *niṣpāvaḥ*, *abhilāvaḥ*.

By the rule *nyudo graḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.20), the suffix *ghañ* occurs after the root *gṛ* (*girati*) when preceded by *ni-* or *ud-*. Examples: *nigāraḥ*, *udgāraḥ*. Why specify "after *ni-* and *ud-*"? [Consider: *garaḥ*.

*kṝ* in the sense of grain (Pāṇini 1.3.21): the suffix *ghañ* occurs after the root *kṛ* when it refers to grain. For example, *utkāra* of grain. Why "grain"? [To show that] *puṣpotkaraḥ* (a heap of flowers) is not included. *nivārāḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.22).
The word *nivāra* is an irregular formation (*nipātana*) when denoting a type of grain.
Regarding the rule *yajñe saṃstāvaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.23), the word *saṃstāva* is an irregular formation when referring to the context of a sacrifice; it has a different meaning in other cases.

*Prastaraḥ* elsewhere than in the sacrifice (1.3.24): after the root *stṛ* preceded by *pra*, the suffix *ghañ* occurs when used in a sense other than the sacrifice. Thus, *prastāraḥ*. However, in the context of the sacrifice, it is *barhiḥ-prastaraḥ* (the sacrificial grass-bundle).
*Viprathanaḥ* when not meaning sound (1.3.25).

When "expansion" (*prathana*) is to be expressed, the suffix *ghañ* is applied after the root *stṛ* preceded by the prefix *vi*, except when it refers to sound. For example: *paṭasya vistāraḥ* ("the expansion of a cloth"). Why say "except when it refers to sound"? Consider: *vākyavistaraḥ* ("an elaboration of a sentence"). Regarding the name of a meter (*chandonāman*):
the suffix *ghañ* is applied after the root *stṛ* when the subject is the name of a meter. For example: *prastārapaṅktiḥ*, *viṣṭārapaṅktiḥ*, and *āstārapaṅktiḥ* as names of meters.

*Avāt traś ca* (1.3.27): After the prefix *ava*, the suffix *ghañ* is applied to the roots *tṛ* (to cross) and *stṛ* (to spread). Thus, *avatāraḥ* (descent) and *avastāraḥ* (a covering). Due to the rule of *bahulādhikāra* (diversity of application), we also have *avataraḥ*. *Nyāyo naye* (1.3.28): The word *nyāya* is formed with the suffix *ghañ* after the root *nī* (to lead) when it means "leading" or "method."
The word *nyāya* is an irregularly formed (nipātita) term in the sense of "guidance" (*naya*). *Nyaya* has another meaning.
The word *paryāya* is an irregularly formed term in the sense of "sequence" (*krama*). *Paryaya* has another meaning.

Pāṇini 1.3.30: After the prefix *vi-* and after the prefix *upa-*, the suffix *ghañ* is applied to the root *śīṅ* in the sense of "order" (*krama*). Thus: *tava rājaviśāyaḥ* ("your turn for sleeping with the king"), *mama rājopaśāyaḥ* ("my turn for sleeping with the king"). Only in the sense of "order": otherwise, *upaśayaḥ* ("resting place"). Pāṇini 1.3.31: [The suffix *ghañ* is applied] to the root *ci* when the object is something reachable by the hand (*hastaprāpya*), provided it is not a theft (*asteya*).

The suffix *ghañ* occurs after the root *ci* ("to gather") when the object is reachable by the hand and it does not mean "stealing. Example: *puṣpapracāyaḥ* ("a gathering of flowers"). Why "reachable by the hand"? Consider: *vṛkṣāgre puṣpapracayaḥ* ("a gathering of flowers on the top of a tree"). Why "not stealing"? Consider: *puṣpapracayaṃ hastena karoti cauraḥ* ("the thief gathers flowers with his hand [by way of theft]"). By rule 1.3.32, *ghañ* occurs after the root *ci* in the senses of "pile," "dwelling," and "body," and the letter *ca* is replaced by *ka*. Examples: *ākāyam agniṃ cinvīta* ("one should pile the fire-altar up to its peak"); *gomayanikāyaḥ* ("a heap of cow dung"); *brāhmaṇanikāyaḥ* ("a community of Brahmins"); *kāyaḥ* ("the body").

In the case of *saṃgha* meaning "a supreme or inferior collection" (*anuttarādhara*)—that is, a multitude of living beings devoid of superior or inferior status—the suffix *ghañ* is applied to the root *ci*, and the letter *c* is replaced by *k*. Thus, *vaiyākaraṇanikāyaḥ* ("the assembly of grammarians"). Why specify "supreme or inferior"? [To exclude cases like] *sūkaranicayaḥ* ("a heap of pigs"). [The rule continues:
After the prefix *ud*, the suffix *ghañ* is applied to the roots *śri*, *iṇ*, *pū*, and *dru*. (Pāṇini 1.3.34)

The suffix *ghañ* occurs after the roots beginning with *śri*, when preceded by the prefix *ud*. Examples: *ucchrāyaḥ*, *udyāvaḥ*, *utpāvaḥ*, *uddrāvaḥ*. Why "preceded by *ud*"? [To exclude cases such as] *praśrayaḥ*. How then is *samucchrayaḥ* formed? By virtue of the rule of *bahulam* (diversity).

(1.3.35) When reproach (*ākrośa*) is implied, the suffix *ghañ* occurs after the root *grah* preceded by *ni* and *ava*. Examples: *nigrāhas te vṛṣala bhūyāt* ("May you suffer a seizure, O wretch!"); *avagrāhas te vṛṣala bhūyāt*. Why "when reproach is implied"? [To exclude cases such as] *nigrahaḥ* (restraint) and *avagrahaḥ* (obstruction).

(1.3.36) *samo muṣṭau*: after the root *grah* preceded by *sam*, the suffix *ghañ* occurs when the meaning is "fist. For example, *saṃgrāho mallasya* ("the clinch of the wrestler"). Why specify "fist"? [To show that] *saṃgrahaḥ* ("gathering") is not included. (1.3.37) *parer yajñe*: [The suffix *ghañ* occurs after *pari* in connection with *grah*] when the context is a sacrifice.

After the prefix *pari*, the root *grah* takes the suffix *ghañ* when the context is that of a sacrifice (*yajña*). Example: *uttaraparigrāhaḥ*. Why "in the context of a sacrifice"? [Counter-example: *parigrahaḥ*. *Pra* [is added] when there is a desire to obtain (*lipsā*) (Pāṇini 1.3.38).

After the prefix *pra*, the root *grah* takes the suffix *ghañ* when a desire to obtain is understood. Example: *pātrapragrāheṇa carati bhikṣuḥ piṇḍapātārthī* ("The mendicant wanders with a bowl for the purpose of obtaining alms"). Why "when there is a desire to obtain"? [Counter-example: *pragrahaḥ*.

(1.3.39) *vā vaṇijām*: When a meaning related to merchants (*vaṇij*) is to be expressed, the suffix *ghañ* optionally occurs after the root *grah* preceded by *pra*. A merchant operates with a balance-suspension (*tulāpragrāheṇa*). A merchant operates with a balance-suspension. A merchant operates with a balance-suspension. (1.3.40) *raśmau*: [The suffix *ghañ* is applied when the sense is] "reins."
After the root *grah* preceded by *pra*, the suffix *ghañ* optionally occurs when "ray" is the meaning expressed. Thus: *pragrāhaḥ* or *pragrahaḥ*.

According to Pāṇini 1.3.41 (*avād varṣavibandhe*), after the prefix *ava*, the suffix *ghañ* optionally occurs after *grah* when there is an obstruction of rain. Thus: *avagrāhaḥ* or *avagrahaḥ* of rain.

(1.3.42) *āṅo ruploḥ*: After the prefix *āṅ*, the suffix *ghañ* optionally occurs after the roots *ru* (to cry out) and *plu* (to float). Thus: *ārāvaḥ* and *āplāvaḥ*; [alternatively] *āravaḥ* and *āplavaḥ*. (1.3.43) *vṛña ācchāde*: [The suffix *ghañ* occurs after the root *vṛ* when meaning "to cover."]

The suffix *ghañ* optionally occurs after the root *vṛ* when it has the sense of "covering. Thus: *prāvāraḥ*, *prāvaraḥ*. According to Pāṇini 1.3.44, *ghañ* optionally occurs after the root *bhū* preceded by *pari* when it signifies "disdain. Thus: *paribhāvaḥ*, *paribhavaḥ*. Why specify "disdain"? [To exclude cases such as: "being everywhere" (*sarvato bhavanam*) is *paribhavaḥ* in its primary sense.

After a verbal root ending in *i* or *u*, the suffix *ac* occurs when the action is for the sake of another action (*kriyārtha*). Examples: *cayaḥ*, *jayaḥ*, *bhayam*. The letter *c* is a marker (*cihna*) indicating that the suffixes *thā*, *tha*, *ghañ*, *ktā*, *ac*, *ap*, *tra*, and *as* have a final augment *it*.
*sthāsnāpāvyadhihaniyudhaḥ kaḥ* (1.3.46): After the roots *sthā*, *snā*, *pā*, *vyadh*, *hi*, *han*, and *yudh*, the suffix *ka* occurs when the action is for the sake of another action.

After the roots *sthā* and others, the suffix *ka* occurs in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāva*) or a participant in an action (*kāraka*). *Ākhūtthaḥ vartate* ("a rat-trap exists"). *Prasthaḥ*: "that in which they stand firmly" (*pratiṣṭhante 'smin*). *Prasnaḥ*: "that in which they bathe" (*prasnānty asmin*). *Prapā*: "that in which they drink" (*prapibanty asyām*). *Āvidhaḥ*: "that by which one pierces" (*āvidhyate 'nena*). *Vighnaḥ*: "that in which one is obstructed" (*vihanyate 'smin*). *Nighnaḥ*, *upaghnaḥ*, *stambaghnaḥ*. *Āyudham*: "that by which they fight" (*āyudhyante 'nena*). By the rule *ṛdor ap* (Pāṇini 3.3.57), the suffix *ap* occurs after roots ending in *ṛ* and those ending in *u*. *Karaḥ*, *gharaḥ*. *Bhavaḥ*, *pavaḥ*. The letter *d* [in the sūtra] is for the purpose of removing ambiguity.

*grahavṛdṛniścigamavaśaraṇaḥ* (1.3.48): The suffix *ap* occurs after the roots *grah*, *vṛ*, *dṛ*, *niści*, *gam*, *vaś*, and *raṇ*. [Examples: *grahaḥ*; by *kapirikādīnām* (6.3.46), the *r* is changed to *l*: *glahaḥ*. [Further examples: *varaḥ*, *daraḥ*, *niścayaḥ*, *gamaḥ*, *vaśaḥ*, *raṇaḥ*. *prādibhyo 'daḥ* (1.3.49).

The suffix *ap* occurs after the root *ad* when preceded by *pra* and other such prefixes. For example: *praghasaḥ*. Why specify "after *pra* and others"? [Answer: Because [otherwise] it would be *ghāsaḥ*.
(Pāṇini 3.3.50) When preceded by *ni*, the suffix *ṇa* occurs after *ad*, and *ap* also occurs. For example: *nyādaḥ*, *nighasaḥ*.

Pāṇini 1.3.51: *vyadhajapo 'prādeḥ*. The roots *vyadh* and *jap* take the suffix *ap* when they are not preceded by an *upasarga* (prefix). Examples: *vyadhaḥ*, *japaḥ*. Why "not preceded by an *upasarga*"? Consider: *āvyādhaḥ*, *upajāpaḥ*. Pāṇini 1.3.52: *svanahasor vā*. [The suffix *ap* is optionally applied after the roots *svan* and *has* when not preceded by an *upasarga*.]
The suffix *ap* optionally occurs after the roots *svan* and *has*. [Examples: *svanaḥ*, *svāvaḥ*; *hasaḥ*, *hāsaḥ*. This applies only when the prefix is not *pra*: *prasvānaḥ*, *prahāsaḥ*.

(1.3.53) The suffix *ap* optionally occurs after the root *yam* when preceded by *sam*, *vi*, *upa*, or when without a prefix (*aprādi*). [Examples: *saṃyamaḥ*, *saṃyāmaḥ*; *viyamaḥ*, *viyāmaḥ*; *upayamaḥ*, *upayāmaḥ*; *yamaḥ*, *yāmaḥ*.

(1.3.54) After the root *yam* preceded by the prefix *ni*, the suffix *ap* optionally occurs. Thus: *niyamaḥ* and *niyāmaḥ*. The separation of this rule (*yogavibhāga*) is for the sake of what follows.
(1.3.55) [The suffix *ap* also occurs after] the roots *gad*, *nad*, *paṭh*, and *svan*.

The suffix *ap* optionally occurs after the roots *gada* and others when preceded by the prefix *ni*. Thus: *nigadaḥ* or *nigādaḥ*; *ninadaḥ* or *ninādaḥ*; *nipaṭhaḥ* or *nipāṭhaḥ*; *nisvanaḥ* or *nisvānaḥ*. Regarding *kvaṇo vīṇāyāś ca* (Pāṇini 1.3.56): the suffix *ap* optionally occurs after the root *kvaṇ* when preceded by *ni*, provided it is not preceded by *pra* and so forth, and also when it refers to a lute (*vīṇā*). Thus: *nikvaṇaḥ* or *nikvāṇaḥ*; *prakvaṇaḥ* [of a lute] or *prakvāṇaḥ*; *kvaṇaḥ* or *kvāṇaḥ*.
*Paṇaḥ parimāṇe* (Pāṇini 1.3.57): The suffix *ap* occurs after the root *paṇ* when it denotes a measure (*parimāṇa*). Thus, *paṇaḥ*. Why "when denoting a measure"? [Consider] *pāṇaḥ*.
*Mado 'prādeḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.58).

The suffix *ap* occurs after the root *mad* when it is not preceded by a prefix. [Example: *madaḥ*. Why "not preceded by a prefix"? [Counter-example: *pramādaḥ*. Regarding Pāṇini 1.3.59 (*prasaṃbhyāṃ harṣe*): the suffix *ap* occurs after the root *mad* preceded by *pra* or *sam* when it means "joy. [Examples: *pramadaḥ kanyānām* ("the joy of maidens"); *saṃmadaḥ kokilānām* ("the joy of cuckoos").

(1.3.60) *sam* and *ut* [as prefixes], when followed by *aja*, take the suffix *ap* in the sense of "animals. After *sam* and *ut* preceding *aja*, the suffix *ap* occurs when the subject is animals. *Samajaḥ paśūnām* ("a gathering of animals"); the meaning is "a collection. *Udajaḥ paśūnām* ("the driving out of animals"); the meaning is "driving forth. Why "in the sense of animals"? [Consider: *samājaḥ brāhmaṇānām* ("an assembly of Brahmins") and *udājaḥ śakunīnām* ("the flight of birds"). (1.3.61) *sartiḥ* [takes the suffix *ap*] in the sense of "procreation."
In the sense of "the first conception," the root *sṛ* takes the suffix *ap*. Thus, *gavām upasaraḥ* ("the first gathering of cows"). Any other gathering is called *upasāraḥ*. Regarding *havaḥ*:
the word *hava* is also irregularly formed (*nipātyate*) from the root *hvā*. Thus: *havaḥ*, *nihavaḥ*, *abhihavaḥ*, *upahavaḥ*, *vihavaḥ*, *āhavaḥ*.

(1.3.63) *nipānam* [is derived as] *āhāvaḥ*: the word *āhāvaḥ* is an irregularly formed (*nipātita*) term when it means a watering place for animals; otherwise, it is *āhvāyaḥ*. (1.3.64) *vadhaḥ* [is derived as] *ghātaḥ*.

The word *vadha* is irregularly formed (*nipātyate*) from the root *han* in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāve*), as is also *ghāta*. In the sense of a solid mass (*mūrti*), *ghana* is irregularly formed; any other [derivative] is *ghāta*. *Antarghaṇa* is the name of a specific region among the Bāhīkas, and in this case, the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* occurs by rule 6.4.102. Likewise, *praghaṇa* is indeed used as a technical name (*saṃjñā*) for a portion of a house.

*gṛhāṃśe praghāṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.66): The term *praghāṇa* is prescribed as a substitute for *agāraikadeśe* (a portion of a house). That over which wooden beams are struck is called *udghana*, meaning "that which has risen up densely. *Apaghana* is a designation for the hands and feet; it is established by means of the prefix *apa-* joined with *ghana*. Similarly, there are *ayoghana* (iron mace) and *vighana*. In the word *drughaṇa*, the substitution of *ṇa* occurs when it is a technical name (*saṃjñā*). *Stambaghana* is established by means of the prefix *stamba-* joined with *ghana*. *Parigha-udghani-ghāḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.67).
The forms *parighaḥ*, *udghaḥ*, and *nighaḥ* are derived as irregular (*nipātyante*) from the root *han*. In the rule *saṃghe 'nuttarādhara* (Pāṇini 2.4.2), the word *saṃghaḥ* [is used].
According to *ḍvitaḥ ktriḥ* (Pāṇini 3.3.88), the suffix *ktri* follows a verbal root ending in *ḍu* or *ṭu* when it expresses an action for the sake of another action. Thus: *kṛtrimam*, *paktrimam*.
*ṭvito 'thuc* (Pāṇini 3.3.89): The suffix *athuc* occurs after verbal roots ending in *ṭu*. Examples: *vepathuḥ*, *kṣavathuḥ*, *śvayathuḥ*.
*vicharakṣo naṅ* (Pāṇini 3.3.90): The suffix *naṅ* occurs after the roots *vi*, *cara*, and *rakṣ*.

The suffix *naṅ* occurs after these two [roots]: *viśnaḥ*, *rakṣṇaḥ*. How are forms such as *yācñā* derived? They result from specific grammatical exceptions (*nipātana*): from the rule *ṭuyācṛ yācñāyām* (Dhātupāṭha 1.591); from *śīṅ svapne* (Dhātupāṭha 2.51); from *praśnākhyānayor iñ ca* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.92); from *yajñe saṃstāvaḥ* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.23); and from *yatnakathopayogeṣu* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.78). Regarding *prādibhyo dādhaḥ kiḥ* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.71): the suffix *ki* occurs after the roots *dā* and *dhā* when preceded by prepositions (*prādi*). Thus we have *ādiḥ* and *nidhiḥ*. How is *antardhiḥ* formed? It results from the exception (*nipātana*) in the rule *tiro 'ntardhau* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.2.33).

(1.3.72) *vyāpyād ādhāre*: after the roots *dā* and *dhā*, preceded by an object (*vyāpya*), the suffix *ki* occurs when the locus (*ādhāra*) is expressed. Examples: *vāladhiḥ* (tail), *iṣudhiḥ* (quiver).
(1.3.73) *abhividhāv inuṇ*: [The suffix *inuṇ* occurs] in the sense of pervasion (*abhividhi*).
The suffix *inuṇ* occurs after a verbal root to denote pervasion (*abhivyāpti*). Examples: *sāṃkūṭinam*, *sāṃrāviṇam*.
Regarding the rule *striyāṃ ktin* (Pāṇini 3.3.94): the suffix *ktin* occurs in the feminine gender to denote an abstract action (*bhāva*) or an agent (*kāraka*). Examples: *kṛtiḥ*, *iṣṭiḥ*.

*Ūti*, *yūti*, *jūti*, *sāti*, *heti*, and *kīrti*: these words are correct forms when they have the acute accent on the final syllable (*antodātta*). *Ūti* is derived from the root *ava*. *yūti* is derived from the root *yu*. *jūti* is derived from the root *ju*. *sāti* is derived from either the root *si* or *su*. *heti* is derived from the root *hi*. *kīrti* is derived from the root *kīrti*.
[The suffix] *ṇac* [is applied] in the sense of reciprocal action (*vyatihāra*). (Pāṇini 1.3.76)
In the sense of reciprocal action, the suffix *ṇac* occurs in the feminine: *vyāvahāsī*, *vyāvacarcī*.
Regarding names, by the rule *nāmni ktic* (Pāṇini 3.3.94), the suffix *ktic* occurs when it is a technical name (*saṃjñā*): *tantiḥ*, *rantiḥ*, *vantiḥ*, *bhūtiḥ*.
Pāṇini 3.3.78: *samaja-manavidasu-śībhṛñiṇo bhāve kyap*.

The suffix *kyap* occurs after the roots *samaja*, *man*, *vid*, *su*, *śī*, *bhṛ*, and *iṇ* in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāva*), when a technical name (*saṃjñā*) is formed. Thus: *samajyā*, *manyā*, *vidyā*, *sutyā*, *śayyā*, *bhṛtyā*, and *ityā*. Due to the rule of diversity (*bahulādhikāra*), the forms *āsutiḥ*, *bhṛtiḥ*, and *samitiḥ* also occur. Why specify "in the sense of an abstract action"? [Consider: *bhāryā* (a wife). Why specify "when it is a name"? [Consider: *saṃvittiḥ* (consciousness). Pāṇini 3.3.79: *neḥ satpataḥ*. [The suffix *kyap* occurs] after the root *pat* following the prefix *ni*.

The suffix *kyap* occurs after the roots *sad* and *pat* when preceded by the prefix *ni-*. Thus: *niṣadyā* (sitting down), *nipatyā* (falling down). From the roots *kṛ*, *vraj*, and *yaj*, the suffix *kyap* occurs [by Pāṇini 3.3.100]: *kṛtyā* (action), *vrajyā* (wandering), *ijyā* (sacrifice).

In the rule *mṛgayāṭātye* (Pāṇini 1.3.81), these two words *mṛgayā* and *aṭāṭyā* are irregularly formed (*nipātyete*) in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāve*). From the root *mṛgaya-* comes *mṛgayā*; from *aṭāṭya-* comes *aṭāṭyā*. How is it that [the forms] *icchā* and *kriyā* are established? They are established by the irregular formation (*nipātana*) [of the rule] *icchāyāṃ kriyāyām*.
In the rule *pareḥ sṛcaro yaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.82)...
The suffix *ya* occurs after the roots *sṛ* and *car* when preceded by *pari*, and it is feminine: *parisaryā*, *paricaryā*. [Vt. 24] After the root *jāgṛ*, the suffix *ya* occurs: *jāgaryā*.

Aḥ *sanādyantāc ca* (Pāṇini 3.1.84): the suffix *a* occurs after roots ending in *san* and so forth, as well as after those ending in *sanādi*. Examples: *jāgarā*, *cikīrṣā*, *jihīrṣā*, *putrīyā*. From the root *aṭāṭyati*, we have *aṭāṭā*. The form *kaṇḍūtiḥ* is derived by virtue of the rule of "variety" (*bahulādhikāra*). *guror halaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.85).

The suffix *a* follows verbal roots ending in a consonant that belong to the *gurumat* class. [Examples: *īhā*, *īkṣā*. How is it that [the forms] *āptiḥ* and *rāddhiḥ* occur? It is due to the rule of "diversity" (*bahulādhikāra*).
[Furthermore,] the suffix *aṅ* follows roots such as *bhid* (Pāṇini 3.3.104).

The suffix *aṅ* occurs after roots beginning with *bhid* and after those marked with the *ṣit* designation when forming feminine nouns. Examples: *īṣatkaraḥ kaṭo bhavatā* ("the mat is easily made by you"), *duṣkaraḥ*, *sukaraḥ*. The form *īṣallabhyaḥ* is established by virtue of the governing principle of *bahula* (diversity).

P. 3.3.126: *kartrāpyābhyāṃ ca bhūkṛñoḥ*. The suffix *khal* occurs after the roots *bhū* and *kṛ*, when they follow the words *īṣat*, *dur*, or *su*, provided that these words denote the agent (*kartṛ*) or the instrument (*āpya*). Examples: *īṣad āḍhyena bhavanam* (the becoming wealthy by one who is slightly [wealthy]) → *īṣadāḍhyaṃbhavam*. *dur āḍhyena bhavanam* → *durāḍhyaṃbhavam*. *sv āḍhyena bhavanam* → *svāḍhyaṃbhavam*. *īṣad āḍhyaḥ kriyate* (one is made slightly wealthy) → *īṣadāḍhyaṃkaraḥ*. *durāḍhyaṃkaraḥ*. *svāḍhyaṃkaraḥ*. Answer: Because the root *kṛ* has the meaning of "manifesting what was previously non-existent" (*abhūtaprādurbhāva*). In this case, since the wealth already exists in some measure, it is not a case of its manifestation from non-existence. Thus, the suffix does not apply.

*Āto yuc* (Pāṇini 3.3.105): The suffix *yuc* occurs after a verbal root ending in long *ā*, when it follows words such as *īṣat* and others, provided that the root has the sense of action (*kriyārtha*). Examples: *īṣatpānaḥ* (easy to drink), *duṣpānaḥ* (difficult to drink), *supānaḥ* (well-drunk).
*Śāsi-yudhi-dṛśi-dhṛṣi-mṛṣaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.3.106): [The suffix *yuc* occurs] after the roots *śās*, *yudh*, *dṛś*, *dhṛṣ*, and *mṛṣ*.

The suffix *yuc* occurs after verbal roots such as *śās*, preceded by particles like *īṣat* and others. Examples: *duḥśāsanaḥ*, *duryodhanaḥ*, *durdarśanaḥ*, *durdharṣaṇaḥ*, *durmarṣaṇaḥ*. Because of the rule of "great scope" (*bahulādhikāra*), the suffixes *khal* and *yuca* occur only in the sense of the action itself (*bhāva*) and the agent (*kartṛ*). The status of being past or future, however, is determined by the context of the matter, other words, and so forth; even that which is proximate to the present is treated as the present itself. Regarding the past and future tenses as well, the present indicative (*laṭ*) occurs as before. When there is a failure of action (*kriyātipatti*), the conditional (*lṛṅ*) occurs optionally in the past, but necessarily in the future: *kathaṃ nāma tatrabhavān vṛṣalam ayājayiṣyat* ("How indeed would His Honor have officiated for a low-born man?"). Why "when censure is implied"? [Consider: *kathaṃ nāma tatrabhavān brāhmaṇam ayājayat* ("How indeed did His Honor officiate for a Brāhmaṇa?"). In this manner, the aorist (*luṅ*) and other suffixes follow according to their respective times. *kimvṛtte liṅ-lṛṭau ca* (Pāṇini 3.3.144).

When the word *kim* is used in the sense of censure (*garhā*), the conditional (*lṛṭ*) and the optative (*liṅ*) occur. For example: *ko nāma tatra vṛṣalaḥ?* ("What sort of low-born man is he there?"), *kataro nāma vṛṣalaḥ?* ("Which low-born man is he?"), *katamo nāma vṛṣalaḥ?* ("Which one indeed is that low-born man?")—referring to him whom your honor will cause to sacrifice, or might cause to sacrifice. Because of the non-connection with the mention of "or" (*vā*), the aorist (*luṅ*) and other such moods do not occur. Only when censure is intended: *ko nāma brāhmaṇo yaṃ tatrabhavān yājayed?* ("What sort of Brahmin is he whom your honor would cause to sacrifice?"). When there is the non-performance of an action (*kriyātipatti*), the conditional (*lṛṅ*) occurs optionally in the past, but necessarily in the future. Example: *ko nāma vṛṣalo yaṃ tatrabhavān ayājayiṣyat?* ("What sort of low-born man is he whom your honor would have caused to sacrifice?"). [The rule continues: *In cases of anger or lack of faith...* (Pāṇini 1.3.111).

The *lṛṭ* (future tense suffix) occurs, as well as the *liṅ* (optative), in the senses of intolerance (*amarṣa*) and impossibility (*anavakḷpti*). [Examples: "I cannot endure it," "I do not believe it," or "I find it impossible that your honor will cause a low-caste man (*vṛṣala*) to perform a sacrifice"—[expressed as] "he will cause him to sacrifice" (*yājayiṣyati*) or "he might cause him to sacrifice" (*yājayet*). When there is the non-occurrence of the action (*kriyātipatti*), the *lṛṅ* (conditional) is used for the past, and it is obligatory for the future: "I cannot endure it," "I do not believe it," or "I find it impossible that your honor would have caused a low-caste man to perform a sacrifice"—[expressed as] "he would have caused him to sacrifice" (*ayājayiṣyat*).
[Furthermore, the *lṛṭ* occurs after the particles] *kiṃkila* and words having the sense of *asti* (existence). (Pāṇini 3.3.145–147; 1.3.112)

When the words *kiṃkila* and those expressing existence (*asti-artha*) are present, the *lṛṭ* (future tense) alone occurs for the meanings of anger and lack of faith, and not the *liṅ* (optative). For example: *kiṃkila tatrabhavān vṛṣalaṃ yājayiṣyati?* ("Is it true that your honor will officiate at a sacrifice for a low-born man? [This implies: "I do not tolerate it; I do not believe it; I do not accept it. Or: *asti nāma*, *bhavati nāma*, *vidyate nāma yat tatrabhavān vṛṣalaṃ yājayiṣyati?* ("Is it possible, is it likely, is it known that your honor will officiate at a sacrifice for a low-born man?"). [In these cases, the *liṅ* is used when the particles] *yadi*, *yadiya*, *yadā*, *jātu*, etc., are present, according to Pāṇini 1.3.113.

When *yad* and the others are present, the conditional (*liṅ*) alone occurs for *krodha* (anger) and *aśraddhā* (lack of faith), and not the future (*lṛṭ*). For example: *yat tatrabhavān vṛṣalaṃ yājayet*, *yadi tatrabhavān vṛṣalaṃ yājayet*, *yadā tatrabhavān vṛṣalaṃ yājayet*, *jātu tatrabhavān vṛṣalaṃ yājayet*; [the sense being] "I do not tolerate it," "I do not believe it," "I do not accept it. When there is the non-performance of an action, the conditional (*lṛṅ*) occurs optionally in the past, but necessarily in the future: *yat tatrabhavān vṛṣalam ayājayiṣyat*. [The particle *ca* applies] to *yac* and *yat* when expressing censure (Pāṇini 1.3.114).

When the words *yacca* and *yatra* are present, the *liṅ* (optative) suffix occurs when censure (*garhā*) is implied, as well as in cases of anger (*krodha*) and lack of faith (*aśraddhā*). For example: *yaca tatrabhavān vṛṣalaṃ yājayet* ("that Your Honor should cause a low-caste man to sacrifice") and *yatra tatrabhavān vṛṣalaṃ yājayet* ("where Your Honor should cause a low-caste man to sacrifice"). This expresses censure: "I condemn it," "I do not tolerate it," "I have no faith in it," or "I do not consider it possible. When there is a lapse of action (*kriyātipatti*), the *lṛṅ* (conditional) suffix is used either for the past or necessarily for the future: *yaca tatrabhavān vṛṣalam ayājayiṣyat* ("if Your Honor had caused a low-caste man to sacrifice"). [The rule continues: "In the case of wonder (*āścarya*)," (Pāṇini 1.3.115).

When the words *yac* and *yatra* are present, the conditional (*liṅ*) occurs when wonder is implied: "It is wonderful, it is marvelous, it is strange that His Honor should cause a low-caste man (*vṛṣala*) to sacrifice," or "That His Honor should cause a low-caste man to sacrifice. When there is the non-occurrence of an action (*kriyātipatti*), the conditional (*lṛṅ*) is used for the past, and it is mandatory for the future: "If His Honor had caused a low-caste man to sacrifice" (past), or "If His Honor were to cause a low-caste man to sacrifice" (future).
In all other cases, the future (*lṛṭ*) is used (Pāṇini 3.3.139).

The *lṛṭ* (future tense suffix) does not occur after *yat* and *ca* when there is another cause for wonder (*āścarya*). [Examples of such wonders: "It is a marvel, it is extraordinary, it is strange—that a blind man should climb a mountain; that a deaf man should hear a sound. Because the rule regarding *liṅ* (prescriptive/optative suffix) in the sense of "it is a marvel if he should eat" (*āścaryaṃ yadi sa bhuñjīta*) supersedes it, the *lṛṭ* will not occur. When there is the non-occurrence of the action (*kriyātipatti*), the *lṛṅ* (conditional suffix) is used either for the past or necessarily for the future. [Furthermore,] *liṅ* occurs after *uta* and *api* in the sense of "certainly" (*bāḍha*). (Pāṇini 3.3.154–156; 1.4.97).

When *uta* and *api* are employed in the sense of "certainly" (*bāḍha*), the potential suffix (*liṅ*) occurs after a verb used for the sake of another action. For example: *uta kuryāt* ("He would certainly do it") and *api kuryāt* ("He would certainly do it"). The meaning is "he would certainly do it. Why say "in the sense of certainly"? [Consider: *uta daṇḍaḥ patiṣyati?* ("Will the staff fall? and *apidhāsyate dvāram* ("The door will be closed"). Here, a question and an obstruction are understood respectively. The rule *bhūte vā* (108) is no longer applicable here. Therefore, when there is a lapse of action (*kriyātipatti*) in the past or future within the scope of the potential suffix, the conditional suffix (*lṛṅ*) must invariably be seen [as applied]. For example: *utākariṣyat* ("He would certainly have done it") and *apy akariṣyat* ("He would certainly have done it").

In the sense of making known one's desire (*kāmapravedana*), the suffix *liṅ* will occur [in the sense of] "request" (*prārthanā*)—for example, "I desire that you eat. However, it will not occur in the case of a mere question, such as "Is your mother living?", because there is no request involved.
[This is governed by the rule: *saṃbhāvane ’lam-arthe tadarthāprayoge* (Pāṇini 1.3.118).

The suffix *liṅ* occurs when the sense of "sufficiency" (*alam-artha*) is implied as the subject matter, provided that the word expressing that meaning is not actually employed. For example: *api parvataṃ śirasā bhindyāt* ("He might even split a mountain with his head") and *api droṇapākaṃ bhuñjīta* ("He might even eat a meal cooked by Droṇa"). Why say "when the sense of sufficiency is implied"? Consider: *videśasthāyī Devadatto grāmaṃ gamiṣyati* ("Devadatta, though staying abroad, will go to the village"). Why say "provided that the word expressing that meaning is not employed"? Consider: *vasati cet Surāṣṭreṣu bhokṣyate 'laṃ lavaṇena* ("If he stays in the Surāṣṭra country, he will eat enough salt"). In the case of the non-occurrence of an action (*kriyātipatti*), the suffix *lṛṅ* necessarily occurs: *api vajrāhato nāpatiṣyat* ("Even if struck by a thunderbolt, he would not have fallen"). [This rule applies] when the verbal root itself expresses [the sense], except in the case of *yad*. (Pāṇini 1.3.119)

When expressing possibility (*saṃbhāvanā*) or when a potentiality is indicated, the optative (*liṅ*) is used provided that the word *yat* is not employed. [Examples: "I consider it possible," "I believe," or "I accept as valid": *bhuñjīta bhavān* ("May you eat") or *abhuṅkta bhavān* ("You might have eaten"). Why say "provided that *yat* is not employed"? [Counter-example: *saṃbhāvayāmi yat sa bhuñjīta* ("I consider it possible that he might eat"). When there is the non-occurrence of an action (*kriyātipatti*), the conditional (*lṛṅ*) is indeed used: *saṃbhāvayāmi nābhokṣyata bhavān* ("I consider it possible that you would not have eaten"). [This rule applies] to cause and effect (*hetu-phala*). (Pāṇini 3.3.156–157)

The *liṅ* suffix optionally occurs after a verbal root expressing an action when that action functions as a cause or as a result of another action. For example: *dakṣiṇena ced yāyān na śakaṭaṃ paryābhavet* ("If he were to go by the right, the cart would not overturn") or *dakṣiṇena ced yāsyati na śakaṭaṃ paryābhaviṣyati* ("If he will go by the right, the cart will not overturn"). Why does it not occur here: *hantīti palāyate* ("He flees because [he thinks] 'he strikes'") or *varṣatīti dhāvati* ("He runs because [he thinks] 'it rains'"? It is because the relationship of cause and effect (*hetu-hetumadbhāva*) is already indicated by the word *iti* itself. As for the one who says:

Since this yoga pertains to the future tense, one might think that it would not apply to the present, such as in the case: "He will flee because he thinks, 'He will kill me. However, the conditional (*lṛṅ*) certainly occurs when there is a failure of action (*kriyātipatti*): "If he had gone by the southern road, the cart would not have overturned. One employs [the conditional] by inferring the failure of a future action through some sign. Furthermore, usage is seen even for the past:
"The earth, with its great mountain-king bound, would have sunk into the waters like Nārāyaṇa, O glorious one, if you had not held it up."

In the sense of "desire" (*icchārtha*), the optative (*liṅ*) and imperative (*loṭ*) suffixes shall occur by the rule *prārthanā* (Pāṇini 3.3.160): *icchāmi bhuñjīta bhavān* ("I desire that you eat"), *icchāmi bhuṅktāṃ bhavān* ("I desire that you eat"). Otherwise, forms such as *icchan karomi* ("desiring, I do") would also be possible. [The forms] *icchati bhoktum*, *kāmayate bhoktum*, and *gaveṣayati bhoktum* are established by the rule *tumunṇvulau kriyāyāṃ kriyārthāyām* (Pāṇini 3.3.10), which prescribes the suffix *tumun* in the sense of an action intended for another action. Because of the re-statement [in 3.3.160], these [suffixes] would also occur here in the sense of "desiring": *icchan karoti*. As for *bhuñjīyeti icchati*, the optative will occur by the rule *prārthanā* (Pāṇini 3.3.157). In *icchet* and *kāmayeta*, only an injunction (*vidhi*) is understood.

(1.3.121) *vidhi-saṃpraśna-prārthaneṣu* (in the cases of injunction, inquiry, and entreaty). An injunction (*vidhi*) is an unestablished command, whether its purpose is visible or invisible, or whether it involves a consequence upon refusal—whether that consequence is harmful or harmless—and whether it is preceded by respect or contempt.
