Inquiry (*saṃpraśna*) is deliberation. Entreaty (*prārthana*) is begging and the expression of a desire for a wished-for object. In these cases—namely, injunction and the others—the *liṅ* suffix occurs after a verb whose meaning is for the sake of another action. For example: "May you make a mat" (*kaṭaṃ kuryād bhavān*), "he should sacrifice" (*yajet*), "he should give" (*dadyāt*). Where there is a consequence upon the refusal of what has been accepted, that is an invitation (*nimantraṇa*).

"May you eat here"—this is an invitation (*āmantraṇa*), where there is freedom of action (*kāmacāra*) regarding the refusal [of the request]. "May you sit here. A command preceded by courtesy is a request (*adhyeṣaṇa*): "May you teach the boy. A command preceded by contempt is an order (*praiṣa*); regarding that, he will state the *loṭ* suffix. In the sense of inquiry (*saṃpraśna*): "O sir, what indeed should I study—grammar? In the sense of supplication (*prārthana*): "May I obtain alms. "May you live. [The *loṭ* suffix is used in these senses. (Pāṇini 1.3.122).

In the case of injunctions and the like, the imperative suffix *loṭ* occurs after a verbal root whose meaning is an action. For example: "May you make a mat" (*kaṭaṃ karotu bhavān*); "Cut off craving" (*tṛṣṇāṃ chinddhi*); "Cultivate forbearance" (*bhaja kṣamām*); "Abandon pride" (*jahi madam*); "Practice compassion" (*kuru dayām*); "May you eat here" (*iha bhavān bhuṅktām*); "May you sit here" (*iha bhavān āstām*); "May you teach the boy" (*māṇavakaṃ bhavān adhyāpayatu*). [Examples of other uses: "O sir, shall I indeed study grammar? (*kiṃ nu khalu bho vyākaraṇam adhyayai?*); "Give me alms" (*dehi me bhikṣām*); "May you live long" (*jīvatu bhavān*). [These occur] in the sense of command (*praiṣa*), permission (*anujñā*), and the arrival of the proper time (*prāptakāla*)—Pāṇini 1.3.123.

The *loṭ* suffix occurs in the sense of *praiṣa* (command) and so forth: "Go to the village. *Anujñā* (permission) is the granting of consent to one who desires to act: "Do it thus," or "Make a mat; the time has come for you to make a mat.
Furthermore, the *liṅ* suffix is used when [the permission] pertains to a period exceeding one hour (*ūrdhvamauhūrtika*). (Pāṇini 1.3.124)

When an action refers to a time subsequent to one *muhūrta* from the present, the suffixes *liṅ* and *loṭ* are used for the purpose of issuing commands (*praiṣa*) and so forth. For example: *ūrdhvaṃ muhūrtāt kaṭaṃ kuryāḥ*; *kaṭaṃ kuru*. *Ūrdhvaṃ muhūrtād evaṃ kuryāḥ*; *evaṃ kuru*. *Ūrdhvaṃ muhūrtāt kaṭaṃ kuryād bhavān*; *kaṭaṃ karotu bhavān*: for it is now the time for you to make the mat. [In this context,] the suffix *loṭ* is also used when the particle *sma* is employed (Pāṇini 1.3.125).

When the particle *sma* is employed, after a verb signifying an action occurring more than a moment (*ūrdhvamauhūrtika*) from the present, the imperative suffix (*loṭ*) alone is used for commands (*praiṣa*) and the like. For example: "May you go to the village after a moment," "May you do so," or "May you make a mat. This is because it is now your time to make the mat.
[This applies] in the sense of a formal request (*adhīṣṭi*). (Pāṇini 1.3.126)

When the particle *sma* is used in an exhortation (*adhyeṣaṇā*), only the imperative (*loṭ*) occurs: *aṅga sma vidvan māṇavakam adhyāpaya* ("Come now, learned one, teach the boy"). In cases of command (*praiṣa*) and so forth, as well as elsewhere, the suffixes *tavya* and the rest are indeed established: *bhavatā khalu kaṭaḥ kartavyaḥ*, *karaṇīyaḥ*, *kāryaḥ*, *kṛtyaḥ*. Likewise, when referring to a time within an hour (*ūrdhvamauhūrtika*) and in the sense of "deserving" (*arha*) and so forth, the same applies. [Examples are: *kālo bhoktum*, *samayo bhoktum*, *velā bhoktum*; here the suffix *tumun* is the very same as the previous one. Alternatively, the verbal root *bhū* may be used because its meaning is understood; for [the rule] *kālasamayavelāsu liṅ yadi* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 3.3.167).

When words such as *kāla* (time), etc., are employed together with the word *yat*, the suffix *liṅ* occurs in the sense of an action (*kriyārtha*). For example: *kālo yad bhavān bhuñjīta* ("it is time that you eat"), *samayo yad bhavān bhuñjīta* ("it is the occasion that you eat"), *velā yad bhavān bhuñjīta* ("it is the hour that you eat").
[This applies also] in the sense of fitness (*arha*) and capability (*śakti*) according to Pāṇini 1.3.128.

The optative (*liṅ*) occurs in the sense of fitness (*arha*) and capability (*śakti*). "You indeed should marry a maiden" (*bhavān khalu kanyāṃ vahet*); [here] you are fit (*arhaḥ*) and you are capable (*śaktaḥ*). In the case of "one who has performed the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice" (*agniṣṭomayājī*), the time is strictly past. In the case of "his son will be born" (*asya putro janitā*), future time is understood through its connection with another word. Likewise: "the mat was made, it will be tomorrow"; "there was a task to be done, there was"; "there was one possessing cows" (*gomān āsīt*); "there will be one possessing cows" (*gomān bhavitā*). "Cut! Cut!"—thus he cuts.

"Study! Study!"—this is precisely how he has studied; this is the imperative (*loṭ*) in the second person singular. This reduplication expresses frequency (*ābhīkṣṇya*); it means that he performs that action so urgently that he seems to be urging others to do it as well. Thus: "He cuts, [saying] 'Cut! Cut! "He studies, [saying] 'Study! Study! Likewise, even regarding other times: "He cut, [saying] 'Cut! Cut! (he has cut); "He cut" (past tense); "He will cut" (future); "He shall cut" (periphrastic future).

The same should be applied to the word *sva* as well. Likewise, in the case of conjunction (*samuccaya*): "He wanders [only] to the monastery and to the monastery; he wanders thus. "Study the Veda and study grammar; he studies thus. However, when there is a difference in activity, the subsequent application (*anuprayoga*) occurs because the general term alone is pervasive: "Eat rice, drink barley-gruel, and eat parched grain; he consumes thus. Regarding the rule *alaṃkhalvoḥ pratiṣedhe ktvā vā* (Pāṇini 1.4.65): [When *alam* or *khalu* express prohibition, the suffix *ktvā* is optionally used].

When the words *alaṃ* and *khalu*, which have the sense of prohibition (*pratiṣedha*), are employed, the suffix *ktvā* optionally occurs. For example: *alaṃ kṛtvā* or *khalu kṛtvā*; *alaṃ kṛtena* or *khalu kṛtena*. Why [is it said] "of *alaṃ* and *khalu*"? Consider: *mā kārṣīḥ* ("do not do"). Why [is it said] "prohibition"? Consider: *alaṃkāraḥ* ("ornament"). [The rule] *meṅaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.130) states that the suffix *ktvā* optionally occurs after the root *mā* (*meṅ*). This rule is commenced for the purpose of [indicating] that the action denoted by the first verb does not precede the second. Examples: *apamitya yācate* ("having borrowed, he begs") or *apamātum yācate*; *yācitvāpamayate* ("having begged, he borrows").

(1.3.131) *ekakartṛkayoḥ pūrvāt*: Between two actions performed by the same agent, the suffix *ktvā* occurs after the word expressing the action that precedes the other. Example: *bhuktvā vrajati* ("Having eaten, he goes"). Because the dual number is not restrictive, one may say: *bhuktvā pītvā vrajati* ("Having eaten and drunk, he goes"). Or [the rule applies] with reference to another [action]. Why specify "by the same agent"? Consider: *bhuktavati Devadatte Yajñadatto vrajati* ("While Devadatta has eaten, Yajñadatta goes"). Why specify "from the preceding"? Consider: *bhuṅkte ca pacati ca* ("He eats and cooks"). In the cases of *aprāpya nadīṃ parvataḥ* ("Before reaching the river, there is a mountain") and *atikramya parvataṃ nadī* ("After passing the mountain, there is a river"), since the root *bhū* is possible in all instances, both the state of having the same agent and the state of being prior in time are understood.

*Ābhīkṣṇye ṇamul ca* (Pāṇini 3.4.22): The suffix *ṇamul* is applied after a verb denoting an action intended for another action, provided that both actions have the same agent and the preceding action is characterized by frequency (*ābhīkṣṇya*); the suffix *ktvā* is also applied in this case. Examples: *bhojaṃ bhojaṃ vrajati* ("he goes after eating repeatedly") or *bhuktvā bhuktvā vrajati* ("having eaten repeatedly, he goes"). The reduplication [of the word] occurs by virtue of the rule *ābhīkṣṇye* (Pāṇini 8.1.4). When the word *yat* is used—as in *yad ayaṃ bhuṅkte tato vrajati* ("when he eats, then he goes")—the suffix *ktvā* does not apply because the sequence is expressed by the word *tataḥ*. Furthermore, because the sense of frequency (*ābhīkṣṇya*) is absent, the suffix *ṇamul* also does not apply.

Since the word *punaḥpunaḥ* itself expresses frequency (*abhīkṣṇya*)—as in "he goes because he eats again and again"—the [suffix] does not occur there. In the case of "having eaten, he goes; therefore, he studies," the suffix *ktvā* is used to express the sequence between eating and going. However, since the sequence between going and studying is expressed by the word *tataḥ*, the [suffix] will not occur there.
[This is governed by the rule: *pūrvāgreprathameṣu* (Pāṇini 2.3.29).

When words such as *pūrva* and others are employed, the suffixes *ṇamul* and *ktvā* occur. For example: *pūrvaṃ bhojaṃ vrajati* ("he goes after having first eaten") or *pūrvaṃ bhuktvā vrajati*; *agre bhojaṃ vrajati* ("he goes after having first eaten") or *agre bhuktvā vrajati*; *prathamaṃ bhojaṃ vrajati* ("he goes after having first eaten") or *prathamaṃ bhuktvā vrajati*. However, in the case of *pūrvaṃ bhuṅkte tato vrajati* ("he eats first, then he goes"), these two suffixes will not occur, because the sequence is already expressed by the word *tataḥ*. Furthermore, according to Pāṇini 3.4.27, the suffix *khamuñ* occurs after the root *kṛ* when it follows an object (*vyāpya*) in the sense of reviling (*ākrośe*).

The suffix *khamuñ* occurs after the root *kṛ*, when it is preceded by an object that pervades [the agent], provided that an insult (*ākrośa*) is understood. Example: *dasyuṃkāram ākrośati* ("he insults him by calling him a thief"). Why "insult"? [Observe: *sādhuṃ kṛtvā stauti* ("having done well, he praises him").
[Also, the suffix applies] after words meaning "tasty" (*svādu*), provided they do not end in a long vowel. (Pāṇini 1.3.135)

The suffix *khamuñ* occurs after the root *kṛ-* when followed by a word ending in *-svādu-* that does not have a long vowel as its final element. Examples: *svāduṃkāraṃ bhuṅkte* (he eats making it sweet), *saṃpannaṃkāraṃ bhuṅkte* (he eats making it well-prepared), *lavaṇaṃkāraṃ bhuṅkte* (he eats making it salty). Why is it said "not having a long vowel"? Consider: *svādūkṛtya bhuṅkte* (having made it sweet, he eats). [This is formed with the suffix *ktvā*, not *khamuñ*. Regarding *anyathākāraṃ bhuṅkte*, *evaṃkāram*, *kathaṃkāram*, and *itthaṃkāram*—the suffix *ṇamul* need not be explicitly taught here, because these forms are already established through the use of nouns ending in *ghañ* as adverbs (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*). For example: *odanapākaṃ śete* (he lies down while the rice is being cooked).

"In this way, according to the form [of the object], so shall I eat; what is that to you? He chooses a maiden as a bride (*kanyā-darśam*). He feeds the Brahmins according to their Vedic knowledge (*brāhmaṇa-vedam*). He eats as much as he knows (*yāvad-vedam*). He studies for as long as he lives (*yāvaj-jīvam*). He gives a full hide (*carma-pūram*). He eats until his belly is full (*udara-pūram*). It has rained until it fills a cow's footprint (*goṣpada-pūram*). Water that reaches the depth of a cow's footprint is called *goṣpada-pram*. It has rained to the extent of a cow's footprint (*goṣpada-pram*). And so it is with all case endings; in a compound, the case ending is elided. Likewise: "It has rained until it soaked the clothes" (*cela-knopam*).

The god rained down until the clothes were soaked (*vastraknopa*). [He rained] until the garments were soaked (*vasanaknopam*). He scrapes away until the roots are torn out (*nimūlakāṣaṃ kasati*). He scrapes away until the roots and all are gone (*samūlakāṣaṃ kasati*). He grinds it into dry powder (*śuṣkapeṣaṃ pinaṣṭi*). [He grinds it into] fine powder (*cūrṇapeṣam*). [He grinds it into] coarse powder (*rūkṣapeṣam*). He destroys it by uprooting it entirely (*samūlaghātaṃ hanti*). He does what has not been done before (*akṛtakāraṃ karoti*). He strikes the altar with his palms (*pāṇighātaṃ vedīṃ hanti*). He grinds it with water (*udapeṣaṃ pinaṣṭi*). He grinds it with oil (*tailapeṣaṃ pinaṣṭi*). He turns it with his hands (*hastavartaṃ vartayati*). He nourishes himself to the full extent of his capacity (*svapoṣaṃ puṣṇāti*). [He nourishes himself to the full extent of his] cow’s capacity (*gopoṣam*). [He nourishes himself to the full extent of his] wealth’s capacity (*raipoṣam*). He is bound in the manner of a prison guard (*cārakabandhaṃ baddhaḥ*). [He is bound] in the manner of a curlew (*krauñcabandham*). He is ruined so that his livelihood is lost (*jīvanāśaṃ naṣṭaḥ*). He carries [the load] like a man-drawn beast of burden (*puruṣavāhaṃ vahati*). It is dried until it is shriveled upward (*ūrdhvaśoṣaṃ śuṣkaḥ*). It is filled until it overflows upward (*ūrdhvapūraṃ pūrṇaḥ*).

*Jīvād graho ṇamul sa cānu* (Pāṇini 3.4.42): After the root *grah*, when it follows the object *jīva*, the suffix *ṇamul* occurs, provided that this root *grah* is subsequently employed (*anuprayujyate*). Example: *jīvagrāhaṃ gṛhṇāti* ("he seizes [him] alive"). *Hastena* (Pāṇini 3.4.43).

The suffix *ṇamul* occurs after the root *grah* when preceded by *hasta* or *kara*, and that [root] is subsequently employed (*anuprayujyate*). Examples: *hastagrāham gṛhṇāti* ("he takes by the hand"), *karagrāham gṛhṇāti* ("he takes by the hand"). From Pāṇini 1.3.138: *upamānāt kartuś ca*: The suffix *ṇamul* occurs after a verb used for the purpose of another action (*kriyārtha*), provided it follows a word denoting a standard of comparison (*upamāna*) or an agent (*kartṛ*) which is the object (*vyāpya*) of that action; and that verb used for the purpose of another action is subsequently employed. Examples: *cūḍakanāśam naṣṭaḥ* ("he was lost like a crest-jewel"), *suvarṇanidhāyam nihitaḥ* ("it was deposited like a hoard of gold"), *odanapācam pakvaḥ* ("it was cooked like a pot of rice"). [Note: If the suffix *ghañ* were used instead, there would be the change of *p* to *k* (*kutva*). Why "from a standard of comparison"? [Counter-example: *cūḍako naṣṭaḥ* ("the crest-jewel was lost").

*Upadaṃśas tṛtīyāyām* (Pāṇini 1.3.139): When *daṃśati* preceded by *upa* has a word ending in the third case as its *upapada*, the suffix *ṇamul* occurs. Examples: *mūlakenopadaṃśaṃ bhuṅkte* ("he eats with a radish as a side-dish") or *mūlakopadaṃśaṃ bhuṅkte*. This is also established by using the suffix *ghañ*. Why specify "in the third case"? [Consider: *mūlakam upadaśya bhuṅkte* ("having bitten the radish, he eats"). *Hiṃsārthād ekāpyāt* (Pāṇini 1.3.140).

The suffix *ṇamul* occurs after a root meaning "to injure" (*hiṃsā*) when it is used with a subsequent verb (*anuprayoga*) that has the same object (*samānavyāpya*), provided that the word ending in the third case (*tṛtīyānta*) is present as an attendant word (*upapada*). Example: *daṇḍenopaghātaṃ gāḥ kalayati* ("He drives the cows, striking them with a stick"). Or: *daṇḍopaghātam*. Why is it said "even though there is only one [object]" (*ekāpyāt*)? Consider: *daṇḍenopahatya bhūmiṃ gāḥ śādayati gopālako yaṣṭyā* ("The cowherd, having struck the ground with a stick, makes the cows lie down").
Also: *upāt pīḍarudhakarṣaḥ saptamyām* (Pāṇini 1.4.141).

The suffix *ṇamul* occurs after verbs such as *pīḍa* ("to press") when preceded by the prefix *upa*, provided that a word ending in the seventh case (*saptamī*) or the third case (*tṛtīyā*) is used as an upapada. Examples: *pārśvayor upapīḍaṃ śete* (he lies pressing against his sides). *pārśvenopapīḍam*. *pārśvopapīḍam*. *vraje uparodhaṃ gāḥ śādayati* (he shuts the cows in the pen). *vrajenoparodham*. *vrajoparodham*. *pāṇāv upakarṣam*. *pāṇinopakarṣam*. *pāṇyupakarṣam*.

(1.3.142) When proximity (*pratyāsatti*) is implied, the suffix *ṇamul* occurs after a verb intended for action (*kriyārtha*), provided a word ending in the seventh case is used as an upapada. Example: *keśeṣu grāhaṃ yudhyante* (they fight seizing [each other] by the hair). *keśagrāham*.

(1.3.143) *pramāṇe*: When the sense of "measure" (*pramāṇa*) is understood, the suffix *ṇamul* is applied after a verb intended to express an action, provided that a word ending in the seventh case (*saptamī*) is used as a subordinate element (*upapada*). Example: *dvyaṅgulotkarṣaṃ gaṇḍikāṃ chinatti* ("He cuts the joint with an elevation of two fingers"). [This means] *dvyaṅgule utkarṣam*. (1.3.144) *pañcamyāṃ tvarāyām*: [The suffix *ṇamul* is applied] when a word ending in the fifth case (*pañcamī*) is used, provided that there is a sense of haste (*tvarā*).

When a word ending in the fifth case (*pañcamī*) is used as an *upapada* and haste is implied, the suffix *ṇamul* occurs after a verb intended for the sake of another action. *śayyotthāyaṃ vrajati* ("he goes having risen from his bed"). [Alternatively: *śayyāyā utthāyaṃ vrajati*. Why "when haste is implied"? [Counter-example: *āsanād utthāya dhāvati* ("having risen from his seat, he runs"). Regarding the rule *dvitīyāyām* (Pāṇini 3.4.23): when a word ending in the second case (*dvitīyā*) is used as an *upapada* and haste is implied, the suffix *ṇamul* occurs after a verb intended for the sake of another action. *yaṣṭigrāhaṃ yudhyante* ("they fight seizing staffs"). [Alternatively: *yaṣṭīr grāham*.

(1.3.146) *adhruve svāṅge*: When an inconstant (*adhruva*) part of one’s own body (*svāṅga*) ending in the accusative case is used as an *upapada*, the suffix *ṇamul* occurs after a verb intended for the purpose of another action (*kriyārtha*). Example: *bhrūvikṣepaṃ jalpati* ("he speaks while twitching his eyebrows"). [Alternatively: *bhruvaṃ vikṣepam*. Why "inconstant" (*adhruva*)? Example: *utkṣipya śiraḥ kathayati* ("he speaks having raised his head").

A part of one's own body (*svāṅga*) is that which is not liquid (*adrava*), possesses form (*mūrtimat*), resides in a living being (*prāṇistha*), and is not produced by a transformation (*avikāraja*).
"And that which is not situated there, yet is seen there; by that, it is joined as such.

(Pāṇini 3.4.54). When "affliction" (*pīḍā*) is understood, the suffix *ṇamul* occurs after a verb meaning "to perform an action," provided that a word ending in the second case denoting one's own limb (*svāṅga*) is the attendant word (*upapada*). For example: *uraḥpratipeṣaṃ yudhyante* ("They fight, crushing chest against chest") or *urāṃsi pratipeṣam*.

Pāṇini 1.3.148: *viśi-pati-padi-skandām vīpsā-bhīkṣṇyayoḥ*. When distributive repetition (*vīpsā*) or frequency (*abhīkṣṇya*) is to be understood, the suffix *ṇamul* is applied after the verbs *viś*, *pat*, *pad*, and *skand*, provided that a word ending in the second case (*dvitīyā*) is used as a governing word (*upapada*). Examples: *gehānupraveśam āste* ("He sits [repeatedly] entering the houses"). This means: *gehaṃ geham anupraveśam* ("entering house after house"), or *geham anupraveśam anupraveśam* ("entering, entering each house"). *gehānuprapātam āste* ("He sits [repeatedly] jumping into the houses"). This means: *gehaṃ geham anuprapātam* ("jumping into house after house"), or *geham anuprapātam anuprapātam* ("jumping, jumping into each house"). *gehānuprapādam āste* ("He sits [repeatedly] stepping into the houses"). This means: *gehaṃ geham anuprapādam* ("stepping into house after house"), or *geham anuprapādam anuprapādam* ("stepping, stepping into each house"). *gehāvaskandam āste* ("He sits [repeatedly] leaping upon the houses"). This means: *gehaṃ geham avaskandam* ("leaping upon house after house"), or *geham avaskandam avaskandam* ("leaping, leaping upon each house").

*geham geham avaskandam*, *geham avaskandam avaskandam*. Why [is it specified] "in the sense of distributive repetition (*vīpsā*) and frequency (*abhīkṣṇya*)"? [Consider: *geham anupraviśyāste* ("having entered the house, he sits"). [The rule] *asutṛṣaḥ kāleṣu vicchede* (Pāṇini 1.3.149).

The suffix *ṇamul* is applied after the roots *as* ("to throw") and *tṛṣ* ("to thirst") when time-periods ending in the second case (*dvitīyānta*) are used as subordinate words (*upapada*), provided that a cessation (*viccheda*) is understood. Examples: *dvyahātyāsaṃ gāḥ pāyayati* — He makes the cows drink [water] with intervals of two days. *dvyaham atyāsam* — With intervals of two days. *dvyahatarṣam* — With intervals of two days [of thirst]. *dvyahaṃ tarṣam* — With intervals of two days [of thirst]. Why is it said "after *asu* and *tṛṣ*" (*asutṛṣa*)? Example: *dvyaham upoṣya bhuṅkte* — Having fasted for two days, he eats. Why is it said "in the case of time-periods" (*kāleṣu*)? Example: *pañca piṇḍān atyasya jalaṃ pibati* — Having thrown five mouthfuls [of food] aside, he drinks water. Why is it said "when a cessation is understood" (*vicchede*)? Example: *ahar atyasyeṣūn gataḥ* — He went having thrown his arrows aside for a day [without using them]. [The rule *nāmni grahādiśaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.150) applies here.]

When the word *nāman* ending in the accusative case is used as an *upapada*, the suffix *ṇamul* is applied after the roots *grah* and *ā-diś*. Examples: *nāmagrāhaṃ dadāti* (he gives while pronouncing the name); *nāmāni grāhaṃ dadāti*; *nāmādeśaṃ dadāti*; *nāmāny ādeśaṃ dadāti*. As for *nīcaiḥkāram ācaṣṭe* (he speaks in a low voice) and *uccaiḥkāram ācaṣṭe* (he speaks loudly), these are established by means of the suffix *ghañ*. Furthermore, the suffix *ktvā* also occurs: *nīcaiḥ kṛtvā*, *nīcaiḥkṛtya*. Likewise: *tiryakkāram*, *tiryak kṛtvā*, *tiryakkṛtya*. *Mukhataḥkāram*, *mukhataḥ kṛtvā*, *mukhataḥkṛtya*.

Having become manifest from the mouth, having become manifest from the mouth, having become manifest from the mouth; having made manifold, having made manifold, having made manifold; having made twofold, having made twofold, having made twofold; having become silent, having become silent, having become silent; having become following after, having become following after, he stands having become following after.

"He is able to eat," "he dares to eat," "he knows how to eat," "he is weary of eating," "he strives to eat," "he begins to eat," "he proceeds to eat," "he obtains [the means] to eat," "he is eager to eat," "he deserves to eat," "there is [opportunity] to eat," "it exists to eat"—in these cases, the suffix *tumun* is indeed established by the rule *tumun bhāve kriyāyāṃ tadarthāyām* (Pāṇini 3.3.10). Likewise: "he is capable of eating" (*pārayati bhoktum*), "he has the power to eat" (*prabhavati bhoktum*).

It is established that [the suffixes] *prabhuḥ*, *samarthaḥ*, *paryāptaḥ*, and *alaṃ* occur everywhere with the root *bhū* (to become), as in: "he becomes able to eat," "he becomes capable of eating," "he becomes sufficient for eating," and "he becomes fit for eating. This is just as one says: "the mind is for eating" (*bhoktuṃ manaḥ*), "the ear is for hearing" (*śrotuṃ śrotram*), "the eye is for seeing" (*draṣṭuṃ cakṣuḥ*), "the bow is for fighting" (*yoddhuṃ dhanuḥ*); or "he is dull-witted for speaking" (*vaktuṃ jaḍaḥ*), "he is slow for going" (*gantuṃ mandaḥ*), "he is lazy for acting" (*kartum alasaḥ*). However, the actual utterance depends upon the speaker. The third quarter of the first chapter is completed.
*laḥ*, *tiptasjhisipthasthamipvasmastātāṃjhathāsāthāṃdhvamiṭvahimahiṅ* (Pāṇini 1.4.1).

In place of the *lakāra* of the *laḍ*-class and others, the substitutes *tiP* and so forth occur. The letter *p* is for the purpose of the operations pertaining to a *pit* suffix. The letter *ṭ* serves as an indicator (*cihna*) for the rule *iṭo 't* (Pāṇini 1.4.38). The letter *ṇ* is for the purpose of forming the *pratyāhāra* *tiṅ*. [The forms are: *pacati*, *pacataḥ*, *pacanti*; *pacasi*, *pacathaḥ*, *pacatha*; *pacāmi*, *pacāvaḥ*, *pacāmaḥ*. *pacate*, *pacete*, *pacante*; *pacase*, *pacethe*, *pacadhve*; *pace*, *pacāvahe*, *pacāmahe*. [By the rule] *ata ātaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.4.2), [the substitution of *i* occurs].

Therefore, the letter *i* is substituted for the letter *ā* of the *tiṅ* suffixes that follow [the vowel *a*]. Examples: *pacete*, *pacethe*; *pacetām*, *pacethām*. Why is it said "after *a*" (*ataḥ*)? [Consider: *dadāte*, *dadhāte*. Because of the mention of the base form (*prakṛtigrahaṇāt*), this substitution does not occur here: *pacāni*.
By the rule *jho 'ntaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.4.3), the letter *jha* of the *tiṅ* suffixes is replaced by the letter *ant*. Examples: *pacanti*, *pacante*; *yajanti*, *yajante*; *yajantu*, *yajantām*.
From a reduplicated [root] (1.4.4):
after a reduplicated root, the substitute *ad* is applied in place of the *jh* of the *tiṅ* suffixes. Examples: *juhvati*, *bibhyati*; *juhvatu*.
From the five beginning with *jakṣ* (1.4.5).

The substitution of *ad* occurs for the letter *jh* following these five roots: *jakṣ*, *jāgṛ*, *daridra*, *cakās*, and *śās*. Examples: *jakṣati*, *jāgrati*, *daridrati*, *cakāsati*, *śāsati*. Why "following these five"? [Consider: *dviṣanti*. (1.4.6) *taṅy anataḥ*: The substitution of *ad* occurs for the letter *jh* following a root that does not end in *a*, when it is followed by an affix belonging to the *taṅ* class. Examples: *lunate*, *lunatām*; *punate*, *punatām*. Why "not ending in *a*"? [Consider: *pacante*.
Pāṇini 1.4.7: *śīṅo rat* — For the letter *jha* following the root *śīṅ*, the substitute *ra* is applied. [Examples: *śerate*, *śeratām*, *aśerata*.
Pāṇini 1.4.8: *vetter vā* — [The substitute *ra* is optionally applied] after the root *vid*.

The substitution of *ra* optionally occurs for the letter *jha* that follows a root ending in *v*. Thus: *saṃvidrate*, *saṃvidate*. Why "having a *luk*-suffix"? So that it does not apply to the root *vid* (to find): [in *vindante*, there is no substitution]. Only when *taṅ* (the *ātmanepada* endings) follows: [in *vidanti*, there is no substitution]. Regarding *liṭa irac* (Pāṇini 7.2.69):
the substitution of *irac* occurs for the letter *jha* that is a substitute for *liṭ*. Thus: *pecire*, *śekire*. Only when *taṅ* follows: [in *pecuḥ*, there is no substitution].
For that [element], namely the *takāra* which is a substitute for *liṭ*, there is the substitution of *eś*. [Examples: *pece*, *śeke*.
For those not belonging to the *taṅ* [class], there are the substitutes *ṇal*, *atus*, *us*, *thal*, *atha*, *us*, *ṇal*, *vam*, and *ma*. (Pāṇini 1.4.11)

For those substitutes of *liṭ* that are not included in *taṅ*, the substitutes beginning with *ṇal* occur: *papāca*, *pecatuḥ*, *pecuḥ*; *papaktha*, *pecitha*, *pecathuḥ*, *peca*; *papāca*, *peciva*, *pecima*. According to Pāṇini 1.4.12, *vido laṭo vā*: for the substitutes of *laṭ* following the root *vid*, the substitutes beginning with *ṇal* optionally occur when they are not included in *taṅ*. Thus: *veda*, *vidatuḥ*, *viduḥ*; *vettha*, *vidathuḥ*, *vida*; *veda*, *vidva*, *vidma*. And [when the *taṅ* substitutes are used], they do not occur: *vetti*, *vittaḥ*, *vidanti*; *vetsi*, *vitthaḥ*, *vittha*; *vedmi*, *vidvaḥ*, *vidmaḥ*.

(1.4.13) *bruvaḥ pañcānām ādita āha ca*: For the five [personal endings] following the root *brū*, which are not of the *ātmanepada* (*ataṅ*), the first five substitutes beginning with *ṇal* optionally occur, and for the root *brū*, the substitute *āha* also occurs. [Examples: *āha*, *āhatuḥ*, *āhuḥ*, *āttha*, *āhathuḥ*. And [the regular forms] do not occur: *bravīti*, *brūtaḥ*, *bruvanti*, *bravīṣi*, *brūthaḥ*. Why "of the five"? [To exclude: *brūtha* (2nd person plural). Why "the first"? [So that it does not apply] to the subsequent [endings]. (1.4.14) *āto ṇala auḥ*: For the root ending in *ā*, the substitute *au* occurs in place of *ṇal*.
The substitution of *au* occurs for the *ṇal* suffix following a verbal root ending in the vowel *ā*. For example: *papau*, *tasthau*.

By the rule *ṭittaṅām et* (Pāṇini 1.4.15), the substitution of *e* occurs for the final sound of the *taṅ* suffixes that are substitutes for a *ṭit* *l*-suffix. For example: *pacate*, *pacante*, *pacadhve*. Why is it specified as "ending in *ṭit*"? [Consider: *apacata*.

(1.4.16) *āmaḥ*: For the *āna* belonging to [an affix] characterized by *ṭi* or *l*, *e* is substituted. [Examples: *pacete*, *pacethe*. (1.4.17) *thāsaḥ se*: [In the same context, for the *thās* of the second person singular, *se* is substituted.]
In place of *thās*, which belongs to the *ṭi* class, there is the substitution of *se*. [Example: *pacase*.
Regarding *luṭ*: "In place of the first three substitutes of *luṭ*, there are the substitutions *ḍā*, *rau*, and *ras*. [Examples: *paktā*, *paktārau*, *paktāraḥ*.

For the *taṅ* [ātmanepada] substitutes of the *luṅ* [aorist], the first three also undergo the substitutions *ḍā*, *rau*, and *ras*. [Examples: *adhyetā*, *adhyetārau*, *adhyetāraḥ*. Due to the indicative mark (*liṅga*) beginning with *eś*, there is an absence of the substitution of *et*.
*Loṭa er uḥ* (1.4.20).
The substitution of *u* occurs for the *i* that is the substitute of the *loṭ* [imperative] ending. [Examples: *pacatu*, *pacantu*.

By the rule *ser hiṅ* (Pāṇini 1.4.21), the substitute *hiṅ* occurs for the *sip* [second person singular imperative] ending. [Examples: *juhudhi*, *lunīhi*. The letter *ṅ* is for the purpose of indicating that [the suffix] is not *pit*.

*āśiṣi tuhyos tātaṅ vā* (1.4.22): In the domain of benediction (*āśis*), the *tātaṅ* substitute optionally occurs for the [suffixes] *tu* and *hi*, which are related to the imperative (*loṭ*). Thus: *jīvatāt bhavān*, *jīvatu bhavān*; *kurutāt tvam*, *kuru tvam*.
The substitute *mip* of the imperative (*loṭ*) takes the substitute *āni*. [Examples: *pacāni*, *karavāṇi*.
According to Pāṇini 1.4.24, *ām* is substituted for the *e* of the imperative. [Examples: *pacatām*, *pacetām*, *pacantām*.
Regarding *svo vāmau* (1.4.25):
for the phoneme *e* that follows the *sakāra* and *vakāra* which are substitutes for the imperative (*loṭ*), the replacements *va* and *am* respectively occur. [Examples: *pacasva*, *pacadhvam*.
Regarding *iḍādīnām aip* (1.4.26): [the replacement *aip* occurs for the phoneme *e*] of those beginning with *iṭ*.

In place of *iṭ* and the following suffixes belonging to the imperative (*loṭ*), *eta* and *aip* are substituted. [Examples: *karavai*, *karavāvahai*, *karavāmahai*. The letter *p* is for the purpose of excluding *eṅ*.

By Pāṇini 1.4.27, *ṭāp* is substituted after the suffixes *v* and *mū* belonging to the imperative. [Examples: *karavāva*, *karavāma*; *karavāvahai*, *karavāmahai*. The letter *ṭ* is for the purpose of indicating that this is a substitute rule (*ādeśavidhi*), while the letter *p* is for the purpose of preventing the application of *eṅ*.
(1.4.28) *tasthasthānāṃ tāntantā ṅitaś ca*:

For the substitutes *tas*, *thas*, and *tha* belonging to *ṅit* *lakāras* and for those of the *loṭ* [mood], the substitutes *tām*, *tam*, and *ta* respectively occur. Examples: *apacatām*, *apacatam*, *apacata*; *pacatām*, *pacatam*, *pacata*.
(1.4.29) *vasmasor lopaḥ*: There is elision (*lopa*) of the suffixes *vas* and *mas*.
There is elision of the final [element] of the *vas* and *mas* endings of the *ṅit* *l*-suffixes and of the imperative (*loṭ*). [Examples: *apacāva*, *apacāma*; *pacāva*, *pacāma*.

According to Pāṇini 1.4.30 (*ito ’taṅi*), there is elision of the *ikāra* (*i*) belonging to those *ṅit* *l*-suffixes that do not pertain to the *taṅ* (middle voice). [Examples: *apacat*, *apacan*; *akariṣyat*, *akariṣyan*.
*mipo ’m* (Pāṇini 1.4.31): For the *lakāra*s marked with the *ṅ*-sign, the substitution of *am* occurs in place of *mip*. [Examples: *akaravam*, *akārṣam*, *akariṣyam*.
*liṅaḥ sīyuṭ* (Pāṇini 1.4.32).

The augment *sīyuṭ* is applied to the substitutes of the optative (*liṅ*). [Examples: *pakṣīṣṭa*, *yakṣīṣṭa*. Regarding Pāṇini 1.4.33, *yāsuṭ ataṇaḥ kit*: the augment *yāsuṭ* is applied to a substitute of the optative that is not marked with *taṅ* (i.e., not an *ātmanepada* ending), and it is treated as having the *kit* designation. [Examples: *bhūyāt*, *bhūyāstām*, *bhūyāsuḥ*. Why does the rule say "not marked with *taṅ*" (*ataṅ*)? [Consider: *laviṣīṣṭa*.

(1.4.34) *ṅid anāśiṣi*: In a context other than a benediction (*āśis*), the *liṅ* suffix takes the augment *yāsuṭ* marked with the *ṅit* designation. Examples: *yajet*, *yajetām*, *yajeyuḥ*. Why "in a context other than a benediction"? [Counter-example: *ijyāt*. [The rule applies] only when the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) markers are absent: *yajeta*. (1.4.35) *ata iy*: [The substitution of *iy* for *yāsuṭ* occurs] after a short *a*.

Therefore, the substitution of *iy* occurs for the *yāsuṭ* augment that follows [the suffix *liṅ*]. Examples: *pacet*, *pacetām*, *paceyuḥ*. Why does it say "following *at*" (*ataḥ*)? [Consider: *kuryāt*. It must be specified as "not in the benedictive" (*anāśiṣi*): [consider] *cikīrṣyāt*.

By the rule *so lopo 'nantyasya* (Pāṇini 1.4.36), there is elision of the non-final *s* of the *liṅ* suffix. Examples: *kuryāt*, *kuryātām*. Why does it say "non-final" (*anantyasya*)? [Consider: *kuryuḥ*. It must be specified as "not in the benedictive" (*anāśiṣi*): [consider] *bhūyāstām*, *bhūyāsuḥ*.
*jhasya ran* (Pāṇini 1.4.37): For the *jh* that is a substitute for *liṅ*, the substitution of *ran* occurs. [Examples: *paceran*, *pakṣīran*.
*iṭo 't* (Pāṇini 1.4.38).
The augment *iṭ* undergoes the substitution of *ad* in place of the *liṅ* suffix. [Examples: *paceya*, *pakṣīya*.
According to Pāṇini 1.4.39 (*suṭ tathoḥ*), the augment *suṭ* is applied to the *takāra* and *thakāra* of the *liṅ* suffix. [Examples: *pakṣīṣṭa*, *pakṣīyāstām*, *pakṣīṣṭhāḥ*.
Regarding *jher jus* (Pāṇini 1.4.40):
*jus* is the substitute for *jhi* after the optative (*liṅ*). Examples: *paceyuḥ*, *kuryuḥ*. Regarding *sicaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.4.41).
The substitution of *jus* occurs for the following *jhi*. For example: *akārṣuḥ*. [Pāṇini 3.4.109] *ātaḥ*:

the substitution of *jus* occurs for *jhi* following only that which ends in long *ā*, from which the *sic* suffix has been elided. For example: *aduḥ*, *adhuḥ*. It does not occur after forms that do not end in long *ā*: *abhūvan*.

(1.4.43) *laṅo dviṣaś ca vā*: After the root *dviṣ* and after a verbal base ending in long *ā*, the substitution of *jus* for the *jhi* of the *laṅ* occurs optionally. Examples: *adviṣuḥ*, *adviṣan*; *ayuḥ*, *ayān*. (1.4.44) *vidaḥ*: [The substitution of *jus* for the *jhi* of the *laṅ* occurs] after the root *vid*.
In the case of *vida* meaning "to know," the substitution of *jus* for the *jhi* ending of the *laṅ* occurs invariably due to the division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*). Example: *aviduḥ*.

By the rule *ati* (Pāṇini 3.4.45), *jus* is substituted for the *jhi* ending following the *laṅ* after reduplicated roots and after the group of roots beginning with *jakṣ*. Examples: *abibharuḥ*, *abibhayuḥ*, *ajāgaruḥ*.
*Taṅānā yathāpāṭham* (1.4.46):

*taṅ* (the ātmanepada endings) and *āna* (the present middle participle suffix) follow a verbal root intended for action (*kriyārtha*) according to their respective order in the grammatical recitation; e.g., *vardhate*, *vardhamānaḥ*; *vartate*, *vartamānaḥ*.
*Bhāvāpyayoḥ* (1.4.47).

The *taṅ* (ātmanepada) and *āna* (passive) affixes occur when the meaning is either the state (*bhāva*) or that which is pervaded by it (*tadvyāpya*). Examples: *bhūyate*, *bhūyamānam*; *kriyate kaṭaḥ*, *kriyamāṇaḥ kaṭaḥ*. The preceding and following rules prescribe [these affixes] when the agent (*kartṛ*) is intended.
By the rule *ṅitaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.48), *taṅ* and *āna* affixes occur after roots marked with the indicator *ṅ* when they have the sense of action (*kriyārtha*). Examples: *pāpacyate*, *pāpacyamānaḥ*.

In the sense of *vinimaya* (1.4.49)—that is, when there is an exchange of actions—the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) and *āna* (passive) suffixes occur after a verb denoting an action. Examples: *vyatilunate*, *vyatipunate*.
However, this does not apply to verbs meaning motion (*gati*), injury (*hiṃsā*), sound (*śabda*), or the root *has* (to laugh), as stated in 1.4.50.

When there is an exchange of actions (*kriyāvinimaya*), the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) and *āna* (passive) suffixes do not occur after roots meaning "to go" (*gati*) and the like, even when they are in the present tense. Examples: *vyatigacchanti*, *vyatighnanti*, *vyatijalpanti*, *vyatihasanti*. How is it that [one says] *vyatiharante bhāram* ("they exchange the burden") and *vyativahante bhāram* ("they carry the burden across")? These two [roots] do not mean "to go. What then? They mean "to cause to reach another place. Similarly, in *saṃpraharante rājānaḥ* ("the kings strike together"), the root *hṛ* does not have the sense of "injury" (*hiṃsā*).

However, when *itaretara*, *anyonya*, and *paraspara* are used in conjunction [with a verb], because the reciprocal exchange of action (*kriyāvinimaya*) is already expressed by another word, the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) and *āna* (passive) suffixes do not occur. For example: *itaretarasya vyatilunanti*, *anyonyasya vyatilunanti*, *parasparasya vyatilunanti*. Regarding the rule *ner viśaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.17): after the prefix *ni*, the roots *viś* take the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) and *āna* (passive) suffixes. Examples: *niviśate*, *nyaviśata*. Why is there a mention of the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhyā*) in the rule? [To show that the prefix must be immediately preceding]; as in: *madhuni viśanti bhramarāḥ* ("Bees enter the honey").
(1.4.52) *parivyavāt krīñaḥ*: After the roots beginning with *pari*, the suffixes *taṅ* and *āna* occur after the root *krī*. [Examples: *parikrīṇīte*, *vikrīṇīte*, *avakrīṇīte*.
(1.4.53) *viparābhyāṃ jeḥ*: [The suffixes *taṅ* and *āna* occur] after the root *ji* when preceded by *vi* or *parā*.

By these two [rules], *taṅ* and *āna* affixes occur after the verb *ji* when it is qualified by [the prepositions] *vi* and *parā*. Thus: *vijayate*, *parājayate*. How is it that in [sentences like] *bahuvi jayati vanam* ("he conquers the forest extensively") and *parā jayati senā* ("the army conquers"), [the *taṅ* affixes do not occur]? In these cases, the verb *ji* is not qualified by the words *vi* and *parā*. Alternatively, here there is the inclusion of only those [prepositions] listed in the *prādi* group, because they occur in mutual association (*sāhacarya*). *Āṅo daḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.25): After the root *dā* preceded by *āṅ*, *taṅ* and *āna* affixes occur. Thus: *ādatte*.

(1.4.55) *na svaprasāraṇe*: When the root *dā* (to give) occurs with the vowel substitution (*prasāraṇa*) [of *ā* for *i*], the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) and *āna* (passive) endings do not occur, provided that this *prasāraṇa* pertains to itself. Examples: *āsyaṃ vyādadāti* (he opens his mouth); *vipādikāṃ vyādadāti* (he opens a sore on the foot); *nadī kūlaṃ vyādadāti* (the river opens its bank). Why is the word *sva* ("its own") mentioned? [Counter-example: *vyādadate pipīlikāḥ pataṅgasya mukham* (the ants open the mouth of the moth). (1.4.56) *gameḥ kṣāntau*: [The *taṅ* endings are used after the root *gam*] in the sense of forbearance.

The *taṅ* (middle voice) and *āna* (passive) affixes occur after the causative (*ṇi*) of the root *gam*, when it signifies "to wait" (*kṣānti*). Example: *āgamayasva tāvat* ("Wait for a moment"). Why specify "when signifying to wait"? [Counter-example: *āgamayati* ("He causes to come"). Regarding *anu-pracchaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.4.57):
the *taṅ* and *āna* affixes occur after the roots *nau* preceded by *āṅ* and *praccha*. Examples: *ānute śṛgālaḥ* ("The jackal howls") and *āpṛcchate gurūn* ("He takes leave of his teachers").

*krīḍo ’nuparibhyāṃ ca* (Pāṇini 1.4.58): When the root *krīḍ* is joined with *anu*, *pari*, or *āṅ*, the *taṅ* suffixes (the middle voice endings) are employed. Examples: *anukrīḍate*, *parikrīḍate*, *ākrīḍate*. Why does it not occur here: *māṇavakam anu krīḍati* ("He plays after the boy")? Because in this case, the root *krīḍ* is not joined with the prefix *anu*; therefore, [the *taṅ* suffixes] will not apply. *samo ’kūjane* (Pāṇini 1.4.59).

After the root *krīḍ* preceded by the prefix *sam*, the *taṅ* and *āna* affixes occur when it does not mean "making a sound. Example: *saṃkrīḍate*. Why "not making a sound"? [Objection: *saṃkrīḍanti śakaṭāni* ("the carts play together"). How is [the form] *śikṣate* derived? *Śikṣi* is indeed one that possesses the *taṅ* and *āna* affixes. How is *śikṣati* derived? It means "he desires to be able," thus *śikṣati*. *Apaskiraḥ* (Pāṇini 1.4.60): After the root *kṛ* preceded by *apa* and accompanied by the augment *suṭ*, the *taṅ* and *āna* affixes occur. Example: *apaskirate vṛṣabho hṛṣṭaḥ* ("the bull, being joyful, digs up [the earth]"). *apaskirate kukkuṭo bhakṣārthī* ("the cock, seeking food, digs up"). *apaskirate śvā nivāsārthī* ("the dog, seeking a dwelling, digs up"). Why "preceded by *apa*"? [Objection: *upaskiranto lunanti Madrakāḥ* ("the Madrakas cut while digging around"). Why "accompanied by *suṭ*"? [Objection: *apakirati*.

Regarding *hṛñ* in the sense of habitual movement (Pāṇini 1.4.61): when the root *harati* signifies habitual movement, the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) and *āna* (passive) suffixes are employed. Example: *paitṛkam aśvā anuharante* ("the horses habitually follow their father's way"). Why is "movement" (*gati*) mentioned? [Counter-example: *pitaram anuharati* ("he resembles his father").
Regarding *nāth* in the sense of benediction (Pāṇini 1.4.62).

The *taṅ* (ātmanepada) and *āna* (the affix *ānaC*) occur after the verb *nāth* when it signifies a blessing (*āśis*). Example: *sarpiṣo nāthate* ("he hopes for ghee"). Why "when signifying a blessing"? Observe: *māṇavakam upanāthati* ("he entreats the boy [for instruction]").

(1.4.63) After the root *śap*, when it has the sense of making a curse (*śapatha*), the *taṅ* and *āna* occur. Example: *Devadattāya śapate* ("he curses Devadatta"). In other cases: *Devadattaṃ śapati* ("he reviles Devadatta").
*sthaḥ pratijñā-nirṇaya-prakāśaneṣu* (1.4.64):

When the meanings of promise (*pratijñā*), determination (*nirṇaya*), and manifestation (*prakāśana*) are understood from the root *sthā*, the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) endings and the suffix *āna* occur. He maintains the doctrine that sound is eternal (*nityaṃ śabdam ātiṣṭhate*). The dispute rests with you (*tvayi tiṣṭhate vivādaḥ*). The maiden remains faithful to the students (*tiṣṭhate kanyā chātrebhyaḥ*). *saṃ-vi-prāvāt* (1.4.65).

After the root *sthā* preceded by *sam*, *vi*, *pra*, or *ava*, the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) and *āna* (passive) affixes occur: *saṃtiṣṭhate*, *vitiṣṭhate*, *pratiṣṭhate*, *avatiṣṭhate*. By the rule *udo ’nūrdhvehāyām* (Pāṇini 1.3.24), after the root *sthā* preceded by *ud*, when it does not signify an upward physical movement (*anūrdhvecchā*), the *taṅ* and *āna* affixes occur: *muktāv uttiṣṭhate* ("he emerges from his bonds"). Why "not upward" (*anūrdhva*)? [Counter-example: *āsanād uttiṣṭhati* ("he rises from his seat"). Why "in the sense of effort" (*īhāyām*)? [Counter-example: *asmād grāmāc chatam uttiṣṭhati* ("a hundred [coins] come out from this village").

(1.4.67) *upān mantreṇa*: After the root *sthā* preceded by the prefix *upa*, the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) endings occur when the instrument (*karaṇa*) is a mantra. Example: *sāvitryā upatiṣṭhate*. Why say "by a mantra"? [Counter-example: *aśvenopatiṣṭhati rājānam* ("He attends upon the king with a horse"). Why is there a mention of the third case (*tṛtīyā*)? [Counter-example: *sāvitrīm upatiṣṭhati* ("He attends upon the Sāvitrī [verse]"). (1.4.68) *pathyārādhanayoḥ*.

When the meanings of "path," "agent," or "propitiation" are understood, the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) endings occur after the root *sthā* preceded by the prefix *upa*. This path leads to (*upatiṣṭhate*) Sṛughna; he propitiates the sun (*ādityam upatiṣṭhate*); he attends upon the charioteers (*rathikān upatiṣṭhate*); he attends upon the high officials (*mahāmātrān upatiṣṭhate*).

By the rule *vā lipsāyām* (Pāṇini 1.3.69), when the sense of "desire to obtain" is understood, the *taṅ* endings occur optionally after the root *sthā* preceded by *upa*. A beggar attends upon the family of a Brahmin (*upatiṣṭhate*), or [alternatively], he attends upon it (*upatiṣṭhati*).

(1.4.70) *Avyāpyāt*: After the root *sthā* preceded by the prefix *upa*, when it is devoid of an object (*avyāpya*), the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) and *āna* (passive) suffixes occur. Example: *bhojanakāle upatiṣṭhate* ("He attends at the time of eating"). Why "when devoid of an object"? [Consider: *rājānam upatiṣṭhati* ("He stands before the king").

(1.4.71) *Samo gamṛchiprachisvṛśruvettyartidṛśaḥ*: [The *taṅ* and *āna* suffixes occur] after the roots *gam*, *ṛ*, *chi*, *prach*, *svṛ*, *śru*, *vid*, *ṛ*, *tṛ*, and *dṛś* when preceded by the prefix *sam*.

The *taṅ* (middle voice endings) and *āna* (the suffix *āna*, forming the present participle) occur after the roots *gam* and others when preceded by the prefix *sam*. Examples: *saṃgacchate*, *samṛcchate*, *saṃpṛcchate*, *saṃsvarate*, *saṃśṛṇute*, *saṃvitte*. Because of the specific mention of *vetti* ("he knows"), the form *saṃvindati* does not occur. Examples: *samārata*, *saṃpaśyate*. Only when [the action] is not directed toward an object (*avyāpyāt*): *saṃgacchati suhṛdam* ("he meets a friend").

*(Pāṇini 1.4.72) prādibhyo 'sūho vā:* The *taṅ* and *āna* optionally occur after the roots *as* ("to throw") and *ūh* ("to push") when preceded by prefixes beginning with *pra*. Examples: *nirasyate*, *nirasyati*; *samūhate*, *samūhati*. Only when [the action] is not directed toward an object: *nirasyati śatrūn* ("he casts out the enemies"); *samūhati padārthān* ("he pushes aside the objects").

(1.4.73) *āṅo yamahanaḥ svāṅgāpyāc ca*: After the roots *yam* and *han* preceded by the prefix *āṅ*, when they do not have an external object (*avyāpya*) or when they have a body part as their object (*svāṅgāpya*), the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) endings are employed. Examples: *āyacchate*, *āhate*. *āyacchate pādam* ("he stretches out his foot"), *āhate udaram* ("he strikes his belly"). When there is another object: *āyacchati rajjum* ("he pulls the rope"), *āhanti vṛṣalam* ("he strikes the low-born man"). Why is the mention of "body part" (*sva*) necessary? [Consider: *Devadatto Yajñadattasya pāṇim āhanti* ("Devadatta strikes Yajñadatta's hand").
(1.4.74) *vyudastapaḥ*: [The *taṅ* endings are used after the root *tap* preceded by *vi* or *ud*.]

The affixes *taṅ* (the middle voice endings) and *āna* (the passive marker) occur after the root *tap* when it is not preceded by the prefixes *vi-* or *ud-*, even when its object is one's own limb (*svāṅga*). Examples: *vitapate*, *uttapate*. *Vitapate pāṇim*, *uttapate pāṇim*. Only when it is "not preceded by *vi-* or *ud-*" and "its object is one's own limb": *ādityaḥ pṛthivīṃ vitapati* (the sun heats the earth); *suvarṇakāraḥ suvarṇam uttapati* (the goldsmith heats the gold); *Devadatto Yajñadattasya hastam uttapati* (Devadatta heats Yajñadatta’s hand). Why "preceded by *vi-* or *ud-*"? [Observe: *nitapati*. Regarding *tapaāpyāt* (Pāṇini 1.4.75): the affixes *taṅ* and *āna* occur after *tap* when that which is heated (*tapaḥ*) is its object (*āpya*). Example: *tapyate tapas tāpasaḥ* (the ascetic performs penance). The meaning is "he performs penance."

Pāṇini 1.4.76: *ni-sam-vi-ūpebhyo hvaḥ*. After the roots *hve* preceded by *ni*, *sam*, *vi*, or *upa*, the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) endings are employed. Examples: *nihvayate*, *saṃhvayate*, *vihvayate*, *upahvayate*. Pāṇini 1.4.77: *spardhāyām āṅaḥ*. [The *taṅ* endings are used after *hve*] when preceded by *āṅ* in the sense of rivalry.

The *taṅ* (middle voice) and *āna* (passive) affixes occur after the root *hve* preceded by the prefix *ā*, when it signifies rivalry. Example: *mallo mallam āhvayate* ("one wrestler challenges another"). Why "when signifying rivalry"? Counter-example: *gopālako gām āhvayati* ("the cowherd calls the cow").
(Also, the *taṅ* affixes occur after the root *kṛ* when used in the senses of pointing out, throwing, serving, acting with violence, exertion, speaking, and employment. Pāṇini 1.4.78.

The *taṅ* (ātmanepada) and *āna* (passive) endings occur after the root *kṛ* when it has the meanings of "indicating" (*sūcana*) and so forth. "Indicating" (*sūcana*) is the disclosure of another's faults motivated by malice; "disparaging" (*avakṣepaṇa*) is contempt; "service" (*sevā*) is the acquisition of another's wealth; "recklessness" (*sāhasa*) is that which is done without prior reflection; "effort" (*yatna*) is the imparting of a new quality to something already existing; "discourse" (*kathā*) is speaking; and "utilization" (*upayoga*) is the application for a purpose such as religious duty (*dharma*). Regarding "indicating": *ayam imam utkurute*. The meaning is "he indicates. Regarding "disparaging": *śyeno vartakām apakurute*. (The hawk disparages the quail.)

The meaning is "he reviles. In the sense of service (*sevā*): *mahāmātrān prakurute*, *gaṇakān prakurute*; the meaning is "he serves. In the sense of violence (*sāhasa*): *paradārān prakurute*; the meaning is "he acts with violence toward them. In the sense of effort (*yatna*): *kāṇḍaguṇasyopaskurute*, *edhodakasyopaskurute*; the meaning is "he bestows another quality upon it. In the sense of narration (*kathā*): *janavādān prakurute*; the meaning is "he tells [them] extensively. In the sense of application (*upayoga*): *śataṃ prakurute*; the meaning is "he applies a hundred [coins] for the sake of dharma and so forth.
Regarding *adhi* in the sense of capability (*śakti*), [Pāṇini 1.4.79].

The *taṅ* (middle voice) and *āna* (passive) suffixes occur after the root *kṛ* when preceded by the prefix *adhi*, provided it denotes capability (*śakti*). Example: *taṃ hādhicakre*. Why "provided it denotes capability"? Observe: *adhikaroti*. [Rule 1.4.80: After the root *kṛ* preceded by the prefix *vi*, the *taṅ* and *āna* suffixes occur, provided that "sound" (*śabda*) is its object (*vyāpya*). Example: *kroṣṭā vikurute svarān*. Why "sound"? Observe: *vikaroti mṛdam*. Why "provided [it is] an object"? Observe: *śabdena matim vikaroti* ("he alters his mind by means of sound").
(1.4.81) *Avyāpyāt*:

after the root *kṛ* preceded by *vi*, when it is devoid of an object (*avyāpya*), the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) and *āna* (passive) suffixes occur. Example: *vikurvate saindhavāḥ*. The meaning is: "The Saindhava horses behave well; they gallop beautifully.

(1.4.82) *Pūjotsaṅgopanayanajñānabhṛtivyayavigaṇaneṣu niyaḥ*: After the root *ni*, the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) suffixes occur when [the action] refers to honoring, taking onto one's lap, leading away, knowing, maintaining, spending, or disregarding.

In senses such as "honoring" (*pūjā*) and so forth, the roots take the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) terminations. *Pūjā* means "to honor. For example: *nayate pāṇinir vyākaraṇe*. The meaning is that he attains honor. Also: *nayate cārvī lokāyate*. Here, *cārvī* refers to the intellect; because of its connection with that [intellect], the teacher is also called *cārvī*. He "leads" (*nayate*)—that is, he causes to be understood—the categories of existence in the *Lokāyata* system, having established them through logical arguments and taught them to his disciples. When these [categories] are thus established by reasonings, they become honored and respected.

*Utsaṅga* means lifting up or raising; *udānayate māṇavakam*. The meaning is that he lifts the boy, who was standing below, onto his lap. Regarding *upanayana*: *upanayana* is the action of a teacher (*ācārya*). He brings the boy near to himself by such a procedure that the one who leads him (*upanetṛ*) himself becomes the teacher. *Māṇavakam upanayate*. The meaning is that, making himself a teacher, he causes the boy to reach his own presence. *Jñāna* is the ascertainment of the object of knowledge (*prameya*).

*Kātyāyana* leads [students] in grammar; the meaning is that he determines the objects of knowledge (*prameya*). *Bhṛti* means wages. He brings laborers near; the meaning is that he draws them close by the payment of wages. *Vyaya* is the expenditure for religious duties and so forth. He expends a hundred; the meaning is that he applies it [to those purposes]. *Vigaṇanam* is the settlement of debts and the like. The Madrakas pay the tax (*kāram vinayante*); the meaning is that they discharge it. *Kāra* is simply *kara*, the portion to be taken by the king, which is assigned by farmers for the sake of protection. Why "in these [senses]"? [Because otherwise: he leads the goat to the village.

(1.4.83) *kartṛsthāmūrtāpyāt*: After a root whose object is situated in the agent (*kartṛstha*), is formless (*amūrta*)—that is, not solid—and is liquid (*āpya*), the suffixes *taṅ* and *āna* occur after the root *nī*. Examples: *krodhaṃ vinayate* ("he subdues his anger"); *manyuṃ vinayate* ("he subdues his resentment"). Why "situated in the agent"? Example: *Devadatto Yajñadattasya manyuṃ vinayati* ("Devadatta subdues Yajñadatta's resentment [for him]"). Why "formless"? Example: *gaṇḍuṃ vinayati* ("he removes a boil"). Why "liquid"? Example: *buddhyā vinayati* ("he leads by means of intelligence"). (1.4.84) *vṛttyutsāhatāyaneṣu kramaḥ*: The root *kram* takes the *taṅ* suffixes when it signifies subsistence (*vṛtti*), exertion (*utsāha*), or extension (*tāyana*).

The suffixes *taṅ* and *āna* occur after [the root] *kram* when the meanings are "proceeding" (*vṛtti*) and so forth. "Proceeding" (*vṛtti*) means absence of obstruction. "Zeal" (*utsāha*) is a mental factor (*caitasika-dharma*). "Expansion" (*tāyana*) means flourishing. In the sense of "proceeding": *ṛkṣasya kramate buddhiḥ*. The meaning is that his intellect is not obstructed. In the sense of "zeal": *vyākaraṇādhyayanāya kramate*. The meaning is that he exerts zeal. In the sense of "expansion": *nītimati śriyaḥ kramante*. Prosperities proceed toward one who possesses statesmanship; treatises proceed toward the wise. The meaning is that they flourish. [The rule continues: *paropāt* (Pāṇini 1.3.85).

When preceded by *parā* or *upa*, the roots beginning with *kram* take the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) and *āna* (passive) endings in the senses of "activity" (*vṛtti*) and so forth. For example: *parākramate*, *upakramate*. Why "preceded by *parā* or *upa*"? [Observe: *saṃkrāmati*. Why "in the senses of activity and so forth"? [Observe: *parākrāmati* (meaning "exerts effort"). Regarding *āṅo jyotirudgatau* (Pāṇini 1.4.86):

when preceded by *āṅ*, the root *kram* takes the *taṅ* and *āna* endings when it signifies the rising of a light. For example: *ākramate sūryaḥ* ("the sun rises"). Why "light" (*jyotis*)? [Observe: *ākrāmati dhūmaḥ* ("the smoke rises"). Why "rising" (*udgati*)? [Observe: *agnir indhanam ākrāmati* ("the fire consumes the fuel").

*veḥ pādābhyām* (1.4.87): After the prefix *vi-*, the *taṅ* and *āna* [terminations] are employed after the root *kram-* if that action is performed with the two feet. Example: *sādhu vikramate* ("He strides well"). Why "with the two feet"? Example: *aśvena vikrāmati* ("He strides with a horse"). *propād ārambhe* (1.4.88).

The *taṅ* (middle voice) and *āna* (passive) suffixes occur after the root *kram* when preceded by *pra* or *upa*, provided it signifies "commencement" (*ārambha*). Examples: *prakramate bhoktum* (he begins to eat), *upakramate bhoktum* (he begins to eat). Acceptance (*aṅgīkaraṇa*) is also considered a form of commencement. Example: *prakramate śuśrūṣām* (he undertakes service). Why specify "commencement"? Consider: *pūrvedyuḥ prakrāmati* (on the previous day he sets out); the meaning here is "he goes. *paredyur upakrāmati* (on the following day he sets out); the meaning here is "he comes. Alternatively, according to Pāṇini 1.4.89 (*aprāder vā*), the *taṅ* and *āna* suffixes optionally occur after *kram* when it is not preceded by a *prādi* prefix. Examples: *kramate* or *krāmati*. Why specify "not preceded by a *prādi*" (*aprādeḥ*)? Consider: *saṃkrāmati* (he moves together/ascends).

(1.4.90) *nihnave jñaḥ*: When the root *jñā* (to know) is used in the sense of concealment (*nihnava*), the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) and *āna* (passive) suffixes occur. Concealment (*nihnava*) means denial (*apahnava*) or evasion (*apalāpa*). Moreover, it occurs when preceded by a prefix (*sapratyaya*), not when used alone. Example: *śatam apajānīte*. The meaning is "he denies [having received] a hundred. Why say "in the sense of concealment"? [Consider: *na tvaṃ kiṃcid api jānāsi* ("you do not know anything at all"). (1.4.91) *avyāpyāt*: [The same applies] when [the verb] is not connected with an object (*avyāpya*).

The *taṅ* (ātmanepada) and *āna* (passive) suffixes occur after the root *jñā* when it is devoid of an object (*avyāpya*). Example: *sarpiṣo jānīte*. The meaning is: "He proceeds by means of ghee (*sarpiṣ*) as a stratagem. Since the activity is preceded by knowledge, the instrument such as ghee is intended to be expressed through its relationship [to the action], and thus the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is used. Why say "when devoid of an object"? Consider: *svareṇa putraṃ jānāti* ("He recognizes his son by his voice"). Regarding the rule *saṃprater asmṛtau* (Pāṇini 1.3.46): the *taṅ* and *āna* suffixes occur after the root *jñā* preceded by *sam* and *prati* when it does not mean "remembering" (*asmṛti*). Examples: *saṃjānīte*, *pratijānīte*. Why say "not remembering"? Consider: *mātuḥ saṃjānāti* ("He remembers his mother").

The *taṅ* (ātmanepada) and *āna* (passive) suffixes occur after the root *vad* when it has meanings such as "knowledge" (*jñāna*) and so forth. For example: *Patañjalir vyākaraṇe vadate*. The meaning is that he speaks with prior knowledge. Since speaking preceded by knowledge is the same as [speaking] for the sake of illumination (*bhāsana*), it need not be stated separately. With the sense of "effort" (*yatna*): *ko 'smin kṣetre vadate?* ("Who speaks in this field?"). With the sense of "persuasion" (*upacchandana*): *karmakarān upavadate* ("He persuades the laborers"); *paradārān upavadate* ("He seduces another's wife"). Regarding *anor avyāpyāt* (Pāṇini 1.3.79): the *taṅ* and *āna* suffixes occur after *vad* preceded by *anu* when it is not accompanied by an object (*avyāpya*). Example: *anuvadate Kaṭhaḥ Kālāpasya* ("The Kaṭha student repeats what was said by the Kālāpa teacher"). Why say "when not accompanied by an object"? Consider: *pūrvam eva yajur uditam anuvadati* ("He repeats the Yajurvedic text already spoken"). Here, because it is an object, the *parasmaipada* is used.

(1.4.95) *vimatau*: When expressing differing opinions, the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) and *āna* (passive) suffixes are used after the root *vad*. Example: *gehe vivadante* ("they dispute in the house"). (1.4.96) *vyaktaṃ sahoktau*: [The same applies] when expressing something clearly in the sense of accompaniment.

When words are uttered together with distinct articulation (*vyaktākṣara*), the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) endings occur. For example: *saṃpravadante grāmyāḥ* ("the villagers converse together"). Why "with distinct articulation"? Consider: *varatanu saṃpravadanti kukkuṭāḥ* ("O fair-limbed one, the cocks are crowing"). Why "when uttered together" (*sahoktau*)? Consider: *vadati brāhmaṇaḥ* ("the Brahmin speaks").
[And there is the rule: *tayor vā* (Pāṇini 1.4.97).

When there is disagreement (*vimati*), when [the action] is clearly manifest (*vyakta*), and when simultaneous utterance (*sahokti*) is intended for a single subject, the *taṅ* and *āna* suffixes optionally occur after the verb *vad*. Examples: *Vipravadante mauhūrtāḥ* / *vipravadanti mauhūrtāḥ* ("The astrologers disagree"). Only when there is disagreement: *saṃpravadante grāmyāḥ* ("The villagers talk together"). Only when it is clearly manifest: *vipravadanti śakunayaḥ* ("The birds chatter"). Only when there is simultaneous utterance: *ekaikaśo vipravadante mauhūrtāḥ* ("The astrologers speak one by one"). Regarding *ava-giraḥ* (Pāṇini 1.4.98): the *taṅ* and *āna* suffixes occur after the root *gṛ* preceded by *ava*. Example: *avagirate* ("He swallows"). Why "preceded by *ava*"? Observe: *girati* ("He swallows"). Because of the specific mention of the form *giraḥ*, it does not apply here: *avagṛṇāti* ("He repeats").

*samaḥ pratijñāyām* (1.4.99): When the sense of "promising" (*pratijñā*) is understood, the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) and *āna* (passive) suffixes occur after the root *gṛ* preceded by the prefix *sam*. Example: *śataṃ saṃgirate* ("He promises a hundred"). Why say "when promising"? Observe: *saṃgirati* ("He swallows"). Why say "after *sama*"? Observe: *śataṃ girati* ("He swallows a hundred"). *kirādiśranthagranthasanām āpye* (1.4.100): After the roots beginning with *kṝ*, as well as *śranth*, *granth*, and *san*, the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) suffixes occur when there is a recipient (*āpya*).

The *taṅ* (ātmanepada) and *āna* (the suffix *ānaC*) occur after roots beginning with *kṛ* and those beginning with *śranth*, when they have an implied object (*āpya*) and express the agent (*kartṛ*). The elephant grooms himself (*avakirate hastī svayam eva*). The garland unties itself (*śrathnīte mālā svayam eva*). The garland knots itself (*grathnīte mālā svayam eva*). The mat desires to be made (*cikīrṣate kaṭaḥ svayam eva*). Why is it said "when there is an implied object"? [Example: The elephant scatters [grass] for the mahout (*avakirati hastī hastipakam*). In the case of the *luṅ* (aorist), [the substitution of *iṭ* occurs] after a vowel (*acaḥ*), according to Pāṇini 1.4.101.

In the context of the *luṅ* (aorist), when the sense of pervasion (*vyāpya*) is present and the agent (*kartṛ*) is not ending in a vowel, the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) and *āna* (kṛt suffixes) occur. *ahauṣṭa haviḥ svayam eva* (the oblation offered itself). *ajeṣṭa rogaḥ svayam eva* (the disease cured itself). Why say "in the *luṅ*"? [So that] *juhuta* (they sacrifice) does not occur. Why say "not ending in a vowel" (*aca*)? [So that] *aghasta* (he ate) does not occur. Only when there is pervasion: *ahauṣīt* (he sacrificed). *snu-nam-aḥ svayam* (Pāṇini 1.3.102): After the roots *snu* and *nam*, the *taṅ* and *āna* occur when the agent is not prompted by another. *prasnute gauḥ svayam eva* (the cow secretes milk by herself). *namate daṇḍaḥ svayam eva* (the stick bends by itself). Why say "by herself" (*svayam*)? [So that] *prasnauti gaur dogdhuḥ kauśalena* (the cow secretes milk through the skill of the milker) [is not included]. *namati pallavo vātena* (the sprout bends because of the wind).

*sṛjaḥ śrāddhe* (Pāṇini 1.4.103): When the agent is endowed with faith (*śraddhā*), the suffixes *taṅ* (the ātmanepada endings) and *āna* (the present participle marker) are applied after the root *sṛj*. Example: *sasṛje mālāṃ dhārmikaḥ* ("The righteous man fashioned a garland [with devotion]"). Why "when endowed with faith"? Example: *sasarja mālāṃ mālikaḥ* ("The garland-maker fashioned a garland"). *śe śyan* (Pāṇini 1.4.104).

The affix *śyan* occurs after the root *sṛj* when it has the sense of "to weave" (*śrāddha*) and the agent (*kartṛ*) is expressed. Example: *dhārmikaḥ sṛjyate mālām* ("the virtuous man weaves a garland"). Only when it means "to weave": *mālikaḥ sṛjati mālām* ("the garland-maker makes a garland"). Regarding the rule *luṅi te ciṇ* (Pāṇini 3.1.60):

when the *luṅ* tense follows and the *ta*-affixes are present, the affix *ciṇ* occurs after *sṛj* when the agent is "one who weaves. Example: *asarji mālāṃ dhārmikaḥ* ("the virtuous man wove a garland"). Why specify "*ta*" (the *ta*-affixes)? Consider: *asṛkṣātāṃ mālāṃ dhārmikau* ("the two virtuous men wove a garland"; here the *ātām* affix is used). Only when it means "to weave": *vyatyasṛṣṭa mālāṃ mālikasamūhaḥ* ("the group of garland-makers interwove a garland"). How is the expression *māsaṃ yujyate brahmacārī* ("the student devotes himself for a month") explained? It is established by [the root] belonging to the *divādi* class.

*udaś caraḥ sāpyāt* (Pāṇini 1.4.106): After the root *car-* preceded by the prefix *ud-*, when it is connected with an object (*vyāpya*), the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) endings and the affix *ānaC* occur. Example: *geham uccarate*. Why "when connected with an object"? Consider: *dhūma uccarati*.
*samas tṛtīyāyuktāt* (Pāṇini 1.4.107): [The same applies] after the root *sam-* when it is connected with an instrument expressed by the third case.

When the verb *carati* is used with the prefix *sam*, the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) endings are employed provided it is joined with a word ending in the third case that qualifies the subject. Example: *rathena saṃcarate* ("he moves about by means of a chariot"). Why "with *sam*"? Observe: *rathena carati* ("he moves by means of a chariot"). Why "joined with a third-case word"? Observe: *ubhau lokau saṃcarasi imam cāmuṃ ca devalaka* ("O Devalaka, you move between both worlds, this one and that one").
[The rule continues: *dāṇaḥ sā cec caturthy-arthe* (Pāṇini 1.3.55).

The roots *dāṇ* (to give), *tan*, and *kṛñ* take the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) endings when joined with a word ending in the third case that is coreferential with the object, provided that this third case occurs in the sense of the fourth case (*saṃpradāna*). For example: *dāsyā saṃprayacchate*. This third case is used here because there is an intention to express the recipient as the instrument (*karaṇa*). Furthermore, this intention is a worldly one occurring only in the conduct of the unrefined (*aśiṣṭa*), for in that context, [the servant] is the most effective means (*sādhakatama*) [of the action]. Why specify "provided that it is in the sense of the fourth case"? Consider: *dāsyā saṃprayacchati bhikṣām* ("He gives alms to the slave girl"). [The rule applies] only when joined with a word in the third case; otherwise, as in *dāsyai saṃprayacchati bhikṣām* ("He gives alms to the slave girl"), the *taṅ* endings do not apply. [The root *dāṇ* takes the *taṅ* endings] in the sense of "marriage" (*upayama*) when referring to a wedding (*udvāha*). (Pāṇini 1.4.109)

When the root *yama* preceded by *upa* is used in the sense of "marrying," the *taṅ* (middle voice) and *āna* (periphrastic perfect suffix) affixes occur. Example: *kanyām upayacchate* ("he marries a girl"). Why specify "marrying"? [Counter-example: *śāṭakam upayacchati* ("he takes a cloth").

Regarding the rule *āmaḥ kṛñaḥ prāgvat* (Pāṇini 1.3.63): after the root *kṛ* followed by the suffix *ām*, the *taṅ* and *āna* affixes occur or do not occur according to how they were observed for the preceding root-form (*prakṛti*). Examples: *īhāṃcakre*, *īkṣāṃcakre*, *bibharāṃcakre*, *bibharāṃcakāra*, *jāgarāṃcakāra*. Why specify "*kṛñaḥ*"? [Counter-example: *īhāṃbabhūva*.
*sanaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.4.111):

In the section already stated and that which is about to be stated, the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) and *āna* (passive) suffixes occur after a root with the desiderative suffix *san*, just as they were observed for the original root (*prakṛti*). For example: from *ās* (to sit), *āsisiṣate*; from *bhuj* (to eat), *bubhukṣate*.
*smṛdṛśaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.4.112).

The *taṅ* (middle voice) and *āna* (desiderative suffix) affixes occur after the roots *smṛ* and *dṛś* when followed by the desiderative suffix *san*. Examples: *susmūrṣate*, *didṛkṣate*. (1.4.113) *ananor jñaḥ*: The *taṅ* and *āna* affixes occur after the root *jñā* when it follows the desiderative suffix *san* and is not preceded by the prefix *anu*. Example: *jijñāsate dharmam* ("he desires to know dharma"). Why say "not preceded by *anu*"? Consider: *putram anujijñāsati* ("he wishes to examine his son").

*Śruvo ’nāṅprateḥ* (1.4.114): After the root *śru*, when it is followed by the suffix *san* and is not preceded by *āṅ* or *prati*, the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) endings occur. Example: *śuśrūṣate gurūn* ("he desires to serve his teachers"). Why "not preceded by *āṅ* or *prati*"? [Counter-examples: *āśuśrūṣati*, *pratiśuśrūṣati*. *Śadeḥ śiti* (1.4.115): [The *taṅ* endings occur after the root *śad*] when a *śit* suffix follows.

In the domain of *śit* affixes, the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) and *āna* (passive) suffixes occur after the root *śad*. Example: *śīyate*. Why specify "in the domain of *śit*"? [Because otherwise it would apply to: *śatsyati*. *mṛṅ* takes *taṅ* and *āna* in the domains of *luṅ*, *liṅ*, and *śit* (Pāṇini 1.3.61). Examples: *amṛta* (domain of *luṅ*), *mṛṣīṣṭa* (domain of *liṅ*), *mriyate* (domain of *śit*). Why specify "in these [domains]"? [Because otherwise it would apply to: *mamāra*.

Pāṇini 1.4.117: *prāder ajādyantād yujer ayajñapātreṣu*. After prefixes (*prādi*) and after words beginning with vowels (*aja-*) or ending in vowels, the *taṅ* and *āna* suffixes (the middle voice endings) are employed following the root *yuj*, provided that its usage does not concern sacrificial vessels (*yajñapātra*). Examples: *upayuṅkte*, *niyuṅkte*, *udyuṅkte*, *prayuṅkte*. Why "after words beginning with vowels"? [Counter-example: *saṃyunakti*. Why "not concerning sacrificial vessels"? [Counter-example: *yajñapātrāṇi prayunakti*. Pāṇini 1.4.118: *samaḥ kṣṇuvaḥ*. [The *taṅ* and *āna* suffixes are employed after the root *kṣṇu* when preceded by the prefix *sam*.]
After the root *kṣṇu* preceded by *sam*, the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) endings occur: *saṃkṣṇute śastram* ("he sharpens the weapon"). [The rule] *bhujo 'pālane* (Pāṇini 1.3.66) [is also applied].

The *taṅ* affixes (the middle voice endings) occur after the root *bhuji* when it signifies "not protecting. He eats (*bhuṅkte*). Why "not protecting"? [Observe: "The king protects the earth" (*bhunakti pṛthivīṃ rājā*). In the examples "The elephant mounts itself" (*ārohayate hastī svayam eva*) and "The king shows himself" (*darśayate rājā svayam eva*), the *taṅ* affix occurs by virtue of Pāṇini 1.3.74 (*phalavati*). The fruit for him is comfort. Otherwise, he would be tormented by the mahouts, and the king would not delight his servants. Even in the case of insentient objects, there is a desire to express the fruit of the action, as in "He dries the rice in the sun" (*śoṣayate vrīhīn ātapa*); how much more so, then, in the case of sentient beings? [The rule] "After the causative suffix *ṇi*, the *taṅ* affixes occur after the roots *bhī* and *smi* when used in the sense of the instigator" (Pāṇini 1.3.68).

The *taṅ* (ātmanepada) endings and the *āna* suffix occur after a causative (*ṇic*) that follows those two roots which signify "frightening" (*bhīṣmi*) when used in a causal sense. Example: *muṇḍo bhīṣayate* ("He causes the shaven-headed man to be frightened"). Example: *jaṭilo vismāpayate* ("He causes the one with matted hair to be amazed"). Why specify "from a causer"? Consider: *kuñcikayainaṃ bhāyayati* ("He frightens him with a key"). Regarding the rule *gṛdhivañcyoḥ pralambhane* (Pāṇini 1.4.121): the *taṅ* endings and *āna* occur after the causatives of *gṛdh* and *vañc* when they signify "deceiving. Examples: *māṇavakaṃ gardhayate* ("He deceives the boy"). Example: *māṇavakaṃ vañcayate* ("He deceives the boy"). Why specify "deceiving"? Consider: *śvānaṃ gardhayati* ("He makes the dog greedy") and *ahiṃ vañcayati* ("He avoids the snake").

*liyaḥ pūjābhibhavayoś ca* (Pāṇini 1.4.122). When the sense of honoring (*pūjā*) is understood, or in the sense of overcoming (*abhibhava*)—that is, deception—the roots *lī* or *līṅ* followed by the causative suffix (*ṇic*) take the *ātmanepada* endings (*taṅ*). *jaṭābhir ālāpayate*. The meaning is: "He attains honor by means of his matted locks. *śyeno vartakām apalāpayate*. The meaning is: "The hawk overcomes the quail. *Kas tvām ullāpayate?* The meaning is: "Who deceives you? Why say "in [the senses of] honoring and so forth"? [Observe: *ghṛtaṃ vilīnayati* ("He melts the ghee"). *Mithyāyoge kṛño 'bhyāse* (Pāṇini 1.4.123). [When the root *kṛ* is used] in connection with a falsehood (*mithyāyoga*), provided there is repetition (*abhyāsa*), [the *ātmanepada* endings are used].

When used in conjunction with the word *mithyā*, the *taṅ* (middle voice) and *āna* (passive) suffixes occur after the root *kṛ* when it is followed by the causative marker (*ṇi*), provided there is repetition. Example: *padaṃ mithyā kārayate* ("He repeatedly makes the word incorrect"). Why "in conjunction with *mithyā*"? Example: *padaṃ sādhu kārayati* ("He makes the word correct"). Why "the root *kṛ*"? Example: *padaṃ mithyā vācayati* ("He causes the word to be spoken incorrectly"). Why "repetition"? Example: *sakṛt padaṃ mithyā kārayati* ("He makes the word incorrect once"). [Rule 1.4.124: When the agent possesses a result [of the action], the *taṅ* and *āna* suffixes occur after the causative root (*ṇi*). Example: *kārayate* ("He causes [it] to be done for his own benefit"). Why "when the agent possesses a result"? Example: *kārayati* ("He causes [someone else] to do it").

(1.4.125) *pāṭhe vibhāṣitāt*: After roots that are optionally marked with the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) designation in the grammatical recitation (*pāṭha*), the *taṅ* endings and the *āna* suffixes occur when the agent is the recipient of the fruit of the action. Examples: *pacate*, *kurute*. Why specify "in the recitation"? Consider *kramate* and *krāmati*; here the *taṅ* and *āna* suffixes occur even without a connection to the fruit of the action. Why specify "when the agent is the recipient of the fruit"? Consider *pacanti karmakarāḥ* ("the laborers cook"). (1.4.126) *ñitaḥ*: [The *taṅ* suffixes and *āna* occur] after roots marked with *ñ*.

After this [root], when it has an action as its object, the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) and *āna* (passive) suffixes occur if the agent is the recipient of the fruit [of the action]. *kaṇḍūyate*. In other cases, *kaṇḍūyati*.

Regarding *apavadaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.4.127): after the root *vad*, preceded by *apa*, the *taṅ* and *āna* suffixes occur if the agent is the recipient of the fruit. *apavadate*. In other cases, *apavadati*.

(Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.128) *sam-ud-āṅ-bhyaḥ yame ’granthē*: After the prefixes *sam*, *ud*, and *āṅ* preceding the root *yam*, when the action does not concern a book (*agrantha*) and the agent is the one who benefits from the action (*phalavati kartari*), the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) endings are used. Examples: *vrīhīn saṃyacchate* (he gathers the rice for his own benefit); *bhāram udyacchate* (he lifts the burden for himself); *rajjum āyacchate* (he draws in the rope for himself). In other cases: *vrīhīn saṃyacchati* (he gathers the rice [for another]). Why say "not concerning a book" (*agrantha*)? Example: *udyacchati cikitsāṃ vaidyaḥ* (the physician applies medical treatment [as a book]). (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.129) *aprapad-e jñaḥ*: [The ātmanepada endings are used after the root *jñā*] except when preceded by *pra*.

The *taṅ* (ātmanepada) and *āna* (passive) suffixes occur after the root *jñā* when it is devoid of prefixes (*prādi*) and when the agent possesses the fruit of the action. Example: *gāṃ jānīte* ("he recognizes the cow [for himself]"). In other cases: *gāṃ jānāti* ("he recognizes the cow [on behalf of another]"). Why "devoid of prefixes"? Consider: *svargalokaṃ prajānāti* ("he knows the heavenly world"). When the agent's possession of the fruit of the action is understood through another word, the *taṅ* and *āna* suffixes occur optionally. Examples: *svaṃ kaṭaṃ kārayate*, *svaṃ kaṭaṃ kārayati* ("he has his own mat made"); *svaṃ yajñaṃ yajate*, *svaṃ yajñaṃ yajati* ("he performs his own sacrifice"). This applies everywhere. [Pāṇini 1.4.131: "Not after *anu* and *parā* with the root *kṛ*."

When preceded by *anu* or *parā*, the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) and *āna* (passive) suffixes do not occur after the root *kṛ* when the agent possesses the fruit of the action (*phalavatkartṛ*). Examples: *anukaroti*, *parākaroti*. How is it that [the form] *gaṅgām anu kurute tapaḥ* ("he performs penance along the Ganges") is explained? In this case, the root *kṛ* is not qualified by *anu*. Regarding the rule *pratyatyabhīnāṃ kṣipaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.4.92):

when preceded by *prati*, *ati*, or *abhi*, the *taṅ* and *āna* suffixes do not occur after the root *kṣip* when the agent possesses the fruit of the action. Examples: *pratikṣipati*, *atikṣipati*, *abhikṣipati*. Why is there a mention of the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhīnirdeśa*)? [To exclude cases where the agent is not the possessor of the fruit, as in: *māṇavakaṃ prati kṣipate* ("he throws toward the boy").
*prād vahaḥ* (1.4.133):

After the root *vah* preceded by *pra*, the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) and *āna* (passive) endings do not occur when the agent (*kartṛ*) receives the fruit of the action. Example: *pravahati*. Why [is it said] "after *pra*" (*prāt*)? [Observe: *vahate*. *parer mṛṣaś ca* (1.4.134): [The *taṅ* and *āna* endings do not occur after the root *mṛṣ*] when preceded by *pari*.

When *mṛṣ* and *vah* are qualified by *pari*, the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) and *āna* (passive) suffixes do not occur when the agent (*kartṛ*) possesses the fruit [of the action]. For example: *parimṛṣyati*, *parivahati*. How is it that one says *māṇavakaṃ pari mṛṣyate* ("he touches the boy thoroughly") and *vanaṃ pari vahataḥ* ("the two carry the forest thoroughly")? These two are not qualified by *pari* in those instances. Regarding *ram* with *vyāṅ* and *pari* (Pāṇini 1.4.135): when *ram* follows *vi*, *āṅ*, or *pari*, the *taṅ* and *āna* suffixes do not occur when it is qualified [by these prepositions]. For example: *viramati*, *āramati*, *pariramati*. How is it that one says *gṛhaṃ pari ramate* ("he rests at home thoroughly")? In this case, *ram* is not qualified by *pari*.
After the prefix *upa*, the roots beginning with *ram* do not take the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) endings. Example: *kaṃcit kālam uparamati* ("he rests for some time").
(1.4.137) *avyāpyād vā*: Or [the roots beginning with *ram* do not take the *taṅ* endings] when they are not preceded by an object.

After the root *ram* preceded by *upa*, when it is devoid of a pervading object (*avyāpya*), the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) endings or the suffix *āna* do not necessarily occur. Thus: *uparamate* or *uparamati*.
[This applies] to the causative suffix *ṇi* when the agent of the non-causative action possesses consciousness (*cittavat*). (Pāṇini 1.4.138)

When a root ending in *ṇic* has an agent possessing consciousness (*cittavat*) and is devoid of an object (*avyāpya*), then the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) and *āna* (passive) suffixes—which would otherwise be obtained by the rule *ṇer aṇau yat karma ṇau cet sa kartānādhyāne* (1.3.67)—do not occur. Examples: *āste māṇavakaḥ* ("The boy sits"); *āsayati māṇavakam* ("He causes the boy to sit"). Why "when not having an object" (*aṇau*)? Consider: *ārohayamāṇaṃ prayojayati* ("He causes [the elephant] that is mounting to mount"); *ārohayate*. Why "having an agent possessing consciousness" (*cittavatkartṛkāt*)? Consider: *śuṣyanti vrīhayaḥ* ("The rice grains dry"); *śoṣayate vrīhīn ātapaḥ* ("The sun causes the rice grains to dry"). It must be "devoid of an object" (*avyāpyāt*) as well; consider: *kaṭaṃ kurvāṇaṃ prayojayati* ("He causes [someone] making a mat to do so"); *kārayate*.
[This applies except for roots] meaning movement or eating (*calanāhārārthāt*, Pāṇini 1.4.139).

Because [the roots] *cal* and *āhṛ* have the meanings "to move" and "to eat" respectively, the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) and *āna* (passive) endings do not apply when they are followed by the causative suffix *ṇic* and the action results in the agent (*phalavati*). Thus, one says *calayati* ("he moves") and *kampayati* ("he shakes"); *āśayati* ("he causes to eat") and *bhojayati* ("he feeds").
