[This is governed by the rule: *prudrusrubudhayudheṅnaśajanaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.4.140).

The *taṅ* (ātmanepada) and *āna* (passive) endings, which would otherwise apply by rule 124 (*ebhyo ṇyāntebhyaḥ phalavati*), do not occur after these roots ending in *ṇi*. *Prāvayati*; the meaning is "he causes to reach. *Drāvayati*; the meaning is "he causes to flow. *Srāvayati*; the meaning is "he causes to flow. However, regarding roots with the sense of motion (*gatyartha*), the prohibition is already established by rule 139 (*calanārthāt*). Examples: *bodhayati māṇavakaṃ ślokam* ("He causes the boy to understand the verse"); *yodhayati kāṣṭham* ("He causes the wood to fight"); *adhyāpayati māṇavakaṃ vedam* ("He causes the boy to study the Veda"); *nāśayati rogam* ("He causes the disease to perish"); *janayati sukham* ("He produces happiness"). [Note: The suffix *ṇic* is not applied after the following roots: *pāda*, *māya*, *māyasa*, *parimuha*, *ruc*, *nṛt*, *dheṭ*, *vada*, and *vasa*. (Pāṇini 1.4.141).

The *taṅ* (ātmanepada) and *āna* (passive) endings, which would otherwise apply by the rule "after [roots] beginning with *pā* and ending in *ṇic*, when the fruit [of the action] accrues to the agent" (Pāṇini 1.3.74), do indeed occur; they are not excluded. This is because there is a counter-exception (*punar-pratiṣedha*) to the prohibition stated in "for *pā*, *ad*, and *dheṭ* when meaning 'to eat'" (Pāṇini 1.3.89). Furthermore, this applies to *nṛt* when it means 'to move' (1.3.89) and to roots where no other agent is involved (*aṇau avyāpyāt*) (1.3.88). The same holds for the remaining roots. Examples:
*pāyayate*, *damayate*, *āyāmayate*, *āyāsayate*, *parimohayate*, *ādayate*, *rocayate*, *nartayate*, *dhāpayate*, *vādayate*, *vāsayate*.
Also, "optionally after a root ending in *kyaṣ*" (Pāṇini 1.3.90).
The *taṅ* (ātmanepada) and *āna* (passive) suffixes optionally occur after roots ending in *kyap*. Thus: *lohitāyati*, *lohitāyate*.

According to Pāṇini 1.4.143 (*dyudbhyo luṅi*), the *taṅ* and *āna* suffixes optionally occur after roots beginning with *dyut* when followed by the *luṅ* (aorist) tense. Thus: *vyadyutat*, *vyadyotiṣṭa*; *aśvitat*, *aśvetiṣṭa*.

Pāṇini 1.4.144: *vṛdbhyaḥ syasanoḥ* (After the roots beginning with *vṛt*, the *taṅ* [ātmanepada] and *āna* [the affix *śānac*] are optionally used after the suffixes *syat* [future] and *san* [desiderative]). Examples: *vartsyati*, *vartiṣyate*; *vivṛtsati*, *vivartiṣate*; *vartsyati*, *vardhiṣyate*; *vivṛtsati*, *vivardhiṣate*; *kalpsyati*, *kalpiṣyate*; *cikḷpsati*, *cikalpiṣate*. Why specify "after *syat* and *san*"? [Observe: *vartate* (present tense). Pāṇini 1.4.145: *luṭi kḷpaḥ* (The *taṅ* and *āna* are optionally used after the root *kḷp* when the suffix *luṭ* [first future] follows).
In the *luṭ* [future] tense, the *taṅ* [ātmanepada] endings optionally occur. [Examples: *kalptā*, *kalpitā*.

(1.4.105) "The three middle [persons] occur when *yuṣmad* [the second person pronoun] is the *kāraka*. When *yuṣmad* is employed as the *kāraka*, the three middle persons occur for both the *taṅ* and *ataṅ* [parasmaipada] endings. [Examples: *tvaṃ pacasi*, *yuvāṃ pacathaḥ*, *yūyaṃ pacatha*; *tvaṃ pacase*, *yuvāṃ pacethe*, *yūyaṃ pacadhve*. Because they are obtained through the force of the context (*sāmarthya*), the three middle persons occur even when [the pronoun] is not explicitly employed: *pacasi*, *pacathaḥ*, *pacatha*; *pacase*, *pacetha*, *pacadhve*.

*Asmady uttamam* (Pāṇini 1.4.107): When the *asmad* pronoun is employed as the agent (*kāraka*), the three persons of the *uttama* (first person) occur, whether they belong to the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) or *ataṅ* (parasmaipada) classes. For example: *ahaṃ pacāmi*, *āvāṃ pacāvaḥ*, *vayaṃ pacāmaḥ*; or *ahaṃ pace*, *āvāṃ pacāvahe*, *vayaṃ pacāmahe*. This applies even when the pronoun is not explicitly used. The three persons of the *prathama* (third person), however, are prescribed generally; because they are superseded by the *madhyama* (second person) and *uttama* (first person) in the respective domains of *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, they remain only in the "remainder" (*śeṣe*). Thus, in examples such as *ehi manye rathena yāsyasi*, *na hi yāsyasi*, or *yātas te pitā*, the *madhyama* and *uttama* persons occur precisely within their own proper domains.

Regarding the rule *ekadvibahuṣu* (Pāṇini 1.4.148): the three [numbers] as previously described apply respectively to the singular (*eka*), dual (*dvi*), and plural (*bahu*). For example: *sa pacati* (he cooks), *tau pacataḥ* (the two cook), *te pacanti* (they cook), and so forth.
Thus ends the first chapter in the Cāndra grammar.

*sv-au-ja-s-auṭ-ch-aṣ-ṭā-bhyām-bhis-ṅ-e-bhyām-bhyas-ṅ-as-i-bhyām-bhyas-ṅ-as-os-ām-ṅ-i-os-sup* (Pāṇini 4.1.2). Three of these [sup-affixes] each occur in the singular, dual, and plural numbers. And by virtue of their functional capacity (*sāmarthya*), these occur after words that denote meanings possessing singularity and so forth. For this very reason, they do not occur after verbs, because there is no connection between an action—which is non-substantial (*asattvabhūta*)—and singularity and the other numbers, and because they are superseded by the suffixes *tavya* and others. They do not occur after verbal endings (*tiṅanta*), because singularity and the rest have already been expressed by the verbal endings themselves. They occur after the remaining [bases]. *dṛṣat*, *dṛṣadau*, *dṛṣadaḥ*;

*dṛṣadam*, *dṛṣadau*, *dṛṣadaḥ*; *dṛṣadā*, *dṛṣadbhyām*, *dṛṣadbhiḥ*; *dṛṣade*, *dṛṣadbhyām*, *dṛṣadbhyaḥ*; *dṛṣadaḥ*, *dṛṣadbhyām*, *dṛṣadbhyaḥ*; *dṛṣadaḥ*, *dṛṣadoḥ*, *dṛṣadām*; *dṛṣadi*, *dṛṣadoḥ*, *dṛṣatsu*. Likewise: *kumārīm*, *kumāryau*, *kumāryaḥ*. Likewise: *khaṭvām*, *khaṭve*, *khaṭvāḥ*. These seven groups of three constitute the seven case-endings (*vibhakti*), since they are divisions (*vibhāga*).
Hence [the rule]: *ato bhisa ais* (Pāṇini 7.1.9).

The substitution of *ais* for the case-ending *bhis* occurs after a word ending in the vowel *a*. For example: *vṛkṣaiḥ*, *plakṣaiḥ*. Why is it specified "after *a*" (*ataḥ*)? [Consider: *agnibhiḥ*. Why is it specified that the *a* is followed by *t* (*taparaḥ*)? [Consider: *mālābhiḥ*. Regarding the rule *ikamadasoḥ kāt* (Pāṇini 7.1.2): the substitution of *ais* for *bhis* occurs only after the *ka*-suffix of *idam* and *adas*. For example: *imakaiḥ*, *amukaiḥ*. Why is it specified "after *ka*" (*kāta*)? [Consider: *ebhiḥ*, *amībhiḥ*.
(2.1.4) *ṭāṅasor inasyau*: for the two [suffixes] *ṭā* and *ṅasi*, when following a word ending in *a*, the substitutes *ina* and *sya* respectively occur. [Examples: *vṛkṣeṇa*, *vṛkṣasya*.
(2.1.5) *ṅeṅasyor yātau*.

When the case endings *ṅe* and *ṅasi* follow a word ending in the vowel *a*, the substitutes *ā* and *āt* respectively take their place. Thus: *vṛkṣāya*, *vṛkṣāt*. Regarding the rule *sarvādibhyaḥ smaismātau* (Pāṇini 7.1.16):

when *ṅe* and *ṅasi* follow words beginning with *sarva-* that end in *a*, the substitutes *smai* and *smāt* respectively take their place. Thus: *sarvasmai*, *sarvasmāt*; *viśvasmai*, *viśvasmāt*. The restriction "only after [a word ending in] *a*" (*ataḥ*) applies here as well: *bhavate*, *bhavataḥ*.

The words *sarva*, *viśva*, *ubha*, *ubhayī*, *ḍatara*, *ḍatama*, *itara*, *anya*, *anyatara*, *tva*, *tvad*, *nema*, *sama*, *sima*, and the terms *pūrva*, *para*, *avara*, *dakṣiṇa*, *uttara*, *apara*, and *adhara*—when used in their specific sense (*vyavasthā*) and not as proper names (*asaṃjñāyām*)—are called *sarvanāman*. Also *sva* when it does not mean "kinsman" or "wealth"; *antara* when it means "outside" (*bahiryoga*) or "inner garment" (*upasaṃvyāna*); and *tyad*, *tad*, *yad*, *adas*, *idam*, *etad*, *eka*, *dvi*, *yuṣmad*, *asmad*, *bhavat*, and *kim*. [Furthermore, by Pāṇini 7.1.15: for the case-ending *ṅi*, the substitute *smin* is applied. (2.1.7)
The substitution of *smin* occurs for the word *ṅi* when it follows [any member] from the group beginning with *sarva*. [Example: *sarvasmin*. Only when [the stem ends in] *at*: [example] *bhavati*.
(Pāṇini 7.1.17) The substitution of *śī* occurs for *jas* when it follows [any member] from the group beginning with *sarva*. [Example: *sarve*. Only when [the stem ends in] *at*: [example] *sarvāḥ*.

*Ād āmaḥ sām* (2.1.9): After words beginning with *sarva-* that end in the vowel *a*, the substitute *sām* is applied to the case-ending *ām*. For example: *sarveṣām*, *sarvāsām*. Why does it say "after [an *a*-ending word]" (*ād*)? Consider: *bhavatām*.
Furthermore, this substitution does not apply to other nouns that are not primary (*apradhāna*). (2.1.10)

That which has been prescribed for the words beginning with *sarva*—both when they function as proper names (*nāmabhūta*) and when they do not (*apradhānabhūta*)—as well as any other grammatical operation belonging to the *sarvādi* group, does not take place [in these cases]. For example: *viśvo nāma kaścit*, *tasmai viśvāya dehi* ("A certain person is named Viśva; give to that Viśva"); *ativiśvāya*; *priyaviśvāya*. Regarding the rule "when joined with the sense of the third case" (*tṛtīyārthayoge*, Pāṇini 2.1.11):

when joined with the sense of the third case, that which has been prescribed for the *sarvādi* group, as well as any other grammatical operation belonging to the *sarvādi* group, does not take place. For example: *māsena pūrvāya*, *māsapūrvāya*.

In the case of a compound expressing the sense of *ca* ("and"), whatever has been prescribed for words beginning with *sarva*, as well as any other operation pertaining to the *sarva*-group, does not take place. For example: *dakṣiṇottarapūrvāṇām*. Why is it said "in a compound"? Witness: *amuṣmai ca tasmai ca dehi*.
[The rule] *śī vā* (Pāṇini 2.1.13) applies.

In the domain of compound meanings (*arthasamāsa*), the substitution of *śī* for the nominative plural marker occurs optionally for those words for which it has been prescribed after the group beginning with *sarva*. Thus: *pūrvottare*, *pūrvottarāḥ*. The substitution of *śī* occurs optionally for *prathama* and the others from the group beginning with *prathamacaramatayāyālpārdhanemakatipayāt* (Pāṇini 2.1.14), for those words for which its application has been prescribed. Thus: *prathame*, *prathamāḥ*; *carame*, *caramāḥ*; *dvitaye*, *dvitayāḥ*; *dvaye*, *dvayāḥ*; *alpe*, *alpāḥ*; *ardhe*, *ardhāḥ*; *neme*, *nemāḥ*; *katipaye*, *katipayāḥ*.

(2.1.15) *pūrvādibhyo navabhyaḥ smātsminau ca*: After the nine beginning with *pūrva*, the suffixes *smāt* and *smin* occur in their respective places, and the substitution of *śī* optionally takes place. [Examples: *pūrvasmāt*, *pūrvāt*; *pūrvasmin*, *pūrve*; *pūrve*, *pūrvāḥ*. *parasmāt*, *parāt*; *parasmin*, *pare*; *pare*, *parāḥ*. Why "after nine"? [Counter-example: *tyasmāt*, *tyasmin*, *tye*. (2.1.16) *smai ca tīyāt*: [The suffix *smai* also occurs] after a word ending in the ordinal suffix *tīya*.

The suffixes *smai*, *smāt*, and *smin* optionally occur in place of [the case endings] following a word ending in the ordinal suffix *-tīya*, according to their respective positions: *dvitīyasmai* or *dvitīyāya*; *dvitīyasmāt* or *dvitīyāt*; *dvitīyasmin* or *dvitīye*. (2.1.17) *āpa autaḥ śīḥ*: The substitution of *śī* occurs for the dative-locative dual ending *au* (*aukārasya*) when it follows a stem ending in *ā*. *māle tiṣṭhataḥ* (The two garlands stand). *māle paśya* (Behold the two garlands).

(2.1.18) *napuṃsakāt*: After a neuter [stem], the substitution of *śī* occurs for the following *au*. Examples: *kuṇḍe tiṣṭhataḥ* ("the two pots stand"), *kuṇḍe paśya* ("look at the two pots"). The letter *ś* is for the purpose of specification in the rule *āc chīṅyoḥ* (5.4.34).
(2.1.19) *jasśasoḥ śiḥ*: The substitution of *śi* occurs for *jas* and *śas*.

The substitution of *śi* occurs for the case endings *jas* and *śas* when they follow a neuter noun. *Kuṇḍāni tiṣṭhanti* ("the pots stand"); *kuṇḍāni paśya* ("look at the pots"). *Aṣṭābhya auś* (Pāṇini 7.1.21):

The substitution of *auś* occurs for *jas* and *śas* when they follow the word *aṣṭan*. *Aṣṭau tiṣṭhanti* ("eight [are] standing"); *aṣṭau paśya* ("look at the eight"). Why is the vowel *ā* specified in the rule? [To show that it applies only when the stem ends in *ā*, as in: *aṣṭa tiṣṭhanti*, *aṣṭa paśya* ("eight [neuter stems ending in -a] stand"; "look at the eight").

*ṣṇaḥ saṃkhyāyā luk* (2.1.21): There is elision (*luk*) of *jas* and *śas* following a numeral ending in *ṣ* or *n*. For example: *ṣaṭ tiṣṭhanti*, *ṣaṭ paśya*; *pañca tiṣṭhanti*, *pañca paśya*. *kateḥ* (2.1.22).
The elision (*luk*) occurs after the word *kati* when followed by the case-endings *jas* and *śas*. [Examples: *kati tiṣṭhanti?*; *kati paśya*. [From Pāṇini 7.1.23:
*svamor napuṃsakāt*:
The elision occurs after a neuter noun when followed by the case-endings *su* and *am*. [Examples: *jatu tiṣṭhati*; *jatu paśya*.

*ato'm* (Pāṇini 7.1.24): *am* is substituted for the dual case endings *sva* and *am* when they follow a neuter noun ending in *a*. For example: *kuṇḍaṃ tiṣṭhati* ("the pot stands") and *kuṇḍaṃ paśya* ("look at the pot").
*ḍatarādibhyaḥ pañcabhyo 'nekatarāt taḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.25): The suffix *ta* is substituted for *sva* and *am* after the five beginning with *ḍatara*, excluding *anekataḥ*.

The letter *t* is substituted for the *s* of the nominative-accusative dual suffixes *su* and *am* when they follow the five neuter stems beginning with *katara*, excluding *ekatara*. *katarat tiṣṭhati?* "Which one stands? *katarat paśya.* "Look at which one. *katamat tiṣṭhati?* "Which one stands? *katamat paśya.* "Look at which one. *itarat tiṣṭhati,* *itarat paśya.* "The other stands; look at the other. *anyat tiṣṭhati,* *anyat paśya.* "Another stands; look at another. *anyatarat tiṣṭhati,* *anyatarat paśya.* "One of two stands; look at one of two. Why say "from the five"? [To exclude: *pūrvaṃ tiṣṭhati,* *pūrvaṃ paśya.* ("The former stands; look at the former. Why say "excluding *ekatara*"? [To exclude: *ekataraṃ tiṣṭhati,* *ekataraṃ paśya.* ("One of two stands; look at one of two. [Next rule: *yuṣmadasmadbhyāṃ ṅaso 'ś* (Pāṇini 2.1.26). "After *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, the genitive singular suffix *ṅas* is replaced by *aś*."
The substitution of *aś* occurs for *ṅasi* following *yuṣmad* and *asmad*. [Thus: *tava*, *mama*.

By Pāṇini 2.1.27, *am* is substituted for *ṅe* and for those [suffixes] marked with *suṬ* that follow *yuṣmad* and *asmad*. [Thus: *tubhyam* is given, *mahyam* is given; *tvam*, *aham*; *yuvām*, *āvām*; *yūyam*, *vayam*; *tvām*, *mām*; *yuvām*, *āvām*.

For *śas* following *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, the initial *ś* is replaced by *n*, and the *s* [at the end of the stem] undergoes elision due to being a final consonant cluster (*saṃyogāntalopa*). [The forms are] *yuṣmān* and *asmān*.
*bhyaso 'bhyam* (2.1.29): [For *bhyas* following *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, the replacement is] *abhyam*.
The substitution of *abhyam* occurs for *bhyas* following *yuṣmad* and *asmad*. [Examples: *yuṣmabhyam dīyate*, *asmabhyam dīyate*.
From the rule *ṅaseś ca* (Pāṇini 7.1.30), the substitution of *at* occurs for *ṅasi* and for *bhyas* which is co-occurrent with it. [Examples: *tvat*, *mat*; *yuṣmat*, *asmat*.
*āma ākam* (2.1.31): For the *ām* following *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, the substitute *ākam* is applied. [Thus we have] *yuṣmākam* and *asmākam*.
*hrasvāpo nuṭ* (2.1.32).

The augment *nuṭ* is added to the case-ending *ām* following a word ending in a short vowel or in the vowel *ā*. For example: *paṭūnām*, *vṛkṣāṇām*, *khaṭvānām*. Regarding the rule *saṃkhyāyā anataḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.55): the augment *nuṭ* is added to the case-ending *ām* following a numeral that does not end in the sound *a*. For example: *caturṇām*, *pañcānām*, *ṣaṇṇām*. Why is it specified "not ending in *a*" (*anataḥ*)? Consider these examples: *triṃśatām*, *tāvatām*. In these cases, the augment *nuṭ* is not applied because the stems end in *a*.
(2.1.34) Regarding the three [cases]: the word *tri* ending in the suffix *am* is irregularly formed as *trayāṇām*. (2.1.35) After *strī* and *yū* [the suffix *ṅīp* is applied].

The augment *nuṭ* is applied to the case ending *ām* following the feminine suffixes *ī* and *ū*. Examples: *kumārīṇām*, *brahmabandhūnām*. Why is the word "feminine" (*strī*) mentioned? [To exclude cases like] *grāmaṇyām*, *khalapvām*. Why is it said "following the two vowels *ī* and *ū*"? [To exclude cases like] *śaradām*. Regarding the rule *seyuvo vā* (Pāṇini 7.1.36): the augment *nuṭ* optionally applies to the case ending *ām* following those stems in which the vowels *i* and *u* (*iy* and *uv*) are found. Examples: *śriyām* or *śrīṇām*. The form *śrīṇām* occurs only in the Vedic language due to a fixed option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*). Examples: *bhruvām* or *bhrūṇām*.
the form *strīṇām* is an irregularly prescribed (*nipātita*) form ending in the suffix *ām*.
(2.1.38) *supo 'saṃkhyāl luk*: there is elision (*luk*) of the case endings (*sup*) when they do not denote number (*asaṃkhyā*).

The *sup* suffixes of another [word] that do not denote a number (*asaṃkhyā*) undergo elision (*luk*). For example: *uccaiḥ*, *nīcaiḥ*. From this very indicative mark (*liṅga*), it is inferred that *sup* suffixes arise even from words that do not denote a number.

When there is unity of meaning (*aikārthya*), that is, when there is a state of unified meaning (*ekārthībhāva*), the *sup* suffixes undergo elision. For example: *putrīyati*, *rājapuruṣaḥ*, *aupagavaḥ*.

Prior to the term *kāraka* (Pāṇini 2.1.40)—that is, before the technical designation *kāraka*—the elision (*luk*) of the nominal suffix (*sup*) occurs when there is a unification of meaning (*aikārthya*). Examples: *upāgni*. Why "prior to *kāraka*"? [Consider: *kaṣṭaśritaḥ*. [Also:
*nāto 'm apañcamyāḥ* (Pāṇini 2.1.41).

Before a *kāraka* suffix, the elision (*luk*) of a *sup* case-ending following a monosyllabic stem ending in short *a* does not occur; however, the suffix *am* is applied, except in the case of the fifth case (*pañcamī*). Example: *upakumbham*. Why "except in the case of the fifth case"? Example: *upakumbhād ānaya* ("bring from near the jar"). (2.1.42) *tṛtīyāsaptamyor vā*: Before a *kāraka* suffix, the suffix *am* optionally occurs after a monosyllabic stem ending in short *a* when followed by the third or seventh case endings. Examples: *upakumbhaṃ kṛtam* or *upakumbhena kṛtam* ("made near the jar"); *upakumbhaṃ nidhehi* or *upakumbhe nidhehi* ("place near the jar").
*Pāṇini 2.1.43*: "The second case ending (*dvitīyā*) is used for that which is pervaded by an action (*kriyāpye*).

The second case ending occurs for that which is pervaded by an action. For example: *kaṭaṃ karoti* ("he makes a mat"), *odanaṃ pacati* ("he cooks rice"), *ādityaṃ paśyati* ("he sees the sun"). In the sentence *odanaḥ pacyate* ("the rice is being cooked"), the state of being pervaded is not understood from the word *odana*, but rather from the verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*). In the expression *kaṭaṃ karoti vipulaṃ darśanīyam* ("he makes a mat, vast and beautiful"), the state of being pervaded certainly exists for that which is endowed with qualities (*guṇa*). Since it is also pervaded [by the action], the second case is established even in the case of what is desired (*īpsita*): *gāṃ dogdhi payaḥ* ("he milks the cow for milk"), *pauravaṃ gāṃ yācate* ("he begs a cow from the descendant of Puru"), *gām avaruṇaddhi vrajam* ("he shuts the cow in the pen").

He asks the student the way. He begs a cow from the descendant of Puru. He gathers fruits from the tree. He tells the student the Dharma. He instructs the student in the Dharma. Thus it also occurs with that which is not desired [as the primary object]: "He leaps over the snake"; "He consumes poison. It also occurs in the case of that which is neither desired nor undesired: "While going to the village, he approaches the roots of the trees. (Pāṇini 1.4.52) [The accusative case is used] for the prompted agent (*prayojya*) of verbs meaning motion, cognition, eating, making sound, and taking nourishment.

The second case ending occurs for the indirect object (*prayojya*) when the agent is the instigator (*kartṛ*), in the case of verbs meaning "to go," "to know," "to eat," "to sound," and those that do not require an object (*anāpya*). And by implication, it is understood that its status as an "object" (*vyāpyatā*) arises solely through the operation of the instigator. Examples: *gamayati māṇavakaṃ grāmam* ("he causes the boy to go to the village"); *yāpayati māṇavakaṃ grāmam* ("he causes the boy to travel to the village"). *bodhayati māṇavakaṃ ślokam* ("he causes the boy to understand the verse"); *vedayati māṇavakaṃ dharmam* ("he causes the boy to know the Dharma"). *bhojayati māṇavakam odanam* ("he causes the boy to eat rice"); *āśayati māṇavakam odanam* ("he causes the boy to consume rice").

He causes the boy to study the Veda; he causes the boy to recite the Veda. He causes Devadatta to sit; he causes Devadatta to lie down. Why [specify] "of these very [roots]"? [Because in cases like: he causes Devadatta to cook the rice. Why [specify] "the prompted agent" (*prayojya*)? [Because in cases like: Devadatta goes. But when Yajñadatta causes Devadatta to go, and another prompts him, then it should be *gamayati devadattaṃ yajñadattena* ("he causes Devadatta to go by means of Yajñadatta"), because the root *gam-* does not have the sense of "going" [in this context].
[The rule] *hṛkror vā* (Pāṇini 1.4.53) applies.

After the roots *hṛ* ("to carry") and *kṛ* ("to do"), when the agent is the one being prompted (*prayojya*), the second case ending optionally occurs. For example: *hārayati bhāraṃ devadattam* or *devadattena*; *abhyavahārayati saktuṃ devadattam* or *devadattena*; *kārayati kaṭaṃ devadattam* or *devadattena*. [This is because of the rule: "The ātmanepada endings are used after the roots *dṛś*, *abhivād*, and *ās*. (Pāṇini 1.3.46).

When the roots *dṛś* ("to see") and *abhivād* ("to salute") are used in a construction where the agent of the action is the object of the causative (*prayojya*), the *ātmanepada* endings (*taṅ*) are optionally employed, provided that the *ātmanepada* is not otherwise required by specific rules. Thus, one may say either *darśayate rājā bhṛtyān* or *bhṛtyaiḥ*; or *abhivādayate guruṃ Devadattam* or *Devadattena*. Why specify "when the *ātmanepada* is not otherwise required"? Consider: *darśayati citraṃ Devadattena* (he shows the painting by means of Devadatta); *abhivādayati guruṃ māṇavakena* (he causes the boy to salute the teacher). [This rule is subject to the exception:
*na nīkhādyadihvāśabdāyakrandaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.4.52), which excludes certain roots such as *nī*, *khād*, etc., from this application.

The second case ending (*dvitīyā*) is not used for the prompted agent (*prayojya-kartṛ*) in the case of *nī* and other such verbs. For example: *nāyayati devadattena*, *khādayati devadattena*, *ādayati devadattena*, *āhvāyayati devadattena*, *śabdāyayati devadattena*, *krandayati devadattena*. Regarding the rule *vāher aniyantṛke* (Pāṇini 1.4.52): the second case ending is not used for the prompted agent when the verb *vah* lacks a driver (*aniyantṛka*). For example: *vāhayati bhāraṃ devadattena*. Why does it say "lacking a driver"? Consider: *vāhayati balīvardān* ("He causes the oxen to carry [the load]"). Here, the oxen are the drivers, so the second case is used.

(2.1.49) *bhakṣer aniṃsāyām*: When the root *bhakṣ* (to eat) does not mean "harming," the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) is not used for the agent of the prompted action (*prayojya*). Example: *bhakṣayati piṇḍīṃ devadattena* ("He causes Devadatta to eat the cake"). Why "not meaning harming"? Example: *bhakṣayati balīvardān sasyam* ("He feeds the oxen on the grain"—here the eating involves harm to the oxen). In the case of *grāmam adhiśete*, there is simply the intention to express the object of pervasion (*vyāpyavivakṣā*). Similarly: *grāmam adhitiṣṭhati*, *vṛkṣam adhyāste*, *dharmam abhiniviśate*, *trirātram upavasati*, *grāmam anuvasati*, *parvatam adhivasati*, and *āvasatham āvasati*. In some instances, there is the intention to express the locus (*ādhāravivakṣā*).

The notion (*saṃjñā*) adheres to the object of the notion (*saṃjñin*). One says "he plays with dice" when there is a desire to express the instrument (*karaṇa*); "he plays at dice" when there is a desire to express the object (*vyāpya*); "he plays on the dice" when there is a desire to express the locus (*ādhāra*). For grammatical relations (*kārakas*) arise from the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*). For example: "The lightning flashes from the cloud"; "the lightning flashes upon the cloud"; "the lightning flashes for the cloud"; "the lightning flashes from the cloud"; "the lightning flashes in the cloud"; "the lightning flashes by means of the cloud. [This is governed by the rule: *samayā-nikaṣā-hā-dhig-antar-antareṇa-yukte* (Pāṇini 2.3.5).

The second case ending (*dvitīyā*) occurs when [words] are joined with *samaya* and so forth. Examples: *samayā grāmam* (near the village), *nikaṣā grāmam* (close to the village), *hā Devadattam* (alas for Devadatta), *dhik Devadattam* (shame on Devadatta), *antarā gārhapatyam āhavanīyaṃ ca vediḥ* (the altar is between the Gārhapatya and Āhavanīya fires). Because the word *antarā* signifies "in the middle," the altar is not joined with the word *antarā* in its primary sense; therefore, the second case does not occur there. [Example: *antareṇa dharmaṃ sukhaṃ na bhavati* (without dharma, there is no happiness). Why is it that the second case does not occur here?

"What is the use of your going between Keśava and Arjuna?"—because this [use of the genitive] is technical (*lākṣaṇika*), its inclusion [in the rule] does not occur. "Nothing appears to one who is hungry" means that nothing is manifest to the hungry person. However, when there is a [direct] relationship, the genitive is used: "It does not appear to Devadatta.
[The genitive is also used] with words such as *adhi* when expressing duality, according to Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.3.51.

When these [words] are joined with *adhi* and others, the second case (*dvitīyā*) shall apply to them when they are in the dual number. By the rule (Pāṇini 6.3.3), *adhi*, *upari*, and *adhas* undergo reduplication when expressing proximity: *adhyadhi grāmam*, *uparyupari grāmam*, *adho'dho grāmam*. Why "in the dual"? [As in: *harmyasyopari prāsādaḥ* ("the palace is above the mansion"). In *māsam adhīte* ("he studies for a month") and *krośam adhīte* ("he studies for the distance of a *krośa*"), the second case applies only because of the object of the action (*kriyāpya*). Likewise, in *krośaṃ kuṭilā nadī* ("the river is winding for the distance of a *krośa*"), it is because the root *bhū* is understood; and because time, state, and distance are pervaded by all actions.

In the expression *māsena anuvāko ’dhītaḥ* ("A lesson has been studied in a month"), the third case (*tṛtīyā*) is used precisely because [the month] is the instrument (*karaṇa*). In the expression *māsam adhīto ’nuvāko na cānena gṛhītaḥ* ("The lesson was studied for a month, but it was not mastered by him"), there is no status of being an instrument here, because it is not the most effective means (*asādhakatamatvāt*). In the expression *adya bhuktvā Devadatto dvyahād bhoktā* ("Having eaten today, Devadatta will eat after two days"), the fifth case (*pañcamī*) is used because [the time] is the limit (*avadhi*) of the action. In the expression *dvyahē bhoktā* ("He will eat in two days"), the seventh case (*saptamī*) is used because [the time] is the locus (*ādhāra*). In the expression *ihastho ’yam iṣvāsaḥ krośāl lakṣyaṃ vidhyati* ("This archer standing here hits the target from a distance of a *krośa*"), the fifth case is used because [the distance] is the limit. In the expression *krośe lakṣyaṃ vidhyati* ("He hits the target at a *krośa*"), the seventh case is used because [the distance] is the locus. [Regarding the rule] *sarvābhiparyubhayāt tasā* (Pāṇini 2.1.52): [this refers to the formation of compounds with words ending in the suffix *tas*].

The second case suffix shall be used after a word joined with any of the words beginning with *sarva* that end in the suffix *tasi*. For example: *sarvataḥ grāmam*, *abhitaḥ grāmam*, *paritaḥ grāmam*, *ubhayataḥ grāmam*.
By the rule *enapā* (Pāṇini 2.3.31), the second case suffix shall be used in connection with a word ending in the suffix *enap*. For example: *dakṣiṇena grāmam*, *uttareṇa grāmam*.

Pāṇini 2.1.54: *lakṣaṇavīpsetthaṃbhūteṣv abhinā*—when used in conjunction with the word *abhi*, the second case ending shall be employed in the senses of "marking" (*lakṣaṇa*), "desire" (*vīpsā*), and "being in such a state" (*itthaṃbhūta*). For example: *vṛkṣam abhi vidyotate* ("It lightens toward the tree"); *vṛkṣaṃ vṛkṣam abhi tiṣṭhati* ("He stands facing each tree"); *sādhur devadatto mātaram abhi* ("Devadatta is well-behaved toward his mother"). Pāṇini 2.1.55: *pratiparibhyāṃ bhāge ca*—in conjunction with *prati* and *pari*, the second case ending shall be used when the sense is that of "portion" (*bhāga*), as well as in the senses mentioned above.

When joined with *prati* or *pari*, the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) shall be used in the sense of a characteristic mark (*lakṣaṇa*), and so forth, as well as in the sense of a portion (*bhāga*). Examples: *vṛkṣaṃ prati vidyotate* (It lightens toward the tree). *vṛkṣaṃ vṛkṣaṃ prati tiṣṭhati* (He stands facing each tree). *sādhur Devadatto mātaraṃ prati* (Devadatta is kind toward his mother). *yad atra māṃ prati syāt* (Whatever may belong to me in this matter). *vṛkṣaṃ pari vidyotate* (It lightens around the tree). *vṛkṣaṃ vṛkṣaṃ pari tiṣṭhati* (He stands around each tree). *sādhur Devadatto mātaraṃ pari* (Devadatta is kind toward his mother). *yad atra māṃ pari syāt* (Whatever may belong to me in this matter). [Also] with *anu* (2.1.56).

The second case ending shall be used after a word joined with *anu* when it signifies the sense of "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*) and so forth, as well as the sense of "portion" (*bhāga*). *vṛkṣam anu vidyotate* ("It flashes near the tree"). *śākalyasya saṃhitām anu prāvarṣat* ("It rained following Śākalya’s *saṃhitā*"). For a cause (*hetu*) is also a characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*). *vṛkṣaṃ vṛkṣam anutiṣṭhati* ("He stands near every tree"). *sādhur Devadatto mātaram anu* ("Devadatta is kind toward his mother"). *yad atra mām anu syāt* ("Whatever may be mine in this matter"). (2.1.57) Regarding the sense of "concomitance" (*sahārtha*): the second case ending shall be used after a word joined with *anu* when it signifies concomitance. *nadīm anv avasitā senā* ("The army has encamped along the river"). The meaning is: "together with the river" (*nadyā saha*).

(2.1.58) *hīne*: When joined with *anu* in the sense of inferiority, the second case ending shall be used. Example: *anv Arjunam yoddhāraḥ* ("The warriors are inferior to Arjuna"). (2.1.59) *upena*: [When joined with *upa*, the second case ending shall be used.]
The second case ending (*dvitīyā*) shall occur after a word joined with *upa* when it signifies inferiority. For example: *upārjunam yoddhāraḥ* ("warriors are inferior to Arjuna").

Regarding the rule *saptamy ādhikye* (Pāṇini 2.3.9): the seventh case ending (*saptamī*) occurs after a word joined with *upa* when it signifies excess. For example: *upa khāryāṃ droṇaḥ* ("a *droṇa* measure is in excess of a *khārī*").

(2.1.61) *svāmye 'dhinā*: When the sense of ownership (*svāmya*) is expressed, the seventh case ending occurs after a word joined with *adhi*. For example: *adhi Brahmadatte Pañcālāḥ* ("The Pañcālas are under the sovereignty of Brahmadatta") and *adhi Pañcāleṣu Brahmadattaḥ* ("Brahmadatta is over the Pañcālas").
(2.1.62) *kartari tṛtīyā*: The third case ending occurs when the agent (*kartṛ*) is expressed.
The third case ending occurs for the agent (*kartṛ*) among the *kārakas*. For example: *caitreṇa kṛtam* ("done by Caitra"). Regarding the instrument (*karaṇa*):

[Pāṇini 2.3.18] "The third case ending shall occur for the instrument among the *kārakas*. For example: *dātreṇa lunāti* ("he cuts with a sickle"), *paraśunā chinatti* ("he chops with an axe"). In cases such as *prakṛtyābhirūpakaḥ* ("handsome by nature"), *prāyeṇa yājñikaḥ* ("mostly a ritualist"), and *gotreṇa gārgyaḥ* ("a Gārgya by lineage"), since the root *bhū* ("to become") is applicable in all these instances, the third case ending occurs specifically for the instrument. Likewise: *samena dhāvati* ("he runs on level ground"), *viṣameṇa dhāvati* ("he runs on uneven ground"), *dvidroṇena dhānyaṃ krīṇāti* ("he buys grain for two *droṇas*"), and *pañcakena paśūn krīṇāti* ("he buys animals for five [coins]").

*parikrayaś caturthī ca* (Pāṇini 2.1.64): In the sense of the root *pari-krī* ("to hire"), the fourth case ending (*caturthī*) is used for the instrument (*karaṇa*) kāraka, as is the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*). Example: *śatāya parikrīto 'nubrūhi* ("Recite [the hymn], having been hired for a hundred") or *śatena parikrīto 'nubrūhi*. *sahārthena* (Pāṇini 2.1.65). [The word *saha* is used with a word meaning "accompanied by" (*sahārtha*).]

The third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) shall occur when there is a connection with the meaning of the word *saha* ("together with"). For example: *putreṇa sahāgataḥ* ("He has come together with his son") or *putreṇa sārdham āgataḥ* ("He has come along with his son"). Like the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*), the third case also denotes that which is not the primary agent (*apradhāna*).

In the sense of a characteristic mark (*lakṣaṇa*), the third case shall occur after a word signifying a characteristic mark. For example: *kamaṇḍalunā chāttram adrākṣīt* ("He saw the student by means of his water-pot") or *akṣṇā kāṇaḥ* ("He is one-eyed in his eye"). For it is by means of that limb that the deformity of the whole body (*aṅgin*) is indicated.

*saṃjño vyāpye vā* (Pāṇini 2.3.67): After the verb *saṃjñā*, the third case ending optionally occurs for that which is the object (*vyāpya*). He recognizes [her] with his mother; he recognizes her as his mother. *Hetau* (Pāṇini 2.3.68).
The third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) shall be used when [the cause] is fit for that action. *Annena vasati* ("He dwells because of food"). *Vidyayā yaśaḥ* ("Fame [arises] from knowledge").
Regarding debt (*ṛṇa*), the fifth case ending (*pañcamī*) is used (Pāṇini 2.3.24):

when the cause is a debt, the fifth case ending occurs. *Śatād baddhaḥ* ("Bound on account of a hundred [pieces of money]"). How is it that one says *śatena bandhitaḥ* ("Caused to be bound by a hundred")? In this case, the third case ending will apply to the agent (*kartṛ*).

Or, when a quality (*guṇa*) is the cause that has become subordinate to another (*parāṅgabhūta*), the fifth case (*pañcamī*) optionally occurs: *jāḍyād baddhaḥ* (bound because of dullness), *jāḍyena baddhaḥ* (bound by means of dullness); *upalabdheḥ san*, *upalabdhyā san* (being [so] because of perception). By virtue of the rule of fixed optionality (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*), in some cases only the third case (*tṛtīyā*) is used: *buddhyā muktaḥ*, *prajñayā muktaḥ* (liberated through intellect, liberated through wisdom).
[The sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is used] with the word *hetu*: *hetunā*. (Pāṇini 2.3.23–24)
When used in conjunction with the word *hetu* ("cause"), the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) occurs in the sense of cause. For example: *annasya hetor vasati* ("He dwells for the sake of food").
[This is governed by the rule: *sarvāḥ sarvādibhyo hetvarthaiḥ* (Pāṇini 2.3.27).

When joined with words expressing the sense of "cause" (*hetu*), all case endings occur after the words beginning with *sarva*. For example: *kena hetunā* ("by what cause?"), *kasmai hetave* ("for what purpose?"), *kasmād dhetoḥ* ("from what cause?"), *kasya hetoḥ* ("of what cause?"), *kasmin hetau* ("in what cause?"), *kiṃ kāraṇam* ("what is the reason?"), *kena kāraṇena* ("by what means? [and likewise] *prayojanena* ("by what motive?"). Why is it said "after the words beginning with *sarva*"? Consider: *annasya hetor vasati* ("he dwells for the sake of food"). Why is it said "with words expressing the sense of cause"? Consider: *kena kṛtam* ("by whom was it done?"). [The suffixes do not apply] after words where the name is not the primary factor, precisely because of the prior prohibition. [Furthermore,] the fourth case ending is used in the sense of the recipient (*saṃpradāna*). (Pāṇini 2.3.13 and 2.3.16).

The dative case occurs for that to which something is properly given. For example: *devebhyaḥ puṣpaṃ dadāti* ("He gives flowers to the gods"). Why specify "properly given" (*saṃpradāne*)? [Observe: *rajakasya vastraṃ dadāti* ("He gives a garment to the washerman").
[Also, the rule applies to] that which involves pleasure (*rucimati*). (Pāṇini 2.3.17)

The fourth case ending occurs when the agent is associated with the sense of "pleasing" (*ruc*). For example: *Devadattāya rocate* ("It pleases Devadatta"). How so? [In examples such as: *Devadattāya ślāghate*, *Devadattāya hnute*, *tiṣṭhate kumārī chāttrebhyaḥ*, *Devadattāya śapate*, and *puṣpebhyaḥ spṛhayati*. In these cases, the fourth case will occur because of the sense of "being for the sake of that" (*tādarthye*). However, when there is an intention to express the object of action (*vyāpya*), one says: *Devadattaṃ ślāghate* or *puṣpāṇi spṛhayati*.
[Regarding the rule] *dhārer uttamarṇe* (Pāṇini 2.3.75): [the fourth case is used for the creditor].

The fourth case ending occurs for the agent (*kāraka*) who is a creditor (*uttamarṇa*) in relation to the verb *dhārayati* ("to owe"). Example: *devadattāya gāṃ dhārayati* ("He owes a cow to Devadatta"). Why "creditor"? [Observe: *gāṃ dhārayati devadattaḥ* ("Devadatta owes a cow [to someone]").
This is also governed by *kopasthāne 'nāpye* (Pāṇini 1.4.37).

The fourth case ending occurs when the object of anger (*kopa*) is an *anāpya* (unapproachable). Examples: *devadattāya krudhyati* (he is angry with Devadatta); *caitrāya druhyati* (he bears malice toward Caitra); *maitrāyerṣyati* (he envies Maitra); *yajñadattāyāsūyati* (he finds fault with Yajñadatta). Why is it specified as *anāpya*? [Observe: *devadattam abhikrudhyati* (he is angry at Devadatta); *yajñadattam abhyasūyati* (he finds fault with Yajñadatta). How is it that [the following] are established: *devadattāya rādhyati* (he seeks success through Devadatta) and *devadattāyekṣate daivam* (he consults the fate regarding Devadatta)? These are established by the fourth case used in the sense of "for the sake of" (*tādarthya*). Likewise: whether requested or unrequested by Devadatta, he promises to Devadatta (*devadattāya pratiśṛṇoti*); he listens to Devadatta (*devadattāyāśṛṇoti*). [This is governed by the rule:
*pratyanubhyāṃ gṛṇo vyāpye* (Pāṇini 1.4.40), which prescribes the fourth case for the object of the verb *gṛ* (to recite/declare) when preceded by *prati* or *anu*.

The fourth case occurs with the object of the verb *gṛṇāti* when preceded by *prati* or *anu*. For example: *hotre pratigṛṇāti* ("He responds to the Hotṛ priest") and *potrē 'nugṛṇāti* ("He responds to the Potṛ priest"). In the expression *grāmāya gacchati*, the fourth case is used in the sense of purpose (*tādarthye*). In the expression *grāmaṃ gacchati*, the second case is used for the object of the action (*karmāpye*). In the expression *mārgabhraṣṭo 'prāptāya pathe gacchati*, the fourth case is used in the sense of purpose. In the expression *panthānaṃ gacchati*, the second case is used for the object of the action. In the expression *pathā gacchati*, the third case is used for the instrument (*karaṇe*).

The fourth case ending (*caturthī*) is used in the sense of "for the sake of" (*tādarthye*), as in: *edhebhyo vrajati* ("he goes for fuel"), *pākāya vrajati* ("he goes for cooking"), *mūtrāya kalpate yavāgūḥ* ("the gruel serves for urine"), *vātāya kapilikā vidyut* ("a reddish lightning portends wind"), and *ātapāya lohinī vidyut* ("a red lightning portends heat").
By Pāṇini 2.3.16, *namaḥ-svasti-svāhā-svadhā-vaṣaṭ-chakty-arthaḥ*:

when joined with *namas* and so forth, as well as words having the sense of "capability" (*śakti*), the fourth case ending occurs. Examples: *namo devebhyaḥ* ("salutation to the gods"), *svasti gobhyaḥ* ("well-being to the cows"), *svāhā devebhyaḥ* ("svāhā to the gods"), *svadhā pitṛbhyaḥ* ("svadhā to the ancestors"), *vaṣaḍ Rudrebhyaḥ* ("vaṣaṭ to the Rudras"). Also: *alaṃ mallo mallāya* ("the wrestler is a match for the wrestler") and *samartho mallo mallāya* ("the wrestler is capable against the wrestler").

*tādarthye* (2.1.79): *tadartham* means "for the sake of that. When the state of being for the sake of something (*tadartha*) is to be expressed, the fourth case ending occurs. For example: *yūpāya dāru* ("wood for a sacrificial post"), *śrāddhāya nigṛhṇāti* ("he prepares for a funeral rite"), *yuddhāya saṃnahyate* ("he arms himself for battle"), *patye śete* ("she lies down for her husband").

*manyāpye kutsāyām anāvādau vā* (2.1.80): [The fourth case ending is used] optionally after a word denoting a person who is censurable, provided it is not preceded by *anu* or *ava*, when the sense is one of reproach.

When the object of the verb *man* (to consider) is something other than a boat (*nau*) and so forth, and when contempt is implied, the fourth case ending (*caturthī*) optionally occurs. Examples: *na tvā tṛṇāya manye*; *na tvā tṛṇaṃ manye*. *na tvā śune manye*; *na tvā śvānaṃ manye*. Why is it said "of the verb *man*" (*manyateḥ*)? [Counter-example: *na tvā tṛṇaṃ cintayāmi* ("I do not think of you as grass"). Why is there a reference to the *śyan*-affix (*śyanā nirdeśaḥ*)? [Counter-example: *na tvā tṛṇaṃ manve* ("I do not consider you as grass"—using the root *man* with the *kvin* suffix). Why is it said "when contempt is [implied]" (*kutsāyām*)? [Counter-example: *na tvā tṛṇam manye* ("I consider you as grass"—without the sense of contempt).

"I consider the stone to be a grindstone; I consider the wood to be a mortar. Why [is this not so] in the case of "anāvadāv"? [Because it says: "I do not consider you to be a boat; I do not consider you to be food; I do not consider you to be a crow; I do not consider you to be a jackal. Why does this [substitution] not occur for *yuṣmad*? If it were to occur, the sense of censure would not be conveyed.
[The rule] "the ablative case ending is used after a word denoting the limit of separation" (Pāṇini 2.3.28).

The fifth case ending occurs after a word denoting the limit (*avadhi*) of an object. He comes from the village. He goes from the village. He fears the thieves. He protects from the thieves. He fails because of his studies. He keeps the cow away from the barley. He restrains the cow from the barley. He hides from the teacher. He studies from the teacher. In the expression "he hears from the actor," the sense of relationship (*saṃbandha*) is intended. An arrow is produced from the horn. The Ganges originates from the Himalayas. He feels disgust toward unrighteousness. He abstains from unrighteousness.

He deviates from unrighteousness. [He is] other than Devadatta; different from Devadatta; distinct from Devadatta; far from Devadatta; the opposite of Devadatta. [Examples of spatial relations: to the east of the village; before the village; to the south of the village; to the south of the village. When a relationship of connection (*saṃbandha*) is intended to be expressed, the genitive case is not prohibited: in front of the village; to the south of the village; above the mountain; above the village. When a limit (*avadhi*) is intended to be expressed, the ablative case occurs even when used in conjunction with words having the sense of *tasi* (i.e., adverbs of direction): *adharmāt pramādyati*. *anyo Devadattāt*. *bhinno Devadattāt*. *vyatirikto Devadattāt*. *ārād Devadattāt*. *itaro Devadattāt*. *pūrvo grāmāt*. *prāg grāmāt*. *dakṣiṇā grāmāt*. *dakṣiṇāhi grāmāt*. In the case where a relationship of connection (*saṃbandha*) is intended to be expressed, the genitive case is not barred: *puro grāmasya*. *dakṣiṇato grāmasya*. *upari śailasya*. *upari grāmasya*. When a limit (*avadhi*) is intended to be expressed, the ablative case indeed occurs even in connection with words having the sense of *tasi*:

After that (*tataḥ paścāt*), above that (*tata upariṣṭāt*). Having ascended the palace, he looks out; "he looks out from the palace" (*prāsādāt prekṣate*)—here the ablative case is used for the point of departure (*avadhi*). Likewise: having sat down on the seat, he looks out; "he looks out from the seat" (*āsanāt prekṣate*). Similarly, also in the context of asking and answering questions: "From where do you come?"—"From Pāṭaliputra. Likewise, also in the measurement of distance and time: "Rājagṛha is seven *yojanas* from Pāṭaliputra," or "at seven *yojanas* [from Pāṭaliputra]. Similarly: "The month [between] Kārttikī and Āgrahāyaṇī. [Also: "By *pari* and *apa*, when excluding" (Pāṇini 2.1.82).

The fifth case ending occurs in connection with the prepositions *pari* and *apa* when they signify exclusion (*varjana*). *Pari trigartebhyo vṛṣṭo devaḥ* ("It has rained outside the Trigartas"). *Apa trigartebhyo vṛṣṭo devaḥ* ("It has rained away from the Trigartas"). The meaning is "having excluded the Trigartas. Why is it specified "when signifying exclusion"? [Consider: *vṛkṣaṃ pari vidyotate* ("It flashes around the tree"). In the expression *ā pāṭaliputrād vṛṣṭo devaḥ* ("It has rained as far as Pāṭaliputra"), the fifth case ending is used for the limit (*avadhi*) itself, whether it denotes a boundary (*maryādā*) or an inclusive limit (*abhividhi*). The sense is "excluding Pāṭaliputra" or "including [Pāṭaliputra]. [The rule] *pratinā pratinidhipratidānayoḥ* (Pāṇini 2.3.11) [states that the third case ending is used after a word joined with *prati* when it signifies a representative or an exchange].

When used in the sense of "substitute" (*pratinidhi*) or "exchange" (*pratidāna*), the fifth case (*pañcamī*) occurs in connection with the word *prati*. *Abhimanyur Arjunataḥ prati* ("Abhimanyu is the substitute for Arjuna"). *māṣān asmai tilebhyaḥ prati prayacchati* ("He gives him beans in exchange for sesame seeds"). Why specify "in the sense of substitute or exchange"? [Because otherwise: *vṛkṣaṃ prati vidyotate vidyut* ("The lightning flashes toward the tree"). In the expressions *kuto 'dhy āgacchati* ("From where does he come? and *kutaḥ pary āgacchati* ("From where does he come around?"), the fifth case is used solely to denote the limit (*avadhi*). *ṛte dvitīyā ca* (Pāṇini 2.3.29): In connection with the word *ṛte*, the second case (*dvitīyā*) and the fifth case (*pañcamī*) occur. *ṛte Pārtham*, *ṛte Pārthāt* ("Except for Pārtha").
*Vinā tṛtīyā ca* (Pāṇini 2.3.85): In connection with the word *vinā*, the third, fifth, and second case endings occur. For example: *vinā vātena*, *vinā vātāt*, *vinā vātam*.
*Pṛthagnānābhyām* (Pāṇini 2.3.86).
When used in conjunction with these two [words], the third and fifth case endings occur. *pṛthag* Devadattena, *pṛthag* Devadattāt; *nānā* Devadattena, *nānā* Devadattāt.

[The third case ending occurs after] *stoka*, *alpa*, *kṛcchra*, and *katipaya* when they do not denote a sentient being (*asattvārtha*), provided they function as the instrument (*karaṇa*). (Pāṇini 2.3.87)

The third and fifth case endings occur after words such as *stoka* when they denote an instrument (*karaṇa*) that does not express a substance (*asattvavacana*). Examples: *stokena muktaḥ*, *stokān muktaḥ*; *alpena muktaḥ*, *alpān muktaḥ*; *kṛcchreṇa muktaḥ*, *kṛcchrān muktaḥ*; *katipayena muktaḥ*, *katipayān muktaḥ*. Why "not expressing a substance"? [Observe: *stokena viṣeṇa hataḥ* ("killed by a small amount of poison"). Why "instrument"? [Observe: *stokaṃ calati* ("it moves slightly"). In the examples *dūraṃ grāmāt* and *antikaṃ grāmāt*, the fifth case ending occurs solely because of the limit (*avadhi*).

In the expressions *dūraṃ grāmasya* ("far from the village") and *antikaṃ grāmasya* ("near the village"), the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is used because of the relationship [of distance]. In *dūraṃ gataḥ* ("gone far") and *antikaṃ gataḥ* ("gone near"), the accusative case (*dvitīyā*) is used because [distance] is the object of the action (*karmapravacanīya*). In *dūreṇa gataḥ* ("gone by means of a distance") and *antikena gataḥ* ("gone by means of a nearness"), the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*) is used because [distance] is the instrument (*karaṇa*). In *dūrād āgataḥ* ("come from afar") and *antikād āgataḥ* ("come from nearby"); *dūreṇa tiṣṭhati* ("stands by means of a distance") and *antikena tiṣṭhati* ("stands by means of a nearness"); and *dūre tiṣṭhati* ("stands at a distance") and *antike tiṣṭhati* ("stands nearby"), the various cases are used in their own respective senses (*svārtha*). In *dūraṃ panthāḥ* ("a path that is far") and *antikaṃ panthāḥ* ("a path that is near"), [distance] functions as an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*), because the sense of "being" (*bhavati*) is understood. [The locative case is used] for the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) according to Pāṇini 2.3.36 (*saptamy adhikaraṇe*).

The seventh case ending occurs in the sense of a locus (*ādhāra*). For example: "He sits on a mat" (*kaṭe āste*); "Birds [are] in the sky" (*ākāśe śakunayaḥ*); "Oil in sesame seeds" (*tileṣu tailam*); "Cows [are] in the Ganges" (*gaṅgāyāṃ gāvaḥ*); and "one who has studied grammar" (*adhītī vyākaraṇe*)—in these cases, the seventh case is used precisely in the sense of a locus.

By the rule *nimittād vyāpyena* (Pāṇini 2.3.89), the seventh case is employed when there is a connection with a motive (*nimitta*) through its correlate (*vyāpya*), that is, when it functions as the purpose (*prayojana*).
One kills the leopard for its skin; one kills the elephant for its tusks;
one kills the yak for its hair; the musk deer is killed for its scent-gland.
[A word denoting] the action which is the mark of another action [is compounded with that other action]. (Pāṇini 2.1.90)

When one action serves as a sign for another action, the locative case (*saptamī*) is employed. For example: *goṣu duhyamānāsu gataḥ* ("He went while the cows were being milked"), *dugdhāsv āgataḥ* ("He returned when they had been milked"); *brāhmaṇeṣu bhuñjāneṣu vṛṣalā āsate* ("While the Brāhmaṇas are eating, the Śūdras sit"); *vṛṣaleṣv āsīneṣu brāhmaṇā bhuñjate* ("While the Śūdras are sitting, the Brāhmaṇas eat"); *vṛṣaleṣu bhuñjāneṣu brāhmaṇā āsate* ("While the Śūdras are eating, the Brāhmaṇas sit"); *brāhmaṇeṣv āsīneṣu vṛṣalā bhuñjate* ("While the Brāhmaṇas are sitting, the Śūdras eat"). Why "action" (*kriyā*)? [Consider: *yo jaṭābhiḥ sa bhuṅkte* ("He who has matted hair, he eats"). Why "sign of an action" (*kriyācihnam*)? [Consider: *yo bhuṅkte sa Devadattaḥ* ("He who eats, he is Devadatta").
[Furthermore,] the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is also used in the sense of disregard (*anādare*), according to Pāṇini 2.3.38.

When an action serves as the mark (*cihna*) of another action, the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) and the locative (*saptamī*) case endings are used, provided that disregard (*anādara*) is implied. Examples: *krośataḥ prāvrājīt* (He went forth into homelessness despite [his] crying out); *krośati prāvrājīt* (He went forth into homelessness while [he] was crying out). In the sense of a relationship (*saṃbandha*), the genitive is used: *gavāṃ svāmī* (the owner of cows). In the sense of a sphere or domain (*viṣaya*), the locative is used: *goṣu svāmī* (the owner among the cows). Similarly: *gavām īśvaraḥ*, *goṣv īśvaraḥ*; *gavām adhipatiḥ*, *goṣv adhipatiḥ*; *gavāṃ dāyādaḥ*, *goṣu dāyādaḥ*; *gavāṃ sākṣī*, *goṣu sākṣī*; *gavāṃ pratibhūḥ*, *goṣu pratibhūḥ*.

Born among cows (*gavām prasūtaḥ*), born among cows (*goṣu prasūtaḥ*). Appointed to the making of mats (*āyuktaḥ kaṭakaraṇasya*), appointed to the making of mats (*āyuktaḥ kaṭakaraṇe*). Skilled in the making of mats (*kuśalaḥ kaṭakaraṇasya*), skilled in the making of mats (*kuśalaḥ kaṭakaraṇe*).
[The genitive is used] when there is a selection from a group (*yato nirdhāraṇam*, Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.1.92).

Selection (*nirdhāraṇa*) is the separation of one part from a whole by means of genus, quality, or action. The genitive and locative cases occur after the word from which that selection is made. Examples: *Śālayaḥ śūkadhānyānāṃ pathyatamāḥ*; *śālayaḥ śūkadhānyeṣu pathyatamāḥ*. (Of awned grains, rice is the most wholesome. *Kṛṣṇā gavāṃ saṃpannakṣīratamāḥ*; *kṛṣṇā goṣu saṃpannakṣīratamāḥ*. (Among cows, the black ones yield the most abundant milk. *Gacchatāṃ dhāvantaḥ śīghratamāḥ*; *gacchatsu dhāvantaḥ śīghratamāḥ*. (Of those who are walking, the runners are the swiftest.)

In the expression *māthurāḥ pāṭaliputrakebhyaḥ sukumāratarāḥ* ("The people of Mathurā are more delicate than those of Pāṭaliputra"), the ablative case (*pañcamī*) is used solely to denote the point of reference (*avadhi*). In *mātari sādhuḥ* ("good toward his mother") and *pitari nipuṇaḥ* ("skilled toward his father"), the locative case (*saptamī*) is used solely to denote the sphere of application (*viṣaya*). Similarly, one says *asādhuḥ mātari*. Likewise, in *keśeṣu prasitaḥ* ("addicted to his hair") and *keśeṣūtsukaḥ* ("anxious about his hair"), the third case (*tṛtīyā*) is used either for the agent (*kartṛ*) or the instrument (*karaṇa*), as in *keśaiḥ prasitaḥ* or *keśair utsukaḥ*. Similarly, in *puṣyeṇa pāyasam aśnīyāt* ("one should eat milk-rice under the asterism Puṣya"), the locative case (*saptamī*) is used solely to denote the locus (*ādhāra*), as in *puṣye pāyasam aśnīyāt*. According to Pāṇini 2.1.93, the nominative case (*prathamā*) is used when the mere meaning of the word itself is intended.

The first case ending occurs when there is no distinction [from the nominal stem], in the mere meaning of the word (*śabdārtha*). For example: *vṛkṣaḥ* ("tree"). Gender—whether feminine, masculine, or neuter—is also part of the meaning of the word. Likewise, measure—such as *droṇaḥ*, *khārī*, or *āḍhakaḥ*—is also part of the meaning of the word. Number—such as one, two, or many—is also part of the meaning of the word. Regarding address (Pāṇini 2.3.47): the first case ending occurs in the sense of addressing. Examples: *he devadatta* ("O Devadatta!"), *hā devadatta* ("Alas, Devadatta!"), *dhik devadatta* ("Shame on Devadatta!").

The sixth case-affix (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is used in the sense of a relationship (*saṃbandha*). (Pāṇini 2.3.50) When a relationship is to be expressed, the sixth case-affix occurs. For example: *rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ* ("the king's man"); *sarpiṣo jānīte* ("he recognizes [the smell of] ghee"). Even in the case of erroneous cognition (*bhrāntijñāna*), there is no status as an instrument (*karaṇa*) for the non-existent ghee. However, when the intention is to express it as an instrument: *svareṇa putraṃ jānāti* ("he recognizes his son by his voice"). When expressing the mother as the object (*vyāpya*): *mātuḥ smarati* ("he remembers his mother"), *sarpiṣo dayate* ("he feels compassion for the ghee"), *lokasyeṣṭe* ("he rules over the world"). But when the intention is to express them as objects (*vyāpya*), only the second case-affix is used: *mātaraṃ smarati*, *pṛthivīṃ dayate*, *lokaṃ īṣṭe*. Similarly, *edhodakasyopaskurute* ("he prepares fuel and water"). When the intention is to express them as objects: *edhodakam upaskurute*.

Thus, one says *caurasya rujati* (he causes pain to the thief) or *cauraṃ rujati* (he causes pain to the thief). Even with the roots *√jvar* (to fever) and *√tap* (to heat), the genitive case occurs when there is an intention to express a relationship: *caurasya jvarayati* (he causes the thief to suffer from fever) and *caurasya saṃtāpayati* (he causes the thief to suffer). However, when there is an intention to express the object (*vyāpya*), one says *cauraṃ jvarayati* (he causes the thief to suffer) and *cauraṃ saṃtāpayati* (he causes the thief to suffer). One says *sarpiṣo nāthate* (he entreats for ghee) and *māṇavakam upanāthati* (he entreats the boy). One says *caurasyojjāsayati* (he causes the thief to flee) or *cauram ujjāsayati*. One says *caurasya nihanti* (he strikes down the thief) or *cauraṃ nihanti*. One says *caurasya prahanti* (he strikes the thief) or *cauraṃ prahanti*.

They strike down the thief: *caurasya niṣprahanti*, *cauraṃ niṣprahanti*. They strike down the thief: *caurasya praṇihanti*, *cauraṃ praṇihanti*. They pull out the thief: *caurasyonnāṭayati*, *cauram unnāṭayati*. They cause the thief to die: *caurasyotkrāthayati*, *cauram utkrāthayati*. [The form] *krāthayati* occurs because it belongs to the *ghaṭādi* group. He grinds the thief: *caurasya pinaṣṭi*, *cauraṃ pinaṣṭi*. Even in the sense of non-violence: he grinds the grains, *dhānāḥ pinaṣṭi*, *dhānānāṃ pinaṣṭi*. For in this connection, the sixth case (genitive) is not prohibited; indeed, a connection with a finite verb (*tiṅanta*) also certainly occurs.

One gives a garment to the washerman (*rajakasya vastraṃ dadāti*), one gives a blow to the back of the striker (*ghnataḥ pṛṣṭhaṃ dadāti*), or one gives to the Brahmin (*brāhmaṇasya dadāti*). Likewise: "He deals with a hundred" (*śatasya vyavaharati*), "he bets a hundred" (*śatasya paṇate*), or "he plays for a hundred" (*śatasya dīvyati*). In all these cases, the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) is used when there is an intention to express the object (*vyāpya*). For example: *akṣair dīvyati* ("he plays with dice") is used when the dice are the instrument (*karaṇa*); *akṣān dīvyati* ("he plays the dice") when they are the object (*vyāpya*); *akṣeṣu dīvyati* ("he plays on the dice") when they are the locus (*ādhāra*); and *akṣāṇāṃ dīvyati* ("he plays for the sake of the dice") when it is a relationship (*saṃbandha*).

Thus: *śatasya pradīvyati*, *śataṃ pradīvyati*, *śatena pradīvyati*, and *śate pradīvyati*. In the sense of connection (*saṃbandha*), as in "he eats five times a day"; in the sense of locus (*ādhāra*), as in "he eats twice a day"; and in the sense of instrument (*karaṇa*), as in "he eats with two [days] a day. In the sense of connection, the genitive occurs in *bhavata āsikā* ("the sitting of you") and *apāṃ sraṣṭā* ("the creator of waters"). Likewise: *cikīrṣā Devadattasya kaṭasya* ("Devadatta's desire to make a mat"), *bhedikā Yajñadattasya kāṣṭhānām* ("Yajñadatta's splitting of the wood"), and *śobhanā Pāṇineḥ sūtrasya kṛtiḥ* ("Pāṇini’s excellent composition of the sūtras").

"Pāṇini’s composition of the Sūtra is excellent"—here the third case (instrumental) is used for the agent (*kartṛ*). Likewise: "The milking of cows by one who is not a cowherd is wonderful," and "The milking of cows belonging to one who is not a cowherd is wonderful"—here the sixth case (genitive) is used for the relationship (*saṃbandha*). Similarly: "He is esteemed by kings"; "This is their sitting"; "The student’s laughing is beautiful"—here the third case is used for the agent in the phrase "the student’s laughing is beautiful. "Cooking rice" (*odanaṃ pacan*) and "cooking rice" (*odanaṃ pacamāna*)—here the second case is used for the object (*vyāpya*). Likewise: "Desiring to make a mat" (*kaṭaṃ cikīrṣuḥ*).

They say that the *rakṣ* [of the root *rākṣ*] is one that goes toward Vārāṇasī (*āgāmuka-vārāṇasīm*). Having made a mat, he went to the village (*kaṭaṃ kṛtvā grāmaṃ gataḥ*); he has gone to the village (*grāmaṃ gatavān*). How many here are putting on armor? He is studying the *pārāyaṇa*. "He will make mats" (*kartā kaṭān*). But when a relationship is intended to be expressed, as in "the lover of a maidservant" (*dāsyāḥ kāmukaḥ*), it is different. In the case of "a mat is easy to make for you" (*īṣatkaraḥ kaṭo bhavate*), the third case ending is used for the agent (*kartari*). But in the case of a relationship, the sixth case ending must certainly be used. Likewise, "hating the thief" (*caurasya dviṣan*). However, in "hating the thief" (*cauraṃ dviṣan*), the second case ending is used for the object (*vyāpye*).

Likewise, [we have] *kaṭaṃ kārako vrajati* ("the mat-maker goes"), *grāmaṃ gamī* ("going to the village"), and *śataṃ dāyī* ("one who will give a hundred"). In the cases of *varṣaśatasya pūrakaḥ* ("filling a hundred years"), *putrapautrasya darśakaḥ* ("seeing sons and grandsons"), and *śatasya dāyī* ("giver of a hundred"), the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is used because of the relationship (*saṃbandha*). Similarly, in *bhavataḥ kaṭaḥ kartavyaḥ* ("a mat must be made for you"), the genitive is used; however, in *bhavatā kaṭaḥ kartavyaḥ* ("a mat must be made by you"), the third case (*tṛtīyā*) is used because of the agent (*kartṛ*). Likewise, in *grāmaṃ kraṣṭavyā śākhā Devadattena* ("the branch must be pulled to the village by Devadatta"), the third case is used; whereas in *grāmaṃ kraṣṭavyā śākhā Devadattasya* ("the branch must be pulled to the village [for] Devadatta's"), the genitive is used because of the relationship. [And: *tulyārthais tṛtīyā vā* (Pāṇini 2.3.72).

When used in conjunction with words having the sense of "equal" (*tulya*), the genitive case is employed, or optionally the instrumental. *Tulyo Devadattasya* ("equal to Devadatta") or *tulyo Devadattena*. *Sadṛśo Devadattasya* ("resembling Devadatta") or *sadṛśo Devadattena*. Why is the instrumental not used here: *Arjunasya tulā nāsti* ("there is no equal to Arjuna") and *Keśavasyopamā na* ("there is no likeness to Keśava")? These two [words, *tulā* and *upamā*] do not have the meaning of "equal" (*tulya*); rather, they have the meaning of "the state of being equal" (*tulyatva*) and "comparison" (*aupamya*). Furthermore, with the words *hita* ("beneficial") and *sukha* ("pleasant"), the dative case is also used [alongside the genitive]. (Pāṇini 2.3.73).

When there is connection with *hita* (beneficial) and *sukha* (happiness), both the fourth (*caturthī*) and the sixth (*ṣaṣṭhī*) cases occur: *hitaṃ devadattāya*, *hitaṃ devadattasya*; *sukhaṃ devadattāya*, *sukhaṃ devadattasya*. [Also, the fourth case is used] in expressions of benediction (*āśis*) with words meaning long life (*āyuṣya*), auspiciousness (*bhadra*), welfare (*artha*), and skill (*kuśala*). (Pāṇini 2.3.73)

When words meaning "long life" (*āyuṣya*) and so forth, or words meaning "welfare" (*hita*) and "happiness" (*sukha*), are used in conjunction [with another word], the genitive and dative cases occur, provided that a benediction (*āśis*) is being expressed. For example: *āyuṣyaṃ Devadattasya* ("May there be long life for Devadatta") or *āyuṣyaṃ Devadattāya*. Likewise: *ciraṃ jīvitam*; *bhadram*, *madram*; *arthaḥ*, *prayojanam*; *kuśalam*, *anāmayam*; *hitam*, *pathyam*; *sukham*, *śarma bhūyāt* ("May there be happiness"). The first quarter of the second chapter is completed. *sup supaikārtham* (2.2.1).

It should be understood that this is the governing rule (*adhikāra*): "A word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*) becomes a single unified meaning (*ekārtha*) with another word ending in a case-suffix. And that unification of meanings (*ekārthībhāva*) of words that originally have distinct meanings is called a compound (*samāsa*). [The following items are indeclinables (*asaṃkhyam*): the case endings (*vibhakti*), proximity (*samīpa*), absence (*abhāva*), renown (*khyāti*), "after" (*paścāt*), "according to" (*yathā*), "simultaneously" (*yugapat*), completion (*sampad*), and entirety (*sākalya*). (Pāṇini 2.2.2)

An indeclinable (*asaṃkhya*) ending in a *sup* suffix, when expressing the sense of case-endings (*vibhakti*) and so forth, becomes a single unified meaning (*ekārtha*) with another word ending in a *sup* suffix. In that regard, first, regarding the sense of a case-ending (*vibhaktyartha*): "A conversation took place among women" is expressed as *adhistri*. Regarding proximity (*samīpa*): "In the vicinity of a jar" is expressed as *upakumbham*. Non-existence (*abhāva*) is of many kinds due to the diversity of its relata. Among these: - Regarding the absence of prosperity (*ṛddhyabhāva*): "The prosperity of the Yavanas has departed" is expressed as *duryavanam*. - Regarding the absence of objects (*arthābhāva*): "The absence of flies" is expressed as *nirmakṣikam* or *nirmaśakam*. - Regarding the absence of transgression (*atikramābhāva*): [The example follows].

*Atigata* (passed beyond): *atitṛṇāni*, *nistṛṇam* (grassless). In the sense of absence: *atitaitsṛkam ācchādanam* (a covering that has lost its threads). In the sense of renown: *Pāṇineḥ khyātiḥ*, *itipāṇini*, *tatpāṇini*. In the sense of "afterwards": *anurathaṃ pādātam* (infantry following the chariots). The meaning of *yathā* is manifold; therein, in the sense of suitability: *anurūpaṃ svarūpo bhavati* (he becomes conformable to his own nature). In the sense of distributive repetition (*vīpsā*): *pratyarthaṃ śabdā abhiniviśante* (words apply to each respective object). In the sense of not exceeding: *yathāśakti* (according to one's ability). In the sense of similarity: *sadṛśaḥ kikhyā*, *sakikhi* (like a crow). In the sense of succession:

*Yathāvṛddham*, *anujyeṣṭham*: according to seniority. In the case of simultaneity (*yaugapadya*): *sacakraṃ nidhehi*. The meaning is "place the wheels down simultaneously. *Saṃpad* is twofold: perfection of one's own being (*ātmabhāvasaṃpatti*) and prosperity (*samṛddhi*). *Saṃpannaṃ brahma*: the Veda is mastered by the Bābhravas; it refers to their excellence. Prosperity is seen among the Madras: *sumadram*. In the sense of totality (*sākalya*): *satṛṇam abhyavaharati* ("he eats everything, even the grass"). *Sāgny adhīte* ("he studies, including the Agni-portion"). Regarding *yathā na tulye* (Pāṇini 2.1.7):

the word *yathā* does not form a single compound with a case-inflected word when it has the sense of "equality" (*tulya*). For example: *yathā Devadattas tathā Yajñadattaḥ* ("As is Devadatta, so is Yajñadatta").

(2.2.4) *yāvad iyattve*: The word *yāvat* expresses a limited quantity (*iyattā*) when it forms a single semantic unit with a nominal ending (*subanta*). Example: *yāvadamatraṃ brāhmaṇān āmantrayasva* ("Invite as many Brahmins as there are vessels"). Why say "limited quantity"? [Counter-example: *yāvad dattaṃ tāvad bhuṅktām* ("Let him eat as much as has been given"). (2.2.5) *pratinā mātrārthe*: [The sixth case ending is used] with *prati* when it signifies a measure (*mātrārtha*).

A word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*) becomes a single syntactical unit (*ekārtha*) with *prati* when it has the sense of "measure" (*mātrārtha*). Examples: *sūpaprati*, *śākaprati*. Why "in the sense of measure"? [Consider: *vṛkṣaṃ prati vidyotate vidyut* ("the lightning flashes toward the tree").

[The rule] *saṃkhyākṣaśalākāḥ pariṇā dyūte 'nyathāvṛttau* (Pāṇini 2.1.6): [Words denoting] numbers, dice, or counting-sticks, when combined with *pari* in the context of gambling, form a single unit when there is a change in the outcome.

Words such as *saṃkhyā* (count) and others have the same referent as *pari* in the context of gambling, when a change from the previous state is understood. For example, in a game with five dice, when all fall either face-up or face-down, the thrower wins. When there is a change from that previous state—when it does not happen as before by even a single die—that is *ekapari*. Likewise, *dvipari*, *tripari*, and *catuṣpari*.

With two dice in a game of dice, it did not turn out as it had before by means of one die; this is *akṣapari*. It did not turn out as it had before by means of one counter-stick; this is *śalākāpari*. Why "in a game of dice" (*dyūte*)? [Because] by means of one arrow, it did not turn out as it had before. Why "when it has turned out otherwise" (*anyathāvṛttau*)? Because by means of the die, it turned out exactly as it had before.
[The rule] *paryapāṅbahirañcaḥ pañcamyā vā* (Pāṇini 2.2.7) [is applied].

Words such as *pari* and others may optionally form a single semantic unit with a word ending in the fifth case (*pañcamyanta*). For example: *paritrigartaṃ vṛṣṭo devaḥ* (the god rained all around Trigarta); *pari Trigartebhyo vṛṣṭo devaḥ* (the god rained all around the Trigartas). *apatrigartaṃ vṛṣṭo devaḥ* (the god rained away from Trigarta); *apa Trigartebhyo vṛṣṭo devaḥ* (the god rained away from the Trigartas). *āpāṭaliputraṃ vṛṣṭo devaḥ* (the god rained up to Pāṭaliputra); *ā Pāṭaliputrād vṛṣṭo devaḥ* (the god rained up to Pāṭaliputra). *bahirgrāmam*, *bahir grāmāt* (outside the village). *prāggrāmam*, *prāg grāmāt* (east of the village). The word *vā* (optionally) is a governing heading (*adhikāra*). [The next rule is: *lakṣaṇenābhipratī* (2.2.8).

The terms *abhi* and *prati* have the same meaning as *lakṣaṇa* (mark/direction). Examples: *abhyagni śalabhāḥ patanti* (moths fall toward the fire); *pratyagni śalabhāḥ patanti* (moths fall toward the fire). Why [is it said] "with *lakṣaṇa*"? Example: *srughnaṃ prati gataḥ* (he went toward Srughna). Why [are it said] "*abhi* and *prati*"? Example: *yenāgnis tena gataḥ* (he went in the direction where the fire is). Even in the sense of another word-meaning (*anyapadārtha*), it occurs by virtue of another rule: *abhyaṅkā gāvaḥ* (cows with marks on their foreheads). *Anu* [is used] in the senses of proximity and extension (Pāṇini 2.1.14).

The word *anu*, when signifying proximity (*sāmīpya*) or extension (*āyāma*), forms a single semantic unit with a nominal stem ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*). Examples: *anuvanam aśanir gatā* ("the thunderbolt struck along the forest"); *anugaṅgaṃ Vārāṇasī* ("Vārāṇasī is situated along the Ganges"). Why specify "proximity and extension"? [Consider: *vṛkṣam anu vidyotate vidyut* ("the lightning flashes near the tree"). [This concludes the section on] *tiṣṭhadgu* and so forth (Pāṇini 2.1.17).

The group beginning with *tiṣṭhadgu* are irregularly formed (*nipātita*) in the sense of forming a single integrated meaning (*ekārthībhāva*). *tiṣṭhadgu*: at the time when cows stand [to be milked]; *vahadgu*: at the time when cows are being driven; *āyatīgavam*: at the time when cows are coming home; *khaleyavam*: when barley is in the threshing-floor; *lūnayavam*: when barley has been reaped; *lūyamānayavam*: when barley is being reaped; *pūtayavam*: when barley has been winnowed; *pūyamānayavam*: when barley is being winnowed; *saṃhṛtayavam*: when barley has been gathered; *saṃhriyamāṇayavam*: when barley is being gathered; *saṃhṛtabusam*: when the chaff has been gathered; *saṃhriyamāṇabusam*: when the chaff is being gathered; *samaṃbhūmi*: level ground; *samaṃpadāti*: level for a pedestrian; *suṣamam*: very even; *viṣamam*: uneven; *niṣṣamam*: quite even; *duṣṣamam*: difficult to traverse; *aparasamam*: not even; *āyatīsamam*: even in the future.

*prāhṇam*, *praratham*, *pramṛgam*, *pradakṣiṇam*, *saṃprati*, *asaṃprati*, *pāpasamam*, *puṇyasamam*, etc. Pāremadhye ṣaṣṭhyā vā (2.2.11): The two words *pāre* and *madhye* optionally form a single compound with a word ending in the genitive case when they have the same referent (*ekārtha*). Their form ending in *-e* is due to irregular derivation (*nipātana*). Examples: *pāregaṅgam* (the further bank of the Gaṅgā), *madhyegaṅgam* (the middle of the Gaṅgā). Because of the repetition of the word "optionally" (*vā*), we also have *Gaṅgāpāram* and *Gaṅgāmadhyam*. In the case of *madhyandinam* (midday), the nasal augment (*num*) is prescribed because [the compound] is analyzed as *madhyasya dinam* (the day's middle).

(2.2.12) *saṃkhyā vaṃśyena*: Numerical words optionally form a single referent (*ekārtha*) with nominal stems denoting lineage (*vaṃśya*) that end in case endings (*subanta*). For example: "two sages belonging to the lineage of grammar" (*dvau munī vyākaraṇasya vaṃśyau*) may be expressed as *dvimuni vyākaraṇasya* or *dvimuni vyākaraṇam*. (2.2.13) *nadībhiḥ*: [Numerical words optionally form a single referent] with words for rivers (*nadī*).

Numerical words form a single unified meaning (*ekārtha*) when combined with words denoting rivers. For example: *dviyamunam* ("two Yamunās"), *triyamunam* ("three Yamunās"). Regarding the rule *anyārthe nāmni* (Pāṇini 2.1.24): a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*) forms a single unified meaning with river names when it denotes something other than the members of the compound themselves, provided it is a proper name (*nāman*). Examples: *Unmattagaṅgam* ("the region where the Gaṅgā is mad"), *Tūṣṇīṃgaṅgam* ("the region where the Gaṅgā is silent"). Why does the rule specify "denoting something else" (*anyārthe*)? Consider: *Kṛṣṇaveṇṇā*, which is the name of a river itself. Why does the rule specify "when it is a proper name" (*nāmni*)? Consider: *śīghragaṅgo deśaḥ* ("the region of the swift Gaṅgā"), which is not a proper name.
"That which has been mentioned above is to be understood as neuter" (2.2.15). And it has been illustrated in exactly that manner.
"A *kāraka* [is compounded] diversely" (2.2.16).

A case-inflected word (*kāraka*) frequently forms a single integrated meaning (*ekārthībhāva*) when combined with another case-inflected word. Examples: *kaṣṭaṃ śritaḥ* (one who has resorted to hardship) becomes *kaṣṭaśritaḥ*; *kāntārātītaḥ* (one who has passed beyond the wilderness); *śvabhraṃ patitaḥ* (one who has fallen into a pit) becomes *śvabhrapatitaḥ*; *grāmaṃ gataḥ* (one who has gone to the village) becomes *grāmagataḥ*; *taraṅgātyastaḥ* (one who has leaped over the waves); *sukhaprāptaḥ* (one who has attained happiness), *sukhāpannaḥ* (one who has entered into happiness), *duḥkhāpannaḥ* (one who has entered into suffering); *grāmagamī* (one who goes to the village), *grāmāgāmī* (one who comes from the village); *odanaṃ bubhukṣuḥ* (one who desires to eat rice) becomes *odanabubhukṣuḥ*. In some cases, the compound formation (*vṛtti*) occurs only in specific instances: *kumbhakāraḥ* (potter), *śvapacaḥ* (outcaste). Also, *khaṭvārūḍhaḥ* (one who has mounted the bed) is used in a derogatory sense.

In some cases, it is simply a sentence: *odanaṃ bhuktavān* ("he has eaten rice"). *Svayaṃdhautau pādau*; the meaning is "by oneself" (*ātmanā*). And that [word] is indeed a *kāraka*. *Sāmikṛtam*; the meaning is "half-done. And that is established as being precisely a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*). Times measured by days are those completed by nights: *sarvarātrakalyāṇī* ("beautiful throughout the entire night"). *Giriṇā kāṇaḥ*, *girikāṇaḥ* ("blind in one eye because of a mountain [fall]"). *Dhānyenārthaḥ*, *dhānyārthaḥ* ("in need of grain"). *Māsena pūrvaḥ*, *māsapūrvaḥ* ("preceded by a month"). *Māsāvaraḥ*, *māsavikalaḥ*, *māsonaḥ* ("lacking a month," "deficient by a month," "short by a month").

"Conflict with a sword" is *asinā kalahaḥ*, which becomes *asikalahaḥ*. "Skilled in speech" is *vāgnipuṇaḥ*; "mixed with molasses" is *guḍamiśraḥ*; "smooth in speech" is *vākślakṣṇaḥ*. In all these cases, this third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is characterized by its status as a *kāraka* (grammatical participant), because in the state of being "one-eyed" (*kāṇa*) and so forth, the mountain (*giri*) and other such things function as the instrument (*karaṇa*), or because in the sense of "doing," they function as the agent (*kartṛ*). How is it that [the forms] *pitṛsadṛśaḥ* ("resembling his father") and *pitṛsamaḥ* ("equal to his father") are formed? They will be formed with the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*), just as in the expression *pitṛtulyam* ("equal to the father"). "Killed by the king" is *rājñā hataḥ*, which becomes *rājahataḥ*. "Cut by a sword" is *asinā chinnaḥ*, which becomes *asicchinnaḥ*. In these instances, there is indeed a compound formation (*vṛtti*): "carried by the feet" is *pādābhyāṃ hriyate*, which becomes *pādahārakaḥ*.

One who sleeps on his side is called *pārśvaśayaḥ*. In these cases, there is only a syntactical connection (*vākya*): "he has reaped with a sickle" (*dātreṇa lūnavān*), "he has cut with an axe" (*paraśunā chinnavān*). When expressing an additional meaning by means of suffixes such as *-tavya*, we have: "a well to be licked by dogs" (*śvalehyaḥ kūpaḥ*), "a river to be drunk from by crows" (*kākapeyā nadī*). It does not occur otherwise: "to be drunk by crows" (*kākaiḥ pātavyā*). In some instances it does occur: "to be ignited by chaff" (*busopendhyam*), "to be struck by a mallet" (*ghanaghātyam*). "Rice mixed with curds" (*dadhyodanaḥ*)—rice sprinkled with curds (*dadhnā upasikta odanaḥ*). "Parched grain mixed with molasses" (*guḍadhānāḥ*)—parched grain mixed with molasses (*guḍena miśrā dhānāḥ*). Since the action is already manifested by the word used in the compound formation (*vṛtti*), there is no lack of semantic capacity (*asāmarthya*).

That which is to be given to the gods is *devadeyam*; a flower fit for the gods is *devadeyam*. Wealth to be given to a Brahmin is *brāhmaṇadeyam*. A maiden to be given as a boon is *varapradeyā*. Here it does not occur: *brāhmaṇāya dātavyam* (to be given to a Brahmin). Fear of a wolf is *vṛkabhayam*; one afraid of a wolf is *vṛkabhītaḥ*; fear of a wolf is *vṛkabhītiḥ*; one who fears a wolf is *vṛkabhīḥ*. One gone out from a village is *grāmanirgataḥ*; one who loathes unrighteousness is *adharmajugupsuḥ*; fallen from a branch is *śākhāpetaḥ*; pushed off by the feet is *pādāpoḍhaḥ*; released from a wheel is *cakramuktaḥ*; fallen from a bed is *mañcapatitaḥ*; terrified by a wave is *taraṅgāpatrastaḥ*. Here it does not occur: *prāsādāt patitaḥ* (fallen from the palace). One intoxicated with dice is *akṣaśauṇḍaḥ*.

*akṣadhūrtaḥ*, *akṣakitavaḥ* (a cheat at dice); *kāmpilye siddhaḥ*, *kāmpilyasiddhaḥ* (one who has attained perfection in Kāmpilya); *chāyāśuṣkaḥ*, *kumbhīpakvaḥ*, *carakabandhaḥ*, *cakrabandhaḥ*; *tīrthadhvāṅkṣaḥ*, *tīrthakākaḥ*, *tīrthavāyasaḥ*—in these cases, the use of words such as *dhvāṅkṣa* (crow) serves only to express contempt. Here it does not occur: *tīrthe kākaḥ* (a crow at a sacred bathing place). *māse deyam ṛṇam*, *māsadeyam* (a debt to be paid in a month); *pūrvāhṇe geyaṃ sāma*, *pūrvāhṇageyam* (a Sāman hymn to be sung in the forenoon). Here it does not occur: *māse deyā bhikṣā* (alms to be given in a month).

In the formation of names such as *araṇyetilakāḥ* ("wild sesame plants") and *araṇyemāṣakāḥ* ("wild beans"), there is no elision (*aluk*) [of the case-ending]. For example: *pūrvāhṇe kṛtam* → *pūrvāhṇakṛtam*; likewise, *tatra kṛtam*, and so on, including *avataptenakulasthitam*. Regarding *pātresamitāḥ* and others for which there is no elision, these are also syntactic phrases (*vākya*), and since there is no other compound form for them, there is no fault in their having separate meanings. By this same rule, forms such as *udumbaramaśakaḥ* ("a gnat in a fig tree") are also established. In some cases, there is only a compound (*vṛtti*):

*upasarajaḥ* ("born from a secondary source"), *svāduṃkāraṃ bhuṅkte* ("he eats making it sweet"), *saṃpannaṃkāraṃ bhuṅkte* ("he eats making it excellent"). In other cases, there is only a phrase (*vākya*): *agre bhuktvā* ("having eaten first"), *agre bhojam* ("eating first").

*Caturthī prakṛtyā* (2.2.17): A word ending in the fourth case (*caturthī*) and ending in a *sup*-suffix becomes a single referent (*ekārtha*) when combined with a word ending in a *sup*-suffix that denotes the material cause (*prakṛti*). Example: *yūpāya dāru* → *yūpadāru* ("wood for a sacrificial post"). Why say "by the material cause"? [Counter-example: *randhanāya sthālī* ("a pot for cooking"). How then are forms such as *tadartham* ("for its sake") and *mātrartham* ("for the sake of a measure") formed? They will be formed under the rule for the "other referent" (*anyapadārtha*). How then are *kuberabaliḥ*, *go hitam*, *gosukham*, and *gorakṣitam* formed? They are established by the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*). *Viśeṣaṇam ekārthena* (2.2.18).
