An attributive word ending in a case-suffix becomes a single unified meaning when combined with a substantive ending in a case-suffix that is in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*). For example: "that which is blue and is a lotus" is *nīlotpalam* (blue lotus). Because of the rule of diversity (*bahulādhikāra*), sometimes the sentence form remains: *dīrghaś cārāyaṇaḥ* (the long Cārāyaṇa), *lohitas takṣakaḥ* (the red Takṣaka). Sometimes there is only the compound form: *kṛṣṇasarpaḥ* (black snake), *lohitaśāliḥ* (red rice). Why say "attributive"? [To exclude: *takṣakaḥ sarpaḥ* (Takṣaka is a snake). Why say "with a single unified meaning"? [To exclude: *anyaḥ kṛṣṇāt* (other than black).

How is "chinnaprarūḍha" (grown back after being cut) an example of a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*)? It is established as such by its very nature. Likewise: *ekapuruṣa* (one man), *sarvānna* (all food), *jaraddhastī* (an old elephant), *purāṇadhānya* (old grain), *navaudana* (fresh rice), *kevalānna* (exclusive food); *Pūrveṣukāmaśamī*, *Saptarṣayaḥ* (the Seven Sages); *pañcakapālaṃ haviḥ* (an oblation in five vessels), *pañcagavadhana* (wealth consisting of five cows), *pañcapūlī* (a bundle of five); *yājñikakitava* (a fraudulent sacrificer), *pāpakulāla* (a wicked potter), *aṇakanāpita* (a mean barber). In some cases, the qualifier functions as a standard of comparison (*upamāna*): *śastrīva śyāmā* (dark like a knife) becomes *śastrīśyāmā*; *śarakāṇḍagaurī* (fair as a reed-stalk).

In some cases, the qualifier becomes the object of comparison (*upamāna*): "This man is like a tiger" becomes *puruṣavyāghraḥ* ("tiger-like man") or *puruṣasiṃhaḥ* ("lion-like man"). In this manner, other terms such as *vyāghra* and so forth—whether explicitly mentioned or not—are to be applied accordingly. Examples include: *pūrvapuruṣaḥ*, *aparapuruṣaḥ*, *prathamapuruṣaḥ*, *caramapuruṣaḥ*, *jaghanyapuruṣaḥ*, *samānapuruṣaḥ*, *madhyapuruṣaḥ*, *madhyamapuruṣaḥ*, and *vīrapuruṣaḥ*. Those who were not ranks (*aśreṇayaḥ*) were made into ranks (*śreṇayaḥ*) become *śreṇikṛtāḥ*.

In this same manner, other compounds such as *śreṇī* and so forth should also be applied with the terms *kṛta* and the rest, whether they have been explicitly mentioned or not. For example: *kṛtākṛtam*, *kṛtāpakṛtam*, *bhuktābhuktam*, *bhuktavibhuktam*; *gatapratyāgatam*, *yātānuyātam*, *aśitānaśitam*, *kliṣṭākliśitam*; *krayākrayikā*, *puṭāpuṭikā*, *phalāphalikā*, *mānonmānikā*; *satpuruṣaḥ*, *mahāpuruṣaḥ*, *paramapuruṣaḥ*, *uttamapuruṣaḥ*. In the case of *puruṣottamaḥ*, the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) comes after [the qualified] due to the rule of "frequent occurrence" (*bahulādhikāra*).

An excellent man (*utkṛṣṭapuruṣaḥ*); a bull among cows (*govṛndārakaḥ*), an elephant among men (*puruṣanāgaḥ*), a noble elephant among men (*puruṣakuñjaraḥ*). Who is a bad Kaṭha? Which [specific] Kaṭha? What kind of king is he who does not protect? What kind of cow is it that does not carry? What kind of man is he, a *kinnara*? A young female merchant (*ibhyapoṭā*), a young female merchant (*ibhyayuvatiḥ*), a small fire (*agnistokaḥ*)—these are qualifiers that follow [the noun], due to the rule of "frequently" (*bahulādhikārāt*). Likewise: a little curd (*dadhikatipayam*), a cow that has calved once (*gogṛṣṭiḥ*), a milch cow (*godhenuḥ*), a cow that has ceased to give milk (*go-vaśā*), a cow whose calf has died (*govehat*), a cow that has borne only once (*gobaṣkayaṇī*).

A reciter of the *Kaṭha* [branch], a learned scholar of the *Kaṭha*, a teacher of the *Kaṭha*, a rogue of the *Kaṭha*; a preeminent cow, a superior horse. A young bald man, a young bald woman. A young gray-haired man, a young gray-haired woman. A young wrinkled man, a young wrinkled woman. A young old man, a young old woman. Food that is hot; equally white, similarly black. White-black, black-white. A female ascetic who is still a child, a cow that is pregnant. One whose shoulders are slumped like those of a peacock: *mayūravyaṃsaka*.

Alternatively, *vyaṃsaka* means one whose shoulders (*aṃsau*) have fallen away; like a peacock, he is a deceiver, thus a *mayūravyaṃsaka*. Likewise, a *chāttravyaṃsaka*. Like a Kāmboja, he is shaven-headed, thus a *kambojamuṇḍa*. Likewise, a *yavanamuṇḍa*. That which is both high (*uccam*) and low (*avacam*) is *uccāvacam*; likewise, *uccanīcam*. "Nothing exists" or "there is nothing belonging to him," thus *akiñcana*. The elision of the vowel and the addition of the suffixes should be understood according to the rule for words beginning with *pṛṣodara* (Pāṇini 6.3.109). However, expressions such as *snātvākālakaḥ* ("one who has become dark after bathing") are merely syntactical compounds (*vākyasamāsa*).

The word *ehivāṇija* exists here [as a compound], and by virtue of belonging to the *arśa-ādi* group (Pāṇini 4.2.147), the suffix *ac* is applied. Thus, *ehivāṇijā* refers to the action [of "come, merchant"]. The same applies to *utpatanipatā* and so forth. [The compound] *pūrvakāya* consists of *pūrva* (fore-) and *kāya* (body); the word *kāya* is used here for a part of the body. Why does this not apply in the case of *kāyasya pūrvam ardham* ("the front half of the body")? Because that [compound] would be dependent (*sāpekṣatvāt*). Similarly: *aparakāya*, *adharakāya*, *uttarakāya*, *madhyamakāya*; as well as *madhyāhna* (midday) and *sāyāhna* (evening). And [the compound] *ardhapippalī* consists of *ardham* (half) and *pippalī* (pepper).

"Pippalyardham" is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). And we see such usage even in cases of unequal division, as in "the southern half of Meru," "half of heaven" (*svarārdham*), "half of the body" (*kāyārdham*), and "twenty-nine [fingers] including half of the crest" (*cūlikārdham*); for one cannot accept the "half-old-woman" fallacy (*ardhajaratīya*) here. Furthermore, "second alms" (*dvitīyabhikṣā*) means that which is both second and alms; "alms-second" (*bhikṣādvitīyam*) is a genitive compound. Likewise: "third alms" (*tṛtīyabhikṣā*), "alms-third" (*bhikṣātṛtīyam*); "fourth alms" (*caturthabhikṣā*), "alms-fourth" (*bhikṣācaturtham*).

*turyabhikṣā*, *bhikṣāturyam*; *turīyabhikṣā*, *bhikṣāturīyam*. The prohibition [stated] in Pāṇini 2.2.23, "not with a word denoting a part," does not apply here, because of the governing principle of *bahulam* ("diversely"). [This is also governed by] Pāṇini 2.2.19: "The words *prāpta* and *āpanna* [form a compound] with a word in the second case, and [the final vowel of the first member] becomes long."

The words *prāpta* ("attained") and *āpanna* ("incurred") form a single semantic unit with a word ending in the second case (*dvitīyā*), and the final vowel of these two [words] becomes short (*atva*). Examples: *prāpto jīvikām* → *prāptajīvikaḥ* (one who has attained a livelihood). *prāptā jīvikām* → *prāptajīvikā* (a woman who has attained a livelihood). *āpanno jīvikām* → *āpannajīvikaḥ* (one who has incurred a livelihood). *āpannā jīvikām* → *āpannajīvikā* (a woman who has incurred a livelihood). *Māso jāto 'sya* ("a month has been born for him") → *māsajātaḥ* ("born after a month"). It is indeed desired that a word ending in the suffix *-kta* be placed last when following words such as *jāti*, *kāla*, and *sukha*. A genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) will not occur here because it would be redundant with a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*). [The rule for] *nañ* (Pāṇini 2.2.20).

The particle *nañ* becomes one in meaning with a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*). For example: *na brāhmaṇaḥ* = *abrāhmaṇaḥ* ("one who is not a Brāhmaṇa"). Due to the rule of "diversity" (*bahulādhikāra*), this occurs even with certain words that are semantically incompatible: *asūryampaśyāni mukhāni* ("faces that do not see the sun"), *apunar-geyāḥ ślokāḥ* ("verses not to be sung again"), *aśrāddhabhojī* ("one who does not eat at a funeral feast"). By the rule *īṣad-guṇena* (Pāṇini 2.2.21), the word *īṣat* ("slightly") becomes one in meaning with a word denoting a quality (*guṇa*). For example: *īṣat-kaḍāraḥ* ("slightly tawny"), *īṣat-piṅgalaḥ* ("slightly reddish-brown"). Why specify "with a quality"? [Consider: *īṣad bhoktavyam* ("it should be eaten slightly").

A word ending in the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) that ends in a nominal suffix (*subanta*) forms a single unified meaning (*ekārtha*) when combined with another word ending in a nominal suffix. For example: *rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ* ("the king's man") becomes *rājapuruṣaḥ* ("king's man").

(2.2.23) *na l-anirdhārya-pūraṇa-bhāva-tṛptārthaiḥ*: [The sixth case does not compound] with words denoting selection (*anirdhārya*), ordinal numbers (*pūraṇa*), abstract states (*bhāva*), or words having the sense of satisfaction (*tṛptārtha*).

A word ending in the genitive case does not form a single unified meaning (*ekārtha*) with a word denoting that which is being singled out (*nirdhāryamāṇa*), a word denoting completion (*pūraṇa*), a word denoting an abstract state (*bhāva*), or words denoting satisfaction (*tṛpta*). Examples: *mātuḥ smaran* (remembering his mother). *sarpiṣo dayamānaḥ* (feeling compassion for the ghee). *gavāṃ kṛṣṇāḥ saṃpannakṣīratamāḥ* (among the cows, the black ones have the most abundant milk). *chātrāṇāṃ pañcamaḥ* (the fifth among the students). *paṭasya śuklatā*, *paṭasya śuklatvam*, *paṭasya śauklyam* (the whiteness of the cloth). Due to the rule of "diversity" (*bahulādhikāra*), it sometimes occurs: *vartamānasāmīpyam* (proximity to the present time).

How is it that [the compound] *brāhmaṇasya śuklā dantāḥ* ("the Brahmin’s white teeth") does not occur? It will not occur because of its dependency (*sāpekṣatva*). But here it certainly does occur: *candanagandhaḥ* ("the fragrance of sandalwood"), *nadīghoṣaḥ* ("the sound of a river"), *kanyārūpam* ("the beauty of a maiden"), *stanasparśaḥ* ("the touch of a breast"), and *phalarasaḥ* ("the juice of fruit"). [Similarly: *phalānāṃ tṛptaḥ* ("satisfied with fruits"), *phalānāṃ suhitaḥ* ("well-nourished by fruits"), *phalānām āśitaḥ* ("eaten of fruits"). [And: *brāhmaṇasyoccair gṛham* ("the Brahmin’s high house") will not occur because of its dependency. However, the formation *brāhmaṇasya kartavyam* ("the Brahmin’s duty") and *brāhmaṇakartavyam* ("the Brahmin’s duty") is also accepted as a valid usage (*vṛtti*).

In the expression *rājñaḥ pāṭaliputrakasya dhanam* ("the wealth of the king of Pāṭaliputra"), the genitive case is used because of a relationship with wealth; however, [in the absence of such a relationship], it will not occur. In the case of *rājño gauś cāśvaś ca puruṣaś ca* ("the king's cow, horse, and man"), where there is a plurality of referents, it remains merely a sentence (*vākya*). In *rājño go'śvapuruṣāḥ* or *rājago'śvapuruṣāḥ*, the compound (*vṛtti*) occurs through the unification of meaning (*ekārthībhāva*). In the case of *sarpiṣo jñānam* ("the knowledge of ghee"), a compound indeed occurs with a genitive of relation: *sarpirjñānam*.

And likewise, examples such as *mātṛsmaraṇam* (remembering one's mother), *sureśvaraḥ* (lord of the gods), *idhmavraścanaḥ* (wood-cutter), and *palāśaśātanaḥ* (leaf-shatterer) are observed. [Examples of the genitive of relation: *rājñāṃ mataḥ* (approved by kings), *rājñāṃ buddhaḥ* (known by kings), *rājñāṃ pūjitaḥ* (honored by kings); *idam eṣām āsitam* (this is their sitting); *āścaryo gavāṃ doho ’gopālakena* (wonderful is the milking of cows by one who is not a cowherd). [Examples of the genitive of agent: *bhavata āsikā* (the act of sitting by you), *apāṃ sraṣṭā* (the creator of waters), *odanasya pācakaḥ* (the cooker of rice). A compound with the genitive of relation certainly occurs; that prohibition does not exist at all.

Likewise, terms such as *brāhmaṇayājaka* ("one who sacrifices for Brahmins") and *gurupūjaka* ("one who honors his teacher") are indeed accepted by grammarians such as Yājñavalkya and others. Because they are conventional (*rūḍhi*) in the sense of "play" or "livelihood," they form obligatory compounds (*nityasamāsa*): *uddālapuṣpabhañjikā* ("the game of breaking *uddāla* flowers"), *daṇḍalekhaka* ("a staff-scribe"), and *nakhalekhaka* ("a nail-scribe").
This is governed by the rule *kuprādayo 'supvidhau nityam* (Pāṇini 2.2.18).

The word *ku* and the particles beginning with *pra* (prādayaḥ) are always of one meaning when combined with a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*), except in cases other than those governed by the rules for case-suffixes (*sup*). Examples: *kubrāhmaṇaḥ* (a bad Brahmin), *koṣṇam* (slightly warm); *praṇāyakaḥ* (a leader), *abhiṣekaḥ* (anointment); *prakṛtya*, *prakṛtam*; *duṣpuruṣaḥ*, *duṣkṛtam*; *supuruṣaḥ*, *sukṛtam*; *atistutam*, *abhiṣṭutam*; *ākaḍāraḥ*, *ābaddhaḥ*. The particles beginning with *pra* (prādayaḥ), when used in the sense of "gone" (*gata*) and so forth, are compounded with a word in the nominative case: *pragata ācāryaḥ* (the teacher has gone away) becomes *prācāryaḥ*; *prāntevāsī* (the student has departed). The particles beginning with *ati* (atyādayaḥ), when used in the sense of "transgressed" (*krānta*) and so forth, are compounded with a word in the accusative case: [e.g., *atikrāntaḥ khaṭvām* becomes *atikhaṭvaḥ*].

*Atikrāntaḥ khaṭvām* (having passed beyond the bed) becomes *atikhaṭvaḥ*. Similarly, *atimālaḥ*. Words beginning with *ava-* [form compounds] with a word in the third case when expressing the sense of "called out" (*kruṣṭa*) and so forth: *avakruṣṭaṃ kokilayā vanam* (the grove called out by the cuckoo) becomes *avakokilam*; likewise, *avamayūram*. Words beginning with *pari-* [form compounds] with a word in the fourth case when expressing the sense of "exhausted" (*glāna*) and so forth: *pariglāno 'dhyayanāya* (exhausted regarding study) becomes *paryadhyayanaḥ*. Words beginning with *nis-* [form compounds] with a word in the fifth case when expressing the sense of "departed" (*krānta*) and so forth: *niṣkrāntaḥ kauśāmbyāḥ* (departed from Kauśāmbī) becomes *niṣkauśāmbiḥ*. Why is it said "when a *sup*-suffix is prescribed"? [Consider: *vṛkṣaṃ prati vidyotate* (it flashes toward the tree)—here no compound is formed. *Rodasī iva* (like heaven and earth) remains a sentence only. Likewise, words such as *punarpravṛddha* and others [are treated similarly]. Or, [compounding occurs] under the rule *anyapadārthe sup supā* (when the meaning is that of another word, a *sup*-ending word is compounded with a *sup*-ending word).

Pāṇini 2.2.25: *ūry-ādi-kārikā-cvi-ḍācaḥ kriyā-arthaiḥ*. Words beginning with *ūrī*, the word *kārikā*, and words ending in the suffixes *cv-* and *ḍāc* become one in meaning (*ekārtha*) with verbal nouns (*subanta*) that express an action. Examples: *ūrīkṛtya*, *ūrīkṛtam*; *urarīkṛtya*, *urarīkṛtam*.

*ūrī*, *urarī*, *urasī*, *pāpī*, *tālī*, *ātālī*, *vetālī*, *dhūlī*, *dhūṣī*, *śalākā*, *saṅkalā*, *dhvaṃsakalā*, *bhraṃśakalā*, *guluguhā*, *sajūs*, *phalūs*, *phalī*, *viklī*, *āklī*, *alambī*, *kevālī*, *sevālī*, *vārdālī*, *masamasā*, *samasamā*, *śrauṣaṭ*, *vauṣaṭ*, *vaṣaṭ*, *svāhā*, *svadhā*, *prādus*, *śrat*, *āvis*. [The following are used] as if they were onomatopoeic sounds (*anukaraṇam*): *kārikākṛtya*, *śuklīkṛtya*, *paṭapaṭākṛtya*. (Pāṇini 5.4.57–58).

An imitative word (*anukaraṇa-śabda*) becomes a single semantic unit with words ending in case-suffixes (*subanta*) that denote an action. For example: *khāṭkṛtya*. How so? [In the sentence] *khāḍ iti kṛtvā niraṣṭhīvat* ("Having made the sound 'khāṭ', he spat"), it will not apply because of the intervention by the word *iti*.

(2.2.27) *bhūṣaṇādarānādareṣv alaṃsadasataḥ*: In the senses of adornment (*bhūṣaṇa*), respect (*ādara*), and disregard (*anādara*), the words *alam*, *sat*, and *asat* become a single semantic unit with words ending in case-suffixes that denote an action. Examples: *alaṃkṛtya*, *satkṛtya*, *asatkṛtya*. Why "in the senses of adornment and so forth"? Consider: *alaṃ bhuktvā gataḥ* ("He went after eating enough"), *sat kṛtvā gataḥ* ("He went after doing well"), *asat kṛtvā gataḥ* ("He went after doing poorly"). In these cases, the rule does not apply.

*agrahe 'ntaḥ* (Pāṇini 2.2.28): The word *antaḥ*, when not meaning "seizing," becomes a single semantic unit (*ekārtha*) with case-inflected words (*subanta*) that express an action. Example: *antarhatya*. Why does it say "not meaning seizing"? Consider: *antar hatvā mūṣikāṃ gataḥ*. The meaning here is "having caught the mouse, he went. *kaṇemanasī tṛptau* (Pāṇini 2.2.29): [The words *kaṇe* and *manasi* become single semantic units with case-inflected words expressing an action] when satisfaction (*tṛpti*) is meant.

The two words *kaṇe* and *manas*, when expressing satiety, become synonymous with nominalized verbal forms (*subanta*) used for the sake of an action. Examples: *kaṇehatya payaḥ pibati* ("he drinks milk until he is satisfied"); *manohatya payaḥ pibati* ("he drinks milk until he is satisfied"). The meaning is: "he drinks as much as is necessary to be satiated. Why specify "when expressing satiety"? [Counter-example: *kaṇe hatvā*, *mano hatvā gataḥ* ("having struck at the ear," "having struck at the mind, he departed").
*puro‘stam asaṃkhyam* (Pāṇini 2.1.30).

The two words *puras* and *astam*, when lacking a number, become one in meaning with words ending in case-suffixes (*subanta*) that denote an action. Examples: *puraskṛtya*, *astaṃkṛtya*. Why does it say "lacking a number"? [Consider: *tisraḥ puraḥ kṛtvā gataḥ* ("having made three cities his front, he went") and *astaṃ kṛtvā kāṇḍaṃ gataḥ* ("having made the arrow its end, he went").
*Accha* [is compounded] with words denoting motion and with the word *vad* along with words ending in case-suffixes (Pāṇini 2.1.13).
The word *accha* becomes one in meaning with words ending in case-suffixes that have the sense of motion and with the word *vad*. Examples: *acchagatya*, *acchavrajya*; *acchodya*.

*ado 'nupadeśe* (2.2.32): The word *adas*, when used in the sense of "not pointing out," becomes a single semantic unit with inflected words (*subanta*) that denote an action. Example: *adaḥkṛtya cintayati* ("having done that, he thinks"). Why say "when not pointing out"? Observe: *adaḥ kṛtvā gataḥ* ("having done this, he went"). *tiro 'ntardhau* (2.2.33): [The word *tiras* is compounded] when it means "disappearance."

The word *tiras* signifies "disappearance" (*antardhāna*) and forms a single semantic unit with indeclinables ending in case endings that denote an action. For example: *tirobhūya* ("having become hidden"). Why say "in the sense of disappearance"? Consider: *tiro hatvā mūṣikāṃ gataḥ* ("having killed the mouse, he went away [out of sight]"). Alternatively, by rule 2.2.34 (*kṛñā vā*), the word *tiras* optionally forms a single semantic unit with the verb *kṛ* when it is accompanied by a case-ending. Thus: *tiraskṛtya* or *tiraḥ kṛtvā* ("having set aside" or "having disregarded").
*Upāje’nvāje* (Pāṇini 2.2.35):

These two words, *upāje* and *anvāje*, optionally form a single syntactical unit with a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*) when used with the root *kṛ*. [Examples: *upājekṛtya*, *upāje kṛtvā*; *anvājekṛtya*, *anvāje kṛtvā*. *Sākṣādādīni* (Pāṇini 2.2.36).

Words such as *sākṣāt* and others either form a single semantic unit with the nominalized verb *kṛ* (to do), or they stand independently. Examples include: *sākṣātkṛtya*, *sākṣāt kṛtvā*; *mithyākṛtya*, *mithyā kṛtvā*. The following words [combine with *kṛ*]: *sākṣāt*, *mithyā*, *cintā*, *bhadrā*, *locanā*, *āryā*, *asthā*, *prājaryā*, *prājaruhā*, *bījaruhā*, *saṃsaryā*, *arthe*, *lavaṇam*, *uṣṇam*, *śītam*, *udakam*, *ārdram*, *namas*.
[Furthermore, according to Pāṇini 2.1.37: In the sense of "not placing upon" (*anatyādhāne*), [the words] *uras*, *manas*, *madhya*, *pade*, and *nivacane* [combine with *kṛ*].

Except when there is the sense of "placing upon" (*atyādhāna*), words such as *uraḥ* and others, when combined with the verb *kṛ*, may optionally form a single semantic unit with a word ending in a case-suffix. For example: *urasikṛtya* or *urasi kṛtvā*; *manasikṛtya* or *manasi kṛtvā*; *madhyekṛtya* or *madhye kṛtvā*; *padekṛtya* or *pade kṛtvā*; *nivacanekṛtya* or *nivacane kṛtvā*. Why does it say "except when there is the sense of placing upon"? Consider: *urasi kṛtvā pāṇiṃ śete* ("Having placed his hand upon his chest, he lies down"). Or: *hastinaḥ pade kṛtvā śiraḥ śete* ("Having placed his head at the foot of the elephant, he lies down").
[The following rule applies: *nityaṃ hastepāṇāv udvāhe* (Pāṇini 2.2.38): [In the sense of marriage, the forms] *haste-kṛtya* and *pāṇau-kṛtya* are always used.

The two words *haste* and *pāṇau* always form a single semantic unit with a finite verb (*karoti*) when followed by a nominal ending (*subanta*), provided they refer to marriage (*udvāha*). Examples: *hastekṛtya*, *pāṇaukṛtya*. Why "provided they refer to marriage"? Witness: *haste kṛtvā kārṣāpaṇaṃ gataḥ* ("having taken a kārṣāpaṇa coin in his hand, he departed"). Regarding the rule *prādhvam bandhe* (Pāṇini 2.1.39): the word *prādhvam* always forms a single semantic unit with a finite verb (*karoti*) when followed by a nominal ending (*subanta*), provided it refers to binding (*bandha*). Example: *prādhvaṃkṛtya*. Why "provided it refers to binding"? Witness: *prādhvaṃ kṛtvā śakaṭaṃ gataḥ* ("having made the cart ready for the journey, he departed").
Regarding the rule *jīvikopaniṣadāv aupamye* (2.2.40):

these two words, when used in the sense of comparison (*aupamye*), are always synonymous with the word *kṛ* followed by a nominal suffix (*suvantena*). Examples: *jīvikākṛtya*, *upaniṣatkṛtya*. Why "in the sense of comparison"? [Example: *jīvikāṃ kṛtvā gataḥ* ("having made a living, he departed").

Regarding the rule *asaṃkhyaṃ vānabhipretākhyāne ktvā* (2.2.41): [the suffix *ktvā* is optionally used after a verbal root] when expressing something that is not intended, provided it is not a number.

An indeclinable (*asaṃkhya*) ending in *su* becomes a single semantic unit with the verb *karoti* when it ends in *ktvā*, provided that the verbal expression is not intended as a direct report (*anabhipretākhyāna*). Example: "O Brahmin, a son has been born to you! [The other replies: "What then, O low-born one? Did you say this 'having done it low' (*nīcaiḥ kṛtvā*)? [The first asks: "Why 'low'? [The second replies: "Indeed, what is pleasant should be told 'loudly' (*uccaiḥ*). Why does it say "provided that the verbal expression is not intended as a direct report"? Consider: "having done it loudly" (*uccaiḥ kṛtvā*). *tiryak* with the sense of completion (*samāpti*) (Pāṇini 2.2.42): The word *tiryak* becomes a single semantic unit with the verb *karoti* when it ends in *ktvā* in the sense of completion. Examples: *tiryakkṛtya*, *tiryak kṛtvā*. Why does it say "in the sense of completion"? Consider: "Having placed the arrow sideways, he went" (*tiryak kṛtvā kāṇḍaṃ gataḥ*). Here, the action of placing the arrow sideways is not yet finished; he merely did so before departing.

(2.2.43) *svāṅgāt tas-nādhārthaṃ bhuvā ca*: A word ending in *tas* derived from a part of one's own body (*svāṅga*) optionally forms a single compound with the verb *karoti*, with words having the sense of *dhā* (the suffix *-tra*), and with the verb *bhavati*, provided they end in the suffix *ktvā*. Examples: *mukhataḥkṛtyācaṣṭe*, *mukhataḥ kṛtvā* (having made [it] in front). *mukhatobhūya*, *mukhato bhūtvā* (having become in front). *nānākṛtya*, *nānākṛtvā* (having made diverse). *nānābhūya*, *nānā bhūtvā* (having become diverse). *dvidhākṛtya*, *dvidhā kṛtvā* (having made twofold). *dvidhābhūya*, *dvidhā bhūtvā* (having become twofold). *aikadhyamkṛtya*, *aikadhyam kṛtvā* (having made into one). *aikadhyambhūya*, *aikadhyam bhūtvā* (having become one).

Due to the mutual association (*sāhacarya*) of *tas* and the others, [the suffix] does not occur here: *mukhe tasyati*, *mukhataḥ kṛtvā*, or *pṛthak kṛtvā*. When that which is already existing is made otherwise, why does [the suffix] not occur? Because of its connection only with what is heard from the root *kṛ* (i.e., the verbal form itself). *tūṣṇīm* (Pāṇini 2.2.44): The word *tūṣṇīm* either has the same meaning as the root *bhū* followed by a suffix ending in *ktvā*. Thus: *tūṣṇīṃbhūya* or *tūṣṇīṃ bhūtvā*.

(2.2.45) *anvak* [is used] in the sense of conformity (*ānukūlya*). The word *anvak* optionally forms a single syntactical unit with a verbal root ending in the suffix *ktvā*, when conformity is understood. Examples: *anvagbhūyāste* (he stands conforming to him), *anvagbhūtvā*. Why say "in the sense of conformity"? [Counter-example: *anvagbhūtvā tiṣṭhati śatruḥ* (having followed behind, the enemy stands). (2.2.46) *anekam* [is used] in the sense of "another" (*anyārtha*).

A plurality of inflected words (*subanta*), when functioning in the sense of another inflected word, becomes a single meaning (*ekārtha*). For example: "he whose cows are brindled" is *citraguḥ*; "that forest in which many elephants are intoxicated" is *mattabahumātaṅgam*; "that tree upon which a monkey has climbed" is *ārūḍhavānaraḥ*; "he by whom guests have been honored" is *pūjitātithiḥ*; "to whom an animal has been offered" is *upahṛtapaśuḥ*; and "that from which *t* follows" is *taparaḥ*.

Ten have approached these: they are *upadaśāḥ*. They are near ten (*āsannadaśāḥ*), not far from ten (*adūradaśāḥ*), or more than ten (*adhikadaśāḥ*). Their measure is thirty (*tridaśa*): they are *tridaśāḥ*. How does the word *daśan* function in the sense of a number? Through proximity to a word denoting a measure (*parimāṇa*); just as when one says, "five is their measure: *pañcakāḥ* birds. Or two or three is their measure: *dvitrāḥ*. The word *vā* has the sense of "or": two or three, *dvitrāḥ* birds.

The intermediate space between the southern and eastern directions is the south-eastern direction (*dakṣiṇapūrvā dik*); or, being both southern and eastern, it is the south-eastern direction. "He has come with his son" (*saputra āgataḥ*) means he has come together with his son. "Hairy" (*salomakaḥ*) means having existing hair. Likewise, "having wings" (*sapakṣakaḥ*). In the expression "the Brāhmaṇī who possesses milk" (*astikṣīrā brāhmaṇī*), the word *asti* is not a numeral. In certain cases, because the meaning is already understood, other words are not employed. "He whose black [color] resides on his neck" (*kaṇṭhekālaḥ*).

His face is like the face of a camel: *uṣṭramukhaḥ*. A mass of hair is his crest: *keśacūḍaḥ*. An ornament made of gold is his [adornment]: *suvarṇālaṃkāraḥ*. Fallen leaves belong to him: *prapatitaparṇaḥ*. Leaves have departed from him: *praparṇaḥ*. Sons do not exist for him: *avidyamānaputraḥ*. Sons are not present for him: *aputraḥ*. In some cases, the suffix does not occur: *pañcabhir bhuktam asya* ("five have been eaten by him") and *bhrātuḥputro 'syāsti* ("he has a brother's son"), because of the rule regarding "frequency" (*bahulādhikāra*).

Regarding the rule *tatra gṛhītvā tena prahṛtya yuddhe sarūpam* (Pāṇini 2.2.47): when multiple words of identical form ending in the locative case (*saptamyanta*) and the instrumental case (*tṛtīyānta*) occur, signifying the two senses of "having seized there" and "having struck with that," they form a single compound in the sense of battle (*yuddha*), which is the external referent (*anyapadārtha*). For example: *keśeṣu ca keśeṣu ca gṛhītvā yuddhaṃ vṛttam* ("Having seized each other by the hair, a battle took place") becomes *keśākeśi*. Similarly, *daṇḍaiś ca daṇḍaiś ca prahṛtya yuddhaṃ vṛttam* ("Having struck each other with sticks, a battle took place") becomes *daṇḍādaṇḍi*. Likewise, *muṣṭāmuṣṭi*. The suffix *ic* is applied by the rule *ij vyatihāre* (Pāṇini 5.4.116). By the rule *ici* (Pāṇini 5.2.48), the substitution of long *ā* (*ātvam*) occurs.

In that context, what is meant by "by means of that" (*tena*)? [Example: "Having struck body against body, a battle took place. Why say "having seized and having struck"? [Counter-example: "Standing in chariot against chariot, a battle took place. Why say "battle"? [Counter-example: "Having grasped hand in hand, friendship was formed. Why say "of the same form" (*sarūpa*)? [Counter-example: "Having struck with clubs and with maces, a battle took place. This refers to the sense of "and" (*ca*). (Pāṇini 2.2.48)

Multiple words ending in case-suffixes (*subanta*) become a single meaning in the sense of *ca* (and). There are many senses of *ca*: conjunction (*samuccaya*), sequential mention (*anvācaya*), mutual connection (*itaretarayoga*), and collective totality (*samāhāra*). Among these, the process of becoming a single meaning (*ekārthībhāva*) is possible in the cases of mutual connection and collective totality, but not in conjunction nor in sequential mention. "A horse and a bull" (*aśvaś ca balīvardaś ca*) results in *aśvabalīvardau* (mutual connection) or *aśvabalīvardam* (collective totality).

In this section concerning the formation of a single meaning (*ekārthībhāva*), that which was mentioned first occurs first, because there is no purpose for deviating from the sequence. In some cases, however, the reverse is observed due to the governing rule of "frequently" (*bahulādhikāra*): *dantānāṃ rājā*, i.e., *rājadantaḥ*. In other cases, out of disregard for the sequence, even that which pertains to the earlier time is placed last: *liptavāsitaḥ*, *nagnamuṣitaḥ*, *siktasammṛṣṭaḥ*, *bhṛṣṭaluñcitaḥ*, *avaklinnapakvaḥ*, *arpitotaḥ*, *uptagāḍhaḥ*.

Regarding the principle of semantic unity (*aikārthya*), in certain cases a word ending in *i* or *u* is placed first: *agnivātau*, *paṭuguptau*. In other cases, the subsequent word is placed first: *citrāsvātī*, *bhāryāpatī*, *jaṃpatī*, *daṃpatī*, *putrapatī*, *putrapaśū*, *keśaśmaśru*, *śirovidu*. In some instances there is no fixed rule: *sarpirmadhunī*, *madhusarpiṣī*; *antādī*, *ādyantau*; *guṇavṛddhī*, *vṛddhiguṇau*; *paṭumṛduśulkāḥ*, *paṭuśuklamṛdavaḥ*.

In some cases, a word beginning with *aja-* or ending in *-a* is placed first: *aśvakharam*, *uṣṭrakharam*. In other cases, the reverse is also observed: *śūdrāryam*, *āryaśūdram*; *Avatyaśmakam*; *Viṣvaksenārjunau*. In some instances there is no fixed rule: *dharmārthau*, *arthadharmau*; *śabdārthau*, *arthaśabdau*; *kāmārthau*, *arthakāmau*; *candrārkau*, *arkacandrau*; *Indrāgnī*, *Agnīndrau*; *candrārkendrāḥ*, *arkacandrendrāḥ*, *Indrārkacandrāḥ*.

In some cases, the word with fewer syllables comes first: *plakṣanyagrodhau* (the Plakṣa and Nyagrodha trees), *dhavakhadirau* (the Dhava and Khadira trees). In other cases, the order is reversed: *ulūkhalamusale* (mortar and pestle), *taṇḍulakiṇvam* (rice and fermenting agent), *Citrarathabāhlīkau* (Citraratha and the Bāhlīkas), *snātakarājānau* (the graduate and the king), *akṣibhruvam* (the eye and the eyebrow), *dāragavam* (wife and cow). In other cases, there is no fixed rule: *Dhanapatirāmakeśavāḥ* (Kubera, Rāma, and Keśava). According to Pāṇini 3.1.117, the suffix *kvin* is applied after the roots *vipūya*, *vinīya*, and *jitya* when followed by the words *muñja*, *kalka*, and *hali* respectively. Regarding seasons and lunar mansions, those with similar vowels follow their natural sequence: *hemantaśiśirau* (winter and cool season), *kṛttikārohiṇyau* (the Kṛttikās and Rohiṇī constellations).

Regarding the rule that among words of unequal length and few syllables, the one with fewer syllables should be placed first—as in *grīṣmavasantau* (summer and spring)—that is incorrect, because we see it otherwise: "In autumn, summer, and spring, curd is generally forbidden. Also, "A man desiring an abundance of fruit should travel under the asterisms Śravaṇa, Dhaniṣṭhā, and Aśvinī. They also desire the prior placement of numerals, names of brothers, and castes in their respective order—as in *pañca ca ṣaṭ ca*, i.e., *pañcaṣaṭ*; or *Yudhiṣṭhirārjunau*; or *brāhmaṇakṣatriyavaiṣyaśūdrāḥ*. That too is incorrect, as deviations are observed.

The dual and singular endings are used for two and one [respectively] (Pāṇini 1.4.22). [In compounds, words] excluding those denoting three or two [categories] are placed first. For example: *Arjunabhīmasenau* (Arjuna and Bhīmasena); *śūdraviṭkṣatriyaviprāṇām* (the Śūdra, Vaiśya, Kṣatriya, and Brāhmaṇa). A word with fewer syllables is placed first: *kuśakāśam* (Kuśa grass and Kāśa grass). Yet even this is subject to exceptions, as seen in the expression *kāśakuśāvalambanam* (clinging to Kāśa and Kuśa grass). A more venerable person is placed first: *Vasudevārjunau* (Vāsudeva and Arjuna). Even in that case, an exception is observed in the form *Naranārāyaṇau* (Nara and Nārāyaṇa).

Since cognition does not proceed toward a qualified object (*viśeṣya*) until its qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) has been apprehended, the qualifier is placed first. For example: *nīlotpalam* (blue lotus), *citraguḥ* (one who possesses variegated cows). Because words such as *sarva-* are also qualifiers, they likewise take the first position: *sarvaśvetaḥ* (all-white), *sarvakṛṣṇaḥ* (all-black). Similarly, numerals take the first position: *pañcaraktaḥ* (five-red), *saptonnataḥ* (seven-tall), *dvyanyaḥ* (other-than-two), *tryanyaḥ* (other-than-three). Even words ending in the locative case take the first position because they function as qualifiers: *kaṇṭhekālaḥ* (Kāla on the throat), *vahegaḍuḥ* (a goitre on the shoulder).

How are [the compounds] *gaḍukaṇṭhaḥ*, *gaḍuśirāḥ*, and *vajrapāṇiḥ* formed? *Gaḍukaṇṭhaḥ* means "one whose throat is marked by a goitre" (*gaḍūpalakṣitaḥ kaṇṭho 'sya*). Otherwise, it would be *kaṇṭhegaḍuḥ*. Similarly, *gaḍuśirāḥ* means "one whose head has a goitre" (*śirasigaḍuḥ*). *Vajrapāṇiḥ* means "one whose hand is a thunderbolt" (*pāṇivajraḥ*). Even for words ending in a past passive participle (*ktānta*), there is prior placement [of the participle] precisely because they function as qualifiers: *kṛtakaṭaḥ* ("one who has made a mat") and *bhikṣitabhikṣaḥ* ("one who has begged alms"). In the analysis (*vigraha*) "a mat was made by him" (*kaṭe kṛtam anena*), there is freedom of usage, as seen in the expression *mahāhavaripuskandhaghṛṣṭacakrāya Cakriṇe* ("to the Wielder of the Discus, whose discus was rubbed against the shoulders of the enemies in the great battle").

In the case of *udyatāsiḥ* (one with a raised sword) and *asyudyataḥ* (one by whom a sword is raised), both forms are possible because the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and the qualified (*viśeṣya*) may be placed in either order as desired. Similarly: *āhitāgniḥ* (one who has established the sacred fires) and *agnyāhitaḥ*; *jātadantaḥ* (one whose teeth have grown) and *dantajātaḥ*; *jātaputraḥ* (one whose son is born) and *putrajātaḥ*; *jātaśmaśruḥ* (one whose beard has grown) and *śmaśrujātaḥ*; *pītatailaḥ* (one who has drunk oil) and *tailapītaḥ*; *pītaghṛtaḥ* (one who has drunk ghee) and *ghṛtapītaḥ*; *ūḍhabhāryaḥ* (one who has married a wife) and *bhāryoḍhaḥ*. The same applies elsewhere. Likewise, in the case of words denoting genus (*jāti*), time (*kāla*), pleasure (*sukha*), and so forth: *sāraṅgajagdhī* (one by whom a spotted deer was eaten) and *jagdhasāraṅgaḥ*.

One who has eaten onions (*palāṇḍubhakṣitaḥ*), one by whom onions have been eaten (*bhakṣitapalāṇḍuḥ*). One born a month ago (*māsajātaḥ*), one in whom a month has been born (*jātamāsaḥ*). One devoid of happiness (*sukhahīnā*), one from whom happiness has departed (*hīnasukhā*). Likewise: one fond of molasses (*guḍapriyaḥ*), one for whom molasses is dear (*priyaguḍaḥ*). Similarly, even when the meaning of the final member [is predominant]: Kaḍāra Jaimini (*kaḍārajaiminiḥ*), Jaimini the tawny (*Jaiminikaḍāraḥ*). Gaḍula the one-eyed (*gaḍulakāṇaḥ*), the one-eyed Gaḍula (*kāṇagaḍulaḥ*). Lame Kuṇḍa (*khañjakuṇḍaḥ*), Kuṇḍa the lame (*kuṇḍakhañjaḥ*). Lame-bowed Khālāti (*khoḍakhalatiḥ*), Khālāti the lame-bowed (*khalatikhoḍaḥ*). A white old man (*gauravṛddhaḥ*), an old white man (*vṛddhagauraḥ*). A tawny mendicant (*bhikṣupiṅgalaḥ*), a tawny mendicant (*piṅgalabhikṣuḥ*).

Thin and dull-witted (*tanuvaṭharaḥ*), dull-witted and thin (*vaṭharatanuḥ*). Black and white (*kṛṣṇaśvetaḥ*), white and black (*śvetakṛṣṇaḥ*), and so forth. In the sense of a collective aggregate, the neuter gender is used (Pāṇini 2.4.29).

In the sense of a collective compound (*samāhāra*), that which has a single referent becomes neuter. This has already been illustrated and will be further illustrated. [An example occurs] in the rule regarding the restatement of Vedic schools: *caraṇānāṃ stheṇor luṅi* (Pāṇini 2.4.3).

In the case of the mention (*anuvāda*) of Vedic schools (*caraṇa*), there is indeed a collective singular (*samāhāra*) when the roots *sthā* and *i* are used with the suffix *luṅ*. For example: *pratyaṣṭhāt Kaṭhakauthumam*, *udagāt Kaṭhakālāpam*. Here, the verbal expression of the rise and establishment of these [schools], which are already known through other means of knowledge, constitutes a mention (*anuvāda*). In other cases: *udaguḥ Kaṭhakālāpāḥ*. Why "of the Vedic schools" (*caraṇānām*)? [Observe: *udagur mīmāṃsakavaiyākaraṇāḥ*. Why "of the roots *sthā* and *i*" (*stheṇoḥ*)? [Observe: *agaman Kaṭhakālāpāḥ*. Why "with *luṅ*" (*luṅi*)? [Observe: *atiṣṭhan Kaṭhakālāpāḥ*. [The rule] *adhvaryukratūnām anapuṃsakānām* (Pāṇini 2.4.51).

A collective singular sense (*aikārthya*) occurs in the case of a combination of sacrifices prescribed in the *Yajurveda* that do not have neuter gender endings. For example: *arkāśvamedham*. Why is the term "Adhvaryu" mentioned? [To exclude cases such as] *pañcaudana-daśaudanau* (the five-rice and ten-rice offerings). Why "of sacrifices"? [To exclude cases such as] *darśapaurṇamāsau* (the New and Full Moon sacrifices), for only a sacrifice accompanied by Soma is termed a *kratu*. Why "not neuter"? [To exclude cases such as] *vājapeya-rājasūye* (the Vājapeya and Rājasūya).
[This applies to those] whose recitation is proximate (*saṃnikṛṣṭapāṭhānām*). (Pāṇini 2.4.52)

When there is a collection (*samāhāra*) of words whose study is not separated [in time], they form a single referent (*aikārthya*). This applies to the *padaka* and *kramaka* recensions. Why is the term "proximate" (*saṃnikṛṣṭa*) mentioned? [To exclude cases like] "the sacrificer and the grammarian" (*yājñika-vaiyākaraṇau*). Why is the term "recitation" (*pāṭha*) mentioned? [To exclude cases like] "father and son" (*pitā-putrau*). Regarding the rule *aprāṇijātīnām* (Pāṇini 2.4.53): for general terms referring to non-living things (*aprāṇi-viṣaya*), there is a formation of a single referent when they are collected. Examples: *ārāśastri* ("saw and axe"), *dhānāśaṣkuli* ("fried grain and cake"). Why is the term "non-living" (*aprāṇi*) mentioned? [To exclude cases like] "a Brāhmaṇa and a Kṣatriya" (*brāhmaṇa-kṣatriyau*). Because of the mention of those "similar to living beings," it does not apply to categories that are not substances (*adravya-jāti*): e.g., "color, taste, smell, and touch" (*rūpa-rasa-gandha-sparśāḥ*). Why is the term "categories" (*jātīnām*) mentioned? [To exclude proper names, such as] "Nandaka and Pāñcajanya" (*Nandaka-pāñcajanyau*).

(2.2.54) *nadīdeśanagarāṇāṃ bhinnaliṅgānām*: In the case of rivers, regions, and cities that have different genders, there is a formation of a single compound meaning when they are combined in a collective sense (*samāhāra*). Examples: *Gaṅgāśoṇam* (the Ganges and the Śoṇa), *Kurukurukṣetram* (the Kuru and Kurukṣetra), *Mathurāpāṭaliputram* (Mathurā and Pāṭaliputra). Since the term "regions" (*deśānām*) already establishes this for regions, this statement is for the purpose of restriction (*niyama*): it should apply only to cities, and not to villages. Example: *Jāmbavaśālūkinyau* (the Jāmbava and the Śālūkinī). How is it here: *Śauryaṃ ca nagaraṃ Ketavatā ca grāmaḥ*, [forming] *Śauryaketavatam*? For the rule applies to cities, whereas there is no prohibition regarding villages.

Regarding the phrase "of rivers, regions, and cities": what is the purpose? [The examples are] *kukkuṭamayūryau* ("the cock and the peahen"). By the mention of "region" (*deśa*), a country (*janapada*) is understood, because "river" (*nadī*) is mentioned separately. [Another example is] *Gaurīkailāsau* ("Gaurī and Kailāsa"). Regarding the phrase "of those with different genders": what is the purpose? [The counter-examples are] *Gaṅgāyamune* ("the Gaṅgā and Yamunā"), *Madrakekayau* ("the Madras and Kekayas"), and *Mathurātakṣaśile* ("Mathurā and Takṣaśilā"). (2.2.55) *nityaṃ vairiṇām*: for those who are eternally at enmity, there is a formation of a collective singular (*aikārthya*) in the sense of a copulative compound (*samāhāra*). [Examples are] *ahinakulam* ("snake and mongoose"), *aśvamahiṣam* ("horse and buffalo"), and *kākolūkam* ("crow and owl"). Why is the word "eternally" (*nitya*) used? [To exclude cases like] *Gopālakaśālaṅkāyanāḥ* ("the Gopālakas and Śālaṅkāyanas").

(2.2.56) Regarding artisans (*kārūṇām*): when there is a collective compound (*samāhāra*) of artisans, it becomes a single referent (*aikārthya*). For example: *takṣāyaskāram* (carpenter and blacksmith), *rajakatantravāyam* (washerman and weaver).
(2.2.57) Regarding cows, horses, and so forth (*gavāśvādīnām*).

In the case of a collective compound (*samāhāra*) of cows, horses, and so forth, there is a unity of meaning (*aikārthya*). Examples include: *gavāśvam* (cows and horses), *gavāvikam* (cows and sheep), *gavaiḍakam* (cows and goats), *ajāvikam* (goats and sheep), *ajaiḍakam* (goats and rams), *kubjavāmanam* (the hunchback and the dwarf), *kubjakairātam* (the hunchback and the Kirāta), *putrapautram* (sons and grandsons), *śvacaṇḍālam* (dogs and Caṇḍālas), *strīkumāram* (women and children), *dāsīmāṇavakam* (female slaves and young Brahmins), *śāṭīpucchakam* (cloths and tails), *uṣṭrakharam* (camels and donkeys), *uṣṭraśaśam* (camels and rabbits), *mūtraśakṛt* (urine and dung), *mūtrapurīṣam* (urine and excrement), *yakṛnmedam* (liver and fat), *māṃsaśoṇitam* (flesh and blood), *darbhaśaram* (Darbha grass and Śara grass), *darbhapūtikam* (Darbha grass and Pūtīka grass), *Arjunapuruṣam* (Arjuna trees and men), and *tṛṇolapam* (grass and Ulapa grass).

"Male and female slaves," "hut and cottage," "the Blessed One and his consort. Why is there this instruction regarding the substitution of *avaṅ*? [Because it applies to] "cow and horse," "cow and horses.
Regarding the rule *prāṇitūryāṅgānām* (Pāṇini 2.4.2):

for parts of living beings and parts of musical instruments, there is a unification of meaning (*aikārthya*) in a collective compound (*samāhāra*). [Examples: "hands and feet"; "the drummers and the panpipe players."

(2.2.59) *senāṅgānāṃ bahutve*: When the members of an army are expressed in the plural, their collective combination (*samāhāra*) results in a single unified meaning. For example: *hastinaś cāśvāś ca* (elephants and horses) becomes *hastyaśvam*. Why does it say "in the plural"? [Consider: *hastī cāśvaś ca* (an elephant and a horse) becomes *hastyaśvau* (the two: elephant and horse). (2.2.60) *kṣudrajantūnām*: [The same applies] for small creatures.

In the collective grouping of small creatures (*kṣudrajantu*), there is a single unified meaning. For example: *yūkālikṣam* ("lice and nits"). Only when there is plurality [does the dual apply]: *yūkā ca likṣā ca*, *yūkālikṣe* ("a louse and a nit").
A small creature may be one that has no bones, or one that is simply minute. Or it may be those whose weight is a hundred *prasṛta*; some say even down to the mongoose (*nakula*).

(2.2.61) *phalānām*: When there is a collective grouping (*samāhāra*) of fruits, they attain the status of a single referent (*aikārthya*). Example: *badarāmalakam* (the jujube and the myrobalan). Only when there is plurality [is this rule applied]; otherwise: "the jujube and the myrobalan," i.e., *badarāmalake*. (2.2.62) *vā vṛkṣatṛṇadhānyamṛgaśakuniviśeṣāṇām*: Or [the singular may optionally be used] for specific types of trees, grasses, grains, wild animals, and birds.

For specific types of trees and so forth, when they exist in plurality, there occurs either a collective compound (*samāhāra*) expressing a single meaning, or [the dual or plural forms]. Examples: *plakṣanyagrodham* / *plakṣanyagrodhāḥ*; *kuśakāśam* / *kuśakāśāḥ*; *tilamāṣam* / *tilamāṣāḥ*; *rurupṛṣatam* / *rurupṛṣatāḥ*; *haṃsacakravākam* / *haṃsacakravākāḥ*. The rule specifies "in plurality" (*bahutve*) precisely for this reason: *plakṣaś ca nyagrodhaś ca* results in *plakṣanyagrodhau* (dual). Why does the rule "for non-living species" (*aprāṇijātīnām*, Pāṇini 2.4.6) not apply here in the case of a collective compound? Because these denote individual substances (*dravyavacanatvāt*). This is governed by the rule *vyañjanānām* (Pāṇini 2.4.63).

In the case of a collection (*samāhāra*) of specific subordinate members (*vyañjana*), there may optionally be a single referent (*aikārthya*). For example: *dadhighṛtam*, *dadhighṛte*; *sūpaśākam*, *sūpaśāke*. This rule is introduced because the previous rule [Pāṇini 2.4.2], "of things not belonging to the class of living beings" (*aprāṇijātīnām*), would have made this obligatory. Regarding *aśvavaḍavau* (Pāṇini 2.4.12): in the collection of a horse and a mule, there may optionally be a single referent. This is already established by the rule for the sense of "and" (*cārtha*, Pāṇini 2.2.29). However, in the case of mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*), the masculine gender is prescribed as a formal exception (*nipātana*). Thus: *aśvavaḍavam*, *aśvavaḍavau*. From this very indicative mark (*jñāpaka*), it is understood that elsewhere, when there is a single referent in the sense of "and," the gender of the subsequent member (*paravalliṅga*) prevails. For example: *kukkuṭamayūryau* ("a cock and a peahen").

(2.2.65) *virodhinām adravyāṇām*: For words expressing opposites that do not denote substances (*adravya*), there is optionally a unification of meaning (*aikārthya*) in a collective compound (*samāhāra*). Examples: *sukhaduḥkham* or *sukhaduḥkhe*. Why "of opposites" (*virodhinām*)? [Counter-example: *kāmakrodhau* ("desire and anger"). Why "not denoting substances" (*adravyāṇām*)? [Counter-example: *sukhaduḥkhāv imau grāmau* ("these two villages, Sukha and Duḥkha").
(2.2.66) *na dadhipay-ādīnām*: [The rule does not apply] to *dadhipayas-* and similar compounds.

In the case of *dadhipayas* and similar compounds, there is no unity of meaning (*aikārthya*) in their collective sense. Examples include: *dadhipayasī*, *sarpirmadhunī*, *madhusarpiṣī*, *Brahmaprajāpatī*, *Śivavaiśravaṇau*, *Skandhaviśākhau*, *parijyākauśikau*, *pravargyopaniṣadau*, *yājyānuvākye*, *śuklakṛṣṇe*, and *idhmābarhiṣī*; in these cases, the lengthening of the vowel occurs by way of irregular derivation (*nipātana*). Furthermore: *dīkṣātapasī*, *medhātapasī*, *udūkhalamusale*, *ādyavasāne*, *śraddhāmedhe*, *ṛksāme*, and *vāṅmanase*.

In the enumeration "these ten are drummers and lute-players," because the meaning is intended to be expressed with distinction, there is no collective compound (*samāhāra*), just as in the case of the [ten] directions. However, when the proximity to a number is intended, the desire to express with either distinction or non-distinction is not contradictory; thus, in certain cases, a collective compound occurs: *upadaśaṃ pāṇipādam*, *aśvabalīvardam*, *aśvabalīvardau*; *adharottaram*, *adharottare*; *pūrvāparam*, *pūrvāpare*—and this is established by the rule *cārthe* (Pāṇini 2.2.29).
Regarding names, the genitive case is used before *kantha* in the sense of the Uśīnara people (Pāṇini 2.2.67).

A *kanthā* that follows a word ending in the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) becomes neuter in gender when it denotes a single object in the region of Uśīnara, provided it is used as a proper name (*saṃjñā*). Example: *sauśamikantham*. Why does [the rule] say "as a name" (*nāmni*)? Consider: *vīraṇakanthā*. Why does it specify "in the region of Uśīnara"? Consider: *dākṣikanthā*.
[The rule] *upajñopakramaṃ tadāditve* (Pāṇini 2.4.21) [applies here].

When a word ending in the sixth case (genitive) is followed by *upajñā* or *upakrama*, and when they signify a single object (*aikārthya*) and denote the beginning of that object (*tadāditva*), it becomes neuter. *Pāṇinopajñam akālakaṃ vyākaraṇam* (The grammar [known as] Akālaka is the invention of Pāṇini). *Candropajñam asaṃjñakaṃ vyākaraṇam* (The grammar [known as] Asaṃjñaka is the invention of Candra). *Nandopakramāṇi mānāni* (The measurements began with Nanda). Why "denoting the beginning of that" (*tadāditva*)? *Devadattopajñā mṛnmayaprākāraḥ* (The mud-brick wall is the invention of Devadatta). Only after the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhyāḥ*)? *anupajñā*, *sadupajñā*. This rule is formulated because the gender of the principal element would otherwise apply. *Sabhā* (assembly) following a word meaning "lord" (*īśvara*), provided it does not mean "king" (*arājñaḥ*), [is feminine]. (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.4.23)

A word ending in the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*), denoting a master (*īśvara*) but excluding the word *rājan*, when followed by the word *sabhā* in a sense of identity (*aikārthya*), becomes neuter. Examples: *inasabham*, *īśvarasabham*. Why "excluding *rājan*"? [To show: *rājasabhā*. How is *Candraguptasabhā* [justified]? This is not in the sense of a "master," as it is seen in other contexts as well. Only [when following] the sixth case: *īśvarasabhā*. [The rule continues: "After a word denoting a non-human being" (Pāṇini 2.4.23).

A word ending in the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*) denoting something other than a human, followed by the word *sabhā*, becomes neuter when there is identity of meaning (*aikārthya*). Examples: *piśācasabham* (an assembly of piśācas), *rākṣasasabham* (an assembly of rākṣasas). Why "other than a human"? [Consider: *devadattasabhā* (the assembly of Devadatta). Because the term refers to those resembling humans, this rule does not apply here: *kāṣṭhasabhā* (a wooden assembly). *aśālā* (Pāṇini 2.4.24):

A word ending in the sixth case followed by *sabhā* in the sense of a non-dwelling (*aśālārūpā*) becomes neuter when there is identity of meaning. Example: *gopālasabham*. The meaning is "a herd of cowherds."

*senāsurāśālāniśā vā* (2.2.72). The words *senā* and so forth, when following a word ending in the genitive case, optionally take the neuter gender when forming a single compound meaning (*aikārthya*). Examples: *brāhmaṇasenā* (the army of the Brāhmaṇas), *yavasuram*, *yavasurā*; *gośālam*, *gośālā*; *śvaniśam*, *śvaniśā*. Only when [the preceding word] ends in the genitive: *paramasenā* (the supreme army). *chāyā* (2.2.73). [The word *chāyā* follows a word ending in the genitive and takes the neuter gender when forming a single compound meaning.]
The word *chāyā* following a word ending in the sixth case optionally becomes neuter when there is identity of referent (*aikārthya*). For example: *kuḍyacchāyam*, *kuḍyacchāyā*.
Regarding the rule for multiplicity (*bāhulye*, 2.2.74):

when multiplicity is understood, the word *chāyā* following a word ending in the sixth case necessarily becomes neuter when there is identity of referent, because of this repeated prescription. For example: *iṣucchāyam*, *śalabhacchāyam*. Why "when multiplicity" (*bāhulye*)? [To show that it does not apply otherwise: *vṛkṣacchāyam*, *vṛkṣacchāyā*.

*patho 'saṃkhyāt* (2.2.75): When the word *pathin* follows a non-numerical [term], it becomes neuter when there is a single unified meaning (*aikārthya*). Examples: *apatham*, *utpatham*. Why "after a non-numeral"? Consider *rājapathaḥ* (royal road). Because this discussion concerns the alteration of gender based on the primary referent (*pradhāna*), the neuter form does not apply when the compound has a different referent: *apathā nagarī* (a city without a path), *utpatho deśaḥ* (a region with a deviant path). *Saṃkhyādiḥ samāhāre* (2.2.76): [A compound] beginning with a numeral [ending in *pathin*] is neuter when it denotes a collective (*samāhāra*).

In a collective compound (*samāhāra*), when there is a unity of meaning, words beginning with a numeral become neuter. For example: *pañcagavam* ("a collection of five cows"), *catuṣpatham* ("a crossroads"). Because the collective is a single entity, it takes the singular number. Why "beginning with a numeral" (*saṃkhyādi*)? Consider *dhavakhadiram* ("the *dhava* and *khadira* trees"); here, by the subsequent rule, the feminine gender does not apply. Why "in a collective" (*samāhāra*)? Consider *pañcakapālaḥ puroḍāśaḥ* ("a sacrificial cake on five potsherds") and *triputraḥ* ("having three sons"); these are not collectives. *aḥ strī* (2.2.77): A word beginning with a numeral that ends in the vowel *a*, when forming a collective in a state of unified meaning, becomes feminine. For example: *pañcapūlī* ("a bundle of five bundles"). "In a collective" (*samāhāra*) is understood [from the previous rule]: thus, *pañcakapālaḥ puroḍāśaḥ* remains masculine as it is not a collective.

*vāp* (Pāṇini 2.2.78): A compound beginning with a numeral and ending in *āp* optionally takes the feminine gender when expressing a collective (*samāhāra*). Examples: *pañcakhaṭvam*, *pañcakhaṭvī*. Only when it is a collective: *pañca khaṭvāḥ*.
[In this context,] there is the elision of the suffix *an* (Pāṇini 2.2.79).

In a collective compound (*samāhāra*) denoting a single unified meaning, there is elision of the final vowel of numerals such as *ananta* and others; furthermore, the feminine gender may optionally occur. For example: *pañcatakṣam*, *pañcatakṣī*. Only when it is a collective compound: *bahurājā* (a country with many kings).
"Not *pātra* and so forth" (Pāṇini 2.4.80): words beginning with *pātra* do not take the feminine suffix. Examples: *dvipātram*, *caturyugam*, *tribhuvanam*.
*rātrāhnavākāḥ puṃsi* (2.2.81): Words ending in *rātra*, *ahna*, and *vāka* are masculine. Examples: *ahorātraḥ*, *sarvarātraḥ*; *pūrvāhṇaḥ*; *anuvākaḥ*, *sūktavākaḥ*.
*aho 'sudinapuṇyāt* (2.2.82).

The word *aha-* occurs in the masculine when it follows the words *sudina-* and *puṇya-*, or any other [word] besides them. Examples: *ekāhaḥ*, *dvyahaḥ*, *tryahaḥ*. Why "except after *sudina-* and *puṇya-*"? [Answer: *sudināham*, *puṇyāham*. And in the neuter, [the words] beginning with *ardharca-* [are optionally masculine]; (Pāṇini 2.4.31). The words beginning with *ardharca-* function as both neuter and masculine. Examples: *ardharcam* / *ardharcaḥ*; *śatamānam* / *śatamānaḥ*; *vārabāṇam* / *vārabāṇaḥ*; *aṣṭāpadam* / *aṣṭāpadaḥ*.

In the exposition of gender through compounds (*samāsa*), words such as *gomaya* (cow-dung) need not be mentioned; likewise, those that possess both masculine and feminine genders, such as *gauḥ*, *iṣuḥ*, *aśaniḥ*, and *yoniḥ*; those with feminine and neuter genders, such as *arcis*; those with all genders, such as *taṭaḥ* and *śṛṅkhalā*; those with each single gender, such as *vṛkṣaḥ*, *khaṭvā*, and *kuṇḍam*; and those that are without gender, such as *yuṣmad* and *asmad*—all of these would have to be explicitly stated. Now, if it is desired that their gender be established either from common usage (*loka*) or from a grammatical treatise on gender (*liṅgānuśāsana*).
In exactly the same way, this will also apply to cow dung and other such things. But what are those [entities] that are feminine, masculine, and neuter?

Those objects regarding which worldly convention is established as "this is a woman," "this is a man," or "this is a thing" (idam)—those are designated by the world as feminine, masculine, and neuter.

*supi hrasvaḥ* (2.2.84): When a case-ending (*sup*) follows, a word standing in the neuter gender undergoes shortening. *rai-* becomes *atiri*; in place of the palatal (*tālavya*) [r], a palatal *i* is substituted. *nau-* becomes *atinu*; in place of the labio-velar (*kaṇṭhoṣṭhya*), a labio-velar *u* is substituted. Why "when a case-ending follows" (*supi*)? [Observe: *kāṇḍe*, *kuḍye*. *gor apradhānasyāntyasya* (2.2.85): [The final vowel] of the word *go-* when it is not the principal member [of a compound] is shortened.

When the word *go* occurs at the end of a compound as a subordinate member (*upasarjana*) followed by a case-ending (*sup*), it becomes short. For example: *citraguḥ*. Why specify "of the subordinate"? [Observe: *sugauḥ*. Why specify "at the end"? [Observe: *gokulam*. By the rule *ṅy-ādīnām* (Pāṇini 1.2.48), a feminine suffix such as *ṅīp* and others that ends a subordinate member becomes short. For example: *niṣkauśāmbiḥ*, *bahukhaṭvaḥ*, *ativāmoruḥ*. Why specify "of the subordinate"? [Observe: *rājakumārī*, *brahmabandhūḥ*. Why specify "at the end"? [Observe: *kumārīpriyaḥ*. How is the form *bahuśreyasī* derived? It will be stated later that the suffix *īyasun* undergoes the substitution of *ī*.

*lug aṇādiluky agoṇyādīnām* (Pāṇini 2.4.87): When there is elision (*luk*) of an *aṇ* suffix or others, there is elision of the feminine markers (*ṅyādi*) and so forth, but not of *goṇī* and the like. Example: *pañcendrāṇyo devatā asya* ("The five Indrāṇīs are its deities") becomes *pañcendraḥ*. Why mention "of an *aṇ* suffix or others"? [To exclude cases such as: *bahunāḍiḥ*. Why mention "elision" (*luk*)? [To exclude cases such as: *bahupatnīkaḥ*. Why mention "not of *goṇī* and the like"? [To exclude cases such as: *pañcabhir goṇībhiḥ krītaḥ* ("bought for five *goṇīs*"), which remains *pañcagoṇiḥ*; likewise, *pañcasūciḥ*. [The rule applies] only when the feminine marker is subordinate: *paramāvantī*. [The rule applies] only to the final vowel: *Avantīkulam*. *Varaṇā* is a name for both a city and a river; *Pañcālāḥ* is a name for both a country and its inhabitants.

In the case of *pañcālāmathurā*, since the case ending is not heard, the dual number applies only to the number of the referents of the nouns. In *harītakyaḥ phalāni*, the word retains its feminine gender even when referring to fruits. In *khalatikam vanāni*, *khalatika* is the singular name for those forests. Indeed, a difference in gender and number is observed among words even when they have the same meaning: *āpaḥ* (feminine plural) and *jalam* (neuter singular), or *dārāḥ* (masculine plural), *kalatram* (neuter singular), and *bhāryā* (feminine singular).

In the expression "the handsome Vadhrikā," the term "handsome" is an attribute of the person (*manuṣya*) and not of Vadhrikā herself. In "The Pañcālas have much food, much milk, and much ghee," it refers to the Pañcālas [as a collective]; in "The country of Pañcāla has many garlands and fruits," it refers to the country (*janapada*). In "the barley is abundant," the singular is used for the genus (*jāti*); in "the barley grains are abundant," the plural is used for distinct individuals (*vyakti*). In "we," there is a distinction between external and internal [persons], as in the case of teachers; however, in "I," the singular is used when one intends to express non-distinction.

"Kadā pūrve phālgunyau": the dual number is used because there are two stars. "Kadā pūrvāḥ phālgunyaḥ": the plural number is used when plurality is possible due to the inclusion of the moon. Likewise, "kadā pūrve proṣṭhapade" and "kadā pūrvāḥ proṣṭhapadāḥ. "Tiṣyapunarvasū": the dual number is used because there are two constellations. "Tiṣyapunarvasu": the singular number is used in the sense of a collective compound (*samāhāra*).

When there is an intention to express a distinction between individual stars—that is, when there is an intention to express a distinction in the number of constellations—the plural number does not exist at all because [the plurality] is absent. Since a word can have multiple meanings, the formation of a *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) is purposeless. For even a single word can be the designator of multiple objects, just as the word *rodasī* denotes both heaven and earth. Furthermore, there is the designation of objects belonging to different classes by a single word, as in "dice," "feet," or "beans"; how much more so, then, for those of the same class?

Since Gārgyāyaṇa also possesses the quality of being a Gārgya, when there is a desire to express non-difference, the form is *gārgyau*. When there is a desire to express difference, as in *baida-baidau*; however, when there is a desire to express non-difference, it must indeed be *baidau*, because in that case there is no prohibition [of the dual ending]. Since Gārgī also possesses the quality of being a Gārgya, Gārgī and Gārgyāyaṇa are *gārgyau*. Since a hen (*kukkuṭī*) also possesses the quality of being a cock (*kukkuṭa*), the hen and the cock are *kukkuṭau*. Likewise, father and mother are *pitarau*; but when there is a desire to express difference:

Mother and father: likewise, father-in-law and mother-in-law are *śvaśurau*; likewise, brother and sister are *bhrātarau*; son and daughter are *putrau*. However, because the neuter possesses the nature of being common to all genders, when there is a designation of both neuter and non-neuter [entities], only the neuter is employed: "white" (masculine), "white" (feminine), and "white" (neuter)—these are "the white ones" (*śuklāni*). But when non-difference is intended to be expressed, it is "this white thing" (*tad idaṃ śuklam*).

Since words such as *tyad* and others are also general denoters (*sāmānyavacana*), they are employed even when expressing another meaning. For example: *sa ca Devadattaś ca, tau* ("He and Devadatta, those two"). And [in the case of] *gāva imāḥ*, the feminine gender [is used] because those [cows] have been deprived of the masculine [gender]. The second quarter of the second [chapter] is completed. [The rule] *striyām* (2.4.1).
This is the governing heading (*adhikāra*). [The rule] *ṛno ṅīp* (Pāṇini 4.1.5):

after a word ending in *ṛ* or *n*, the suffix *ṅīp* occurs in the feminine. Examples: *kartrī*, *daṇḍinī*. The letter *ṅ* is for the purpose of indicating that the suffix is marked with *ṅ* (to trigger the substitution of *ṅy* for the final vowel and consonant, as per Pāṇini 6.1.69). The letter *p* is for the purpose of the accent. "In the feminine" (*striyām*) is specified only so that it does not apply to *kartā* or *daṇḍī*, which denote masculine agents. It also does not apply to *pañca* or *sapta*, because they lack the feminine gender. Nor will it apply to *svasṛ*, because the feminine gender is already expressed even without the suffix *ṅīp*. Similarly: *duhitā*, *nanandā*, *yātā*, *mātā*; *tisraḥ*, *catasraḥ*.
(2.3.3) *ugitaḥ*: The suffix *ṅīp* occurs after a word ending in an *ugit* vowel when it denotes a feminine. Examples: *bhavatī*, *vadantī*.
(2.3.4) *añcaḥ*: [The suffix *ṅīp* occurs] after a word ending in *añc*.

The suffix *ṅīp* occurs after a verbal root ending in *u* or *ū* (*ugit*) when it functions as a noun denoting an action (*kriyārtha*). Examples: *prācī*, *pratīcī*. It does not occur here: *parṇadhvad-brāhmaṇī*. [Rule 2.4.71: *ahośo vano ra ca* (2.4.71).

After a word ending in the suffix *van* prescribed by *ahaśas* (i.e., Pāṇini 3.2.75), the suffix *ṅīp* occurs in the feminine, and by its application, the final syllable is replaced by *ra*. Example: *dhīvarī*. Why say *ahaśas*? [Counter-example: *sahayudhvā-brāhmaṇī*.

Or, when another meaning is intended (Pāṇini 4.1.5): the suffix *ṅīp* is applied after a word ending in *van* when it denotes something other than the word's own referent, and the letter *r* is substituted for the final vowel. Examples: *bahudhīvarī*, *bahudhīvā*. [The rule concerning] *pāda-* (Pāṇini 4.1.8).

The suffix *ṅīp* optionally occurs after a word ending in *pād* when it functions as a member of a compound other than that which ends in *pād*. [Examples: *dvipadī*, *dvipāt*; *tripadī*, *tripāt*. [Question: How is it that we have *tripadā gāyatrī* ("the Gāyatrī has three feet") and *pañcapadā paṅktiḥ* ("the Paṅkti has five feet")? [Answer: This is established by using the word *pada*, which has the same meaning as the word *pāda*. [Objection: In that case, the forms *dvipāt* and *tripāt* would also apply to a Vedic verse (*ṛc*). [Response: That is indeed desired, because we see the expression *catuṣpād ṛk* ("a four-footed verse"). [Objection: Then the suffix *ṅīp* would also apply to a Vedic verse. [Response: It will not occur due to the rule of restricted optionality (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*). [This concludes the section on] *anaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.8).

The suffix *ṅīp* occurs after an *anaṅt* stem when it denotes something other than its own meaning, provided it refers to a feminine. For example: *bahurājñī pṛthivī* ("the earth with many kings"); [in the masculine: *bahurājā*, *bahurājānau*, *bahurājānaḥ*. Since *adhirājñī* is the name of a certain village, it is a proper noun ending in *ṅīp*; therefore, it is not used without that suffix. Only when denoting "something else" [does this apply]: *atikrāntā rājānam* ("one who has surpassed the king") results in *atirājñī*. [The rule] *ūdhaso naś ca* (Pāṇini 4.1.9) [states: [The suffix *ṅīp* is added to *ūdhah* and] the final *n* is substituted for the *s*.

After the word *ūdhas*, when it functions as the meaning of another member of a compound (*anyapadārtha*), the suffix *ṅīp* occurs in the feminine, and *na* is substituted for the final [s]. Examples: *kuṇḍodhnī*; *dvyūdhnī*, *tryūdhnī*; *atyūdhnī*, *dvividhodhnī*. Only when it has the meaning of "another" (*anyārtha*) does this apply: *prāptodhāḥ* (where the cow has reached its udder). Only when it is in the feminine does this apply: *mahodhaḥ* (a bull with large udders); *dhainukam* (a herd of milch cows). (2.3.10) *dāmnaḥ saṃkhyādeḥ*: After the word *dāman*, when preceded by a numeral and functioning as the meaning of another member of a compound, the suffix *ṅīp* occurs in the feminine. Examples: *dvidāmnī*, *tridāmnī*. Why say "preceded by a numeral"? Consider: *uddāmā vaḍavā* (a mare with loose reins).

(2.3.11) *hāyanād vayasi*: After the word *hāyana*, when preceded by a numeral and used in the sense of another word (*anyapadārtha*), the suffix *ṅīp* occurs in the feminine when age is understood. Examples: *dvihāyanī*, *trihāyaṇī*, *caturhāyaṇī*. [The substitution of] *ṇ* [for *n*] occurs by rule 6.4.107: *tricaturbhyāṃ hāyano vayasi*. Why "when age is understood"? Example: *trihāyanā śālā* ("a three-year-old shed"). Why "preceded by a numeral"? Example: *atītahāyanā gauḥ* ("a cow that has passed one year"). (2.3.12) *nopāntavataḥ*: [The suffix *ṅīp* does not occur] after a word ending in *hāyana* that has a penultimate *u*.

The suffix *ṅīp* does not occur after a word ending in *upāntavat* (having a penultimate vowel) that ends in *anant* when it functions as an external referent (*anyapadārtha*). Examples: *suparvā*, *suparvāṇau*; *suśarmā*, *suśarmāṇau*. Only when it refers to an external referent: *atiparvaṇī yaṣṭiḥ* ("a staff with too many joints"). [The rule for] *manas-* follows (Pāṇini 4.1.11).

The suffix *ṅīp* does not occur after a feminine stem ending in *man*. Examples: *dāmā*, *dāmānau*; *sīmā*, *sīmānau*. The inclusion of the terms *an*, *in*, *as*, and *man* in the rule causes the application of the "ending-in" (*tadanta*) principle to both meaningful and meaningless forms, because they refer to the mere form itself. The phrase "for another purpose" (*anyārtha*) is no longer operative here, due to the separation of the rules (*yogavibhāga*). Otherwise, the author would have simply stated: *na manupāntavadbhyām*. By the rule *tābhyāṃ ḍāp* (Pāṇini 4.1.14), the suffix *ḍāp* occurs in the feminine after those two—namely, after stems ending in *man* and *an* that do not end in *anat*. Examples: *bahurājā*, *bahurāje*; *suparvā*, *suparve*; *dāmā*, *dāme*; *sīmā*, *sīme*.

*ajādyataḥ* (2.3.15): The suffix *ḍāp* occurs in the feminine after words beginning with *ajā* and after words ending in short *a*. Examples: *ajā*, *Devadattā*. Although the rule could have been established simply by saying "after [words] ending in *a*," the specific mention of the group beginning with *ajā* is for the purpose of overriding other potential rules. In the case of *ajā*, *eḍakā*, *kokilā*, *aśvā*, *caṭakā*, and *mūṣikā*, although the suffix *ṅīṣ* would normally apply by virtue of their being genus names (*jāti*), *ḍāp* takes its place instead. In the case of *bālā*, *hoḍā*, *pākā*, *vatsā*, *mandā*, and *vilātā*, although the suffix *ṅīp* would normally apply because they denote age (*vayasi acarama* 4.1.20), *ḍāp* takes its place instead.

In the case of *pūrvāpahāṇā*, *aparāpahāṇā*, and *saṃprahāṇā*, although the suffix *ṅīp* would have been required by the rule for words ending in *ṭi*, the form is established through irregular derivation (*nipātana*), and the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* also occurs. Regarding the words *saṃbhastra*, *ajina*, *śaṇa*, and *piṇḍa* followed by *phala*, although the suffix *ṅīṣ* would have been required by the rule for words ending in *phala*, the forms are *saṃphalā*, *bhastraphalā*, *ajinaphalā*, *śaṇaphalā*, and *piṇḍaphalā*. Why does the rule specify "from these"? Consider *vāsīphalī*. How is *triphalā* formed? It is *triphalā* because it contains three fruits (*trīṇi phalāny asyām*).

In the case of *saṃhati*, because it is not a genus (*ajāti*), the suffix *ṅīṣ* does not apply; and because it is not a collective (*asamāhāra*), the suffix *ṅīp* also does not apply. Regarding the rule "after *sat*, *prāk*, *kāṇḍa*, *prānta*, *śata*, and *eka*, when [the word] *puṣpa* follows": since the suffix *ṅīṣ* would otherwise be required by the characteristic of ending in *puṣpa*, we have: *satpuṣpā*, *prākpuṣpā*, *kāṇḍapuṣpā*, *prāntapuṣpā*, *śatapuṣpā*, *ekapuṣpā*. Why "after these"? [Consider: *śaṅkhapuṣpī*. "And *śūdrā* is [a feminine form] when it denotes a genus and is not preceded by the word *mahat*. That is, *śūdrā* ends in the suffix *ḍāp* when it denotes a genus and is not preceded by *mahat*. Thus, *śūdrā* refers to a Śūdra woman who is a wife, but not one who belongs to a Śūdra man.

Why does the rule specify "not preceded by *mahat*"? [Consider] *mahāśūdrī*, which belongs to the *ābhīra* caste. From this very indicative mark (*jñāpaka*), it is understood that in this section, the rule of "application to what ends with [a specific stem]" (*tadantavidhi*) applies. [Examples: *atibhavatī*, *atidhīvarī*. Why does the rule specify "a genus" (*jāti*)? [Consider] the wife of a *śūdra*, *śūdrī*; here the suffix *ṅīṣ* occurs precisely because it is characterized by connection with a male (*puṃyoga*). In the case of *kruñcā*, *uṣṇihā*, and *devaviśā*, the absence of elision [of the final vowel] occurs only due to irregular derivation (*nipātana*). Alternatively, the suffix *ḍāp* may be applied after stems ending in *a* due to irregular derivation; thus, the form *uṣṇig* is also established.

In the case of *jyeṣṭhā*, *kaniṣṭhā*, and *madhyamā*, the suffix *ḍāp* indeed occurs after these [words] because they denote a specific state (*vyavasthāvācin*), and thus the suffix *ṅīp*—which characterizes age—is not applicable; furthermore, because they are not words denoting a relationship with a male (*puṃyoga*), the suffix *ṅīṣ* is also not applicable. Nor should it be said that [the rule] "after *mūla*, when preceded by the negative particle *nañ*" applies here: for in the case of *amūlā*, the suffix *ṅīṣ*—which would otherwise apply because the word ends in *mūla*—does not occur, since it does not denote a genus (*ajāti*). Why does the suffix *ḍāp* not occur here in *pañcājī* and *daśājī*? Because in these cases the word *aja* does not refer to a female; and that which refers to a female here is not the word *aja*.

By the rule of *tadanta-vidhi* (application of a grammatical operation to that which ends with a specified element), [the suffix] would apply; however, due to the principle of *vipratiṣedha* (conflict between rules), the suffix *ṅīp* will occur by the rule *saṃkhyādeḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.26). What is the purpose of including *ta* (the long vowel *ā*) in the technical term *tapara*? [Consider the examples: *kīlālapāḥ* and *śubhaṃyāḥ*. The word *ataḥ* is a governing heading (*adhikāra*). From this point forward, whatever is prescribed for the feminine gender in the section beginning with *svārthe* (Pāṇini 4.1.15) should be understood as applying when the base denotes its own meaning (*svārthe vartamānāt*).

Pāṇini 4.1.15: *ṭiḍḍhāṇañṭhakṭhañnañsnañkañkvarapkhyunaḥ*. The suffix *ṅīp* occurs in the feminine in its own sense after a stem ending in a *ṭi*-marker and so forth. For example, *kurucarī*. It does not occur in *vidyā paṭhitā*, because although the addition of *tuṭ* would have sufficed for the formation, the *ṭi*-marker is specifically employed to indicate that the suffix itself is *ṭit*. It does not occur in *pacamānā* because it possesses two *anubandhas*. However, it certainly occurs after suffixes such as *lyuṭ*, by virtue of the force of the *ṭi*-marker. Since there is no *ḍha* suffix without an *anubandha*, the rule includes both *ḍhak* and *ḍhañ*. Furthermore, although there is a *ḍha* in the rule *śilāyā ḍhaś ca* (4.3.80), it is not used in the feminine. Examples include *sauparṇeyī*, *vainateyī*, and *śābaleyī*.

*āṇ*: *kumbhakārī*, *aupagavī*. *añ*: *autsī*, *baidī*. *ṭhak*: *ākṣikī*. *ṭhañ*: *lāvaṇikī*. *nañ-snañ-au*: *straiṇī*, *pauṃsnī*. *kañ*: *tādṛśī*. *kvarap*: *itvarī*. *khyun*: *āḍhyaṃkaraṇī*. [The suffixes apply] only when the sense is that of the base itself (*svārthe*): *priyakurucarā nagarī*. Regarding the rule *yañaṣāvaṭāt* (Pāṇini 4.1.78): after a word ending in *yañ*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* occurs, provided that the suffix was not prescribed after a word ending in *ṣakāra* or after the word *avaṭa*. Examples: *gārgī*, *vātsī*. Why "not after *ṣa* or *avaṭa*"? [Counter-examples: *śārkarākṣyā*, *pautimāṣyā*, *gāukakṣyā*, *āvaṭyā*. In the last case, the suffix *ḍāp* applies by the rule *ataḥ* (4.1.5).

*ṣpho vā* (2.3.19). The [restriction] *aṣāvaṭāt* does not apply here. After a word ending in *yañ*, the suffix *ṣpha* optionally occurs in the feminine. Examples: *Gārgī*, *Gārgyāyaṇī*; *Vātsī*, *Vātsyāyanī*; *Sārkarākṣyāyaṇī*, *Pautimāṣyāyaṇī*, *Gaukakṣyāyaṇī*; *Āvaṭyāyanī*. Because it has the marker *ṣ*, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied. The mention of the option (*vā*) is for the sake of the form *āvaṭyāyanī*. [The rule continues: *lohitādibhyaḥ śakalāntebhyaḥ* (2.3.20).

From the words beginning with *lohita* and ending with *śakala*, which take the suffix *yañ*, only the suffix *ṣpha* occurs, because of its mandatory re-formation. Thus: *lauhityāyanī*, *sāṃśityāyanī*. From the word *manāyī*, [the form] is *mānāyyāyanī*. The substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) does not occur by the rule *yaño 'ñādau* (Pāṇini 6.3.32), due to the force of the specific recitation [of the word]. The form *mānavyāyanī* is established precisely from the recitation of the word *manu*. From the word *vataṇḍa*, when it does not denote a descendant of Aṅgiras, [the form] is *vātaṇḍyāyanī*; however, due to its inclusion in the *Śivādi* group, [the form] is also *vātaṇḍī*.

In the case of *Āṅgirasa*, however, [the suffix] *yañ* is applied; and for its feminine form, by [Pāṇini 4.1.63], *jāter astryām akṛtrimam*, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is added: *Vataṇḍī*. From the word *Kapi*, only when it is an *Āṅgirasa* is *yañ* applied: *Kāpyāyanī*; but when not an *Āṅgirasa*, it is *Kāpeyī*. [Similarly,] *Kātyāyanī* and *Śākalyāyanī*. Why is it said "from those ending in *Śakala*"? [Consider: *Kāṇvī*, *Kāṇvyāyanī*. However, *Kuru* and *Katānaḍuha* should be listed before *Lohita*, because for these two, neither the grammatical operation starting with *Lohita* nor that starting with *Śakala* is desired. [This is taught in the rule: *kauravyāsurimāṇḍūkāt* (Pāṇini 2.4.70).

The suffix *ṣpha* occurs in the feminine after the word *kauravya*, which ends in *ṇya*; after the word *āsuri*, which ends in *iñ*; and after the word *māṇḍūka*, which ends in *aṇ*. This is an exception to the suffixes *ṅīp* and *ḍāp*. [Examples: *kauravyāyaṇī*, *āsurāyaṇī*, *māṇḍūkāyanī*. How is the form *kauravī* [used for] "an army" (*senā*) derived? It is established by [the rule] *tasyedam* (Pāṇini 4.3.120). [Regarding the rule] *vayasy acaramē* (Pāṇini 2.3.22):

The suffix *ṅīp* occurs after a feminine stem when it refers to one who is not in the final stage of life. For example: *kumārī*, *kiśorī*, *varkarī*; *karabhī*, *kalabhī*; *taruṇī*, *talunī*; *vadhūṭī*, *ciriṇṭī*. Why "not in the final stage"? [As in] *sthavirā*, *vṛddhā*. How is it that [the suffix does not apply in] *dvivarṣā*, *trivarṣā*, *uttānaśayā*, *lohitapādikā*, *madhyā*, *madhyamā*, *jyeṣṭhā*, and *kaniṣṭhā*? Because in these cases, the first stage of life is understood from the sense (*artha*), not from the word itself (*śabda*).

How is *kanyā* [formed]? It is by virtue of the irregular derivation (*nipātana*) in the rule *kanyāyāḥ kanīna ca* (Pāṇini 2.4.46). How is *vṛddhakumārī* [formed]? In this case, the word *vṛddha-* conveys the later stage of life, not the word *kumāra-*. Therefore, [the suffix] applies only in such cases: *śiśuḥ* (an infant). Regarding the rule *saṃkhyādeḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.23):

the suffix *ṅīp* occurs after a word beginning with a numeral, ending in the vowel *a*, and denoting a feminine. For example: *pañcapūlī* (a collection of five bundles); *daśapūlī* (a collection of ten bundles). The restriction "in its own sense" (*svārthe*) applies as well: *dvikhārīkā* (a measure of two *khārīs*).

(2.3.24) *parimāṇāl luky asaṃkhyākālavistācitakambalyāt*: When there is elision (*luk*) [of the case-ending] after a word denoting measure (*parimāṇa*), provided it begins with a numeral and ends in short *a*, but excludes numerals, time, *visti*, *ācita*, and *kambalya*, the suffix *ṅīp* occurs. For example: *dvikuḍavī*. Why "after a measure"? Consider *pañcāśvā* ("five horses"). Why "when there is elision"? Consider *dvipaṇyā* ("worth two coins"). Since elision of the case-ending (*sup*) occurs everywhere, it is not understood here [as the intended *luk*]. Why "excluding numerals, time, *visti*, *ācita*, and *kambalya*"? Consider *dviśatā* ("two hundred"), *dvivarṣā* ("two years old"), *dvivistā*, *dvyācitā*, and *dvikambalyā*. (2.3.25) *kāṇḍād akṣetre*: [The suffix *ṅīp* occurs after *kāṇḍa* when it does not refer to a field.]

After a word beginning with a numeral and ending in *kāṇḍa*, the suffix *ṅīp* occurs when there is elision (*luk*) of the [secondary] suffix, provided that it does not refer to a field (*akṣetre*). Example: *dvikāṇḍī*. Why "not a field"? Consider: *dvikāṇḍā kṣetrabhaktiḥ* ("a two-sectioned division of a field"). Only after a measure (*parimāṇāt*): *dvikāṇḍā* meaning "bought for two sections. (2.3.26) *puruṣād vā*:

After a word beginning with a numeral and ending in *puruṣa*, the suffix *ṅīp* optionally occurs in the feminine. Examples: *dvipuruṣī* or *dvipuruṣā* "a staff [measuring] two men. Only after a measure: *pañcapuruṣā* meaning "bought for five men."

Regarding the rule *kevalamāmakabhāgadheyapāpāvarasamānāryakṛtasumaṅgalabheṣajān nāmni* (Pāṇini 4.1.30): the suffix *ṅīp* occurs after the words *kevala* and the others when they function as proper names (*saṃjñā*). Examples: *kevalī*, *māmakī*, *bhāgadheyī*, *pāpī*, *avarī*, *samānī*, *āryakṛtī*, *sumaṅgalī*, *bheṣajī*. Why does the rule specify "when it is a proper name"? [To exclude cases such as: *kevalā*, *māmikā*. Regarding the rule *antarvatnī garbhiṇyām* (Pāṇini 4.1.32): the word *antarvatnī* is used in the sense of "pregnant."

The suffix *matup* is irregularly formed (*nipātyate*) as *antarvatnī*, with the addition of the augment *nuk*, in the sense of "pregnant" (*garbhiṇī*). In other cases: "there is [something] inside the house" (*antarasyāṃ śālāyām asti*).
