Regarding the word *pativatnī* (2.3.29): the form *pativatnī* is irregularly formed from the suffix *matup* by changing *m* to *v* and adding the augment *nuk*, in the sense of "a wife. In other cases: *patimatī*.
(2.3.30) *patyuḥ na ūḍhāyām*:

When the word *pati* refers to a married wife (*bhāryā*), the substitution of *na* occurs [for the final syllable], and the suffix *ṅīp* is also applied. Thus, *patnī*. Why does it say "when she is married" (*ūḍhāyām*)? So that it does not apply to one who has merely been taken in marriage [but not yet wedded]. Why does it say "to a wife" (*bhāryāyām*)? So that it does not apply to one who is married [only] by name [or for a specific purpose]. (2.3.31) *sapūrvasya vā*: [The substitution of *na* and the suffix *ṅīp* occur] optionally when the word is preceded by another word.
The substitution of *n* for the word *pati* when it is preceded by another word, and the suffix *ṅīp*, optionally occur in the feminine. For example: *āśāpatnī* or *āśāpatiḥ*.

According to Pāṇini 2.3.32, when the word *pati* occurs in a compound where the referent is something other than the wife (*anyapadārtha*), the substitution of *n* and the suffix *ṅīp* optionally occur in the feminine. For example: *dṛḍhapatnī* or *dṛḍhapatiḥ*.

(2.3.33) *samānādibhyaḥ*: For the word *pati* following [the words] beginning with *samāna*, there is the substitution of *n* for the final vowel when it denotes a female, and the suffix *ṅīp* is also applied, because this is a mandatory rule (*nitya*). Thus: *sapatnī*, *ekapatnī*. In the case of *sāpatna*—meaning "the offspring of a *sapatnī*"—the *n* does not disappear even in the absence of *ṅīp*, because it was prescribed as not being joined [with any other element]. [The members of the *samānādi* group are: *samāna*, *eka*, *vīra*, *piṇḍa*, *putra*, *bhrātṛ*. (2.3.34) *śyetaitaharitarohitāt to naḥ*: After the words *śyeta*, *eta*, *harita*, and *rohita*, the *t* is replaced by *n*.

After the words *śyeta* and others, the suffix *ṅīp* optionally occurs in the feminine, and the letter *t* is replaced by *n*. Thus: *śyenī*, *śyetā*; *enī*, *etā*; *hariṇī*, *haritā*; *rohiṇī*, *rohitā*. By the rule *kapirikādīnām* (Pāṇini 6.3.46), there is the substitution of *l* for *r*: *lohinī*, *lohitā*. By the rule *kno 'sitapalitāt* (Pāṇini 2.3.35), the suffix *ṅīp* optionally occurs after the words *asita* and *palita* in the feminine, and the letter *t* is replaced by the substitute *kn*. Thus: *asiknī*, *asitā*; *paliknī*, *palitā*.

*ṣitaḥ ṅīṣ* (Pāṇini 4.1.41): After a word ending in a *ṣit* suffix, the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* occurs. Examples: *nartakī*, *khanakī*, *pātrī*. Because of the division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) regarding *daṃṣṭrā* and others, this is not mandatory. *gaurādibhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.41).

The suffix *ṅīṣ* occurs after [the words] *gaura* and so forth when denoting a female. Examples: *gaurī*, *śabalī*, *kalmāṣī*, *sāraṅgī*, *piśaṅgī*, *matsī*. The list includes: *gaura*, *śabala*, *kalmāṣa*, *sāraṅga*, *piśaṅga*, *matsya*, *manuṣya*, *śṛṅga*, *gavaya*, *haya*, *mukaya*, *ṛśya*, *puṭa*, *druṇa*, *droṇa*, *arīhaṇa*, *aroṣa*, *vaṭhara*, *okaṇa*, *āmalaka*, *kuvala*, *badara*, *bimba*, *tarkāra*, *śarkāra*, *ṣaṣkaṇḍa*, *suṣava*, *ālinda*, *alaja*.

The following [words ending in -i] are derived from the names of artisans: pāṇḍaṣa, āḍhaka, āsanda, sṛpāṭa, śaṣkula, sūrya, sūci, śūrpa, dūṣa, yūṣa, dhātaka, vallaka, mālata, vetasa, bṛsa, atasī, bhṛṅga, maha, maṭha, śvan, anaḍuh, and eṣaṇa; as well as dehala, kākādana, gavādana, tejana, lavaṇa, pāṇa, medha, gautama, ayasthūṇa, bhauriki, bhauliki, bhauliṅgi, audgāhamāni, ālambi, ālaji, and ālaki.

-Ālandhi, Kālambi, Āraṭa, Doṭa, Nāṭa, Mūlāṭa, Śātana, Pātana, and Āstaraṇa [form derivatives] in the sense of location; [the suffix *cha* is applied after] Āgrahāyaṇa, Pratyavarohaṇa, and Sevana when expressing a name; [the suffix *aṇ* is applied after] Sumaṅgala when expressing a name; [the suffix *aṇ* is applied after] Maṇḍala, Maṇḍara, Paṭa, Piṇḍa, Ūrda, Gurda, Sūrda, Pāṇḍāra, Ātaṇḍa, Kadara, Kadala, Kardama, Kadalpa, Bṛhat, Mahat, Saudharma, Rohiṇī, and Revatī when referring to a lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*); [the suffix *aṇ* is applied after] Vikala, Niṣkala, and Puṣkala.

— *kaṭa* [is added] after *śroṇi*; and *pippalyādayaḥ*: *pippalī*, *harītakī*, *kośātakī*, *śamī*, *karīra*, *pṛthivī*, *mātāmaha*, *pitāmaha*, *kroṣṭu*. Because it is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open class), [it includes] *nada*, *bhaṣa*, *plava*, *cara*, *cora*, *gāha*, *sūda*, *deva*, *putra*. [The suffix *aṇ* is applied] after *bhāja*, *goṇa*, *nāga*, *sthala*, *kuṇḍa*, *kāla*, *kuśa*, *kāmuka*, and *kabara*, when they respectively mean *pakva* (cooked), *āvapana* (sowing), *sthūla* (large), *akṛtrima* (unartificial), *amatra* (vessel), *kṛṣṇāyasa* (iron), *riraṃsu* (desirous of sport), and *keśaveśa* (arrangement of hair). (Pāṇini 2.4.38)

The suffix *ṅīṣ* occurs after words such as *bhāja* when they refer to meanings such as "cooked" (*pakva*) and so forth, in the feminine gender. *Bhājī* means "cooked"; otherwise, it is *bhājā*. *Goṇī* means "a container for grain" (*āvapana*); otherwise, it is *goṇā*. *Nāgī* means "thick" (*sthūla*); otherwise, it is *nāgā*. However, when referring to the species (*jāti*), it is simply *nāgā*, because that [species] lacks thickness. *Sthalī* means "natural ground" (*akṛtrimā*); otherwise, it is *sthalā*. *Kuṇḍī* means "a vessel" (*amatra*); otherwise, it is *kuṇḍā*. *Kālī* means "black" (*kṛṣṇā*); otherwise, it is *kālā*. *Kuśī* means "made of iron" (*āyasī*); otherwise, it is *kuśā*.

If it means "desirous of love," [the word *kāma*] becomes *kāmukī*; otherwise, it is *kāmukā*. If it means "an arrangement of hair," [the word *kabara*] becomes *kabarī*; otherwise, it is *kabarā*. (2.3.39) *nīlāt prāṇyoṣadhyoḥ*: After the word *nīla*, when referring to a living being (*prāṇin*) or a plant (*oṣadhi*), the suffix *ṅīṣ* occurs in the feminine. Examples: *nīlī vaḍavā* ("a dark mare") and *nīlī oṣadhiḥ* ("a dark medicinal herb"). Why specify "living being or plant"? [Consider: *nīlā śāṭī* ("a blue garment").
Or [the suffix] optionally [is applied] after "nīla" when it is a name (Pāṇini 2.3.40). Thus, *nīlī* or *nīlā*.
[The suffix] is applied after "śoṇa" and others (Pāṇini 2.3.41).

After words such as *śoṇa* and others, the suffix *ṅīṣ* optionally occurs in the feminine. Thus: *śoṇī*, *śoṇā*; *caṇḍī*, *caṇḍā*. [The list includes: *śoṇa*, *caṇḍa*, *arāla*, *kamala*, *kṛpaṇa*, *vikaṭa*, *viśāla*, *viśaṅkaṭa*, *bharuja*, and when referring to the river Candrabhāgā; also *kalyāṇa*, *udāra*, *purāṇa*, and *ahan*. By rule 2.3.42, *er aktinaḥ*:

after a word ending in the vowel *i* that is not the suffix *ktin*, the suffix *ṅīṣ* optionally occurs in the feminine. Thus: *dhūlī*, *dhūliḥ*; *ālī*, *āliḥ*; *āvalī*, *āvaliḥ*; *paddhatī*, *paddhatiḥ*; *aṅgulī*, *aṅguliḥ*. Why "not *ktin*"? [Consider: *paktiḥ*.

Or, by rule 2.3.43 (*or guṇād akharusaṃyogopāntāt*), the suffix *ṅīṣ* optionally occurs in the feminine after a word denoting a quality (*guṇa*) ending in *u*, with the exception of the word *kharu* and words having a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*) as their penultimate letter (*upānta*). Examples: *paṭvī*, *paṭuḥ*; *bahvī*, *bahuḥ*. Why [is it said] "ending in *u*" (*or*)? Consider *sitā* (white). Why [is it said] "denoting a quality" (*guṇāt*)? Consider *ākhuḥ* (mouse). Why [is it said] "with the exception of *kharu* and words having a conjunct consonant as their penultimate letter" (*akharusaṃyogopāntāt*)? Consider *kharur brāhmaṇī* (a harsh Brahmin woman) and *pāṇḍur brāhmaṇī* (a pale Brahmin woman).
By rule 2.3.44 (*puṃnāmno yogād apālakāntāt*), [the suffix *ṅīṣ* is added] after a masculine noun when it is joined [to another word], provided that the compound does not end in *pālaka*.

The suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied after a word denoting a male, provided that it is used to denote a female through connection with a male, and does not end in *pālaka*. For example, the wife of a *praṣṭha* is *praṣṭhī*. Why is the mention of "denoting a name" (*nāman*) necessary? [Consider: *prasūtā* ("one who has given birth"). Why is it said "not ending in *pālaka*"? [Consider: *gopālikā*, *paśupālikā*.
[Furthermore, for the words] *pūtakratu*, *vṛṣākapi*, *agni*, *kusita*, and *kusīda*, the vowel *ai* is substituted [for the final *u* before the feminine suffix]. (Pāṇini 4.1.37–38)

The suffix *ṅīṣ* occurs after words such as *pūtakratu* when they denote a woman through connection with a male, and the vowel *ai* is substituted for the final syllable. Thus: *pūtakratāyī*, *vṛṣākapāyī*, *agnāyī*, *kusitāyī*, *kusīdāyī*. Only because of the condition "through connection with a male": she by whom the sacrifices (*kratavaḥ*) have been purified is called *pūtakratuḥ*. (2.3.46) *manor au vā*:

After the word *manu* when it denotes a woman through connection with a male, the suffix *ṅīṣ* optionally occurs, and the vowel *au* is substituted for the final syllable, or *ai*. Thus: *manāyī*, *manāvī*, *manuḥ*.
*Sūryā devī* (2.3.47):
*Sūryā* is the wife of Sūrya, provided she is a goddess (*devī*). Any other [female] is *Sūrī*.
*Indra-varuṇa-bhava-śarva-rudra-mṛḍānām ānuk ca* (2.3.48).

The suffix *ṅīṣ* occurs after words such as *indra*, when they denote a female through connection with a male, and the augment *ānuk* is added. Thus: *indrāṇī*, *varuṇānī*, *bhavānī*, *śarvāṇī*, *rudrāṇī*, *mṛḍānī*.
Regarding *ācāryānī* (Pāṇini 2.3.49): for the word *ācārya*, the augment *ānuk* is prescribed along with the substitution of *aṇ* for the final vowel. The wife of an *ācārya* is *ācāryānī*.
(2.3.50) *mātulopādhyāyād vā*:

After the words *mātula* and *upādhyāya*, the suffix *ṅīṣ* occurs when a feminine is denoted, and there is optionally the addition of *ānuk*. [Examples: *mātulānī*, *mātulī*; *upādhyāyānī*, *upādhyāyī*. (2.3.51) *āryakṣatriyāc ca*: [The same applies] after the words *ārya* and *kṣatriya*.

After *ārya* and *kṣatriya*, the suffix *ṅīṣ* optionally occurs, as does *ānuk*. The *ca* (and) is for the purpose of connecting [the suffixes] with the word "optionally" (*vā*). This statement is made to exclude the case of connection with a male (*puṃyoga*), because they are listed separately. Thus: *āryāṇī*, *kṣatriyāṇī*; [and when not connected with a male: *āryā*, *kṣatriyā*. But in the case of connection with a male: *āryī*, *kṣatriyī*.

(2.4.52) After *himā* and *araṇya*, the suffix *ṅīṣ* occurs in the feminine when greatness is implied, as does *ānuk*. Great snow: *mahad dhimam*, *himānī*. A great forest: *mahad araṇyam*, *araṇyānī*.

*yavād doṣe* (Pāṇini 2.3.53): After the word *yava*, when it signifies a defect (*doṣa*), the suffix *ṅīṣ* occurs and *ānuk* is added [to the stem]. When a barley-corn is defective, it is called *yavānī*. *yavanāl lipyām* (Pāṇini 2.3.54): [The suffix *ṅīṣ* occurs] after *yavana* when it refers to a script (*lipi*).

After *yavana*, the suffix *ṅīṣ* occurs when a feminine word is formed, and *ānuk* is added [to the stem], provided that "script" (*lipi*) is the meaning expressed. For example: *yavanānī lipiḥ* ("the Greek script"). [Rule 2.3.55: *krītāt karaṇādeḥ*. After the word *krīta*, the suffix *ṅīṣ* occurs in the feminine when it has the sense of "purchased," provided that its initial member is an instrument (*karaṇa*). Example: *vastrakrītī* ("purchased with a garment"). Why is the mention of "instrument" (*karaṇa*) necessary? Consider *sukrītā* ("well-purchased"); here the suffix does not apply because the word is not derived from an instrument. Why is the mention of "initial member" (*ādi*) necessary? Consider *aśvena krītā* ("purchased with a horse"); here the suffix does not apply because the instrument is not the initial member, due to the absence of a single compound form (*aikapadya*). How then is *dhanakrītā* ("purchased with wealth") formed? This is a compound with a word ending in a *taddhita* suffix [namely, *dhana*]. The term *ataḥ* ("from this [stem]") continues to apply.

(2.3.56) *ktād alpoktau*: After a word ending in a *kta* suffix, the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* occurs when the instrument (*karaṇa*) or other [case-relation] is designated as "small. Example: *abhraviliptī dyauḥ* ("the sky is lightly covered with clouds"). Why say "when there is the designation of smallness"? Example: *candanānuliptā yoṣit* ("a woman well-anointed with sandalwood paste"). (2.3.57) *svāṅgād akṛtamitajātapratipannād anyārthe*: [The suffix *ṅīṣ* occurs after a word denoting a limb of one's own body (*svāṅga*), provided it is not preceded by the particles *akṛta*, *mita*, *jāta*, or *pratipanna*, and provided another meaning [than that of the base itself] is intended.]

The suffix *ṅīṣ* occurs after a word ending in *kta* that denotes a part of one's own body (*svāṅga*) when it functions as a member of a compound whose referent is something else (*anyapadārtha*), with the exception of words such as *kṛta*. Example: *śaṅkhabhinnī* ("one who has broken a conch"). Why "after a part of one's own body"? Consider: *vastracchannā* ("covered by a cloth"). Why "with the exception of *kṛta*-type words"? Consider: *dantakṛtā*, *dantamitā*, *dantajātā*, *dantapratipannā* ("made by the teeth," "measured by the teeth," "born from the teeth," "attained by the teeth"). Why "when the referent is something else"? Consider: *hastābhyāṃ patitā* ("fallen by means of the hands"), which becomes *hastapatitā*. Regarding *pāṇigṛhīty ūḍhā* (Pāṇini 4.1.52):
the word *pāṇigṛhītī* is formed [with *ṅīṣ*] if she is a married woman; otherwise, she is *pāṇigṛhītā*.

(2.3.59) *Jāter anācchādād vā*: After a word denoting a genus (*jāti*), provided it is not a word for clothing (*anācchāda*) and ends in a *kta* suffix, the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* optionally occurs when the word functions as a member of a compound referring to something other than its own primary meaning (*anyapadārtha*). Examples: *palāṇḍubhakṣitī*, *palāṇḍubhakṣitā*. Why "after a genus word" (*jāteḥ*)? [Counter-example: *māsajātā* ("born a month ago"). Why "not clothing" (*anācchādāt*)? [Counter-example: *vastracchannā* ("covered with clothes"). The restriction "except for words beginning with *kṛta*" (*akṛtādibhyaḥ*) still applies: *kuṇḍakṛtā*, *kuṇḍamitā*, *palāṇḍujātā*, *vṛkṣapratipannā*. (2.3.60) *Saṃjñāyām*: [The suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied] when the word is a proper name (*saṃjñā*).
The suffix *ṅīṣ* optionally occurs after a word ending in a *kta* suffix when it denotes a name (*saṃjñā*). Examples: *pravṛddhavilūnī*, *pravṛddhavilūnā*.
[Regarding Pāṇini 4.1.54: "After a word denoting a body part (*svāṅga*) that is not principal (*apradhāna*), [the suffix] *ṅīṣ* optionally occurs in the feminine. Example: *dīrghakeśī*, *dīrghakeśā*.

A limb (*svāṅga*) is that which is non-fluid (*adrava*), possesses form (*mūrtimat*), resides in a living being (*prāṇistha*), is not produced by modification (*avikāraja*), and—if it is seen elsewhere than in its natural location—is joined with that [being] in such a way [as if it were there]. Why "non-fluid"? [In the case of] *bahukaphā* ("having much phlegm"). Why "possessing form"? [In the case of] *bahujñānā* ("having much knowledge"). Why "residing in a living being"? [In the case of] *dīrghamukhā śālā* ("a hall with a long entrance"). Why "not produced by modification"? [In the case of] *bahuśothā* ("having much swelling"). If it is seen elsewhere than in its natural location, that too is a limb: *dīrghakeśī rathyā* ("a street with long hair") and *dīrghakeśā* ("having long hair"). If it is joined with that [being] in such a way: *pṛthustanī pratimā* ("an image with large breasts") and *pṛthustanā* ("having large breasts").

Because it relies on a non-primary measure, *atikeshī* (one whose hair has surpassed [the usual length]) or *atikeśā* means "one who has surpassed her hair," as in "a garland of hair. Why [is it specified] "from a part of the body" (*svāṅgāt*)? [Consider: *bahuyavā* (one who has many barley grains). Why "from a non-primary [part]" (*apradhānāt*)? [Consider: *śikhā* (the crest/topknot).
[The suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied after the following: *nāsikā*, *udara*, *oṣṭha*, *jaṅghā*, *danta*, *karṇa*, *śṛṅga*, *aṅga*, *gātra*, and *kaṇṭha* (Pāṇini 4.1.55).

Since [the suffix] is already established, this rule is for the purpose of restriction: the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is optionally applied after words ending in "nose" (*nāsikā*) or "belly" (*udara*) that have more than two syllables, and after words beginning with "lip" (*oṣṭha*) etc. that end in a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*). Examples: *śaṅkunāsikī*, *śaṅkunāsikā* (having a pointed nose); *talodarī*, *talodarā* (having a flat belly); *bimboṣṭhī*, *bimboṣṭhā* (having lips like the *bimba* fruit); *dīrghajaṅghī*, *dīrghajaṅghā* (having long shanks); *samadantī*, *samadantā* (having even teeth); *cārukarṇī*, *cārukarṇā* (having beautiful ears); *tīkṣṇaśṛṅgī*, *tīkṣṇaśṛṅgā* (having sharp horns); *mṛdvaṅgī*, *mṛdvaṅgā* (having soft limbs); *cārugātrī*, *cārugātrā* (having beautiful body parts).
*raktakaṇṭhī*, *raktakaṇṭhā*. Why [is it said] "from these very [words]"? [Examples: *pṛthujaghanā*, *pṛthugulphā*.
From the word *puccha* (2.3.63), when it is not the principal member of a compound, the suffix *ṅīṣ* optionally occurs. [Examples: *dīrghapucchī*, *dīrghapucchā*.

(2.3.64) After the word *puccha* ("tail"), when it follows [the words] *kavara*, *maṇi*, *viṣa*, or *śara*, and when it is not the principal member of the compound, the suffix *ṅīṣ* occurs in the feminine; this is because it is prescribed as a mandatory rule (*nitya*). Examples: *kavarapucchī*, *maṇipucchī*, *viṣapucchī*, *śarapucchī*.
(2.3.65) [The suffix *ṅīṣ* also occurs after *puccha*] when preceded by a word used as a standard of comparison (*upamāna*), etc.
The suffix *ṅīṣ* occurs after a word ending in *puccha* when it follows a word used as a standard of comparison (*upamāna*), provided the word is feminine. Example: *ulūkapucchī* ("owl-tailed").
(2.3.66) The suffix *ṅīṣ* occurs after a word ending in *pakṣa* when it follows a word used as a standard of comparison, provided the word is feminine. Example: *ulūkapakṣī* ("owl-winged").

(2.3.67) *na kroḍādibhyaḥ*: The suffix *ṅīṣ* does not occur after feminine nouns beginning with *kroḍa* and others. Examples: *kalyāṇakroḍā*, *kalyāṇakhurā*. The list consists of: *kroḍa*, *khura*, *gokhā*, *ukhā*, *vāla*, *śapha*, *guda*. This is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open class); examples include *subhagā* and *sugalā*. (2.3.68) *sahanajvidyamānādeḥ*: [The suffix *ṅīp* is applied] after words beginning with *saha*, *nañ*, and *vidyamāna*.

The suffix *ṅīṣ* does not occur after a word beginning with *saha*, *vidyamāna*, or the like, when it refers to one's own body part (*svāṅga*). Examples: *sakeśā*, *ākeśā*, *vidyamānakeśā*; *sanāsikā*, *anāsikā*, *vidyamānanāsikā*. Regarding the rule *nakhamukhān nāmni* (Pāṇini 4.1.58):

the suffix *ṅīṣ* does not occur after the words *nakha* and *mukha* when they form a proper name (*saṃjñā*). Examples: *Śūrpaṇakhā*, *Gauramukhā*. Why is it specified "when it is a proper name"? Consider: *tuṅganakhī* ("having high nails").

The forms *sakhi* and *aśiśvī* are correct when used as technical designations (*saṃjñā*). [Furthermore,] the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied after a word denoting a genus (*jāti*) that does not refer exclusively to females and ends in a consonant other than *y*.

The suffix *ṅīṣ* occurs after a general term (*jāti*) that does not end in *y*, provided it is seen [used] in the feminine or elsewhere. Examples: *kukkuṭī*, *mayūrī*, *sūkarī*. Why "after a genus term" (*jāteḥ*)? [Answer: *muṇḍā*. Why "not having the feminine as its exclusive domain" (*astrīviṣayāt*)? [Answer: *makṣikā*. Why "not ending in *y*" (*ayopāntāt*)? [Answer: *kṣatriyā*. It is for the sake of the word's own meaning (*svārthe*) alone: *priyakukkuṭā Mathurā*. It is only after [a stem] ending in *a* (*ataḥ*): *tittiriḥ*.
[Also after those ending in] *pāka*, *karṇa*, *parṇa*, *puṣpa*, *phala*, *mūla*, and *bāla*: (Pāṇini 4.1.64).

The suffix *ṅīṣ* occurs in the feminine after words denoting a genus (*jāti*) that end in *pāka* and so forth: *odanapākī*, *ākhukarṇī*, *maṅgaparṇī*, *śaṅkhapuṣpī*, *dāḍimaphalī*, *darbhamūlī*, *govālī*.

By the rule *ito nṛjāteḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.65), the suffix *ṅīṣ* occurs in the feminine after words ending in *ikāra* (the vowel *i*) that denote a human genus (*nṛjāti*): *Avantī*. Because the word "genus" (*jāti*) is mentioned again [in the rule], the suffix also applies after words ending in *ya*: *Audapeyī*. Why is the word "human" (*nṛ*) mentioned? [To exclude non-human genera: *tittiriḥ* (a partridge).
*iñaḥ* (2.3.74): The suffix *ṅīṣ* occurs after a word ending in *iñ*, and also after others. [Example: That which was produced by Sutaṃgama is *Sautaṃgamī*.

The suffix *ūṅ* occurs after a word ending in *udanta* when denoting a feminine. Example: *brahmabandhūḥ*. This applies only to words denoting human species; thus, *dhenuḥ* [is not formed with *ūṅ*]. This applies only to words whose penultimate letter is not *ya*; thus, *adhvaryubrāhmaṇī*. Why is the *tapara* (the *t* following the vowel) specified? Consider *khalapve*. (2.3.76) *aprāṇinām arajjvādibhyaḥ*: The suffix *ūṅ* occurs in the feminine after words denoting non-living beings, provided they do not belong to the *rajju*-class. Example: *alābūḥ*. Why "non-living beings"? Consider *kṛkavākuḥ*. Why "not of the *rajju*-class"? Consider *rajjuḥ* and *hanuḥ*.
(2.3.77) *bāhv-antaka-druka-maṇḍalubhyo nāmni*:

The suffix *ūṅ* occurs after words ending in *bāhu*, as well as after *kadru* and *kamaṇḍalu*, when they form a proper name (*nāman*). Examples: *Madrabāhūḥ*, *Kadrūḥ*, *Kamaṇḍalūḥ*. Why "when it is a proper name"? In the case of a descriptive compound (*vṛtti*), such as "she whose arms are round" (*vṛttabāhuḥ*), [the suffix does not apply]; nor does it apply to the names *kadruḥ* or *kamaṇḍaluḥ* when not proper names. (2.3.78) *paṅgūḥ śvaśrūḥ*: The suffix *ūṅ* is applied to *paṅgu* when it refers to a mother-in-law (*śvaśrū*). Example: *paṅgūḥ śvaśrūḥ*. (The suffix does not apply if she is not a mother-in-law.)
These two words are irregularly formed (*nipātita*) as feminine nouns by [Pāṇini 4.1.69]:
*ūror upamā-saṃhita-sahita-saha-śapha-vāmalakṣmaṇād eḥ*.

The suffix *ūṅ* occurs after the word *ūru* when preceded by a word used as a standard of comparison (*upamāna*) or others, in the feminine gender: *karabhorūḥ*, *saṃhitorūḥ*, *sahitorūḥ*, *sahorūḥ*, *śaphorūḥ*, *vāmorūḥ*, *lakṣmaṇorūḥ*. It need not be stated that the suffix *ṅīn* applies after the *yañ* [patronymic] suffixes beginning with *Śārṅgarava*; for after those ending in *añ*, the suffix *ṅīp* already exists. Furthermore, the suffix *ṅīṣ* applies after words derived from *Śārṅgarava* and others that end in *aṇ*, those ending in *ḍhak*, and those ending in *yañ* which denote a genus (*jāti*). It also applies after words ending in the vowel *i*: for example, *Śaibyā*. And after a word ending in *yañ*, there must be the suffix *cāp*. However, in the case of the *Śibi* tribe, the suffix *ṅīp* applies to the *aṇ* [patronymic] suffix in the sense of "belonging to this" (*tasyedam*) when denoting a genus.

Even for *bhogavat* and *gaurimat*, the suffix *ṅīp* applies by the rule *ugitaś ca*. However, in the case of the comparative suffixes such as *tarap*, the short vowel [of the feminine] occurs invariably due to the fixed option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*). Furthermore, there is no occurrence of feminine forms at all for *nṛ* and *nara*. From the suffix *aṇ* [derived] by the rule *tasyedam*, the suffix *ṅīp* is applied: *nārī*.

By the rule *yaṅaś cāp* (Pāṇini 4.1.74), the suffix *cāp* is applied to a word ending in *yaṅ* in the feminine: *Kārīṣagandhyā*, *Āmbaṣṭhyā*, *Vārāhyā*. This statement is intended to set aside the suffix *ṅīṣ* characterized by being a genus (*jāti*) as well as the suffix *ḍāp*.
*yūnas tiḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.77): For *yuvan*, the suffix *ti* occurs when forming the feminine. [Thus: *yuvatiḥ*.

*anṛṣer gurūpottamād gotre ’ṇiñoḥ ṣyaṅ* (Pāṇini 4.1.78): After a patronymic (*gotra*) that does not derive from a seer’s name (*anṛṣi*), provided the penultimate syllable is heavy (*gurūpottama*), the suffix *ṣyaṅ* replaces the suffixes *aṇ* and *iñ*.

For those two suffixes *aṇ* and *iñ*, which are prescribed after a word that does not denote a seer (*anṛṣi*) and where the penultimate syllable is heavy (*gurūpottama*), the substitution of *ṣyaṅ* occurs in the feminine when they form a *gotra* (lineage) name. Examples: *Kārīṣagandhyā*, *Vārāhyā*. By its very nature, the word *uttama* refers to three or more syllables. Why "not denoting a seer"? Example: *Vāsiṣṭhī* (denotes a seer). Why "where the penultimate syllable is heavy"? Example: *Aupagavī* (the penultimate syllable is not heavy). Why "in a *gotra* name"? Example: *Āhicchattrī* (this is a place-name, not a *gotra*). Why "*aṇ* and *iñ*"? Example: *Ārtabhāgī*. Here, *añ* is applied because it belongs to the *bidādi* group. Regarding the rule *kulanāmnaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.140):
for a word used as a family name, the substitution of *ṣyaṅ* occurs in the feminine when *aṇ* or *iñ* are prescribed in the sense of a *gotra*. Examples: *Pauṇikyā*, *Maukharyā*.

(2.3.84) *Krauḍyādīnām*: For the group beginning with *Krauḍi*, the suffix *ṣyaṅ* is applied in the feminine for the [patronymic] suffixes *aṇ* and *iñ*. Examples: *Krauḍyā*. [The list includes: *Krauḍi*, *Lāḍi*, *Āpiśali*, *Āpikṣiti*, *Caupayata*, *Saikayata*, *Bailvavata*, *Saudhātaki*, [applied] to a female Sūta or a young woman; [applied] to a Bhoja who is a Kṣatriya; *Bhauriki*, *Bhauliki*, *Śālāsthali*, *Kāpiṣṭhali*.
(2.3.85) *Daivayajñi-śaucivṛkṣi-sātyamugri-kāṇṭheviddhīnāṃ vā*: For the descendants of Daivayajñi, Śaucivṛkṣi, Sātyamugri, and Kāṇṭheviddhi, the suffix *ṣyaṅ* is optionally applied in the feminine.

For feminine nouns ending in *iñ* derived from *daivayajñi* and others, the suffix *ṣyaṅ* optionally occurs. Examples: *daivayajñī*, *daivayajñyā*; *śaucivṛkṣī*, *śaucivṛkṣyā*; *sātyamugrī*, *sātyamugryā*; *kāṇṭheviddhī*, *kāṇṭheviddhyā*. The option (*vā*) is understood as a governing rule. The second chapter, third quarter, is completed.
From here until the rule for *añ* (2.4.1), the suffix *aṇ* applies.

The suffix *aṇ* occurs in the sense of those meanings that precede the mention of the word *jita*. For example: *aupagavaḥ*. Because the word "or" (*vā*) is understood [from a previous rule], one also has: *upagvapatyam*. Regarding the rule *dityadityādityayamāṇ ṇyaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.85): after the words *diti*, etc., the suffix *ṇya* occurs in place of the *aṇ* that precedes *jita*. Examples: *daityaḥ*, *ādityaḥ*, *ādityaḥ*, *yāmyaḥ*. How is *daiteyaḥ* formed? It will be derived from a word ending in a *ṅī* suffix by means of the suffix *ḍhak*.

(2.4.3) *Patyur anaśvādyādeḥ*: After the word *pati*, when it is preceded by a term other than those beginning with *aśva* and so forth, the suffix *ṇya* (which replaces *jit-āṇ*) occurs. Example: *Bārhaspatyaḥ*. Why "not preceded by *aśva* and so forth"? [Counter-examples: *āśvapatam*, *śātapatam*, *ādhipatam*. [The list of excluded terms is: *aśva*, *śata*, *dhana*, *gaṇa*, *rāṣṭra*, *kula*, *gṛha*, *paśu*, *dhānya*, *dhanvan*, *sabhā*, *prāṇa*, *adhi*, *senā*, *kṣetra*.
(2.4.4) *Aḥ sthāmnaḥ*: [The suffix *a* occurs after *sthāman*].
The suffix *aṅ* follows a word ending in *sthāman*, provided it does not end in *jit*. For example: *Aśvatthāmaḥ*. Regarding the rule *lomno ’patyeṣu* (Pāṇini 2.4.58):

the suffix *aṅ* follows a word ending in *loman* when there are many descendants. For example: the sons of *Uḍuloman* are *Uḍulomāḥ*. Why is the plural used [in the rule]? Consider: *Auḍulomiḥ*. Here, the suffix *iñ* is applied because the word belongs to the *bāhv-ādi* group.

*pṛthivyā ñaḥ* (2.4.6): Before *jit*, the suffix *ña* is applied after *pṛthivī*. [Thus: *pārthivaḥ*. Because it is read in the *utsādi* group, the suffix *añ* is also applied: *pārthivī*, *pārthivā*.
[This is governed by] *utsādibhyo ’ñ* (2.4.7).

The suffix *añ* occurs after [the words] beginning with *utsa*, provided they have been previously mentioned in the section on *jit* [roots]. For example: *autsaḥ* (from *utsa*) and *audapānaḥ* (from *udapāna*). [The list of bases is: *utsa*, *udapāna*, *vikara*, *vinada*, *mahānada*, *mahānasa*, *mahāprāṇa*, *taruṇa*, *taluna*, *baṣkaya*—provided they do not occur in a compound; *dhenu*, *pṛthivī*, *paṅkti*, *jagatī*, *triṣṭubh*, *anuṣṭubh*, *janapada*, *Bharata*, *Uśīnara*, *grīṣma*, *pīlukuṇa*, *udasthāna* when referring to a region (*deśa*); *bṛhatī* when referring to a biting insect (*daṃśa*); *bhallakīya*, *rathantara*, *madhyandina*, *bṛhat*.
After the words *mahat*, *mahit*, *sātvat*, *kuru*, *pañcāla*, *indrāvasāna*, *uṣṇih*, *kakubh*, and *suvarṇa*, the suffix *añ* follows a word ending in *deva* (Pāṇini 2.4.8). For example: *daiva*.
The suffix *yañ* (2.4.9) occurs after the word *deva* when it precedes *jita*; thus, *daivyaḥ*.
After *bahiṣ*, the suffixes *ṭīk* and *ka* also occur (2.4.10).

The suffix *ṭīkañ* occurs after the word *bāhīka*, provided it is derived from *bāhya*. Furthermore, after a numeral that denotes the thing numbered, when no patronymic suffix follows, there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix *añ* and its derivatives, provided the stem does not begin with *aj*. (Pāṇini 5.3.49–50) *bāhīkaḥ*, *bāhyaḥ*. (When the suffix *añ* is applied to *bāhya* to denote a person from that region, the form is *bāhīkaḥ*; otherwise, it remains *bāhyaḥ*. Regarding the rule "After a numeral denoting the thing numbered, when no patronymic suffix follows, there is elision of the suffix *añ* and its derivatives, provided the stem does not begin with *aj*, and this elision is not doubled": (Pāṇini 5.3.49).

The suffixes beginning with *a* (and so on) that are prescribed after words denoting numbers—ending in the word denoted by the number—and which occur before the patronymic suffix *ñi*, provided they do not denote a descendant, undergo elision (*luk*), but not in the case of *dvi*. For example: "prepared in five vessels" (*pañcasu kapāleṣu saṃskṛtaḥ*) becomes *pañcakapālaḥ*. Why say "beginning with a number"? Consider *paurvaśālaḥ* ("one who comes from the eastern hall"). Why say "from a word denoted by the number"? Consider *trividyā* ("knowledge consisting of three parts"); one who studies that is called *traividyaḥ*. Consider *ṣaṭkulam* ("the family of six"); one born therein is *ṣāṭkulaḥ*. Consider *pañcanadaṃ nagaram* ("the city of the five rivers"); one born therein is *pāñcanadaḥ*.

In the case of *pañcakapālya*, however, the form is *pañcakapāla* itself, because the meaning is that of a countable object (*saṃkhyeya*). Why [is the word] "without offspring" (*anapatya*) used? [To exclude forms such as] *dvaimāturaḥ*. Why [is the word] "beginning with *aja*" (*ajādeḥ*) used? [To exclude forms such as] *pañcagargarūpyaḥ*. Why [is the word] "not after *dvi*" (*advi*) used? [To exclude forms such as] *pāñcakapālaḥ*, meaning a fragment of a five-pot-sherd sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*). Only up to the suffix *-jit* [is this rule applied]: thus, *dvināvikaḥ*. [Furthermore, by the rule] "before the suffix *-vat*, [the suffix] *ḍhak* [is applied] after *agni* and *kali*" (Pāṇini 4.2.12).

Before the mention of the suffix *vat*, the suffix *ḍhak* occurs after the words *agni* and *kali* when these meanings are intended: the offspring of Agni is *Āgneyaḥ*; [the offspring] of Kali is *Kāleyaḥ*. A *Sāman* seen by Agni is *Āgneyam*; [a *Sāman* seen by] Kali is *Kāleyam*. That which has Agni as its deity is *Āgneyaḥ*; [that which has] Kali as its deity is *Kāleyaḥ*. That which belongs to Agni is *Āgneyam*; [that which belongs to] Kali is *Kāleyam*. That which is caused by Agni—whether it be a conjunction or a portent—is *Āgneyaḥ*; [that which is caused by] Kali is *Kāleyaḥ*. Why say "before *vat*"? [To exclude cases such as: *agnivat*, *kalivat*; *agnitvam*, *kalitvam*. Or rather, [the suffixes are optional]: *agnisvam*, *kalisvam*.
After the words *strī* and *puṃs*, the suffixes *nañ* and *snañ* [are applied respectively]. (Pāṇini 4.1.87)
Before the suffix *vat*, the suffixes *nañ* and *snañ* are applied after the words *strī* and *pums*. Thus: *straiṇam* and *pauṃsnam*. Only before *vat*: *strīvat* and *puṃvat*.
Regarding the state (*bhāva*), there is an option (Pāṇini 2.4.14):
after *strī* and *pums*, the suffixes *nañ* and *snañ* optionally occur to denote the state. Thus: *straiṇam* or *strītvam*; *pauṃsnam* or *puṃstvam*.

*gor aci* (2.4.15): When an affix beginning with a vowel (*ac*) follows the word *go*, the substitution *yat* occurs. *gavi bhavam* (existing in a cow) becomes *gavyam*. *goḥ svam* (the property of a cow) becomes *gavyam*. *gaur devatāsya* (that which has a cow as its deity) becomes *gavyam*. Why does it say "when an affix beginning with a vowel"? [Consider: *gor āgataḥ* (come from a cow) becomes *gorūpyaḥ*. *tasyāpatyam* (2.4.16). [The suffix *yat* is applied after the word *go* when the sense is "his offspring."]

After a word ending in the sixth case, the suffixes *aṇ* and others, as prescribed, occur to denote offspring (*apatya*). Examples: *aupagavaḥ*, *daityaḥ*, *bārhaspatyaḥ*. (2.4.17) *Ādyāt*: Those suffixes such as *aṇ* and others that occur to denote offspring are applied to the very first ancestor (*paramaprakṛti*) alone. For that [person] is the offspring of all the preceding ancestors; or rather, by figurative usage (*upacāra*), the term for the first ancestor is used to denote the descendant. The offspring of Upagu is *Aupagavaḥ*; his offspring is *Aupagavaḥ*. The offspring of Devadatta is *Daivadattiḥ*; his offspring is *Daivadattiḥ*. The offspring of Garga is *Gārgyaḥ*; his offspring is *Gārgyaḥ*.

(2.4.18) *pautrāder astriyāṃ gurvāyatte*: In the case of a descendant starting with the grandson (*pautra*), when dependent upon a teacher (*guru*)—provided the descendant is not female—the suffixes *aṇ* and so forth are applied. For example: *Gārgyāyaṇaḥ*. Why does it say "not female" (*astriyām*)? [Because] *Gārgī* [is formed with a feminine suffix]. Why is the word "teacher" (*guru*) mentioned? [To indicate that] *Gārgyaḥ* refers to one who is the offspring of someone other than the teacher. Why is the word "dependent" (*āyatta*) mentioned? One who, even while the teacher is alive, conducts himself independently, is called *Gārgyaḥ* in a sense of reproach (*kutsā*). Even though one might say, "This scoundrel (*jālma*) is a *Gārgyāyaṇa*," the reproach is understood from the word *jālma*, not from the word *Gārgyāyaṇa*.

By this, however, the subject matter is demonstrated: that even when one is properly dependent upon a guru, there are those who do not act accordingly. But he who does not become self-willed even when the guru is no longer present is said to be "Gārgyāyaṇa" for the sake of praise, because he remains dependent [on the guru] by following what was previously instructed by him, even after the guru has died. Furthermore, even one who is dependent on a guru of a different lineage is intended to be called "Gārgyāyaṇa" because he is a fit object of praise. However, one who is dead is not dependent on anyone, and thus he is called "Gārgya."

Now, is he called "Gārgyāyaṇa" because he was previously dependent on his guru? Even so, there is no fault. In all cases, the word *gārgya* exists when the specific [lineage] is not intended to be expressed.

Thus, by the rule *ata iñ* (Pāṇini 4.1.95), the suffix *iñ* occurs after a word ending in *a* in the genitive case to denote offspring. The offspring of Dakṣa is *Dākṣi*. Why is the *t* in *taparaḥ* [specified]? [Consider the example: *kailālapaḥ*.

(2.4.20) *bāhvādibhyo gotrādibhyaḥ*: The suffix *iñ* is applied after words beginning with *bāhu* when they belong to the class of *gotra* (lineage). Examples: *Bāhaviḥ*, *Aupabāhaviḥ*. Why "after words beginning with *gotra*"? Consider one named *Bāhu* in the present day; his descendant would be called *Bāhavaḥ* [by the suffix *aṇ*].

Bāhu, Upabāhu, Nibāhu, Upabindu, Vṛkalā, Kṛkalā, Cūḍā, Balākā, Mūṣikā, Bhagalā, Lagahā, Dhruvakā, Dhuvakā, Sumitrā, Durmitrā, Puṣkarasad, Anurahat, Anaḍuh, Agniśarman, Devaśarman, Kunāman, Sunāman, Pañcan, Saptan, Aṣṭan, Sudhāvat, Udañc, Śiras, Māṣaśarāvin, Kṣemadhṛtvin, Śṛṅkhalanodin, Kharanādin, Nagaramardin.

Prākāramardin, Loman, Ajīgarta, Kṛṣṇa, Yudhiṣṭhira, Arjuna, Sāmba, Gada, Pradyumna, and Bhūyo'mbha—[the suffix *iñ* is applied after these,] and there is the elision of the vowel *a* in *amita-ūjas*. This is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open class): [examples include] Jāṅghi, Aindraśarmi, and Ājadhenavi. (2.4.21) *vyāsādīnām akaṅ ca*: After the names in the group beginning with Vyāsa, the suffix *iñ* is applied to denote a descendant, and the substitution *akaṅ* occurs [in place of the final part of the name]. Examples: Vaiyāsaki, Saudhātaki, Vāruṭaki. [The members of this group are: Vyāsa, Sudhātṛ, Varuṭa, Niṣāda, Caṇḍāla, and Bimba.

*Bidādibhyo ’ñ* (2.4.22): The suffix *añ* occurs after [names] such as Bida and others to denote a descendant. For example: Baidaḥ, Aurvaḥ. Only when referring to a *gotra* (clan name), etc.: if there is someone named Bida who is not a *gotra*, his descendant is Baidiḥ. The list is: Bida, Urva, Kaśyapa, Kuśika, Bharadvāja, Upamanyu, Kilāta, Kindarbha, Viśvānara, Ṛṣṭiṣeṇa, Ṛtabhāga, Haryaśva, Priyaka, Apastambha, Kucavāra, Śaradvat, Śunaka, Dhenu, Gopavana, Śigru, Bindu, Bhājana, Aśvāvatāna.

Śyāmāka, Śyāmāka, Śyāparṇa, Harita, Kiṃdāsa, Vasyaska, Arkaluṣa, Vadhyoga, Viṣṇuvṛddha, Pratibodha, Rathītara, Rathantara, Gaviṣṭhila, Gaviṣṭhira, Niṣāda, Maṭhara, Mṛdāku, *punarbhū*-son, daughter, sister-in-law, another’s wife, and the axe. (2.4.23) *ṛṣeḥ pautrādau*: After the names of sages (*ṛṣi*) beginning with Bida, the suffix *añ* occurs for a descendant from the grandson onwards. Examples: *Baidaḥ*, *Kauśikaḥ*. Why "of a sage"? [Counter-example: *dauhitraḥ* ("daughter's son"). Why "from the grandson onwards"? [Counter-example: *Baidiḥ* ("grandson").
*gargādibhyo yañ* (Pāṇini 4.1.105):

the suffix *yañ* occurs after [names] such as *garga* and others to denote a descendant in the line beginning with the grandson. For example: *Gārgyaḥ*, *Vātsyaḥ*. Only for the line beginning with the grandson: *Gārgiḥ*. Only from those belonging to the *gotra* [lineage]: suppose there is someone named *Garga*; his descendant in the line beginning with the grandson is *Gārgiḥ*.

Garga, Vatsa, Vāja (in the uncompounded form), Saṃkṛti, Asaṃkṛti, Aja, Vyāghrapād, Vidabhṛt, Prācīnayoga, Pulasti, Eka, Rebha, Agniveśa, Śaṅkha, Śaṭha, Dhūma, Avaṭa, Manasa, Dhanañjaya, Vṛkṣa, Viśvāvasu, Jaramāṇa, Kurukata, Anaḍuh, Lohita, Saṃśita, Babhru, Babhlu, Maṇḍu, Maṅkṣu, Śabhlu (?), Ligu, Guhalu, Vijigīṣu, Mantu, and Manu.

Tanu, Manāyī, Sruva, Kaṇṭhaka, Ṛkṣa, Tarukṣa, Tarakṣa, Taṇḍa, Vataṇḍa, Kapi, Kata, Śakala, Kaṇva, Gokakṣa, Agastya, Kuṇḍinī, Yājñavalkya, Abhayajāta, Tirohita, Vṛṣagaṇa, Rahogaṇa, Śaṇḍila, Mudgala, Musala, Parāśara, Jatūkarṇa, Mantrita, Aśmaratha, Śarkarakṣa, Pūtimāṣa, Sthūṇā, Rarākā, Piṅgala, Kṛṣṇa, and Golanda.

Ulūka, Titimbha, Bhiṣaj, Bhaṇḍita, Dalbha, Cikita, Devahū, Indrahū, Ekalū, Pippalū, Bṛhadagni, Jamadagni, Alābhin, Uktha, Ṛktha (?), and Kuṭīgu. How is it that [the son] of Jamadagni is called Jāmadagnya and the son of Parāśara is called Vyāsa Pārāśarya? For even a son may be designated in such a way because he performs the duties of a grandson and so forth. However, when immediate descent is intended, the suffix *ṛṣyaṇ* alone is used: Jāmadagnaḥ, Pārāśaraḥ.
[The rule] "after *madhu*, [the suffix *yañ* is used] for a Brāhmaṇa" (2.4.25).
From the word *madhu*, the suffix *yañ* occurs when a Brāhmaṇa is the descendant: *mādhavyaḥ* as a Brāhmaṇa; otherwise, *mādhavaḥ*. Regarding *babhroḥ kauśike* (Pāṇini 4.1.104):

because *babhru* is included in the *gargādi* list, the suffix *yañ* applies only when the descendant is specifically Kauśika: *bābhravyaḥ*; elsewhere, *bābhravaḥ*. However, its inclusion in the *gargādi* list is for the purpose of the feminine suffix *ṣpha*: *bābhravyāyaṇī*.

Regarding *kaper āṅgirase* (Pāṇini 2.4.27): because of its inclusion in the list beginning with *garga*, the suffix *yañ* applied after *kapi* occurs only when it refers to a descendant of Aṅgiras. Thus, [the form] is *kāpyaḥ*. In other cases, it is *kāpeyaḥ*. Because of its inclusion in the list beginning with *garga*, the feminine form is *kāpyāyanī*.
Regarding *bodhāt* (2.4.28).
The suffix *yañ* occurs after *Bodha* when the descendant belongs to the lineage of Aṅgiras. Thus, *Baudhyaḥ*; another [descendant] is *Baudhiḥ*.

Regarding *vataṇḍāt* (Pāṇini 2.4.29): after *Vataṇḍa*, the suffix *yañ* occurs only when the descendant belongs to the lineage of Aṅgiras. Thus, *Vātaṇḍyaḥ*. However, if he does not belong to the lineage of Aṅgiras, then because of its inclusion in both the *Garga*-group and the *Śiva*-group, the forms are *Vātaṇḍyaḥ* and *Vātaṇḍaḥ*.

*striyāṃ luk* (2.4.30): After the word *vataṇḍa*, when the feminine descendant is an Āṅgirasa, there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix *yañ*. Thus, *vataṇḍī*. But when she is not an Āṅgirasa, [the forms are] *vātaṇḍī* or *vātaṇḍyāyanī*. *aśvādibhyaḥ phaṅ* (2.4.31).

The suffix *phañ* (*āyana*) is applied after [the bases] beginning with *aśva* to denote a descendant in the third generation or beyond. Examples: *Āśvāyanaḥ*, *Āśmāyanaḥ*. The bases are: *aśva*, *aśman*, *śaṅkha*, *vida*, *puṭa*, *rohiṇa*, *kharjūra*, *piñjala*, *bhaḍila*, *bhaṇḍila*, *bhaḍita*, *bhaṇḍita*, *prahṛta*, *rāmoda*, *kṣātra*, *grīvā*, *ākāśa*, *kāṇa*, *golāṅka*, *arkasvana*, *vana*, *pāda*, *cakra*, *kula*, *tula*, *śraviṣṭhā*, *pavitrā*, *pavindā*, *gomin*, *śyāma*, and *dhūma*.

Vāgmin, Viśvānara, Kuṭaśa, Ātreya (?), Jaḍa, Vata, Grīṣma, Arha, Vīkṣya, Viśampa, Viśāla, Giri, Capala, Dāsaka, Bailya, Dharmya, and Ānaḍuhya—these [names] form patronymics in the masculine from the word *jāta*. After *Śapa*, when followed by *Ātreya*, [the suffix *iñ* is applied]; likewise after *Arjuna*, *Śūdraka*, *Sumanas*, and *Durmanas*. After *Ātreya*, when followed by *Bhāradvāja*, [the suffix *iñ* is applied]; and after *Bhāradvāja*, when followed by *Ātreya*. [The suffix *iñ* is also applied] after *Utsa*, *Anāya* (?), *Atava*, *Kitava*, *Śiva*, and *Khadira*. After *Bharga*, when followed by *Traigarta*, [the suffix *iñ* is applied]. (Pāṇini 2.4.32)

The suffix *phañ* occurs after *Bharga* when the descendant is a grandson or later, provided he belongs to the Traigarta lineage. Example: *Bhārgāyaṇaḥ*. Why "Traigarta"? [Counter-example: *Bhārgaḥ*. The suffix *phyañ* occurs after the *kuñja*-group when the descendant is a grandson or later. Examples: *Kauñjāyanyaḥ*, *Kauñjāyanyau*; *Brādhnāyanyaḥ*, *Brādhnāyanyau*. Why "grandson or later"? [Counter-example: *Kauñjiḥ*. The *kuñja*-group consists of: *Kuñja*, *Bradhna*, *Śaṅkha*, *Bhasman*, *Gaṇa*, *Loman*, *Śaṭha*, *Śāka*, *Śuṇḍā*, *Śubhrā*, *Vipāśa*, *Skanda*, and *Skambha*.

*strībahuṣu phak* (Pāṇini 4.1.98): When there are many female descendants, the suffix *phak* occurs after [the group of words] beginning with *kuñja*. For example: *kauñjāyanī* (a single female descendant). When there are many: *kauñjāyanāḥ*. Only when referring to descendants from the third generation (*pautra*) onwards does this apply; otherwise, one has *kauñjī* or *kauñjayaḥ*. *naḍādibhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.99).

The suffix *phak* occurs after [the group of stems beginning with] *naḍa* and so forth, to denote a descendant in the third generation (*pautra*) or beyond. For example: *Nāḍāyanaḥ*, *Cārāyaṇaḥ*. The restriction "in the third generation or beyond" is applied because otherwise [the form] would be *Nāḍiḥ*. The restriction "after [stems belonging to] the *gotra* category and so forth" is applied because otherwise [the form] would be *Nāḍiḥ*—referring to someone simply named *Naḍa*; his descendant [in the immediate sense] is *Nāḍiḥ*. The list is: *naḍa*, *cara*, *baka*, *muñja*, *itika*, *itiśa*, *upaka*, *lamaka*, *śalaṅku* (and *śalaṅka*).

Because the word *Śālaṅki* is recited among [the names] beginning with *Paila*, the suffix *iñ* also occurs: Saptala, Vājavya, Vyatika, Agniśarman, Vṛṣagaṇa, Prāṇa, Nara, Sāyaka, Dāsamitra, Dvīpa, Piṅgara, Piṅgala, Kiṃkara, Kiṃkala, Kātara, Kāthala, Kāśya, Kāśyapa, Nāvya, Aja, Amuṣya, Kṛṣṇa, and Raṇa when they are Brāhmaṇas of the Vasiṣṭha lineage; Amitra, Ligu, Citra, Kumāra, and Kroṣṭu—with *Kroṣṭa* substituted for it; as well as Loha, Durga, and Stamba.

Śiṃśapā, Agra, Tṛṇa, Śakaṭa, Sumanas, Durmanas, Sumata, Mimata, Jālandhara, Yugandhara, Haṃsaka, Daṇḍin, Hastin, Pañcāla, Camasin, Sukṛtya, Sthiraka, Brāhmaṇa, Aśvala, Caṭaka, Badara, Adhvara, Kharapa, Kāmuka, Brahmadatta, Udumbara, Śoṇa, Aloha, Daṇḍapa, Lohita.
[The suffix] *añ* is applied after these words beginning with *harita* (Pāṇini 2.4.36).

The suffix *phak* occurs after words ending in *añ* derived from *harita* and others, due to their inclusion in the *bidādi* group, when forming a patronymic in the sense of "offspring. Examples: *Hāritāyanaḥ*, *Kaiṃdāsāyanaḥ*.

By the rule *yañiñaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.101), the suffix *phak* occurs after words ending in *yañ* or *iñ* when forming a patronymic for a descendant from the third generation (*pautra*) onwards. Examples: *Gārgyāyaṇaḥ*, *Dākṣāyaṇaḥ*.

(2.4.38) After *śaradvat*, *śunaka*, and *darbha*, the suffix *phak* occurs in the sense of a descendant beginning with a grandson when [the patronymic] belongs to the *Bhārgava*, *Vātsya*, or *Āgrāyaṇa* groups. Thus, *Śāradvatāyana* is formed if he is a *Vātsya*; otherwise, he is a *Śaunaka*, in which case the suffix *añ* is applied because they belong to the *Bida* group. *Dārbhāyaṇa* is formed if he is an *Āgrāyaṇa*; otherwise, he is a *Dārbhi*. The rule "beginning with a grandson" applies here as well: thus, *Śāradvata*.
(2.4.39) After *parvata* and *jīvanta*, the suffix is optional.

The suffix *phak* optionally occurs after *parvata* and *jīvanta* when the descendant is a grandson or later. Thus: *pārvatāyanaḥ* or *pārvatiḥ*; *jaivantāyanaḥ* or *jaivantiḥ*. The restriction "when the descendant is a grandson or later" remains in force: hence *pārvatiḥ* [as a grandson]. Regarding *droṇāt* (Pāṇini 4.1.109):

the suffix *phak* optionally occurs after *droṇa* for any descendant. Thus: *drauṇāyanaḥ* or *drauṇiḥ*. Due to the separation of the rule (*yogavibhāga*), the restriction "when the descendant is a grandson or later" is no longer applicable here.

*Śivādibhyo ’ṇ* (Pāṇini 4.1.112): The suffix *aṇ* occurs after words such as *Śiva* and others when denoting simply "offspring. Examples: *Śaivaḥ*, *Prauṣṭhaḥ*. This rule is restated in order to override other potential exceptions. For instance, in the case of *Ārṣṭiṣeṇaḥ*, the suffix *ṇya* does not apply. From the word *Gaṅgā*, because it is included here [in the *Śiva* list], the suffix *aṇ* applies: *Gāṅgaḥ*; because it is included in the *Śubhra* group, the suffix *ḍhak* applies: *Gāṅgeyaḥ*; and because it is included in the *Tika* group, the suffix *phiñ* applies: *Gāṅgāyaniḥ*. From the word *Vipāś*, because it is included here [in the *Śiva* list], the suffix *aṇ* applies: *Vaipāśaḥ*; because it is included in the *Kuñja* group, the suffix *phyañ* applies: *Vaipāśāyanyaḥ*.

Śiva, Proṣṭha, Prauṣṭhika, Caṇḍa, Jambha, Bhūri, Kuṭhāra, Anabhiglāna, Sandhi, Muni, Kakustha, Kohaḍa, Kakubha, Rodha, Pirala, Vataṇḍa, Tṛṇa, Karṇa, Kṣīrahrada, Jalahrada, Pariṣika, Gopikā, Kapilikā, Jaṭilikā, Badhirikā, Amañjarīka, Vṛṣṇika, Khañjāra, Khañjāla, Rekha, Lekha, Sulekha, Viśravaṇa, Ravaṇa, and Vartanākṣa.

-Piṭaka, -Piṭāka, Bṛkṣāka, Nabhāka, Ūrṇanābha, Jaratkāru, Utkāru, Utkāya (?), Purohitikā, Āryaśvetā, Supiṣṭa, Piṣṭa, Mayūrakarṇa, Khadūraka, Takṣan, Ṛṣṭiṣeṇa, Gaṅgā, Vipāśā, Yaska, Druhya, Lahya, Ayasthūṇa, Tṛṇakarṇa, Kalandana, Virūpākṣa, Bhūmi, Ilā, Sapatnī; [names] with two vowels [ending in] a vowel other than *ā* when followed by a river name—Triveṇī and Trivaṇa; and for names of rivers and female humans, [the suffix *cha* is applied] after a stem ending in a vowel other than *ā*, provided it begins with a consonant. (Pāṇini 4.1.42)

The suffix *aṇ* occurs after a word denoting a river or a female human being when forming a derivative meaning "offspring," provided that the diphthongs *ai* and *au* do not occur among the vowels at the beginning of the word. Examples: *Yāmunaḥ*, *Caititah*. Why mention "river" and "female human"? [Counter-example: *Sauparṇeyaḥ*. Why mention "name" (*nāman*)? [Counter-example: from *Śobhanikā*, we have *Śaubhanikeyaḥ*. Why specify "provided that *ai* and *au* do not occur among the initial vowels"? [Counter-example: from *Vāsavadattā*, we have *Vāsavadatteyaḥ*. By rule 2.4.43, the suffix *aṇ* occurs after the words *kruñcā* and *kokilā* to form a derivative meaning "offspring. Examples: *Krauñcaḥ*, *Kaukilaḥ*.
(2.4.44) *ṛṣikuruvṛṣṇyandhakāt*: The suffix *aṇ* occurs after words denoting sages (*ṛṣi*) and so forth to form a patronymic. Examples: *Vāsiṣṭhaḥ*, *Nākulaḥ*, *Vāsudevaḥ*, *Śvāphalkaḥ*.

(2.4.45) *mātur ut saṃkhyāsaṃbhadrādeḥ*: [The suffix *aṇ* is applied] after the word "mother" (*mātṛ*), with the substitution of *u* for the final vowel, when preceded by a numeral or the words *saṃ* and *bhadra*, etc.

The suffix *aṇ* occurs after the word *mātṛ* when preceded by a numeral or similar element in the sense of "offspring," and the letter *u* is substituted for the final vowel. Examples: *dvaimāturaḥ*, *sāṃmāturaḥ*, *bhādramāturaḥ*. Why specify "not preceded by *vi*, *saṃ*, *bhadra*, etc."? Because the offspring of *vimātṛ* is *vaimātreyaḥ*. Regarding the rule *kanyāyāḥ kanīna ca* (Pāṇini 4.1.116):
the suffix *aṇ* occurs after *kanyā* in the sense of "offspring," and *kanīna* is substituted [for *kanyā*]. Example: *kānīnaḥ*, as in the case of Karṇa.

(2.4.47) *Śuṅgacchagalavikarṇād bhāradvājavātsyātreyeṣu*: After the words *śuṅga* and others, the suffix *aṇ* occurs when the descendants belong to the lineages of Bhāradvāja, Vātsya, and Ātreya respectively. If he is a descendant of Bhāradvāja, he is called *Śauṅga*; otherwise, he is *Śauṅgi*. Because a specific gender is included when the name itself is mentioned, the descendant of *Śuṅgā* (feminine) is also *Śauṅga*. If he is a descendant of Vātsya, he is called *Chāgala*; otherwise, he is *Chāgali*. If he is a descendant of Ātreya, he is called *Vaikarṇa*; otherwise, he is *Vaikarṇi*. (2.4.48) *Pīlāmaṇḍūkād vā*: [The suffix *aṇ* is applied] optionally after the words *pīlā* and *maṇḍūka*.
The suffix *aṇ* optionally occurs after *pīla* and *maṇḍūka* when denoting offspring. [Thus: *Pailaḥ*, *Paileyaḥ*; *Māṇḍūkaḥ*, *Māṇḍūkiḥ*.
By rule 2.4.49 (*ḍhak*), the suffix *ḍhak* optionally occurs after *maṇḍūka* when denoting offspring. [Thus: *Māṇḍūkeyaḥ*, *Māṇḍūkeyī*; *Māṇḍūkaḥ*, *Māṇḍūkiḥ*.

Pāṇini 4.1.99 (*ṅyāptyūṅaḥ*): The suffix *ḍhak* occurs after words ending in feminine suffixes marked with *ṅ*, words ending in *ā*, words ending in *tyap*, and words ending in *ūṅ*, when forming a patronymic. Examples: *sauparṇeyaḥ*, *vainateyaḥ*, *pārvateyaḥ*, *kāmaṇḍaleyaḥ*. Why "after these"? [Counter-example: *daradaḥ* is the offspring of *daradaḥ*; here it is not formed with *ḍhak*. Pāṇini 4.1.100 (*dvyacaḥ*): [The suffix *ḍhak* occurs] after a word consisting of two syllables.
The suffix *ḍhak* occurs after a word ending in a vowel beginning with *ṅ*, provided it consists of two syllables (*dvyac*), when forming a patronymic. For example: *Dātteyaḥ*.

The suffix *ḍhak* occurs after a word ending in *i*, provided it does not end in the suffix *ini*, when forming a patronymic. For example: *Ātreyaḥ*, *Vārṣṇeyaḥ*. Why "not ending in *ini*"? Consider: *Dākṣāyaṇaḥ*. The requirement that it consist of two syllables (*dvyac*) remains: for example, *Mārīcaḥ*.

(2.4.53) *Śubhrādibhyaḥ*: The suffix *ḍhak* occurs after [names] beginning with *śubhra* when forming a patronymic (*apatya*). Examples: *Śaubhreyaḥ*, *Vaiṣṭapureyaḥ*. The list [of the *śubhra*-group] is as follows: *śubhra*, *viṣṭapura*, *brahmakṛta*, *śaradvāra*, *śalāthala*, *śalākābhrū*, *lekhābhrū*, *vidhavā*, *kṛkasā*, *rohiṇī*, *rukmiṇī*, *diś*, *dharmiṇī*, *śālūka*, *ajabasti*, *śakandhi*, *lakṣaṇa* and *śyāma* [when referring to] a descendant of *vasiṣṭha* (*vāsiṣṭha*), *godhā*, *kṛkalāsa*, *atithi*, *pravāhaṇa*, *bhārata*, *bhārama*, *kamaṣṭu*, *yamaṣṭu*.

Mṛkaṇḍu, Karpūra, Mṛdu, Itara, Anyatara, Devatara, Ālīḍha, Sudanta, Sudakṣa, Sukāman, Kadru, Guda, Akaśāya, Kumārikā, Kiśorikā, Jihmāśin, Paridhi, Vīradatta, Vāyudatta, Śabala, Khadūraka, Ambikā, Aśokā, Gandhapiṅgalā, Khaḍonmattā, Kudantā, Kuśamba, Anusṛṣṭi, Jaratin, Śuka, Śukra, Ugra, Bīja, Śvan, Aśva, Ajira, and Ahi. This is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open class of words): [e.g.,] Gāṅgeya, Vaimātreya.

(2.4.54) After *vikarṇa* and *kuṣītaka*, the suffix *ḍhak* occurs when *Kāśyapa* is the descendant. Thus: *Vaikarṇeyaḥ*, *Kauṣītakeyaḥ*. Why "when *Kāśyapa* [is the descendant]"? [Otherwise: *Vaikarṇiḥ*, *Kauṣītakiḥ*.
(2.4.55) *Bhrauveyaḥ*.
From the word *bhrū*, when the suffix *ḍhak* is applied to denote offspring, the letter *v* is substituted [for the final *ū*].

For words beginning with *kalyāṇī*, the suffix *ḍhak* occurs to denote offspring, and there is also the substitution of *inaṅ*. [Examples: *kālyāṇineyaḥ*, *saubhāgineyaḥ*. [The list of words is: *kalyāṇī*, *subhagā*, *durbhagā*, *bandhakī*, *anusṛṣṭi*, *jaratī*, *balīvardī*, *jyeṣṭhā*, *kaniṣṭhā*, *madhyamā*, *parastrī*.
(2.4.57) *Kulaṭāyā vā*:
for the word *kulaṭā*, the substitute *inaṅ* optionally occurs; however, the suffix *ḍhak* is already established by the preceding rule. Thus: *kaulaṭineyaḥ* and *kaulaṭeyaḥ*.
(2.4.58) *Caṭakād airak*: [the suffix] *airak* [is applied] after *caṭaka*.

The suffix *airak* occurs after the word *caṭaka* when meaning "offspring. Thus, *cāṭakairaḥ*. Because the feminine form is also included [in the rule], the offspring of *caṭakā* is also *cāṭakairaḥ*.
Regarding the rule *luk striyām* (Pāṇini 4.1.120):

the suffix *airak* added to *caṭaka* undergoes elision (*luk*) in the feminine, resulting in *caṭakā*. This is so that the suffix *airak* itself might not be heard [in the feminine]. However, there indeed exists the word *caṭakā* as a term denoting a genus (*jāti*).
After the words *jāṇḍa* and *pāṇḍa*, the suffix *ārak* occurs to denote offspring: *jāṇḍāraḥ*, *pāṇḍāraḥ*. After the word *godhā*, [the suffix *ārak* occurs]. (Pāṇini 4.1.85–86)
The suffix *ārag* occurs after *godhā* in the sense of offspring:
*gaudhāraḥ*. By [Pāṇini 4.1.129], *erak* occurs after *godhā* in the sense of offspring: *gaudheraḥ*.

(2.4.63) *vā kṣudrābhyaḥ*: after words denoting low-caste women (*kṣudrā*), the suffix *erañ* optionally occurs in the sense of offspring. *kāṇeraḥ*, *kāṇeyaḥ*; *dāseraḥ*, *dāseyaḥ*. Low-caste women are those who are physically deformed or have had sexual relations with multiple men. (2.4.64) *bhrātuḥ vyat*: [the suffix *vyat* occurs after the word *bhrātṛ* in the sense of offspring].

The suffix *vyat* occurs after the word *bhrātṛ* when meaning "offspring. Thus, *bhrātṛvyaḥ*. However, he will state that the word *bhrātṛvya* has its first syllable acute-accented (*ādyudātta*) when it means "rival.
By [Pāṇini 4.1.135], the suffix *cha* occurs after *bhrātṛ* in the sense of offspring. Thus, *bhrātrīyaḥ*.
After *svasuḥ* (2.4.66), the suffix *cha* occurs in the sense of offspring; thus, *svasrīyaḥ*. After *pitṛ*, *mātṛ*, and so forth, the suffix *chaṇ* occurs (2.4.67).

The suffix *chaṇ* is applied after the words *pitṛ-*, *mātṛ-*, and so forth, as well as after *svasu-* [to form patronymics]. Thus: *paitṛṣvasrīyaḥ* (son of the father’s sister), *mātṛṣvasrīyaḥ* (son of the mother’s sister).
Regarding the rule *ḍhaki lopaḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.68):

when the suffix *ḍhak* follows, there is elision of the final phoneme of *pitṛ-*, *mātṛ-*, and so forth, as well as of *svasu-*. The suffix *ḍhak* is understood from this very indicative mark (*liṅga*). Thus: *paitṛṣvaseyaḥ*, *mātṛṣvaseyaḥ*.

*kṣatrāj jātau ghaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.138): after the word *kṣatra*, the suffix *gha* occurs when a lineage (*jāti*) is to be understood as the offspring. [The form is] *kṣatriyaḥ*. Why "when a lineage is to be understood"? [Consider: *kṣātriḥ*.
*rājño yat* (Pāṇini 4.1.139).
When the offspring of a king (*rājan*) is to be expressed, the suffix *yañ* is applied: *rājanyaḥ*. Only when referring to a caste (*jāti*) is this so; otherwise: *rājanaḥ*.
From *śvaśura* (Pāṇini 4.1.137), the suffix *yañ* is applied to denote offspring: *śvaśuryaḥ*. Only when denoting a lineage (*gotra*) and so forth is this so; otherwise: *śvāśuriḥ*.
(2.4.72) *kulād ḍhakañ ca*:
after the word *kula*, the suffix *ḍhakañ* occurs in the sense of offspring, as well as [the suffix *ya*]. [Examples: *kauleyakaḥ* and *kulyaḥ*.
(2.4.73) *khaḥ padāntāc ca*: [The suffix *kha*] also [occurs] after a word ending in *pad*.

The suffix *kha* occurs after the word *kula* when it appears at the end of a compound or as a standalone term, in the sense of "offspring. Examples: *āḍhyakulīnaḥ* ("born of a wealthy family"), *kulīnaḥ* ("of noble birth").

Regarding the rule *duro ḍhag vā* (Pāṇini 4.1.141): the suffix *ḍhak* optionally occurs after the word *kula* when preceded by *dus*, in the sense of "offspring. Examples: *dauṣkuleyaḥ*, *duṣkulīnaḥ*.

(2.4.75) *mahākulād añkhañau*: after the word *mahākuḷa*, the suffixes *añ* and *khañ* are optionally applied in the sense of offspring (*apatya*). [Examples: *māhākulaḥ*, *māhākulīnaḥ*, *mahākulīnaḥ*. (2.4.76) *catuṣpādbhyo ḍhañ*: after words meaning "four-footed," the suffix *ḍhañ* is applied.
The suffix *ḍhañ* occurs after words denoting quadrupeds to form derivatives meaning "offspring. For example: *śābaleyaḥ*, *bāhuleyaḥ*. Regarding the rule *gṛṣṭyādibhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.135):

the suffix *ḍhañ* occurs after the group of words beginning with *gṛṣṭi* to form derivatives meaning "offspring. This statement is made for the purpose of excluding quadrupeds. Examples: *gārṣṭeyaḥ*. The members of the *gṛṣṭyādi* group are: *gṛṣṭi*, *hṛṣṭi*, *hali*, *vāli*, *viśri*, *kudri*, *ajabasti*, and *mitrayu*.

*Revatyādibhyaṣ ṭhak* (2.4.78): The suffix *ṭhak* is applied after [the words] beginning with *revatī* to denote a descendant (*apatya*). Examples: *Raivatikaḥ*, *Āśvapālikaḥ*. The list begins: *revatī*, *aśvapālī*, *dvārapālī*, *maṇipālī*, *vṛkavañcin*, *vṛkagrāha*, *karṇagrāha*, *daṇḍagrāha*, *kukkuṭākṣa*. *pautrādeḥ striyāḥ kutsite ṇa ca* (2.4.79): After a feminine word denoting a descendant starting from the grandson (*pautra*) onwards, the suffix *ṇa* is applied [along with *ṭhak*] when contempt is expressed.

The suffixes *ṭhak* and *ṇa* are applied after [patronymic stems] beginning with *pautra* when denoting the contemptible offspring of a female; [the suffix *ṅīṣ* is also applied]. Examples: *gārgikaḥ* "a contemptible Gārgī" or *gārgaḥ* "a contemptible Gārgī. Why "beginning with *pautra*"? [Consider: *kārikeyaḥ* "a contemptible Kārikā. Why "of a female"? [Consider: *aupagaviḥ* "a contemptible Aupagavī. Why "contemptible"? [Consider: *gārgeyaḥ* "a descendant of Garga. Regarding the Sauvīras, it is optional (Pāṇini 2.4.80).

The suffix *ṭhak* is optionally applied to denote a despicable descendant of those who are well-known among the Sauviras as belonging to [specific] lineages (*gotra*) and so forth. For example: the despicable descendant of Bhāgavitti is *Bhāgavittikaḥ* or *Bhāgavittāyanaḥ*. The descendant of Tārṇabindava is *Tārṇabindavikaḥ* or *Tārṇabindaviḥ*. The descendant of Ākaśāyeya is *Ākaśāyeyikaḥ* or *Ākaśāyeyiḥ*. Why "among the Sauviras"? [Consider: *Aupagaviḥ* is a despicable person. Why "despicable"? [Consider: *Bhāgavittāyanaḥ* [is not despicable]. [Also: *pheś cha ca* (Pāṇini 4.1.150).

After a word ending in *phiñ* such as *pautrādi*, which is well-known among the Sauviras, the suffix *cha* is applied to denote a descendant who is contemptible, and *ṭhak* is also applied. The descendant of *Yāmundāyani* is *Yāmundāyanīyaḥ* or *Yāmundāyanikaḥ*. The descendant of *Sauyāmāyani* is *Sauyāmāyanīyaḥ* or *Sauyāmāyanikaḥ*. The descendant of *Vārṣyāyaṇi* is *Vārṣyāyaṇīyaḥ* or *Vārṣyāyaṇikaḥ*. Only when referring to the Sauviras [is this rule applied]: *Taikāyaniḥ* is a rogue. [In this case,] there is elision (*luk*) by the rule "after a word ending in *ñi* or *ārṣeya*, there is elision of *aṇ* and *iñ*" (Pāṇini 2.4.58). Only when denoting contempt [is the rule applied]: *Yāmundāyaniḥ*. [Furthermore,] after *Phāṇṭāhṛti*, the suffixes *ṇa* and *phiñ* are applied (Pāṇini 4.1.82).

The suffixes *ṇa* and *phiñ* occur after [the patronymic] *Phāṇṭāhṛti* when the descendant of a grandson or later is denoted. [Examples: *Phāṇṭāhṛtaḥ*, *Phāṇṭāhṛtāyaniḥ*. Only when referring to the Sauvīras: *Phāṇṭāhṛtāyanaḥ*. [Rule 2.4.83: *Mimātāt*.

The suffixes *ṇa* and *phiñ* occur after *Mimata* when the descendant is denoted. [Examples: *Maimataḥ*, *Maimatāyaniḥ*. Only when referring to the Sauvīras: *Maimatāyanaḥ*. [In this case,] *phak* applies because [the base] belongs to the *Naḍādi* group.

*ṇya* after *Kuru* and others (Pāṇini 4.1.172): the suffix *ṇya* occurs after words such as *Kuru* and the like to denote a descendant. Thus: *Kauravyaḥ*, *Gārgaryaḥ*. The inclusion of the word *Kuru* here is for the purpose of excluding the meaning "Kṣatriya" [which would otherwise require *yañ*]. In the plural: *Kauravyāḥ*. Due to its inclusion in the *Tika*-group, the suffix *phiñ* applies: *Kauravyāyaṇiḥ*. A *rathakāra* (chariot-maker) is a distinct caste; however, when used in the sense of a craftsman (*kāru*), the suffix *ṇya* is applied by that same rule. Because the word *Keśinī* is indicated with the feminine suffix *ṅīp*, there is no substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*). Thus: *Kaiśinyaḥ*. Since the word *takṣan* is included here, the suffix *ṇya* applies: *tākṣaṇyaḥ*. Furthermore, by virtue of its inclusion in this list, the suffix *iñ*—which is prescribed for craftsmen—is not applied.

From *tākṣṇa* [the patronymic suffix] *aṇ* is applied after the recitation beginning with *śiva*: *tākṣṇaḥ*. According to the rule "for *vāmaratha*, as in the case of *śakala* and others," there is elision (*luk*) when referring to many: *vāmarathāḥ*. From the rule "from *śakala* and others, which belong to the *gotra* group" (Pāṇini 4.1.102), the suffix *aṇ* is applied: the students (*chāttrāḥ*) of *vāmarathya* are *vāmarathāḥ*. By the rule "in the sense of a corporation (*saṃgha*), a mark (*aṅka*), a clan-name (*ghoṣa*), or a characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), [the suffixes] *añ*, *yañ*, and *iñ* are replaced by *aṇ*" (Pāṇini 4.3.127): the mark (*aṅka*) of *vāmarathya* is *vāmarathaḥ*.

The Kuru, Gārgara, Maṅguṣa, Ajamāra, Rathakāra, Caṣaṭṭaka, and Samrāj lineages among the Kṣatriyas; as well as the Kavi, Mati, Vāk, Pitṛmat, Aindrajāli, Vātaki, Dāmoṣṇīṣi, Kārṇakāri, Kaiśori, Kāpiñjala and others, the Kūṭa, Śalākā, Mura, Eḍaka, Śubhra, Darbha, Keśinī, Vena, Śūrpaṇāya, Śyāvanāya, Śyāvaputra, Vaivākavi, Nitāntavṛkṣa, Indravṛkṣa, Amravṛkṣa, and Satyaṃkāra lineages.

Vahatiṃkāra, Pathikārin, Mūḍha, Śākaṃbhū, Hanu, Śaṅku, Ina, Piṇḍī, Takṣan, and [the patronymic] of Vāmaratha, like Śakala and others; and after Senānta, Kārula, and Lakṣmaṇa, there is also the suffix iñ. (Pāṇini 4.1.152–153)

After words ending in *senā* that denote artisans, as well as after *Lakṣmaṇa*, the suffix *iñ* occurs to form patronymics, and *ṇya* also occurs. Thus: *Hāriṣeṇiḥ*, *Hāriṣeṇyaḥ*; *Tāntravāyiḥ*, *Tāntravāyyaḥ*; *Lākṣmaṇiḥ*, *Lākṣmaṇyaḥ*. These two suffixes also occur after words ending in *senā* when they denote sages (*ṛṣi*), Kurus, Vṛṣṇis, or Andhakas: *Jātaseniḥ*, *Jātasenyaḥ*; *Bhaimaseniḥ*, *Bhaimasenyaḥ*; *Vaiṣvakseniḥ*, *Vaiṣvaksenyaḥ*; *Augraseniḥ*, *Augrasenyaḥ*. [The suffix] *phiñ* occurs after [words beginning with] *tika* (Pāṇini 4.1.154).

The suffix *phiñ* occurs after [the words] *tika* and others to denote a descendant. Thus: *Taikāyaniḥ*, *Kaitavāvaniḥ*. Because of its association with the word *Aurasa*, the word *Kauravya* denotes a *kṣatriya*; however, if it were derived from the *kurv-ādi* group ending in *iñ*, it ought to be formed with that suffix.

*Tika*, *kitava*, *saṃjñā*, *bāla*, *ukhā*, *urasa*, *śāṭya*, *saindhava*, *yamunda*, *rūpya*, *taila*, *nīla*, *amitra*, *kuru*, *devaratha*, *taitila*, *aurasa*, *kauravya*, *bhauriki*, *bhauliki*, *caupayata*, *caiṭayata*, *śaikayata*, *kṣaijayata*, *candramas*, *śubha*, *gaṅgā*, *vareṇya*, *vasu*, *ārathya*, *vahyakā*, *khalyakā*, *lomakā*, *suyāman*, *udanya*, and *yajña*.
The suffix *yuṭ* is applied after the words *dagu*, *kośala*, *karmāra*, *chāga*, *vṛṣa*, and *adri*. (Pāṇini 4.1.140)

The suffix *phiñ* is applied after [words beginning with] *dagu* and others to denote a descendant (*apatya*), and the augment *yuṭ* is added. Examples: *Dāgavyāyaniḥ*, *Kauśalyāyaniḥ*, *Kārmāryāyaṇiḥ*, *Chāgyāyaniḥ*, *Vārṣyāyaṇiḥ*.

By the rule *dvyaco ’ṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.88), the suffix *phiñ* is applied after a word ending in the suffix *aṇ* that consists of two syllables (*dvyac*) to denote a descendant. Examples: *Hautrāyaṇiḥ*, *Yāskāyaniḥ*. Why is it said "consisting of two syllables" (*dvyac*)? Consider *Aupagaviḥ* (which does not take *phiñ*). Why is it said "ending in *aṇ*" (*aṇaḥ*)? Consider *Dākṣāyaṇaḥ* (which takes *phak* instead).
(2.4.89) *tyadādibhyo vā*: After words such as *tyad* and others, the suffix *phiñ* optionally occurs to denote a descendant. [Examples: *tyādāyaniḥ*, *yādāyaniḥ*; *tyādaḥ*, *yādaḥ*.
(2.4.90) *agotrād ādaijādyacaḥ*: [The suffix *phiñ* is applied] after a word that is not a *gotra* name and begins with *ā*, *ai*, or *aij*, provided it ends in a single vowel (*ac*).

The suffix *phiñ* optionally occurs after a word that begins with *ā*, *ai*, or *au*, provided that its initial vowel is not a *gotra* name, when forming a patronymic (*apatya*). Examples: *Śālaguptāyaniḥ*, *Śālaguptiḥ*. Because it is subsequent in the order of rules, *phiñ* is applied even after words denoting a profession (*kāru*): *nāpitāyaniḥ*. Why "not a *gotra* name"? Example: *Aupagaviḥ*. Why "beginning with *ā*, *ai*, or *au*"? Example: *Daivadattiḥ*. Regarding *vākinādīnāṃ kuk ca* (Pāṇini 4.1.157): the suffix *phiñ* optionally occurs after the group of words beginning with *vākina* to form a patronymic, and the augment *kuk* is added. Examples: *Vākinakāyaniḥ*, *Vākiniḥ*; *Gāreṭakāyaniḥ*, *Gāreṭiḥ*. [The members of this group are: *vākina*, *gāreṭa*, *kārkaṭya*, *kāka*, *laṅkā*, *carmin*, *varmin*.

(2.4.92) *Putrāntāt vā*: After a word ending in *putra*, provided it does not denote a *gotra*, the suffix *phiñ* optionally occurs in the sense of offspring; and when *phiñ* is applied, the augment *kuk* is optionally added. Examples: *Gārgīputrakāyaṇiḥ*, *Gārgīputrāyaṇiḥ*, *Gārgīputriḥ*. (2.4.93) *Phin bahulam*: The suffix *phin* is applied diversely.

The suffix *phin* is frequently applied after a word that is not a *gotra* [patronymic] when forming a derivative denoting offspring. Examples: *glucukāyaniḥ*, *glaucukiḥ*. Why "frequently"? [To account for exceptions: *dākṣiḥ*, *daivadattiḥ*, *rājadattiḥ*. Only after what is not a *gotra*: *aupagaviḥ*.
Regarding the rule *manor jātau yat ṣuk ca* (Pāṇini 4.1.160):

When the word *manu* denotes a genus (*jāti*), the suffix *yat* is applied to form a derivative denoting offspring, and the augment *ṣuk* is added. Example: *manuṣyaḥ*. Why "when denoting a genus"? [To exclude cases where it does not denote a genus: *mānavaḥ*.
AÑ (Pāṇini 4.1.95): The suffix AÑ is applied after the word *manu* to form a patronymic, and the augment *ṣuk* is added. [Thus: *mānuṣaḥ*. (Pāṇini 4.1.96):
[The suffix AÑ is applied] after the name of a country when it denotes a Kṣatriya, and also when denoting the king thereof.

The suffix *añ* occurs after a *kṣatriya* name that is also the name of a *janapada* (country), when forming a patronymic or denoting a king. Examples: *Pāñcālaḥ*, *Aikṣvākaḥ*. Why "of a *janapada* name"? [Consider] *Dāśarathiḥ* (the son of Daśaratha). Why "after a *kṣatriya* [name]"? [Consider] *Pāñcāliḥ*, the son of a Brāhmaṇa named Pañcāla. From *Gāndhāri* and *Śālveya* (2.4.97), the suffix *añ* occurs after these two when forming a patronymic or denoting a king. Examples: *Gāndhāraḥ*, *Śālveyaḥ*. Because the meaning is connected with each [word] individually, there is no correspondence according to the order of the items (*yāthāsaṃkhyam*).
Pāṇini 2.4.98: *ādaijādyaco ñyaṅ*.

After the name of a *janapada* (region) denoting a *kṣatriya*, the suffix *ñyaṅ* occurs to form a patronymic (*apatya*) or to denote a king (*rājan*), provided the name begins with a vowel (*ā, ai, au*) or the vowel *a*. Example: *Āmbaṣṭhyaḥ*. Pāṇini 2.4.99: *itkośalājādāt*. [The suffix *ñyaṅ* is applied] after names beginning with *i*, as well as after *Kośala* and *Ājāda*.

The suffix *ñyaṅ* occurs after the words *Kośala* and *Ājada* to denote a descendant or a king. Examples: *Āvantyaḥ*; *Kauśalyaḥ*, *Ājādyaḥ*. Why is the *t* in *taparaḥ* specified? [To exclude: There is a country named *Kumārī*; the descendant or king of a Kṣatriya belonging to that name is *Kaumāraḥ*.
The suffix *aṇ* occurs after the words *Aṅga*, *Magadha*, *Kaliṅga*, and *Sūramasa* to denote a descendant or a king. Examples: *Āṅgaḥ*, *Vāṅgaḥ*; *Māgadhaḥ*, *Kāliṅgaḥ*, *Sauramasaḥ*.
The suffix *ṇya* is applied after the word *kuru* and words beginning with *na*, in the sense of a descendant (*apatya*) or a king (*rājan*). Examples: *Kauravyaḥ*, *Naiṣadhyaḥ*.
The suffix *ḍyaṇ* is applied after the word *pāṇḍu*. (Pāṇini 2.4.102)
The suffix *ḍyaṇ* occurs after the word *pāṇḍu* when it means "offspring" or "king. Thus: *pāṇḍyaḥ*. [The suffix *aṇ* applies] only when it is the name of a country: thus, *pāṇḍavaḥ*.
[The suffix] *iñ* occurs after *śālva*, *aṃśa*, *pratyagratha*, *kalakūṭa*, and *aśmaka*:
[the examples are] *audumbaraḥ*, *tailakhalaḥ*, *madrakāraḥ*, and *yaugandharaḥ*.
The Bhuliṅgas, the Śaradaṇḍas, and those designated as parts of the Śālvas [are formed with *iñ*].

The suffix *iñ* occurs after the names of Kṣatriyas such as Śālvāvayava, Pratyagratha, and others, to denote a descendant or a king. Examples: Audumbari, Tailakhali; Prātyagrathi, Kālakūṭi, Āśmaki. [By rule 2.4.104: "There is elision (*luk*) after [the name] Kamboja and others."
The elision (*luk*) occurs of the suffix prescribed after *Kamboja* and others when denoting a descendant or a king. Examples: *Kambojaḥ*, *Colaḥ*, *Keralaḥ*, *Śakaḥ*.

(2.4.105) After *Kuru*, *Kunti*, and *Avanti*, the elision occurs of the suffix prescribed for a female descendant. Examples: *Kurūḥ*, *Kuntī*, *Avantī*. Why specify "in the feminine"? [To exclude] *Āvantyaḥ* (a male descendant). [The rule applies] only to names of countries (*janapada*): [as in] *Kauravyāḥ* (the descendants of the Kuru country).

Therefore, by the rule *ato ’prācyabhargādibhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.106), there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix *a* prescribed for a female descendant, provided it is not prescribed after [clans] from the East (*prācya*) or after the *Bharga*-group. Examples: *Śūrasenī*, *Madrī*. Why say "not after [clans] from the East or the *Bharga*-group"? [Counter-examples: *Āṅgī*, *Vāṅgī*; *Bhārgī*, *Kārūṣī*. Why say "in the feminine" (*striyām*)? [Counter-example: *Mādraḥ* (masculine). The *Bharga*-group consists of: Bharga, Karūṣa, Kekaya, Kaśmīra, Śālva, Susthāla, Urasa, and Kauravya. By the rule *yañañor bahuṣv astriyām* (Pāṇini 2.4.107): [The suffixes] *yañ* and *añ* are elided when forming a plural, provided they do not refer to a feminine.

The suffix *yañ* is elided when applied to many descendants, provided they are not feminine. Examples: *Gargāḥ*, *Bidāḥ*, *Pañcālāḥ*. Why "to many"? [Counter-examples: *Gārgyaḥ*, *Baidaḥ*. Why "not feminine"? [Counter-examples: *Gārgyaḥ* [denoting] women; *Baidyaḥ*. Only in the sense of "descendant": *bāhyāḥ*, *autsāḥ*. In the case of *priyagārgyāḥ*, this *yañ* is not applied to many [individuals]. In *priyagargaḥ*, however, *yañ* is applied to many [individuals]. The family of *Gārgya* is called either *gārgyakulam* or *gargakulam*. For the family that belongs to *Gārgya* is also the family of the *Gargas*; thus it is expressed without distinction. *Kuṇḍināḥ* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.4.108).

After the word *kuṇḍinī*, when plurality is expressed, there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix *yañ* and the feminine form ending in short *a* is substituted by irregular derivation (*nipātana*). Only when plurality is intended: *kauṇḍinyāḥ*. Only when not in the feminine: *kauṇḍinyāḥ striyaḥ* ("the women who are Kauṇḍinyas"). By the rule *ñyādīnām* (Pāṇini 2.4.109), there is elision of the suffixes beginning with *ñya* when they have been prescribed for the expression of plurality. Examples: *ambaṣṭhāḥ*, *aṅgāḥ*, *kuravaḥ*. Only when plurality is intended: *āmbaṣṭhyaḥ*. Only when not in the feminine: *āmbaṣṭhyāḥ striyaḥ*. Only when referring to offspring (*apatya*): "these belong to the Aṅgas," *āṅgāḥ*.

*yaskādibhyaḥ* (2.4.110): The elision (*luk*) occurs for the suffix prescribed after *Yaska* and others when [the descendant] is plural. *Yaskāḥ*. Only when plural: *Yāskaḥ* (singular). Only when not feminine (*astriyām*): *Yāskyaḥ striyaḥ* (feminine plural). Only when referring to a descendant (*apatye*): *Yāskāś chāttrāḥ* (the students of Yaska). [The list begins with: Yaska, Lahya, Druhya, Ayasthūṇa, Tṛṇakarṇa, Kalandana;

From these [names] listed under Śiva and others, there is elision (*luk*) of the *aṇ* suffix: Sadāmatta, Kamvalahāra, Bahiryoga, Karṇāṭaka, Piṇḍījaṅgha, Bakasaktha, Rakṣomukha, Jaṅghāratha, Utkāsa, Kaṭuka, Manthaka, Viṣapuṭa, Uparimekhala, Kroṣṭupāda, Śīrṣamāya, Padaka, Varṣaka. From these, by the rule *ata iñ*, [the patronymic suffix *iñ* is applied]: Puṣkarasad; from the class beginning with bāhu, by the rule *bāhvāditvād iñaḥ*: Viśri, Kudri, Ajabasti.

From these, by virtue of their inclusion in the *gṛṣṭyādi* group, there is the suffix *ḍhañ*: *Maitreya*. From this [the next], by virtue of the suffix *aṇ*: *Kharapa*. From this, by virtue of its inclusion in the *naḍādi* group, there is the suffix *phak*: *Bhaḍila*, *Bhaṇḍila*, *Bhaḍita*, *Bhaṇḍita*; from these, by virtue of their inclusion in the *aśvādi* group, there is the suffix *phañ*. According to Pāṇini 2.4.111, *atribhṛgukutsavasiṣṭhāṅgirogotamāt*, the elision (*luk*) occurs for the patronymic suffixes when many descendants are produced from these [lineages]: *Atrayaḥ*, *Bhṛgavaḥ*, *Kutsāḥ*, *Vasiṣṭhāḥ*, *Aṅgirasaḥ*, *Gotamāḥ*. Only when "many" is intended: *Ātreyaḥ*, *Bhārgavaḥ*. Only when "not feminine" is intended: *Ātreyyaḥ*.
*Agastayaḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.112):

When there are many descendants of Agastya, the elision (*luk*) of the suffix and the substitution of the form *Agasti-* are prescribed by irregular derivation (*nipātana*). Thus: *Agastayaḥ*. Only when "many" is intended: *Āgastyaḥ* (when there is one). Only when "not feminine" is intended: *Āgastyaḥ striyaḥ* ("the women who are descendants of Agastya"). *Bahvacaḥ prācyād iñaḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.113): [The same applies] to the patronymic suffix *iñ* after a name from the Eastern region that has more than two syllables.

The suffix *iñ* prescribed after a *prācya* (eastern) gotra-name that consists of more than two syllables undergoes elision (*luk*). Examples: *Pānnāgārāḥ*, *Manthareṣaṇāḥ*, *Yudhiṣṭhirāḥ*, *Uddālakāḥ*. Why "consisting of more than two syllables"? [Counter-example: *Caiṅkayaḥ*. Why "from a *prācya* [gotra]"? [Counter-example: *Hāstidāsayaḥ*. The rule applies only when there is a plurality [of descendants]: *Pānnāgāriḥ*. [Optionally] from *Upaka* and others: *upakādibhyo vā* (Pāṇini 2.4.114).

The elision (*luk*) optionally occurs for the patronymic suffix prescribed after many descendants, such as *Upaka* and others. For example: *Upakāḥ* or *Aupakāyanāḥ*; *Lamakāḥ* or *Lāmakāyanāḥ*. [The list includes: Upaka, Lamaka, Bhraṣṭaka, Kapiṣṭhala, Vaḍāraka, Gaḍuka, Supiṣṭa, Piṣṭa, Mayūrakarṇa, Kharījaṅgha, Śalāthala, Patañjali, Kaṭheraṇi, Kuṣītaki, Kāśakṛtsna, Kadāmatta, Kalaśīkaṇṭha, Dāmakaṇṭha, Kṛṣṇājina, Kṛṣṇasundara, and Karṇaka.

Parṇaka, Jaṭilaka, Badhiraka, Jantuka, Anuloma, Anupada, Piñjalaka, Pratiloma, Pratāna, Anabhihita. [The suffix *cha* is applied after these and after *tikakitava* etc., when there is identity of meaning. (Pāṇini 2.4.115)

When there is a unity of meaning (*aikārthya*) regarding the sense [of the suffix], there is elision (*luk*) of the plural marker for those suffixes prescribed after the groups beginning with *Tika* and *Kitava*. Examples: *Taikāyanas* and *Kaitavāyanas* become *Tikakitavāḥ*; here there is elision of the *phiñ* suffix prescribed after the group beginning with *Tika*. *Vāṅkharayas* and *Bhāṇḍīrathayas* become *Vaṅkharabhaṇḍīrathāḥ*; here there is elision of the *iñ* suffix prescribed after the word ending in *at*. In the same way: *Prahṛtakanarakāḥ*, *Bakanakhaguḍapariṇaddhāḥ*, *Laṅkaṭaśāntamukhāḥ*, *Ubjakakubhāḥ*.

*Ubja* [is derived] from *ata-ijaḥ* (the suffix *iñ* after a base ending in *at*); *kakubha* [is derived] from *śivādyaṇaḥ* (the suffix *aṇ* after bases beginning with *śiva*); *urasa-laṅkaṭāḥ*. From *urasa-* and *tikā*-type bases, [the suffix] *phiñ* [is applied]: *agniveśa-duśerakāḥ*. From *agniveśa*, [the suffix] *yañ* [is applied] according to the *gargādi* group; from *daśeraka*, [the suffix] *ata-ijaḥ* (the suffix *iñ* after a base ending in *at*): *upaka-lamakāḥ*. From *naḍādi* bases, [the suffix] *phak*: *bhraṣṭaka-kapiṣṭhalāḥ*; *kṛṣṇājina-kṛṣṇasundarāḥ*, [from which] *ata-ijaḥ* (the suffix *iñ* after a base ending in *at*). Since the three starting with *upaka-lamaka* are already established by the preceding rule, their recitation here is for the purpose of making them obligatory (*nitya*). [The exception applies: "Not [after] the eight [bases] beginning with *gopavana*" (Pāṇini 2.4.116).

The elision (*luk*) does not occur for the suffix *añ* prescribed after the eight [gotra-names] beginning with Gopavana, because they are listed in the *Bidādi* group. Examples: *Gaupavanāḥ*, *Śaiṅgravāḥ*, *Baindavāḥ*. Why "after the eight"? Consider: *Haritāḥ*. [This is governed by] Pāṇini 2.4.117: *prāgjitīye 'ci*.

When elision (*luk*) has been prescribed for a suffix in the sense of "many," that elision does not take place when a suffix beginning with a vowel (*aj-ādi*) belonging to the *prāgjītīya* group is to be applied. Examples: *atrīṇāṃ chāttrāḥ* ("the pupils of the Atris") becomes *Ātreyīyāḥ*; *Āgastyīyāḥ*. Why "belonging to the *prāgjītīya* group"? Consider: *Gargebhyo hitaḥ* ("beneficial for the Gargas") becomes *Gargīyaḥ*. Why "beginning with a vowel"? Consider: *Gargebhya āgataḥ* ("come from the Gargas") becomes *Gargarūpyaḥ*. The rule applies only when the sense is "many": *Kambojasyāpatyam* ("the descendant of Kamboja") is *Kambojaḥ*; his pupils are *Kāmbojāḥ*. [This is because of the rule: *gotrāl luk* (Pāṇini 2.4.64).

When a suffix prescribed after a *gotra* [patronymic] stem is to be elided (*luk*) before a *prāgjitiya* [eastern] suffix beginning with a vowel, its elision occurs. For example: the descendant of Phāṇṭāhṛti is Phāṇṭāhṛta; his pupils are Phāṇṭāhṛtāḥ. When the *ṇa* is elided, the suffix *aṇ* is applied by rule 4.2.80 (*iñaḥ*). Only when it is a *prāgjitiya* suffix does this apply: that which is beneficial for Bhāgavittika is Bhāgavittikīyaḥ. Only when the suffix begins with a vowel does this apply: Phāṇṭāhṛtarūpyaḥ. [The elision of] *phak* and *phiñ* is optional by rule 2.4.119.

When a suffix beginning with a vowel (*aj-ādi*) that falls under *prāgjiti* (Pāṇini 4.1.93–167) is to be applied, there is optionally elision (*luk*) of the suffixes *phañ* and *phiñ* when they have been prescribed after a *gotra* [patronymic] stem.
