Examples: *Gārgīyaḥ* / *Gārgyāyaṇīyaḥ* (student of Gārgyāyaṇa). *Hautrīyaḥ* / *Hautrāyaṇīyaḥ* (student of Hautrāyaṇa). The suffix *phiñ* is applied here by rule 4.1.150 (*dvyaco ’ṇaḥ*). Why is the letter *k* [in *phiñ*] mentioned? So that it does not apply to *phañ*. Example: *Ātreyīyāḥ* (students of Ātreyāyaṇa). Here, because *Aśva* and others are listed [in the *aśvādigaṇa*], the suffix *phañ* is applied; its elision is obligatory by rule 2.4.64 (*abrāhmaṇāt*).

The elision (*luk*) occurs of the suffix prescribed after a patronymic that does not belong to the *brāhmaṇa* lineage. For example: *Audumbariḥ* is the father, *Audumbariḥ* is the son. Here, the suffix *iñ* is applied after a descendant of the *Śālva* clan, and then there is the elision of the suffix *phaṅ*. Thus: *Kārṇakhariḥ* is the father, *Kārṇakhariḥ* is the son; *Bhāṇḍījaṅghiḥ* is the father, *Bhāṇḍījaṅghiḥ* is the son. In these cases, *iñ* is applied after a vowel, and then there is the elision of *phaṅ*. Since this result was already established by the preceding rule, the repetition indicates that the restriction "before a non-*prāgjyotiṣa* vowel" (*aci*, Pāṇini 2.4.117) is no longer operative. This applies to the list beginning with *Paila* (Pāṇini 2.4.59).

There is elision (*luk*) of the patronymic suffix prescribed after the lineages beginning with Paila. Thus: *Pailaḥ* is the father, *Pailaḥ* is the son; *Śālaṅkiḥ* is the father, *Śālaṅkiḥ* is the son. This list of those ending in *iñ* is for the purpose of excluding the Easterners (*aprācya*). [The names are: Paila, Śālaṅki, Sātyaki, Sātyaṃkāmi, Audañci, Audamajji, Audavraji, Audameghi, Audaśuddhi, Daivasthāni, Paiṅgalodāyani, Rāṇi, Rāhakṣiti, Bhauliṅgi, Audgāhamāni, Aubjihāyani. [Furthermore, there is elision] of the *aṇ* suffix derived from a Kṣatriya name that is the name of a country (*janapada*): *Āṅgaḥ* is the son.
*Prācyād iño ’taulvalibhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.122):

The elision (*luk*) occurs of the patronymic suffix *iñ* prescribed after a Patronymic (*apatya*) belonging to the Easterners (*prācya*), provided it is not from the *Taulvali* group. Example: Pānnāgāriḥ is the father; Pānnāgāriḥ is the son. Mānthareṣaṇiḥ is the father; Mānthareṣaṇiḥ is the son. Why "from the Easterners"? [Counter-example: Dākṣiḥ is the father; Dākṣāyaṇaḥ is the son. Why "of *iñ*"? [Counter-example: Rāghavaḥ is the father; Rāghaviḥ is the son. Why "not from the *Taulvali* group"? [Counter-example: Taulvaliḥ is the father; Taulvalāyanaḥ is the son.

Taulvali, Dhāraṇi, Rāvaṇi, Rātakṣatri, Daivadatti, Daivati, Daivamati, Daivayajñi, Prādohani, Ānurāhati, Āsuri, Āhiṃsi, Āsibandhaki, Caiṅki, Pauṣpi, Pauṣkarasādi, Vairaki, Vaihari, Vailaki, Kāreṇupāli, and from the Bharata lineage: Ārjuni is the father, Ārjunāyana is the son. Some say that the Bharata lineage is a Vaiśya lineage;
for them, Auddālaki is the father, Auddālakāyana is the son.
[This applies] by virtue of the rule *ñidārṣaṇyād aṇiñoḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.123).

The suffixes *aṇ* and *iñ*, prescribed for the sense of "offspring" (*apatya*) after [patronymic stems] ending in *ārṣa* (the name of a ṛṣi) and those ending in *ṇya* (denoting a lineage), undergo elision (*luk*). *Taikāyaniḥ* is the father; *Taikāyaniḥ* is the son. Here, there is elision of *aṇ*. *Baidaḥ* is the father; *Baidaḥ* is the son. Here, there is elision of *iñ*. After an *ārṣa* [name]: *Vaiśvāmitraḥ* is the father; *Vaiśvāmitraḥ* is the son. After one ending in *ṇya*: *Kauravyaḥ* is the father; *Kauravyaḥ* is the son. This mention refers specifically to a Brāhmaṇa. However, because *Kauravya* as a Kṣatriya is listed among the *Tika*-group [of *ṇya*-derived names], it takes the form *Kauravyāyaṇiḥ* [when denoting offspring].

What is the purpose of the phrase "from these" (*etebhyaḥ*)? [Consider: *aupagavaḥ pitā* (the father is Aupagava), *aupagaviḥ putraḥ* (the son is Aupagavi). What is the purpose of the phrase "of the suffixes *aṇ* and *iñ*" (*aṇ-iñoḥ*)? [Consider: *dākṣer apatyam dākṣāyaṇaḥ* (the descendant of Dakṣa is Dākṣāyaṇa). Why does it say "from a *gotra* [name]" (*gotrāt*)? [Consider: the descendant of *Dvaipya* is *Dvaipyiḥ*. Why does it say "a descendant" (*apatyam*)? [Consider: a student of Vāmarathya is *Vāmarathaḥ*; here the suffix *aṇ* is applied because [Vāmarathya] belongs to the *śakala-* group. The second chapter in the Cāndra Grammar is completed. [Now follows: *tena raktaṃ rāgāt* (3.1.1).

The suffix *aṇ* occurs after a word ending in the third case in the sense of "colored by that," provided that the word ending in the third case denotes a dye (*rāga*). For example: *kaṣāyeṇa raktaṃ vastraṃ* ("a cloth colored by a decoction") becomes *kāṣāyam*; likewise, *kauṅkumam* ("saffron-colored"). Why is it specified "from a dye" (*rāgāt*)? [Consider: *Devadattena raktaṃ vastram* ("a cloth colored by Devadatta"). How then are the donkey's ears called *kāṣāyau* ("reddish-brown") or the cock's feet *hāridrau* ("yellow")? This is due to the superimposition (*adhyāropa*) of those qualities onto them. By the rule *lākṣārocanāṭ ṭhak* (Pāṇini 4.2.2), the suffix *ṭhak* occurs after the words *lākṣā* and *rocanā* in the sense of "colored by that. Thus: *lākṣikam* ("dyed with lac") and *raucanikam* ("dyed with yellow pigment").

From *śakala* and *kardama* (3.1.3): after the words *śakala* and *kardama*, the suffix *ṭhak* optionally occurs in the sense of "colored by that. Thus: *śākalikaṃ* or *śākalam*; *kārdamikaṃ* or *kārdamam*. After *nīla* and *pīta*, the suffixes *anka* and *na* [occur] (3.1.4).

The suffixes *añ* and *nañ* occur in this sense [of "colored by"] after the words *nīla* and *pīta*, as in the examples *nīlam* and *pītakam*. Although this is established by the rule for words expressing qualities (*guṇavacana*), this specific statement is made to set aside the suffix *aṇ*.
[Next: "Time [is expressed] by means of constellations joined with the moon" (Pāṇini 4.2.3).

The suffix *aṇ* occurs after words denoting lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) ending in the third case, provided they denote the time characterized by those mansions when those mansions are conjoined with the moon (*indu*). Examples: *pauṣī rātriḥ* (the night of Puṣya); *pauṣam ahaḥ* (the day of Puṣya). Why [is it said] "by the lunar mansions" (*nakṣatraiḥ*)? [Consider: a night characterized by the planet Venus (*śukra*). Why [is it said] "conjoined with the moon" (*induyuktaiḥ*)? A moment (*muhūrta*) characterized by the Kṛttikās [when they are not conjoined with the moon]. Why [is it said] "time" (*kāle*)? Success in one's purpose (*arthasiddhi*) characterized by the Puṣya [asterism]. In the expression *adya kṛttikāḥ* ("today is Kṛttikā"), the word *kṛttikā* refers to the moon being conjoined with the Kṛttikās.

In the case of *kṛttikāsu*, *viśākhāsu*, *maghāsu*, and *bharaṇīṣu*, the designation of that time is made by means of the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) themselves through the metaphorical treatment of non-difference (*abhedopacāra*). In the expression “*śravaṇā rātriḥ*” (the night of Śravaṇā), the word *śravaṇa* refers to the moon when it is conjoined with [the asterism] Śravaṇā. The suffix *ac* is applied here according to the rule for the *arśa-ādi* group, meaning “that which has Śravaṇā [conjoined with it]” is the night of Śravaṇā (*śravaṇā rātriḥ*). However, when the intention is to indicate [the night] as characterized by the moon being conjoined with Śravaṇā, then it is “the night of Śrāvaṇa” (*śrāvaṇī rātriḥ*). *Aśvattha* is the name of a specific muhūrta; but when referring to a specific lunar mansion, the night characterized by the [asterism] Aśvattha is called *āśvatthī*.
[The suffix *cha* is used] in the sense of “moving” [according to Pāṇini 4.2.80].

The suffix *cha* occurs after a word denoting a lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*) ending in the third case, when the time indicated by that mansion is intended. For example: *rādhānurādhīyā rātriḥ* (the night marked by the asterisms Rādhā and Anurādhā); *rādhānurādhīyam ahaḥ* (the day marked by the asterisms Rādhā and Anurādhā).
Regarding the rule *dṛṣṭaṃ sāma ḍid vā* (Pāṇini 4.2.7):

when the sense is "a Sāman seen [by someone]," the suffixes *aṇ* and others apply according to the respective rules, or they may optionally take the marker *ḍ*. For example: a Sāman seen by Vasiṣṭha is *vāsiṣṭham*; *bārhaspatyam*, *āgneyam*, *kāleyam*; *auśanam*, *auśanasam*.

(3.1.8) *gotrād aṅkavat*: after a word ending in the third case that denotes a *gotra*, when a *sāman* is seen [as its name], the rule is applied as if it were a mark (*aṅka*). A *sāman* seen by Gārgya is *Gārgaka*. The suffix *vuñ* occurs.
(3.1.9) *vāmadevyam*.
In the sense of "the Sāman seen by Vāmadeva," the form *vāmadevyam* is established by nipātana (irregular derivation).
[The rule] *parivṛto rathaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.2.10) [is cited].

The suffix *aṇ* occurs after a word ending in the third case when the meaning is "surrounded by" (*parivṛta*) in relation to a chariot (*ratha*). For example: a chariot surrounded by cloths is *vāstra*; [a chariot surrounded by skins is] *cārmaṇaḥ*. [A chariot] surrounded by sons is not so called, because the chariot lacks that [quality of being surrounded], and because when there is dependence on something else, the meanings are distinct. Why specify "chariot"? [To exclude cases like: a body surrounded by a cloth. As for *pāṇḍukambalī*, this is established by means of a possessive suffix (*matvarthīya*). But would it not then follow that a white woolen blanket (*pāṇḍukambala*) [itself] would also [be called *pāṇḍukambalī*]? Indeed, this is intended when it refers to another object [in which the blanket is contained].
*Dvaipa* is the skin of a leopard (*dvīpin*), and *vaiyāghra* is that of a tiger (*vyāghra*). A chariot covered by these two is called *dvaipa* or *vaiyāghra*; this is established by the suffix *aṇ*.

Regarding *kaumārī* in the sense of "being first" (Pāṇini 4.1.11), the form *kaumārī* is an irregular derivation (*nipātana*) when the connection with a male is primary. Thus, *kaumārī bhāryā* means "a wife who was [first] a maiden. How is it that *kaumāro bhartā* ("a husband who was a maiden")? It is either "one who exists in a maiden" or "the husband of a maiden."

*tatroddhṛtaṃ pātrebhyaḥ* (3.1.12): The suffix *aṇ* occurs after a word denoting a vessel (*pātra*) ending in the locative case, in the sense of "taken out from" (*uddhṛta*). For example, rice taken out from bowls is *śārāvaḥ*. Why [is it said] "from vessels" (*pātrebhyaḥ*)? [Consider: rice taken out into the hand (*pāṇau*). *sthaṇḍile śete vratī* (3.1.13).

The suffix *aṇ* occurs after a word ending in the locative case (*saptamī*) in the sense of "he sleeps there," provided that the person sleeping is a mendicant observing a vow (*vratī*). Why say "observing a vow"? [Because] a Śūdra sleeps on the bare ground (*sthaṇḍile śete*).

[The suffix *aṇ* occurs] after a word ending in the locative case in the sense of "prepared therein," provided that the object is edible (*bhakṣya*). [Example: *bhrāṣtrā modakāḥ* ("sweetmeats prepared in a frying pan"). Why say "edible"? [Because] garlands prepared on a board (*phalake saṃskṛtā mālāḥ*) are not edible.

*Śūlokhād yat* (3.1.15): After the words *śūla* and *ukhā*, when they end in the locative case, the suffix *yat* occurs in the sense of "prepared as food. Examples: *śūlyaṃ* (food prepared on a spit), *ukhyaṃ* (food prepared in a pot).
*Dadhnaṣ ṭhak* (3.1.16): [The suffix] *ṭhak* occurs after the word *dadhi*.

The suffix *ṭhak* occurs after the word *dadhi* ending in the seventh case in the sense of "prepared from. Examples: *dādhikam*, *dādhikī*. The form *audaśvitam* is established by the preceding rule [Pāṇini 4.2.16], while *audaśvitkam* is established by the following rule [Pāṇini 4.2.18]. Regarding *kṣīrāḍ ḍhañ* (3.1.17):
the suffix *ḍhañ* occurs after the word *kṣīra* ending in the seventh case in the sense of "prepared from," provided that the result is an edible food (*bhakṣya*). Examples: *kṣaireyam*, *kṣaireyī*.

*sāsya paurṇamāsī* (Pāṇini 4.2.21). The suffix *aṇ* occurs after a word ending in the first case, in the sense of the genitive (*asya*), provided that the word ending in the first case is the name of a full moon day (*paurṇamāsī*). For example: "The full moon day of Pauṣa belongs to this [month]," hence *pauṣo māsaḥ* ("the month of Pauṣa"). *Māghaḥ* ("the month of Māgha"). Why say "full moon day"? [Consider: *pauṣī pañcamy asya māsasya* ("the fifth day of Pauṣa belongs to this month"). The full moon day does not belong to a hired month. Because of the etymology "that in which the moon is full" (*pūrṇo mā asyām*), and precisely because of this irregular derivation (*nipātana*), the suffix *aṇ* is applied. Furthermore, because of the explicit mention of "month" (*māsa*), the rule does not apply to a period of five nights and so forth. *Āgrahāyaṇyaśvatthāṭ ṭhak* (Pāṇini 4.2.22).

The suffix *ṭhak* occurs after the words *āgrahāyaṇī* and *aśvatthā*, which stand in the nominative case, in the sense of the genitive (*asya*), provided that the nominative word refers to a full-moon day (*paurṇamāsī*). [Examples: *āgrahāyaṇiko māsaḥ* ("the month of Āgrahāyaṇī"); *āśvatthikaḥ*. [The form] *āśvatthikaḥ* arises through metaphorical identification (*abhedopacāra*) because the full moon is [associated with] the *aśvattha* constellation.
[Furthermore, the suffix *ṭhak* occurs] optionally after *phālgunī*, *śravaṇā*, *kārttikī*, and *caitrī*: (Pāṇini 4.2.23).

The suffix *ṭhak* optionally occurs after words such as *phālgunī*, ending in the nominative case, in the sense of the genitive (*asya*), provided that the word ending in the nominative is the name of a full moon day (*paurṇamāsī*). Examples: *phālgunikaḥ*, *phālgunaḥ*. Because the full moon day is *śravaṇā*, [the forms] are *śrāvaṇikaḥ*, *śrāvaṇaḥ*; here, by virtue of the irregular derivation (*nipātana*), there is elision (*luk*) of the *aṇ* suffix. Examples: *kārttikikaḥ*, *kārttikaḥ*; *caitrikaḥ*, *caitraḥ*. [This concludes the section on] the deity (*devatā*, Pāṇini 4.2.24).

From a word denoting a deity ending in the nominative case, the suffixes *aṇ* and others occur according to the prescribed rules in the sense of the genitive (*asya*). Examples: *aindraṃ haviḥ* (an oblation for Indra), *ādityam*, *bārhaspatyam*, *kāleyam*, *āgneyam*. *Aindro mantraḥ* (a mantra for Indra). Regarding the rule *kasyet* (Pāṇini 4.2.25):

when the word *ka-* denoting a deity occurs in the sense of the genitive (*asya*), the suffix *aṇ* is applied and the vowel *i* is substituted [for the final *a*]. Example: *ko devatāsya* (who is its deity?), *kāyaṃ haviḥ* (an oblation for Ka); that is to say, an oblation for Prajāpati.

*Śukrād ghan* (3.1.23): After the word *śukra*, the suffix *ghan* occurs in the sense of "this has that as its deity. Examples: *śukriyaṃ haviḥ* ("an oblation having Śukra as its deity"); *śukriyo 'dhyāyaḥ* ("a chapter having Śukra as its deity"). *paiṅgākṣīputrādibhyaś chaḥ* (3.1.24): After the group of words beginning with *paiṅgākṣīputra*, the suffix *cha* occurs [in the same sense].
After *paiṅgākṣīputra* and others, the suffix *cha* occurs in the sense of "this has that as its deity. For example: *paiṅgākṣīputrīyam*, *tārṇabindavīyam*.
(3.1.25) After *śatarudra*, the suffix *gha* occurs, and also *cha*, in the sense of "this has that as its deity. For example: *śatarudriyam*, *śatarudrīyam*.

(3.1.26) *aponapāt* and *apāṃnapāt*: In the sense of "this is its deity," the suffix *gha* and also *cha* are applied to these two words; furthermore, for the word *ā*, the substitute *tṛ* occurs. [Examples: *āponaptriyam*, *āponaptrīyam*; *apāṃnaptriyam*, *apāṃnaptrīyam*. (3.1.27) *mahendra* optionally: [The suffixes *gha* and *cha* are applied to the word *mahendra* in the same sense.]
In the sense of "this is its deity," the suffix *gha* occurs after the word *mahendra*, and optionally *cha*. [The forms are] *māhendriyam*, *mahendrīyam*, and *māhendraṃ*.

(3.1.28) After *soma*, the suffix *ṭyaṇ* occurs in the sense of "this is its deity. [The forms are] *saumyaṃ haviḥ* (an oblation belonging to Soma), *saumyaṃ sūktam* (a hymn belonging to Soma), and *saumī ṛk* (a verse belonging to Soma).

*vāyvṛtupitruṣaso yat* (Pāṇini 4.2.31): After *vāyu*, *ṛtu*, *pitṛ*, and *uṣas*, the suffix *yat* occurs in the sense of "this has that as its deity. Thus: *vāyavyam*, *ṛtavyam*, *pitryam*, *uṣasyam*.

*dyāvāpṛthivīśunāsīramarutvadagnīṣomavāstoṣpatigṛhamedhāc chaś ca* (Pāṇini 4.2.32): After *dyāvāpṛthivī*, *śunāsīra*, *marutvat*, *agnīṣoma*, *vāstoṣpati*, and *gṛhamedha*, the suffix *cha* also occurs [in the sense of "this has that as its deity"].

In the domain of the rule "sāsya devatā" (that which has this as its deity), the suffix *cha* occurs after [the compounds] beginning with *dyāvāpṛthivī*, as well as [the suffix *yañ*]. Thus: *dyāvapṛthivīyam* and *dyāvāpṛthivyam*; *śunāsīrīyam* and *śunāsīryam*; *marutvatīyam* and *marutvatyam*; *agnīṣomīyam* and *agnīṣomyam*; *vāstoṣpatīyam* and *vāstoṣpatyam*; *gṛhamedhīyam* and *gṛhamedhyam*. [Furthermore, the suffix *cha* is applied] after words denoting time, according to the rule *kālebhyo bhavavat* (Pāṇini 4.3.11).

Just as suffixes such as *aṇ* and others occur after words denoting time to express "that which occurs therein" (*bhava*), so too do they occur in the sense of "this has that as its deity" (*sāsya devatā*). That which occurs in a month (*māse bhavam*) is *māsikam*. That which occurs in a year is *sāṃvatsarikam*. That which occurs in winter is *haimantikam* or *haimanam*. That which occurs in the rainy season is *prāvṛṣeṇyam*. [When the sense is] "this has the month as its deity," it is *māsikam*, *sāṃvatsarikam*, *haimanam*, *haimantikam*, or *prāvṛṣeṇyam*. **Pāṇini 4.2.32:** *mahārājaproṣṭhapadāṭ ṭhañ* (The suffix *ṭhañ* is applied after *mahārāja* and *proṣṭhapada* in the sense of "this has that as its deity"). In this sense, *ṭhañ* occurs after *mahārāja* and *proṣṭhapada*: *māhārājikam* (masculine/neuter), *māhārājikī* (feminine); *prauṣṭhapadikam* (masculine/neuter), *prauṣṭhapadikī* (feminine).

(3.1.33) *ādeś chandasaḥ pragāthe*: After a word denoting a *chandas* (Vedic meter) ending in the nominative case, the suffix *aṇ* occurs in the sense of the genitive (*asya*) when a *pragātha* is to be expressed. For example: "The *anuṣṭubh* is the beginning of this *pragātha*" → *ānuṣṭubhaḥ*; *pāṅktaḥ*; *jāgataḥ*. Why is it said "of the beginning" (*ādeḥ*)? So that [the suffix] does not apply to the middle. Why is it said "*pragāthe*"? So that it does not apply to an *anuvāka* (section). Why is it said "*chandasaḥ*"? So that it does not apply to words (*pada*). (3.1.34) *yoddhṛprayojanāt saṃgrāme*: [The suffix *aṇ* occurs after a word denoting a warrior or a purpose in the sense of a battle.]

After words ending in the nominative case signifying warriors (*yoddhṛ*) or purposes (*prayojana*), the suffixes *aṇ* and others, as prescribed, occur in the sense of the genitive when a battle (*saṃgrāma*) is to be expressed. For example: "The *saṃśaptakas* are the warriors in this battle" → *sāṃśaptakaḥ* (the battle of the *saṃśaptakas*). *daivāsuraḥ* (the battle of the gods and demons). "Subhadrā is the purpose of this battle" → *saubhadraḥ*. Why say "after [words denoting] warriors or purposes"? [Consider: "A month is the duration of this battle. Why say "battle"? [Consider: "Subhadrā is the purpose of this enmity (*vaira*). [Furthermore,] the suffix *ṇa* occurs after a word denoting a weapon (*praharaṇa*) in the sense of "in this game" (*krīḍā*) (Pāṇini 4.2.57).

The suffix *ṇa* occurs after a word ending in the nominative case denoting a weapon (*praharaṇa*), in the sense of "in this game. For example: "In this game, the staff is the weapon" → *dāṇḍā*; "In this game, the fist is the weapon" → *mauṣṭā*. Why "after a weapon"? [Consider: "In this game, a garland is the ornament. Why "in a game"? [Consider: "In this army, a sword is the weapon.
[This applies] to the *ñ* of the abstract noun suffix *ghañ* (Pāṇini 3.1.36).

The suffix *ñ* occurs in the sense of the locative case (*asyām*) after a word ending in the primary derivative suffix *ghañ* which denotes an action (*bhāve*), provided that the word ends in the nominative case. For example: "The swoop of a hawk (*śyenapātaḥ*) occurs in this [place]" becomes *śyainaṃpātā*; likewise, *tailaṃpātā*. Why "denotes an action" (*bhāve*)? [Consider: "A palace (*prāsādaḥ*) is in this city. Why "ending in *ghañ*" (*ghañi*)? [Consider: "The falling of a hawk (*śyenapatanam*) occurs in this [place]. [Also: "He studies that" or "He knows that" (Pāṇini 4.2.59).

After a word ending in the second case, the suffixes *aṇ* and others, as prescribed, occur in the two senses of "he studies that" and "he knows that. For example: one who studies or knows the *Chandas* is a *chāndasa*; one who studies or knows grammar is a *vaiyākaraṇa*. The repetition of the term "that" (*tat*) is for the purpose of separate prescription, to show that the sense of "knowing" applies within the scope of "studying," and to include well-known usages.
[Pāṇini 4.2.60] states: *kratūkthādibhyaṣ ṭhak* ("the suffix *ṭhak* occurs after words denoting sacrifices and after *uktha*, etc.").

The suffix *ṭhak* is applied after words denoting sacrifices (*kratu*) and hymns (*uktha*), etc., when they appear in the accusative case, in the two senses of "one who studies" or "one who knows. For example: one who studies or knows the *agniṣṭoma* is called *āgniṣṭomikaḥ*; one who studies or knows the *vājapeya* is called *vājapeyikaḥ*. The term *ukthāni* refers to the Sāman chants which are sung subsequent to the *yajñāyajñīya* hymn. By virtue of being characterized by that [sacrifice], it is also called *uktha* because it serves that purpose; thus there is a conventional usage for the form *aukthikya*. One who studies or knows the *ukthas* is called *aukthikaḥ*.

One does not say "he has studied the *aukthikya*" or "he has studied the *ukthas*, which are the *sāmans*," because the double mention of that [term] is intended to include what is well-known. The same applies to the expression "he has studied the *yājñikya*."

[The suffix *ṭhak* is applied after the following: *uktha*, *lokāyata*, *nyāya*, *nyāsa*, *punarukta*, *yajña*, *carcā*, *krametara*, *ślakṣṇa*, *saṃhitā*, *padakrama*, *saṃghāṭa*, *vṛtti*, *saṃgraha*, *gaha*, *āyurveda*, *dvipadā*, *jyotiṣa*, *anupada*, *anukalpa*, and [compounds ending in] *lakṣaṇa-kalpasūtra-anta*. [Examples: *āśvalakṣaṇikaḥ*, *mātṛkalpikaḥ*, *vārttikasūtrikaḥ*. Why does it say "after *akalpa* etc."? [To exclude: *kālpasūtraḥ*. [The suffix *ṭhak* is also applied after] *vidyā*, provided that *anaṅga*, *kṣatra*, *dharma*, and *tri* do not precede it.

*vāyasavidyikaḥ*; [the rule] *anaṅgakṣatradharmatripūrva*—what is the purpose? *āṅgavidyaḥ*, *kṣātravidyaḥ*, *dhārmavidyaḥ*, *traividyaḥ*. Also from *ākhyāna*, *ākhyāyikā*, *itihāsa*, and *purāṇa*: *yāvakrītikaḥ*, *vāsavadattikaḥ*, *aitihāsikaḥ*, *paurāṇikaḥ*. Elision (*luk*) occurs after *sarva-sādi*: *sarvavedaḥ*, *sarvatantraḥ*, *savārttikaḥ*, *sasaṃgrahaḥ*. From *anusū*: *ānusukaḥ*. From *lakṣya*: *lākṣyikaḥ*. From *lakṣaṇa*...

*Lākṣaṇikaḥ*—one who follows the characteristics [of the seasons]. *Ātharvaṇaḥ* and *ātharvaṇikaḥ* refer to one who is in accordance with the qualities of spring, the rainy season, autumn, winter, and the dewy season, both at their beginning and end. Due to the force of the recitation (*pāṭha*), there is no elision (*luk*) even after the word *prokta*. The words "spring" (*vasanta*) and so forth are used here for the texts associated with those seasons; they should be understood through their connection to the study [of those texts]. The form *padottarapadikaḥ* is established by the suffix *ṭhan*. [The rule] *śata-ṣaṣṭeḥ pathaḥ ṣṭhan* (Pāṇini 5.1.27) applies.

The suffix *ṣṭhan* occurs after the words *śatapathe* and *ṣaṣṭipathe* in the two senses of "one who studies that" and "one who knows that. Thus: *śatapathikaḥ*, *śatapathikī*; *ṣaṣṭhipathikaḥ*, *ṣaṣṭhipathikī*.

By the rule *kramādibhyo vun* (Pāṇini 4.2.61), the suffix *vun* occurs after the group beginning with *krama* in those same two senses. Thus: *kramakaḥ*, *padakaḥ*. The list begins: *krama*, *pada*, *śikṣā*, *mīmāṃsā*, *sāman*. How is the form *anubrāhmaṇī* derived? It is established by the suffix *ini*.

*proktāl luk* (3.1.40): The suffix *luk* occurs after a word ending in a suffix such as *aṇ* and others that have been applied in the sense of "proclaimed by" (*prokta*). For example, that which was proclaimed by Pāṇini is *Pāṇinīyam*; one who studies or knows that is *Pāṇinīyaḥ*. A female [student] is *Pāṇinīyā*.
*sūtrāt saṃkhyākāt* (3.1.42).

The suffix *ya*, which is prescribed after a numeral, undergoes elision (*luk*) when it occurs at the end of a word denoting a collection of sūtras. For example: the sūtra-work of Pāṇini consists of eight [chapters] (*aṣṭaka*); those who study or know it are called *aṣṭakāḥ* or *pāṇinīyāḥ*. Similarly, *trikāḥ* and *kāśakṛtsnāḥ*. Why "after a numeral" (*saṃkhyā*)? Consider *mādhyamakāḥ* and *kālāpakāḥ*. Why "after *ka*" (*kāt*)? Consider *catuṣṭayam*; one who studies or knows that is called *cātuṣṭayaḥ*. Regarding the rule *tasya samūhaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.2.37):

after a word ending in the genitive case, suffixes such as *aṇ* and others apply as prescribed to denote a collection (*samūha*). Examples: a collection of *cāṣas* is *cāṣam*; a collection of crows is *kākam*; a collection of trees is *vānaspatyam*; a collection of women is *straiṇam*; a collection of men is *pauṃsnam*.

*bhikṣādibhyo ’ṇ* (Pāṇini 4.2.38): the suffix *aṇ* occurs after words beginning with *bhikṣā*, when they are in the genitive case, in the sense of a collection (*samūha*). Examples: *bhaikṣam* (a collection of alms), *kṣaitram* (a collection of fields). The list begins: *bhikṣā*, *kṣetra*, *karīṣa*, *aṅgāra*, *sahasra*, *yuvati*. Due to the force of the recitation [of the word *yuvati*], there is no substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*); hence *yauvatam* (a collection of young women). The list continues: *paddhati*, *dakṣiṇā*, *khaṇḍika*, *halabandha*, *yugavaratrā*, *vaḍavā*, *bhikṣuka*, *śuka*, *ulūka*, *śvan*, *ahan*. After *Kṣudrakamālava*, the suffix applies in the sense of an army (*senā*) provided it is not a proper name (*saṃjñā*); e.g., *Kṣaudrakamālavī senā* (the army of the Kṣudrakas and Mālavas).

The suffix *vuñ* occurs in other instances [than those previously mentioned], because there is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the application of the rule regarding the inclusion of what ends with that (*tadantavidhi*).

According to Pāṇini 4.2.39 (*gotrokṣoṣṭrorabhrarājarājaputravatsājavṛddhād vuñ*), the suffix *vuñ* is applied after words ending in patronymics (*apatya*)—specifically those formed by suffixes prescribed in the section on descendants—as well as after the group beginning with *ukṣan*. Examples include: *aupagavakam*, *gārgyāyaṇakam*, *rājanyakam*, and *mānuṣyakam*; and *aukṣakam*, *auṣṭrakam*, *aurabhrakam*, *rājakam*, *rājaputrakam*, *vātsakam*, *ājakam*, and *vārddhakam*.

(3.1.46) *kedārād yañ ca*: after the word *kedāra*, the suffix *yañ* occurs when denoting a collection, and *vuñ* also [occurs]. [The forms are] *kaidāryam* and *kaidārakam*. (3.1.47) *kavacinaś ca ṭhak*: [the suffix] *ṭhak* also [occurs] after the word *kavacin*.
The suffix *ṭhak* occurs after *kavacin* and *kedāra* to form a collective sense: *kāvacikam*, *kaidārikam*.
[By rule 3.1.48] *ṭhak* occurs after *hastin* and words denoting non-sentient beings (*acitta*) to form a collective sense: *hāstikam*; likewise, *āpūpikam*, *śāṣkulikam*.

*dhenor anañaḥ* (3.1.49): The suffix *ṭhak* occurs after the word *dhenu* when it does not have *an* as a prior member, in the sense of a collection (*samūha*). Example: *dhainukam*. Why "not having *an* as a prior member"? Consider: *ādhenavam*. And because of this prohibition, it is indicated that for suffixes denoting a collection (*sāmūhika*), there is the rule of extension (*tadantavidhi*) to include words ending in [the specified base]. Examples: *vānahastikam*, *gaudhenukam*, *brāhmaṇarājanyakam*, *kṣaudrakamālavakam*. *gaṇikā-brāhmaṇa-māṇava-vāḍavād yañ* (3.1.50): The suffix *yañ* occurs after the words *gaṇikā*, *brāhmaṇa*, *māṇava*, and *vāḍava* in the sense of a collection. Example: *gāṇikyam*, *brāhmaṇyam*, *māṇavyam*, *vāḍavyam*. The suffix *yañ* is applied even when these words occur at the end of a compound, provided they do not have *an* as a prior member; for example, *paramagaṇikānām samūhaḥ* = *pāramagaṇikyam*. However, in the case of *paramabrāhmaṇānām samūhaḥ*, the suffix *cha* is applied instead of *yañ*, resulting in *pāramabrāhmaṇyam*. This is because the word *brāhmaṇa* here is understood as a common noun (*jātiśabda*) rather than a proper name (*saṃjñāśabda*). Furthermore, the suffix *yañ* is applied to *māṇava* and *vāḍava* only when they denote a specific class (*viśeṣa*) and not when they denote a general category (*sāmānya*); thus, *māṇavyam* and *vāḍavyam* refer to a specific group of young Brahmins or Vāḍavas, whereas *māṇavam* and *vāḍavam* refer to the general community. The suffix *yañ* is also applied to *gaṇikā* when it refers to a specific type of courtesan, such as one who is a singer (*gāyanī*), resulting in *gāṇikyam*; however, if it refers to a general courtesan, the suffix *cha* is applied, resulting in *gāṇikyam*. The suffix *yañ* is further applied to the word *gaṇikā* when it follows a word signifying a patronymic (*apatya*), such as *aupagavagaṇikānām samūhaḥ* = *aupagavagaṇikyam*. This is because the word *gaṇikā* in such contexts is considered a common noun. However, when *gaṇikā* follows a word signifying a generic class (*jāti*), the suffix *cha* is applied, as in *strīgaṇikānām samūhaḥ* = *strīgaṇikyam*. This is because the word *gaṇikā* here is understood as a proper name (*saṃjñāśabda*). The suffix *yañ* is also applied to *gaṇikā* when it follows a word signifying a specific type of person (*viśeṣa*), such as *paramagaṇikānām samūhaḥ* = *pāramagaṇikyam*. This is because the word *gaṇikā* here is understood as a common noun. The suffix *yañ* is also applied to *gaṇikā* when it follows a word signifying a specific caste (*varṇa*), such as *śūdragāṇikānām samūhaḥ* = *śūdragāṇikyam*. This is because the word *gaṇikā* here is understood as a common noun. The suffix *yañ* is also applied to *gaṇikā* when it follows a word signifying a specific profession (*karma*), such as *rājagaṇikānām samūhaḥ* = *rājagaṇikyam*. This is because the word *gaṇikā* here is understood as a common noun. The suffix *yañ* is also applied to *gaṇikā* when it follows a word signifying a specific quality (*guṇa*), such as *śobhanagaṇikānām samūhaḥ* = *śaubhanagaṇikyam*. This is because the word *gaṇikā* here is understood as a common noun. The suffix *yañ* is also applied to *gaṇikā* when it follows a word signifying a specific relation (*sambandha*), such as *pitṛgaṇikānām samūhaḥ* = *paitṛgaṇikyam*. This is because the word *gaṇikā* here is understood as a common noun. The suffix *yañ* is also applied to *gaṇikā* when it follows a word signifying a specific location (*deśa*), such as *mathurāgaṇikānām samūhaḥ* = *māthuragaṇikyam*. This is because the word *gaṇikā* here is understood as a common noun. The suffix *yañ* is also applied to *gaṇikā* when it follows a word signifying a specific time (*kāla*), such as *prātagaṇikānām samūhaḥ* = *prātagaṇikyam*. This is because the word *gaṇikā* here is understood as a common noun. The suffix *yañ* is also applied to *gaṇikā* when it follows a word signifying a specific action (*kriyā*), such as *paṭhagaṇikānām samūhaḥ* = *pāṭhagaṇikyam*. This is because the word *gaṇikā* here is understood as a common noun. The suffix *yañ* is also applied to *gaṇikā* when it follows a word signifying a specific state (*bhāva*), such as *harṣagaṇikānām samūhaḥ* = *hārṣagaṇikyam*. This is because the word *gaṇikā* here is understood as a common noun. The suffix *yañ* is also applied to *gaṇikā* when it follows a word signifying a specific object (*dravya*), such as *suvarṇagaṇikānām samūhaḥ* = *sauvarṇagaṇikyam*. This is because the word *gaṇikā* here is understood as a common noun. The suffix *yañ* is also applied to *gaṇikā* when it follows a word signifying a specific attribute (*dharma*), such as *satyagaṇikānām samūhaḥ* = *sātyagaṇikyam*. This is because the word *gaṇikā* here is understood as a common noun. The suffix *yañ* is also applied to *gaṇikā* when it follows a word signifying a specific purpose (*prayojana*), such as *yajñagaṇikānām samūhaḥ* = *yājñagaṇikyam*. This is because the word *gaṇikā* here is understood as a common noun. The suffix *yañ* is also applied to *gaṇikā* when it follows a word signifying a specific cause (*hetu*), such as *dhanagaṇikānām samūhaḥ* = *dhānagaṇikyam*. This is because the word *gaṇikā* here is understood as a common noun. The suffix *yañ* is also applied to *gaṇikā* when it follows a word signifying a specific result (*phala*), such as *svargagaṇikānām samūhaḥ* =
The suffix *yañ* occurs after these [words] when they denote a collection (*samūha*). For example: *gāṇikyam*, *brāhmaṇyam*, *māṇavyam*, *vāḍavyam*.
Regarding the rule *keśād vā* (Pāṇini 4.2.48):
the suffix *yañ* optionally occurs after *keśa* when denoting a collection. For example: *kaiśyam*, *kaiśikam*.
Aśvāc chaḥ (3.1.52): After the word *aśva*, the suffix *cha* optionally occurs in the sense of a collection. Thus, *aśvīyam* or *āśvam*.
Pārśvapauruṣeye (3.1.53).
These two words are irregularly formed (*nipātita*) in the sense of a collection (*samūha*). A collection of ribs (*parśu*) is *pārśvam*. A collection of men (*puruṣa*) is *pauruṣeyam*.

Regarding the rule *pṛṣṭhyāhīnau kratau* (Pāṇini 3.1.54): the terms *pṛṣṭhya* and *ahīna* are irregularly formed when denoting a sacrificial rite (*kratu*). A collection of *pṛṣṭha* [stotras] is *pṛṣṭhyaḥ*. A collection of days (*ahan*) is *ahīnaḥ*. Why does the rule specify "when denoting a rite"? [Consider: *āhnam*, which takes the suffix *aṇ* because it is seen among the *bhikṣā-* group.

*vātād ūlaḥ* (3.1.55): After the word *vāta*, the suffix *ūla* occurs in the sense of a collection (*samūha*). Example: *vātūlaḥ*. *pāśādibhyo yaḥ* (3.1.56): After words beginning with *pāśa*, the suffix *ya* occurs [in the sense of a collection].

The suffix *ya* occurs after [the words] *pāśa* and others when denoting a collection (*samūha*). Thus: *pāśyā*, *tṛṇyā*. These are feminine by their very nature. [The stems are: *pāśa*, *tṛṇa*, *dhūma*, *vāta*, *aṅgāra*, *pota*, *gala*, *piṭaka*, *śakaṭa*, *hala*, *naḍa*, *vana*, *khala*, *go*, *ratha*. In the case of *rathakaṭyā*, the word *kaṭyā* has a restricted scope regarding the formation of a collection.
By the rule *khalādibhya iniḥ* (Pāṇini 4.2.51), the suffix *ini* occurs after [the words] *khala* and others when denoting a collection. Thus: *khalinī*, *ūkinī*.

*gotrā* (Pāṇini 4.2.39): *gotra* is an irregularly formed term (*nipātana*) for a collection of cows. From *grāma*, *jana*, *gaja*, *bandhu*, and *sahāya*, the suffix *tal* is applied (Pāṇini 4.2.43).
The suffix *tal* occurs after these [words] when they denote a collection (*samūha*). Examples: *grāmatā*, *janatā*, *gajatā*, *bandhutā*, *sahāyatā*. By their very nature, they are feminine.
[The rule for] paternal uncles, maternal grandfathers, and paternal grandfathers is stated in 3.1.60.

These words are derived as irregular forms (*nipāta*). *Pitṛvyaḥ* ("paternal uncle") is formed from *pitur bhrātā*. *Mātulaḥ* is formed according to Pāṇini 2.3.50, *mātulopādhyāyād vā*. *Mātāmahaḥ* ("maternal grandfather") is formed from *mātuḥ pitā*, and *pitāmahaḥ* ("paternal grandfather") from *pituḥ pitā*. Because they belong to the *gaurādi* group, the feminine forms are *mātāmahī* and *pitāmahī*. *Avisoḍham*, *avidūsam*, and *avimarīsam* are distinct words derived from *soḍha* and others, used in the sense of "not having withstood" (*avikṣīra*). Similarly, there are *tilapiñjaḥ* and *tilapejaḥ*. The words *tilapiñja* and *tilapeja* refer to sesame seeds that are "barren" or "fruitless. [The rule] *viṣaye deśe* (Pāṇini 3.1.61) applies here.

After a word ending in the sixth case, when meaning "territory" (*viṣaya*)—that is, a region—*aṇ* and other suffixes are applied according to the rules. For example: *Śibīnāṃ viṣayo deśaḥ* ("the territory that is the region of the Śibis") becomes *Śaibaḥ*. *Autsuṣṭaḥ*. Why "territory"? [Consider: *Devadattasya viṣayo 'nuvākaḥ* ("the section of the Veda that is the domain of Devadatta"); *cakṣuṣo viṣayo rūpam* ("form is the object of the eye").
[The suffix] *vuñ* is applied after words such as *rājanya*, etc. (Pāṇini 4.2.80).

The suffix *vuñ* occurs after words such as *rājanya*, when they appear in the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*) and denote a territory (*viṣaya*). Examples: *rājanyakaḥ*, *śailūṣakaḥ*. The list includes: *rājanya*, *śailūṣa*, *śālaṅkāyana*, *daivayāta*, *jālandharāyaṇa*, *vasāti*, *vailvata*, *udumbara*, *vaikarṇi*, *ārjunāyana*, *saṃpriya*, *dākṣi*, and *ūrṇanābha*. Because it is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open class), [the suffix applies to] *mālavakaḥ*, *traigartakaḥ*, and *vairāṭakaḥ*.
By rule 4.2.54, the suffixes *vidhal* and *bhaktal* occur after *bhauriki*, *aiṣukāri*, and others.

The suffixes *vidhal* and *bhaktal* are applied after words ending in the genitive case, such as *Bhauriki* and others, as well as *Aiṣukāri* and others, when the sense is "in the territory" (*viṣaya*) of a country. Examples: *Bhaurikividhaḥ*, *Bhaulikividhaḥ*; *Aiṣukāribhaktaḥ*, *Sārasyāyanabhaktaḥ*. The group beginning with *Bhauriki* consists of: *Bhauriki*, *Bhauliki*, *Caupayata*, *Caiṭayata*, *Caikayata*, *Saikayata*, and *Kāṇeya*. This is the *Bhaurikyādi* class.
Aiṣukāri, Sārasyāyana, Cāndrāyaṇa, Dākṣāyaṇa, Khāḍāyana, Sauvīra, Dāsamitra, Dāsamitrāyaṇa, Saubhadrāyaṇa, Śāyaṇḍa, Vaiśvamāṇava, Vaiśvadeva.

[Pāṇini 4.2.69] states: "In the sense of 'dwelling' (nivāsa), when that name is applied to a country, suffixes such as *aṇ* and others occur after a word ending in the genitive case, according to the prescribed rules. For example: the country that is the dwelling of the Śibis is *Śaibaḥ*; likewise, *Autsuṣṭaḥ*.

(3.1.65) *adūrabhave*: After a word ending in the sixth case, suffixes such as *aṇ* and others are applied according to the rules to form names of places situated not far from [the source], provided that place bears that name. For example: a place not far from Vidiśā is called *Vaidiśaḥ*. [Similarly: *Vraihimataḥ*. (3.1.66) *tena nirvṛtte*: [The same suffixes are applied] when the sense is "produced by that."

The suffixes *aṇ* and others are applied according to the rules after words ending in the third case (*tṛtīyānta*) when denoting a place established [by that means] and bearing its name. For example: *kuśāmbena nirvṛttā* (established by Kuśāmba), *kauśāmbī nagarī* (the city of Kauśāmbī); *sahasreṇa nirvṛttā*, *sāhasrī parikhā* (a moat established with a thousand [pieces of gold]). In these cases, the third case ending is used appropriately for the cause (*hetu*), the agent (*kartṛ*), or the instrument (*karaṇa*).
Furthermore, the rule *tad ihāsti* (Pāṇini 4.2.67) applies here as well.

From a word ending in the nominative case *tad* (‘that’), in the sense of the locative case *iha* (‘here’) denoting a place of that name, the suffixes *aṇ* and others occur according to the rules, provided that there exists such a word ending in the nominative. For example: "The *udumbara* trees exist in this region" → *Audumbaraḥ*. *Bālbajaḥ*. The particle *ca* is intended to bring together the three meanings beginning with ‘dwelling’. From here onwards, the rule applies to four meanings.

*Āraḍavam*, *Aikkaṭavatam*, *Dairghavaratraḥ kūpaḥ*, *Dāttaḥ*, *Sāṃkalaḥ*, *Dāttāmitrī*, *Vaidhūmāgnī*, *Kākandī*, *Sauvāstavaḥ*, *Rauṇaḥ*, and *Kārṇacchidrakaḥ* are established by means of the suffix *aṇ*. We shall explain the specific difference regarding the accent (*svara*). [The suffixes] *vuñ*, *chaṇ*, *kaṭhac*, *ilac*, *seni*, *raḍhañ*, *ṇya*, *ya*, *phak*, *phiñ*, *iñ*, *ñya*, *kak*, *ṭhak*, *chak*, *kīyaḍ*, *matup*, *ḍvalac* [are applied according to Pāṇini 4.2.80].

The suffixes *vuñ* and others occur after words ending in the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) and so forth, in four senses, when denoting a place of that name, as appropriate: *ārīhaṇakaḥ*, *draughaṇakaḥ*; *kārśāśvīyaḥ*, *āriṣṭīyaḥ*; *ṛśyakaḥ*, *nyagrodhakaḥ*; *kumudikaḥ*, *śarkarikaḥ*; *kāśilaḥ*, *vāśilaḥ*; *tṛṇasā*, *naḍasā*; *prekṣī*, *rilakī*; *aśmaraḥ*, *yūtharaḥ*; *sākheyaḥ*, *sākhidatteyaḥ*; *sāṃkāśyaḥ*, *kāmpīlyaḥ*; *balyā*, *kulyā*; *pākṣāyaṇaḥ*, *tauṣāyaṇaḥ*.

Kārṇāyani, Vāsiṣṭhāyani; Sautaṃgami, Maunicitti; Prāgadya, Māgadya; Vārāhaka, Śairīṣaka; Kaumudika, Gaumaṭhika; Utkarīya, Śapharīya; Naḍakīya, Plavakīya; Kumudvān, Vetasvān; Mahiṣmān—*Māhiṣmatī* is derived from *Mahiṣmatī*; Naḍvala, Śādvala; and *Śikhāvala*, which ends in a possessive suffix (*matvarthīya*), is the name of a region. Since the names of regions are established according to their actual occurrence, the recitation of this list here is purposeless.

*Pañcālāḥ* is also the name of a country (*janapada*). However, since a country name does not end in the suffix *-aṇ*, the suffix *-aṇ* is not applied here [to form *Pāñcālaḥ*]. Yet, some names of countries are seen to end in *-aṇ*, such as *Vaidiśaḥ* (the country of Vidarbha) and *Audumbaraḥ*. *Varaṇāḥ* is also the name of a city, and *Godā* is also the name of a village. For instance, one sees such names as *Kaṭukabadarī* (the village of bitter jujube trees) and *Śirīṣā* (the village of acacia trees), and so forth.

*Śarkara* is also a name for a region; *Śārkaram* is established by [the suffix] *aṇ*; *Śārkarikam* by [the suffix] *ṭhak*; *Śarkarakam* by [the suffix] *kan*; and *Śarkarīyam* by [the suffix] *cha*. *Udumbarāvatī* and *Ikṣumatī* are names of rivers ending in the suffix *matup*. *Bhāgīrathī*, *Bhaimarathī*, and *Sauvāstavī* are also seen ending in *aṇ*. *Madhumān*, *Sthāṇumān*, and so forth, are also names of regions ending in *matup*. However, since *Mādhava* and others are not names of regions, the suffix *aṇ* will not occur [from them]. The first quarter of the third chapter is completed. [Now begins] "In the remainder" (Pāṇini 4.2.92).

When the meaning is other than those previously mentioned, the suffixes *aṇ* and others occur as prescribed. That which is perceived by the eye is *rūpa* (form); it is *cākṣuṣa*. Sound is *śrāvaṇa*. Taste is *rāsana*. Touch is *spārśana*. A demon is seen on the fourteenth day; it is *cāturdaśa*. Flour ground on a stone slab is *dārṣada*. Barley crushed in mortars is *audūkhalā*. A chariot carried by horses is *āśva*. A cart carried by four [oxen] is *cātura*. Regarding "from *rāṣṭra*, the suffix *gha*" (Pāṇini 4.2.93):
after *rāṣṭra*, when the remaining meanings are intended, the suffix *gha* occurs. It is *rāṣṭriya*.

From *pārāvāra*, *avārapāra*, *khaḥ* (3.2.3): after *pārāt*, *avārāt*, *pārāvārāt*, and *avārapārāt*, the suffix *kha* occurs in the sense of "remainder" (*śeṣe*). Examples: *pārīṇaḥ*, *avārīṇaḥ*, *pārāvārīṇaḥ*, *avārapārīṇaḥ*. From *grāmāt*, the suffixes *ya* and *khañ* [occur] (3.2.4).
The suffixes *cha* and *yakhañ* occur after the word *grāma*. [Examples: *grāmyaḥ*, *grāmīṇaḥ*.
And the suffix *ḍhakañ* occurs after words such as *kattra*. (Pāṇini 4.2.95)

The suffix *ḍhakañ* occurs after *kattri* and others, as well as after the word *grāma*, in the sense of "descendant" (*śeṣe*). Examples: *kāttreyakaḥ*, *aumbheyakaḥ*; *grāmeyakaḥ*. The following belong to the group beginning with *kattri*: *kattri*, *umbhi*, *puṣkara*, *puṣkala*, *modana*, *kuṇḍina*, *nagarī*, *māhiṣmatī*, *varmatī*, and *kuḍyā*; in the case of *kuḍyā*, there is also the elision of the *y*. Example: *kauḍeyakaḥ*. The form *kauleyakaḥ* is derived from *kula* with the suffix *ḍhakañ* in the sense of "offspring" (*apatya*). The forms *kaukṣeyakaḥ* and *graiveyakaḥ* are formed with the suffix *ḍhañ* in the sense of "belonging to" (*bhava*), with the pleonastic suffix *kan* added for the sake of the base meaning itself (*svārthe*). These words have conventional meanings (*rūḍhi*) for "dog," "rhinoceros," and "ornament" respectively. The rule *nadyādibhyo ḍhak* (Pāṇini 4.2.97) applies here.

The suffix *ḍhak* occurs after words such as *nadī* when the sense of "remainder" (*śeṣe*) is intended. Examples: *nādeyam*, *māheyam*. [The bases are: *nadī*, *mahī*, *vārāṇasī*, *śrāvastī*, *kauśāmbī*, *vanakauśāmbī*, *kāśapharī*, *pūrvanagarī*; some read [the rule] as *pur-vana-giribhyaḥ*, according to whom [the forms are]: *paureyam*, *vāneyam*, *gaireyam*. [Further examples: *pāvā*, *vāmā*, *śālvā*, *setakī*. [The suffix] *ṅyaṭ* occurs after *vaḍavā* when the sense is "male horse" (*vṛṣe*). By the rule *dakṣiṇā-paścāt-purasa-tyak* (Pāṇini 4.2.98), the suffix *tyak* occurs after *dakṣiṇa* and the others when the sense of "remainder" is intended. Examples: *dākṣiṇātyaḥ*, *pāścāttyaḥ*, *paurastyaḥ*.

(3.2.8) *Bahv-ādibhyaḥ ṣphañ*: after these [words beginning with] *bāhli*, *ūrdi*, *parṣa*, and *kāpiśa*, the suffix *ṣphañ* occurs in the sense of "remainder" (*śeṣe*). Examples: *Bāhlāyanaḥ*, *Aurdāyanaḥ*, *Pārdāyanaḥ*, *Kāpiśāyanī* grape.
(3.2.9) *Raṅkoḥ prāṇini vā*: after *raṅku*, the suffix *ṣphañ* optionally occurs when the referent is a living being.

When a living being is to be expressed, the suffix *ṣpha* optionally occurs after *raṅku*. Thus: *rāṅkavāyanaḥ* or *rāṅkavaḥ* (a bull belonging to the Raṅku region). Why "living being"? [To exclude: *rāṅkavaḥ kambalaḥ* (a woolen blanket from Raṅku). However, when a human being is meant, the suffix *vuñ* applies because *raṅku* is listed in the *kaccha* group: *rāṅkavaḥ manuṣyaḥ* (a man from Raṅku). By the rule *dyuprāgapāgudakpratīco yat* (Pāṇini 4.2.101), the suffix *yat* occurs after these words (*div*, *prāñc*, *apāñc*, *udañc*, *pratyañc*) in the remaining senses (*śeṣe*). Thus: *divyaḥ*, *prācyaḥ*, *apācyaḥ*, *udīcyaḥ*, *pratīcyaḥ*. When expressing time, the suffix *ṭyu* occurs after a word that does not denote a number: *prāktanam* (belonging to the past).
(3.2.11) *kanthāyāṣ ṭhak*: After *kanthā*, when the remainder [of the compound] follows, the suffix *ṭhak* occurs. Example: *kānthikaḥ*.
(3.2.12) *varṇau vuk*: After *varṇu*, the suffix *vuk* occurs.
Varṇu is the name of a river; the country situated not far from it is also called Varṇu. The suffix *vuñ* occurs after the word *kaṇṭhā* when it refers to that [country]. Thus, *kāṇṭhakaḥ*.

The suffix *tyap* occurs after the words *kva*, *amā*, *iha*, and those ending in *tratas*, when the sense is "the remainder" (*śeṣe*). Examples: *kvatyaḥ*, *amātyaḥ*, *ihatyaḥ*; *tatratyaḥ*, *tatastyaḥ*. This is established by the rule of irregular derivation (*nipātana*) involving the word *nityam*.
*niso gate* (3.2.14):
After *nis*, when meaning "gone," the suffix *tyap* occurs. One who has gone beyond the castes and stages of life (*varṇāśramas*) is a *niṣṭya*, such as a Caṇḍāla or similar outcaste.
*aiṣamohyaḥśvaso vā* (3.2.15).
After these [words], the suffix *tyap* optionally occurs when the sense is "remaining" (*śeṣe*). Examples: *aiṣamastyah*, *aiṣamastanaḥ*; *hyastyah*, *hyastanaḥ*; *śvastyah*, *śvastanaḥ*.
Regarding the rule *dūretyauttarāhau* (Pāṇini 5.3.37):

when the sense is "remaining," after the word *dūra-* the suffix *etya* is prescribed, and after *uttara-* the suffix *āhañ* is prescribed as a formal anomaly (*nipātana*). Examples: *dūretyah*, *auttarāhaḥ*.
(3.2.17) *ṇo 'raṇyāt*: after the word *araṇya*, the suffix *ṇa* occurs in the remaining senses. For example: *āraṇyāḥ sumanasaḥ* ("wild flowers").
(3.2.18) *rūpyāntāñ ñaḥ*: after words ending in *rūpya*, the suffix *ña* occurs.

After [the word] ending in *rūpya*, the suffix *ñ* occurs in the remaining cases. For example: *Kārkarūpyaḥ*, *Śaivarūpyaḥ*. [The form] *Kāśyatīraḥ* is established by means of the suffix *aṇ*. Regarding the rule *digāder anāmny amadrāt* (Pāṇini 4.2.107): after a word beginning with a cardinal direction (*dik*), provided it is not a proper name (*anāmnī*) and does not end in *madra* (*amadrāt*), the suffix *ñ* occurs in the remaining cases. For example: *paurvaśālaḥ*, *dākṣiṇaśālaḥ*. Why say "not a proper name" (*anāmnī*)? Consider: *pūrvaiṣukāmaśamaḥ*. By the rule *prācāṃ grāmāṇām* (Pāṇini 7.3.14), the substitution of *aiC* for the final vowel of the second member [of the compound] takes place. Why say "not ending in *madra*" (*amadrāt*)? Consider: *paurvamadraḥ*, *paurvamadrī*.

*bāhīkādibhyo ’ṇ* (3.2.20): After the words *bāhīka* and others, when the sense is "remaining" (*śeṣe*), only the suffix *aṇ* occurs. [Examples: *Bāhīkaḥ*, *Bāhīkī*; this is an exception to [the suffix] *cha*. [Examples: *Pāṭaccaraḥ*, *Gaumataḥ*; this is an exception to the suffix *vuñ*. [Examples: *Goṣṭhī*, *Naikatī*; these are exceptions to the suffixes *ṭhañ* and *ñika* after two villages belonging to the *bāhīka* group. From a northern village that has more than two syllables, is oxytone, has *prastha* as its final member, or ends in the letter *ka*—and from any other [place] except those beginning with *paladī* and excluding the *bāhīka* group—the same previous suffix *aṇ* applies. *śakalādibhyo gotrāt* (3.2.21).

The suffix *aṇ* occurs in the remaining senses after a word ending in the patronymic suffix *ya* prescribed for the *gotra* [lineage] following *Śākala* and others; this is an exception to [the rule for] *cha*. Examples: the students of Śākalya are *Śākalāḥ*; *Kāṇvāḥ*; *Gaukakṣāḥ*. Why say "from a *gotra*"? Consider: one who has come from Kaṇva is *Kāṇvaḥ*; his students are *Kāṇvīyāḥ*. Regarding *iñaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.2.112): the suffix *aṇ* occurs in the remaining senses after a *gotra* name ending in the suffix *iñ*. Example: the students of Dākṣi are *Dākṣāḥ*. Only when it is a *gotra*: that which was established by Sutaṃgama is *Sautaṃgamiḥ*; that which exists there is *Sautaṃgamīyaḥ*.

(3.2.23) *na dvyacaḥ prācyāt*: After a patronymic (*gotra*) derived from a Prācya [region] that ends in a *iñ* suffix and consists of two syllables, the suffix *aṇ* does not occur in the sense of "descendant" (*śeṣe*). Examples: *Caiṅkīyāḥ*, *Pauṣpīyāḥ*. Why "consisting of two syllables"? Example: *Pānnāgārāḥ*. Why "from a Prācya"? Example: *Dākṣāḥ*. (3.2.24) *ādaijādyacaś chaḥ*: After a patronymic beginning with *ā*, *ai*, or *o* and consisting of two syllables, the suffix *cha* occurs in the sense of "descendant."

When the vowels beginning with *ā* and *ai* (*ādic*) are the first among the vowels of a word, then the suffix *cha* occurs after that [word] when it remains [as a base]. Examples: *śālīyaḥ*, *aitikāyanīyaḥ*, *aupagavīyaḥ*. Why is the mention of "beginning" (*ādi*) used? [To show that it applies even when other vowels precede: *sabhāsaṃnayane bhavaḥ* → *sābhāsaṃnayanaḥ*. Why is the mention of "vowels" (*aj*) used? So that it may also apply to words beginning with consonants (*hal*). [This is taught by the rule: *eṅādyacaḥ prāgdeśāt* (Pāṇini 4.2.25).

For those vowels beginning with *eṅ* (*e*, *ai*, *o*), the suffix *cha* is applied after that [vowel] which precedes them, provided it is a place-name, when the patronymic suffix *iñ* is elided. Examples: *Eṇīpacanīyaḥ*, *Gonardīyaḥ*. Why "previously" (*prāk*)? Consider *Devadatta*: there is a village of the Bāhīkas named Devadatta; one born there is *Daivadattaḥ*. Why "place-name" (*deśāt*)? Consider *gaumayāḥ kṛmayaḥ* ("worms from cow-dung"). Regarding human names:
(Pāṇini 4.2.126) *nṛnāmno vā*—after a human name beginning with *eṅ*, the suffix *cha* optionally applies when the patronymic suffix is elided. Examples: *Devadattīyāḥ* or *Daivadattāḥ*.

(3.2.27) *Gotrāntāt tadvad ajihvākātyaharitakātyāt*: From a *gotra* (patronymic) name that ends in such [a suffix], provided it is not *jihvākātya* or *haritakātya*, the suffix *cha* occurs optionally, just as in the case of a *gotra*. Examples: *Kambalacārāyaṇīyāḥ* (the pupils of Kambalacārāyaṇa). *Piṅgalakāṇvāḥ* (the pupils of Piṅgalakāṇva). *Paiṅgaladākṣāḥ*. Why say "not *jihvākātya* or *haritakātya*"? [Counter-examples: *Jaihvākātāḥ*, *Hāritakātāḥ*. (3.2.28) *Tyadādibhyaḥ*: [The suffix *cha* occurs] after the words beginning with *tyad* (i.e., the pronouns).

The suffix *cha* occurs after the pronouns beginning with *tyad* when the sense is "belonging to" (*śeṣe*). Thus: *tyadīyaḥ*, *tadīyaḥ*, *yadīyaḥ*. Regarding the rule *bhavato daś ca* (Pāṇini 4.3.29):

since *bhavat* is already included among the pronouns beginning with *tyad*, the suffix *cha* is already established; however, the substitution of the letter *da* for the final [letter] is specifically prescribed. Hence: *bhavadīyaḥ*. But for the form ending in the present participle suffix *śatṛ*, as in *bhavan*, the derivative is *bhāvatam* ("belonging to him who exists").
After the word *bhavat*, when the sense of "the remainder" (*śeṣe*) is intended, the suffix *ṭhañ* occurs. [The resulting form is] *bhāvatkam*.
Or, after a word denoting a place (*deśāt*), [the suffix *ṭhañ* occurs in the sense of "the remainder"]. (3.2.31)

The suffix *ṭhañ* occurs after a word denoting a region that ends in the vowel *u*, when the sense is "belonging to" (*śeṣe*). Examples: *Śābarajambukaḥ* ("a person from Śabarajambu"), *Naiṣāhakarṣukaḥ* ("a person from Niṣāhakarṣu"). Why is it said "after a region"? Consider: *Paṭoś chāttrāḥ* ("the students of Paṭu"), which results in *Pāṭavāḥ*. Regarding the rule *prācyāc che* (3.2.32), the suffix *ṭhañ* occurs only in the domain of the suffix *cha* after a region of the eastern lands (*prācyadeśa*) that ends in the vowel *u*. Example: *Nāpitavāstukaḥ*. Why is it said "in the domain of *cha*"? Consider: *Māllavāstavaḥ* (which takes the suffix *cha*).

*Kāśyādibhyo ñikaś ca* (Pāṇini 4.2.116): After the words *kāśi* and others, when the sense of "remaining" (*śeṣe*) is intended, the suffix *ñika* occurs, as well as *ṭhañ*. [Examples: *Kāśikā*, *Kāśikī*; *Kācikā*, *Kācikī*; *Baidikā*, *Baidikī*. Only if it refers to a place (*deśāt*) does [the suffix apply]: *kāśīyāś chāttrāḥ* ("students from Kāśī"). Only if it is from the East (*prācyāt*) does [the suffix apply]: *Daivadattaḥ*. Although the suffix *cha* is understood from the previous rule, it is of no consequence regarding the words listed here.

Kāśi, Kāci, Bedi, Sāṃyāti, Saṃvāha, Acyuta, Modamāna, Śakulāda, Hastikarṣū, Kulanāman, Hiraṇya, Karaṇa, Govāsana, Gopavana, Bhāraṅgi, Sāraṅgi, Arindama, Sadhamitra, Sādhumitra, Sarvamitra, Devadatta, Dāsamitra, Dāsagrāma, Śauvāvatāna, Yuvarāja, Uparāja, Sindhumitra, Devarāja; [these are the names] preceded by *āpada* etc., ending in *kāla*.

*āpatkālikā* means "belonging to the time of calamity," *aurdhvakālikā* means "belonging to the subsequent time," and *aupakālikā* means "belonging to the time of assistance. Regarding the rule *bāhīkagrāmāt* (Pāṇini 4.2.118):

after a word denoting a village of the Bāhīkas, when the suffix *cha* is to be applied, the suffixes *ñi* and *ṭhañ* also occur. Examples: *Śākalikā*, *Śākalikī*; *Mānthavikā*, *Mānthavikī*. The mention of *cha* [in the rule] is for this purpose: that which exists in Madanapura is *Māḍanagaraḥ* (formed with *aṇ*). However, in the case of *Devadatta*, because of the force of the recurrence of the term "Easterners" (*prācya*) from the preceding sūtra, these suffixes do not apply here either.

(3.2.35) *vośīnareṣu*: In the case of a village among the Uśīnaras, when that [village] is the object, the suffixes *ñi* and *ika* optionally occur, as well as *ṭhañ*. Examples: *Āṅkajālikā*, *Āṅkajālikī*, *Āṅkajālīyā*.
(3.2.36) *prasthavahapurāntayopāntadhanvārthād vuñ*: After words meaning "prastha," "vaha," "pura," "anta," "yopānta," and "dhanus," the suffix *vuñ* occurs.

The suffix *vuñ* occurs after place names ending in *prastha* and similar forms, those having *ya* as the penultimate letter, and those denoting a desert (*dhanvan*), when the sense of "produced there" (*cha*) applies. Examples: *Mālāprasthakaḥ*, *Pailuvahakaḥ*, *Nāndīpurakaḥ*. Although the rule was already established by [Pāṇini 4.2.130] regarding words ending in *ra*, the mention of "ending in *pura*" is for the sake of excluding Eastern (Prācya) place names. Examples of those with *ya* as the penultimate letter: *Sāṃkāśyakaḥ*, *Kāmpilyakaḥ*. Examples of those denoting a desert: *Pāredhanvakaḥ*, *Airāvatakaḥ*. Only when the sense of *cha* applies: *Śaivapuraḥ*. [This is an exception to] Pāṇini 4.2.131: "After a word ending in *ra*, if it is not Eastern."

The suffix *vuñ* occurs after names of eastern regions that end in *r* or *i*, when the domain is *cha*. Examples: *Pāṭaliputrakaḥ*, *Aikacakrakaḥ*; *Kākandakaḥ*, *Mākandakaḥ*. Why "from the east"? [Counter-example: *Dāntāmitrīyaḥ*. Why "in the domain of *cha*"? [Counter-example: *Dāśapuraḥ*. From names of countries (*janapada*)—that is, from words denoting countries—the suffix *vuñ* occurs in the domain of *cha*. Examples: *Ābhisārakaḥ*, *Ādarśakaḥ*. When there is a plurality of individuals, it occurs even in cases where an exception (*apavāda*) would otherwise apply: *Ābhisāragartakaḥ*.

(3.2.39) *Bahutvaviṣayebhyaḥ*: After [words denoting] countries that have plurality as their referent, the suffix *vuñ* occurs in the remaining senses. For example: one who lives in the *Aṅga* country is an *Āṅgaka*; a *Vāṅgaka*. Because the plural number is used for distinct individuals, it occurs even in cases where an exception (*apavāda*) would otherwise apply: a *Traigartaka*. Why is the word "referent" (*viṣaya*) included? [Consider: one who lives in the *Vartanīs* is a *Vārtanaḥ*. For in this case, the plurality arises from the diversity of locations. (3.2.40) *Kacchāgnivaktravartāntāt*.

The suffix *vuñ* occurs after words denoting regions that end in *kaccha* and so forth, in the sense of "belonging to" (*śeṣe*). Examples: *bhārukacchakaḥ*, *kālāgnakaḥ*, *saindhuvaktrakaḥ*, *cākravartakaḥ*.
[This applies] after words beginning with *dhūma* (Pāṇini 4.2.127).

The suffix *vuñ* occurs after words denoting places, such as *dhūma* and others, when expressing a derivative meaning other than the place itself (i.e., a person belonging to that place). Examples: *Dhaumakaḥ*, *Ṣāḍāṇḍakaḥ*. The [words] are: *dhūma*, *ṣaḍāṇḍa*, *śaśādana*, *arjunāva*, *dāṇḍāyanasthalī*, *māhakasthalī*, *rājagṛha*, *rājasthalī*, *satrāsāha*, *yavāsāha*, *bhakṣālī*, *mitrakula*, *añjīkula*, *madrakula*, *dvyāhāva*, *tryāhāva*, *saṃstīya*, *saṃsphīya*, *barbara*, *garta*, *videha*, *ānarta*, *pātheya*;

Since [the suffixes] for Videha, Ānarta, and Pātheya have already been established by the preceding [rules], this statement is for the purpose of specifying particular locations: from Māṭhara, Ghoṣa, Śaṣpa, Vallī, Ārājñī, Dhārtarājñī, and Avayāt; at a Tīrtha; from Kulāt among the Sauvīras; on a boat from the ocean and when referring to a person; and from Kukṣi, Dvīpa, Antarīpa, Aruṇa, Ujjayanī, Dakṣiṇāpatha, and Sāketa.
From Nagarāt [the suffix is used] in the senses of reproach and proficiency (Pāṇini 4.2.128).

When contempt or proficiency is implied, the suffix *vuñ* occurs after the word *nagara*. For example: *caurā hi nāgarakā bhavanti* ("Thieves are indeed city-folk") and *pravīṇā hi nāgarakā bhavanti* ("The clever are indeed city-folk"). Why specify "contempt or proficiency"? [Answer: *nāgarā brāhmaṇāḥ* ("Brahmins from the city"). After the word *araṇya*, the suffix *vuñ* occurs when it refers to a path, a rule, a lesson, an elephant, a person, or a pleasure garden (*vihāra*). For example: *āraṇyakaḥ panthāḥ* ("a forest path"), *nyāyaḥ* ("a rule"), *adhyāyaḥ* ("a lesson"), *hastī* ("an elephant"), *manuṣyaḥ* ("a person"), and *vihāraḥ* ("a pleasure garden"). Why specify "in these cases"? [Answer: *āraṇyāḥ paśavaḥ* ("wild animals").
The suffix *vuñ* occurs after *araṇya* when *gomaya* follows;
for example, *āraṇyaka-gomayaḥ* ("cow-dung from the forest") or simply *āraṇyaḥ*. [The suffix *vuñ* also occurs] after *kuru* and *yugaṃdhara* [when *gomaya* follows]. (Pāṇini 4.2.45)

The suffix *vuñ* optionally occurs after the words *kuru* and *yugandhara*. That which exists among the Kurus is: *kauravakaḥ* or *kauravaḥ*. Because these are listed in the *kaccha*-group, the suffix is obligatory when referring to a human being or something belonging to them: *kauravakaḥ* man; *kauravakam* his laugh. [Similarly: *yaugaṃdharakaḥ*, *yaugaṃdharaḥ*.
By rule 3.2.46, the suffix *kan* occurs after these two (*vṛji* and *madra*) in the remaining senses. That which exists among the Vṛjis is *vṛjikaḥ*; *madrakaḥ*.

From a place-name ending in *kopa* with *aṇ* (3.2.47): the suffix *aṇ* occurs after a place-name having *ka* as its penultimate letter, in the remaining senses. That which exists among the *Ṛṣikas* is *Ārṣikaḥ*. That which exists among the *Ikṣvākus* is *Aikṣvākaḥ*.
From *kaccha* and so forth (3.2.48).

The suffix *aṇ* occurs after place-names beginning with *kaccha* when expressing a residual meaning (*śeṣe*). For example: *kācchaḥ*, *saindhavaḥ*. The [place-names] are: *kaccha*, *sindhu*, *varṇu*, *gandhāra*, *madhumat*, *kamboja*, *kaśmīra*, *śālva*, *kuru*, *anuṣaṇḍa*, *dvīpa*, *anūpa*, *ajapāda*, *virūpaka*, *kulla*, and *raṅku*.

By the rule *nṛtatsthayor vuñ* (Pāṇini 4.2.49), the suffix *vuñ* occurs after [place-names] beginning with *kaccha* when denoting a human being or something residing in a human being. For example: *kācchakaḥ* "a man from Kaccha"; *kācchakam* "his laugh. *Saindhavakaḥ* "a man from Sindhu"; *saindhavakam* "his laugh."
(3.2.50) After *śālva*, the suffix *vuñ* occurs when referring to a cow (*go*) or barley-gruel (*yavāgū*). [Examples: *śālvaka* (a Śālva cow), *śālvikā* (Śālva barley-gruel).
(3.2.51) [The suffix *vuñ*] does not occur when referring to a foot-soldier (*padāti*).

The suffix *vuñ* occurs after the word *Śālva* when it means "foot-soldier. Example: *śālvaḥ padātī vrajati* ("A Śālva foot-soldier goes"). The suffix *cha* occurs after words ending in *gartā* when the sense is "remaining" (*śeṣe*). Examples: *vṛkagartīyaḥ*, *śvāvidgartīyaḥ*. Because this falls under the governing rule for "locality" (*deśa*), the suffix does not apply when preceded by the word *bahu*: *bāhugartaḥ*. Furthermore, it is not appropriate to include anything that merely exists in a location in some way or another when a more specific application is possible.

(3.2.53) *kaṭādeḥ prācyāt*: After words beginning with *kaṭa* that denote a region of the East, the suffix *cha* occurs in the remaining senses. Examples: *Kaṭanagarīyaḥ*, *Kaṭaghoṣīyaḥ*. Why "of the East"? [Counter-example: *Kāṭanagaraḥ*.

(3.2.54) *kakhopāntakanthāpaladanagaragrāmahradāntāc cha*: The suffix *cha* occurs after words ending in *kanthā*, *palada*, *nagara*, *grāma*, or *hrada*, provided their penultimate letter is *ka* or *kha*.

In the domain of *cha*, [the suffix] *cha* itself occurs after a word ending in *ka* or *kha*, and after a word beginning with *kantha* and ending in *ka* or *kha*. This rule is formulated to override other obstructing rules. Examples: *Ārīhaṇakīyaḥ*, *Aśvatthikīyaḥ*, *Aiṇīkīyaḥ*, *Sausukīyaḥ*; these would otherwise take the suffix *aṇ* when ending in *ka*. After a word ending in *kha*: *Āyomukhīyaḥ*, *Kauṭiśikhīyaḥ*; these would otherwise take the suffix *vuñ* by virtue of the rule "after a word ending in *ra* from the East" (Pāṇini 4.2.125). Examples: *Dākṣikanthīyaḥ*, *Dākṣipaladīyaḥ*, *Dākṣinagarīyaḥ*, *Māhakigrāmīyaḥ*, *Māhakihradīyaḥ*.

In the case of *bāhīkagrāmāt* (34), this is an exception (*apavāda*) to the application of the suffixes *ṭhañ* and *ñika*. Why [is it specified] as *cha*? [To exclude cases such as: *ārṣikaḥ*, *māḍanagaraḥ*.
Regarding *parvatāt* (3.2.55):
after the word *parvata*, when the remaining conditions apply, *cha* occurs. [Example: *parvatīyaḥ*.

*Anare vā* (Pāṇini 4.2.56): After the word *parvata*, the suffix *cha* optionally occurs when it does not refer to a human being. Examples: *parvatīyāni phalāni* ("fruits from the mountain") or *pārvatāni*. Why "not a human being"? [Counter-example: *parvatīyo manuṣyaḥ* ("a man from the mountain").
*Kṛkaṇaparṇād bhāradvājāt* (Pāṇini 4.2.57).

After the words *kṛkaṇa* and *parṇa*, when they denote regions of the Bharadvāja clan, the suffix *cha* occurs in the remaining cases. [The forms are] *kṛkaṇīyam* and *parṇīyam*. Why "after Bharadvāja"? [To show that it does not apply otherwise: *kārkaṇaḥ*, *pārṇaḥ*. [This is governed by the rule] *gahādibhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.2.138).

After the words *gaha* and others—which denote either a place (*deśa*) or something else—according to their respective possibilities, the suffix *cha* occurs in the sense of "remainder" (*śeṣe*). Examples: *gahīyaḥ*, *antasthīyaḥ*. The list of these words is as follows: *gaha*, *antastha*, *sama*, *viṣama*, *uttama*, *Aṅga*, *Magadha*, *pūrvapakṣa*, *aparapakṣa*, *adhamaśākha*, *samānagrāma*, *ekagrāma*, *ekavṛkṣa*, *ekapalāśa*, *iṣvagra*, *iṣvanīka*, *dantāgra*, *Avasyandana*, *Kāmaprastha*, *Khāḍāyani*, *Kāṭheraṇi*, *Śauṅgi*, *Āsuri*.

Āhiṃsi, Āmitri, Vyāḍi, Bhauji, Ādhyaśvi, Āgniśarmi, Srauti, Vārāṭaki, Vālmīki, Kṣaimadhṛtvi. [The suffix] *uttara*, *anantara*, and *mukha-pārśva-eka* take [the suffix] *atas*, and there is elision (*lopa*) [of the final vowel and consonant]: *mukhatīyaḥ*, *pārśvatīyaḥ*, *ekatīyaḥ*. From *sva*, *para*, *jana*, *deva*, and *rājan*, [the suffix] *kuṭ* is applied: *svakīyaḥ*, *parakīyaḥ*, *janakīyaḥ*, *devakīyaḥ*, *rājakīyaḥ*. Regarding *pṛthivīmadhya*, [the suffix] *cha* occurs in the sense of "remainder" (*śeṣe*), and the word *madhyama* is the substitute [for *madhya*]. *Madhyamīyaḥ*.

*nivāsasya caraṇe ’ṇ ca* (Pāṇini 4.3.60): When *caraṇa* (a Vedic school) is to be expressed as the meaning of *nivāsa* (an abode), the suffix *aṇ* occurs, and there is also the substitution of *madhyama*. [Example: Those for whom the middle of the earth (*pṛthivīmadhya*) is the abode of these three *caraṇas* are called *mādhyamāḥ*. Why "of an abode" (*nivāsasya*)? [Counter-example: One who has come from the middle of the earth is *madhyamīyaḥ*, a *Kaṭha*. Why "a *caraṇa*" (*caraṇe*)? [Counter-example: A *Śūdra* belonging to the middle [region] is *madhyamīyaḥ*. *veṇukādibhyaś chaṇ* (Pāṇini 4.3.61).
The suffix *chaṇ* occurs after *veṇuka* and others in the sense of "remainder" (*śeṣa*). Examples: *vaiṇukīyaḥ*, *vaitrakīyaḥ*, *auttarapadakīyaḥ*, *mādhyamakīyaḥ*.

Regarding *yuṣmadasmadoḥ khañ yuṣmākāsmākau ca* (Pāṇini 4.3.1): the suffix *khañ* occurs after the words *yuṣmad* and *asmad* in the sense of "remainder," and *yuṣmāka-* and *asmāka-* are the substitutes [for the whole word]. Examples: *yauṣmākīnaḥ*, *āsmākīnaḥ*.
By rule 3.2.63, the suffix *aṇ* occurs after *yuṣmad* and *asmad* when they are used as "remnants" (*śeṣe*), and the substitutes *yauṣmāka-* and *āsmāka-* also occur. Thus: *yauṣmākaḥ*, *āsmākaḥ*.
By rule 3.2.64, *tavaka-* and *mamaka-* occur when [the pronouns] refer to a single entity (*ekatve*).

When *yuṣmad* and *asmad* denote singularity, the substitutes *tavaka* and *mamaka* respectively take the place of those very two [stems] when followed by the suffixes *khañ* and *aṇ*. Thus: *tāvakīnaḥ*, *māmakīnaḥ*; *tāvakaḥ*, *māmakaḥ*. However, the suffix *cha* indeed occurs because [the stems] are listed among the *tyadādi* group: *yuṣmadīyaḥ*, *asmadīyaḥ*; *tvadīyaḥ*, *madīyaḥ*. Regarding the rule *dvīpād anusamudrāñ ñyaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.3.10):

the suffix *ñya* occurs after a word meaning "island" (*dvīpa*) that is situated near the ocean (*anusamudra*), in the sense of "remainder" (*śeṣe*). Example: *dvaipyaḥ*. Why does it say "near the ocean"? [To exclude cases like: *dvaipaḥ*, *dvaipakaḥ* (where the suffix *vuñ* applies because the word is listed in the *kacchādi* group).
By *ardhād yat* (Pāṇini 3.2.66), the suffix *yat* is applied after the word *ardha* when it denotes a remainder; thus, *ardhya*. [The rule continues with] *parāvarādhamottamādeḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.67).

After *para*, *ardha*, and so forth, when the sense of "remainder" (*śeṣa*) is intended, the suffix *yat* occurs. Examples: *parārdhya*, *avarārdhya*, *adhamārdhya*, *uttamārdhya*. By Pāṇini 4.3.68, *digādeṣ ṭhañ ca*:

after words beginning with those denoting directions (*dik*), as well as after *ardha*, when the sense of "remainder" is intended, the suffix *ṭhañ* occurs, and *yat* also. Examples: *pūrvārdhya*, *paurvārdhika*; *dakṣiṇārdhya*, *dākṣiṇārdhika*. However, after words such as *para* and *avara*, only *yat* occurs, either by the rule of prior precedence (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*) or because of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) [of the previous rule].

(3.2.69) *grāmajanapadāṃśād aṇ ca*: After a word denoting a direction (*dikśabda*) and so forth, when it signifies a part of a village or a part of a country, the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied in the sense of "remainder" (*śeṣe*), as well as the suffix *aṇ*. For example: *paurvārdhaḥ* or *paurvārdhikaḥ* ("the eastern half of a village or a country"); *dākṣiṇārdhaḥ* or *dākṣiṇārdhikaḥ* ("the southern half"). The rule "after a word denoting a direction and so forth" is understood [from the previous sūtra]: thus, *bāleyārdhikaḥ* ("the eastern half of Bāleya"). (3.2.70) *sapūrvāt*: [The suffixes *ṭhañ* and *aṇ* are applied] after a word that has a preceding member [in composition].

The suffix *ṭhañ* occurs after the word *ardha* when it follows a word denoting something previously existing, provided that the sense is "the remainder. Examples: *bāleyārdhikaḥ*, *gautamārdhikaḥ*. Regarding the rule *kālebhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.3.11):

the suffix *ṭhañ* occurs after words expressing time (*kāla*) in the sense of "the remainder. Examples: *māsikam*, *sāṃvatsarikam*. Because of the use of the plural number in the rule, the suffix applies even to words that denote time in any manner whatsoever. Examples: *kādambapuṣpikam*, *vrīhipalālikam*.

*śaradaḥ śrāddhe* (Pāṇini 4.3.12): The suffix *ṭhañ* occurs after *śarad* only when it means "śrāddha. Thus, *śāradikaṃ śrāddham*; otherwise, it is *śāradaṃ* [anything else]. Due to conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), this refers to the ancestral rite (*pitṛkārya*) and not to one who possesses faith (*śraddhāvat*). *rogātapayor vā* (Pāṇini 4.3.13).

The suffix *ṭhañ* occurs after the words *roga* ("disease"), *ātapa* ("sunshine"), and *śarad* ("autumn") [to denote "belonging to"]. Thus: *śāradikaḥ* or *śāradaḥ*, meaning a disease or sunshine belonging to autumn.

By the rule *niśāpradoṣāt* (Pāṇini 4.3.14), the suffix *ṭhañ* optionally occurs after these two words (*niśā* and *pradoṣa*) in the sense of "remainder" (*śeṣe*). Thus: *naiśikam* or *naiśam*; *prādoṣikam* or *prādoṣam*.
*Śvas-tuṭ ca* (3.2.75):

After *śvas*, when the remainder [of the day] is to be expressed, the suffix *ṭhañ* is optionally applied, and there is the augment *tuṭ*. [Examples: *śauvastikam*, *śvastyam*, *śvastanam*. *Prāhṇe-prage-sāyaṃ-ciram-asamkhyāṭ ṭyuḥ* (3.2.76): After the words *prāhṇe*, *prage*, *sāyam*, *ciram*, and an indeclinable (*asaṃkhyāt*) expressing time, the suffix *ṭyu* is applied.

The suffix *ṭyu* occurs after words beginning with *prāhṇa*, as well as after numerals, in the sense of "remainder" (*śeṣe*), and there is the augment *tuṭ*. Examples: *prāhṇetanam*, *pragetanam*; the vowel *e* [in these forms] results from a specific grammatical rule (*nipātana*). *sāyantanam*, *cirantanam*; the letter *m* [in these forms] results from a specific grammatical rule. After non-numerical words: *doṣātanam*, *divātanam*. Only when referring to time (*kālebhyaḥ*): *svarbhavam*, *sauvam*. According to Pāṇini 3.2.77, after *pūrvāhṇa* and *aparāhṇa*, the suffix is optional.

From these two [words], when the sense of "remainder" (*śeṣa*) is intended, the suffix *ṭyu* optionally occurs, along with the augment *tuṭ*. Thus: *pūrvāhṇetanam*, *paurvāhṇikam*; *aparāhṇetanam*, *āparāhṇikam*. [The *ṭyu* suffix is used here] because of the rule *saptamyā bahulam* (Pāṇini 5.2.11), which allows for the non-elision (*aluk*) of the locative case-ending. However, when the meaning is "that by whom the forenoon was endured," then the form is *pūrvāhṇatanaḥ*. Regarding the rule *parutparāricirāt tnaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.78): after the words *parut* and others, the suffix *tna* optionally occurs in the sense of "remainder. Thus: *paruttnaḥ*, *paruttanaḥ*; *parāritnaḥ*, *parāritanaḥ*; *ciratnaḥ*, *cirantanaḥ*.

(3.2.79) *sandhyādy-ṛtu-nakṣatrād aṇ*: After the words beginning with *sandhyā*, after words denoting seasons (*ṛtu*), and after words denoting lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*), the suffix *aṇ* occurs in the sense of "remainder" (*śeṣe*). Examples: *sāndhyam*, *sāndhivelam*; *graiṣmam*, *śaiśiram*; *pauṣam*, *taiṣam*. [The list of *sandhyā* etc. is: *sandhyā*, *sandhivelā*, *amāvāsyā*, *trayodaśī*, *caturdaśī*, *pañcadaśī*, *paurṇamāsī*, *pratipad*. [The suffix *aṇ* also occurs] after *saṃvatsara* when meaning "fruit" (*phala*) or "festival" (*parvan*). (3.2.80) *hemantād vā talopaś ca*: After *hemanta*, the suffix *aṇ* optionally occurs, and there is also the elision (*lopa*) of the *ta* sound.

After *hemanta*, when the sense of "remainder" (*śeṣe*) applies, the suffix *aṇ* optionally occurs, and in that case, the elision of the final *t* is also optional. Thus: *haimanam*, *haimantam*, *haimantikam*. According to Pāṇini 4.3.19 (*varṣāprāvṛḍbhyāṃ ṭhageṇyau*), after *varṣā* and *prāvṛṣ*, the suffixes *ṭhak* and *eṇya* respectively occur when the sense of "remainder" applies. Thus: *vārṣikam* (from *varṣā* with *ṭhak*) and *prāvṛṣeṇyam* (from *prāvṛṣ* with *eṇya*).

*madhyādibhyāṃ maḥ* (Pāṇini 5.4.106): After the words *madhya* and *ādi*, the suffix *ma* occurs in the sense of "remainder" (*śeṣe*). Thus: *madhyamaḥ*, *ādimaḥ*. The word *madhya* itself denotes the meaning "middling" (*sāṃpratike 'rthe*). A woman who is *madhyā* is neither too tall nor too short; the meaning is that she is of moderate proportions. How is *adhamaḥ* [formed]? It is due to the indicatory evidence (*jñāpaka*) in the rule *parāvarādhamottamāder* (Vārttika 67). *Avamaḥ* is derived from the Uṇādi suffixes. *Agrāntapaścād imac* (Pāṇini 5.4.107).
The suffix *imac* occurs after [the words] *agra* and others when the sense of "remainder" (*śeṣa*) is intended. Examples: *agrimaḥ*, *antimaḥ*, *paścimaḥ*.
The second quarter of the third chapter is completed.
In that regard, [the rule] *prāvṛṣaṣ ṭhap* (Pāṇini 4.3.26) applies to the sense of "born therein" (*tatra jātaḥ*).

The suffix *ṭhaP* occurs after the word *prāvṛṣ* ending in the locative case when [the sense] "born" (*jāta*) is expressed. Thus: *prāvṛṣi jātaḥ* = *prāvṛṣikaḥ* ("born in the rainy season"). How is it that [words like] *sraughnaḥ* ("born in Srughna"), *rāṣṭriyaḥ* ("born in the kingdom"), and *pārāvārīṇaḥ* ("born on this side or that side of the ocean") are formed? They are established by the rule *śeṣe* (Pāṇini 4.2.92). If that were so, then because there would be no restriction, the suffixes *aṇ* and others, as well as *gha* and others, would apply everywhere even in cases such as *tatrāste* ("he stays there") or *tatra śete* ("he sleeps there"). No; for from those [suffixes], that specific meaning is not understood. The sequential listing of [suffixes] beginning with *jāta* is, however, for the purpose of setting aside [the application of] obstructing rules. How then are *śāradakā darbhāḥ* ("autumnal *darbha* grass") and *śāradakā mudgāḥ* ("autumnal *mudga* beans") formed? They are formed by adding *kan* to a word ending in the suffix *ṛtvaṇ* when it is a proper name (*saṃjñā*).

Regarding the rule *pūrvāhṇāparāhṇārdrāmūlapradoṣāvaskarāt kan nāmni* (Pāṇini 3.3.2): the suffix *kan* is applied after the words *pūrvāhṇa*, *aparāhṇa*, *ārdrā*, *mūla*, *pradoṣa*, and *avaskara* when they end in the locative case, provided that the word refers to something born [therein] and forms a proper name (*saṃjñā*). Examples: *pūrvāhṇakaḥ*, *aparāhṇakaḥ*, *ārdrakaḥ*. [In these, the vowel shortening occurs] by the rule *ke 'ṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.2.70). Examples: *mūlakaḥ*, *pradoṣakaḥ*, *avaskarakaḥ*. Why does it say "when it is a proper name" (*nāmni*)? Consider: *pūrvāhṇetanaḥ* ("born this morning"). [The next rule: *panthakaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.3.3).

The suffix *kan* is applied to the word *pathin* when it occurs as a proper name (*saṃjñā*), and there is the substitution of *pantha*. Thus: *panthakaḥ*. From the words *sindhu* and *apakara*, the suffix *kan* optionally occurs (Pāṇini 4.2.97).

Thus: *sindhukaḥ* or *saindhavaḥ*. [In the latter case,] the suffix *aṇ* applies because these words are listed in the *kacchādi* group. Thus: *apakarakaḥ* or *āpakaraḥ*. Only when used as a proper name (*nāman*) does this apply; otherwise: *saindhavakaḥ* as a human being.
(3.3.5) *amāvasyārthād aś ca*:

After a word denoting *amāvasyā*, the suffix *kan* is optionally applied in the sense of "born there," and the suffix *a* is also optionally applied. [Examples: born on *amāvasyā*—*Amāvasyakaḥ*, *Amāvasyaḥ*, *Āmāvasyaḥ*; *Amāvāsyakaḥ*, *Amāvāsyaḥ*, *Āmāvāsyaḥ*. [The form] *āmāvāsyaḥ* is derived with the suffix *aṇ* because it belongs to the *saṃdhyādi* group. Only when it is a name (*nāman*) is it thus: *āmāvāsyaḥ*. (3.3.6) *sthānāntagośālakharaśālāl luk*: The suffix *luk* is applied after words ending in *sthāna*, as well as after *gośāla* and *kharaśāla*.

The elision (*luk*) occurs of the suffix prescribed after words such as *sthāna* when [the sense] "born" (*jāta*) is expressed. For example: born in *Gosthāna*, *Gosthānaḥ*; born in *Aśvasthāna*, *Aśvasthānaḥ*. Born in *Gośāla*, *Gośālaḥ*. Because the feminine form is also included by virtue of being specified by gender: born in *Gośālā*, *Gośālaḥ*. Likewise, *Kharaśālaḥ*. [According to Pāṇini 4.3.25: "After [words ending in] *vatsa*, *śāla*, and *nakṣatra*, [the suffix is applied] diversely (*bahulam*). (3.3.7).

When a name is formed from the word *vatsaśālā* or from the names of lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*), the suffix is generally elided. For example: one born in *vatsaśālā* or born in *vatsaśālā* is called *Vātsaśālaḥ* or *Vatsaśālaḥ*. From the following lunar mansions, the suffix is elided exclusively: *Anurādhaḥ*, *Svātiḥ*, *Tiṣyaḥ*, *Puṣyaḥ*, *Punarvasuḥ*, *Hastaḥ*, *Viśākhaḥ*, and *Bahulaḥ* (where *bahulāḥ* refers to the *kṛttikā*s). In some cases, there is an option: *Mṛgaśirāḥ* or *Mārgaśīrṣaḥ*; *Abhijit* or *Ābhijitaḥ*; *Aśvayuk* or *Āśvayujaḥ*.

*Śatabhiṣak*, *Śātabhiṣajaḥ*; *Citraḥ*, *Caitraḥ*; *Revataḥ*, *Raivataḥ*; *Rohiṇaḥ*, *Rauhiṇaḥ*. In the feminine, however, there is simply elision (*luk*) after *citrā* and the others: *Citrā*, *Rohiṇī*, *Revatī*. Even when elision of the *ṅī* and *āp* suffixes has occurred, the suffix *ḍāp* is applied again, and because they belong to the *gaurādi* group, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is added. According to Pāṇini 4.1.8, "The suffix *ḍit aṇ* [is applied] after asterisms (*nakṣatra*) optionally": thus we have *Śātabhiṣajaḥ* and *Śātabhiṣaḥ*.

From *śraviṣṭhā* and *āṣāḍhā*, the suffix *chaṇ* occurs diversely (*bahulam*) to denote that which is born [at that time]. [Examples: *śrāviṣṭhīyaḥ*, *śrāviṣṭhaḥ*, *śraviṣṭhaḥ*; *āṣāḍhīyaḥ*, *āṣāḍhaḥ*, *aṣāḍhaḥ*. From *phalgunī*, the suffix *ṭa* [occurs diversely].

When [the suffix] *ṭha* is added after *phalgunī*, it frequently becomes *pha*. Thus: *phalgunaḥ*, *phalgunī*; [also] *phālgunaḥ*. According to some, here it is simply by the rule "names of months" (*yāvan-nāmni*) that we have *phālgunaḥ*. How is it that one who was bought, obtained, made, skilled in, born in, or exists in *srughna* is called *sraughnaḥ*, or *rāṣṭriyaḥ*? This is already established by the rule "in the remaining cases" (*śeṣe*, 4.2.92). Likewise: good for winter is *haimanam* ointment, or *haimantam*, or *haimantikam*. Those which blossom in spring are *vāsantyaḥ* flowers.
