Those that ripen in autumn are *śāradāḥ* rice plants; those sown in winter are *haimanāḥ* barley. Regarding the rule *aśvayujyām upte vuñ* (Pāṇini 4.3.11): the suffix *vuñ* occurs after the locative form of the word *aśvayujī* when it means "sown. Thus, *āśvayujakāḥ* refers to beans sown on the full moon day of the month of Āśvayuja.

After *grīṣma* and *vasanta*, the suffix *vuñ* is optionally applied when [the crop] is sown during those seasons. Thus: *graiṣmakam* or *graiṣmam* "a crop sown in summer"; *vāsantakam* or *vāsantam* "a crop sown in spring.
After a word denoting time, the suffix *vuñ* is applied to express a debt to be paid at that time. (Pāṇini 4.3.13)

The suffixes *ṭhañ* and others, as prescribed, occur after time-denoting words ending in the locative case (*saptamī*) when that which is to be given (*deya*) is a debt (*ṛṇa*). For example, a debt to be paid in a month is *māsikam*. Likewise, *graiṣmam*. Why specify "debt"? [Consider: alms to be given in a month (*māse deyā bhikṣā*). By rule 3.3.14, *vun* occurs after the words *kalāpī*, *aśvattha*, and *yavabusā* when they end in the locative case and indicate time, in the sense of "a debt to be given. For instance: a debt to be given when the peacocks have their plumage (*kalāpiṣu*), when the *aśvattha* trees bear fruit, or when the chaff of barley (*yavabusāḥ*) has appeared: *kalāpakam*, *aśvatthakam*, *yavabusakam*.
(3.3.15) *grīṣmāvarasamād vuñ*: After the words *grīṣma* and *avarasama*, the suffix *vuñ* occurs in the sense of "a debt to be paid" (*deyam ṛṇam*). [Examples: *graiṣmakam*, *āvarasamakam*.
(3.3.16) *saṃvatsarāgrahāyaṇyāṣ ṭhañ ca*: After the words *saṃvatsara* and *agrahāyaṇī*, the suffix *ṭhañ* also [occurs] [in the same sense].

The suffix *ṭhañ* (and also *vuñ*) occurs in this sense: "a debt to be paid after a year" (*saṃvatsarāt*) or "on the full moon day of Āgrahāyaṇī" (*āgrahāyaṇyāḥ*). Examples: *sāṃvatsarikam*, *sāṃvatsarakam*; *āgrahāyaṇikam*, *āgrahāyaṇakam*. However, when the meaning is "interest to be paid after a year," the mention of *ṭhañ* is made so that the suffix *aṇ*—which would apply by virtue of its inclusion in the *saṃdhy-ādi* group—does not occur. As for the forms *naiśaḥ* and *naiśikaḥ* in the sense of "a wild animal crying out at night," they are already established by [Pāṇini 4.3.12], which governs the remaining meanings (*śeṣe*). Furthermore, even for something other than a wild animal, these suffixes certainly occur in the sense of "belonging to" (*bhava-artha*).

For whoever speaks at night becomes one who exists at night (*naiśa*). And it is the threefold derivation (*traiśabdya*) that is to be established here. Thus, *naiśa* or *naiśika* means either "night is endurable for him" or "study at night is endurable for him.
[This is derived] by the rule *digādibhyo yad bhaviṣye* (Pāṇini 4.3.54).

The suffix *yat* occurs after words ending in the locative case, such as *diś* and others, when the sense is "belonging to" (*bhave*). Examples: *diśyam*, *vargyam*. The list includes: *diś*, *varga*, *pūga*, *gaṇa*, *pakṣa*, *dhāyyā*, *mitra*, *medhā*, *antar*, *pathin*, *rahas*, *alīka*, *ukhā*, *sākṣin*, *ādi*, *anta*, *mukha*, *jaghana*. The reading [of *mukha* and *jaghana*] is for the purpose of excluding parts of the body: *mukhyaḥ* (foremost), *jaghanyaḥ* (lowest). [The suffix *yat* occurs] after *megha*, *yūtha*, and *udaka* when forming a proper name (*saṃjñāyām*): *udakyā* (a menstruating woman). [The suffix *yat* occurs] after *nyāya*, *vaṃśa*, *anuvaṃśa*, *deśa*, *kāla*, and *ākāśa*. [The suffix *yat* occurs] after a word denoting a part of the body, according to Pāṇini 4.3.55 (*adehāṃśāt*).

That which arises from a part of the body [is expressed by the suffix *yañ*]: dental (*dantya*), labial (*oṣṭhya*). According to Pāṇini 4.3.55, *dṛtikukṣikalaśivastyastyaher ḍhañ*, the suffix *ḍhañ* occurs after *dṛti* and the others when expressing "originating therefrom" (*bhave*): *dārteya*, *kaukṣeya*, *kālaśeya*, *vāsteya*, *āsteya*, *āheya*.
(3.3.20) *grīvāto ’ṇ ca*:
after *grīvā*, when [the suffix] *aṇ* occurs, there is also *ḍhañ*. Thus: *graivam* and *graiveyam*.
(3.3.21) *gambhīrapañcajanāñ ñyaḥ*: after *gambhīra* and *pañcajana*, the suffix *ñya* occurs.

The suffix *ñya* occurs after the words *gambhīra* and *pañcajana*. Thus, *gāmbhīryaḥ* and *pāñcajanyaḥ*. However, after the words *bahiḥ* and *deva*, [the suffix] is established by the preceding rule. Regarding the rule *cāturmāsyaṃ yājñe* (Pāṇini 4.2.62):

in the sense of "that which occurs during four months" when referring to a sacrifice (*yajña*), the suffix *ñya* is applied as an irregularity (*nipātana*). Thus, *cāturmāsyam*. As for the word *cāturmāsyāni*: the suffix *aṇ* need not be mentioned after *caturmāsa* in the sense of a name (*saṃjñā*), because it is already established by the general rule *śeṣe* (Pāṇini 4.2.92). The word *cāturmāsī* refers to the full moon day (*paurṇamāsī*) of Āṣāḍha, Kārttika, or Phālguna. Furthermore, there is no elision (*luk*) of the suffix, because the specific name is understood.

(3.3.23) *parimukhādibhyaḥ*: The suffix *ñya* occurs after [words] beginning with *parimukha*. That which exists facing the face (*parimukham*) is *pārimukhyaḥ*. *Pārihanavyaḥ*. The list begins with: *parimukha*, *parihanu*, *paryoṣṭha*, *paryulūkhala*, *parisīra*, *anusīra*, *upasīra*, *upasthūṇa*, *upakalāpa*, *anupatha*, *anugaṅga*, *anutila*, *anusīta*, *anusāta*, *anupada*, *anuyūpa*, *anuvaṃśa*, *anumāṣa*, *anuyava*.

The recitation of the case endings (*vibhaktipāṭha*) is for the purpose of making known the predominance of the compound that does not involve a number (*asaṃkhyasamāsa*); therefore, [the suffix] does not apply here: *parimukham* (surrounding the face), and *pārimukhaḥ* (born there). Regarding the rule *antaḥpūrvāt tadarthāt ṭhañ* (Pāṇini 4.3.60): the suffix *ṭhañ* occurs after a word preceded by *antar*, provided that the first member of the compound is predominant in expressing that meaning (*tadartha*). Examples: *āntargehikam* (inside the house), *āntarvaṃśikam* (inside the lineage). This is a compound according to the rule *vibhaktyarthe yad asaṃkhyam* (Pāṇini 2.1.6). Why say "expressing that meaning" (*tadarthāt*)? Consider: *āntaḥkaraṇam* (pertaining to the internal organ), which means "that which exists within the internal organ" (*antaḥkaraṇe bhavam*). Here, the first member is not predominant in expressing that meaning.

(3.3.25) *paryanubhyāṃ grāmāt*: after the words *pari* and *anu* preceding *grāma*, the suffix *ṭhañ* occurs when the sense is "originating therefrom. Examples: *pārigrāmikaḥ*, *ānugrāmikaḥ*. By the rule *tadarthāt* [3.3.14] alone: "the village has been traversed" (*parigato grāmaḥ*); that which originates therein is *pārigrāmaḥ*. (3.3.26) *samānāt*.
The suffix *ṭhañ* occurs after *samāna* when the sense is "belonging to" (*bhave*). Thus: *sāmānikaḥ*.
By the rule *tadādeḥ* (Pāṇini 4.3.27), the suffix *ṭhañ* occurs after words beginning with *samāna* in the sense of "belonging to. Thus: *sāmānagrāmikaḥ*, *sāmānadeśikaḥ*.

(3.3.28) *lokāntāt*: The suffix *ṭhañ* occurs after a word ending in *loka* when the sense is "occurring therein" (*bhave*). Examples: *aihaukikaḥ* ("belonging to this world"), *pāralaukikaḥ* ("belonging to the next world"). By the rule *anuśatikādīnām* (6.1.30), the *aiC* substitution occurs for both members of the compound. (3.3.29) *adhyātmādibhyaḥ*.

The suffix *ṭhañ* occurs after *adhyātma* and the following words when the sense is "occurring therein" (*bhave*). Examples: *ādhyātmika*, *ādhidaivika*, *ādhibhautika*, *aurdhvadehika*. This is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open class of words).
By the rule *jihvāmūlāṅguleś chaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.3.62), the suffix *cha* occurs after these two [words] in the sense of "occurring therein. Examples: *jihvāmūlīya*, *aṅgulīya*.

(3.3.31) After a word ending in a consonant of a *varga* group, the suffix *cha* occurs in the sense of "belonging to. For example: *kavargīyaḥ* ("belonging to the *ka*-group") and *cavargīyaḥ* ("belonging to the *ca*-group").
(3.3.32) When not referring to a sound (*aśabda*), the suffixes *yat* and *kha* also occur.

After the word *śabda*, when followed by the suffix *vargānta*, the suffix *cha* occurs, as well as *yat* and *kha*. Examples: *Arjunavargīyaḥ*, *Arjunavargyaḥ*, *Arjunavargīnaḥ*. Why does it say "not after *śabda*"? [To exclude cases like: *kavargīyaḥ*.

After the word *madhya*, the suffixes *maṇ*, *mīya*, and *cha* occur when expressing "born there" (*bhave*). Examples: *mādhyamaḥ*, *madhyamīyaḥ*, *madhyīyaḥ*. [The term] *mādhyandinaḥ* refers to those who chant the *udgītha*, used figuratively (*tadupacārāt*) based on that connection.
(3.3.34) *kan* is added after *lalāṭa* when the meaning is "ornament. [The form is] *lalāṭikā*.
(3.3.35) After *karṇa*...

The suffix *kan* occurs after *karṇa* when it means "ornament. Thus, *karṇikā*. By rule 3.3.36, *upādeṣ ṭhak*, the suffix *ṭhak* occurs after *karṇa* preceded by *upa* in the sense of "originating therefrom" (*bhave*). Thus, *aupakarṇikam*.

By [Pāṇini 4.3.37], *jānu* and *vī* preceded by *upa*, the suffix *ṭhak* occurs in the sense of "originating therefrom" (*bhava*). Thus: *aupajānuka* ("originating at the knee") and *aupanīvika* ("originating at the navel"). This is already established by [the rule] "also in the sense of 'mostly originating therefrom' (*prāyabhava*).
Furthermore, by [Pāṇini 4.3.38]: "And [the suffix *ṭhak* occurs] after the name of that which is to be explained, in the sense of 'explaining that'."

The suffixes *aṇ* and others, as prescribed, occur after a word ending in the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) denoting that which is to be explained (*vyākhyeya*), when the sense is "explanation" (*vyākhyāna*); and after a word ending in the seventh case (*saptamī*), when the sense is "occurring therein" (*bhava*). For example: *supāṃ vyākhyānam* (the explanation of the case-endings) or *supsu bhavam* (that which occurs in the case-endings), resulting in *saupam*. Similarly, *taiṅam*. Why is it said "after the name of that which is to be explained"? Consider: *Pāṭaliputrasya vyākhyānī Sukosalā* (Sukosalā is the expounder of Pāṭaliputra). How is it so? [In these cases: *Aśvatthāmni bhavaḥ* (that which occurs in Aśvatthāman), resulting in *Aśvatthāmā*; *kṛṣṇājine bhavam* (that which occurs in a black antelope skin), resulting in *kṛṣṇājinam*; *siṃhājinam* (that which occurs in a lion's skin); *agniṣṭome bhavo mantraḥ* (a mantra occurring in the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice), resulting in *agniṣṭomaḥ*.

The *kalpa* is the exposition (*vyākhyāna*) of the *agniṣṭoma*; thus, it is called "Agniṣṭoma" by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*). In that case, would not the suffixes *aṇ* and so forth also apply? Indeed, they are intended when there is the desire to express "this belongs to that. Furthermore, a threefold expression (*traiśabdya*) is to be established here. The simultaneous mention of the scopes for [the suffixes] *bhava* and *vyākhyāna* is for the purpose of subverting what would otherwise subvert them. [This is governed by] Pāṇini 4.3.70: *bahvaco 'ntodāttāṭ ṭhañ*.

The suffix *ṭhañ* occurs after a polysyllabic word that has an oxytone final vowel when expressing "originating from" (*bhava*) or "explaining" (*vyākhyāna*). Examples: *ṣātvaṇatvikam*, *nātānatikam*. [In these cases] the final syllable is oxytone by the rule *samāsasya* [P. 6.1.223]. Why say "polysyllabic"? [Counter-examples: *saupam*, *taiṅam*. Why say "having an oxytone final vowel"? [Counter-examples: *saṃhitāyāḥ*, *sāṃhitam*. [In this case] it is ādyudātta (accented on the first syllable) due to the accentuation rule for *prādi* compounds. Accents such as udātta and others are well known, just like the *visarjanīya* and other grammatical elements. [This concludes the section on] *yajñebhyaḥ* (P. 4.3.115).

The suffix *ṭhañ* occurs after words denoting sacrifices (*yajña*) in the senses of "originating therefrom" (*bhava*) and "commentary thereon" (*vyākhyāna*). Examples: *āgniṣṭomikam*, *vājapeyikam*, *pāñcaudanikam*, *dāśaudanikam*. The plural number is used for the purpose of including all sacrifices. Regarding the rule *adhyāyeṣv evārṣeḥ* (Pāṇini 4.3.72):

the suffix *ṭhañ* occurs after words denoting sages (*ṛṣi*) in the senses of "originating therefrom" and "commentary thereon," provided that the referents are specifically chapters (*adhyāya*). For example, a chapter that is a commentary on a work by Vasiṣṭha, or which originates from it, is called *vāsiṣṭhikaḥ*; likewise, *vaiśvāmitrikaḥ*. Why specify "only in the case of chapters"? Consider: *vāsiṣṭhī ṛk* ("a verse [ṛc] belonging to Vasiṣṭha"). Here, because the referent is not a chapter, the suffix *ṭhak* is applied instead.

*Pauroḍāśapuroḍāśāt ṣṭhan* (3.3.42): From these two [words], *pauroḍāśa* and *puroḍāśa*, the suffix *ṣṭhan* occurs in the senses of "belonging to" (*bhava*) and "explaining" (*vyākhyāna*). [Examples: *pauroḍāśikaḥ*, *pauroḍāśikī*; *puroḍāśikaḥ*, *puroḍāśikī*. *Chandaso yat* (3.3.43).
The suffix *aṇ* occurs after the word *chandas* in the senses of "originating therefrom" (*bhava*) and "explanation" (*vyākhyāna*). [Thus: *chāndasyam*.
By rule 3.3.44, *aṇ* occurs after *chandas* in the senses of "originating therefrom" and "explanation. [Thus: *chāndasam*.

(3.3.45) *ṛgayanādibhyaḥ*: The suffix *aṇ* occurs after the group beginning with *ṛgayana* in the senses of "originating therefrom" (*bhava*) and "explanation" (*vyākhyāna*). Examples: *ārgayaṇaḥ* ("originating from the *ṛgayana*") and *pādavyākhyānaḥ* ("an explanation of the *pāda*"). The list is as follows: *ṛgayana*, *padavyākhyāna*, *chandovyākhyāna*, *chandonāman*, *chandobhāṣā*, *chandoviciti*, *chandovijiti*, *nyāya*, *nirukta*, *punarukta*, *vyākaraṇa*, *nigama*, *vāstuvidyā*, *aṅgavidyā*, *kṣatravidyā*, *kṣatriyavidyā*, *utpāta*, *utpāda*, *saṃvatsara*, *yajña*, *carcā*, *ślakṣṇa*, *muhūrta*, *nimitta*, *upaniṣad*, and *śikṣā*.

Pāṇini 4.3.46: *dvyaj-ṛk-sām-brāhmaṇa-prathama-adhvara-puraścaraṇa-nāma-ākhyāta-ṭhak*. The suffix *ṭhak* is applied after words consisting of two syllables, after those ending in *ṛ*, after the word *ṛc*, and after the group beginning with *brāhmaṇa*, in the senses of "originating therefrom" (*bhava*) and "explaining that" (*vyākhyāna*). Examples: *aiṣṭikam* (relating to a sacrifice), *cāturhotṛkam* (relating to the four officiating priests), *ārcikam* (relating to the *ṛc* verses), *brāhmaṇikam* (relating to a Brāhmaṇa), *prāthamikam* (relating to the first), *ādhvarikam* (relating to a sacrifice), *pauraścaraṇikam* (relating to preparatory rites), *nāmākhyātikam* (relating to nouns and verbs), *nāmikam* (relating to a noun), *ākhyātikam* (relating to a verb). Pāṇini 4.3.47: *āyasthānād āgate*. The suffix *ṭhak* is applied after the word *āyasthāna* in the sense of "come from" (*āgata*). Example: *āyasthānikaḥ* (one who has come from a place of refuge).

The suffix *ṭhak* occurs after words denoting sources of income when they appear in the fifth case (*pañcamī*). For example: *śulkaśālāyā āgataḥ* (come from the toll-house) becomes *śaulkaśālikaḥ*. Similarly, *ātarikaḥ* (from the ferry) and *āpaṇikaḥ* (from the market). How is it that *srughnād āgataḥ* (come from Srughna) results in *sraughnaḥ*, and *rāṣṭriyaḥ* (from the kingdom), and so forth? This is already established by the rule *śeṣe* (Pāṇini 4.2.92).

By the rule *śuṇḍikādibhyo ’ṇ* (Pāṇini 4.3.48), the suffix *aṇ* occurs after words beginning with *śuṇḍika* when meaning "come from. Thus: *śauṇḍikaḥ* (from the tavern) and *kārkaṇaḥ* (from the *karkaṇa* plant). The mention of *aṇ* is for the sake of including *udapāna*. The list is: *śuṇḍika*, *kṛkaṇa*, *udapāna*, *sthaṇḍila*, *upatīrtha*, *bhūmi*, *tṛṇa*, *parṇa*.

*Vidyāyonisaṃbandhād vuñ* (Pāṇini 4.3.77): The suffix *vuñ* occurs after words denoting a connection through learning (*vidyā*) or a connection through birth (*yoni*) when something has come [from that source]. Examples: *aupādhyāyakam* (derived from *upādhyāya*), *śaiṣyakam* (derived from *śiṣya*); *mātāmahakam* (derived from *mātāmaha*), *paitāmahakam* (derived from *pitāmaha*). *Ṛtaḥ kañ* (Pāṇini 4.3.78): The suffix *kañ* occurs after a word ending in the vowel *ṛ*.

The suffix *kañ* occurs after a word ending in *ṛt* in the sense of "come from" (*āgate*). For example: *hautṛkam*, *mātṛkam*. This applies specifically when the relationship is based on learning or biological origin; thus: *sāvitram*. Alternatively, *pitryam* (3.3.51):
in the sense of "come from a father," the form *pitryam* is optionally prescribed as a *nipātana*; thus: *pitryam* or *paitṛkam*.

*rūpya-* (3.3.52): After words denoting "man" (*manuṣya*) and after words denoting "cause" (*hetu*), the suffix *rūpya* optionally occurs in the sense of "come from" (*āgata*). From Devadatta: *devadattarūpyam*, *daivadattam*. Come from the cause "peace" (*sāma*): *samarūpyam*, *samīyam*. [The latter] is formed with the suffix *cha* due to its inclusion in the *gahādi* group. *mayaṭ* (3.3.53).
The suffix *mayaṭ* occurs when [something] has come from human causes. For example: *devadattamayam* ("made by Devadatta"), *samamayam* ("made by Samas").
Regarding the rule *gotrād aṅkavat* (Pāṇini 4.3.126):

after a word ending in a patronymic (*gotra*) suffix that has been prescribed [by the rules], when [something] has come [from them], the suffixes *aṇ* and others occur just as they do in the case of a mark (*aṅka*). Examples: *Aupagavebhya āgatam* → *Aupagavakam* ("come from the descendants of Upagu"); *Baidam*, *Gārgam*, *Dākṣam*; *Śākalam*, *Śākalakam*.

The word *vaidūrya* (3.3.55) is an irregularly formed (*nipātita*) term denoting a specific kind of gem produced in Vidūra. How so? [One might ask: "The Gaṅgā originates from the Himavat, thus she is *Haimavatī*; the path or messenger goes to Srughna, thus it is *Sraughna*; [one born in] a kingdom is *Rāṣṭriya*; the gate issues forth from Srughna, thus it is *Sraughna*; a book composed concerning Subhadrā is *Saubhadra*. [To this we reply: This is already established by the rule *śeṣe* (4.2.92). If that is so, then [the suffix] would apply here as well: [for example, to the word *vaidūrya*].

In cases such as *srughnaṃ gacchati sārthaḥ* ("The caravan goes to Srughna"), *srughnam abhiniṣkrāmati panthāḥ* ("The road leads out to Srughna"), and *subhadrām adhikṛtya kṛtaḥ prāsādaḥ* ("A palace was built concerning Subhadrā"), [the suffix *cha*] is indeed desired when there is the intention to express "his own" (*tasya svam*).

Regarding the rule *śiśukrandādibhyo dvitīyāntebhyo 'dhikṛtya kṛte granthe chaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.3.88): the suffix *cha* occurs after words such as *śiśukranda*, etc., ending in the second case, when a book is composed concerning them. Examples include: *śiśukrandīyaḥ*, *yamasabhīyaḥ*, *indrajananīyaḥ*, and *sītānveṣaṇīyaḥ*.

(3.3.57) *cārthān adevāsurādīn*: After compounds expressing the sense of "and" (*ca*), excluding those beginning with *deva* and *asura*, when a work is composed concerning a noun ending in the second case, the suffix *cha* is applied. Examples: *śyenakapotīyaḥ* ("concerning the hawk and the pigeon"), *saṃvartamaruttīyaḥ* ("concerning Saṃvarta and Marutta"). Why say "excluding those beginning with *deva* and *asura*"? [Counter-examples: *daivāsuram* ("concerning gods and asuras"), *rākṣo'suram* ("concerning Rākṣasas and asuras"), *gauṇamukhyam* ("concerning the secondary and the primary"). How then do we account for *Vāsavadattā* and *Bandhumatī*? This is because there is an intention to express them through the metaphorical treatment of non-difference (*abhedopacāra*). In the case of *Bhaimarathī*, there is no such intention to express non-difference. How then do we derive *Sraughnaḥ* from "Srughna is his residence" (*srughno nivāso 'sya*) or "Srughna is his ancestral home" (*srughno 'syābhijanaḥ*)? [This is derived by the rule 4.3.89.]

Regarding the term *rāṣṭriya*: it is already established by [Pāṇini 4.3.93] *śeṣe*. As for [the formation of] *so 'syābhijanaḥ* from mountains, it is [governed by] [Pāṇini 4.3.112] *giribhyaḥ śastrajīviṣu*.

The suffix *cha* occurs after mountain names denoting one's ancestral home (*abhijana*), when they appear in the nominative case and the sense of the genitive case is intended, provided that those to be designated are weapon-bearers (*āyudhajīvin*). For example: *Hṛdgola* is the mountain that is their ancestral home; thus, the weapon-bearers [living there] are called *Hṛdgolīyāḥ*. Similarly, *Bhojakaṭīyāḥ* and *Rohitagirīyāḥ*. Why "from mountains" (*giribhyaḥ*)? [Consider: *Sāṃkāśyakāḥ* are weapon-bearers [but not from a mountain]. Why "when [the referents] are weapon-bearers" (*śastrajīviṣu*)? [Consider: *Ṛkṣoda* is the mountain that is the ancestral home of these Brahmins; thus, they are called *Ārkṣodāḥ*. In this context, "ancestral home" (*abhijana*) refers to where one's ancestors lived; "residence" (*nivāsa*) refers to where one currently lives.
*Śālāturīyaḥ* (3.3.59):
In the sense of "one whose ancestral home (*abhijana*) is Śalātura," the form *Śālāturīya* is prescribed as an irregular formation (*nipātana*).
*Śaṇḍikādibhyo ñyaḥ* (3.3.60).

The suffix *ñya* is applied after [the words] *śaṇḍika* and others in the sense of "this is his ancestral lineage" (*so 'syābhijanaḥ*). Examples: *śāṇḍikyaḥ*, *kaucavāryaḥ*. [The base words are: *śaṇḍika*, *kucavāra*, *sarvakeśa*, *sarvasena*, *śaka*, *śaṭa*, *vaha*, *śaṅkha*, *bodha*.
[Also, the suffix] *aṇ* is applied after *sindhu* and others [in the same sense]. (Pāṇini 4.3.93; cf. 4.3.61).

The suffix *aṇ* is applied after [the group of words beginning with] *sindhvādi* in the sense of "this is his native place" (*so 'syābhijanaḥ*). Examples: *Saindhavaḥ*, *Vārṇavaḥ*. [Sindhvādi list: Sindhu, Varṇu, Gandhāra, Madhumat, Kamboja, Kaśmīra, Śālva, Kiṣkindhā, Gandika, Urasa, Darad, Takṣaśilā, Vatsoddharaṇa, Kaumedura, Kāṇḍavāra, Grāmaṇī, Śakala, Chagalaka, Kaṃsa, Kiṃnara, Saṃkucita, Siṃhakoṣṭha, Karṇa, Barbara, Avasāna.

As for those [villages] listed among *kaccha* and the others, since the suffix *aṇ* would already apply to them, this rule is stated as an exception (*apavāda*) to *vuñ*. Furthermore, it serves as an exception to both *ṭhañ* and *ñika* for villages belonging to the *bāhīka* region.

Regarding *tudī* and *varmatī*, [Pāṇini 4.3.94] states: "After *tudī* and *varmatī*, the suffix *ḍhañ* occurs" in the sense of "this is his native place" (*so 'syābhijanaḥ*). Thus: *taudeyaḥ*, *vārmateyaḥ*.

In this context, [the rule] *mahārājāṭ ṭhak* (Pāṇini 4.3.63) means that the suffix *ṭhak* occurs after the word *mahārāja* when it ends in the seventh case (*saptamī*), in the sense of "whose devotion is toward this. For example, one whose devotion is toward the Great King (*mahārāja*) is called *māhārājika*. How is it that one whose devotion is toward *Srughna* is called *Sraughna*, or *rāṣṭriya*? This is already established by the rule *śeṣe* (Pāṇini 4.2.92).
[The next rule is: *acittād adeśakālāt* (Pāṇini 4.3.64).

The suffix *ṭhak* occurs in the sense of "one who has devotion (*bhakti*) toward that," provided the word denoting the object is not a name of a sentient being (*acittavācin*) and does not refer to a place or time (*adeśakālāt*). For example: one who has devotion toward cakes (*apūpa*) is called *āpūpikaḥ*; one who has devotion toward *śaṣkuli* is called *śāṣkulikaḥ*. Why "not a name of a sentient being"? [Consider] *Daivadattaḥ*. Why "not a place or time"? [Consider] *Sraughnaḥ* (one from Śrughna) and *Haimanaḥ* (one from winter). Regarding *vāsudevārjunāt kan* (Pāṇini 4.3.98):
the suffix *kan* occurs after these two words in the sense of "one who has devotion toward that. Thus: *Vāsudevakaḥ* and *Arjunakaḥ*.

*Gotrād bahulaṃ vuñ* (3.3.66): After a word ending in a patronymic suffix that has been prescribed [by rules such as 4.1.95], the suffix *vuñ* is optionally applied in the sense of "devoted to that" (*tatra bhaktir asya*). Examples: *aupagavakaḥ*, *dākṣakaḥ*; *pāṇinīyaḥ*. *Kṣatriyāt* (3.3.67): [The suffix *vuñ* is applied] after a word denoting a *kṣatriya*.
The suffix *vuñ* occurs frequently in the sense of "he has devotion toward that" when the base word denotes a *kṣatriya*. Examples: *Nākulakaḥ*, *Sāhadevakaḥ*; *Pauravīyaḥ*.
All [rules] regarding the plural number apply here just as they do for *janapada* names, provided the base word is of the same form [as the name of the people]. (Aṣṭādhyāyī 4.2.129–130)

When there is plurality, because the word denoting a *kṣatriya* has the same form as that denoting a country (*janapada*), the designation "like a country" (*janapadavat*) applies in the sense of "he has devotion to them," and everything [the rules for countries] takes place. For example: he has devotion to the countries of Aṅga or Vaṅga: *Āṅgakaḥ*, *Vāṅgakaḥ*. Similarly, he has devotion to the *kṣatriyas* of Aṅga or Vaṅga: *Āṅgakaḥ*, *Vāṅgakaḥ*. Why say "everything"? So that the base form (*prakṛti*) itself may also be like a country. For example: he has devotion to the Madras or the Vṛjis: *Madrakaḥ*, *Vṛjikaḥ*.

What is the purpose of the phrase *tatsarūpāt* (“from that which has the same form”)? [Consider: *Pauravīyaḥ*. What is the purpose of the phrase *bahutve* (“in the sense of plurality”)? So that [the suffix] may also occur from a stem of a different form when there is singularity or duality. For example: *āṅgo bhaktir asya* or *āṅgayor bhaktir asya* = *āṅgakaḥ*. [The rule applies] only after a word denoting a *kṣatriya*: *pañcāleṣu brāhmaṇeṣu bhaktir asya* = *pāñcālaḥ*. How is it that [we have] *auśanasam*, *bārhaspatyam*, and *pāṇinīyam* for “proclaimed by Uśanas,” “by Bṛhaspati,” and “by Pāṇini”? This is already established by the rule *śeṣe* (A 4.2.92). [Furthermore, the suffix is added] because of the rule *tena proktaṃ vedaṃ vetty adhīte* (A 4.2.59).

After a word ending in the third case, the suffixes *aṇ* and others occur as prescribed in the senses of "one who knows" (*veda*) or "one who has studied" (*adhīta*) a Veda proclaimed by that person. For example: *pippalādena proktaṃ vedaṃ vidanti adhīyate vā* ("they know or study the Veda proclaimed by Pippalāda") results in *paippalādāḥ*. Similarly, *maitrāyaṇīyāḥ*. Why is "Veda" specified? [To exclude cases such as: *pippalādena proktaṃ ślokaṃ vidanti adhīyate vā* ("they know or study the verse proclaimed by Pippalāda"). [The rule] *tittirivaratantukhaṇḍikokhāc chaṇ* (Pāṇini 4.3.102) applies here.

The suffix *chaṇ* occurs after these [words] in the two senses of "one who knows" or "one who has studied" that which was proclaimed by them. For example: one who knows or has studied the Veda proclaimed by Tittiri is a *Taittirīya*. Likewise, *Vāratantavīya*, *Khāṇḍikīya*, and *Aukhīya*. The word "the Veda" (*veda*) is used [in the rule] for this purpose alone: [it does not apply to other texts]. Thus, one who knows or has studied a *śloka* proclaimed by Tittiri [is not called a Taittirīya]. Furthermore, the suffix *ṇini* is applied after the names of the sages Kāśyapa and Kauśika when referring to a *kalpa* [proclaimed by them]. (Pāṇini 4.3.103–104).

The suffix *ṇini* occurs after these two [words] in the sense of "one who knows" (*vetty*) or "one who has studied" (*adhīta*) that which was proclaimed by them. For example: those who know or have studied the Veda and the Kalpa proclaimed by Kāśyapa are called *Kāśyapinaḥ*; likewise, *Kauśikinaḥ*. Why does it say "by two seers" (*ṛṣibhyām*)? [To exclude: the Kalpa belonging to Kāśyapa is *Kāśyapīyaḥ*. Why does it say "and the Kalpa" (*kalpaṃ ca*)? [To exclude: the Purāṇa collection belonging to Kāśyapa is *Kāśyapīyā*. [The rule continues: *śaunakādibhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.3.106).

The suffix *ṇini* occurs after the words *śaunaka* and others in the sense of "one who has proclaimed the Veda" (*prokta*) or "one who knows/has studied [it]" (*adhīta*). Examples: *Śaunakinaḥ*, *Vājasaneyinaḥ*. The word "veda" must be used [in the rule]: *Śaunakīyā śikṣā* ("the Śikṣā belonging to Śaunaka"). The list includes: *śaunaka*, *vājasaneya*, *śārṅgarava*, *śāpeya*, *śāṣpeya*, *khāḍāyana*, *skanda*, *skambha*, *devadarśa*, *rajjubhāra*, *rajjukaṇṭha*, *kaṭhaśāṭha*, *kaṣāya*.
[Also] after the disciples of Kalāpin and Vaiśampāyana (Pāṇini 4.3.104).

The suffix *ṇini* occurs after these two meanings: "one who knows the Veda taught by him" and "one who has studied [it]. In this context, the disciples of Kalāpin are Haridru, Tumburu, Ulapa, and Chagalin. The disciples of Vaiśampāyana are: Ālambi, Piliṅga, and Kamala—these are the Easterners; Śyāmāyana, Kaṭha, and Kalāpin—these are the Northerners; and Ṛcābha, Āruṇi, and Taṇḍa—these are the Middlemen.

In this context, only direct disciples (*sākṣācchiṣyāḥ*) are understood, not grand-disciples (*praśiṣyāḥ*), because the disciples of Kalāpin are treated separately. Furthermore, Khaḍāyana, who is a disciple of Kaṭha, is included among the group beginning with Śaunaka. Those who know or study the Veda proclaimed by Haridru are called *Hāridraviṇaḥ*. Similarly: *Taumburaviṇaḥ*, *Aulapinaḥ*; *Ālambinaḥ*, *Pailiṅginaḥ*, *Kāmalinaḥ*; *Śyāmāyaninaḥ*; *Ārcābhinaḥ*, *Āruṇinaḥ*, *Tāṇḍinaḥ*. [The suffix *ini* is applied after these names]. By the rule *kaṭhacarakāl luk* (Pāṇini 4.3.107), the suffix *ini* is elided after the names Kaṭha and Caraka.

By these two [rules], there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix *ṇini* and of *aṇ*, which are prescribed in the sense of "one who knows" (*veda*) or "one who has studied" (*adhīta*) a Veda proclaimed by such a person. For example: those who know or study the Veda proclaimed by Kaṭha are called *Kaṭhāḥ*; likewise, *Carakāḥ*. Regarding *kalāpino ’ṇ* (Pāṇini 4.3.108):

the suffix *aṇ* occurs after *Kalāpin* in the two senses of "one who knows" or "one who has studied" the Veda proclaimed by him. Thus, *Kālāpāḥ*. Although the prohibition [of *aṇ*] would apply by the rule *anapatye ca* (Pāṇini 4.1.89), the final vowel and following sounds are elided by the rule *Kalāpyādīnām* (Pāṇini 6.4.144).

*chagalino ḍhinuk* (Pāṇini 4.3.107): The suffix *ḍhinuk* occurs after *chagalin* in the two senses of "those who know the Veda taught by him" and "those who study it. [The derivative form is] *Chāgaleyinaḥ*.

*karmandakṛśāśvābhyāṃ bhikṣunaṭasūtram iniḥ* (Pāṇini 4.3.111): The suffix *ini* occurs after *karmanda* and *kṛśāśva* when referring respectively to a mendicant (*bhikṣu*) and a theatrical manual (*naṭasūtra*).

The suffix *in* occurs after these two [names] when they signify that one knows or has studied the *Bhikṣusūtra* and the *Naṭasūtra* taught by them. Those who know or study the *Bhikṣusūtra* taught by Karmanda are the *Karmandinas*, the monks. Those who know or study the *Naṭasūtra* taught by Kṛśāśva are the *Kṛśāśvinas*, the actors. Because the connection with "knowing" and "studying" is established for each [name] individually, there is no correspondence according to the order of enumeration (*yāthāsaṃkhyam*). After the words *Pārāśarya* and *Śilālin*, the suffix *ṇini* is applied. (Pāṇini 4.3.110).

The suffix *ṇini* occurs after these two words [to denote] the meanings "one who knows" or "one who has studied" the *bhikṣusūtra* or the *naṭasūtra* as proclaimed by him. Those who know or study the *bhikṣusūtra* proclaimed by Pārāśarya are the *Pārāśariṇaḥ* monks. Those who know or study the *naṭasūtra* proclaimed by Śilālin are the *Śailālinaḥ* actors. [The suffix *ṇini* occurs after the word *brāhmaṇa*] when preceded by the name of an ancient seer (*purāṇarṣi*). (3.3.79)

The suffix *ṇini* occurs after a word denoting an ancient seer (*purāṇarṣi*) in the two senses of "one who knows" or "one who has studied" a *brāhmaṇa* proclaimed by him. For example: those who know or study the *brāhmaṇa* proclaimed by Śāṭyāyana are called *Śāṭyāyaninaḥ*; [those who know or study the *brāhmaṇa* proclaimed by Itarā are called] *Aitareyiṇaḥ*. Why is the word "ancient" (*purāṇa*) mentioned? [Consider: the *brāhmaṇas* proclaimed by Yājñavalkya are called *Yājñavalkāni*; here the suffix *aṇ* applies because of the recension beginning with Śākala. By this very rule, the word *purāṇa* itself is also established as correct. [This concludes the section on] *kalpa* (Pāṇini 4.3.126).

The suffix *ṇini* occurs after a word denoting a *purāṇarṣi* (an ancient seer) when it means "proclaimed by. For example, that which was proclaimed by Piṅga is the *Paiṅgī Kalpa*. Also, *Āruṇaparājī*. Furthermore, those who know or study the *Paiṅgin Kalpa* are also called *Paiṅginas*. For it has been stated that there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix after a word meaning "proclaimed" [by a seer]. Only when referring to an ancient seer: the *Āśmaratha Kalpa*. [In the case of] Atharvan, the suffix *aṇ* is used for the Veda: [Atharvaveda]. (Pāṇini 4.3.105 and 4.3.112).

The suffix *aṇ* occurs after the word *Atharvan* when it means "proclaimed by him" (*tena prokte*) regarding the Veda. Thus, *Ātharvaṇo vedaḥ*. How is it that [the words] *Atharvā vedaḥ*, *Vasiṣṭho 'nuvākaḥ*, and *Viśvāmitraḥ* are formed? They are so called because of metaphorical application (*upacārāt*), just as [something] is said to be "proclaimed by him. How is it that *Saudāmanī* and *Haimavatī* mean "having the same direction as Sudāman" and "having the same direction as Himavat"? This is already established by the rule *śeṣe* (Pāṇini 4.2.92). How is it that *Sudāmataḥ* means "having the same direction as Sudāman," and *Himavattaḥ* [means the same]? [These are explained by the same principle of metaphorical application.]

Is the direction equal to the chest (*uras*) called *urasta*? In that case, the suffix *tas* will apply by the rule *tata āgataḥ* (4.3.74), which states that [the suffix *tas*] occurs after a word denoting a limit (*avadhi*), as in *hāgruhoḥ*. One direction is identical with the chest; thus, one can say *urasya*, meaning "that which exists near the chest," just as one says *gaṅgāyāṃ gāvaḥ* ("cows on the Ganges" [meaning on the banks]). Therefore, the point is established by the very words "from a part of the body" (18). As for *pāṇinīyam* ("composed by Pāṇini") and *śaivaḥ* ("a work composed by Śiva"), these are established by the rule *śeṣe* (4.2.92), which governs the remaining cases.

In that case, would [the suffix] not also apply to what is not a book (*agrantha*)? Indeed, it is so intended, as in: "a palace made of bricks" (*aiṣṭakaḥ*); "a song composed by Nārada" (*nāradīyam*); "a maiden created by the mind" (*mānasī kanyā*). Now, does it occur in the rule *tasya svam* (Pāṇini 4.3.120)? In that case, even in the expression "a palace built by a carpenter" (*takṣṇā kṛtaḥ prāsādaḥ*), it certainly occurs when there is the intention to express "its property," because there is no prohibition. It also occurs in the sense of a name (*saṃjñā*), as in: "made by bees" (*mākṣikam*).
*gārmutam*, *sāragham*, *pauttikam*, *kṣaudram*, *bhrāmaram*, and *vāṭaram* are established by [the rule] 2.1.30, *śeṣe*.
Regarding the suffix *ḍhañ* after *puruṣa* when denoting "made by" (3.3.82):
the suffix *ḍhañ* occurs after the word *puruṣa* ending in the third case when the sense is "made by. Example: *pauruṣeyam*.

*Vātapād añ* (3.3.83): After *vātapā*, the suffix *añ* occurs when it denotes something made by him, provided it is a proper name (*saṃjñā*). Example: *vātapam*. Why "provided it is a proper name"? Example: *vātapīyam*. *Kulālādibhyo vuñ* (3.3.84): After [the group of words] beginning with *kulāla*, the suffix *vuñ* occurs [when denoting something made by them].

The suffix *vuñ* is applied after words such as *kulāla* when [the sense] "made by him" (*tena kṛtam*) is intended. Examples: *kaulālakam*, *vāruṭakam*. Only when it is a proper name (*saṃjñāyām*) does [the suffix *aṇ* apply]: *kaulālam*. [The list of bases is: *kulāla*, *varuṭa*, *caṇḍāla*, *niṣāda*, *karmāra*, *senā*, *devarāja*, *parṣad*, *vadhū*, *ruru*, *anaḍuh*, *brāhmaṇa*, *kumbhakāra*, *śvapāka*. How is it that [the suffix *aṇ* applies] to form *aupagavam* meaning "Upagu’s own," and *rāṣṭriya* meaning "belonging to the kingdom"? This is established simply by the rule *śeṣe* (Pāṇini 4.2.92). Regarding "one's own" (*sve*), [the suffix *cha* applies] after words for villages, countries, and humans (Pāṇini 4.3.120, Vārttika).

Thus, it should not be said [that this is redundant], because it is observed elsewhere: *aindram*, *bārhaspatyam*, *āgneyam*, *kāleyam*, *vāruṇam*, *paiśācam*, *āsuram*. Regarding the rule *tasya svaṃ rathād yat* (Pāṇini 4.3.121):

the suffix *yat* occurs after the word *ratha* ending in the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*), when "its own" (*svam*) is to be expressed. *rathasya svam* = *rathyam* ("the property of a chariot"). *rathasya voḍhā* = *rathyaḥ* ("the carrier of a chariot"). *dvirathyaḥ*, *trirathyaḥ* ("one who has two chariots," "one who has three chariots"). Because *ratha* functions as a qualifier, there is an application of the rule regarding words ending in that [base] (*tadantavidhiḥ*). Since it does not begin with *añ* or other such suffixes, there is no elision (*luk*) of the feminine marker.

The suffix *añ* (3.3.86) is applied after the word *ratha* when preceded by a word denoting a vehicle (*yāna*), in the sense of "that which belongs to it" (*tasya svam*). Examples: *āśvaratha-* ("belonging to a horse-chariot") and *rāsabharatha-* ("belonging to a donkey-chariot").
[Sūtra 3.3.87: *yānāt*.

The suffix *añ* occurs in the sense of "its own" after the word *vāhana*. Examples: *āśvam*, *rāsabham*. It need not be stated that [the suffix applies] only when [the item] is "to be carried" (*vāhya*), because [the suffix] is also perceived in cases such as *śṛṅkhala* ("chain"). [The forms] *ādhvaryavam* and *pārṣadam* are established by means of the suffix *aṇ*. By rule 3.3.88, *halasīrāṭ ṭhak*:
the suffix *ṭhak* occurs after the words *hala* and *sīra* in the sense of "its own. Examples: *hālikam*, *sairikam*.

Pāṇini 4.3.127: *cārthād vaire vun adevāsurādibhyaḥ*. The suffix *vun* occurs after a word denoting a collection (*cārthavṛtti*)—excluding those beginning with *devāsura*—in the sense of "its own" (*tasya svam*), when enmity (*vaira*) is to be expressed. Examples: *Bābhravaśālaṅkāyanikā* ("hostility between the descendants of Babhru and Śalaṅka"), *Kākolūkikā* ("hostility between crows and owls"). The feminine gender is inherent (*svabhāvāt*). Why exclude those beginning with *devāsura*? [Because for them, the suffix is *aṇ*: *daivāsuram*, *rākṣo'suram*. Pāṇini 4.3.128: *vivāhe*. [The suffix *vun* is added to denote hostility arising from a marriage.]

And by implication, the suffix *vun* occurs after [the word] *naṭa* in the sense of "its own" (*tasya svam*) when the meaning "marriage" (*udvāha*) is to be expressed. For example: *Kutsakuśikikā*, *Atribharadvājikā*.

The suffix *ñya* occurs after *naṭa* in the sense of "its own" (*tasya svam*) when the meaning "dance" (*nṛtya*) is to be expressed. For example: "the property of the actors," *nāṭyam*. Why "when dance is to be expressed"? [Consider: "the house of the actors."

(3.3.92) *chandogaukthikayājñikabahvṛcād dharmāmnāyasaṃgheṣu*: After the words *chandoga*, *aukthika*, *yājñika*, and *bahvṛca*, the suffix *ñya* occurs in the sense of "belonging to that" when the referents are *dharma*, *āmnāya*, or *saṃgha*. Thus: the *dharma*, *āmnāya*, or *saṃgha* of the *chandogas* is *chāndogya*; *aukthikya*; *yājñikya*; *bāhvṛcya*. Why say "when [the referents are] *dharma* etc."? [Because otherwise: the house of the *chandogas* is *chāndogam*. (3.3.93) *ātharvaṇaḥ*.
The suffix *aṇ* is applied to form *Ātharvaṇa*, with the elision of the suffix *ika*, to denote the *dharma*, *āmnāya*, or *saṃgha* of the *Ātharvaṇikas*.

According to Pāṇini 4.3.126 (*caraṇād vuñ*), the suffix *vuñ* is added after words denoting a *caraṇa* (Vedic school) in the sense of "belonging to that" (*tasya svam*), when terms such as *dharma* and so forth are to be expressed. Thus, the *dharma*, *āmnāya*, or *saṃgha* of the *Kaṭhas* is the *Kāṭhaka*; [likewise], the *Paippalādaka*.

(3.3.95) *Gotrād adaṇḍamāṇavāntevāsiṣu*: After a word denoting a *gotra* (lineage) that has been prescribed [to take a suffix], the suffix *vuñ* occurs in the sense of "his own," provided it does not refer to a staff-bearer (*daṇḍa*), a young student (*māṇava*), or a pupil (*antevāsin*). Example: *aupagavakaḥ*. Why "provided it does not refer to a staff-bearer, a young student, or a pupil"? [Consider: *dākṣāḥ*—staff-bearers, young students, or pupils who are primarily characterized by their lineage. (3.3.96) *Raivatikādibhyaś chaḥ*: After words beginning with *raivatika*, the suffix *cha* occurs [in the same sense].

The suffix *cha* occurs in the sense of "belonging to that" (*tasya svam*) after the patronymic lineages (*gotra*) beginning with *Raivatika*. Thus: *Raivatikīyaḥ*, *Svāpiśīyaḥ*. [The lineages are: *Raivatika*, *Svāpiśi*, *Kṣaimadhṛtvi*, *Gauragrīvi*, *Audameghi*, *Audavāpi*, *Baijavāpi*.
By the rule *kaupiñjalahāstipadād aṇ* (Pāṇini 4.3.97), the suffix *aṇ* occurs in the sense of "belonging to that" (*tasya svam*) after these two patronymics. Thus: *Kaupiñjalaḥ*, *Hāstipadaḥ*.
Pāṇini 4.3.127: *saṃghāṅkaghoṣalakṣaṇeṣv añyañiñaḥ* (3.3.98).

After a word ending in *añ*, *yañ*, or *iñ*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied in the sense of "that which belongs to him" (*tasya svam*) when the referents are a *saṃgha* (corporation), an *aṅka* (mark), a *ghoṣa* (herdsmen's station), or a *lakṣaṇa* (characteristic). Examples: *Baidaḥ saṃghaḥ*, *aṅkaḥ*, *ghoṣaḥ*, *Baidaṃ lakṣaṇam*. *Gārgaḥ saṃghaḥ*, *aṅkaḥ*, *ghoṣaḥ*, *Gārgaṃ lakṣaṇam*. *Dākṣaḥ saṃghaḥ*, *aṅkaḥ*, *ghoṣaḥ*, *Dākṣaṃ lakṣaṇam*. Why specify "in the case of *saṃgha* and so forth"? [Otherwise: *Baidānāṃ gṛham* ("the house of the Baidas"). Why specify "from a *gotra* [name]"? [Otherwise: *Vātapīyaḥ*. Pāṇini 4.3.128: *śākalād vā* (3.3.99). [The suffix *aṇ* is optionally applied after *Śākala* in the same senses.]

In the sense of "his own" (*tasya svam*), the suffix *aṇ* optionally occurs after *Śākala* when the referents are a community (*saṃgha*) and so forth. Those who know or study the Veda proclaimed by Śākalya are called *Śākalas*; their community is *Śākalaḥ* or *Śākalakaḥ*. Likewise, a troop (*aṅka*) or a herd (*ghoṣa*) is *Śākalam*, and a characteristic mark (*lakṣaṇa*) is *Śākalakam*. Regarding the rule *vahes tur iṭ ca* (Pāṇini 4.3.100):

after a word ending in the suffix *tṛ* derived from the root *vah*, the suffix *aṇ* occurs in the sense of "his own," and the augment *iṭ* is added to the *tu*. "His own [property] of one who carries" is *sāṃvahitram*.

(3.3.101) *Āgnīdhram* [is formed] when *śaraṇa* [shelter] follows *agnīdh*. When *śaraṇa* is to be expressed as "his own" (*tasya svam*), the suffix *rañ* is irregularly prescribed (*nipātyate*) after *agnīdh*, and there is an absence of *jaśtva* [the substitution of the voiced stop for the voiceless dental *t*]. Thus: *āgnīdhram śaraṇam* [the shelter of the Agnīdh]. (3.3.102) *Ṣeṇyaṇ* [is applied] after *samidh* in the sense of "placing upon" (*ādhāne*).

*Ādhāna* is that by which something is placed; in this sense, the suffix *ṣeṇyaṇ* occurs after the word *samidh*. *Sāmidhenyaḥ* refers to the mantras; *sāmidhenī* refers to the *ṛc* verses. Regarding the rule *vikāre* (3.3.103):

when a modification (*vikāra*) is to be expressed, the suffixes *aṇ* and others occur as prescribed after a word ending in the sixth case. A modification of stone (*aśman*) is *āśmaḥ*; [a modification] of ash (*bhāsmān*) is *bhāsmanaḥ*. Since this is already established by the rule *śeṣe* (4.2.92), the repetition here is for the purpose of excluding the secondary (*śaiṣika*) suffixes. Examples: *hālaḥ*, *sairaḥ*.

(3.3.104) *vṛkṣauṣadhibhyo ’ṃśe ca*: After words denoting trees and medicinal plants, the suffixes beginning with *aṇ* (Pāṇini 4.3.133) are applied to denote a part (*aṃśa*) and a modification (*vikāra*). Examples: *kārīram* stalk; *kārīram* ash. *maurvam* stalk; *maurvam* ash. (3.3.105) *prāṇibhyo ’ñ*: After words denoting living beings, the suffix *añ* is applied.

The suffix *añ* occurs after words denoting living beings when the meaning is a derivative product (*vikāra*) or a part (*aṃśa*). For example: *kāpotam māṃsam* (pigeon meat), *kāpotam sakthi* (pigeon bone); *cāṣam māṃsam* (blue jay meat), *cāṣam sakthi* (blue jay bone). By rule 4.3.106, *tālādibhyo ’ṇ*:

the suffix *aṇ* occurs after the group beginning with *tāla* in the senses of a derivative product or a part. For example: *tālam dhanuḥ* (a bow made of palmyra wood); otherwise, it is *tālamayam* (made of palmyra). Also: *bārhiṇaḥ*. Regarding *tāla* in the sense of a bow: the *tālādi* group consists of *tāla*, *barhin*, *indrādarśa*, *indrālisa*, *indrāyudha*, *cāpa*, *śyāmāka*, *pīyūkṣā*, and *gavedhukā*.

(3.3.107) *hemārthāt parimāṇe*: After words meaning gold (*hema*), when denoting a measure or a derivative product, the suffix *aṇ* occurs. Examples: *hāṭako niṣkaḥ* (a golden *niṣka* coin), *jātarūpaṃ kārṣāpaṇam*, *tāpanīyam*. Why "when denoting a measure"? [Consider: *iyaṃ yaṣṭir hāṭakamayī* (this staff is made of gold). (3.3.108) *trapujatunoḥ ṣuk*: After the words *trapu* (tin) and *jatun* (lac), the augment *ṣuk* is added.

In the case of derivatives from *trapu* and *jatu*, the augment *ṣuk* is applied; however, the suffix *aṇ* is already established [by rule 4.3.139]. For this very reason, it does not supersede the suffix *mayaṭ*. Examples: *trāpuṣam*, *jātuṣam*; *trapumayam*, *jatumayam*. By the rule *mayaḍ abhakṣācchādane* (Pāṇini 4.3.143), the suffix *mayaṭ* occurs after the base alone to denote a modification (*vikāra*) or a part (*avayava*), provided it is neither food nor clothing. Examples: *aśmamayam*, *karīramayam*, *dūrvāmayam*. There is an option between the suffixes *aṇ* and others and *mayaṭ*, as both are prescribed. What is the purpose of the restriction "not food or clothing"? Consider: *maudgaḥ sūpaḥ* ("lentil soup") and *kārpāsam ācchādanam* ("cotton garment"). In these cases, only *aṇ* applies.

*Ekācaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.3.110): The suffix *mayaṭ* occurs after a monosyllabic word to denote a modification (*vikāra*), and because it is restated here, it is obligatory. For example: *vāṅmayam* ("consisting of speech"), *mṛnmayam* ("made of clay"). How is it that *gomayam* ("cow-dung") is used when it is not a modification? It is due to the irregular formation (*nipātana*) taught in *vā gomaye* (3.2.44). [The following rule is: *che* (3.3.111).

The suffix *mayaṅ* is invariably used after words denoting color (*chavi*) when expressing a modification (*vikāra*) or a constituent part (*avayava*). For example: *āmramayam* ("made of mangoes"), *śālamayam* ("made of śāla wood").
According to Pāṇini 3.3.112, *mayaṅ* is used after the word *vrīhi* when referring to a sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) as a modification.
Thus: *vrīhimayaḥ puroḍāśaḥ* ("a sacrificial cake made of rice"). Any other [cake] is simply called *vraiha*.

(3.3.113) *tilayavapiṣṭād asaṃjñāyām*: After *tila*, *yava*, and *piṣṭa*, the suffix *mayaṅ* is invariably applied to denote a modification (*vikāra*) or a part (*avayava*), provided it is not a technical name (*asaṃjñā*). Examples: *tilamayam*, *yavamayam*, *piṣṭamayam*. Why "provided it is not a technical name"? [Counter-examples: *tailam* (sesame oil), *yāvakam* (barley meal), *piṣṭikā* (flour). (3.3.114) *śarādibhyaḥ*: [The suffix *mayaṅ* is applied] after the group beginning with *śara*.

The suffix *mayaṭ* occurs after words such as *śara* when expressing a modification (*vikāra*) or a part (*avayava*). Examples: *śaramayaṃ* (made of reeds), *darbhamayaṃ* (made of *darbha* grass). [The bases are: *śara*, *darbha*, *kuṭī*, *tṛṇa*, *soma*, *balbaja*. (3.3.115) *krītavat parimāṇāt*:

Regarding a modification of a measure, the same rule applies as for what is purchased (*krīta*). Example: a modification of a *niṣka* is *naiṣkikaḥ*; *śatyaḥ*, *śatikaḥ*, *sāhasraḥ*. [Likewise: two *niṣkas* is *dviniṣkaḥ*, *dvinaiṣkikaḥ*.
*Śamyāṣ ṭlañ* (3.3.116): The suffix *ṭlañ* occurs after the word *śamyā* to denote a product (*vikāra*) or a part (*avayava*). [Examples: *śāmīlaḥ*, *śāmīlī*. *Uṣṭrād vuñ* (3.3.117).

The suffix *vuñ* occurs after the word *uṣṭra* to denote a derivative product (*vikāra*) or a part (*avayava*). Example: *auṣṭrakaḥ*. Regarding the rule *umorṇād vā* (Pāṇini 4.3.159): the suffix *vuñ* optionally occurs after the words *uma* and *ūrṇā* to denote a derivative product or a part. Examples: *aumakam* or *aumam*; *aurṇakam* or *aurṇam*.

*eṇīkośāḍ ḍhañ* (3.3.119): The suffix *ḍhañ* occurs after the words *eṇī* and *kośa* to denote a derivative product (*vikāra*) or a constituent part (*avayava*). [Examples: *aiṇeyam* (made from the skin of a black antelope), *kauśeyam* (silk).
*puruṣād vadhe ca* (3.3.120): [The suffix *ḍhañ* occurs] after the word *puruṣa* to denote a derivative product or a constituent part, and also when [the action] involves killing.
The suffix *ḍhañ* occurs after the word *puruṣa* when the meaning is "modification" (*vikāra*) or "killing" (*vadha*). Thus: *pauruṣeya* modification, *pauruṣeya* killing.
Regarding *haiyaṅgavīna*, it is an irregularly formed term (*nipātita*) by rule 3.3.121, *haiyaṅgavīnaṃ saṃjñāyām*.

It is established as *haiyaṅgavīna* in the sense of "a modification of the milk of a cow that has recently calved," provided it is a proper name (*saṃjñā*). Thus: *haiyaṅgavīna*—fresh butter, clarified butter (*ghṛta*) that has been processed immediately [after milking].

*payaso yat* (Pāṇini 4.3.160): the suffix *yat* occurs after the word *payas* when a derivative product of milk is denoted. Example: *payasyam*. How is *gavayam* formed? It is established by [the rule] *gor aci yat* (4.3.160).
Alternatively, it is *āpyam*. (Pāṇini 4.3.161)
From the word *ap*, the suffix *yat* is optionally applied to denote a derivative product (*vikāra*), and the lengthening of the vowel is also prescribed. Thus: *āpyam* and *ammayam*.
From the word *dru* (Pāṇini 3.3.124), the suffix *yat* occurs to denote both a derivative product and a part (*avayava*). Thus: *dravyam*.

*Māne vayaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.3.162): after the word *dru*, the suffix *vaya* occurs in the sense of a measure (*māna*) and in the sense of a modification (*vikāra*). Thus, *druvayaṃ mānam* ("a measure of wood"). How is it that the fruit of the *āmalaka* is called *āmalaka*, as well as *kuvala* and *badara*? This is established because they are distinct base forms (*prakṛti*). But then, would not the suffixes *aṇ* and *mayaṭ* also apply? No, because the fruit is not understood from those [forms] ending in those suffixes. For otherwise, those two suffixes might even apply to the tree instead of the fruit. However, when the fruit is understood, they certainly do apply: *vaiṇavam*, *plākṣam*, *naiyagrodham*, *aiṅgudam*, *kākṣatavam*, *bārhatam*, *jāmbavam*.

*Jambuphalam* is another form [of the compound], because of the metaphorical treatment (*abhedopacāra*) of *jambūḥ* as being identical to the fruit. Likewise: *harītakī*, *kośātakī*, *drākṣā*; *vrīhayaḥ*, *tilāḥ*, *mudgāḥ*, *yavāḥ*, *māṣāḥ*, *śālayaḥ*, *godhūmāḥ*; as in the expression "he eats *śāli* rice with *mudga* beans. Similarly, among flowers and roots: *mallikā*, *navamālikā*, *bṛhatī*, *vidārī*. In some cases there is a distinction: *pāṭalāni kusumāni* (Pāṭala flowers), *airaṇḍāni mūlāni* (Eranda roots). In some cases both [forms occur]: *śairīṣaṃ kusumam*, *śirīṣam*. [The rule] *kāṃsyapāraśavau* (Pāṇini 3.3.126).

These two words are irregularly derived (*nipātita*) in the sense of a modification (*vikāra*). *Kaṃsīya* means "for the sake of bell-metal" (*kaṃsa*), and its modification is *kāṃsya*. *Paraśavya* means "for the sake of an axe" (*paraśu*), and its modification is *pāraśava*.
[The suffix] *na* is not applied twice [in this context]. (Pāṇini 4.3.136–137)

The suffixes *aṇ* and the others do not occur twice for both a modification (*vikāra*) and a part (*avayava*). [For example: "a modification of *kapota*" is *kāpotaḥ*. How then is there the expression "the juice of *kapota*" (*kāpoto rasaḥ*) or "the juice of * kapittha*" (*kāpittho rasaḥ*)? Even in the case of a modification, the word for the material cause (*prakṛti*) is seen [to apply]. In that case, the derivation will occur from the material cause which functions as the modification. Or rather, even a modification of a modification is simply a modification, and even a part of a part is simply a part. How is *drauvayam* [formed]? It will be derived by [the rule] "its own" (*tasya svam*, Pāṇini 4.3.120). How is *gaumayam* [formed]? This is not from a modification. The third quarter of the third chapter is completed.
Before the rule *yataṣ ṭhak* (Pāṇini 3.4.1),
that is, for those meanings prior to the mention of *yat*, the suffix *ṭhak* is to be understood.
[The suffixes are applied] after [words ending in the fifth case when meaning] "conquered by that," "wins by that," "plays with that," or "digs with that" (Pāṇini 3.4.2).

The suffix *ṭhak* occurs after a word ending in the third case when the meanings beginning with "won by" (*jitādi*) are intended. Won by dice: *ākṣikam*. Won by sticks: *śālākikam*. One who wins or plays with dice: *ākṣikaḥ*. One who plays with sticks: *śālākikaḥ*. One who digs with a spade: *khānitrikaḥ*. One who digs with a hoe: *kauddālikaḥ*. "Won by Devadatta" does not apply [to the suffix], nor does "digs with a finger," because the intended meaning is not conveyed.

Regarding the rule for "prepared" (*saṃskṛta*, Pāṇini 4.4.3): the suffix *ṭhak* occurs after a word ending in the third case in the sense of "prepared with. Prepared with curds: *dādhikam*. Prepared with *mārīca*: *mārīcikam*.

(3.4.4) *aṇ* [is added] after *kulattha* and after [words] having *ka* as their penultimate letter, when [the product] is prepared with that. [Examples: *kaulattham*, *tāintilīkam*, *dārdarūkam*. (3.4.5) *tarati* [the suffix *aṇ* is added after a word denoting a means of crossing].

The suffix *ṭhak* is applied after a word ending in the third case in the sense of "one who crosses by means of that. Examples: *auḍupikaḥ* ("one who crosses by means of a raft"), *gaupucchikaḥ* ("one who crosses by means of a cow's tail").

By the rule *dvyajnaubhyāṃ ṭhan* (Pāṇini 4.4.7), the suffix *ṭhan* is applied after a word consisting of two syllables and after the word *nau* in the sense of "one who crosses by means of that. Examples: *ghaṭikaḥ*, *plavikaḥ*; *nāvikaḥ*, *nāvikā*.

(3.4.7) *carati*: after a word ending in the third case, the suffix *ṭhak* occurs in the sense of "he goes about [with that]. Examples: *ghāṇṭikaḥ*, *śākaṭikaḥ*, *śārṅgaverikaḥ*. Some also explain it in the sense of "eating.
(3.4.8) *parpādibhyaḥ ṣṭhan*: after the group beginning with *parpa*, the suffix *ṣṭhan* occurs.

The suffix *ṣṭhan* occurs after the words *parpa* and others in the sense of "one who moves by means of that. Thus: *parpikaḥ*, *parpikī*; *aśvikaḥ*, *aśvikī*. [The bases are: *parpa*, *aśva*, *aśvattha*, *ratha*, *jāla*, *vyāsa*, *vyāla*, *pāda*, *ākarṣa*.
(3.4.9) After the word *śvagaṇa*, the suffix *ṣṭhan* optionally occurs in the sense of "one who moves by means of that. Thus: *śvagaṇikaḥ*, *śvagaṇikī*; *śvāgaṇikaḥ*, *śvāgaṇikī*.

(3.4.10) *vetanādibhyo jīvati*: After the words *vetana* and others, the suffix *ṭhak* is applied in the sense of "one who lives by means of that. Examples: *vaitanikaḥ*, *vāhikaḥ*. [The list includes: *vetana*, *vāha*, *ardhavāha*, *veśa*, *upaveśa*, *preṣaṇa*, *sukha*, *śayyā*, *śakti*, *haya*, *upahasta*, *pāda*, *upasthāna*, *dhanus*, *daṇḍa*: *dhānuṣkaḥ*, *dāṇḍikaḥ*, *dhānurdaṇḍikaḥ*. (3.4.11) *vastrakrayavikrayāṭ ṭhan*: After the compound *vastrakrayavikraya*, the suffix *ṭhan* is applied.
The suffix *ṭhan* occurs in the sense of "one who lives by means of" after words such as *vastra* ("clothing") and others. For example: *vastrikaḥ*, *krayikaḥ*, *vikrayikaḥ*, *krayavikrayikaḥ*.

By the rule *chaś cāyudhāt* (Pāṇini 4.4.14), the suffix *cha* occurs—and *ṭhan* as well—in the sense of "one who lives by means of" after the word *āyudha* ("weapon"). Thus: *āyudhīyaḥ* and *āyudhikaḥ* (and *āyudhikā*).
(3.4.13) *vrātāt khañ*:

"Vrātas" are associations (*saṃghāḥ*) consisting of people of various castes with irregular livelihoods who subsist by manual labor; their work is also called "vrāta. The suffix *khañ* occurs in the sense of "one who lives by that," as in *vrātīnaḥ*.
(3.4.14) *haraty utsaṅgādibhyaḥ*: [The suffix *khañ* is applied after words such as *utsaṅga*] in the sense of "one who carries [something]."

The suffix *ṭhak* is applied after the words *utsaṅga* and others in the sense of "carrying by means of that. Examples: *autsaṅgikaḥ*, *audvāhikaḥ*. [The list includes: *utsaṅga*, *udvāha*, *uttupa*, *utpuṭa*, *piṭaka*, *piṭāka*.

By the rule *bhastrādibhyaḥ ṣṭhan* (Pāṇini 4.4.16), the suffix *ṣṭhan* is applied after the words *bhastrā* and others in the sense of "carrying by means of that. Examples: *bhastrikaḥ*, *bhastrikī*; *bharaṭikaḥ*, *bharaṭikī*. [The list includes: *bhastrā*, *bharaṭa*, *bharaṇa*, *śīrṣabhāra*, *aṃsahāra*.

(3.4.16) *vivadhavīvadhād vā*: after the words *vivadha* and *vīvadha*, the suffix *ṣṭhan* optionally occurs in the sense of "one who carries that by means of it. [Examples: *vivadhikaḥ*, *vivadhikī*; *vīvadhikaḥ*, *vīvadhikī*; *vaivadhikaḥ*, *vaivadhikī*.
(3.4.17) *aṇ kuṭilikāyāḥ*: the suffix *aṇ* occurs after the word *kuṭilikā*.

The suffix *aṇ* occurs after the word *kuṭilikā* in the sense of "he steals by means of that," as in *kauṭilikaḥ*. Regarding the rule *akṣadyūtādibhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.4.19), the suffix *ṭhak* occurs after words such as *akṣadyūta* and others ending in the third case when the sense is "accomplished by means of that" (*nirvṛtte*). For example: that which is accomplished by means of gambling with dice (*akṣadyūtena nirvṛttam*) is *ākṣadyūtikam*; likewise, *jāṅghāprahṛtikam*. The list includes: *akṣadyūta*, *jaṅghāprahṛta*, *pādasvedana*, *kaṇṭakamardana*, *gatāgata*, *yātopayāta*, and *gatānugata*.
*bhāvād imap* (3.4.19): The suffix *imap* occurs after a word expressing an action (*bhāva*) in the sense of "completed by means of that. Examples: *pākimam*, *sekimam*, *kuṭṭimam*.
The suffix *imaP* occurs after [the word] *tryanta* when something is produced therefrom, because of its constant re-employment [in this rule]. For example: *kṛtrimam*, *paktrimam*.

Regarding *apamitya-kak* (Pāṇini 3.4.21): the suffix *kak* occurs after the word *apamitya* when something is produced therefrom. Example: *āpamityakam*. How is *yācitakam* formed? The suffix *kan* occurs here in the sense of contempt (*kutsā*).

(3.4.22) *saṃsṛṣṭe*: after a word ending in the third case, the suffix *ṭhak* occurs when the meaning is "mixed with. *dadhnā saṃsṛṣṭam* ("mixed with curd") becomes *dādhikam*. *paippalikam* ("mixed with barley meal").
(3.4.23) *cūrṇād iniḥ*: after the word *cūrṇa*, the suffix *ini* occurs [in the same sense].
The suffix *ini* occurs after the word *cūrṇa* when it means "mixed with. For example: *cūrṇena saṃsṛṣṭāḥ* = *cūrṇinaḥ apūpāḥ* ("cakes mixed with flour").

Regarding *lavaṇāl luk* (Pāṇini 5.2.24): there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix prescribed after *lavaṇa* when it means "mixed with. For example: *lavaṇaḥ sūpaḥ* ("salted soup"), *lavaṇā yavāgūḥ* ("salted gruel").

*mudgād aṇ* (3.4.25): After *mudga*, the suffix *aṇ* occurs in the sense of "mixed with. Thus, *maudga odanaḥ* ("rice mixed with mung beans"). How is it that rice sprinkled with curd is called *dādhikaḥ* and [rice sprinkled] with ghee is called *sārpiṣkaḥ*? It is established by the very word "mixed" (*saṃsṛṣṭa*).
*ojassaho'mbhasā vartate* (3.4.26).

The suffix *ṭhak* occurs after these words ending in the third case (*tṛtīyā*) in the sense of "he acts by means of that. For example: *ojasā vartate* ("he acts with vigor") becomes *aujasikaḥ*; *sāhasikaḥ*; *āmbhasikaḥ*. Regarding the rule *taṃ pratyanor īpalomakūlāt* (Pāṇini 3.4.27):

the suffix *ṭhak* occurs after words ending in the second case (*dvitīyā*) preceded by *prati*, *anu*, *īpa*, *loman*, and *kūla*, in the sense of "he acts [in that manner]. For example: *pratīpaṃ vartate* ("he acts against the current") becomes *prātīpikaḥ*. Here, the second case is used because the word functions as an adverb (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*). Similarly: *ānvīpikaḥ*; *prātilomikaḥ*, *ānulomikaḥ*; *prātikūlikaḥ*, *ānukūlikaḥ*.

(3.4.28) *parermukhapārśvāt*: When the sense is "he exists by means of," the suffix *ṭhak* is applied after the words *mukha* and *pārśva*, provided they end in the accusative case and are preceded by *pari*. For example: *parimukhaṃ vartate* ("he exists around the face") becomes *pārimukhikaḥ*; *pāripārśvikaḥ* ("one who stands by the side"). (3.4.29) *uñchati*: [The suffix *ṭhak* is applied] when the sense is "he gleans."

The suffix *ṭhak* occurs after a word ending in the second case in the sense of "gathering" (*uñchati*). For example: one who gathers jujube fruits (*badarāṇi*) is a *bādarika*; one who gathers *śyāmāka* grain is a *śyāmākika*.

[Rule 3.4.30] The suffix *ṭhak* occurs after a word ending in the second case in the sense of "protecting" (*rakṣati*). For example: one who protects an assembly (*samāja*) is a *sāmājika*; one who protects a settlement (*sanniveśa*) is a *sāṃniveśika*.

(3.4.31) *śabdadardaraṃ karoti*: the suffix *ṭhak* occurs after the words *śabda* and *dardara* in the sense of "he makes [them] resound. Examples: *śābdikaḥ*, *dārdarikaḥ*. (3.4.32) *pakṣimatsyamṛgān hanti*: [The suffix *ṭhak* occurs after these words] in the sense of "he kills birds, fish, or deer."

The suffix *ṭhak* is applied after words ending in the accusative case, such as *pakṣin* and others, in the sense of "he kills. Examples: *pākṣikaḥ*, *mātsyikaḥ*, *mārgikaḥ*. Because the instruction is based on the primary meaning of the word, it also applies to synonyms and specific varieties: *śākunikaḥ*, *śyainikaḥ*; *mainikaḥ*, *śāpharikaḥ*; *hāriṇikaḥ*, *saukarikaḥ*. Regarding the rule *paripanthaṃ tiṣṭhati ca* (Pāṇini 3.4.33):

the suffix *ṭhak* is applied after the word *paripantha* when it ends in the accusative case, in the two senses of "standing in the way" (*tiṣṭhati*) and "killing" (*hanti*). Example: *pāripanthikaḥ*. By virtue of this very rule, the form *paripantha* itself is also considered grammatically correct.

*ṭhak* is added after words ending in *mātha* and after *padavi*, etc., in the sense of "running after" (*dhāvati*). Examples: *dāṇḍamāthikaḥ*, *śaulkamāthikaḥ*; *pādavikaḥ*, *ānupadikaḥ*, *ākrandikaḥ*.
[The suffix *ṭhak* is added] after *padānta*, *pratikaṇṭha*, *artha*, and *lalāma* in the sense of "seizing" (*gṛhṇāti*). (Pāṇini 3.4.34–35)

The suffix *ṭhak* occurs after a word ending in *pada* as a subsequent member (*uttarapada*) and after words such as *pratikaṇṭha*, in the sense of "one who takes" (*gṛhṇāti*). For example: one who takes the first part (*pūrvapada*) is a *paurvapadika*; one who takes [what is] against the throat (*pratikaṇṭha*) is a *prātikaṇṭhika*; one who takes the meaning (*artha*) is an *ārthika*; one who takes the phlegm (*lālāma*) is a *lālāmika*. Regarding the rule 3.4.36, *garhye*:

when the sense is "one who takes" (*gṛhṇāti*), the suffix *ṭhak* occurs after a word in the accusative case (*dvitīyānta*) provided that something censurable (*garhya*) is expressed. For example: one who takes double (*dviguṇa*) is a *dvaiguṇika*; one who takes triple (*traiguṇa*) is a *traiguṇika*.

Regarding *vṛddher vṛdhuṣ* (Pāṇini 3.4.37): in connection with the suffix *ṭhak*, the substitute *vṛdhuṣ* occurs for *vṛddhi*. One who takes interest is a *vārdhuṣikaḥ*. Regarding *daśaikādaśakusīdāt ṣṭhan* (Pāṇini 3.4.38).

The suffix *ṣṭhan* occurs after the words *daśaikādaśa* and *kusīda* in the sense of "one who takes [this amount]. From *daśaikādaśa*: one who takes eleven for every ten is *daśaikādaśikaḥ* or *daśaikādaśikī*. From *kusīda*: a moneylender is *kusīdikaḥ* or *kusīdikī*. In the sense of "one who practices this," the suffix *ṭhak* occurs after the words *dharma* and *adharma*. From these: one who practices righteousness is *dhārmikaḥ*; one who practices unrighteousness is *ādharmikaḥ*.

*pratipatham eti ṭhaṃś ca* (3.4.40): After the word *pratipatha*, when it ends in the second case, the suffix *ṭhak* is applied, as well as *ṭhañ*, in the sense of "he goes. [The forms are] *pratipathikaḥ* and *prātipathikaḥ*.
*samājārthāt samavaiti* (3.4.41).
The suffix *ṭhak* occurs after the word *samāja*, when it ends in the second case and signifies "one who assembles therein. Examples: *sāmājikaḥ*, *sāmavāyikaḥ*, *sāmūhikaḥ*.
Regarding the rule *pariṣado ṇyaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.4.42): the suffix *ṇya* occurs after the word *pariṣad* in the sense of "one who assembles therein. Example: *pāriṣadyaḥ*.

(3.4.43) *senāyā vā*: In the sense of "he belongs to the army" (*senāyāḥ samavaiti*), the suffix *ṇya* optionally occurs. Thus: *sainyaḥ*, *sainikaḥ*. How is *sainyam* [formed]? By virtue of its inclusion in the group beginning with *cāturvarṇya*.
(3.4.44) *lālāṭikakaukkuṭikau*.

These two words are derived as irregular forms (*nipātana*). One who looks at the forehead (*lalāṭa*) is a *lālāṭika* servant. By "looking at the forehead," staying at a distance is indicated; by that, there is a lack of contact and an absence from [the master's] affairs. A servant who does not apply himself to his master's business is a *lālāṭika*. Alternatively, he is a *lālāṭika* because he looks only at the forehead to discern the signs of anger or favor. One who looks at a hen (*kukkuṭī*) is a *kaukkuṭika*. By the word "hen," the landing of the hen is indicated; by that, the smallness of the place is indicated.

A monk who walks with his gaze fixed straight ahead, restraining his vision to the area where his feet step, is a *kaukkuṭika*. One who likewise displays himself in such a manner is also called a *kaukkuṭika*. The word *kukkuṭī* refers to the behavior of hypocrites (*dāmbhika*); one who practices that is a *kaukkuṭika*. Thus, through this grammatical derivation (*nipātana*), a very great range of meaning is obtained.
[The rule] *paradārādīn gacchati* (Pāṇini 3.4.45).

The suffix *ṭhak* occurs after words such as *paradāra*, ending in the second case, in the sense of "he goes to" (*gacchati*). For example: he goes to another's wife (*paradārān gacchati*) = *pāradārikaḥ*—also called *gaurutalpikaḥ*.
Regarding the rule 3.4.46, *susnātādīn pṛcchati*:

the suffix *ṭhak* occurs after words such as *susnāta*, ending in the second case, in the sense of "he asks about" (*pṛcchati*). For example: he asks about a good bath (*susnātaṃ pṛcchati*) = *sausnātikaḥ*; *saukharātrikaḥ*; *saukhaśāyikaḥ*; *sukhaśayyikaḥ*.

Regarding *prabhūtādīn āha* (3.4.47): after words such as *prabhūta* ending in the accusative case, the suffix *ṭhak* is applied in the sense of "he says. For example: *prabhūtam āha* results in *prābhūtikaḥ*; likewise, *pāryāptikaḥ*. Regarding *mā śabda ityādibhyaḥ* (3.4.48): [the suffix *ṭhak* is applied] after words such as *mā śabda*.

The suffix *ṭhak* occurs after words such as *mā śabdaḥ* in the sense of "he says. For example: *mā śabdaḥ* (silence! he says → *māśabdikaḥ*; *nityaḥ śabdaḥ* (sound is eternal) he says → *naityaśabdikaḥ*; *kāryaḥ śabdaḥ* (sound is produced) he says → *kāryaśabdikaḥ*. This rule for *ṭhak* applies to a sentence (*vākya*). [Treating the next rule: After a word ending in the genitive case, the suffix *ṭhak* occurs in the sense of "that which pertains to it" (*tasya dharmyam*, Pāṇini 4.4.49). For example: that which pertains to a customs house (*śulkaśālā*) → *śaulkaśālikam*; [that which pertains to a market] → *āpaṇikam*.

*ṛmahiṣyādibhyo ’ṇ* (3.4.50): After words ending in the vowel *ṛ* and after the group beginning with *mahiṣī*, the suffix *aṇ* occurs in the sense of "that which pertains to its duty" (*tasya dharmyam*). For example: that which pertains to the duty of a *hotṛ* is *hautram*; *audgātram*; *nāram*; that which pertains to the duty of a *mahiṣī* is *māhiṣam*; that which pertains to the duty of *Prajāpati* is *prājāpatam*. The list [of bases] is: *mahiṣī*, *prajāpati*, *vilepikā*, *pralepikā*, *anulepikā*, *purohita*, *maṇipālī*, *anuvāka*, *yajamāna*, and *nara*. *vaiśastravaibhājitre* (3.4.51): [The suffix *aṇ* occurs after the words *vaiśastra* and *vaibhājitra* in the same sense].*

In the sense of a lawful object, the suffix *aṇ* is applied after the roots *viśas* ("to slaughter") and *vibhāj* ("to divide"), and the augment *iṭ* as well as the causative marker *ṇic* are elided by irregular rule (*nipātana*). Thus: *vaiśastram* ("slaughter") and *vaibhājitram* ("division").

Regarding *avakrayaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.4.52): that by which something is hired is called *avakrayaḥ*; it refers to a fixed price for a lump sum. In this context, the suffix *ṭhak* is applied to a word ending in the genitive case. For example: the hire of a customs house (*śulkaśālā*) is *śaulkaśālikaḥ*; [the hire] of a guard post (*gulma*) is *gaulmikaḥ*.
*tad asya paṇyam* (Pāṇini 4.4.53):

the suffix *ṭhak* occurs after a word denoting merchandise (*paṇya*) ending in the nominative case, in the sense of "this is his merchandise. For example: *apūpāḥ paṇyam asya* ("his merchandise is cakes") results in *āpūpikaḥ*.
From the word *lavaṇa*, the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied (Pāṇini 4.4.54).

The suffix *ṭhañ* occurs in the sense of "that is his merchandise" after the word *lavaṇa*. [Example: "Lavaṇa is his merchandise" → *lāvaṇikaḥ*. There is a difference in accent. The suffix *ṣṭhan* occurs after the group beginning with *kisara* in the sense of "that is his merchandise" (*tad asya paṇyam*). [Examples: "Kisara is his merchandise" → *kisarikaḥ*, *kisarikī*; *naladikaḥ*, *naladikī*. The *kisarādi* group consists of: *kisara*, *nalada*, *sthagala*, *tagara*, *guggulu*, *uśīra*, *haridrā*, *haridru*, and *parṇī*.
After *śalālu*, the suffix *ṣṭhan* optionally occurs in the sense of "that is his merchandise" (*tad asya paṇyam*). Thus: *śalālukaḥ* or *śālālukaḥ*.
[The suffix *ṣṭhan* also occurs after a word denoting] a craft (*śilpam*). (Pāṇini 3.4.57)

The suffix *ṭhak* is applied after a word ending in the nominative case in the sense of "this is his," provided that the nominative word denotes an art (*śilpa*). For example: "the drum is his art" results in *mārdaṅgikaḥ*; likewise, *pāṇavikaḥ*. The word *mṛdaṅga* refers to the playing of the drum because it is the subject thereof.

Regarding the rule *maḍḍukajharjharād aṇ vā* (Pāṇini 4.4.58): after these two words, the suffix *aṇ* optionally applies in the sense of "this is his art. Thus: *māḍḍukaḥ* or *māḍḍukikaḥ*; *jhārjharaḥ* or *jhārjharikaḥ*.

*Praharaṇam* (3.4.59): The suffix *ṭhak* occurs after a word ending in the nominative case in the sense of "this is his weapon," provided that the word ending in the nominative is a weapon (*praharaṇa*). For example: *tomaraṃ praharaṇam asya* ("a lance is his weapon") results in *taumārakaḥ*. Similarly, *dhānuṣkaḥ* ("one whose weapon is a bow") and *pāraśvadhikaḥ* ("one whose weapon is an axe"). *Śaktiyaṣṭyoṣ ṭīkaṇ* (3.4.60): The suffix *ṭīkaṇ* occurs after the words *śakti* ("spear") and *yaṣṭi* ("staff") [in the same sense]. For example: *śāktīkaḥ* and *yāṣṭīkaḥ*.

In the sense of "his weapon is a spear (*śakti*) or a staff (*yaṣṭi*)," the suffix *ṭīkaC* occurs: *śāktīkaḥ*, *yāṣṭīkaḥ*; [and with the feminine suffix] *śāktīkī*, *yāṣṭīkī*. Regarding the rule *asti-nāsti-diṣṭam iti matiḥ* (Pāṇini 4.4.60), the suffix *ṭhak* occurs in the sense of "one whose conviction (*mati*) is based on 'it exists' (*asti*) and so forth. One whose conviction is that "it exists" is *āstikaḥ*; *nāstikaḥ*; *daiṣṭikaḥ*. "Diṣṭa" means fate (*daiva*).

The suffix *ṭhak* is applied after a word ending in the nominative case in the sense of "this is his habit" (*śīlam*), provided that the word ending in the nominative is "habit" (*śīla*). Because the word [ending in the nominative] is metaphorically applied to the person due to their being the object of that habit—or because the act of eating cakes is expressed by that word—the forms *āpūpikaḥ* ("one whose habit is eating cakes") and *śāṣkulikaḥ* ("one whose habit is eating *śaṣkuli* cakes") are derived.
The suffix *ṇa* is applied after words such as *chattra* and others. (Pāṇini 3.4.63)

The suffix *ṇa* occurs in the sense of "this is his habit" (*tad asya śīlam*) after the words *chattra* and others. For example, one whose habit is an umbrella (*chattraṃ śīlam asya*) is a *chāttra*. The meaning is that he is a source of comfort for his teacher, like an umbrella. The list [of bases] is: *chattra*, *śikṣā*, *bubhukṣā*, *bhikṣā*, *puroda*, and *sthā*. The word *sthā* is understood when preceded by *antaḥ*, *sam*, *ava*, or *upa*: *antasthā*, *saṃsthā*, *avasthā*, *upasthā*. Also included are *curā*, *udasthāna*, *kṛṣi*, *karman*, *viśvadhā*, *tapas*, *satya*, *anṛta*, and *viśikā*. [The rule] *karmādhyayane vṛttam* (Pāṇini 5.2.64) applies here.

The suffix *ṭhak* is applied after a word in the nominative case (*prathamāntāt*) in the sense of "this belongs to him" (*asyeti*), provided that the thing denoted by that nominative word is an action related to study (*adhyayanaviṣaye*). If one other action has occurred in the form of a lapse during his study, he is called *aikānyikaḥ*. [Likewise,] *dvaiyanyikaḥ*. Why "in study"? [Consider: one other action, a lapse, has occurred for him while walking. [In this case, the suffix is not applied.
According to Pāṇini 3.4.65, the suffix *ṭhac* is applied after a compound whose prior member (*pūrvapada*) consists of more than two syllables.

The suffix *ṭhañ* occurs after a compound whose prior member consists of more than two syllables (*bahvac-pūrvapada*) in the sense that "this [person] has performed those [actions] during his study. For example: *dvādaśānyikaḥ*, meaning "one who has performed twelve other [tasks] during his study.
By rule 3.4.66, *hitā bhakṣāḥ*:

the suffix *ṭhak* occurs after words denoting food (*bhakṣa*) ending in the nominative case in the sense of "this [person] has these," provided that those foods are beneficial (*hita*). For example: *apūpā hitā asya* → *āpūpikaḥ* ("one for whom cakes are beneficial"); *śāṣkulikaḥ* ("one for whom pastries are beneficial").

*dīyate niyuktam* (Pāṇini 3.4.67): The suffix *ṭhak* occurs after a word ending in the nominative case in the sense of "to whom this is given," provided that what is in the nominative is given regularly (*niyogataḥ*). For example: *āgrabhojanam asya dīyate niyuktam* ("regular first-portion food is given to him") results in *āgrabhojanikaḥ*. Similarly, *āpūpikaḥ*. [Pāṇini 3.4.68 states: *odanāt ṭhaṭ* ("after *odana*, the suffix *ṭhaṭ*").

In this context—[meaning] "that which is assigned as being given to him"—the suffix *ṭhaṅ* occurs after the word *odana*. Thus: *odanikaḥ*, *odanikī*. How is it that [we have] *śrāṇikaḥ*, *śrāṇikī*; *māṃsaudanikaḥ*, *māṃsaudanikī*; *māṃsikaḥ*, *māṃsikī*? [These are] established by the preceding rule (*ṭhaṅ*). However, we shall explain the accentuation. (3.4.69) *bhaktād aṇ vā*:
After the word *bhakta*, when [meaning] "that which is assigned as being given to him," the suffix *aṇ* optionally occurs. Thus: *bhāktaḥ*, *bhāktikaḥ*.

Regarding that [sūtra] *niyuktaṃ* (Pāṇini 3.4.70): the suffix *ṭhak* occurs after a word ending in the locative case when the sense is "appointed to" (*niyukta*). Examples: *śaulkaśālikaḥ* (a customs officer), *dauvārikaḥ* (a doorkeeper).
[The next rule is: *agārāntāt ṭhan* (3.4.71).
In this context, regarding the sense of "appointed" (*niyukta*), the suffix *ṭhan* occurs after a word ending in *agāra*. Example: *devāgārikaḥ* ("one appointed to the temple").

(3.4.72) Regarding the sense of "having studied" (*adhīta*), the suffix *ṭhak* occurs after a word ending in the locative case that denotes a prohibited place or time. Example: one who studies in a cremation ground (*śmaśāna*) is a *śmāśānikaḥ*; one who studies on the fourteenth day is a *cāturdaśikaḥ*. Why say "from a [word denoting] a prohibited place or time"? [Consider: one who studies in *Srughna*; one who studies in the forenoon (*pūrvāhṇa*).

(3.4.73) *kaṭhināntaprastārasaṃsthānād vyavaharati*: The suffix *ṭhak* occurs after words ending in *kaṭhina*, and after *prastāra* and *saṃsthāna*, in the sense of "one who deals with that. Examples: *vāṃśakaṭhinikaḥ* ("one who deals with bamboo mats"), *prāstārikaḥ*, *sāṃsthānikaḥ*. (3.4.74) *nikaṭādiṣu vasati*: [The suffix *ṭhak* occurs] after [words beginning with] *nikaṭa* in the sense of "one who dwells there."

The suffix *ṭhak* occurs in the sense of "dwelling there" when the word *nikaṭa* and others are used. Examples: *naikaṭikaḥ* (one who dwells near), *śmāśānikaḥ* (one who dwells in a cemetery), *ābhyavakāśikaḥ* (one who dwells in the open air), *vārkṣamūlikaḥ* (one who dwells at the foot of a tree), *āvasathikaḥ* (one who dwells in a lodging).
Regarding *satīrthya*: the form *satīrthyaḥ* is derived by irregular derivation (*nipātana*) in the sense of "one who dwells at the same sacred ford."
(3.4.76) *prāg ghitāt*:
before the suffix *ghit*, the suffix *yat* is to be understood in those meanings which occur prior to *ghit*.
(3.4.77) *tad vahati yugaprāsaṅgāt*: [The suffix *yat* is applied] in the sense of "he carries that," provided it is by means of a yoke (*yuga*) or a pole (*prāsaṅga*).

The suffix *yat* occurs after the words *yuga* and *prāsaṅga*, which end in the accusative case, when the sense is "he carries that. Thus: *yugaṃ vahati* ("he carries the yoke") becomes *yugyaḥ*; *prāsaṅgyaḥ*. Regarding *dhuraḥ ḍhak ca* (Pāṇini 4.4.78): in the sense of "he carries the burden," the suffix *ḍhak* occurs, as well as *yat*. Thus: *dhaureyaḥ* and *dhuryaḥ*.
*Pāṇini 3.4.79*: After *sarva*, *uttara*, *dakṣiṇa*, and so forth, the suffix *kha* [is applied].

When the sense is "it carries that which is preceded by *sarva* etc.," the suffix *kha* occurs. For example: *sarvadhuraṃ vahati* → *sarvadhurīṇaḥ*; *uttaradhurīṇaḥ*; *dakṣiṇadhurīṇaḥ*. *Pāṇini 3.4.80*: After *eka* and so forth, there is also elision (*luk*) [of the suffix].

In the sense of "he carries that," there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix *dhur* following words such as *eka*, and the suffix *khaś* is also applied. Thus: *ekadhuraḥ* and *ekadhurīṇaḥ*. How is it that [the word] *śākaṭaḥ* is used in the sense of "a bull that carries a cart"? It is established by the rule *śeṣe* (Pāṇini 4.2.92). How is it that [the words] *hālikaḥ* and *sairikaḥ* are formed? They are established by the rule *tasya svam* (Pāṇini 4.3.85, 88). Regarding the term *janyāḥ* (Pāṇini 4.4.81): when it is a name (*saṃjñā*), the suffix *yan* is irregularly prescribed after the word *janī*, which denotes a bride, in the sense of "they carry her"; furthermore, the plural form is used. Those who carry the bride (*janīm vahanti*) are the *janyāḥ*: the relatives and servants of the newly married woman.

*vidhyaty akaraṇena* (3.4.82): The suffix *yat* is applied after a word ending in the second case when the sense is "pierces," provided that the piercing is not accomplished by means of an instrument (*karaṇa*). Examples: *pādau vidhyanti śarkarāḥ* ("gravel pierces the feet") → *padyāḥ* (gravel); *urasyāḥ kaṇṭakāḥ* ("thorns [piercing] the chest"). Why say "not by means of an instrument"? [Counter-example: *cauraṃ vidhyati dhanuṣā* ("he pierces the thief with a bow"); *ripūn vidhyati śaktyā* ("he pierces the enemies with a spear"). *dhanagaṇaṃ labdhvā* (3.4.83): [The suffix *yat* is applied after a word denoting wealth or a group when it occurs in connection with the act of having obtained.]

That which occurs when [the suffix] is applied to "dhana" and "gaṇa" in the sense of one who has obtained [them]: *dhana* + *labdhṛ* = *dhanyaḥ*; *gaṇyaḥ*. By Pāṇini 3.4.84, *anna* with the suffix *ṇa*:
