The suffix *ti* is added after *pakṣa* (4.2.26).

After the word *pakṣa* ending in the sixth case, the suffix *ti* occurs; thus, *pakṣati*. By the rule *tena vittaś cuñcupcaṇapau* (Pāṇini 5.2.26), the suffixes *cuñcup* and *caṇap* occur after a word in the third case when meaning "renowned for" (*vitta*); for example, one renowned for his hair is *keśacuñcuḥ* or *keśacaṇaḥ*.
The two words *vinā* and *nānā* are treated as irregularly formed (*nipātita*) [by Pāṇini 4.2.28].
[Furthermore, by 4.2.29: after the prefix *vi-*, the suffixes *śālac* and *śaṅkaṭac* are applied.
The suffixes *śālac* and *śaṅkaṭac* occur after the word *vi*. Thus: *viśālaḥ*, *viśaṅkaṭaḥ*.
The suffix *kaṭac* occurs after *sam*, *pra*, *ud*, *ni*, and *vi*. (Pāṇini 5.2.30) Thus: *saṃkaṭaḥ*, *prakaṭaḥ*, *utkaṭaḥ*, *nikaṭaḥ*, *vikaṭaḥ*.
(4.2.31) After *ava*, the suffixes *kuṭāra* and *kaṭa* occur [after the root *kuṭ*].
Thus: *avakuṭāraḥ* and *avakaṭaḥ*. (4.2.32) When denoting the bending of the nose, the suffixes *ṭīṭañ*, *nāṭañ*, and *bhraṭac* occur [after the root *kuṭ*].

When the bending of the nose (*nāsikā*) is to be expressed, the suffixes *avaṭ*, *ṭīṭaja*, and so forth, occur. *Avaṭīṭam* means the bending of the nose; likewise *avanāṭam* and *avabhraṭam*. Through connection with these [suffixes], one speaks of an *avaṭīṭā nāsikā* (a nose that is bent) or an *avaṭīṭaḥ puruṣaḥ* (a person with a bent nose). The words *nibiḍa*, *nibirīṣa*, *cikka*, *cikina*, and *cipiṭa* (Pāṇini 4.2.33) are irregularly formed (*nipātyante*) not only for the bending of the nose, but also in other appropriate senses. Examples include: *nibiḍaḥ* (dense), *nibirīṣaḥ* (thick), *cikkaḥ* (rough), *cikinaḥ* (rough), and *cipiṭaḥ* (flat).
(4.2.34) *klinnacakṣuṣi cillapillacullāḥ*:
when "one whose eyes are moist" (*klinne cakṣuṣī yasya*) is to be expressed as the referent, the forms *cilla*, *pillā*, and *culla* are prescribed [as substitutes for *klinna*].
(4.2.35) *upatyakādhityake*: [The forms *upatyakā* and *adhityakā* are prescribed respectively for the regions at the foot and summit of a mountain.]

These two words are derived as irregular forms (*nipātana*). *Upatyakā* is the land at the foot of a mountain; *adhityakā* is the land upon it. The suffix *kaṭac* need not be prescribed for the dust of *alābu*, *tila*, *umā*, and *bhaṅgā*, because the word *kaṭa* already denotes that dust. Thus: the dust of *alābu*s is *alābūkaṭam*; *tilakaṭam*, *umākaṭam*, *bhaṅgākaṭam*. In some cases, it also occurs in the sense of a "collection": a collection of sheep is *avikaṭaḥ*; a collection of camels is *uṣṭrakaṭaḥ*. The word *paṭa* is also seen in the sense of "extent" (*vistāra*): the extent of sheep is *avipaṭaḥ*.

Even words such as *goṣṭhaja* ("born in a cow-pen") and others need not be explicitly mentioned [in the rule], because they are established by their very nature (*svabhāvasiddha*) in relation to their respective locations and so forth. For the word *goṣṭha* is a synonym for "place": *gogoṣṭham* ("cow-pen"), *mahiṣīgoṣṭham* ("buffalo-pen"). In compounds such as *uṣṭragoyugam* ("pair of camels and cows") and *aśvagoyugam* ("pair of horses and cows"), the compound is formed like *narapuṃgava* ("bull among men"). Similarly, there are *hastiṣaḍgavam* ("six elephants") and *uṣṭraṣaḍgavam* ("six camels"). The conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) is that the word *taila* refers to oil other than clarified butter (*ghṛta*): *sarṣapatailam* ("mustard oil"), *iṅgudatailam* ("inguda oil"). The words *śākaṭa* and *śākin* are synonyms for "field" (*kṣetra*):
*ikṣuśākaṭam* ("sugarcane field") and *mūlaśākinam* ("root-field"). [The suffix] *aṭhac* is applied in the sense of an action when it fits [the context], according to Pāṇini 4.2.36.
The suffix *aṭhac* occurs after a word denoting an action (*karman*) ending in the seventh case when the sense is "skilled in" (*ghaṭamāna*). For example: *karmaṭhaḥ* ("skilled in work").

By the rule *tad asya saṃjātaṃ tārakādibhya itac* (Pāṇini 5.2.36), the suffix *itac* occurs after words beginning with *tāraka* ending in the nominative case, in the sense of the genitive (*asya*), provided that those things have become manifest (*saṃjāta*). For instance: "stars have appeared for him" (*tārakāḥ saṃjātā asya*) results in *tārakitaṃ nabhaḥ* ("the sky is starred"); *puṣpito vṛkṣaḥ* ("the tree is in bloom").

The suffix *mātraṭ* is applied after the following words when they do not denote a living being: *tārakā*, *puṣpa*, *kaṇṭaka*, *ṛjīṣa*, *mūtra*, *niṣkramaṇa*, *purīṣa*, *uccāra*, *vicāra*, *kuḍmala*, *pracāra*, *mukula*, *kusuma*, *stabaka*, *kisalaya*, *vega*, *nidrā*, *tandrā*, *bubhukṣā*, *pipāsā*, *śraddhā*, *abhra*, *roga*, *aṅgāra*, *pallava*, *droha*, *doha*, *sukha*, *duḥkha*, *utkarṣa*, *utkaṇṭhā*, *gara*, *vyādhi*, and *vraṇa*. (Pāṇini 5.2.37–38)

The suffix *mātraṅ* occurs after words ending in the nominative case in the sense of "this is its measure," provided they do not denote a human being (*manuṣya-vṛtti*). For example: *palam unmānam asya* → *palamātram* ("its weight is one *pala*"); *hastaḥ pramāṇam asya* → *hastamātram* ("its measure is one cubit"); *prādeśamātrī samit* ("a sacrificial fuel-stick measuring a span"); *śataṃ mānam asya* → *śatamātram* ("its measure is one hundred"); *prasthaḥ parimāṇam asya* → *prasthamātram* ("its capacity is one *prastha*"). Through metaphorical identification (*abhedopacāra*), the word *prastha* itself may also be used [to mean "that which measures a *prastha*"].
Furthermore, the suffixes *daghnaṭ* and *dvayasaṭ* occur after [words denoting height] in the sense of "reaching up to" (*ūrdhvam*). (Pāṇini 5.2.37–39)

The suffixes *daghnaṭ*, *dvayasaṭ*, and *mātraṭ* occur after the word *ūrdhvamāna* (vertical measurement) in the sense of "belonging to this. Examples are: *ūrudaghnam*, *ūrudvayasam*, *ūrumātram*. A river may be called *jānudaghnī*, *jānudvayasī*, or *jānumātrī*. One might ask: "Are the men twenty *mātra*s or thirty *mātra*s? Or: "Is the river water knee-deep (*jānudvayasam*) or thigh-deep (*ūrudvayasam*)? These are used even in cases of doubt, because such an inference is made. Just as there is a sentence construction meaning "its measure is that much" (*tāvat parimāṇam asya*), so too will there be a compound formation: *tāvanmātram*, *tāvaddvayasam*.

(4.2.40) *hastipuruṣād aṇ ca*: After these two [words], when they are in the nominative case and denote a measure (*ūrdhvamāna*), the suffix *aṇ* occurs, as well as *mātraṭ*, *daghnaṭ*, and *dvayasaṭ*. *Hastī parimāṇam asya* ("An elephant is its measure"): *hāstinam*. *pauruṣam*. *Hastimātram*, *puruṣamātram*. *Hastidaghnam*, *puruṣadaghnam*. *Hastidvayasam*, *puruṣadvayasam*. (4.2.41) *saṃkhyādeḥ saṃkhyeyāl luk*: There is elision (*luk*) of the suffixes after a word beginning with a numeral when it denotes the thing numbered (*saṃkhyeya*).

The suffixes denoting the measure (*māna*) that have been prescribed [by Pāṇini 5.1.58] for words beginning with numerals and ending with the counted object (*saṃkhyeya*) undergo elision (*luk*). For example: *dviprastham* (two *prasthas*), *dviprasthī* (a vessel of two *prasthas*); *dvipuruṣam* (two men), *dvipuruṣī* (a woman who has borne two children). Why say "ending with the counted object"? Consider: *ekādaśamātrā brāhmaṇāḥ santi* (there are eleven Brahmins). Regarding the rule *śañ-śat-śater ḍinir vā* (Pāṇini 5.1.60): after a word ending in *śan*, a word ending in *śat*, and a word ending in *śati*, the suffix *ḍini* optionally occurs in the sense of "that is its measure. Examples: *pañcadaśino 'rdhamāsāḥ* (fifteen-day half-months), *triṃśino māsāḥ* (thirty-day months), *viṃśino 'ṅgirasaḥ* (twenty-membered Aṅgiras clans). Alternatively: *pañcadaśamātrāḥ*, *triṃśanmātrāḥ*, *viṃśatimātrāḥ*.

The suffix *vatup* is optionally applied after the words *yad*, *tad*, and *etad* when they end in the nominative case and denote a measure (*māna*), in the sense of "belonging to this" (*asya*). Thus: that which is its measure is *yāvat*, *tāvat*, or *etāvat*. Likewise: *yanmātram*, *tanmātram*, or *etanmātram*.
The forms *iyat* and *kiyat* are also derived in this way. (Pāṇini 5.2.43–44)
From the pronoun *idam* and from *kim*, the suffix *vatup* is applied; in that context, this form is optionally prescribed as a *nipātana*.

Regarding the rule "In the sense of number, *kati*" (Pāṇini 5.2.41), *kati* is optionally prescribed as a *nipātana* in the domain of number. [Examples: *katy ete?* or *kiyanta ete?* ("How many are these?")?
Pāṇini 4.2.46: *aṃśe saṃkhyāyās tayaṭ*.

The suffix *tayaṭ* occurs after a numeral denoting a part (*avayava*) ending in the nominative case, in the sense of the genitive (*asya*). For example: "this has five parts" (*pañca aṃśā asya*) results in *pañcatayaḥ saṃghaḥ* ("a group consisting of five") or *pañcatayī śālā* ("a hall consisting of five parts").
Pāṇini 4.2.47: *dvitribhyām ayaṭ vā*. [The suffix *ayaṭ* optionally occurs after the words *dvi* and *tri* in the same sense.]

The suffix *ayaṭ* optionally occurs after the words *dvi* and *tri*, ending in the nominative case, in the sense of the genitive (*asya*). Thus: *dvāv aṃśāv asya* becomes *dvayam*, *trayam*, *dvitayam*, or *tritayam*.
Regarding the rule *ubhāt* (Pāṇini 5.2.48):

after the word *ubha*, when it denotes parts and ends in the nominative case, the suffix *ayaṭ* occurs in the sense of the genitive (*asya*), and this application is obligatory due to the separation of the rule (*yogavibhāga*). Examples: *ubhayo maṇiḥ*, *ubhayī sthitiḥ*, *ubhaye devamanuṣyāḥ*.
Regarding *nimāna* and *nimeya*, the suffix *mayaṭ* [is applied] by Pāṇini 4.2.49:

when the words for *nimāna* (the measure) and *nimeya* (the thing measured) denote a portion (*aṃśa*), the suffix *mayaṭ* occurs in the sense of the genitive case (*asya*)—that is, in the sense of "belonging to this"—whether it refers to the measure or the thing measured. When two portions of barley (*yava*) are the measure of this whey (*udaśvit*), it is "two-fold whey" (*dvimayam udaśvid*) of barley; likewise, "three-fold" (*trimayam*). When two portions of whey are the thing measured by these barley grains, they are "two-fold barley" (*dvimayā yavāḥ*) of whey; likewise, "three-fold" (*trimayāḥ*). In this context, the genitive case expresses the relationship between the measure and the thing measured. Why does [the suffix] not occur here? [In the following example: [The text continues with examples where the suffix does not apply.]

Is it that "two parts of barley are the measure of these portions of buttermilk"? No, because there is no connection with the number of barley-parts for them taken collectively. However, if the connection is made individually, it must indeed be so. Likewise, "two portions of buttermilk are the measure of these barley-parts. It is not the case that "one part of barley is the measure of this buttermilk," because there is no conceptualization of a part and a whole in relation to a single unit; rather, in that case, equality is what is understood.

Alternatively, the suffix *mayaṭ* occurs in the sense of the genitive case—meaning "belonging to this"—referring to that very standard of measure (*nimāna*) or the thing measured (*nimeya*), which consists of parts (*aṃśa*) of the standard and the thing measured. For example: *dvimayā yavā udaśvitaḥ* ("two parts of these barley grains belong to the buttermilk") or *trimayāḥ*. Or: *dvimayam udaśvid yavānām* ("two parts of this buttermilk belong to the barley grains") or *trimayam*. Why does one not say, for instance, "one part belongs to the barley grains"? Because the parts belonging to the thing measured (*nimeya*) are not understood [in that formulation].

Why does [the suffix] not occur in *eko ’ṃśa udaśvitaḥ* (“one part of buttermilk”)? Because the parts to be measured (*nimāna*) are not understood. Why does it not occur in *adhyardhaṃ yavānām* (“one and a half barley-corns”)? Because *adhyardha* is not a numeral; for it is separately mentioned in the rule *saṃkhyādhyardhādeḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.38). [The suffix occurs] only when there is the word *aṃśa*: *dvau vrīhiyavāv aṃśāv asya udaśvitaḥ* (“two parts of rice and barley are the measure of this buttermilk”). [The suffix occurs] only when there is a numeral: *aṃśo nimānam asya udaśvitaḥ* (“a part is the measure of this buttermilk”). [The suffix] *ḍa* occurs after a hundred or a thousand that ends in *śat*, *śad*, or *daśan*, provided that the number is greater than these: *śati-śad-daśāntādhikāsmiñ śatasahasre ḍaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.2.50).

The suffix *ḍa* occurs after a numeral ending in *śat*, *śad*, or *daśa*, when it is in the nominative case and used in the sense of the locative "in this," provided that the number is an addition (*adhika*). Furthermore, that which is added—in the sense of "in this"—must be a hundred (*śata*), a thousand (*sahasra*), or a hundred-thousand (*śatasahasra*). For example: *viṃśatir adhikāsmiñ śate* ("twenty is added to this hundred") becomes *viṃśaṃ śatam*. Similarly, *ekaviṃśaṃ śatam* or *ekaviṃśaṃ sahasram*. *triṃśaṃ śatam* (or *triṃśaṃ sahasram*) becomes *ekatriṃśam*. Likewise, *ekādaśam* and *dvādaśam*.

Since the formation is established by the inclusion of *śat* alone, the inclusion of *daśānta* (ending in *daśan*) is for the purpose of excluding [the application of] *kevala* (alone). However, it occurs after a word ending in *śati* or *daśan*, whether that word is *kevala* or not, because the rule specifies the inclusion of those endings themselves. Why [is the term] *śati-śabda-daśānta* used? Consider: *ṣaḍ adhikā asmiñ śate* ("six are added to this hundred"). Why [is the term] *adhika* used? Consider: *pañcadaśa hīnā asmiñ śate* ("fifteen are subtracted from this hundred"). Why [is the term] *asmin* used? Consider: *viṃśatir adhikā asmāc chatāt* ("twenty are added to this hundred"). Why [is the term] *śata-sahasra* used? Consider: *ekādaśa adhikā asyāṃ viṃśatau* ("eleven are added to this twenty"). Why does it not occur here: [in the following case]?

[Question: Does the expression *ekādaśa paṇā adhikā asmin kārṣāpaṇaśate* mean "there are eleven *paṇas* in excess in this hundred *kārṣāpaṇas*"? [Answer: No, because there is no understanding of an excess of *paṇas*. For when it is said *ekādaśaṃ kārṣāpaṇaśatam*, an excess of items of the same kind—namely, *kārṣāpaṇas*—is understood. Regarding the suffix *ḍaṭ* [in the sense] of filling that [number]: by Pāṇini 4.2.51, *ḍaṭ* occurs after a number in the genitive case in the sense of "filling. That which fills a number is the "filler" (*pūraṇa*). The filler of eleven is *ekādaśaḥ*; the twelfth is *dvādaśaḥ* or *dvādaśī*. Because of the mention of "filling a number" (*saṃkhyāpūraṇa*), it does not apply here: *dvādaśānāṃ muṣṭikānāṃ pūraṇo ghaṭaḥ* ("a jar that fills twelve fistfuls").

*Viṃśatyādibhyas tamaṭ vā* (Pāṇini 5.2.56): The suffix *tamaṭ* optionally occurs after words beginning with *viṃśati*, when they are in the genitive case and denote an ordinal number (*pūraṇa*). For example: *viṃśatitamaḥ* or *viṃśaḥ*; *ekaviṃśatitamaḥ* or *ekaviṃśaḥ*; *triṃśattamaḥ* or *triṃśaḥ*; *pañcāśattamaḥ* or *pañcāśaḥ*; *aṣṭāpañcāśattamaḥ* or *aṣṭāpañcāśaḥ*. *Śatādimāsārdhamāsasaṃvatsarāt* (Pāṇini 5.2.57): [The suffix *tamaṭ* is optionally applied] after *śata* and other such words, as well as after *māsa*, *ardhamāsa*, and *saṃvatsara*, [when denoting an ordinal].

The suffix *tamaṭ* occurs after words beginning with *śata* and words beginning with *māsa*, when they end in the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*), provided they denote an ordinal number (*pūraṇa*), because it is prescribed as obligatory (*nityam*). Examples: *śatatamaḥ*, *ekaśatatamaḥ*; *sahasratamaḥ*, *ekasahasratamaḥ*; *māsatamaḥ*, *ardhamāsatamaḥ*, *saṃvatsaratamaḥ*. Regarding the rule *ṣaṣṭhāder asaṃkhyādeḥ* (Pāṇini 5.2.54): the suffix *tamaṭ* occurs obligatorily after words beginning with *ṣaṣṭi* that do not begin with a numeral (*asaṃkhyādi*), when denoting an ordinal number. Examples: *ṣaṣṭitamaḥ*, *saptatitamaḥ*, *aśītitamaḥ*, *navatitamaḥ*. Why does the rule specify "not beginning with a numeral" (*asaṃkhyādeḥ*)? [To exclude cases like] *ekaṣaṣṭaḥ* and *ekaṣaṣṭitamaḥ*.

*maṭ* (Pāṇini 4.2.55): The suffix *maṭ* occurs after a word ending in *n*, provided it is not a numeral, when forming an ordinal (*pūraṇa*). For example: *pañcamaḥ* (fifth), *saptamaḥ* (seventh). Only if it is "not a numeral" [is this rule applied]; thus, *ekādaśaḥ* (eleventh). *thaṭ* (Pāṇini 4.2.56): The suffix *thaṭ* occurs after the words *ṣaṣ*, *kati*, and *katipaya*.
The suffix *thaṭ* occurs after these [words] when expressing a ordinal number (*pūraṇa*). For example: *ṣaṣṭhaḥ*, *katithaḥ*, *katipayathaḥ*.
Regarding the rule 4.2.57, *caturaḥ*:
the suffix *thaṭ* occurs after the word *catur* when expressing a ordinal number. For example: *caturthaḥ*.

*yacchau calopaś ca* (Pāṇini 4.2.58): When the suffixes *yac* and *śas* follow [the word] *catur*, the forms *yac* and *śas* occur, and there is elision (*lopa*) of the letter *ca*. Thus: *turyaḥ* and *turīyaḥ*.
[The rule for] *dvitīya* and *tṛtīya* is given by 4.2.59.
These two words are irregularly formed (*nipātyete*) in the sense of "filling" (*pūraṇe*).
According to Pāṇini 4.2.60, *tithaṭ* is applied after *bahu*, *pūga*, *gaṇa*, and *saṃgha* when expressing a ordinal number (*pūraṇe*). Thus: *bahutithaḥ*, *pūgatithaḥ*, *gaṇatithaḥ*, *saṃghatithaḥ*.

*vator ithaṭ* (4.2.61): After a word ending in *vatu*, the suffix *ithaṭ* occurs in the sense of ordinal number (*pūraṇa*). [Examples: *yāvatithaḥ*, *tāvatithaḥ*. *bhāge ’ṣṭamāñ ño vā* (4.2.62): In the sense of a "portion" (*bhāga*), the suffix *ñ* optionally occurs after *aṣṭama*.

The suffix *ñ* optionally occurs in the sense of the base itself after the word *aṣṭama*, when it denotes a part. Thus, "the eighth part" is *aṣṭamaḥ* or *āṣṭamaḥ*. By this same rule, the form is also established when it refers to a limb of an animal.
After the word *ṣaṣṭha* (4.2.63), when it denotes a part, the suffix *ñ* optionally occurs in the sense of the base itself. Thus, "the sixth part" is *ṣaṣṭhaḥ* or *ṣāṣṭhaḥ*.

(4.2.64) *māne kaṃś ca*: After the word *ṣaṣṭha*, when it refers to a portion within the context of measurement (*māna*), the suffix *kan* occurs in its own sense (*svārthe*), and *ña* optionally as well. Thus: *ṣaṣṭhakaḥ*, *ṣāṣṭhaḥ*, or *ṣaṣṭhaḥ*—meaning "a sixth part.
(4.2.65) *tena gṛhṇātīti luk ca*: [The suffix *kan* also occurs] after a word ending in the third case, in the sense of "one who takes by means of that," and there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix.

The suffix *kan* is added after a word ending in the third case that expresses a ordinal number (*pūraṇa*), in the sense of "he grasps," and there is elision (*luk*) of the ordinal markers such as *ḍaḍ* and so forth. For example: "He grasps by means of the sixth form" = *ṣaṭkaḥ*; "by means of the fifth" = *pañcakaḥ*. The word *iti* is for the purpose of indicating the intended meaning; therefore, this occurs only when grasping a text. It does not occur here: "He captures the enemy on the fifth day.
Or, [this rule applies] when there is grasping (*grahaṇe*). (Pāṇini 4.2.66)

The suffix *kan* is applied after a word denoting a number when it signifies a book (*pūraṇa*) according to the form in which it is apprehended, and there is optionally a *luk*-elision [of the case-ending]. When one apprehends a book by means of a second form: *dvikam* or *dvitīyakam* "the second apprehension"; *trikam* or *tṛtīyakam*. (4.2.67) *ekād ākinic cāsahāye*:
After *eka*, the suffix *kan* occurs in the sense of "not being accompanied" (*asahāya*), and *ākinic* also occurs optionally. Thus: *ekakaḥ*, *ekākī*, or *ekaḥ*.

(4.2.68) *Ākarṣādiṣu kuśalaḥ*: after words beginning with *ākarṣa* ending in the locative case, the suffix *kan* is applied in the sense of "skilled in. Examples: *ākarṣakaḥ*, *tsarukaḥ*. [The *ākarṣādi* group consists of: *ākarṣa*, *tsaru*, *piśāca*, *picaṇḍa*, *aśani*, *aśman*, *nicaya*, *jaya*, *naya*, *pāda*, *hrada*, *hlāda*, *śakuni*. (4.2.69) *Pathakaḥ*.
This word *śābda* is irregularly formed (*nipātita*) in the sense of "skilled on the road.

Regarding the rule *dhanahiraṇye kāme* (Pāṇini 4.2.70): the suffix *kan* is applied after these two words, *dhana* and *hiraṇya*, when they end in the locative case and denote "desire" (*kāma*). Thus, "one whose desire is for wealth" is *dhanakaḥ*; "one whose desire is for gold" is *hiraṇyakaḥ*.

*svāṅgeṣu saktaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.2.71): after words denoting one’s own limbs (*svāṅga*) ending in the locative case, the suffix *kan* is added when the sense is "attached to. Examples: attached to the teeth—*dantakaḥ*; attached to the mouth—*mukhakaḥ*; attached to the teeth and lips—*dantauṣṭhakaḥ*; attached to the hair and nails—*keśanakhakaḥ*. *audariko 'lase* (Pāṇini 4.2.72).
The suffix *ka* is applied after the word *udara* in the sense of "lazy," meaning "attached to the belly. *Udaraka* has a different meaning. [Pāṇini 4.2.73] states: *sasyena parijātaḥ*.

The suffix *kan* occurs after the word *sasya* ending in the third case in the sense of "fully grown" (*parijāta*). Examples: *sasyakaḥ khaḍgaḥ* (a sword with a hilt made of grain), *sasyako maṇiḥ* (a gem). The meaning is "endowed with substance on all sides."
*aṃśaṃ hārī* (Pāṇini 4.2.74): The suffix *kan* occurs after the word *aṃśa* ending in the accusative case when it means "one who necessarily takes. Example: *aṃśakaḥ*.
*tantrān navoddhṛte* (Pāṇini 4.2.75).
The suffix *kan* occurs after the word *tantra* when it ends in the fifth case (*pañcamyanta*) and denotes "recently brought. For example: *tantrakaḥ paṭaḥ* ("a recently woven cloth").

According to Pāṇini 4.2.76, *brāhmaṇān nāmni*, the suffix *kan* occurs after the word *brāhmaṇa* when it forms a proper name (*saṃjñā*). For example: *Brāhmaṇaka* is the name of a region where the *brāhmaṇas* are "barely touched" by the Vedic sections (*kāṇḍaspṛṣṭāḥ*).
(4.2.77) After *uṣṇa*, the suffix *kan* occurs when a name is formed. *Uṣṇikā* refers to barley-gruel; it is that which contains little food. Some say it refers to a river.
(4.2.78) And after *śīta*, [the suffix *kan* occurs] when denoting an agent.

The suffix *kan* occurs after the words *śīta* and *uṣṇa* when they denote an agent (*kārin*). When necessity (*āvaśyaka*) is implied, the suffix *ṇini* is used. Here, *śīta* and *uṣṇa* function as adverbs (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*). One who is *śītaka* is lazy; one who is *uṣṇaka* is dexterous. After the word *adhika*, the suffix *kan* occurs, and the elision of the final member of the compound (*vṛtty-uttarapada-lopa*) is prescribed by nipātana. When a *droṇa* measure has been added to a *khārī* measure, it is called *adhika*. When a *khārī* measure has been exceeded by a *droṇa*, it is called *adhika* by means of a *droṇa*.

The words *anuka*, *abhika*, and *abhīka* are derived as irregular forms (*nipātana*) when they mean "one who desires" (*kamitṛ*). One who desires after (*anukāmayate*) is called *anuka*. One who desires toward (*abhikāmayate*) is called *abhika* or *abhīka*.
[The suffix *kan* is applied] to one who seeks by the side (*pārśvena-anvicchati*). (Pāṇini 4.2.80–81)

The suffix *kan* is applied after the word *pārśva* ending in the third case when the sense is "he seeks" (*anvicchati*). *Pārśvakaḥ*: one who seeks wealth by an indirect path; this very person is so designated. By rule 4.2.82, the suffix *ṭhak* is applied after the words *ayaḥśūla* and *daṇḍājina* ending in the third case when the sense is "he seeks. An *ayaḥśūla* is a sharp means; one who seeks [wealth] by that is *āyaḥśūlikaḥ*. The meaning is "impetuous" (*rābhasika*). A *daṇḍājina* is a mark of hypocrisy; one who seeks [wealth] by that is *dāṇḍājinikaḥ*. The meaning is "hypocritical" (*dāmbhika*).

The suffix *kan* is added after a word ending in the nominative case in the sense of the genitive (*asya*), provided that the nominative word is "grāmaṇī" (leader). For example: *devadatto grāmaṇīr eṣām* ("Devadatta is the leader of these") becomes *devadattakāḥ*; *yajñadattakāḥ*. Why say "grāmaṇī"? [Counter-example: *devadattaḥ śatrur eṣām* ("Devadatta is the enemy of these"). [Next rule:
The suffix *kan* is added to *śṛṅkhala* (chain) in the sense of "bond" when referring to a camel (*karabha*). (Pāṇini 4.2.84)

The suffix *kan* is applied after the word *śṛṅkhala* ending in the nominative case, in the sense of the genitive (*asya*), when the word *karabha* ("young camel") is to be expressed, provided that the *śṛṅkhala* is a "bond. [Example: *śṛṅkhalaṃ bandhanam asya* ("this has a bond as its fetter"), *śṛṅkhalakaḥ karabhaḥ* ("a young camel with a chain-fetter"). Why say "a bond"? [Counter-example: *śṛṅkhalam asya vāhyaṃ karabhasya* ("the chain is the vehicle for this young camel"). Why say "*karabha*"? [Counter-example: *śṛṅkhalaṃ bandhanam asya goḥ* ("the chain is the bond for this cow"). Regarding *utka* meaning "eager" (*unmanāḥ*): the form *utka* is an irregular derivation (*nipātana*) [from *ud-√kam*], provided that it means "eager."

(4.2.86) *Kāla-hetu-phalāt nāmni*: After words denoting time, when used in the nominative case, and after words denoting cause or effect, the suffix *kan* is added in the sense of the genitive (*asya*) to form a name (*saṃjñā*). For example: *tṛtīyo divasaḥ asya āvirbhāvāya* → *tṛtīyakaḥ jvaraḥ* ("a fever that recurs on the third day"); *caturthakaḥ* ("a fever that recurs on the fourth day"). *viṣapuṣpaṃ kāraṇam asya* → *viṣapuṣpakaḥ* ("that which has a poison-flower as its cause"); *śītaṃ kāryam asya* → *śītakaḥ* ("that for which cold is the effect"); *uṣṇakaḥ*. Why say "in the sense of a name"? Consider: *dvitīyo divasaḥ asya jātasya* ("the second day of this person's birth"). (4.2.87) *Prāyo 'nnam asmin*: [The suffix *kan* is added] in the sense of "mostly food in this."

The suffix *kan* occurs after a word denoting food ending in the nominative case, in the sense of the locative (*asmin*), when it forms a technical name (*saṃjñā*). For example, because there is generally food consisting of *tripuṭā* on this full moon day, it is called *tripuṭikā paurṇamāsī*. Similarly, *kṛsarikā*. The restriction "when it is a name" is essential: [otherwise], although there is generally food consisting of barley meal (*saktu*) on this [day], it would not be so named. By rule 4.2.88, the suffix *aṇ* occurs after the word *kulmāṣa* ending in the nominative case, in the sense of the locative (*asmin*). Because there is generally food consisting of *kulmāṣa* on this full moon day, it is called *kaulmāṣī paurṇamāsī*.

*vaṭakād iniḥ* (Pāṇini 4.2.89): From the word *vaṭaka*, ending in the nominative case, the suffix *in* occurs in the sense of the locative (*asmin*), meaning "in which. For example: *vaṭakāḥ prāyeṇānnam asyām*, "In this [night] food consists mostly of *vaṭaka*s," resulting in *vaṭakinī paurṇamāsī*, "the full-moon night characterized by *vaṭaka*s. *sākṣād draṣṭā* (Pāṇini 4.2.90).

The suffix *ini* occurs after the word *sākṣāt* in the sense of "one who sees directly. Because it is not a number (*asaṃkhyatva*), there is elision of the final vowel and the following consonant (*antyājādilopa*). Thus: *sākṣī*. [The rule applies] only when referring to a name (*nāmni*): one who sees directly.

By the rule *śrāddham anenādya bhuktaṃ ṭhaṃś ca* (Pāṇini 4.2.91), the suffix *ini* and also the suffix *ṭhak* occur after the word *śrāddha* ending in the nominative case, in the sense of the instrumental case (*aneneti tṛtīyārthe*), provided that what is referred to has been eaten on that very day. Thus: *śrāddhī*, *śrāddhikaḥ*.
From *pūrva* (4.2.92):

after the word *pūrva*, the suffix *ini* occurs in the sense of "by this. [Examples: *pūrvam anena bhuktam*, *pītam*, or *kṛtam* = *pūrvī*. Since there can be no agent without an action, by implication (*sāmarthyāt*), an action such as eating and so forth is supplied. The word *pūrvam* is its qualifier. From *sapūrva* (4.2.93).

The suffix *ini* occurs after the word *pūrva* when it is preceded by another word, in the sense of "by this [person]. For example: *bhuktaṃ pūrvam anena* ("this person has eaten before") results in *bhuktapūrvī odanam* ("one who has previously eaten rice"); *kṛtapūrvī kaṭam* ("one who has previously made a mat"). This applies to words such as *iṣṭa* and others, according to Pāṇini 4.2.94.

The suffix *ini* occurs in the sense of "by this" after the words beginning with *iṣṭa*. For example: *iṣṭam anena* (this was sacrificed by him) becomes *iṣṭī yajñe* (he is a sacrificer at a sacrifice); *pūrtī śrāddhe* (he is one who has performed a funeral rite). The list includes: *iṣṭa*, *pūrta*, *upasādita*, *nigadita*, *parigadita*, *nikathita*, *nipaṭhita*, *saṃkalita*, *parikalita*, *saṃrakṣita*, *parirakṣita*, *arcita*, *gaṇita*, *avakīrṇa*, *āyukta*, *gṛhīta*, *āmnāta*, *śruta*, *āsevita*, *avadhārita*, *udgṛhīta*, *avakalpita*, *nirākṛta*, *upakṛta*, *upākṛta*, *anuyukta*, *anugaṇita*, *anupaṭhita*, and *vyākulita*.

(4.2.95) *anupady anveṣṭā*: the form *anupadī* is prescribed as a substitute [for *anupada*] when it means "one who searches. (4.2.96) *kṣetriyac parakṣetre cikitsyaḥ*: [the suffix *yat* with the augment *iC* forms] *kṣetriyac*, meaning "curable in another's field" [i.e., a disease that is transmitted].

The term *kṣetriya* is an irregularly formed (*nipātita*) word in the sense of "to be treated in another's field. The *ca* in the rule is for the sake of the accent. "Field" (*kṣetra*) means the body; poison that must be treated after having entered another's body is *kṣetriya*. A disease that must be treated in the body of the next world is *kṣetriya*; the meaning is "incurable. Grasses that must be treated [removed] in another's field for the sake of the crop are *kṣetriyāṇi*. One who must be treated [punished] in another's field—meaning in another's wife—is a *kṣetriya*, an adulterer. [The suffix *ghañ* forms] *indriya* (Pāṇini 4.2.97).

The term *indriya* is derived as a conventional formation (*nipāta*) for all the senses. It is so called because it is a mark (*liṅga*) of Indra, that is, the Self (*ātman*), since an instrument is employed by an agent; or because it was created by him, since it is produced from his karma; or because it is favored (*juṣṭa*) by him, since it serves as the gateway for his perception.
[The suffix] *matup* is applied according to Pāṇini 4.2.98: "When something belongs to this or exists in this, [the suffix *matup* is added]."

The suffix *matup* occurs after a word ending in the nominative case (*prathamāntāt*) in the two senses of "he has this" (*asya asti*) and "this exists in him" (*asmin asti*). For example: "He has cows" (*gāvaḥ asya santi*) results in *gomān*; "trees exist in this place" (*vṛkṣāḥ asmin deśe santi*) results in *vṛkṣavān*. Because the word "exists" (*asti*) specifies the present time, one is not called *gomān* on account of cows that were past or will be in the future. How so? [One might ask: "He was a cow-possessor" (*gomān āsīt*) or "He will be a cow-possessor" (*gomān bhavitā*). Even then, he is called *gomān* only by virtue of cows that are present at that time. The words "was" (*bhūtaḥ*) and "will be" (*bhāvī*) are separate words [and do not affect the application of the suffix]. The word "iti" (*itiśabdaḥ*) serves to indicate the intended meaning (*vivakṣārthaḥ*). Therefore, [the suffix is used] in cases of abundance (*bhūman*), censure (*nindā*), praise (*praśaṃsā*), constant connection (*nityayoga*), and excellence (*atiśāyana*).
"When there is a desire to express existence in relation to a connection [between a quality and a substance], the suffixes *matup* and others are employed.

Thus, the restriction on usage is justified by the intended meaning. In the expression "a white cloth" (*śuklaḥ paṭaḥ*), the suffix *matup* does not occur because the word "white" (*śukla*) has the capacity to denote the substance itself, just as it does not occur after genus-words such as "cow" (*go*) or "horse" (*aśva*). However, for those adjectives that lack the capacity to denote the substance, the suffix certainly occurs, as in "possessing taste" (*rasavān*), "possessing form" (*rūpavān*), "possessing smell" (*gandhavān*), and "possessing touch" (*sparśavān*).

It need not be stated "from *rasa* etc.," for [the forms] *rasī* and *rasikaḥ*, as well as *rūpī* and *rūpikaḥ*, are desired. Now, if the reading *guṇāt* is intended for the purpose of qualifying *rasa* and so on, even then *gandhikaḥ* is not established. Regarding *prāṇyaṅgād āto laj vā* (Pāṇini 4.2.99): after a word denoting a limb of a living being that ends in long *ā*, the suffix *laj* optionally occurs in the sense of the possessive (*matvarthe*). Examples: *cūḍālaḥ* and *cūḍāvān*. Why is *prāṇi* ("living being") mentioned? [To exclude: *śikhāvān pradīpaḥ* ("a lamp with a flame"). Why is *aṅga* ("limb") mentioned? [To exclude: *icchāvān* ("possessing desire"). Why is *ataḥ* ("ending in *ā*") mentioned? [To exclude: *hastavān* ("possessing hands"). The particle *ca* is for the purpose of overriding the circumflex (*svarita*) accent in cases such as *cūḍālo 'si*. The term *vā* ("optionally") is a governing heading (*adhikāra*).

(4.2.100) *Sidhmādibhyaḥ*: After the words beginning with *sidhma*, the suffix *la* optionally occurs in the sense of possession (*matvartha*). Examples: *sidhmalaḥ* (one who has freckles), *sidhmavān*; *gaḍulaḥ* (one who has goiters), *gaḍumān*. The following belong to the *sidhma* group: *sidhma*, *gaḍu*, *maṇi*, *nābhi*, *bīja*, *niṣpāva*, *pāṃsu*, *hanu*, *saktu*, *māṃsa*, *parśu*, and *pārṣṇi*; [in these cases] the vowel of *dhamani* is also lengthened. In the case of *vāta*, *danta*, *bala*, and *lalāṭa*, the vowel *ū* is substituted [for the final vowel]. *Jaṭā* and *ghāṭā* are included when used in a derogatory sense (*kṣepe*). [The suffix applies] after *parṇa*, *udaka*, *prajñā*, and small creatures (*kṣudrajantu*), as well as after words denoting affliction (*upatāpa*). Examples from "small creatures": *yūkālaḥ* (one who has lice), *makṣikālaḥ* (one who has flies). Examples from "afflictions": *vicarcikālaḥ* (one who has scabies), *vipādikālaḥ* (one who has cracked feet). Also: *mūrchālaḥ* (one who suffers from fainting).

(4.2.101) *vatsāṃsāt snehavalinoḥ*: After the word *vatsa*, when [the sense] is "possessing affection" (*snehavat*), and after *aṃsa*, when [the sense] is "possessing strength" (*balavat*), the suffix *lac* optionally occurs. *Vatsalā gauḥ* ("an affectionate cow"); *aṃsalaḥ puruṣaḥ* ("a strong man"). Why say "when [the sense is] possessing affection or strength"? [Observe: *vatsavatī gauḥ* ("a cow possessing a calf"), *aṃsavān durbalaḥ* ("a weak man with shoulders"). Now, because a specific distinction is being relied upon, even though the word "optionally" (*vā*) is being carried over [from a previous rule], it is of no consequence. This should be understood in other cases as well. (4.2.102) *phenāt*.
The suffix *laC* optionally occurs after the word *phena* in the sense of the possessive (*matvartha*). [Examples: *phenalaḥ*, *phenavān*. Pāṇini 5.2.103: *picchādibhyaś celac*:

After words beginning with *piccha* and after *phena*, the suffix *ilac* optionally occurs in the sense of the possessive. [Examples: *picchilaḥ*, *picchavān*; *urasilaḥ*, *urasvān*; *phenilaḥ*, *phenavān*. [The following words take the suffix *ilac* in the sense of the possessive: *piccha*, *uras*, *dhruvakā*, *jaṭā*, *ghāṭā*, *kālāt* when used in a derogatory sense (*kṣepe*), *parṇa*, *udaka*, *prajñā*, *tunda*, *udara*, *picaṇḍa*, *yava*, *vrīhi*, and [words denoting] a limb of one's own body (*svāṅga*) when it indicates enlargement (*vivṛddhau*).

(4.2.104) *Lomādipāmādibhyaḥ śanau*: After the group beginning with *loman* and the group beginning with *pāman*, the suffix *śa* optionally occurs in the sense of possession (*matvarthe*), and after those beginning with *pāman*, the suffix *na* optionally occurs. Examples: *lomaśaḥ* (hairy), *romaśaḥ* (hairy); *pāmanaḥ* (scabby), *vāmanaḥ* (dwarf). Also: *lomavān* (possessing hair), and so forth. The *lomādi* group consists of: *loman*, *roman*, *babhru*, *valgu*, *hari*, *kapi*, *muni*, *bharu*. The *pāmādi* group consists of: *pāman*, *vāman*, *heman*, *śleṣman*, *dadru*, *vali*, *kṛmi*, *sāman*. [From the word] *aṅga*, [the suffix *na* occurs] in the sense of "being beautiful"; and for *śāki*, *palāli*, and *ikadru*, there is also shortening [of the final vowel].

*Śākinaḥ*, *palālinaḥ*, *kadruṇaḥ*—in these cases, there is elision of the final member of the compound, with sandhi not applied: *viṣuṇaḥ*. [From *lakṣmī*,] *ac* is substituted: *lakṣmaṇaḥ*. [The suffixes] beginning with *pāmā* [are also included]. By Pāṇini 4.2.105, *prajñā-śraddhā-arcā-vṛtti-bhyaḥ ṇaḥ*: the suffix *ṇa* optionally occurs after words such as *prajñā* in the sense of possession (*matvartha*). Thus: *prājñaḥ*, *śrāddhaḥ*, *ārcaḥ*, *vārttaḥ*; and [in the feminine]: *prājñā*, *śrāddhā*, *ārcā*, *vārttā*. [Otherwise, one says] *prajñāvān*, etc.

*Tapas-sahasrābhyām aṇ* (Pāṇini 5.2.106): after these two, the suffix *aṇ* optionally occurs in the sense of possession (*matvartha*). Thus: *tāpasaḥ* (an ascetic), *tapasvān* (possessing austerity); [and] *tapasvī* (one who possesses austerity), according to *asmāyāmedhāsrajo viniḥ* (Pāṇini 5.2.121). *Sāhasraḥ* (thousandfold), *sahasravān* (possessing a thousand); [and] *sahasrī* (having a thousand), according to *ata iniṭhanau* (Pāṇini 5.2.115). *Jyotsnādibhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.2.107).

The suffix *aṇ* optionally occurs after words such as *jyotsnā* in the sense of possession (*matvartha*). Thus: *jyautsnaḥ*, *tāmisraḥ*, *kauṇḍalaḥ*, *kautupaḥ*, *vaisarpaḥ*, *vaipādikaḥ*; or [alternatively] *jyotsnāvān*, and so forth.
According to Pāṇini 4.2.108, the suffix *aṇ* optionally occurs after the words *sikatā* and *śarkarā*. Thus: *saikatam*, *śārkaram*; or [alternatively] *sikatāvān*, and so forth.
*ilaj deśe* (Pāṇini 4.2.109):

When the word *deśa* (region) is to be expressed, the suffix *ilac* optionally occurs after the words *sikatā* (sand) and *śarkarā* (gravel). Thus: *sikatilaḥ deśaḥ* (a sandy region), *saikataḥ*; *śarkarilaḥ deśaḥ*, *śārkaraḥ*. [The forms] *sikatāvān* and *śarkarāvān* also occur. The expressions "the region is sand" (*sikatā deśaḥ*) and "the region is gravel" (*śarkarā deśaḥ*) are used through metaphorical identification (*abhedopacāra*), just as one says, "Bring in the spears" (*kuntān praveśaya*) or "Bring in the staffs" (*yaṣṭīḥ praveśaya*), where those possessing the objects are referred to by the names of the objects themselves. *danturaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.2.110).
The suffix *ra* is applied after the word *danta* in the sense of "having prominent teeth.
Regarding the rule *ūṣādibhyo raḥ* (Pāṇini 5.2.107):

the suffix *ra* occurs after the group of words beginning with *ūṣa* in the sense of possession (*matvartha*). Examples: *ūṣaraḥ* (saline soil), *suṣiraḥ* (hollow), *muṣkaraḥ* (testicular), *madhuraḥ* (sweet), *kharaḥ* (donkey), *mukharaḥ* (talkative), *nakharaḥ* (clawed), *kuñjaraḥ* (elephant), *nagaraḥ* (city), *pāṇḍuraḥ* (pale), *pāṃsuraḥ* (dusty). After the word *kacchū*, there is also shortening [of the vowel]: *kacchuraḥ* (itchy). Because the word "iti" [in the list] serves to restrict the application, the suffix *ra* does not occur in cases such as *ūṣavān ghaṭaḥ* (a pot possessing salt), *madhumān vṛkṣaḥ* (a tree possessing honey), or *kuñjavān giriḥ* (a mountain possessing thickets).
*dyudrubhyāṃ maḥ* (Pāṇini 4.2.112):

After *dyu* and *dru*, the suffix *ma* optionally occurs in the sense of the possessive suffix *mat*. Thus, *dyumaḥ* ("possessing light") and *drumaḥ* ("possessing wood," i.e., a tree). Because these are conventional terms (*rūḍhi*), the suffix *matup* is not used. *keśādibhyo vaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.2.113): After words beginning with *keśa*, the suffix *va* occurs in the sense of the possessive suffix *mat*. Thus, *keśavaḥ* ("having hair").

The suffix *va* optionally occurs after [words beginning with] *keśa* and others. Thus: *keśavaḥ*, *keśavān*, *keśī*, *keśikaḥ*; *maṇivaḥ*, *maṇimān*; *rājīvam*; *kurarāvam*; *iṣṭakāvam*; *bimbāvam*. After *arṇas*, there is also elision [of the final syllable]: *arṇavaḥ*. After *gāṇḍī* and *ajakā*, when used as a proper name (*saṃjñā*), [the suffix *va* is applied]: *Gāṇḍīvam*, *Gāṇḍivam*; *Ajakāvam*, *Ajakavam*. By rule 4.2.114, the suffix *ira* optionally occurs after these two [words] in the sense of possession (*matvartha*). Thus: *medhiraḥ*, *medhāvī*, *medhāvān*; *rathiraḥ*, *rathī*, *rathikaḥ*, *rathavān*.
After these two, the suffix *īrac* optionally occurs in the sense of possession (*matvartha*). Thus: *kāṇḍīraḥ* and *aṇḍīraḥ*; [alternatively] *kāṇḍavān* and *aṇḍavān*.
*Valac* (4.2.116): After [words beginning with] *kṛṣi*, etc., the suffix *valac* occurs.

The suffix *valac* optionally occurs after *kṛṣi* and other such words. Thus: *kṛṣīvalaḥ* ("farmer"). By rule 5.2.135 (*vale*), there is lengthening of the vowel: *āsutīvalaḥ*, *parṣadvalaḥ*, *rajasvalā*, *bhrātṛvalaḥ*, *putravalaḥ*, *utsaṅgāvalaḥ*. After *danta* and *śikhā*, when a name is intended: *dantāvalaḥ* ("elephant") and *śikhāvalaḥ*. Due to the restriction of intended meaning, these are used only in certain cases: *kṛṣimat kṣetram* ("a field with crops"), *rajasvān vāyuḥ* ("wind with dust"). [Also mentioned are] *jyotsnā*, *tāmisra*, *ūrjasvin*, *ūrjasvala*, and *malīmasa* (Pāṇini 4.2.117).

Words such as *jyotsnā* are irregularly formed (*nipātita*) with the sense of the possessive suffix (*matvartha*), according to their respective domains. *Jyotsnā* means "moonlight"; elsewhere, it is *jyotiṣmatī*. *Tamisrā* means "night," *tamisraḥ* means "the dark fortnight," and *tamasvatī* means "a cave. *Ūrjasvī* and *ūrjasvalaḥ* mean "one who possesses vigor" (*ūrj*), or "one who has vigor. *Malīmasaḥ* means "soiled" or "one who has dirt. According to Pāṇini 4.2.118, the suffix *ṭhan* optionally occurs after words beginning with *nau* in the sense of the possessive suffix. Thus, from *nau*, we have *nāvikaḥ* ("boatman"). The words beginning with *nau* are: *nau*, *yava-khāda*, *kumārī*, and *karaṇa*.

*vrīhy-ādibhyaś ca* (Pāṇini 5.2.116): The suffix *ini* is applied after words beginning with *vrīhi* and after words ending in short *a*, in the sense of possession (*matvartha*); and the suffix *ṭhan* is optionally applied as well. Examples: From *vrīhi*: *vrīhī*, *vrīhikaḥ*, *vrīhimān*. Because the word *artha* is also included [in the list], we have: *śālī*, *śālikaḥ*, *śālimān*; *māyī*, *māyikaḥ*, *māyāvān*; *śīrṣī*, *śīrṣikaḥ*, *śīrṣavān*. From words ending in short *a*: *daṇḍī*, *daṇḍikaḥ*, *daṇḍavān*. Because the word *iti* [in the rule] serves to restrict the intended application, these two suffixes do not occur in some cases: *pācakavān*, *dravyavān*, *dhanavān*. However, they do occur when referring to a creditor (*uttamarṇa*): [e.g., *ṛṇī*, *ṛṇikaḥ*].

The suffixes *dhanī* and *dhanikaḥ* [are applied after words ending in *matup*]. However, they do not occur after words ending in *ghañ* and similar suffixes: *pākavān*, *snehavān*, *śabdavān*, *pracayavān*, *svanavān*. In some cases they do occur: *bhogī*, *bhogikaḥ*; *vijayī*, *vijayikaḥ*; *tarī*, *tarikaḥ*; *saṃyamī*, *saṃyamikaḥ*. After words denoting genus (*jāti*), they do not occur in some cases: *vyāghravān*, *siṃhavān*. In other cases they do occur: *taṇḍulī*, *taṇḍulikaḥ*. Even in the domain of suffixes such as *lac* and others, they do not occur in some cases: *sidhmalaḥ*, *phenilaḥ*.
In some cases, your [grammar] provides: *bījī*, *bījikaḥ*; *parṇī*, *parṇikaḥ*; *tundī*, *tundikaḥ*.
According to Pāṇini 4.2.120 (*naikācaḥ*), the suffixes *-in* and *-iṭhan* do not occur after a monosyllabic stem ending in *-a*. For example: *svavān*, *khavān*.
In the sense of the seventh case (locative), the suffixes *ini* and *ṭhan* do not occur after a word ending in *a*. For example: *daṇḍavad gṛham* ("a house possessing a staff").
[The suffix] *ṭhañ* occurs after a word preceded by *eka* or *go*. (Pāṇini 4.2.122)

The suffix *ṭhañ* occurs after [a compound] beginning with *eka* and after one beginning with *go*. Examples: *aikavastrikaḥ* ("worth one thing"), *gosahasrikaḥ* ("worth a thousand cows"). Because the word *iti* is intended to restrict the scope of the application, it does not occur here: *ekadravyavān* ("possessing one substance"). The rule applies only after [a word ending in] *a*: *goviṃśatimān grāmaḥ* ("a village possessing twenty cows"). How is *aikagavikaḥ* formed? It will be formed once the compound-ending suffix (*samāsānta*) has been applied. How is *gauśakaṭikaḥ* formed? It will be formed from the word *śakaṭa*.

After [the words] *niṣka* and so forth, as well as after *śata* and *sahasra*, the suffix *ṭhañ* occurs: *naiṣkaśatikaḥ* ("worth a hundred *niṣkas*"), *naiṣkasahasrikaḥ* ("worth a thousand *niṣkas*").

(4.2.124) *navayajñādibhyaḥ*: The suffix *ṭhañ* occurs after [the group of words] beginning with *navayajña*. For example: *nāvayajñikaḥ*—a region where the *pākayajña* sacrifice is performed. Even that which exists in a place is indeed present there; thus, this is already established by the preceding rule. (4.2.125) *cārtharogagarhitāt prāṇisthād asvāṅgād iniḥ*: The suffix *ini* occurs after a word denoting a collection (*cārtha*), a disease (*roga*), or something censurable (*garhita*), provided it refers to something residing in a living being (*prāṇistha*) but is not a limb of the body (*asvāṅga*).

The suffix *ini* alone occurs in the sense of possession (*matvartha*) after words denoting diseases, contemptible things, and [words] residing in living beings (*prāṇistha*), provided they do not denote body parts (*asvāṅga*). Examples: *kaṭakavalayinī* (“possessing bracelets and bangles”), *jvarī* (“suffering from fever”), *kuṣṭhī* (“suffering from leprosy”), *kakudāvartī* (“having a hump and a curl”), *kākatālukī* (“having a palate like a crow’s”). Why “residing in living beings”? [Counter-example: *puṣpaphalavān vṛkṣaḥ* (“a tree possessing flowers and fruit”). Why “not denoting body parts”? [Counter-example: *stanakeśavatī* (“possessing breasts and hair”). The rule applies only after [stems ending in] *at*: *citralalāṭikāvatī* (“possessing a variegated forehead-mark”). (4.2.126) For *vāta*, *atisāra*, and *piśāca*, the suffix *ini* occurs, and there is also the augment *kuk*. Examples: *vātakī*, *atisārakī*, *piśācakī*.

(4.2.127) *vayasi pūraṇāt*: After a word ending in a *pūraṇa* suffix that has been prescribed [to denote a number], when age (*vayas*) is understood, only the suffix *ini* occurs. Example: *pañcamī bālakaḥ* ("a child who is fifth [in age]"). Why "when age" (*vayasi*)? Consider: *pañcamavān grāmarāgaḥ* ("a musical mode consisting of five [notes]"). (4.2.128) *sukhādibhyaḥ*.

After the words *sukha* and others, only the suffix *ini* occurs. Thus: *sukhī*, *duḥkhī*. [The suffix *ini* is applied] after *sukha*, *duḥkha*, *tṛpra*, *kṛcchra*, *asra*, *kakṣa*, *alīka*, *karuṇa*, *kṛpaṇa*, *śopha*, *pratīpa*, *hala*, and *mālā* when used in a derogatory sense (*kṣepe*). After *bala*, provided it is preceded by *bāhu* or *ūru*: *bāhubalī*, *ūrubalī*. After words beginning with *sarva*: *sarvabījī*, *sarvadhanī*, *sarvakeśī*. How is *arthī* formed? *Artha* is the act of seeking; one who possesses that is *arthī*; [alternatively] *arthikaḥ*. From *pratyartha* comes *pratyarthikaḥ*.
One whose purpose (*artha*) is grain (*dhānya*) is *dhānyārtha*; one who possesses that is *dhānyārthī*.

*dharmaśīlavarṇāntāt* (4.2.129): After words ending in *dharma*, *śīla*, and *varṇa*, only the suffix *ini* occurs in the sense of possession (*matvartha*). Examples: *brāhmaṇadharmī*, *brāhmaṇaśīlī*, *brāhmaṇavarṇī*.
*hastadantāj jātau* (4.2.130): [The suffix *ini* occurs] after *hasta* and *danta* when referring to a genus (*jāti*).
After these two [words], when expressing a genus (*jāti*), only the suffix *ini* occurs. For example: *hastī*, *dantī*. Why "when expressing a genus"? Consider: *hastavān*, *dantavān*.
Pāṇini 4.2.131 states: *varṇād brāhmaṇe*.

After a word denoting a caste (*varṇa*), when a religious student (*brahmacārin*) is to be expressed, only the suffix *ini* occurs. For example: *varṇī*. Why "a religious student"? Consider: *varṇavān*.

(4.2.132) *puṣkarādibhyo deśe*: After the words beginning with *puṣkara*, when referring to a place (*deśa*), only the suffix *ini* occurs. Examples: *puṣkariṇī* ("a lotus pond"), *padminī* ("a lotus pond"). Why "when referring to a place"? [Example: *puṣkaravān hastī* ("an elephant having a trunk-tip like a lotus"). The list begins: *puṣkara*, *padma*, *utpala*, *tamāla*, *kumuda*, *naḍa*, *kapittha*, *bisa*, *mṛṇāla*, *kardama*, *śālūka*, *karīṣa*, *śirīṣa*, *yavāṣa*, *hiraṇya*. (4.2.133) *manmān nāmni*: [The suffix *ini* occurs after a word ending in] *matup* (*man*) when forming a proper name (*nāman*).

The suffix *ini* occurs after words ending in *man* and *mant* when they denote a name (*saṃjñā*). Examples: *prathiminī*, *dāminī*, *sominī*, *hominī*. Why specify "when denoting a name"? [Consider: *somavān*.
[Also, the suffix *ini*] is optional after [words beginning with] *śikha* and so forth (Pāṇini 4.2.134).

The suffix *ini* optionally occurs after the words beginning with *śikhā* in the sense of possession (*matvartha*). Examples: *śikhī*, *śikhāvān*; *mālī*, *mālāvān*. The list includes: *śikhā*, *mālā*, *mekhalā*, *vīṇā*, *saṃjñā*, *vaḍavā*, *aṣṭakā*, *balākā*, *patākā*, *karman*, *varman*, *bala*, *utsāha*, *uddāma*, *cūḍā*, *ula*, *kula*, *mūla*, *āyāma*, *vyāyāma*, *prayāma*, *upayāma*, *āroha*, *avaroha*. Because it is prescribed again after the word *bala*, the suffix *ini* supersedes *ṭhan*; because of the mention of "optionally" (*vā*), it does not supersede *matup*.
By rule 4.2.135, the suffix *yaP* is applied after the word *rūpa* when the meanings are "struck" (*āhata*) or "praiseworthy" (*praśasya*).

The suffix *yap* occurs after the word *rūpa* when it means "struck" (*āhata*) or "praiseworthy" (*praśasya*). For example: *rūpyā gauḥ* ("a cow that has been struck"). Why specify "when meaning struck or praiseworthy"? [Answer: Because otherwise it would be *rūpavān*. After words beginning with *hima*, the suffix *yap* optionally occurs. For example: *himyaḥ parvataḥ* ("a snowy mountain") or *himavān*. [Similarly,] *guṇyaḥ brāhmaṇaḥ* ("a praiseworthy Brahmin") or *guṇavān*.

Pāṇini 4.2.137: *asmāyāmedhāsrajo viniḥ*. The suffix *vini* optionally occurs after words ending in the suffix *asan*, as well as after *māyā* and the others. Examples: *yaśasvī*, *tapasvī*; *māyāvī*, *medhāvī*, *sragvī*; and *yaśasvān*, etc.
Pāṇini 4.2.138: *āmayāvī*.
The suffix *vin* is applied in the sense of the possessive (*matvartha*), and the lengthening of the vowel is also prescribed as a nipātana. Thus, *āmayāvī*.
From *vṛnda*, the suffix *ārakan* is applied (Pāṇini 4.2.139). From *vṛnda*, the suffix *ārakan* optionally occurs. Thus: *vṛndārakaḥ*, *vṛndī*, or *vṛndavān*.
From *śṛṅga*, the suffix *ārakan* optionally occurs: *śṛṅgārakaḥ*, *śṛṅgī*, *śṛṅgavān*.
From *phala*, *barha*, and *malā*, the suffix *inañ* occurs.
The suffix *inac* optionally occurs after the words *phala* and others, as well as after *śṛṅga*. Thus: *phalinaḥ*, *barhiṇaḥ*, *malinaḥ*, *śṛṅgiṇaḥ*; [alternatively] *phalavān*, and so forth.

According to Pāṇini 4.2.142 (*parvamarudbhyāṃ tap*), the suffix *tap* optionally occurs after these two words (*parvan* and *marut*) in the sense of possession (*matvartha*). Thus: *parvataḥ* (mountain), [alternatively] *parvavān*; *maruttaḥ*, [alternatively] *marutvān*.

*svāmin* [is used] in the sense of *īśvara* (master/owner), according to Pāṇini 4.2.143; it is an irregular form (*nipātana*). Any other [word ending in] *-sva* means "possessing. *Gomin* [is used] in the sense of "worthy of honor," according to Pāṇini 4.3.144.
The word *gomin* is derived from *gomān*, which is treated as an irregular form (*nipātyate*) when it denotes one worthy of honor; otherwise, it is simply *gomān*.
According to Pāṇini 4.2.145, the suffix *gmin* is applied to the word *vāc* in the sense of possession (*matvarthe*). Thus, *vāggmī*.
*Ālaj* and *āṭac* are used in the sense of censure (Pāṇini 4.2.146). When censure of speech is implied, the suffixes *ālaj* and *āṭac* are applied. [Examples: *vācālaḥ*, *vācāṭaḥ*.
[The suffix] *ac* is applied after words such as *arśas* (Pāṇini 4.2.147).

The suffix *ac* occurs after words such as *arśas* and others in the sense of possession (*matvartha*). Examples: *arśasaḥ* ("suffering from hemorrhoids"), *urasaḥ* ("having a broad chest"). The list includes: *arśas*, *uras*, *tunda*, *catura*, *palita*, *jaṭā*, *ghāṭā*, *abhra*, *āmla*, *lavaṇa*; and when referring to a limb of one's own body (*svāṅga*), provided it is not small (*hināt*) and is a color term (*varṇāt*). This is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open class); whatever [word] denotes the possessor by means of a non-differentiated form [from the quality itself] should all be understood as included here.

(4.2.148) *tuṇḍi-vali-vaṭer bhaḥ*: After *tuṇḍin*, *valin*, and *vaṭin*, the suffix *bha* occurs in the sense of possession. Examples: *tuṇḍibhaḥ*, *valibhaḥ*, *vaṭibhaḥ*. [The word *valibhaḥ* is derived] because *valin* is listed in the *pāmādi* group (Pāṇini 5.2.100).
(4.2.149) *kaṃśaṃbhyām*: After these two [stems], *kam* and *śam*, which end in the letter *m*, the suffix *bha* occurs. Thus: *kambhaḥ*, *śambhaḥ*. (4.2.150) *titubayastāḥ*.
These suffixes follow the words *kaṃ* and *śam*. [The forms are: *kantiḥ*, *śantiḥ*; *kantuḥ*, *śantuḥ*; *kambaḥ*, *śambaḥ*; *kaṃyaḥ*, *śaṃyaḥ*; *kantaḥ*, *śantaḥ*.
Regarding the suffix *yus* (Pāṇini 4.2.151): *yus* follows *kaṃ* and *śam*. [The forms are: *kaṃyuḥ*, *śaṃyuḥ*.
(4.2.152) *ūrṇāhaṃśubh-ebhyaḥ*: The suffix *yus* occurs after *ūrṇā*, *ahan*, and *śubham*. [Examples: *ūrṇāyuḥ*, *ahaṃyuḥ*, *śubhaṃyuḥ*.
(4.2.153) *sūktasāmnoś chaḥ*: The suffix *cha* occurs after the words *sūkta* and *sāman*.

The suffix *cha* occurs in the sense of possession (*matvartha*) after the words *sūkta* and *sāman* when they function as the objects denoted [by the derivative]. For example: *acchāvākīyam* and *asyavāmīyam* as names of *sūktas*. Because these are words of imitation (*anukaraṇaśabda*), this case ending does not occur [in their own forms]. For example: *yajñāyajñīyam* as a name of a *sāman*. (4.2.154) *adhyāyānuvākayor lug vā*:

When *adhyāya* and *anuvāka* are the objects denoted, the suffix *cha* occurs in the sense of possession, and there is optionally the elision (*luk*) of this suffix. For example: *gardabhāṇḍa* as the name of an *adhyāya*, or *gardabhāṇḍīya*; *palitastambha* as the name of an *anuvāka*, or *palitastambhīya*.

*Vimuktādibhyaṣ ṭhañ* (Pāṇini 4.2.155): After the words *vimukta* and others, the suffix *aṇ* occurs in the sense of possession (*matvartha*) when referring to an *adhyāya* or an *anuvāka*. Examples: *vaimuktaḥ*, *daivāsūraḥ*. The list [of *vimuktādi*] is: *vimukta*, *devāsura*, *rakṣo'sura*, *parisāraka*, *upasad*, *vasu*, *patnīvant*, *Daśārha*, *Satvantu*, *Daśārṇa*, *vayas*, *havirdhāna*, *mahitrī*, *Somāpūṣan*, *iḍā*, *Agnāviṣṇu*, *Vṛtrahan*, *asyahatya*.
*Gosadādibhyo vun* (Pāṇini 4.2.156): After the words *gosada* and others, the suffix *vun* occurs in the same sense.

The suffix *vun* occurs after the words *gosada* and others when expressing the sense of possession (*matvartha*) in relation to a chapter (*adhyāya*) or a section (*anuvāka*). Examples: *gosadakaḥ*, *iṣetvakaḥ*. The [words] *gosad*, *iṣe tvā*, *mātariśvan*, *devasya tvā*, *devīr āpaḥ*, *kṛṣṇo ’sy ākhareṣṭhā*, *devīṃ dhiyam*, *rakṣohaṇa*, *añjana*, *pratūrta*, and *kṛśānu* [belong to this class]. [Furthermore, the suffix *valuc* occurs after the words] *nidrā*, *tandrā*, *aśraddhā*, *adayā*, and *ahṛdaya* [in the sense of possession]. (Pāṇini 4.2.157)

The suffix *āluc* optionally occurs after words such as *nidrā* in the sense of possession (*matvartha*). Examples: *nidrāluḥ*, *tandrāluḥ*, *śraddhāluḥ*, *dayāluḥ*, *hṛdayāluḥ*. [These correspond to] *nidrāvān* and so forth. Why does the suffix *matup* not occur in the expression "in this country there are those possessing cows" (*gomanto 'smin deśe santi*)? Because of the contradiction of an action operating upon itself. For at the time of the application of the rule for *matup*, there is no base ending in *matup*; however, where such a base exists, the suffix certainly occurs: e.g., *daṇḍimatī śālā* ("a cow-stall possessing staffs"). [Pāṇini 5.2.90: *śītoṣṇatṛpraṃ na sahate* ("it does not endure cold, heat, or thirst").
The suffix *āluc* occurs after words ending in the second case, such as *śīta* ("cold") and others, in the sense of "not enduring. Examples: *śītāluḥ*, *uṣṇāluḥ*, *tṛprāluḥ*.
By rule 4.2.159, *celuḥ* occurs after the word *hima* ("snow") ending in the second case, in the sense of "enduring. Example: *himeluḥ*.

*Balavātaṃ cūlaḥ* (4.2.160): After the words *bala* and *vāta*, ending in the accusative case, the suffix *cūla* is applied in the sense of "one who endures. Thus: *balūlaḥ* ("enduring strength") and *vātūlaḥ* ("enduring wind"). The second quarter of the fourth chapter is completed.

In the sense of "having different sides" (vyāśraye), the suffix *tas* optionally follows a word ending in the sixth case when it refers to having various opposing sides. For example: *devā arjunato 'bhavan*, *ādityāḥ karṇato 'bhavan* ("the gods were on Arjuna's side; the Ādityas were on Karṇa's side"). This means: *devā arjunasya pakṣe 'bhavan*. Why say "in the sense of having different sides"? [Observe: *vṛkṣasya śākhā* ("the branch of the tree").
[The suffix *tas* is used] after a word denoting a disease in the sense of its remedy (*pratīkāre*). (Pāṇini 4.3.2)

When a remedy is understood, the suffix *tas* optionally occurs after a word denoting a disease that ends in the genitive case. *pravāhikātaḥ pratikuru* / *pravāhikāyāḥ pratikuru*. Why "when a remedy [is understood]"? [Answer: *pravāhikāyāḥ kopaḥ* ("an aggravation of dysentery").
(4.3.3) The suffix *tas* occurs after a word ending in the third case when it does not denote the agent, provided that the meaning is "scolding," "excessive grasping," or "distress."

The suffix *tas* optionally occurs after a word ending in the third case (*tṛtīyā*) prescribed [by rule 2.3.18] when it is not the agent (*akartari*), provided that meanings such as "scorned" (*kṣepa*) and so forth are understood. For example: *vṛttataḥ kṣiptaḥ* or *vṛttena kṣiptaḥ*. *vṛttato 'tigṛhyate* or *vṛttenātigṛhyate*. The meaning is that he is taken up surpassing others, or he is taken up with excellence. *vṛttato na vyathate* or *vṛttena na vyathate*. The meaning is that he does not waver. Why say "when it is not the agent"? [Consider: *Devadattena kṣiptaḥ* ("thrown by Devadatta"). [Also see: *hīyamānapāpayuktāt* (Pāṇini 5.4.47).

The suffix *tas* optionally occurs after a word ending in the third case that denotes something inferior (*hīyamāna*) or something wicked (*pāpa*). Examples: *vṛttato hīyate* or *vṛttena hīyate*; *vṛttataḥ pāpam* or *vṛttena pāpam*. This statement is made for the purpose of expressing the true state of affairs (*tattvākhyāna*).

(4.3.5) *pratinā pañcamyāḥ*: When used in conjunction with *prati*, the suffix *tas* optionally occurs after a word ending in the fifth case. Example: *Pradyumno Vāsudevataḥ prati* or *Vāsudevāt prati*.

*avadhāv ahāgruhoḥ* (4.3.6): The suffix *tas* optionally occurs after a word ending in a fifth case (*pañcamī*) when it denotes a limit (*avadhi*), provided that this limit is not related to the verbs *hā* (to abandon) or *ruh* (to descend). Examples: *grāmata āgacchati* / *grāmād āgacchati* ("He comes from the village"); *caurato bibheti* / *caurebhyaḥ* ("He fears the thief"). Why say "not related to *hā* or *ruh*"? Consider: *sārthād dhīyate*, *sārthād dhīnaḥ* ("He is abandoned by the caravan"); *parvatād avarohati* ("He descends from the mountain"). What is the purpose of the letter *k* [in *tas*]? Consider: *bhūmita ujjihīte* ("He rises up from the ground"). *sarvādibahubhyo 'dvyādibhyaḥ* (4.3.7): [The suffix *tasil* occurs] after the group beginning with *sarva* and after words meaning "many," but excluding those beginning with *dvi*.

The suffix *tas* optionally occurs after many words beginning with *sarva*, excluding *dvi* and so forth, when they are in the fifth case (*pañcamī*). Examples: *sarvataḥ* or *sarvasmāt*; *tataḥ* or *tasmāt*; *bahutaḥ* or *bahubhyaḥ*. Since this was already established by the preceding rule, this statement is made for the purpose of excluding the forms ending in *ha* and *agra*. Why does it say "excluding *dvi* and so forth"? [Because] *dvābhyām* is not included. How then are forms such as *tvattaḥ*, *mattaḥ*, *yuṣmattaḥ*, and *asmattaḥ* explained? They will take the suffix *tas* by the rule *avadhāv ahāgruhoh* (Pāṇini 5.4.45). [Also see] *kuto 'ta itaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.3.8).

The suffix *tas* is optionally prescribed after the word *kimaḥ* ending in the fifth case, and the change to *ku* is also applied as a *nipātana*. For *etado*, the substitution *aś* occurs; for *idamaḥ*, the substitution *iś* occurs. Thus: *kutaḥ* (from where), *kasmāt*; *ataḥ* (from here), *etasmāt*; *itaḥ* (from here), *asmāt*. How is the form *abhitaḥ* (on both sides) or *paritaḥ* (all around) established? It is established because the second case is prescribed when used in conjunction with those words. Regarding *ādyādibhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.4.45): the suffix *tas* is optionally added after the group beginning with *ādi*. Thus: *ādau*, *āditaḥ*; *madhyataḥ*; *antataḥ*; *pṛṣṭhataḥ*; *pārśvataḥ*; *mukhataḥ*.

The suffix *tral* is optionally applied after many words beginning with *sarva*, excluding those starting with *dvi*, when they end in the locative case (*saptamī*). For example: *sarvatra* (in all), *sarvasmin* (in all); *yatra* (where), *yasmin* (where); *bahutra* (in many), *bahuṣu* (in many). It is only after words other than those starting with *dvi* that this applies; thus: *dvayoḥ* (in two), *tvayi* (in you), *mayi* (in me).
[Furthermore, the suffixes] *kva*, *kutra*, *iha*, and *atra* [are used for the locative]. (Pāṇini 5.3.10–11)

The word *kimaḥ* ending in the locative case is optionally substituted by *kva* or *kutra*; likewise, *idam* becomes *iha*, and *etad* becomes *atra*. [The suffix *traL* is added] after *bhavat*, *dīrghāyus*, *āyuṣmat*, *devānāmpriya*, and other words [ending in the seventh case]. (Pāṇini 4.3.12)

In your yoga, those forms beginning with *tasa* and so forth may optionally occur after other case endings as well: *sa bhavān*, *tato bhavān*, *tatra bhavān*; *taṃ bhavantam*, *tato bhavantam*, *tatra bhavantam*; *tena bhavatā*, *tato bhavatā*, *tatra bhavatā*; *tasmai bhavate*, *tato bhavate*, *tatra bhavate*; *tasya bhavataḥ*, *tato bhavataḥ*, *tatra bhavataḥ*.

In this manner, "he is long-lived," "he is venerable," and "he is beloved of the gods" should be applied everywhere. Likewise for "who are you? and "from where are you? and so forth; similarly for "this is you," "from here are you," and "here are you," and so forth. Regarding the rule *sarva-ekānya-kiṃ-yat-tadaḥ kāle dā* (Pāṇini 5.3.15): after these words—*sarva*, *eka*, *anya*, *kim*, *yat*, and *tad*—when they refer to time and end in the locative case (*saptamī*), the suffix *dā* is optionally added. Examples: *sarvasmin kāle* → *sarvadā* ("at all times"); *ekasmin kāle* → *ekadā* ("once"); *anyasmin kāle* → *anyadā* ("at another time"); *kasmin kāle* → *kadā* ("when?"); *yasmin kāle* → *yadā* ("when"); *tasmin kāle* → *tadā* ("then"). Why specify "time"? [To exclude cases like: *sarvatra deśe* ("in every place").
The words *sadā*, *adhunā*, *idānīm*, and *tadānīm* are derived as irregular forms (*nipātana*). *Sadā* means "at all times. *Adhunā* and *idānīm* mean "at this time. *Tadānīm* means "at that time.

According to Pāṇini 4.3.15: *kiṃ-yad-anya-ad-anadyatane rhil vā*, the suffix *rhil* is optionally applied after the words *kim*, *yad*, *anya*, and *ad*, when referring to a time other than the current day.

The suffix *rhil* optionally occurs after the words *kim* and others, when they denote non-recent time (*anadyatana*) and end in the locative case. Thus: *karhi*, *kadā*; *yarhi*, *yadā*; *anyarhi*, *anyadā*.

Regarding *tarhi*, *etarhi*, *sadyaḥ*, and *paredyavi* (Pāṇini 5.3.16): the words *tarhi* and so forth are established as irregular forms (*nipātana*) derived from those beginning with *tad*, when they end in the locative case and denote time. [Examples: in that time—*tarhi*; in this time—*etarhi*. On the same day—*sadyaḥ*; on the following day—*paredyavi*. The forms *adya*, *parut*, *parāri*, and *aiṣamaḥ* are established through specific irregular derivations (*nipātana*).

From *pūrva*, *anya*, *anyatara*, *itara*, *apara*, and *adhara*—when these denote time and end in the locative case—the suffix *edyus* optionally occurs. In the previous day: *pūrvedyus*. In another day: *anyedyus*. In one of two days: *anyataredyus*. In a later day: *aparedyus*. In a lower day: *adharedyus*. In a subsequent day: *uttaredyus*.
After *ubhaya*, the suffix *dyus* also occurs. (Pāṇini 4.3.18)

The suffix *dyus* optionally occurs after a word denoting time ending in the locative case *ubhaya*; *edyus* is also used. In the sense of "on both days": *ubhayadyuḥ*, *ubhayedyuḥ*. Regarding the suffix *thāl* (Pāṇini 5.3.23): after words beginning with *sarva* and after numerals, *thāl* occurs when a specific manner is intended. For example: *sarvathā* ("in every way"); *yathā*, *tathā* ("in which way," "so"). Regarding the rule *kathaṃliṅ* (1.3.109), [the word] *katham* is used. Regarding the rule *itthaṃbhūteṣu* (2.1.54), [the word] *ittham* is used.

*dhā* [is added] after a numeral (4.3.20). The suffix *dhā* follows a word expressing a number when it signifies a manner (*prakāra*). For example: "He makes two ways" or "He makes two types," *dvidhā karoti*; "He makes many ways," *bahudhā karoti*. "He makes one heap into five types," *pañcadhā karoti*. "He makes five types into one type," *ekadhā karoti*.
Or [the form] *ṣoḍhā* [is used] (4.3.21).
Or *ṣoḍhā* is derived as an irregular form (*nipāta*). [Examples: *ṣoḍhā*, *ṣaḍḍhā*.
Regarding *aikadhyam* (Pāṇini 5.3.43): the suffix *dhyamuñ* is optionally prescribed after the word *eka* when expressing "in one way. [Examples: *aikadhyam karoti*, *ekadhā karoti*.
*dvitrer dhamuñ* (4.3.23): After *dvi* and *tri*, the suffix *dhamuñ* optionally occurs in the sense of "manner. Thus: *dvaidham*, *traidham*; [alternatively] *dvidhā*, *tridhā*.
The suffix *edhāc* occurs after the words *dvi* and *tri* when expressing a mode [of division]. Thus: *dvedhā*, *tredhā*.
By the rule *tadvati dhaṇ* (Pāṇini 4.3.25), the suffix *dhaṇ* occurs after *dvi* and *tri* when expressing that which possesses such modes. Thus: *dvaidhāni*, *traidhāni*.

*jātīyar* (4.3.26): The suffix *jātīyar* occurs after a word denoting a general quality when it refers to something possessing that quality. For example: *paṭujātīyaḥ* ("of a clever kind"), *mṛdujātīyaḥ* ("of a soft kind").
*kan* (4.3.27): [The suffix *kan* occurs] after words such as *sthūla*.

The suffix *kan* is applied after words such as *sthūla* when they denote a kind or variety (*prakāra*). Examples: *sthūlakaḥ*, *aṇukaḥ*. [The following are the specific bases: *sthūla*, *aṇu*, *aṇumāṣa*; *kṛṣṇatileṣu*, *yavavrīhiṣu*; *ikṣutilavāṭyakālāvadātasurāyām*; *gomūtrācchādane*, *surāhau*; *jīrṇaśāliṣu*; *pattramūle* (both used together or separately); *kumārīputra*, *kumārīśvaśura*, *maṇicañcat*, *bṛhat*.

From words denoting direction (*dik*), provided they signify direction, place, or time, the suffix *astāti* is applied after those ending in the locative (*saptamī*), ablative (*pañcamī*), or nominative (*prathamā*) case endings. (Pāṇini 5.3.27).

The suffix *astāti* optionally follows a word denoting a direction (*diś*), provided it is well-known as such and ends in the locative, ablative, or nominative case, when referring to direction, place, or time. He dwells in the eastern direction: *pūrvasyāṃ diśi vasati*, or *purastād vasati*. He has come from the eastern direction: *pūrvasyā diśa āgataḥ*, or *purastād āgataḥ*. The eastern direction is delightful: *pūrvā dig ramaṇīyā*, or *purastād ramaṇīyam*. He dwells in the eastern region or time: *pūrvasmin deśe kāle vā vasati*, or *purastād vasati*. He has come from [there]: *purastād āgataḥ*. It is delightful [there]: *purastād ramaṇīyam*. Why specify "from a word denoting a direction"? [Consider: He dwells in the direction of Indra (*aindryāṃ diśi vasati*).

What is the purpose of [specifying] "from the point of view of direction, place, time, or object"? [Example: *pūrvasmin gurau vasati* ("He dwells with the teacher who is to the east"). What is the purpose of [specifying] "after the seventh, fifth, and first case endings"? [Example: *pūrvaṃ grāmaṃ gataḥ* ("He has gone to the eastern village"). Because of the connection with words denoting direction, there is no mutual correlation between the words for direction (*dig-ādi*) and the case endings beginning with the seventh; thus, there is no application according to numerical order (*yathāsaṃkhyam*). *Añco luk* (Pāṇini 5.3.29): There is elision (*luk*) of the suffix *astāti* after a word for direction ending in *añc*. [Examples: *prācyāṃ diśi vasati*, *prāg vasati*; *prāg āgataḥ*, *prāg ramaṇīyam*. By the rule *lug aṇādiluki* (Pāṇini 1.1.62), the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is elided. In the same way, one should apply [the analysis] to such cases as *prāci deśe kāle vā vasati* ("He dwells in the eastern region or time"), and so forth.

*Upary upariṣṭāt* (Pāṇini 4.3.30): In the sense of the word *ūrdhva*, when the suffix *astāti* is to be applied, the forms *upa* and *upariṣṭāt* are prescribed as substitutes. He dwells in the upward direction: *ūrdhvāyāṃ diśi vasati*, *upari vasati*. He has come from above: *upary āgataḥ*; it is beautiful above: *upari ramaṇīyam*. He dwells from above: *upariṣṭād vasati*; he has come from above: *upariṣṭād āgataḥ*; it is beautiful from above: *upariṣṭād ramaṇīyam*. In the same way, this should be applied to dwelling in an upward region or at an upward time. *Pūrvādharayoḥ puradhau ca* (Pāṇini 4.3.31).

The substitution of *asta* occurs for the words *pūrva* and *adhara* when they end in the seventh case (*saptamī*) or other cases; furthermore, *pura* and *adhas* are the respective substitutes. Thus: *purastād vasati*, *purastād āgataḥ*, *purastād ramaṇīyam*; *adhastād vasati*, *adhastād āgataḥ*, *adhastād ramaṇīyam*. By rule 4.3.32, the suffix *as* is applied to *pūrva* and *adhara* when they end in the seventh case or other cases; furthermore, *pura* and *adhas* are the substitutes. Thus: *puro vasati*, *pura āgataḥ*, *puro ramaṇīyam*; *adho vasati*, *adha āgataḥ*, *adho ramaṇīyam*.

(4.3.33) *avarasya*: For the word *avara*, when it ends in the locative case or other cases beginning with the locative, *as* is substituted [for the case-ending], and *ava* is the substitute for the word itself. Examples: *avo vasati*, *ava āgataḥ*, *avo ramaṇīyam*.

When the suffix *āsti* follows the word *avara*, it optionally undergoes the substitution of *ava*. Thus: *avastād vasati* or *avarastād vasati*; *avastād āgataḥ* or *avarastād āgataḥ*; *avastād ramaṇīyam* or *avarastād ramaṇīyam*. In the case of *paścāt* (Pāṇini 4.3.35), the substitution of *pañca* for *avara* and the suffix *āti* are prescribed as a nipātana (irregular formation). Thus: *paścād vasati*, *paścād āgataḥ*, *paścād ramaṇīyam*. How is the form *dakṣiṇapaścāt* explained? It is that which is both southern (*dakṣiṇam*) and western (*paścāt*); hence, *dakṣiṇapaścāt*.
*Paścārdham* (4.3.36):

*paścārdham* is an irregularly formed (nipātita) word in the sense of "the latter half" (*avarārdham*). Furthermore, that which is both "northern" (*uttaram*) and "the latter half" (*paścārdham*) is *uttarapaścārdham*. Because gender is not a restrictive factor, [the word] *paścārdhaḥ* is also valid.
(4.3.37) *parāvarāt tas vā*: [The suffix] *tas* is optionally applied after the words *para* and *avara*.

The suffix *tas* optionally occurs after the words *para* and *avara*, when they end in the seventh (*saptamī*) or first (*prathamā*) case endings. *parato vasati* (he dwells beyond), *parato ramaṇīyam* (it is pleasant beyond). *parastād vasati* (he dwells beyond), *parastād ramaṇīyam* (it is pleasant beyond). *avarato vasati* (he dwells below), *avarato ramaṇīyam* (it is pleasant below). *avarastād vasati* (he dwells below), *avarastād ramaṇīyam* (it is pleasant below). Regarding *parata āgataḥ* (come from beyond) and *avarata āgataḥ* (come from below), since these are already established by the preceding rule [Pāṇini 5.3.27], the mention of the fifth case (*pañcamī*) is withdrawn. This is also established for the feminine gender because of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*). [Then follows: *dakṣiṇottarād ā ca* (4.3.38).

The suffix *āt* is added after the words *dakṣiṇa* and *uttara*, when they end in the seventh or first case, and the suffix *taḥ* is also added. *dakṣiṇā vasati* (he dwells to the south), *dakṣiṇā ramaṇīyam* (the pleasant place is to the south); *dakṣiṇato ramaṇīyam* (the pleasant place is to the south). *uttarā vasati* (he dwells to the north), *uttarā ramaṇīyam* (the pleasant place is to the north); *uttarato vasati* (he dwells to the north), *uttarato ramaṇīyam* (the pleasant place is to the north). [Furthermore, the suffixes *āt* and *taḥ* are added] also after [words denoting] distance (*dūra*). (Pāṇini 5.3.39)

The suffix *āhi* follows the words *dakṣiṇa* and *uttara*, when they end in the seventh or first case, provided that the point of reference (*avadhimān*) is distant. Thus: *dakṣiṇāhi vasati*, *dakṣiṇāhi ramaṇīyam*; *dakṣiṇā vasati*, *dakṣiṇā ramaṇīyam*. Likewise: *uttarāhi vasati*, *uttarāhi ramaṇīyam*; *uttarā vasati*, *uttarā ramaṇīyam*. Why "distant"? [Observe: *dakṣiṇato vasati*.
Also, after *adhara*, the suffix *āt* is added [under the same conditions]. (Pāṇini 5.3.35–36)

The suffix *āt* is substituted for the final vowel of the words *adhas*, as well as those ending in the seventh (*saptamī*) or first (*prathamā*) case, when followed by *dakṣiṇa* or *uttara*. Examples: *adharād vasati* (he dwells below), *adharād ramaṇīyam* (it is pleasant below). *dakṣiṇād vasati* (he dwells to the south), *dakṣiṇād ramaṇīyam* (it is pleasant to the south). *uttarād vasati* (he dwells to the north), *uttarād ramaṇīyam* (it is pleasant to the north). In the cases of *adharād āgataḥ*, *dakṣiṇād āgataḥ*, and *uttarād āgataḥ* ("come from below," "come from the south," "come from the north"), the substitution is already established by the fifth case (*pañcamī*), because these refer to directions based on a distinction of spatial orientation. Furthermore, the suffix *enap* may optionally be used in the sense of "not far" (Pāṇini 4.3.41).

The suffix *enap* is optionally applied after words ending in the seventh or first case—namely *adhara*, *dakṣiṇa*, and *uttara*—when they denote a direction that is not distant. Examples: *adhareṇa vasati*, *adhareṇa ramaṇīyam* (he dwells or it is pleasant to the south). *adharād vasati*, *adharād ramaṇīyam* (he dwells or it is pleasant to the south). *dakṣiṇena vasati*, *dakṣiṇena ramaṇīyam* (he dwells or it is pleasant to the south). *dakṣiṇād vasati*, *dakṣiṇād ramaṇīyam* (he dwells or it is pleasant to the south). *uttareṇa vasati*, *uttareṇa ramaṇīyam* (he dwells or it is pleasant to the north). *uttarād vasati*, *uttarād ramaṇīyam* (he dwells or it is pleasant to the north). Why is it specified "not distant" (*adūra*)? Consider: *uttarato Himavān* (the Himalayas are to the north [of here]). In this case, the suffix *tas* is used because the distance is implied.

Some do not follow the rule for *adharādi* compounds: *pūrveṇa vasati*, *pūrveṇa ramaṇīyam*. Regarding Pāṇini 4.3.42, *nindye pāśap*: the suffix *pāśap* occurs in the sense of the base itself (*svārthe*) after a word denoting something contemptible (*kutsite*). A contemptible grammarian is a *vaiyākaraṇapāśaḥ*; a *chāndasapāśaḥ*. Why does it say "contemptible"? [Consider: *vaiyākaraṇaḥ*. Why does it not apply here: *vaiyākaraṇaś cauraḥ*? In this case, it is not the state of being a grammarian that is contemptible; rather, it is the act of theft (*cauryam*).

*bhūtapūrve caraṭ* (Pāṇini 4.3.43). *Bhūtaḥ pūrvam* means "previously been. The compound is formed either by this very rule of irregular derivation (*nipātana*) or by *sup supā* (2.2.1). The suffix *caraṭ* occurs after a word denoting something that existed previously. Examples: *āḍhyacaraḥ* ("one who was formerly wealthy"), *darśanīyacaraḥ* ("one who was formerly handsome").
*Ṣaṣṭhyā rūpyac ca* (4.3.44). [The suffix *rūpya* also occurs after a word in the genitive case.]

When that which has previously existed is to be expressed, the suffixes *rūpya* and *caraṭ* follow a word ending in the sixth case. For example: *devadattasya bhūtapūrvaḥ* (one who formerly belonged to Devadatta) becomes *devadattarūpyo gauḥ* (a cow formerly belonging to Devadatta) or *devadattacaraḥ*.
Regarding two or more [entities], when excellence is to be expressed, the suffixes *tarap* and *tamap* are used. (Pāṇini 5.3.57; 5.3.55)

The suffixes *tarap* and *tamap* occur after a word expressing a quality when that quality exists in two or in many, denoting a single or multiple degree of excellence respectively. For example: "Of these two, this one is wealthier" (*ayam anayor āḍhyataraḥ*); "Of these two, this one is a better cook" (*ayam anayoḥ pācakataraḥ*); "Among these, this one is the wealthiest" (*ayam eṣām āḍhyatamaḥ*); "Of these, these two are the best cooks" (*imāv eṣāṃ pācakatamau*); "These three among these cooks are the very best cooks" (*ime traya eṣāṃ pācakānāṃ pācakatamāḥ*). How is it that [the comparative suffix] occurs in the expression "The people of Mathurā are more delicate than the people of Pāṭaliputra"? In this case as well, since there is a comparison between two groups, the suffix *tarap* occurs because it denotes the excellence of one [group] over the other.

The plural number, however, depends on the individual members [of a group], as in: "In this village, the merchants are wealthier. Likewise: "Between us and Devadatta, Devadatta is more handsome. In the expression "the teeth of Dantauṣṭha are glossier," the singular number depends on the whole. In the statement "The people of Mathurā are more delicate than those of Sāṃkāśya and those of Pāṭaliputra," there is a comparative excellence (*prakarṣa*) of only one from each pair.

Regarding the inhabitants of Sāṃkāśya and the inhabitants of Pāṭaliputra, in the expression "the inhabitants of Pāṭaliputra are most delicate," the superlative suffix (*tarap*) expresses a high degree of excellence based on a comparison with many. However, when the comparison is between two, there ought to be only the comparative suffix (*tarap*). Yet, because even a single entity can be considered different through a difference in state, the superlative must indeed occur; for example: "Last year you were clever, but this year you are more clever" (*paṭutaraḥ*). Furthermore, when there is a further degree of excellence even among those already excellent, the comparative (*tarap*) and superlative (*tamap*) suffixes certainly occur, as in: "Yudhiṣṭhira is the most excellent of the Kurus" (*śreṣṭhatamaḥ*). [Pāṇini 5.3.46: "The suffixes *kim*, *etiṅ* (verbs), and numerals, ending in *ām* when not denoting a substance..."

The suffixes *tarap* and *tamap*, as well as *āmu* and *ān*, occur after words such as *kim* when they express excellence (*prakarṣa*), provided that a substance (*dravya*) is not the meaning to be expressed.
