Examples: *kiṃtarām*, *kiṃtamām*; *pūrvāhṇetarām*, *pūrvāhṇetamām*; *pacatitarām*, *pacatitamām*; *uccaistarām*, *uccaistamām*. Why "provided that a substance is not the meaning to be expressed"? Consider: *uccaistaro vṛkṣaḥ* ("the very tall tree").
[Also, the suffixes] *īyasun* and *iṣṭhan* occur after a quality word (*guṇa*). (Pāṇini 5.1.120)

The suffixes *īyasun* and *iṣṭhan*, as well as *tarap* and *tamap*, occur after words denoting qualities (*guṇavacana*) when they express excellence (*prakarṣa*). For example: "Of these two, this one is more clever" (*paṭīyān*, *paṭutaraḥ*); "Among these, this one is the most clever" (*paṭiṣṭhaḥ*, *paṭutamaḥ*); "These two among these are the most clever" (*paṭiṣṭhau*, *paṭutamau*); "These three among these are the most clever" (*paṭiṣṭhāḥ*, *paṭutamāḥ*). These suffixes do not occur after words that denote a quality (*guṇavṛtti*) when there is an absence of comparative excellence. [Pāṇini 5.3.65: *vinmator luk* (the suffixes *vin* and *matup* are elided).

The suffixes *īyasun* and *iṣṭhan* occur after words ending in *vin* and *mat*, when used in the dual or plural to express excellence; furthermore, there is elision (*luk*) of *vin* and *mat*, because they are explicitly mentioned [in the rule]. "Of these two garland-bearers (*sragviṇau*), this one is more garlanded (*srajīyān*). "Among these many garland-bearers (*sragviṇām*), this one is the most garlanded (*srajiṣṭhaḥ*). "Of these two spoon-bearers (*srugvatau*), this one is more spoon-bearing (*srucīyān*). "Among these many spoon-bearers (*srugvatām*), this one is the most spoon-bearing (*sruciṣṭhaḥ*). Due to the treatment as if it were *iṣṭhan* (*iṣṭhavadbhāvaḥ*) in the case of the denominative suffix *ṇic*: *srajayati*, *srucayati*. Regarding the rule *praśasyasya śraḥ* (Pāṇini 5.3.60): when *īyasun* or *iṣṭhan* follows, the word *praśasya* ("praiseworthy") undergoes the substitution *śra*. Thus: *śreyān* ("better"), *śreṣṭhaḥ* ("best").

Pāṇini 4.3.50: *vṛddhasya ca jyaḥ*. When the suffix *īyasun* follows both *praśasya* ("praiseworthy") and *vṛddha* ("grown"), the substitute *jya* occurs. Of these two praiseworthy ones, this one is *jyāyān* (more praiseworthy). Of these praiseworthy ones, this one is *jyeṣṭhaḥ* (the most praiseworthy). Of these two grown ones, this one is *jyāyān* (older). Of these grown ones, this one is *jyeṣṭhaḥ* (the oldest). Pāṇini 4.3.51: *bāḍhāntikayoḥ sādhanedau*. [The substitutes *sādhū* and *nedū* occur for *bāḍha* and *antika* respectively when followed by the suffix *īyasun*.]

In the case of *bāḍha* and *antika*, when followed by the suffixes *īyasun* and *iṣṭhan*, the substitutes *sādhu* and *nedu* respectively occur. For example: *ayam anayoḥ sādhīyo ’dhīte* ("this one studies better than these two"), *ayam eṣāṃ sādhiṣṭham adhīte* ("this one studies best among these"); *idam anayor nedīyaḥ* ("this is nearer than these two"), *idam eṣāṃ nediṣṭham* ("this is nearest among these"). There is no correspondence between the causes [the original words] and the results [the substitutes] according to their respective order, because each substitute depends upon both [the suffixes]. Thus it has been set forth. Furthermore, [the rule] *yuvālpayoḥ kan vā* (Pāṇini 5.3.64) applies.

When combined with the suffixes *īyasun* or *iṣṭhan*, the substitution of *kan* optionally occurs for the words *yuvan* and *alpa*. Thus: *ayam anayoḥ yūnoḥ kanīyān* / *yavīyān* ("this one of these two young men is younger"); *ayam eṣāṃ yūnāṃ kaniṣṭhaḥ* / *yaviṣṭhaḥ* ("this one among these young men is the youngest"). Similarly: *ayam anayor alpayoḥ kanīyān* / *alpīyān* ("this one of these two small things is smaller"); *ayam eṣām alpānāṃ kaniṣṭhaḥ* / *alpiṣṭhaḥ* ("this one among these small things is the smallest"). Due to the treatment as if it were *iṣṭhan* (*iṣṭhavadbhāva*) when the causative suffix *ṇic* follows: *yuvānam ācaṣṭe* ("he describes him as young") becomes *kanayati*.

And by rule 4.3.53, *rūpap* occurs after a verbal form (*tiṅanta*) expressing excellence, as well as after a nominal stem (*subanta*). Examples: *pacatirūpam* ("the manner of cooking"), *yajatirūpam* ("the manner of sacrificing"), *vaiyākaraṇarūpaḥ* ("one who is a grammarian"), *corarūpaḥ* ("one who is a thief"), *tasyurūpaḥ* ("one who is like that").

*kiṃcid ūne kalpab-deśya-deśīyaraḥ* (Pāṇini 5.3.67): The suffixes *kalpab*, *deśya*, and *deśīyar* occur after a finite verb (*tiṅanta*) or a nominal stem (*subanta*) that denotes something slightly incomplete. Examples: *paṭukalpaḥ*, *paṭudeśyaḥ*, *paṭudeśīyaḥ*; *pacatikalpam*, *pacatideśyam*, *pacatideśīyam*. How is it that [the form] *bahukṛtam* occurs? This is simply the word *bahu* itself. *Bahukṛtam* means "not much was done."

Even when [the word] *bahukṛtam* is used in the sense that "Yajñadatta has done much for Devadatta," or "Yajñadatta is a great benefactor to us," even then it is clearly understood that the meaning is simply "much. In expressions such as *bahutailā prasannā* ("clear wine with much oil") or *bahuguḍā drākṣā* ("grapes with much molasses"), the word *bahu* likewise [denotes quantity]. Similarly, in the case of verbal forms (*tiṅanta*), the meaning "he does much" (*bahu karoti*) is understood, yet there is no grammatical rule (*vidhi*) for the preceding *bahu* [to undergo any change].
[This is because the rule] *prāg ḍhañaḥ kaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.3.55) applies.

Prior to the mention of the suffix *ḍhañ*, it should be understood that the suffix *ka* is prescribed for the meanings to be stated hereafter. For example: *aśvakaḥ* ("little horse"), *gardabhakaḥ* ("little donkey").

Regarding the rule *tiṅasaṃkhyānām aco 'ntyāt pūrvo 'kac* (Pāṇini 5.3.71): for verbal forms (*tiṅanta*) and for words not denoting number (*asaṃkhyā*), the suffix *akac* should be understood as prescribed prior to the final vowel (*ac*). Examples: *pacataki* ("he cooks [in a certain way]"), *uccakaiḥ* ("highly").

And what is *daḥ*? (Pāṇini 4.3.57): for those words that do not denote numbers, the final letter *ka* becomes *akac*, and the substitute *da* takes the place of the letter *ka*. Examples: *hirakut*, *pṛthakat*.
[The suffix] *tūṣṇīkām* (Pāṇini 4.3.58).
This word is irregularly formed (*nipātita*).
Regarding the rule *tūṣṇīkaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.4.62),
when one is silent by nature (*tūṣṇīṃ-śīla*), the form *tūṣṇīka* is irregularly derived.

(4.3.60) *sarvādīnām*: For words beginning with *sarva*, the suffix *akac* is inserted before the final vowel, prior to the addition of *ḍhañ*. [Examples: *sarvakaḥ*, *viśvakaḥ*; *yuṣmakābhiḥ*, *asmakābhiḥ*; *yuṣmakāsu*, *asmakāsu*. (4.3.61) *supaḥ*: [The following applies] after a case-ending (*sup*).
After the words *sarva* and so forth, when an *aj*-ending case suffix (*sup*) follows, the augment *akac* is inserted immediately before it. Thus: *tvayakā*, *mayakā*; *tvayaki*, *mayaki*.

Regarding the rule *ajñātakutsayoḥ* (Pāṇini 5.3.73): when "unknown" (*ajñāta*) or "contemptible" (*kutsā*) is implied, the suffixes *ka* and *kak* are applied according to the respective rules. (The section ends with *vatsakaḥ*).
In the sense of "compassion" (dayāyām), [the suffix *aṇ* is applied]:
*vatsakaḥ*. [The vocative particle] *ehaki*. [The sentence] *hanta te dhānakāḥ, gṛhād dūraṃ mā gāḥ* ("Alas, here are your grains; do not go far from home").
Regarding names of men (*nṛnāmni*), the suffixes *ṭhañ*, *ghan*, *ilac*, or [the general *aṇ*] are optionally applied. (Pāṇini 4.3.64)

When compassion (*dayā*) toward a person’s name is implied, the suffixes *ṭhañ*, *ghan*, *ilac*, or *a* are optionally applied. Devikaḥ, Deviyaḥ, Devilaḥ, Devakaḥ, Devadattakaḥ, Devadattaḥ. Dattikaḥ, Dattiyaḥ, Dattilaḥ, Dattakaḥ, Devadattaḥ. Vyāghrikaḥ, Vyāghriyaḥ, Vyāghrilaḥ, Vyāghrakaḥ, Vyāghraḥ. Kṛṣṇājinaḥ, Kṛṣṇakaḥ, Ajinakaḥ. Prajāpatidattaḥ, Prajāpatikaḥ, Prajāpatiyaḥ, Prajāpatilaḥ, Prajāpatidattakaḥ.

Śevalikaḥ, Śevaliyaḥ, Śevalilaḥ, Śevalakaḥ, Śevaladattakaḥ, Śevalendradattaḥ. In the same way, [the suffixes] are to be applied to Suparikaḥ, Viśālikaḥ, Varuṇikaḥ, Aryamikaḥ, and so forth. Vāgāśīrdattaḥ, Vāgāśīrdattakaḥ, Vācikaḥ, Vāciyaḥ, Vācilaḥ. Likewise, Tvacikaḥ, Srucikaḥ.
And [the suffix] *ḍa* is used after the prefix *upa-* (Pāṇini 4.3.65).

The suffixes *ṭhañ*, *ghan*, and *ilac* optionally occur after the word *upa* when it is part of a human name, and the suffix *ḍa* also occurs when compassion (*dayā*) is implied. Thus: *Upikaḥ*, *Upiyaḥ*, *Upilaḥ*, *Upaḍaḥ*, and *Upakaḥ*—the latter being formed as before; and *Upendradattaḥ*. The letter *ḍ* is for the purpose of audible pronunciation.
After the word *ṣaṣ* (six), the suffixes *ṭhañ* and so forth optionally occur, and *ḍa* is the substitute for the final syllable. Thus: *Ṣaḍikaḥ*, *Ṣaḍiyaḥ*, *Ṣaḍilaḥ*, *Ṣaṭkaḥ*.

*ṛto layau* (Pāṇini 4.3.67): After a human name ending in *ṛ*, the suffixes *la* and *ya* optionally occur when the sense of "offspring" (*dayā*) is understood. Examples: *Savitṛlaḥ*, *Savitṛyaḥ*, *Savitṛkaḥ*, *Savitṛdattakaḥ*. *udantāt* (Pāṇini 4.3.68): [The suffixes *la* and *ya* optionally occur] after a name ending in *u*.

When compassion (*dayā*) is implied, the suffixes *la* and *ya* optionally occur after a word denoting a human name. Thus: *Bhānulaḥ*, *Bhānuyaḥ*, *Bhānukaḥ*. Because of the mention of the "end" (*anta*), there is the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*): *Bhānudattakaḥ*. Names of this kind are simply alternative names; therefore, no elision (*lopa*) needs to be stated for any of them. *Lahoḍaḥ*, *Lahikaḥ*; *Kahoḍaḥ*, *Kahikaḥ*—these too are simply alternative names.

By the rule *alpe* (Pāṇini 5.3.85), when a word denotes something small (*apacitaparimāṇa*), the suffixes *ka* and *kāc* occur according to the prescribed rules. Thus: *alpaṃ tailam* (a little oil) becomes *tailakam*; *ghṛtakam*; *pacataki*; *uccakaiḥ*.

The suffixes *ka* and *kāca* occur after a word denoting something short—that is, the opposite of long. For example: *vṛkṣakaḥ*, *plakṣakaḥ*. They also occur when forming a name (*saṃjñā*): *vaṃśakaḥ*, *naḍakaḥ*.
After the words *kuṭī*, *śamī*, and *śuṇḍā*, the suffix *ra* occurs [to form names]. (Pāṇini 4.3.71)
The suffix *ra* follows words such as *kuṭī*. Thus: *kuṭīraḥ*, *śamīraḥ*, *śuṇḍāraḥ*. By their very nature, these are masculine.
Regarding *kutupa*: the form *kutupa* is an irregularly prescribed (*nipātita*) shortening [of the final vowel].

Pāṇini 4.3.73: *kāsūgoṇībhyāṃ ṣṭarac*. The suffix *ṣṭarac* occurs after the words *kāsū* and *goṇī* when they are short. A short spear is *kāsūtarī*; a small sack is *goṇītarī*. Pāṇini 4.3.74: *vatsokṣāśvarṣabhāṇāṃ tanutve*. [The suffix *ṭaca* occurs after these words] when their smallness is intended.

When the nature of a calf (*vatsa*) and so forth is perceived as diminished, the suffix *ṣṭaraj* is applied. When childhood (*śaiśava*) is diminished, it is a *vatsatara*. When youth (*yauvana*) is diminished, it is an *ukṣatara*. When the nature of a horse (*aśva*) is diminished, it is an *aśvatara*. When strength (*sāmarthya*) is diminished, it is an *ṛṣabhatara*. This is according to the rule: "The suffix *ḍatarac* is used after one [of two] when there is a selection (*nirdhāraṇa*)" (Pāṇini 5.3.92).

After *yad* and the following two [words], the suffix *ḍatarac* optionally occurs when selecting one out of two. *yataro bhavatoḥ Devadattaḥ, tatara āgacchatu* ("Whichever of you two is Devadatta, let him come"). *yo bhavatoḥ Devadattaḥ, sa āgacchatu* ("Whoever of you two is Devadatta, he shall come"). *yako bhavatoḥ Devadattaḥ, saka āgacchatu* ("Which of you two is Devadatta, that one shall come"). *ekataro bhavatoḥ Devadattaḥ*, *eko bhavatoḥ Devadattaḥ*, *ekako bhavatoḥ Devadattaḥ*.
The suffix *ḍatamac* occurs after these [same words] when selecting one out of many, provided it refers to a genus (*jāti*). (Pāṇini 5.3.93)

When selecting one from many words beginning with *yad* that denote a genus (*jāti*) and are present, the suffix *ḍatamaj* optionally occurs. For example: *yatamo bhavatāṃ kaṭhaḥ*, *tatama āgacchatu* ("Whichever among you is a Kaṭha, let that one come"; "Let that one among you who is a Kaṭha come"). Also: *ekatamo bhavatāṃ kaṭhaḥ* ("One among you is a Kaṭha") and *eko bhavatāṃ kaṭhaḥ*. Why specify "denoting a genus"? [Consider: *yo bhavatāṃ devadattaḥ, sa āgacchatu* ("Whosoever among you is Devadatta, let him come"). [The rule] *tau kimaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.3.92) applies.

In the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*), do these two suffixes, *ḍatarac* and *ḍatamac*, occur? "Which of you two is Devadatta? (*kataro bhavator Devadattaḥ*); "Which among you is a Kaṭha? (*kataro bhavatāṃ Kaṭhaḥ*); "Which among you is a Kaṭha? (*katamo bhavatāṃ Kaṭhaḥ*); "Which among you is Devadatta? (*katamo bhavatāṃ Devadattaḥ*); "O Brahmin, which one among the Bhāradvājas are you? (*Bhāradvājānāṃ katamo 'si brahman*). [Pāṇini 5.3.93: "The suffix *ivaN* occurs after a word denoting a name (*saṃjñā*) or a likeness (*pratikṛti*). (4.2.78).

The suffix *ka* occurs after a word used in the sense of "like" (*iva*), when it denotes a name (*saṃjñā*) or a representation (*pratikṛti*). For example: *aśva iva ayam* ("this is like a horse") becomes *aśvakaḥ*; likewise, *gardabhakaḥ*. Why specify "when denoting a name or a representation"? Consider: *gaur iva gavayaḥ* ("a gayal is like a cow"). Also: *cañceva cañcā* ("a wooden doll is like a beak"), *vadhrikeva vadhrikā* ("a butcher's wife is like a butcher's wife"); here, the designation by that very word arises from the insistence that "this is that. Similarly for statues: *Skandaḥ*, *Viṣṇuḥ*; for paintings: *Bhīmaḥ*, *Arjunaḥ*; for banners: *siṃhaḥ*, *Garuḍaḥ*.

Likewise, in cases such as *devapatha* and *haṃsapatha*, the suffix *ka* will not occur according to the established option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*). However, in some instances it is indeed desired: *hastaka*, *daṇḍaka*, and *puṣpaka*.
Regarding the rule *vaster ḍhañ* (Pāṇini 4.3.79):
the suffix *ḍhañ* occurs after the word *vasti* when it is used in the sense of "like" (*ivārtha*). For example: like a bladder (*vasti*), it is *vāsteyam*.

*Śilāyā ḍhaś ca* (Pāṇini 4.3.80): The suffix *ḍha* is applied after the word *śilā* when it occurs in the sense of "like" (*ivārtha*), as well as the suffix *ḍhañ*. [Examples: *śileyaṃ dadhi* ("curd like stone"), *śaileyam* ("stone-derived").
*Śākhādibhyo yaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.3.81).

The suffix *ya* occurs in the sense of "like" (*iva*) after words such as *śākhā*. For example: *śākheva* = *śākhyam*. [The words *śākhā*, *mukha*, *jaghana*, *śṛṅga*, *megha*, *caraṇa*, *Skanda*, *uras*, *agra*, and *dru* [are included]. Like a tree (*dru*), so is the substance (*dravyam*); the meaning is "essence. This is also seen even in the case of non-essential things such as jars and the like.

By the rule *kuśāgrāc chaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.3.105), the suffix *cha* occurs in the sense of "like the tip of a blade of *kuśa* grass. For example: *kuśāgrīyā buddhiḥ* ("an intellect sharp as the tip of a *kuśa* blade").

The suffix *cha* occurs after the words *ākasmika* when it denotes the sense of "accidental" (*ivārtha*), provided that "accidental" is the meaning to be expressed. That which is accidental, like the meeting of a crow and a palm fruit, is called *kākatālīya*. [Similarly,] *ajākṛpāṇīya*.
After words such as *śarkara*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied [to denote the sense of "made from"]. (Pāṇini 4.3.84)

The suffix *aṇ* occurs after words such as *śarkarā* in the sense of "made of" or "abounding in. Examples: *śārkaram*, *kāpālikam*. [The bases are: *śarkarā*, *kapālikā*, *kapāṭikā*, *puṇḍarīka*, *śatapattra*, *goloman*, *gopuccha*, *narācī*, *nakula*, *sikatā*.

By rule 4.3.85, the suffix *ṭhak* occurs after words beginning with *aṅguli* in the sense of "made of" or "abounding in. Examples: *āṅgulikaḥ*, *bhārujikaḥ*. [The bases are: *aṅgulī*, *bharuja*, *babhru*, *valgu*, *maṇḍara*, *maṇḍala*, *śaṣkula*, *hari*, *kapi*, *muni*, *bharu*, *khala*, *udaśvit*, *goṇī*, *taras*, *kuliśa*.
(4.3.86) *ekaśālāyās ṭhac ca*: after the word *ekaśālā*, the suffixes *ṭhañ* and *ṭhak* occur in the sense of "resembling" (*ivārtha*). [The forms are] *ekaśālikaḥ* and *aikaśālikaḥ*.
(4.3.87) *karkalohitād īkak*: after the words *karka* and *lohita*, the suffix *īkak* occurs.
The suffix *īka* occurs after the words *karka* and *lohitá* in the sense of "belonging to" (*arthe*). For example: *kārkīkaḥ*, *lauhītīkaḥ*. Regarding the rule *pūgāñ ñyaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.3.88):

a *pūga* is a collection (*saṃgha*) of people of various castes whose occupations are not fixed. The suffix *ñya* occurs after a word denoting a *pūga* in its own sense (*svārthe*). For example: *Lauhadhvajyaḥ*, *Lauhadhvajyau*; *Śaibyaḥ*, *Śaibyau*. A word denoting a whole may also apply to a part [of that whole]. Why does it not occur here: *Devadatto grāmaṇīr eṣām, Devadattakāḥ* ("Devadatta is their leader, [they are] the Devadattakas")? Because this [word "Devadatta"] does not inherently denote a *pūga*.

*Vrātād astriyām* (Pāṇini 4.3.89): The suffix *ñya* occurs in its own sense after a word denoting a *vrāta*—a group of people of various castes, of irregular livelihood, who live by manual labor—but not in the feminine. Examples: *Kāpotapākyaḥ*, *Kāpotapākyau*; *Vraihimatyaḥ*, *Vraihimatyau*. Why "not in the feminine"? [Because] *Kapotapākī* is a feminine form. [This rule applies] after words for groups of weapon-bearers among the Bāhīkas, excluding Brāhmaṇas and Rājanyas; the suffix *ñyaṭ* is used here. (4.3.90).

The suffix *ñyaṭ* occurs after a word denoting a group of weapon-bearers among the Bāhīkas, provided that it does not denote Brāhmaṇas or Rājanyas. Examples: *Kṣaudraka* → *Kṣaudrakyah*, *Kṣaudrakyau*; *Mālava* → *Mālavyah*, *Mālvyau*. Why "among the Bāhīkas"? [Consider: *Śabarāḥ* (the Śabaras). Why "provided it does not denote Brāhmaṇas or Rājanyas"? [Consider: *Śālaṅkāyanāḥ*, who are *rājanyāḥ* (members of the royal caste). The term *rājanya* here is taken as its own form (*svarūpagrahaṇa*); the prohibition applies because there is a difference in accentuation for the feminine form. Why "after a group of weapon-bearers"? [Consider: *Mallāḥ* (the Mallas, who are wrestlers, not weapon-bearers). Why mention "group" (*saṃgha*)? [Consider: *Cakraghoṇaḥ* (which refers to a single individual). The letter *ṭ* in *ñyaṭ* is for the sake of adding the augment *ṇi*. See *vṛkāṇ ṇeṇyaṭ* (Pāṇini 4.3.91).

The suffix *ṇyaṭ* occurs after the word *vṛka* when it denotes a community (*saṃgha*) of those who live by weapons. Thus: *vārkeṇyaḥ*, *vārkeṇyau*. It does not occur when it denotes an animal: "Lust and anger are like two wolves that devour men.
[Pāṇini 4.3.92: The suffix *cha* occurs after *dāman* and others.

The suffix *cha* occurs after the names *Dāmanī* and others which denote corporations of weapon-bearers (*śastrajīvi-saṃgha*). [Examples: *Dāmanīyaḥ*, *Aulapīyaḥ*. The list includes: *Dāmani*, *Aulapi*, *Baijavāpi*, *Audaki*, *Ācyutanti*, *Kākandaki*, *Śākuntaki*, *Sārvaseni*, *Bindu*, *Tulabha*, *Mauñjāyana*, *Sāvitrīputra*. Among the Trigartas, there are six more: *Kauṇḍoparatha*, *Dāṇḍaki*, *Krauṣṭuki*, *Jālamāni*, *Brahmagupta*, and *Jānaki*.

Kauṇḍoparathīyaḥ, Dāṇḍakīyaḥ, Krauṣṭukīyaḥ, Jālamānīyaḥ, Brahmaguptīyaḥ, Jānakīyaḥ. Why [specify] "in the Trigarta region"? [Because otherwise it would apply elsewhere, as in: Kauṇḍoparathyaḥ. The suffix *ñya* occurs after the name of a guild (*pūga*).
After words such as *parśu*, the suffix *aṇ* occurs when not denoting the feminine gender (Pāṇini 4.3.93).

The suffix *aṇ* occurs after words denoting groups of weapon-bearers (*śastrajīvi-saṃgha*), such as *parśu* and others, provided they do not refer to a feminine. Examples: *pārśavaḥ*, *āsuraḥ*. Why "provided they do not refer to a feminine"? [Answer: *parśūḥ* (a single female member of the group). Why "after words denoting groups of weapon-bearers"? [Answer: *parśuḥ* (the individual weapon-bearer). [The list of such groups is: *parśu*, *asura*, *rakṣas*, *bāhlīka*, *vayas*, *vasu*, *marut*, *satvant*, *daśārha*, *piśāca*, *aśani*, *kārṣāpaṇa*, *trigarta*, *bharata*, *uśīnara*. How is the form *yaudheyaḥ* derived? It is formed by the suffix *ḍhak* according to the rule *yudhāyā dvayacaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.112).

[The forms] *Śubhra*, *Dhṛta*, *Vṛtta*, *Jyā*, and *Bāṇa* [are derived] from the group beginning with *śubhra*. In [the case of] *Yaudheyī* and others, the suffix *ṅīp* is applied directly after the suffix *ḍhak*. We shall discuss the specific accentuation in the chapter on accents (*svarādhyāya*).

(4.3.94) "There is elision (*luk*) of the suffixes beginning with *ñya* when [the patronymic] refers to many. There is elision of the suffixes beginning with *ñya* when referring to many [members of a clan]. For example: *Lohadhvajāḥ*, *Kapotapākāḥ*, *Kṣudrakāḥ*, *Vṛkāḥ*, *Dāmanayaḥ*. Only provided it is not feminine (*astriyām*): the women are *Lauhadhvajyāḥ*, *Kapotapākyaḥ*, *Dāmanīyāḥ*.
The suffix *yañ* is applied after the words *abhijit*, *vidabhṛt*, *śālāvat*, *śikhāvat*, *śamīvat*, *ūrṇāvat*, and *śrumat* to form patronymics. (Pāṇini 4.1.115)

The suffix *yañ* occurs in the sense of the base meaning itself after those [words] ending in *aṇ* which denote a descendant, starting with *abhijit*. For example: *ābhijityaḥ*, *vaidabhṛtyaḥ*; *śālāvatyaḥ*, *śaikhāvatyaḥ*, *śāmīvatyaḥ*, *aurṇāvatyaḥ*, *śraumatyaḥ*. Why is the mention of "descendant" (*apatya*) necessary? [Consider: *ābhijitaḥ sthālīpākaḥ* ("an *ābhijita* sacrificial porridge"). By the rule "there is elision (*luk*) when there are many," we have: *ābhijitāḥ*. By the rule "provided it is not feminine" (*astriyām*), we have: *abhijityaḥ striyaḥ* ("feminine *ābhijityas*"). Furthermore, because this *yañ* is an affix added in the sense of a descendant or the base meaning itself, the elision prescribed by Pāṇini 2.4.64 (*yañañoś ca*) does not occur at all in the feminine.

The descendant of Ābhijiti is dependent on his teacher, [called] Ābhijityāyana. By the rule *yañiña* (Pāṇini 4.1.101), the suffix *phak* is applied. A student of Ābhijiti is Ābhijitaka. By the rule *gotrād vuñ* (Pāṇini 4.2.115), the suffix *vuñ* is applied. A group of the Ābhijitas is Ābhijita. By the rule *saṃghāṅkaghoṣalakṣaṇeṣv añyañiña* (Pāṇini 4.3.127), the suffix *aṇ* is applied. The third quarter of the fourth chapter is completed. [Now begins:
After words meaning "much" (*bahu*) or "little" (*alpa*), when they denote an agent (*kāraka*), the suffix *śas* is optionally used to express a blessing (*maṅgala*). (Pāṇini 5.4.42).

When a word expressing auspiciousness (*maṅgalavacana*) is understood from a word denoting "much" (*bahu*) or "little" (*alpa*), the suffix *śas* optionally occurs after that word. Give much! / Give in abundance! (*bahu dehi*, *bahuśo dehi*). Give plenty! / Give in plenty! (*prabhūtaṃ dehi*, *prabhūtaśo dehi*). Give little! / Give in small measure! (*alpaṃ dehi*, *alpaśo dehi*). Give a trifle! / Give in trifles! (*stokaṃ dehi*, *stokaśo dehi*). Give with many [gifts]! / Give in many ways! (*bahubhir dehi*, *bahuśo dehi*). Give to many! / Give in many ways! (*bahubhyo dehi*, *bahuśo dehi*). Give among many! / Give in many ways! (*bahuṣu dehi*, *bahuśo dehi*). Why is it said "from a word denoting much or little"? [Consider: Give a cow! (*gāṃ dehi*).

Why is it stated "from a word denoting an agent" (*kārakāt*)? [Consider: *bahūnāṃ svāmī* ("the master of many"). Why is it stated "in the sense of 'auspicious'" (*maṅgale*)? [Consider: *bahūni śrāddhāni dehi* ("give many funeral offerings") and *alpam ābhyudayikaṃ dehi* ("give a small auspicious offering"). [The rule] *saṃkhyaikārthād vīpsāyām* (Pāṇini 5.4.43) applies.

The suffix *śas* optionally occurs after a numeral or a word denoting a single entity (*ekārtha*), when distributive repetition (*vīpsā*) is understood. Examples: *dvau dvau dehi* ("Give two by two") becomes *dviśo dehi*. *triśo dehi*. *gaṇaśaḥ*, *katiśaḥ*, *tāvacchaḥ*. *māṣaṃ māṣaṃ dehi* ("Give bean by bean") becomes *māṣaśo dehi*. *saṃghaśaḥ*, *pūgaśaḥ*, *vṛndaśaḥ*. In the case of *kramaśaḥ*, there is a distinction of sequence due to the distinction among those possessing a sequence. This is already established by the rule [Pāṇini 5.4.43] "when distributive repetition is intended. Why specify "after a numeral or a word denoting a single entity"? Consider: *māṣau māṣau dehi* ("Give two beans, two beans"). Why specify "when distributive repetition is intended"? Consider: *dvau dehi* ("Give two"). The rule applies only when the word denotes a *kāraka* (participant in an action).
Thus: *dvayor dvayoḥ svāmī* ("The owner of each pair"). [The suffix] *vun* follows a numeral and so forth [according to Pāṇini 5.1.22].

The suffix *vun* optionally occurs after numerals and the like when expressing distributive repetition (*vīpsā*). For example: *dvau dvau pādau dadāti* ("he gives two feet each time") becomes *dvipadikāṃ dadāti*; *dviśatikāṃ dadāti*; *dvimodakikāṃ dadāti*. Only when there is distributive repetition does this apply; otherwise, as in *dvau pādau dadāti* ("he gives two feet"), it does not. By virtue of a fixed optionality (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*), it does not occur in some cases, such as *dvau dvau māṣau dadāti* ("he gives two māṣas each time"). [This applies] in the case of giving and punishment (*daṇḍadānayoḥ*). (Pāṇini 5.4.43)

When *daṇḍa* ("punishing") and *dāna* ("giving") are understood, the suffix *vun* optionally occurs after numerals and so forth. Examples: *dvipadikāṃ daṇḍitaḥ* ("he was punished two paces"), *dviśatikām*, *dvimodakikām*. *dvipadikāṃ dadāti* ("he gives two paces"), *dviśatikām*, *dvimodakikām*. By virtue of the fixed optionality (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*), it does not occur in some cases: *dvau māṣau daṇḍitaḥ* ("he was punished two māṣas").
[The suffix] *kṛtvasuc* is used after a numeral denoting frequency (*vāra*). (Pāṇini 5.4.17–18)

The suffix *kṛtvasuc* is optionally used after a numeral that denotes a number of times (*vāra*). Examples: *pañca vārān bhuṅkte* (he eats five times), *pañcakṛtvo 'hno bhuṅkte* (he eats five times during the day). Also: *ṣaṭkṛtvaḥ*, *gaṇakṛtvaḥ*, *katikṛtvaḥ*, *tāvatkṛtvaḥ*. What is the purpose of mentioning "times" (*vāra*)? [To exclude cases like: *pañca bhuṅkte* (he eats five [meals]). Why say "after a numeral" (*saṃkhyāyāḥ*)? [To exclude cases like: *prabhūtān vārān bhuṅkte* (he eats many times). [Also taught is: *bahoś ca dhā cāviprakarṣe* (Pāṇini 5.4.20): after the word *bahu*, the suffix *dhā* is also used, provided there is no great interval between the actions.

The suffix *dhā* and *kṛtvasuc* are applied to a numeral associated with frequency (*vāra*), provided that there is no long interval between the occurrences. For example: *bahudhā divasasya bhuṅkte* ("he eats many times during the day"), *bahukṛtvaḥ*. Why "no long interval"? [Consider: *bahukṛtvo māsasya bhuṅkte* ("he eats many times during the month").

Regarding *dvitricaturaḥ suc* (Pāṇini 5.4.18): the suffix *suc* optionally occurs after the words *dvi*, *tri*, and *catur* when they denote frequency. For example: *dvau vārau bhuṅkte* ("he eats twice") or *dvir bhuṅkte*; *trir bhuṅkte*; *catur bhuṅkte*.
(4.4.8) *sakṛt*: In the sense of "once," the form *sakṛt* is optionally prescribed as a nipātana. For example: *ekaṃ vāraṃ bhuṅkte*, *sakṛd bhuṅkte* ("he eats once").
(4.4.9) *mayaṭ* is applied in the context at hand.

The suffix *mayaṭ* optionally occurs when [the base] denotes the material cause (*prakṛti*). When food is the material cause, we have *annamayaṃ* (made of food), *yavāgūmayaṃ* (made of gruel), or *yavāgūmayī* (feminine). How is it that [the suffix is used] in expressions such as *annamayo yajñaḥ* ("a sacrifice consisting of food") or *vaṭakamayī yātrā* ("a procession consisting of cakes")? This is established by the rule *tasya vikāre* (Pāṇini 4.3.134) when there is an intention to express its predominance (*prādhānya*), as in *śraddhāmayo 'yaṃ puruṣaḥ* ("this person consists of faith"). How is it that when cakes are the material cause, we have *āpūpikaṃ* (a collection of cakes), or when cakes are the material cause in this [sacrifice], we have *āpūpiko yajñaḥ* ("a cake-sacrifice")? This is established by the rule *tasya samūhaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.2.37). In the case of sacrifices and the like, the gender is determined by common usage (*lokataḥ*), or the suffix *ac* is applied because they belong to the *arśas-ādi* group.
(4.4.10) *anantāvasathetihabheṣajāñ-ñaḥ*:

After the words *ananta* and so forth, the suffix *ñya* optionally occurs in the sense of the base itself (*svārtha*). Thus: *ananta* itself is *ānantyam*; *āvasatha* itself is *āvasathyam*; *iti ha* (thus indeed) is *aitihyam*; *bheṣaja* itself is *bhaiṣajyam*. (4.4.11) *tīyād īkak na vidyā cet*: After a word ending in the suffix *tīya*, the suffix *īkak* is added, provided it does not refer to a branch of knowledge (*vidyā*).

The suffix *īka* optionally occurs after a word ending in the third case (*tṛtīyā*) in the sense of the base itself (*svārthe*), provided that it does not denote a branch of knowledge (*vidyā*). [Examples: *dvaitīyīkam*, *dvitīyam*; *tārtīyīkam*, *tṛtīyam*. Why is it said "provided it does not denote a branch of knowledge"? [Counter-examples: *dvitīyā vidyā* (the second science), *tṛtīyā vidyā* (the third science). [The suffix] *kan* occurs after words such as *yāvat* and others [in the sense of the base itself]. (Pāṇini 5.4.12)

The suffix *kan* is optionally added in the sense of the base itself (*svārtha*) after words such as *yāva*. For example: *yāva* itself is *yāvaka*; *maṇi* itself is *maṇika*. This is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open class of words), consisting of: *yāva*, *maṇi*, *asthi*, *candra*, *pīta*, *stabdha*, *ṛtu*, *uṣṇa-śīta*, *paśu*, *lūna-viyāta*, *aṇu* (in the sense of "skillful"), *putra* (in the sense of "artificially made"), *puṇya* (when a student has completed his Vedic studies), *śūnya* (in the sense of "empty"), *dāna* (in the sense of "contemptible gift"), *tanu* (in the sense of "thread"), *bṛhatī* (in the sense of "garment"), and the suffix *īyasun* (as in *jyeṣṭha*). Also included are *jñāta*, *ajñāta*, and toys for young girls (*kumārī-krīḍanakāni*). Furthermore, by rule 4.4.13, *lohitāt maṇau* ("after *lohita* when meaning a gem"): [the suffix *kan* is applied]. For example: *lohita* itself is *lohitaka* when it refers to a gem.

The suffix *kan* optionally occurs after the word *lohita* when it refers to a gem (*maṇi*). For example: *lohitakaḥ maṇiḥ* ("a red gem") or simply *lohitaḥ*. Why "when referring to a gem"? [Observe: *lohito gauḥ* ("a red cow"). Regarding the rule *raktānityayoḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.41): the suffix *kan* optionally occurs after *lohita* when it means "dyed" (*rakta*) or "non-eternal" (*anitya*). For example: *lohitakaḥ*, *lohitaḥ*. A cloth dyed with safflower and the like is called *lohitakaḥ*. One who is red with anger is *lohitakaḥ*. A garment may be *lohitikā* or *lohitā*. Since the feminine form is also included, when the suffix *kan* is added to the word *lohinī*, the result is *lohinikā* or *lohinī*. Why "when meaning dyed or non-eternal"? [Observe: *lohitaṃ rudhiram* ("blood is red").

After a word denoting time, when it signifies "colored" (*rakta*) or "not permanent" (*anitya*), the suffix *kan* optionally occurs. For example: *kālakaḥ kambalaḥ* ("a black blanket") or simply *kālaḥ*; likewise, *kālakaḥ śokena* ("darkened by grief"). Furthermore, after a word ending in the suffix *kta*, *kan* is used when the sense is not absolute (*anātyantika*).

The suffix *kan* optionally occurs after a word ending in a past passive participle (*kta*) when it denotes something that is not final or complete. For example: *anatyantaṃ bhinnaḥ* (not completely split) becomes *bhinnakaḥ*; *chinnakaḥ*. Why "not final"? Because in cases such as *bhinnaḥ* or *chinnaḥ*, the suffix does not apply. [Furthermore,] because the meaning "half-finished" is expressed by a different word (*sāmikṛtam*), the suffix *kan* does not occur there. The forms *brāhmaṇajātīyaḥ* and *kṣatriyajātīyaḥ* are established by means of the suffix *jātīyar*. For a particularity (*viśeṣa*) is a mode (*prakāra*) that distinguishes a general category (*sāmānya*). In the expression *pitṛsthānīyaḥ* ("standing in the place of a father"), the meaning is "one whose position is like that of a father"; that is, *pitṛsthāna* (the father's place).

That which is to be treated with respect in this matter, like a father, is *pitṛsthānīya* ("father-like"). That which is to be treated without restraint in this matter, like a son, is *putrasthānīya* ("son-like"). Regarding the rule *vinayādibhyaṣ ṭhak* (Pāṇini 4.4.17):

the suffix *ṭhak* optionally occurs after the group beginning with *vinaya* (*vinayādi*) in its own sense (*svārthe*). Thus, *vinaya* itself is *vaina-yikaḥ*; likewise, *sāmayikaḥ*. From *vinaya*, *samaya*, and *upāya*, there is also shortening [of the final vowel]. The group [of words] is: *saṃgati*, *akasmāt*, *upacāra*, *samācāra*, *vyavahāra*, *saṃpradāna*, *samutkarṣa*, *samūha*, *viśeṣa*, *atyaya*, and *anugādin*.

In the sense of "message" (vācaḥ saṃdeśe 4.4.18), the suffix *ṭhak* is applied to the word *vāc* when it occurs in the sense of a message. One tells a *vācika* (verbal message). Since there is no occurrence of the word *vāc* in the sense of a message without this suffix, the rule is mandatory (*nitya*). Why say "in the sense of a message"? [Otherwise, it would apply to] *vāk* (speech in general). Likewise, [the suffix] *aṇ* is applied after *karman* (4.4.19).

Just as in the case of *saṃdeśa*, the suffix *aṇ* occurs after *karman*. Thus, *kārmaṇa*. Since subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*) is also performed according to the instruction of the elders, that too is called *kārmaṇa*. [The rule] "after *oṣadhi*, when not denoting a genus" (Pāṇini 4.3.138): the suffix *aṇ* occurs after *oṣadhi* when it does not denote a genus. Thus, *auṣadha*. Why "when not denoting a genus"? [Consider: *oṣadhiḥ*.
Pāṇini 4.4.21:

The suffix *aṇ* occurs after a word ending in *ṇac* and after a word ending in *inuṇ*, in the sense of the base itself (*svārthe*). Examples: *vyāvakrośī* (one who habitually reviles), *vyāvacarcī* (one who habitually disputes); *sāṃkūṭinam* (acting with deceit), *sāṃrāviṇam* (making a loud noise).
Pāṇini 4.4.22: Or [the suffix *aṇ* occurs] after words beginning with *prajña*.

The suffix *aṇ* optionally occurs after words such as *prajña* in their own sense (*svārthe*). One who understands is *prajña*; that same person is *prājña*. Since this is already established by the possessive suffix (*matvarthīya*), the statement is made for the sake of the feminine suffix *ṅīp*: a woman is *prājñī*. [Similarly: *vaṇik*, *vāṇijaḥ*.

*prajña*, *vaṇij*, *uśij*, *uṣṇih*, *pratyakṣavidan*, *ṣoḍan*, *vidyā*, *manas*, *juhvat*, *visārin*, *matsya*, *śrotra*, *śarīra*, *kṛṣṇamṛga*, *cikīrṣita*, *cora*, *śatru*, *dhūrta*, *yodha*, *cakṣus*, *vasu*, *marut*, *kruñc*, *satvan*, *daśārha*, *vayas*, *asura*, *rakṣas*, *piśāca*, *aśani*, *devatā*, *bandhu*. This is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open class).

*Vaikṛtaḥ*, *vaiyātaḥ*, *sāṃtapanaḥ*, *ānuṣṭubham*, *jāgatam*, *āgnīdhram*, *sādhāraṇam*, and *āgrayaṇam*—in these cases, there is substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpatvam*) due to their inclusion in the *śakandhvādi* group. *Āgrahāyaṇam* is derived from *āgrahāyaṇī* by the rule *ṭhak* (Pāṇini 4.2.21), as established by nipātana. By the rule *mṛdas tikan* (Pāṇini 5.4.39), the suffix *tikan* is applied to *mṛd*; thus we have *mṛttikā* and *mṛt*.
The suffixes *sas* and *sn* are optionally used after the word *mṛd* to express praise. Thus: *mṛtsā*, *mṛtsnā*, or *mṛdrūpā*.
The suffix *dheya* is added after the words *nāman* and *rūpa*. (Pāṇini 4.4.25)

The suffix *dheya* is applied in its own sense after the words *nāman* and *rūpa*. [Thus we have] *nāma* and *nāmadheya*; *rūpa* and *rūpadheya*. Furthermore, by the rule *bhāgād yaś ca* (Pāṇini 4.4.26), the suffix *ya* occurs after *bhāga*, and *dheya* also occurs. [Thus we have] *bhāgyāni* and *bhāgadheyāni*.

(4.4.27) *sūramartakṣemayaviṣṭhāt*: after the words *sūra*, etc., the suffix *yat* or [the suffix *ya*] occurs. *sūraḥ*, *sūryaḥ*; *martaḥ*, *martyaḥ*; *kṣemaḥ*, *kṣemyaḥ*; *yaviṣṭhaḥ*, *yaviṣṭhyaḥ*. (4.4.28) *navāt*: [The suffix *yat* or *ya* occurs] after the word *nava*.
Or it may be derived from *nava*. [The forms] *navam* and *navyam* are derived directly. Regarding the rule *tnaptanakhā nū ca* (Pāṇini 5.4.29):
after the word *nava*, the suffixes *tna*, *tana*, and *kha* occur, and furthermore, *nū* is its substitute. Thus, one obtains *nūtnam*, *nūtanam*, and *navīnam*.
(4.4.30) After the word *pra*, when it signifies "ancient," the suffix *na* occurs, as well as *tṛ*, *tana*, and *kha*. [Examples: *praṇam*, *pratnam*, *pratanam*, *prīṇam*.
(4.4.31) After a word ending in *devatā*, the suffix *yat* is added in the sense of "for the sake of that."

After the word *devatā*, when its meaning is to be expressed, the suffix *yat* optionally occurs. For example: *agnidevatārtham idam* (this is for the sake of the deity Agni), *agnidevatyam*; *pitṛdevatyam*. This is established either by the rule *sāsya devatā* (Pāṇini 4.2.24) due to this very nipātana (irregular formation), or by the suffix *yat*. After the word *argha*, the suffix *yat* optionally occurs in the sense of "for that purpose. For example: *arghārtham*, *arghyam*.
when the sense of "water for the feet" is to be expressed, *pādyam* is an irregularly formed word (*nipātana*).
*atither ṇyaḥ* (4.4.34).
The suffix *ṇya* occurs after [a word] meaning "guest" (*atithi*) in the sense of "for the sake of that. Thus: *ātithyam*, meaning "for the sake of a guest" (*atithyartha*).

Regarding the transformation of one thing into another: when used in conjunction with the verbs *kṛ*, *bhū*, or *as*, the suffix *cvi* is applied after a word denoting the thing modified. (Pāṇini 5.4.50).

When there is a connection with the roots *kṛ*, *bhū*, or *as*, the suffix *cv-* occurs after a word denoting a modification (*vikāra*), provided that a thing possessing a certain state (*avasthāvat*) comes into being as that very essence (*tadātmanā*) through a change of state (*avasthāntara*). Examples: * He makes what was not white white: *śuklīkaroti*. * He becomes what was not white white: *śuklībhavati*. * May he become what was not white white: *śuklīsyāt*. Why is it specified "the becoming of that which was not previously so" (*abhūtatadbhāva*)? Consider: *ghaṭaṃ karoti* (He makes a pot). *ghaṭo bhavati* (It becomes a pot). *dadhy asti* (There is curd). [In these cases, the suffix does not apply. Why is it specified "in connection with *kṛ*, *bhū*, or *as*"? Consider: *aśuklaḥ śuklo jāyate* (What was not white is born white). [The suffix does not apply here because the roots are not *kṛ*, *bhū*, or *as*. Why is it specified "from a modification" (*vikārāt*)? So that it does not apply to the original material (*prakṛti*): [e.g., *mṛdaṃ ghaṭīkaroti*—he makes clay into a pot].

Gold becomes a coil (*kuṇḍala*). However, as for that which does not become white even with effort, it will simply not come into being there because of the absence of the transformation of one thing into another (*abhūtatadbhāva*).
[Furthermore, by Pāṇini 4.4.36: "There is elision (*lopa*) of the suffixes *aru*, *manas*, *cakṣus*, *cetas*, *rahas*, and *rajas*."

The final phoneme of *aru* and the following words is elided; furthermore, the suffix *cvi* is established by the preceding rule. *aru* becomes *arū*: *aruṃ karoti*, *aruṃ bhavati*, *aruṃ syāt*. *unmanas* becomes *unmanī*: *unmanīṃ karoti*, *unmanīṃ bhavati*, *unmanīṃ syāt*. *uccakṣus* becomes *uccakṣū*: *uccakṣūṃ karoti*, *uccakṣūṃ bhavati*, *uccakṣūṃ syāt*. *vicetas* becomes *vicetī*: *vicetīṃ karoti*, *vicetīṃ bhavati*, *vicetīṃ syāt*. *virahin* becomes *virahī*: *virahīṃ karoti*, *virahīṃ bhavati*, *virahīṃ syāt*. *virajas* becomes *virajī*: *virajīṃ karoti*, *virajīṃ bhavati*, *virajīṃ syāt*. In the sense of "pervasion" (*abhividhi*), the suffix *sāti* is optionally used with the verb *sam-pad*. (Pāṇini 5.4.52)

When pervasion is understood—either by way of a single part or in its entirety—within the domain of *cvī*, there is optionally the suffix *sāti* when used in conjunction with *saṃpad*, as well as with *kṛ*, *bhū*, and *as*. *agnisāt saṃpadyate śastram* ("The weapon becomes fire"). *agnisāt karoti*, *agnisād bhavati*, *agnisāt syāt*. *agnīkaroti*, *agnībhavati*, *agnīsyāt*. The repetition of the word "optionally" (*vā*) is for the purpose of allowing an alternative construction. [This applies also] in the sense of "dependent on that" (*tadadhīne*). (Pāṇini 5.4.51)

When the object to be expressed is dependent on something else, the suffix *sāti* optionally occurs after a word denoting the owner of that thing, provided it is used in conjunction with the roots *kṛ*, *bhū*, *as*, and *saṃpad*. For example: *rājādhīnaṃ karoti* ("he makes [it] dependent on the king"), *rājasāt karoti*; *rājasād bhavati*, *rājasāt syāt*, *rājasāt saṃpadyate*. Regarding what is to be given, the suffix *trā* is also used [after the same words]. (Pāṇini 5.4.52–53)

When that which is to be given (*deyam*) depends upon someone, and that person is not explicitly mentioned as the object, the suffix *trā* is used in connection with the roots *kṛ*, *bhū*, and *as*, as well as with the verb *saṃ-pad*. The suffix *sāti* is also used. For example: *devādhīnaṃ deyaṃ karoti* ("He makes the gift dependent on the gods") becomes *devatrā karoti*. *deveṣu bhavati* ("It exists among the gods") becomes *devatrā bhavati*. *devatrā syāt*, *devatrā saṃpadyate*. *devasāt karoti*, *devasād bhavati*, *devasāt syāt*, *devasāt saṃpadyate*. [The rule] *devādibhyo dvitīyāsaptamyor bahulam* (Pāṇini 5.4.40) [applies].

After words such as *deva* and others, the suffix *trā* is frequently employed in the sense of the second case (*dvitīyā*) and the seventh case (*saptamī*), when used in conjunction with the verbs *kṛ*, *bhū*, *as*, and others. For example: *devān karoti* (he makes gods), *devatrā karoti*; *deveṣu bhavati* (he exists among the gods), *devatrā bhavati*; *deveṣu syāt* (may he be among the gods), *devatrā syāt*; *devān gacchati* (he goes to the gods), *devatrā gacchati*.

He dwells among the gods (*deveṣu*), he dwells among the gods (*devatrā*). Likewise: he goes to humans (*manuṣyān*) or dwells among humans (*manuṣyeṣu*), [expressed as] *manuṣyatrā*; among men (*puruṣān* or *puruṣeṣu*), [expressed as] *puruṣatrā*; among many men (*purūn* or *puruṣu*), [expressed as] *purutrā*; among mortals (*martyān* or *martyeṣu*), [expressed as] *martyatrā*; among many (*bahūn* or *bahuṣu*), [expressed as] *bahutrā*. And from other words as well, according to usage.
[The suffix] *ḍāc* is added after an unexpressed imitation of sound that consists of more than one syllable, provided it is not followed by the particle *iti* (Pāṇini 4.4.41).

The suffix *ḍāc* is applied after an imitative sound (*avyaktānukaraṇa*) consisting of more than one vowel (*anekāc*), when used in conjunction with the roots *kṛ*, *bhū*, or *as*, provided that it is not followed by the word *iti*. Examples: *paṭapaṭākaroti*, *paṭapaṭābhavati*, *paṭapaṭāsyāt*. Why does the rule specify "after an imitative sound"? Consider: *dṛṣatkaroti* ("he makes a stone"). Why does it specify "consisting of more than one vowel"? Consider: *śratkaroti* ("he hears"). Why does it specify "not followed by *iti*"? Consider: *paṭiti karoti* ("he acts suddenly"). The letter *c* [in *ḍāc*] is for the purpose of providing a specific grammatical designation. [Also: After the words *dvitīya*, *tṛtīya*, *śamba*, and *bīja*, the suffix *ḍāc* is applied when used with the root *kṛ* in the sense of plowing (*kṛṣi*). (Pāṇini 5.4.42)

When used in conjunction with the verb *karoti* (he does/makes) in the sense of plowing, the suffix *ḍāc* is applied after words beginning with the second [case ending]. *dvitīyākaroti*, *tṛtīyākaroti*, *śambākaroti*. The meaning is that he plows again crosswise. *bījākaroti*. Why "in the sense of plowing"? [Consider: *dvitīyaṃ paṭaṃ karoti* (he makes a second cloth). [From Pāṇini 5.4.43:

After a word for a quality (*guṇa*) preceded by a numeral, the suffix *ḍāc* is applied when used in conjunction with *karoti*. *dviguṇākaroti*, *triguṇākaroti*. Only "in the sense of plowing" applies here: *dviguṇāṃ rajjuṃ karoti* (he makes a two-fold rope).

(4.4.44) *samayād yāpanāyām*: When *yāpanā* (delaying/procrastinating) is understood, the suffix *ḍāc* occurs in connection with the verb *kṛ*. *Samayākaroti* means "he delays" or "he wastes time. Why say "when *yāpanā* is understood"? [Answer: *Samayaṃ karoti* ("he makes an agreement"). (4.4.45) *sapattraniṣpattrād ativyathane*: [The suffix *ḍāc* occurs after the words *sapattra* and *niṣpattra* when used in the sense of causing excessive pain.]

When excessive wounding is understood to be occurring through the use of *sapattrā* and *niṣpattrā*, the suffix *ḍāc* is applied. *Sapattrākaroti mṛgam* ("He makes the deer [sapattrā]"). *Niṣpattrākaroti kavacam* ("He makes the armor [niṣpattrā]"). Why "excessive wounding"? [Consider: *Sapattraṃ karoti vṛkṣam* ("He makes the tree [sapattraṃ]") and *niṣpattraṃ karoti kāṇḍam* ("He makes the arrow [niṣpattraṃ]"). Regarding *niṣkulān* in the sense of "extracting from the interior" (Pāṇini 4.4.46): the suffix *ḍāc* is applied to *niṣkulā* when there is an extraction of what was situated within. *Niṣkulākaroti phalam* ("He extracts the fruit [from its interior]"). Why "extraction"? [Consider: *Niṣkulaṃ karoti śatrum* ("He exterminates the enemy").

(4.4.47) *priyasukhād ānukūlye*: When conformity (*ānukūlya*) is implied, the suffix *ḍāc* is applied after the words *priya* and *sukha*. Examples: *priyākaroti*, *sukhākaroti*. Why specify "conformity"? [Consider: *sukhaṃ karoti* ("he makes happy"). (4.4.48) *duḥkhāt prātikūlye*: [The suffix *ḍāc* is applied] after the word *duḥkha* when opposition (*prātikūlya*) is implied.

When the sense of being contrary to suffering (*duḥkha*) is understood, the suffix *ḍāc* is applied. Example: *duḥkhākaroti*. Why "being contrary"? [Counter-example: *duḥkhaṃ karoti* ("he causes pain").

In the case of cooking on a spit (*śūla*), when the sense of cooking on a spit is understood, the suffix *ḍāc* is applied. Examples: *śūle pacati māṃsam* ("he cooks meat on a spit") or *śūlākaroti*. Why "cooking"? [Counter-example: *śūlaṃ karoti* ("he makes a spit").

(4.4.50) *satyād aśapathe*: After the word *satya*, when it does not refer to an oath (*aśapatha*), the suffix *ḍāc* occurs. Example: *satyākaroti vaṇig bhāṇḍam*. This means he creates confidence [in the buyer] that "I must certainly purchase this merchandise. Why say "when it does not refer to an oath"? Observe: *satyaṃ karoti* ("he tells the truth"). (4.4.51) *madrabhadrād vapane*: [The suffix *ḍāc* occurs after the words *madra* and *bhadra* in the sense of shaving.]

When the sense of "shaving" (*vapana*) is implied, the suffix *ḍāc* is applied after the words *madrabhadra*. Examples: *madrākaroti*, *bhadrākaroti*. Why specify "shaving"? [Counter-example: *madraṃ karoti* ("he does what is beneficial").

From this point forward, the suffixes beginning with *añ* that will be mentioned should be understood as forming the final element (*anta*) of a compound. We shall explain the purpose for their being included as the final element in those very rules.

(4.4.53) *na kimaḥ kṣepe*: When the word *kim* is used in a sense of censure (*kṣepa*), the compound suffix does not occur after it. For example: *kiṃrājā yo na rakṣati!* ("What a king he is, who does not protect!"); *kiṃgaur yo na vahati!* ("What an ox he is, who does not carry!"). Why "in censure"? Consider: *keṣāṃ rājā, kiṃrājaḥ* ("the king of whom?"—here it is a question). (4.4.54) *pūjāyāṃ svateḥ prāg anyārthāt*: When expressing praise (*pūjā*), [the suffix] occurs before the word *sva*, provided it does not have another meaning.

(95) When *su* or *ati* precede, a compound-ending suffix (*samāsānta*) does not occur when expressing praise (*pūjā*), prior to the section on other meanings. Examples: *surājā*, *atirājā*; *sugauḥ*, *atigauḥ*. Why "when expressing praise"? Consider: one who has surpassed a king (*atikrānto rājānam*) is called *atirājaḥ*. Why "of *su* and *ati*"? Consider: *paramarājaḥ*. Why "prior to the section on other meanings"? Consider: *susakthaḥ*, *svakṣaḥ*. Regarding *naño 'nanyārthe* (Pāṇini 5.4.71):

after the negative particle *nañ*, a compound-ending suffix does not occur provided that it does not function to express a meaning other than that of the [second] member. Examples: *arājā*, *asakhā*. Why "not expressing another meaning"? Consider: *anṛco māṇavaḥ* ("a student who has no Ṛgveda verses") and *adhuraṃ śakaṭam* ("a cart without a yoke").

*patho vā* (4.4.56): After the word *pathin* when preceded by the negative particle *nañ*, the compound-final suffix (*samāsānta*) optionally occurs. Thus: *nāyaṃ panthāḥ* ("this is not a path") becomes *apanthāḥ* or *apatham*. [The rule applies] only when it does not have another meaning: *apatho 'yam uddeśaḥ* ("this region is pathless").
*purabdhuraś cānakṣasyāc* (4.4.57).

The suffix *añ* is applied as a compound-final (*samāsānta*) to words ending in *pura*, *anta*, and *pathin*, provided they are not connected with the word *akṣa*. Examples: *daśapurī*, *dvipurī*; *dvīpaḥ*, *samīpaḥ*; *dvidhurī*, *tridhurī*. Because the term "compound-final" is specified, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* applies according to Pāṇini 4.1.23 (*ataḥ saṃkhyādeḥ*). Examples: *sthalapathaḥ*, *devapathaḥ*. Why does it say "not connected with *akṣa*"? Consider: *akṣasya dhūḥ* = *akṣadhūḥ*; *dṛḍhadhūr akṣaḥ*.
According to Pāṇini 4.4.58 (*ṛcaḥ*), the suffix *añ* is applied as a compound-final to a compound ending in *ṛc*. Examples: *saptarco mantraḥ*, *ardharcaḥ*.

Pāṇini 4.4.59: *nañbahor māṇavacaraṇayoḥ* — After the negative particle *nañ* and after the word *bahu*, when followed by words ending in *ṛc*, the suffix *añ* is applied to form names for a student (*māṇava*) and a school (*caraṇa*). Examples: *anṛco māṇavaḥ* ("a student who has not mastered the Ṛgveda") and *bahvṛcaś caraṇaḥ* ("the school of the Bahvṛcas"). Why specify "student and school"? [Counter-examples: *anṛkkaṃ sāma* ("a Sāman that does not contain Ṛg-verses") and *bahvṛkkaṃ sūktam* ("a hymn containing many Ṛg-verses"). Pāṇini 4.4.60: *pratyanvavāt sāmalomnaḥ* — After the prefixes *prati*, *anu*, and *ava*, the suffix *añ* is applied to the words *sāman* and *loman*.

The suffix *añ* is applied after a compound ending in *sāman* or *loman* when preceded by *prati*, *anu*, or *ava*. Examples: *pratisāmam*, *anusāmam*, *avasāmam*; *pratilomam*, *anulomam*, *avalomam*. Regarding *akṣṇo 'cakṣuṣaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.4.61):
the suffix *añ* is applied after a compound ending in *akṣi* provided that it does not mean "eye. Examples: *lavaṇākṣaḥ*, *gavākṣaḥ*. Why "not meaning eye"? Consider *brāhmaṇākṣi*.

The following compounds are *dvandva* (copulative) compounds with the first member in its uninflected stem form: *dhenvanaḍuh*, *ṛgyajuṣa*, *akṣibhruv*, *dāragava*, *vaṣṭhīva*, *padaṣṭhīva*, *naktaṃdiva*, *rātriṃdiva*, *ahardiva*, *ahardiva*, *sajūs*, *puruṣāyuṣa*, *dvyāyuṣa*, *tryāyuṣa*, *jātokṣa*, *mahokṣa*, *vṛddhokṣa*, *upaśuna*, and *goṣṭhaśva*. (Pāṇini 2.4.12)

Words ending in vowels such as *dhenu-anaḍuh-* and others are treated as irregular formations (*nipātana*). *Dhenuś ca anaḍvāṃś ca* (the cow and the ox) becomes *dhenvanaḍuhau*. *Ṛk ca yajuś ca* (the Ṛgveda and the Yajurveda) becomes *ṛgyajuṣam*. *Akṣiṇī ca bhruvau ca* (the two eyes and the two eyebrows) becomes *akṣibhruvau*. *Dārāś ca gāvaś ca* (wives and cows) becomes *dāragavam*. *Ūrū cāṣṭhīvantau ca* (the two thighs and the two knees) becomes *ūrvaṣṭhīvam*. *Pādau cāṣṭhīvantau ca* (the two feet and the two knees) becomes *padaṣṭhīvam*. *Naktaṃ ca divā ca* (by night and by day) becomes *naktaṃdivam*. *Rātrau ca divā ca* (at night and by day) becomes *rātriṃdivaṃ bhuṅkte* (he eats [both] night and day). *Rātriś ca divā ca* (night and day) becomes *rātriṃdivam atītam* (it has passed night and day).

In the sense of repetition (*vīpsā*), *ahar-ahar* is prescribed as *ahardivam*. Because this occurs within the section on compounds (*samāsa-prakaraṇa*), it does not preclude the formation of a sentence either. *Saha rajasā* becomes *sarajasam*. This is a compound according to [Pāṇini 2.1.48]: *asaṃkhyam sākalye*. *Puruṣasya āyuḥ* becomes *puruṣāyuṣam*. Two lifespans joined together: *dvyāyuṣam*. Three lifespans joined together: *tryāyuṣam*. A bull that has been born: *jātokṣaḥ*. A great bull: *mahokṣaḥ*. An old bull: *vṛddhokṣaḥ*. Near a dog: *upaśunam*.

The compound *asaṃkhyam vibhaktisamīpe* (Pāṇini 2.2.2) is a [genitive] compound (*samāsa*). *Goṣṭhaśvaḥ* means "a dog in the cow-pen. The suffix *ac* is applied here by virtue of the irregular derivation (*nipātana*) in rule 2.4.13. *Ṛksāme* and *vāṅmanase* do not form compounds under rule 2.2.66 because they belong to the *dadhipaya-ādi* group. Regarding *brahmahastirājapalyād varcasaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.4.63): the suffix *añ* occurs after the word *varcas* when it follows *brahman*, *hastin*, *rājan*, or *pali*. Thus, we have *brahmavarcasam*, *hastivarcasam*, *rājavarcasam*, and *palyavarcasam*.
(4.4.64) After *sam* and the others, the suffix *ac* is applied to *tamas*. Thus: *saṃtamasam*, *avatamasam*, *andhatamasam*.
(4.4.65) [The suffix *ac* is applied] after *śvas* when it means "better than tomorrow."
The suffix *ac* is applied after the word *śvas*, when it follows a word meaning "better" (*vasīyasaḥ*). *Śvovasīyasam* means "well-being" (*kalyāṇam*).

Regarding *niś ca śreyasaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.4.80): the suffix *ac* is applied as a compound-final element (*samāsānta*) after the word *śreyas*, when it follows either *nis* or *śvas*. *Niḥśreyasam*—meaning "definite excellence"—is *nirvāṇa*. *Śvaḥśreyasam* means "well-being."
(4.4.67) *taptānvavād rahasaḥ*: after the words *tapta*, etc., the suffix *ac* occurs after *rahas*. Examples: *taptarahasam*, *anurahasam*, *avarahasam*.
(4.4.68) *prater urasa ādhārāt*: [the suffix *ac* occurs] after *uras* when it denotes a support (*ādhāra*) following the word *prati*.

The suffix *ac* occurs after *prati* when it follows *uras* used in the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇa*). [Example: "it exists upon the chest," *pratyurasam*. This is a compound by the rule "that which does not denote number [is compounded] in the sense of a case ending" (Pāṇini 2.1.2). Why [is it specified] "from a locus"? Consider: "the chest has come toward [him]," *pratyuraḥ*.

[The term] *anugavam* is prescribed as an irregular formation (*nipātana*) when extension (*āyāma*) is implied. [Example: *anugavam śakaṭam* ("a cart [long enough] for cows"). Why [is it specified] "extension"? Consider: "behind the cows," *anugu*.

*dvistāvā* and *tristāvā* [are formed] when the meaning is "twice that much" (*dvis tāvatī*) or "thrice that much" (*tris tāvatī*), provided that the word *vedi* ("altar") follows; in these cases, the compound *dvistāvā* and *tristāvā* are prescribed with the elision of the suffix *-ī*. For while the altar is of a certain size in the archetype sacrifice (*prakṛti-yāga*), it is twice that size in some modified sacrifice (*vikṛti-yāga*), and thrice that size in others. Why specify "*vedi*"? [To exclude cases such as: "a rope twice that long" (*dvis tāvatī rajjuḥ*). [The rule continues: *prādibhyaḥ adhvanaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.4.71).

The suffix *añ* occurs after the word *adhvan* when it follows prepositions such as *pra* and others. For example: *pragato ’dhvānam* (“gone beyond the road”) becomes *prādhvo rathaḥ* (“a carriage that has gone beyond the road”) and *prādhvaṃ śakaṭam* (“a cart that has gone beyond the road”). Also: *atyadhvam*. Why say “after prepositions such as *pra*”? [Because] in *paramādhvā* (“the highest road”), the suffix does not apply. (4.4.72) *pāṇḍūdakkṛṣṇād bhūmeḥ*:

The suffix *añ* occurs after the word *bhūmi* when it follows words such as *pāṇḍu*, *udak*, and *kṛṣṇa*. For example: *pāṇḍubhūmaḥ* (“having pale soil”), *udagbhūmaḥ* (“having northern soil”), and *kṛṣṇabhūmaḥ* (“having black soil”).

(4.4.73) After a numeral, the suffix *aC* is added to the end of a compound consisting of the words *nadī*, *godāvarī*, or *bhūmi*. Examples: *pañcanadam* ("five rivers"), *saptagodāvaram* ("seven Godāvarīs"), *dvibhūmaḥ prāsādaḥ* ("a two-storied palace"), *daśabhūmakam sūtram* ("a ten-chaptered treatise").
(4.4.74) Furthermore, after a numeral other than a specific number (*asaṃkhyā*), the suffix *aC* is added to the word *aṅguli* when it does not mean "another number" (*ananyāsaṃkhyārthe*).

The suffix *ac* is applied after the word *aṅguli* when it is preceded by an innumerable (*asaṃkhyāta*) or a supreme number (*parā*), provided that the compound-ending suffix (*samāsānta*) does not occur when the compound refers to something other than a number (*ananyasaṃkhyārtha*). Examples: *niraṅgulam* (beyond the fingers), *atyaṅgulam* (exceeding the fingers). When two fingers are combined: *dvyaṅgulam*. Why is it specified "not referring to a number" (*ananyasaṃkhyārtha*)? Counter-example: *pañcāṅguliḥ hastaḥ* (a hand with five fingers). Also: *upāṅguli* (near the finger). How [is this derived]?

Is it that "two fingers" (*dvyaṅgula*) means "having two atoms as its measure" (*paramāṇu-mātram asya*)? No; a compound is not prescribed here for the sake of another referent (*anyapadārtha*). Rather, when the suffixes *mātraṭ* and so forth have been elided, the word remains there [in that sense]. Or, the word *aṅgula* is a different base (*prakṛti*) denoting a measure. For example: "a full hundred of fingers by their own finger-measure," or "fourteen fingers. In the case of "a hand having two-finger parts" (*dvyaṅgulāvayavo hastaḥ*), the whole (*samudāya*) functions as the other referent. However, for the word ending in *aṅguli*, there is a compound according to Pāṇini 2.1.57 (*viśeṣaṇaṃ viśeṣyeṇa ekārthena*).

(4.4.75) *Ahaḥ-sarva-ekadeśa-saṃkhyāta-puṇya-varṣa-dīrghāt ca rātreḥ*: After the words *ahar* and so forth, as well as after a numeral and the words *saṃkhyāta*, *puṇya*, *varṣa*, and *dīrgha*, the suffix *ac* is applied to the word *rātri*. From *ahar* and so forth: *ahar ca rātriś ca* becomes *ahorātraḥ*; *sarvarātraḥ*; *pūrvarātraḥ*, *apararātraḥ*. Here, in the case of [the latter two], the word *rātri* refers to a part [of the night]; elsewhere, it is simply *pūrvarātriḥ*. From a numeral: *saṃkhyātarātraḥ*, *puṇyarātraḥ*, *varṣārātraḥ*, *dīrgharātriḥ*. [Examples: *atirātraḥ*, *nīrātraḥ*.

Two nights combined make a *dvirātra* (a two-night period). This is for the purpose of excluding other numbers; for example, *dīrgharātriḥ* (a long night) and *hemantaḥ* (winter), as well as *uparātriḥ* (the final night).

Regarding the rule *sakhyahorājñāṃ ṭac* (Pāṇini 4.4.76): the suffix *ṭac* occurs after words ending in *sakhi*, *ahan*, and *rājan*. Examples include *rājasakhaḥ* (a friend of the king), *paramāhaḥ* (the supreme day), and *Madrarājaḥ* (the king of the Madras). This is for the purpose of excluding other numbers; for example, *Indrasakhā* (friend of Indra) and *upasakhi* (near the friend). Because of the specific mention of *rājan* in the rule, the suffix does not apply when it means "king" [in a general sense]. How then is *madrarājñī* (queen of the Madras) formed from *madrāṇāṃ rājñī*? In this case, there is no inclusion of the feminine form (*liṅgaviśiṣṭagrahaṇa*) because a specific distinction is being relied upon.

*gor aluky acārthe* (Pāṇini 4.4.77): The suffix *ṭac* is applied after the word *go*, provided that the elision (*luk*) has not occurred [in the compound] and the compound does not have the sense of "and" (*ca*). Examples: *rājagavaḥ*, *paramagavaḥ*; *pañcagavadhanam*, *daśagavadhanam*. Why "provided that there is no elision"? [Answer: *pañcabhir gobhiḥ krītaḥ* ("bought for five cows") results in *pañcaguḥ*. Why "not having the sense of 'and'"? [Answer: *ajāśvagāvaḥ* ("goats, horses, and cows"). It is understood as "not having another number" (*ananyasaṃkhyārtha*); thus: *citraguḥ*, *upaguḥ*. *uraso 'gre* (Pāṇini 4.4.78).

The suffix *ṭac* is applied after the word *uraḥ* when it occurs at the end of a compound denoting the principal part [of a body]. For example: *aśvorasam*, *hastyurasam*. The meaning is "the principal part of those. Why does the rule specify *agra* ("forepart")? Consider: *aśvoraḥ*.
[Furthermore, the suffix *ṭac* is applied] after words ending in *an*, as well as *aśman*, *ayas*, and *saras*, when they are names of species (*jāti*). (Pāṇini 5.4.94).

The suffix *ṭac* is applied after a word ending in *ana*, provided it denotes a genus (*jāti*) or a proper name (*saṃjñā*). For example: *upānasa-* as a genus; *mahānasa-* as a proper name. *Amṛtāśma-* as a genus; *piṇḍāśma-* as a proper name. *Kālāyasa-* as a genus; *lohitāyasa-* as a proper name. *Maṇḍūkasarasa-* as a genus; *jalasarasa-* as a proper name. How is it that *bindusara-* and *bakasara-* are [proper names]? These are not [etymological] names; rather, they are understood as proper names by conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), like the name *Śūrpaṇakhī*. [Also taught: "After *grāma* and *kuṭa*, when denoting a carpenter" (Pāṇini 4.4.80).

The suffix *ṭac* is applied after the word *takṣan* when it follows *grāma* or *kauṭa*. *Grāmatakṣaḥ*: one who is common [to the village]; this is the meaning. *Kauṭaḥ* means "one who stays in a hut" (*kuṭyām bhavaḥ*); *kauṭatakṣaḥ* is a carpenter who stays in a hut—one who lives in his own home, is independent, and is not bound to anyone; this is the meaning. Why say "after *grāma* or *kauṭa*"? [Consider: *rājatakṣā* ("king's carpenter"). Only when it has the sense of "belonging to" (*acārtha*) [is the suffix applied]: *grāmatakṣāṇau* (dual). Only when it has the sense of "this person's" (*anayārtha*) [is the suffix applied]: *kauṭas takṣāsyāsti*, *kauṭatakṣā*. [Also: *ateḥ śunaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.4.81).

The suffix *ṭac* occurs after the word *śvan* when it follows the prefix *ati*. *Atiśvaḥ* means "one who has surpassed a dog," as in *atikrāntaḥ śvānam atiśvo varāhaḥ* ("a boar that has surpassed a dog"). The meaning is "extremely swift. *Atiśvaḥ sevakaḥ* ("a dog-like servant") means "one who is very devoted to his master. *Atiśvī sevā* ("dog-like service") means "very base service. Regarding *upamānād aprāṇini* (Pāṇini 5.4.82): when the object of comparison (*upamāna*) is not a living being, the suffix *ṭac* occurs after a word ending in *śvan* used in that sense. For example, *ākarṣaḥ śveva* ("a game-board like a dog") becomes *ākarṣaśvaḥ*; likewise, *phalakaśvaḥ*. Why say "from a word of comparison"? Consider *uttamaśvā* ("an excellent mare"), which does not apply here. Why say "when not a living being"? Consider *vyāghraḥ śveva* ("a tiger like a dog"), which becomes *vyāghraśvā*; this is excluded because a tiger is a living being.

(4.4.83) *mṛgapūrvottarāc ca sakthnaḥ*: The suffix *ṭac* is applied after the word *sakthi* when it follows *mṛga*, *pūrva*, *uttara*, or a word denoting a standard of comparison (*upamāna*). Examples: *mṛgasaktham*, *pūrvasaktham*, *uttarasaktham*. When the thigh is like a plank: *phalakasaktham*.
(4.4.84) *saṃkhyārdhān nāva ekārthāt*: [The suffix *ṭac* is applied] after numerals and the word *ardha* when they denote a single object with a ship (*nau*).

The suffix *ṭac* is applied after a word ending in *nau* that follows a numeral or the word *ardha*, provided these stand in apposition. Examples: *dvināvam*, *trināvam*. Because gender depends on worldly convention (*lokāśrayatva*), the feminine gender does not apply here. Example with *ardha*: *ardhanāvam*. Why specify "from a single entity" (*ekārthāt*)? Consider *dvayor nauḥ*, which becomes *dvinauḥ*. Only when it has no other meaning: *dvinaukaḥ*. Regarding *khārī*, it is optional (Pāṇini 4.4.85).

The suffix *ṭac* is optionally applied after a numeral or the word *ardha* when followed by *khārī*. Thus: *dvikhāram* or *dvikhārī*; *ardhakhāram* or *ardhakhārī*. By the very force of this specific rule, that which ends in *ṭac* does not function as feminine. [The suffix applies] only when there is a single referent (*ekārtha*): *dvayoḥ khārī* becomes *dvikhārī*. [The suffix applies] only when the referent is not something else (*ananyārtha*): *dvikhārīkaḥ*.
[The suffix *kan* is applied] after *añjali* following the words *dvi* and *tri*: (Pāṇini 4.4.86).

The suffix *ṭac* is optionally applied after the word *añjali* when it follows the words *dvi* or *tri*. Thus: *dvyañjalam*, *tryañjalam*; or *dvyañjali*, *tryañjali*. Only when [the compound] has a single referent (*ekārtha*) does this apply; for example: "the *añjali* of two people" is *dvyañjaliḥ*. Only when [the compound] has no other meaning (*ananyārtha*) does this apply; for example: *dvyañjalikaḥ*. Regarding *kumahadbhyāṃ brahmaṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.4.105):

the suffix *ṭac* is optionally applied after the word *brahman* when it follows the words *ku* or *mahat*. Thus: *kubrahmaḥ*, *kubrahmā*; *mahābrahmaḥ*, *mahābrahmā*. Only when [the compound] has no other meaning does this apply; for example: *mahābrahmakaḥ*.

[Rule 4.4.88: *janapadāt*—the suffix *ṭac* is applied after a word ending in *brahman* that follows a word denoting a *janapada* (region/country); this is established as obligatory due to the division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*). Example: *Avantiṣu brahmā* = *Avantibrahmaḥ*; *Kāśiṣu brahmā* = *Kāśibrahmaḥ*. Why say "from a *janapada*"? [Counter-example: *devabrahmā Nāradaḥ* (Nārada is a Brahmin among the gods). The restriction "only when not meaning 'and'" (*acārtha*) applies: *Avantayaś ca brahmā ca* = *Avantibrahmāṇaḥ* (the people of Avanti and the Brahmin). The restriction "only when not having another purpose" (*ananyārtha*) applies: *Avantibrahmakaḥ*. [Rule 4.4.89: *cārthe cudaṣahaḥ samāhāre*—the suffix *ṭac* is applied after words ending in *ca*, *da*, or *ṣa*, when they mean "and" (*cārtha*), provided they form a collective compound (*samāhāra*).

The suffix *ṭac* is applied after a copulative compound (*dvandva*) denoting a collection (*samāhāra*), provided it ends in a letter of the *ca*-class, or in *da*, *ṣa*, or *ha*. Examples: *vāktvacam* (speech and skin), *śrīsrajam* (fortune and garland), *samiddṛṣadam* (firewood and stone), *vāktviṣam* (speech and luster), *chattropānaham* (umbrella and sandals). Because *chattropānaham* ends in the suffix *ini* due to the rule for compound-final elements (*samāsānta*), the suffix *ini* is applied by virtue of the word ending in *at* (Pāṇini 5.4.106). Why specify "denoting a collection"? Consider *dvidṛṣat* (two stones). Why specify "ending in *ca*, *ṣa*, *ha*, etc."? Consider *vāksamit* (speech and mind). Why specify "collection"? Consider *prāvṛṭcharadau* (the rainy season and autumn). [This is governed by] Pāṇini 4.4.90: *śaradādibhyo 'saṃkhyārthe* ("after *śarad* and so on, when not meaning a number").

The suffix *ṭac* is applied as a compound-final element (*samāsānta*) after words beginning with *śarad*, provided they do not denote a number. Examples: *upaśaradam*, *upavipāśam*. Why "provided they do not denote a number"? Consider *paramaśarat*. The list [of bases] is: *śarad*, *vipāś*, *manas*, *upānah*, *div*, *himavat*, *anaḍuh*, *vihas*, *catur*, *tad*, *yad*, *jarā* (which becomes *jaras*), *dṛś*, *akṣi* (after *prati*, *para*, *samanu*), and *pathin*. The inclusion of those ending in *jhay* is for the sake of making the rule obligatory. [Also included is] *anas* (Pāṇini 4.4.91).

The suffix *ṭac* is applied as a compound-final element (*samāsānta*) after the word *ananta* when it does not signify a number. Thus: *adhyātmam*, *pratyātmam*, *uparājam*. Because these end in *ṭac*, the rule *ato ’m apañcamyāḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.82) applies, resulting in the form *am*.

According to *napuṃsakād vā* (Pāṇini 5.4.104), the compound-final suffix *ṭac* is optionally applied after a neuter word ending in *ananta* when it does not signify a number. Thus: *upacarmam* or *upacarma*.

Pāṇini 4.4.93: *girinadīpaurṇamāsyāgrahāyaṇījhayaḥ*. After words beginning with *giri* and ending in a *jhay* consonant, the compound-final suffix *ṭac* is optionally applied when not expressing a number. Examples: *antargiram*, *antargiri*; *upanadam*, *upanadi*; *upapaurṇamāsam*, *upapaurṇamāsi*; *upāgrahāyaṇam*, *upāgrahāyaṇi*; *upasamidham*, *upasamit*; *upadṛṣadam*, *upadṛṣat*. Pāṇini 4.4.94: *nisaḥ śato ḍac*. [The suffix *ḍac* is applied after *niṣ* when it precedes *śata*.]

The suffix *ḍac* optionally occurs after a word ending in *śat* that follows *niś*. Thus: *nistriṃśāni varṣāṇi* ("thirty years [of age]"), or *nistriṃśat* ("thirty"). Also: *niścatvāriṃśāni* ("forty years [of age]"). [In another sense: *nistriṃśaḥ khaḍgaḥ* ("a sword [which has gone beyond thirty fingers]").
[This applies] to a numeral other than *abahu-* when used in a sense other than its own meaning [Pāṇini 4.4.95].

The suffix *ḍac* occurs after a number that excludes "many" (*bahu*), provided it stands at the end of a compound denoting another referent (*anyapadārtha*). Examples: *upadaśāḥ* ("nine or eleven"), *āsannadaśāḥ* ("near ten"), *adūradaśāḥ* ("not far from ten"), *adhikadaśāḥ* ("more than ten"). *Tridaśāḥ*: their number is three times ten. *Dvitrāḥ*: two or three. Why "excluding *bahu*"? Witness *upabahavaḥ* ("slightly more than many"). Why "denoting another referent"? Witness *dvādaśa* ("twelve"). The governing rule for "another referent" extends up to the suffix *kap*. [Pāṇini 5.4.73:
*sakthyakṣṇaḥ svāṅgāt ṣac* ("the suffix *ṣac* occurs after *sakthi* and *akṣi* when they denote a part of one's own body").

The suffix *ṣac* is applied after the words *sakthi* and *akṣi* when they denote one’s own limbs (*svāṅga*). [Examples: *dīrghasakthaḥ*, *dīrghasakthī*; *viśālākṣaḥ*, *viśālākṣī*. Why specify "after *sakthi* and *akṣi*"? [Counter-example: *dīrghajānuḥ*. Why specify "when denoting one’s own limbs"? [Counter-example: *dīrghasakthi śakaṭam* ("a cart with long shafts"); *sthūlākṣir ikṣuḥ* ("a sugarcane with thick joints"). The restriction "only when having another meaning" (*anyārthe*) applies as well: *paramasakthi* ("an excellent thigh"). The letter *ṣ* is for the purpose of introducing the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ*. [Also: *aṅguler dāruṇi* (Pāṇini 4.4.97).

The suffix *ṣaC* occurs after the word *aṅguli*, when it denotes something other than its own meaning, namely a piece of wood. Examples: *dvyaṅgulam dāru* (a two-finger-width piece of wood), *pañcāṅgulam* (a five-finger-width piece of wood). A "finger" here refers to a wooden measure used for scattering grain and the like, consisting of parts similar to a finger. As for [its use] as a measurement, it is established by the previous rule (*pramāṇe* 5.2.37).

Regarding *dvitribhyāṃ mūrdhnaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.4.115): the suffix *ṣaC* occurs after the word *mūrdhan* when it follows the words *dvi* or *tri*. Examples: *dvimūrdhaḥ* (two-headed), *trimūrdhaḥ* (three-headed). Only when it means something other than its own meaning [does this apply]; otherwise: *dvayor mūrdhā* (the head of two), *dvimūrdhā* (two-headed).

*Ap pūraṇyās tāsu* (Pāṇini 5.4.99): After a feminine word ending in a suffix denoting an ordinal number (*pūraṇa*), provided it occurs as the prior member of a compound whose referent is those same ordinal numbers, the compound-final suffix *ap* is applied. For example: *kalyāṇī pañcamy āsāṃ rātrīṇām* ("these nights, of which the fifth is auspicious"), resulting in *kalyāṇīpañcamā rātrayaḥ*. Why does the rule specify *tāsu* ("in those [same ordinals]")? Consider: *kalyāṇapañcamīkaḥ pakṣaḥ* ("a fortnight in which the fifth day is auspicious"). Furthermore, the prohibition of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) applies only when the ordinal numbers themselves are the expressed meaning. *Pramāṇyāḥ* (Pāṇini 5.4.100): [The suffix *ap* is applied] after a feminine word denoting a measure (*pramāṇa*).

The suffix *ap* occurs after the word *pramāṇī*. For example: "those for whom a woman is the authority" (*strīpramāṇāḥ*) refers to householders; likewise, *bhāryāpramāṇāḥ*. Although this is established by the general rule for the word *pramāṇa*, this specific statement is made to set aside the suffix *ka*.

By the rule *antarbahirbhyāṃ lomnaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.4.101), the suffix *ap* occurs after a word ending in *loman* that follows *antar* or *bahis*. For example: *antarlomaḥ* ("having hair on the inside") and *bahirlomaḥ* ("having hair on the outside").

(4.4.102) *nakṣatrān netuḥ*: After the word *nakṣatra*, the suffix *ap* occurs when it is followed by *netṛ*. Examples: *mṛganetrā rātrayaḥ* ("nights having the deer as their leader"), *puṣyanetrāḥ* ("having Puṣya as their leader"). Why "after *nakṣatra*"? [Consider: *Devadattanetṛkaḥ* ("having Devadatta as his leader"). Since this would have been established by the word *netra*, this rule is stated for the purpose of setting aside the suffix *ka*. (4.4.103) *nañ-suv-avyaya-pūrvasya caturo ’c*: When preceded by the negative particle *nañ*, the particles *su*, *avi*, or *upa*, the word *caturo* takes the suffix *ac*.

The suffix *ac* occurs after a word ending in *catur* that follows *nañ* and other such particles. "Its four eyes do not become objects [of perception]," *acaturaḥ*. "Its four [objects] become objects [of perception] even more clearly," *sucaturaḥ*. "Its four [objects] become objects [of perception] in various ways," *vicaturaḥ*. "Four is near to these," *upacaturāḥ*. "Three or four," *tricaturāḥ*.
According to Pāṇini 4.4.104, *ac* occurs after a word ending in *nābhi*. Examples: *padmanābhaḥ*, *ūrṇanābhaḥ*.

*suprātasuśvasudivaśārikukṣacaturaśrāḥ* (Pāṇini 4.4.105). The words *suprāta-* and others ending in the vowel *a* are established as irregular forms (*nipātana*). He whose morning is beautiful is *suprātaḥ*. He whose tomorrow is beautiful is *suśvaḥ*. He whose day is beautiful is *sudivaḥ*. He whose belly is like that of a *śārī* bird is *śārikukṣaḥ*. He whose four corners are [equal] is *caturaśraḥ*. [The forms] *eṇīpadaḥ*, *ajapadaḥ*, and *proṣṭhapadaḥ* are established by means of the word *pada* in the same manner as *bhadrapadaḥ*. Furthermore, due to their conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), these have restricted domains of application. *nañsudurbhyaḥ sakthno vā* (Pāṇini 4.4.106). [The suffix *aC* is applied after the word *sakthi* following the negative particle *nañ*, and the prefixes *su-* and *dur-*, optionally.]

The suffix *ac* optionally occurs after a word ending in *sakthi*, provided that it follows *nañ* and other such particles. Examples: *asakthaḥ*, *asakthiḥ*; *susakthaḥ*, *susakthiḥ*; *duḥsakthaḥ*, *duḥsakthiḥ*. Why specify "after *nañ* and others"? [Consider: *dīrghasakthi śakaṭam* ("a cart with long thighs"). Regarding *prajāyā asic* (Pāṇini 4.4.107):
the suffix *asic* occurs after a word ending in *prajā*, provided that it follows *nañ* and other such particles. Examples: *aprajāḥ*, *suprajāḥ*, *duṣprajāḥ*.

(4.4.108) *mandālpāc ca medhāyāḥ*: The suffix *as* occurs after the word *medhā* when it follows *manda*, *alpa*, or words beginning with *nañ*. Examples: *mandamedhāḥ*, *alpamedhāḥ*, *amedhāḥ*, *sumedhāḥ*, *durmedhāḥ*.
(4.4.109) *nāmni nāsāyā naso 'sthūlāt*: In a name, the substitute *nas* replaces *nāsā* when it does not follow *sthūla*.

When *nāsā* follows a word other than *sthūla*, the compound-final suffix is applied and the substitute *nas* is used for that [word] *nāsā*. Examples: *gonasaḥ*, *vādhrīṇasaḥ*. Why is it said "in a name" (*nāmni*)? [Counter-example: *dīrghanāsaḥ*. Why is it said "other than *sthūla*" (*asthūlāt*)? [Counter-example: *sthūlanāsaḥ*. Regarding *prādibhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.4.110):
when *nāsā* follows words beginning with *pra* and others, the substitute *nas* is used. Examples: *praṇasaṃ mukham*, *unnasam*.
*veḥ khaḥ* (4.4.111): For the word *nāsā* preceded by the prefix *vi*, the substitute *kha* occurs. One whose nose is gone is *vikhaḥ*. *khurakharāṇ ṇas vā* (4.4.112).

The suffix *ṇas* optionally occurs in place of the *nāsā* [of a bahuvrīhi compound] when it follows *khura* or *khara*. Thus: *khuraṇāḥ*, *khuraṇasaḥ*; *kharaṇāḥ*, *kharaṇasaḥ*. According to Pāṇini 4.4.113, *anic* is optionally added after the word *dharma* when it follows a single (i.e., non-compounded) prior member. Thus: *kalyāṇadharmā*, *kalyāṇadharmakaḥ*; *taddharmā*, *taddharmakaḥ*; *viparītadharmā*, *viparītadharmakaḥ*. Why does the rule specify "when following a single [prior member]" (*kevalāt*)? Consider: *paramasvadharmakaḥ* (where *svadharma* is part of a larger compound).

After the words *su*, *harita*, *tṛṇa*, and *soma*, the suffix *anij* occurs after the word *jambha*. Thus: *sujambhā*, *haritajambhā*, *tṛṇajambhā*, *somajambhā*. Why "after *su* and the others"? Consider: *patitajambhaḥ*.
[The word] *dakṣiṇermā* [is formed with *anij*] when used in connection with a hunter (*lubdha*). (Pāṇini 4.4.115)

The form *dakṣiṇermā* is an irregularly formed (*nipātita*) derivative ending in the suffix *anij*, occurring when there is a connection with a disease. *Īrma* means a wound; "one whose right side has a wound" is *dakṣiṇermā*, referring to a deer. Why specify "in connection with a hunter"? [Because otherwise it would apply to other cases: *dakṣiṇermaṃ śakaṭam* ("a cart with a right-side wound"). The suffix *ij* occurs (Pāṇini 5.4.116) when a reciprocal action is understood, applied to a word denoting another object [of that action]. Examples: *keśākeśi* ("hair-to-hair"), *daṇḍādaṇḍi* ("stick-to-stick"). The inclusion of the letter *c* [in the rule] is for the purpose of qualifying [it as belonging to the *ic*-class] by Pāṇini 5.2.48.
*dvidaṇḍyādīni* (Pāṇini 5.4.117):

word-forms such as *dvidaṇḍi* and others ending in the suffix *ij* are treated as irregular formations (*nipātana*). [The formation is as follows: "he has two sticks" (*dvau daṇḍāv asya*) results in *dvidaṇḍi*; likewise, *dvimusali*. Because these are irregular formations, they depend on specific meanings; therefore, it does not apply here: *dvidaṇḍā śālā* ("a field with two rows of sticks").

*dvidaṇḍi*, *dvimusali*, *ubhāñjali*, *ubhayāñjali*, *ubhādanti*, *ubhayādanti*, *ubhākarṇi*, *ubhayākarṇi*, *ubhāhasti*, *ubhayāhasti*, *ubhāpāṇi*, *ubhayāpāṇi*, *ubhābāhu*, *ubhayābāhu*, *ekapadi*, *prohyapadi*, *ācyapadi*, *nikucyakarṇi*, *saṃhatapucchi*. In the case of *prohyapadi dhāvati* ("he runs with his feet lifted") and *nikucyakarṇi dhāvati* ("he runs with his ears flattened"), because these are adverbs (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*), the meaning of the other word (*anyapadārtha*) is the action itself.
[The suffix] *ṭhac* is applied after a word ending in *māsa* when it signifies wages (*bhṛti*). (Pāṇini 4.4.118)
The suffix *ṭhañ* occurs after the word *māsa* when preceded by *bhṛti*. [Examples: *pañcakamāsikaḥ* ("one for whom five months constitute his wages"), *daśakamāsikaḥ*.
By Pāṇini 4.4.119, *jña* is the substitute for *jānu* when preceded by *sampra*. [Example: *saṃjñaḥ* ("one whose knees are joined together"), *prajñaḥ* ("one whose knees are extended").
(4.4.120) *ūrdhvād vā*:
After the word *ūrdhva*, the substitute *jña* optionally occurs in place of *jānu*. For example: one whose knees are raised is called *ūrdhvajñaḥ* or *ūrdhvajānuḥ*.
(4.4.121) *dhanur nāmni*: [The suffix *aṇ* is applied after *dhanus*] when a name is formed.

The word *dhanus* is employed only when it functions as the external referent (*anyapadārtha*) within a compound that forms a proper name (*saṃjñā*). Examples: *dṛḍhadhanuḥ*, *śatadhanuḥ*. Why does the rule specify "in a name" (*nāmni*)? [Consider: *gāṇḍīvadhanvā*. There is another base, *dhanvan*, which is used without distinction whether in a name or not.
