A cow's footprint (*gopada*); a *kiṣku* as a measure (*pramāṇa*); the cave of Kiṣkindhā (*guhā*); a thief (*taskara*) is a robber (*caura*); Bṛhaspati is the deity (*devatā*); a tree that does not flower is a forest-tree (*vanaspati*); a cow that tramples (*prastumpati*), another that tramples (*pratumpati*); and *kustumburu* is coriander (*dhānyaka*).

What is meant by *dhānyakam*? *Kutumburūṇi* means contemptible *tumburu* fruits; those resembling *dhānyaka*. *Āścaryam* and *adbhutam* mean a marvel. *Viṣkiraḥ* or *vikiraḥ* refers to a bird that scatters [its food]. *Pratiṣkaśaḥ* means an assistant, a messenger (*vārttika*), or one who goes ahead. *Praskaṇva* and *Hariścandra* are names of sages (*ṛṣi*). Why "sages"? [To exclude] *Prakaṇva* as a region and *Haricandra* as a young student (*māṇavaka*). *Maskara* and *maskarin* refer to a bamboo staff and a wandering mendicant (*parivrājaka*) respectively; *makara* and *makarī* refer to something else. *Kāstīra* and *ajastunda* refer to two cities; *kātīra* and *ajatunda* refer to something else. *Prāyaścitta* and *prāyaścittin* [refer to expiation and one who performs it]. This is an open-ended class (*ākṛtigaṇa*).
The first quarter of the fifth [chapter] is completed.
It should be understood that "aluk" and "uttarapade" are governing rules (*adhikāra*) for what follows.
(Pāṇini 5.2.1) *Aluk* and *uttarapade*: these two are to be known as governing rules.

(5.2.2) *pañcamyāḥ stokādibhyaḥ*: After words belonging to the group beginning with *stoka*, there is no elision (*aluk*) of the fifth case (*pañcamī*) when followed by a subsequent word (*uttarapada*). Examples: *stokānmuktaḥ* ("freed from a little"), *alpānmuktaḥ* ("freed from a small amount"), *kṛcchrānmuktaḥ* ("freed from difficulty"), *katipayānmuktaḥ* ("freed from a few"). Because these denote non-substances (*asattvavacana*), they appear only in the singular. The rule "when followed by a subsequent word" is specified because [otherwise] one would have *niḥstokaḥ* in the sense of "gone out from a little. (5.2.3) *brāhmaṇācchaṃsī*.

In the case of the word *brāhmaṇa* followed by a fifth-case form ending in a suffix marked with *śaṃ*, the elision (*luk*) of the case-ending is not applied when a subsequent member follows. According to Pāṇini 5.2.4, *khiti ca ekāco 'maḥ*: after a monosyllabic stem ending in *i* or *ī*, the case-ending *ām* is not elided when a subsequent member ending in *khit* follows. Examples include: *gāṃmanyaḥ*, *strīṃmanyaḥ* (or *striyaṃmanyaḥ*), *nāvaṃmanyaḥ*, *śriyaṃmanyaḥ*, and *bhruvaṃmanyaḥ*. The term *śriyaṃmanyaḥ* means "a Brahmin family that considers itself like Śrī. This is because there is no occurrence of a neuter form for a word that has the same coreferentiality as the self (*ātmasamānādhikaraṇa*), and because the gender is fixed (*āviṣṭaliṅgatva*). Others, however, read the form as *śriyaṃmanyam*.

Just as words such as *praṣṭhī* and others occur in the feminine, so too does this [word *hariṇī*] occur in the neuter. Furthermore, this is not an exception (*apavāda*) to the elision (*luk*) of the nominative and accusative singular endings (*su* and *am*), because it is prescribed when a subsequent member (*uttarapada*) follows. Why is it said "ending in *khi*"? Consider *strīmānī*. Why is it said "ending in *ic*"? Consider *vāṅmanyaḥ*. Why is it said "having a single vowel" (*ekāc*)? Consider *hariṇīmanyaḥ*. (5.2.5) *ojaḥ-sahaḥ-amhas-tapa-añjasaḥ tṛtīyāyāḥ*: After the third case ending following *ojas* and the others, there is no elision (*aluk*) before a subsequent member. Examples: *ojasākṛtam*, *sahasākṛtam*, *ambhasākṛtam*, *tapasākṛtam*, *añjasākṛtam*.

(5.2.6) *manaso nāmni*: The elision (*aluk*) of the third case ending of the word *manas*, when it is followed by another [word] in a compound, does not occur when the compound forms a proper name (*saṃjñā*). Example: *Manasādevī*. Why "when it is a proper name"? Example: *Manodattā*.
(5.2.7) *ājñāyini*.
The third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) does not undergo elision (*aluk*) when it follows *manas* as a prior member and *ājñāyin* as a subsequent member. Example: *manasājñāyī*.

In the rule *puṃjanurbhyām anujāndhayoḥ* (Pāṇini 5.2.8), the third case ending following *pum̐s* and *janus* does not undergo elision when *anuja* and *andha* are the subsequent members. Examples: *puṃsānujā kanyā* ("a girl younger than a brother") and *januṣāndhaḥ* ("blind from birth").

(5.2.9) *ātmanaḥ pūraṇe*: When a word expressing completion (*pūraṇa*) follows as a final member (*uttarapada*), the elision (*luk*) of the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) of the word *ātman* does not occur. Examples: *ātmanāpañcamaḥ* ("with oneself as the fifth"), *ātmanāṣaṣṭhaḥ* ("with oneself as the sixth"). The compound *ātmanaḥ* is formed because it functions as the fifth member in the state of being the fifth. How is it that [the statement] "Janārdana, however, was himself the fourth" is possible? It is because it refers to something other than the members of the compound. (5.2.10) *nāmni parāc ca caturthyāḥ*: [The elision of the fourth case ending of the word *parāc* does not occur when it forms a name.]

The *aluk* (non-elision) of the fourth case (*caturthī*) occurs after *para*, *ātman*, and *parasmai* when used as technical designations (*saṃjñā*). Examples: *parasmaipada*, *parasmaibhāṣā*; *ātmanepada*, *ātmanebhāṣā*.
[In other cases], the seventh case (*saptamī*) is frequently retained [as *aluk*] (Pāṇini 5.2.11).

The *aluk* (non-elision) of the locative case ending occurs diversely (*bahulam*) before a subsequent word (*uttarapada*). Examples: *stamberamaḥ*, *karṇejapaḥ*; *apsuyoniḥ*, *apsumatiḥ*; *apsucaraḥ*, *goṣucaraḥ*; *varṣāsujaḥ*, *apsujaḥ*; *hṛdispṛk*, *divispṛk*; *prāvṛṣijaḥ*, *śaradijaḥ*, *kālejaḥ*, *divijaḥ*. In some cases there is an option (*vikalpa*): *varṣajaḥ*, *varṣejaḥ*; *kṣarajaḥ*, *kṣarejaḥ*; *śarajaḥ*, *śarejaḥ*; *varajaḥ*, *varejaḥ*. Also: *pūrvāhṇatare*, *pūrvāhṇetare*; *pūrvāhṇatane*, *pūrvāhṇetane*.

*khaśayaḥ*, *kheśayaḥ*; *grāmavāsaḥ*, *grāmevāsaḥ*; *grāmavāsī*, *grāmevāsī*; *madhyaguruḥ*, *madhyeguruḥ*; *antaguruḥ*, *anteguruḥ*; *hastabandhaḥ*, *hastebandhaḥ*; *cakrabandhaḥ*, *cakrebandhaḥ*. In some cases it does not occur: *akṣaśauṇḍaḥ*, *Kurucaraḥ*; *sthaṇḍilaśāyī*, *sthaṇḍilavartī*; *Sāṃkāśyasiddhaḥ*, *Kāmpilyasiddhaḥ*; [ending in a vowel: *cakrabandhaḥ*, *cārakabandhaḥ*.

The suffix *stha* occurs after [words ending in] *sam*, *viṣama*, *kūṭa*, and *parvata*: *samasthaḥ*, *viṣamasthaḥ*, *kūṭasthaḥ*, *parvatasthaḥ*. In some cases it occurs even when not in an *anuttara-pada* (i.e., not at the end of a compound): *apsavyaḥ* (from *apsu bhavaḥ*). In some cases it occurs in proper names (*saṃjñā*): *gaviṣṭhiraḥ*, *yudhiṣṭhiraḥ*, *tvacisāraḥ*; *araṇyetilakāḥ*, *araṇyemāṣakāḥ*; *sūpeśāṇaḥ*, *mukuṭekārṣāpaṇaḥ*, *dṛṣadimāṣakaḥ*, *haledvipadikā*. In some cases it does not occur: *abhyarhitapaśuḥ*, *yūthapaśuḥ*, *avikaṭoraṇaḥ*, *nadīkukkuṭikā*, *bhūmipāśakaḥ*.

In some cases, it occurs when there is an external referent (*anyapadārtha*): *kaṇṭhekālaḥ* ("one who has Kāla on his neck"), *vahegaḍuḥ* ("one with a goitre on the chest"), *urasilomā* ("one with hair on the chest"), *udaremaṇiḥ* ("one with a jewel on the belly"). In other cases, it does not occur: *mūrdhaśikhaḥ*, *mastakaśikhaḥ*, *mukhakāmaḥ*, *aṅgulitrāṇaḥ*, *jaṅghāvaliḥ*. Regarding the rule *ṣaṣṭhyā ākrośe* (Pāṇini 5.4.12): when an insult is implied, there is no elision (*aluk*) of the genitive case-ending before the second member of the compound. Examples: *caurasyakulam* ("the family of a thief"), *dāsasyakulam* ("the family of a slave"). Why "when an insult is implied"? Example: *brāhmaṇakulam* ("the family of a Brahmin").

When *putra* follows as the second member of a compound and reproach (*ākrośa*) is implied, the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) optionally does not undergo elision (*aluk*). Examples: *dāsyāḥputraḥ* (the son of a female slave), *dāsīputraḥ*; *vṛṣalyāḥputraḥ*, *vṛṣalīputraḥ*. Only when reproach is implied: *brāhmaṇaputraḥ* (the son of a Brahmin). (5.2.14) *vāgdikpaśyadbhyo yuktidaṇḍahareṣu*: [The sixth case does not undergo elision] after the words *vāc*, *diś*, and *paśyat* when followed by *yukti*, *daṇḍa*, and *hara* respectively.

The sixth case ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*) of words other than *vāk* and so forth is not elided (*aluk*) when followed by the subsequent words *yukti* and others. Examples: *vācoyuktiḥ*, *diśodaṇḍaḥ*, *paśyatoharaḥ*. (5.2.15) Regarding *adas*: the sixth case ending of *adas* is not elided when followed by the suffixes *phak* or *vuñ*. Example: *āmuṣyāyaṇaḥ*. Here, *phak* is applied because [the word *amuka*] belongs to the *naḍādi* group (Pāṇini 2.4.35). Similarly: *āmuṣyakulikā* and *āmuṣyaputrikā*. Here, *vuñ* is applied because they belong to the *manojñādi* group (Pāṇini 4.1.149). It is precisely by the force of the textual reading that the intervention of *vuñ* is accepted [in the formation of *āmuṣyāyaṇa*]. How is it that *devānāmpriyaḥ* is formed? It is due to the irregular derivation (*nipātana*) in the rule *devānāmpriyais te 'nyābhyaś ca* (Pāṇini 4.3.12).

(5.2.16) *Śunaḥ-śepha-puccha-lāṅgūleṣu nāmni*: When the name [of a person] is intended, there is no elision (*aluk*) of the genitive case ending following the word *śvan* when *śepha*, *puccha*, or *lāṅgūla* follow as the subsequent members [of the compound]. Examples: *Śunaḥśephaḥ*, *Śunaḥpucchaḥ*, *Śunolāṅgūlaḥ*. Why does it say "when it is a name"? [Counter-example: *śvapucchaḥ*. (5.2.17) *Divo dāse*: [There is no elision of the genitive case ending following the word *div*] when *dāsa* follows as the subsequent member [of the compound].

In a compound where *dāsa* is the final member, there is no elision (*aluk*) of the genitive case ending after the word *div*, provided it refers to the "other world" (*parasyāḥ*) and the resulting form is a proper name (*saṃjñāyām*). Example: *Divodāsaḥ*.
This is governed by Pāṇini 5.4.156: *ṛto vidyāyonisaṃbandhāt tatra*.

After a word ending in *ṛ*, which denotes a relationship through learning (*vidyā*) or a relationship through birth (*yoni*), the sixth case suffix (*ṣaṣṭhī*) remains unelided (*aluk*) when it is followed by another word denoting a relationship through learning or birth as the subsequent member (*uttarapada*). Examples: *hotuḥputraḥ* ("the son of the Hotṛ priest"), *hoturantevāsī* ("the pupil of the Hotṛ priest"); *pituḥputraḥ* ("the son of the father"), *piturantevāsī* ("the pupil of the father"). Why "ending in *ṛ*" (*ṛtaḥ*)? [Counter-examples: *ācāryaputraḥ* ("the teacher's son"), *mātulaputraḥ* ("the maternal uncle's son"). Why "relationship through learning or birth" (*vidyāyonisaṃbandhāt*)? [Counter-example: *dātṛputraḥ* ("the giver's son"). Why "in that very [context]" (*tatra*)? [Counter-examples: *hotṛdhanam* ("the property of the Hotṛ priest"), *pitṛgṛham* ("the father's house"). [The rule continues: "In the case of *svasṛ* and *pati*, it is optional" (*svasṛpatyor vā*). (Pāṇini 6.3.24–25)

When the words *svasṛpati* ("sister's husband") and *mātṛpitṛ* ("mother and father") follow as subsequent members (*uttarapada*), the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) following a word denoting a relationship through learning (*vidyā*) or birth (*yoni*) optionally does not undergo elision (*aluk*). Examples: *mātuḥṣvasā*, *mātṛṣvasā* ("mother's sister"); *pituḥṣvasā*, *pitṛṣvasā* ("father's sister"); *duhituḥpatiḥ*, *duhitṛpatiḥ* ("daughter's husband"). Regarding the rule *mātarapitarau cārthe* (Pāṇini 5.2.20): in the context of a compound expressing the sense of "and" (*cārtha*), the form *mātarapitarau* is optionally prescribed by nipātana. Examples: *mātarapitarau*, *mātāpitarau*. Why specify "in the sense of 'and'" (*cārtha*)? Consider: *mātuḥpitarau* ("mother and father [of someone else]"). Here, because the sense is not "and" [but rather a genitive relationship], the elision does not apply.

*Ṛtaḥ tatrānaṅ* (Pāṇini 5.2.21): For a word ending in *ṛt* that denotes a relationship by learning (*vidyā*) or by birth (*yoni*), when it occurs as the first member of a compound with another word ending in *ṛt* that likewise denotes a relationship by learning or by birth, the substitution of *ānaṅ* takes place in the scope of a copulative compound (*cārtha-samāsa*). Examples: *hotāpotārau* ("the Hotṛ and Potṛ priests"), *mātāpitarau* ("mother and father"). The letter *n* is for the purpose of preventing the substitution of *r* (i.e., to ensure the nasal remains). Why "ending in *ṛt*"? Witness *patibhrātarau* ("husband and brother"). Why "in that [context]" (*tatra*)? Witness *pitṛpitāmahau* ("father and grandfather"). Why "copulative sense" (*cārtha*)? Witness *mātṛṣvasā* ("mother's sister"—this is not a copulative compound). Why "relationship by learning or by birth"? Witness *dātṛbhrātarau* ("giver and brother"—no relationship of learning or birth). Why "in that [context]" (*tatra*)? Witness *pitṛbhoktārau* ("father and enjoyer"—no restriction to a specific relationship). *Putre* (Pāṇini 5.2.22).

In the case of a compound whose final member is *putra* and which denotes a relationship based on learning (*vidyā*) or birth (*yoni*), the substitution of *ānaṅ* occurs for the final vowel of the first member when it ends in *ṛ*. This applies to the domain of *arthasamāsa* compounds. Examples: *pitāputrau* ("father and son"), *mātāputrau* ("mother and son").
According to Pāṇini 5.2.23, in the Veda, this substitution also occurs for deities other than *vāyu* when they are mentioned together.

In the Veda, when words denoting deities—excluding *vāyu*—are heard together [in a compound], the substitution *ānaṅ* occurs for the first member (*pūrvapada*) before a word denoting a deity as the second member (*uttarapada*). Examples: *sūryācandramasau*, *mitrāvaruṇau*. Why say "of deities"? Observe: *yūpacaṣāle* ("the sacrificial post and the cup"). Why say "excluding *vāyu*"? Observe: *agnivāyū*, *vāyvagnī*. Why say "in the Veda"? Observe: *śivavaiśravaṇau*, *skandaviśākhau*. Why say "heard together"? Observe: *candrasūryau*, *divākaraniśākarau*. [The following rule applies:
*ānaṅ* does not occur for *agni* before *indra*, except before *viṣṇu*. (Pāṇini 6.3.27)

When *agni-* is followed by a word beginning with *ā*, *ai*, or *au* (*ādaic*), provided that the following word is not *viṣṇu*, the substitution *ānaṅ* does not occur. For example: *āgnimārutam kriyate*. Why "beginning with *ā*, *ai*, or *au*"? Consider: *agnāmarutau*. Why "provided it is not *viṣṇu*"? Consider: *āgnāvaiṣṇavam carum nirvapet*. (5.2.25) *somavaruṇayor īt*: When *soma* or *varuṇa* follows as the second member of a compound, *ī* is substituted for the final vowel of *agni*. Examples: *agnīṣomau*, *agnīvaruṇau*. Why "not when beginning with *ā*, *ai*, or *au*"? Consider: *āgnivāruṇīm anaḍvāhīm ālabheta*.
*divo dyavā* (5.2.26):
In the sense of "heaven" (*div*) and "deities" (*devatā*), the substitution *dyāvā* occurs for *div*. Example: *dyāvābhūmī* (Heaven and Earth).
*divas pṛthivyāṃ vā* (5.2.27): [The substitution *dyāvā* occurs] optionally for *div* when followed by *pṛthivī*.

In a compound where *pṛthivī* is the final member, the substitution of *diva* for *div* optionally occurs. Thus: *divaspṛthivyau* or *dyāvāpṛthivyau*. The explicit mention of the letter *s* is for the purpose of preventing the application of *rutva* (the substitution of *r*).
(5.2.28) *uṣāsoṣasaḥ*: When the word *uṣas* is used in the sense of deities as the final member of a compound, the substitution of *uṣāsā* occurs. Thus: *uṣāsānaktā*.

5.2.29: In a feminine [compound], that which has a corresponding masculine form (*uktapuṃska*), provided it does not end in the suffix *ūṅ*, becomes like the masculine when it occurs in the same grammatical relation (*ekārtha*) with a feminine word that is not a principal ordinal number (*apradhānapūraṇī*) or a word such as *priya* (*priyādi*). When a feminine word denoting a feminine referent (*striyāṃ vartamānam*)—which has a corresponding masculine form (*bhāṣitapuṃskam*) and does not end in the suffix *ūṅ* (*anūṅ*)—is followed by a feminine word in the same case-relation (*samānādhikaraṇe strīliṅge uttarapade*) that is not a principal ordinal number (*apradhānapūraṇī*) or a word from the *priya* group (*priyādivarjite*), it takes the masculine form (*puṃvad bhavati*). Examples: *kumārabhāryaḥ* ("one whose wife is a young girl"), *puṭabhāryaḥ* ("one whose wife is a small basket"), *etabhāryaḥ* ("one whose wife is a ewe"), *dīrghajaṅghaḥ* ("long-shanked"), *yuvajāniḥ* ("one whose wife is young"). Why "in the feminine" (*striyām*)? Consider: *grāmaṇi-kulaṃ dṛṣṭir asya* ("his view is that of a village headman's family"); here, *grāmaṇi* remains feminine because it refers to a family (*kulam*). Why "having a corresponding masculine form" (*uktapuṃskam*)? Consider: *khaṭvābhāryaḥ* ("one whose wife is a bedstead"); since *khaṭvā* has no corresponding masculine form, it does not become masculine. Why "not ending in *ūṅ*" (*anūṅ*)? Consider: *brahmabandhūbhāryaḥ* ("one whose wife is a woman of low Brahmin lineage"); since *brahmabandhū* ends in *ūṅ*, it remains feminine.

What is meant by "having the same referent" (*ekārtha*)? *Kalyāṇyā mātā* → *kalyāṇīmātā* ("the mother who is beautiful"). Why is it said "in the feminine" (*striyām*)? *Kalyāṇī pradhānam eṣām* → *kalyāṇīpradhānā ime* ("those for whom a beautiful woman is the principal one"). Why is it said "when [the word] is not a subordinate term, a ordinal number, or [one of the group] beginning with *priya*"? *Kalyāṇī pañcamī yāsāṃ rātrīṇām* → *kalyāṇīpañcamā rātrayaḥ* ("nights of which the fifth is beautiful"); *kalyāṇīpriyaḥ*, *kalyāṇīmanojñaḥ*. Why is the mention of "principal" (*pradhāna*) made? *Kalyāṇapañcamīkaḥ pakṣaḥ* ("a fortnight having a beautiful fifth day"). [The group beginning with *priya* consists of: *priyā*, *manojñā*, *kalyāṇī*, *subhagā*, *duhitā*, *vāmanā*. [The rule continues: *prasūtā-prajātā-garbhiṇyaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.2.30).

Words such as *prasūta* ("one who has given birth") undergo the masculine substitution (*puṃvat*) when followed by a feminine noun in apposition. Examples: *prasūtabhāryaḥ*, *prajātabhāryaḥ*, *garbhibhāryaḥ*. Although this was already established by the preceding rule, the explicit mention of *prasūta* and so forth is for the sake of restriction: only words like *prasūta* that have been previously mentioned as having a masculine form (*bhāṣitapuṃska*) undergo the masculine substitution when their general form (*ākṛti*) is not identical, and no others. Examples: *droṇībhāryaḥ*, *kuṭībhāryaḥ*. [The suffixes] *trata*, *tarap*, *tamap*, *caraṭ*, *kalpap*, *deśya*, *rūpa*, *pāśap*, *śas*, *thyan*, *kyan*, and *mānin* [are added according to Pāṇini 5.3.31].

In these words beginning with *trā*, when followed by a word expressing pride (*mānin*) as a subsequent member, a feminine form becomes like the masculine (*puṃvat*). Examples: *bahutra*, *bahutaḥ*, *paṭutarā*, *paṭutamā*, *paṭucarī*, *paṭukalpā*, *paṭudeśyā*, *paṭurūpā*, *paṭupāśā*; *bahvībhyo dehi*, *bahuśo dehi*. Because of its association with the group beginning with *trā*, the suffix *śas* is understood here even when it is not a case-ending. Examples: *ajathyā*, *enī*: *etāyate*; *śyenī*: *śyetāyate*. In the case of *darśanīyamāny ayam asyāḥ*, *darśanīyamāninīyam asyāḥ*. The mention of *mānin* is for the purpose of excluding the feminine meaning and for the purpose of [applying to] non-co-referential (*asamānādhikaraṇa*) compounds.
[This applies] when *yat* follows *aṇ* and so forth (Pāṇini 5.2.32).

When followed by a suffix beginning with *ya*, beginning with a vowel (*aj*), or beginning with *aṇ* and so forth, a word denoting a feminine becomes like the masculine form. The state of being a *śyenī* is *śyaityam*. Among these, she who is most clever is *paṭiṣṭhā*. Because of the application of the rule regarding the superlative suffix (*iṣṭhan*) to the suffix *ṇa*, one says *śyetayati* and *paṭayati*. A collection of female elephants is *hāstikam*. Why "beginning with *aṇ* and so forth"? [Observe: *hastinīyati* and *hastinyaḥ*.

Regarding the suffix *ḍha*, in the case of *agnāyī* (Pāṇini 4.1.33), only *agnāyī* becomes like the masculine when the suffix *ḍha* applies. For example: "He whose deity is Agnāyī" is *āgneyaḥ*. Others do not become like the masculine: *śyaineyaḥ*, *rauhiṇeyaḥ*.

(5.2.34) *na tyādivukopāntam*: That which has a *k* preceding it, belonging either to a word beginning with *ty-* or to the suffix *vuñ*, does not undergo the *puṃvat* substitution. Examples: *madrikābhāryaḥ*, *vṛjikābhāryaḥ*; *madrikākalpā*, *vṛjikākalpā*; *madrikāyate*, *vṛjikāyate*; *vailepikam* (meaning "proper for *vilepikā*"); *yācikābhāryaḥ*, *yācikākalpā*; *kārikābhāryaḥ*, *kārikākalpā*. Since the rule would have been established by the phrase "ending in *k*" (*kopāntam*), the inclusion of "beginning with *ty-*" (*tyādi*) and "the suffix *vuñ*" (*vuñ*) is for the purpose of excluding other *k*s: as in *pākabhāryaḥ*. (5.2.35) *saṃjñāpūraṇyoḥ*: [The feminine suffixes of] proper names and ordinal numbers [do not become masculine].

A feminine form ending in a name (*saṃjñā*) or a ordinal number (*pūraṇī*), when it denotes a woman, does not undergo the *puṃvat* substitution. Examples: *dattābhāryaḥ*, *dattākalpā*; *pañcamībhāryaḥ*, *pañcamīkalpā*. [This is because of the rule: "After a vowel other than *a*, and after *āt*, *ait*, and *aut*, there is no substitution when the suffix *cha* (denoting a product) does not signify a coloring or a transformation" (Pāṇini 5.2.36).

When an *ā*, *āT*, or *aiC* is substituted in place of a vowel (*ac*), that which is prescribed as the cause for those substitutions—provided it is not a blood-related derivative (*rakta-vikāra*)—does not cause the final member of the compound to be treated as masculine (*puṃvat*). Examples: *sautāṅgamī-bhāryaḥ*, *vaidiśī-bhāryaḥ*, *nādeyī-bhāryaḥ*; *sautāṅgamī-kalpā*, *vaidiśī-kalpā*, *nādeyī-kalpā*. Why is it said "in place of a vowel" (*acaḥ*)? Consider: *tāvadbhāryaḥ*, *vaiyākaraṇabhāryaḥ*. Why is it said "when there is a cause for an *āT* or *aiC*" (*ādaij-hetuḥ*)? Consider: *ardhaprasthī* (meaning "born in half-a-prastha"); she is his wife, thus *ardhaprasthabhāryaḥ*.

By the rule *nāta* (Pāṇini 6.1.37), the substitution of *āT*, *aiC*, and *auC* does not take place [for the final vowel of the first member]. Why is it said "provided it is not a coloring or a modification" (*arakta-vikāre*)? Consider: *kāṣāyī bṛhatikā asya* ("his cloak is dyed brown") results in *kāṣāyabṛhatikaḥ*. *Lauhī īṣā asya* ("its pole is made of iron") results in *lauheṣaḥ*. Because of the prohibition regarding coloring and modification, and because—by the maxim of the "young cow and the heifer" (*akiśoradhenunyāya*)—the suffixes are understood to apply only to those prescribed after a nominal ending (*sup*), this [substitution] does not occur here: *kumbhakārabhāryaḥ* ("the potter's wife"). [Furthermore, by the rule] *svāṅgād īd amānini* (Pāṇini 5.2.37) [the long *ī* is applied].

When the word *amāninī* follows as the second member (*uttarapada*), a feminine stem ending in the long vowel *ī* that follows an [indeclinable] part of the body (*svāṅga*) does not undergo the masculine form (*puṃvat*). Examples: *dīrghakeśībhāryaḥ*, *dīrghakeśīpāśā*. Why "following an [indeclinable] part of the body"? *paṭubhāryaḥ*. Why "ending in *ī*"? *akeśabhāryaḥ*. Why "*amāninī*"? *dīrghakeśamāninī*. Regarding *jātir aṣphādau ca* (Pāṇini 6.3.41):

A word denoting a genus (*jāti*) occurring in the feminine does not undergo the masculine form when followed by a suffix beginning with *aṣ* or *ph*, or when followed by *amāninī*. Examples: *kaṭhībhāryaḥ*, *bahvṛcībhāryaḥ*. Why "beginning with *aṣ* or *ph*"? *hāstikam*. What is the purpose of the particle *ca* ("and")? [To include: *kaṭhamāninī*.

*Puṃvat svapadārthajātīyadeśīyeṣu* (Pāṇini 5.2.39): A feminine word ending in *ūṅ*, which has a corresponding masculine form (*uktapuṃska*) and is used in the feminine sense, becomes like the masculine when followed by a feminine co-referential (*samānādhikaraṇa*) final member denoting its own meaning (*svapadārtha*), or when followed by the suffixes *jātīya* or *deśīya*. Examples: *Madrakavṛndārikā*, *pācakavṛndārikā*, *Dattavṛndārikā*, *pañcamavṛndārikā*, *Sraughnavṛndārikā*, *ślakṣṇamukhavṛndārikā*, *Vātaṇḍyavṛndārikā*, *Kaṭhavṛndārikā*; *Iḍabiḍvṛndārikā*, *Aiḍabiḍavṛndārikā*.

Daradvṛndārikā, Dāradavṛndārikā; Pṛthuvṛndārikā, Pārthavavṛndārikā; Uśigvṛndārikā, Auśijavṛndārikā. Madrakajātīyā, Madrakadeśīyā; pācakajātīyā, pācakadeśīyā; Dattajātīyā, Dattadeśīyā; pañcamajātīyā, pañcamadeśīyā; Sraughnajātīyā, Sraughnadeśīyā; ślakṣṇamukhajātīyā, ślakṣṇamukhadeśīyā; Kaṭhajātīyā, Kaṭhadeśīyā. Only when [the word] has already expressed the masculine gender: *khaṭvāvṛndārikā*. Only when [the suffix] *-ūṅ* is not present: *brahmabandhūvṛndārikā*.

(5.2.40) *guṇas tvataloḥ*: A quality (*guṇa*) denoting a feminine [entity] becomes like the masculine (*puṃvat*) when followed by the suffixes *tva* or *tal*. For example: the state of being clever (*paṭvī*) is *paṭutvam* or *paṭutā*. Why "a quality"? [Consider: *kaṭhītvam* (the state of being a female Kaṭha).
(5.2.41) *sarvādayo vṛttimātre*: [The words] beginning with *sarva-* [behave as masculines] in all compound formations (*vṛtti*).

Words such as *sarva* and others, when they function as feminine, become masculine when referring merely to their grammatical function (*vṛtti*). For example: *tasyāḥ sukham* becomes *tatsukham*; *yasyāḥ sukham* becomes *yatsukham*. *Tasyā idam* becomes *tadīyam*; *yadīyam*. *Bhavatyā idam* becomes *bhāvatkam* or *bhavadīyam*. *Tasyām* becomes *tatra*; *yatra*. *Tasyāḥ* becomes *tataḥ*; *yataḥ*, *kutaḥ*. *Kayā vṛttyā* becomes *katham*; *tayā vṛttyā* becomes *tathā*. *Tasyāṃ velāyām* becomes *tadā* or *tarhi*.

How is it that "the egg of a hen" is *kukkuṭāṇḍam*, "the milk of a doe" is *mṛgakṣīram*, "the track of a doe" is *mṛgapadam*, and "the chick of a crow" is *kākaśāvaḥ*? Because the genus (*jāti*) is intended to be expressed, the compound will take the masculine gender; however, when the feminine is intended to be expressed, it must indeed be *kukkuṭyaṇḍa* and so forth, just as in the cases of *avīkṣīram* ("ewe's milk") and *ajākṣīram* ("goat's milk").
[This is governed by the rule: *taratamarūpakalpacelaḍbruvagotramatahate ṅyo hrasvaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.3.43).

When *tarap* and so forth, as well as *celaḍ* and so forth, follow, the feminine suffix (*ṅī*) of a word that has a corresponding masculine form undergoes shortening. Examples: *brāhmaṇitarā*, *brāhmaṇitamā*, *brāhmaṇirūpā*, *brāhmaṇikalpā*, *brāhmaṇicelī*, *brāhmaṇibruvā*. By this very rule, in the case of the root *bru-* followed by a vowel, there is no substitution of *vac-*, but rather the substitution of *uv-*. [Examples continue: *brāhmaṇigotrā*, *brāhmaṇimatā*, *brāhmaṇihatā*. Why "after a word ending in *ṅī*"? [Counter-example: *dattātarā*. Why "having a corresponding masculine form"? [Counter-example: *āmalakītarā*. [This concludes the discussion of] *vaikacaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.2.43).

The vowel of a monosyllabic word preceding the suffix *ṅī* is optionally shortened when followed by *tara* and other such suffixes. Thus: *stritarā* or *strītarā*. Only when *ṅī* follows does this apply: *śrītarā*. Regarding the rule *ugitaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.3.44): the vowel of a word ending in an *ugit* suffix preceding the suffix *ṅī*, when followed by *tara* and other such suffixes, is optionally shortened. Thus: *śreyasitarā* or *śreyasītarā*; *viduṣitarā* or *viduṣītarā*. How is it that forms like *śreyastarā* and *vidvattarā* are established? They are established because, prior to the application of excellence (*prakarṣa*), the feminine gender was not intended to be expressed.
(5.2.45) *Ūṅaḥ*: After a word ending in *ūṅ*, the vowel may optionally be shortened before suffixes such as *tara* and others. For example: *brahmabandhutarā* or *brahmabandhūtarā*.

(5.2.46) *Ān mahato jātīyaikārthayor acvyarthe*: The substitution of *ān* for *mahat* occurs before the suffixes *jātīya* and *ekārtha*, provided that they do not have the sense of a verbal derivative (*acv-artha*).

The substitution of *ā* for the final vowel of the word *mahat* occurs when it is followed by a suffix beginning with *jātīya* or by a co-referential (*samānādhikaraṇa*) following member, provided that it does not function in the sense of the suffix *cvī*. Examples: *mahājātīyaḥ*, *mahāpuruṣaḥ*, *mahābāhuḥ*. Why is it specified "when [the meaning] is one with *jātīya*"? Consider: *mahataḥ putraḥ* → *mahatputraḥ*. Why is it specified "not in the sense of *cvī*"? Consider: *amahān mahān saṃpannaḥ* → *mahadbhūtaś candramāḥ* ("the moon has become great"). This is not a figurative usage (*gauṇa*), because it is a state of becoming such; it is like saying "a lump of clay has become a jar.
[In the case of the compound] *ghāsakaraviśiṣṭe*, there is also the masculine form (*puṃvat*). (Pāṇini 5.4.47)

When followed by words such as *ghāsa* that are in a different grammatical relation (*vyadhikaraṇa*), the substitution of *ā* for the final vowel of *mahat* occurs, and there is also the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*). For example: *mahatyā ghāsaḥ* becomes *mahāghāsaḥ*; *mahatyāḥ karaḥ* becomes *mahākaraḥ*; *mahatyā viśiṣṭaḥ* becomes *mahāviśiṣṭaḥ*.
According to Pāṇini 5.2.48, the substitution of *ā* occurs when followed by a word ending in the suffix *ic*: *keśākeśi* and *muṣṭāmuṣṭi*.

(5.2.49) *nāmny aṣṭanaḥ*: When a name is the subject, the substitution of *ā* for *aṣṭan-* occurs when it is followed by another word (*uttarapada*). Example: *aṣṭāvakraḥ* (the sage Aṣṭāvakra). Why "when it is a name"? Example: *aṣṭadaṃṣṭraḥ* (having eight tusks). (5.2.50) *kapāle haviṣi*. [The substitution of *ā* for *aṣṭan-* occurs before the word *kapāla* when it refers to an oblation.]

When *kapāla* follows as the second member of a compound and refers to an oblation (*havis*), the substitution of *āt* for *aṣṭan* occurs. For example: *aṣṭākapālaṃ haviḥ*. Why "referring to an oblation"? [Consider: *aṣṭakapālam annam* ("food on eight potsherds").

In the case of *go* when it follows as the second member of a compound and denotes something yoked to it (Pāṇini 5.2.51), the substitution of *āt* for *aṣṭan* occurs. For example: *aṣṭāgavena śakaṭena* ("a cart yoked to eight oxen"). Why "yoked"? [Consider: *aṣṭagavadhanaṃ brāhmaṇasya* ("the wealth of a Brahmin consisting of eight oxen").
(5.2.52) *dveś ca saṃkhyāyāṃ prāk chatād ananyārthāśītyoḥ*:

Before the word *śata*, when followed by a numeral (*saṃkhyā*) as a subsequent member (*uttarapada*), provided that it does not mean "another thing" (*ananyārtha*) and excludes *aśīti*, the substitution of *ā* for *e* occurs in the words *dvi* and *aṣṭan*. For example: *dvādaśa* (twelve), *dvāviṃśatiḥ* (twenty-two), *dvātriṃśat* (thirty-two); *aṣṭādaśa* (eighteen), *aṣṭāviṃśatiḥ* (twenty-eight), *aṣṭātriṃśat* (thirty-eight). Why is *dveś ca* ("and *dvi*") stated? [To exclude cases like: *pañcadaśa* (fifteen). Why is *saṃkhyāyām* ("when it is a numeral") stated? [To exclude cases where the subsequent member is not a numeral: *dvaimāturaḥ* (having two mothers), *āṣṭamāturaḥ* (having eight mothers). Why is *prāk chatāt* ("before *śata*") stated? [To exclude cases where the subsequent member is *śata* or higher: *dviśatam* (two hundred), *dvisahasram* (two thousand); *aṣṭaśatam* (eight hundred), *aṣṭasahasram* (eight thousand).

What is the purpose of the restriction "except when [the compound] has another meaning or ends in *aśīti*"? Consider: *dvitrāḥ* (two or three); *dvyaśītiḥ* (eighty-two). Regarding the rule *tres trayaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.2.53):

in the context of numerals, the word *tri* undergoes the substitution *trayas*. Thus: *trayodaśa* (thirteen), *trayoviṃśatiḥ* (twenty-three), *trayastriṃśat* (thirty-three). The restriction "in the context of numerals" applies here: *traimāturaḥ* (born of three mothers). The restriction "before *śata*" also applies: *triśatam* (three hundred), *trisahasram* (three thousand). The restriction "except when [the compound] has another meaning or ends in *aśīti*" likewise applies: *tridaśāḥ* (the thirty gods), *tryaśītiḥ* (eighty-three).

(5.2.54) *Catvāriṃśadādau vā*: That which has been prescribed regarding a numeral optionally applies when *catvāriṃśat* (forty) and so forth follow. Thus: *dvācatvāriṃśat* or *dvicatvāriṃśat*; *aṣṭācatvāriṃśat* or *aṣṭacatvāriṃśat*; *trayaścatvāriṃśat* or *tricatvāriṃśat*. *Dvāpañcāśat* or *dvipañcāśat*; *aṣṭāpañcāśat* or *aṣṭapañcāśat*; *trayaḥpañcāśat* or *tripañcāśat*. How is *ekādaśa* (eleven) formed? It is established as *ekādaśa* by the irregular derivation (*nipātana*) in [Pāṇini 5.1.59]: *daśaikādaśakusīdād*. (5.2.55) *Hṛdayasyāṇi hṛt*: [The word *hṛdaya* is replaced by] *hṛt* before the suffix *aṇ*.
After the suffix *aṇ*, *hṛd* is the substitute for *hṛdaya*. *Hārdam*.

In the presence of the suffix *aṇ* ending in *lekha* (Pāṇini 5.2.56), *hṛd* is the substitute for *hṛdaya*. *Hṛdayaṃ likhati* [one who writes the heart], *hṛllekhaḥ*. Only when it is *aṇ* [does the substitution apply]: *hṛdayalekhaḥ*. Since the rule would have been established by the mention of *aṇ* alone, the specific mention of *lekha* is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that, within the governing heading (*adhikāra*) concerning the "subsequent member" (*uttarapada*), there is no inclusion of forms ending in those [words].

(5.2.57) *lāsayatoḥ*: When followed by the suffix *yat* or the root *las*, the substitution of *hṛd* for *hṛdaya* occurs. Examples: *hṛllāsaḥ*, *hṛdyaḥ*. Although the form could have been established by using the word *hṛt*, the rule prescribes the substitution in order to exclude the use of the word *hṛdaya*. In other cases, both forms may be used: *hṛcchokaḥ* / *hṛdayaśokaḥ*; *sauhārdyam* / *sauhṛdayyam*; *hṛdrogaḥ* / *hṛdayarogaḥ*; *hṛcchūlaḥ* / *hṛdayaśūlaḥ*; *hṛcchalyaḥ* / *hṛdayaśalyaḥ*. (5.2.58) *pādasyājyātigopahate padaḥ*: In the words *aji*, *ati*, *go*, and *upahata*, the substitution of *pad* for *pāda* occurs.

The word *pāda* undergoes the substitution *pad* when followed by *aji*, *āti*, *ga*, or *upahata*. Thus: *pādābhyām ajati* becomes *padājiḥ*; *padātiḥ*, *padagaḥ*, *padopahataḥ*. By Pāṇini 5.2.59, *prāṇyaṅgāt khalayavamāṣatilavṛṣabrahmaṇaś ca*, the substitution *pad* occurs for *pāda* when followed by *hima*, *hati*, *kāṣin*, *ṣṭhan*, or *yat*. Thus: *paddhimam*, *paddhatiḥ*, *patkāṣī*. From *pādābhyāṃ carati* comes *padikaḥ*; here *ṣṭhan* is applied because it belongs to the *parpādi* group (Pāṇini 3.4.8). From *pādau vidhyanti* comes *padyāḥ śarkarāḥ* ("pebbles that strike the feet"). Because this section begins with the topic of limbs of living beings (*prāṇyaṅga*), the substitution does not apply here: *dvipādyam*.

*ṛcaḥ śi* (Pāṇini 5.4.74): When followed by a word beginning with *ś*, the substitution of *pad-* occurs for the word *pāda-* when it is related to the *ṛc* (Vedic verse). Example: *paccho gāyatrīṃ śaṃsati* ("He recites the Gāyatrī verse foot by foot"). Why "related to the *ṛc*"? [Counter-example: *pādaśaḥ kārṣāpaṇaṃ dadāti* ("He gives a kārṣāpaṇa coin by the foot [unit]"). Although the desired form is established by the word *paccha-*, the explicit mention of the substitute (*ādeśa*) is for the purpose of excluding the word *pāda-*. Elsewhere, both forms may be used: *padghoṣaḥ* / *pādaghoṣaḥ*; *padmiśraḥ* / *pādamiśraḥ*; *pacchabdaḥ* / *pādaśabdaḥ*; *panniṣkaḥ* / *pādaniṣkaḥ*. *nas nāsikāyās taḥkṣudre* (Pāṇini 5.4.118): In the sense of "small," the substitute *ta-* occurs for the word *nāsikā-* when preceded by *naḥ* (the negative particle *na*). [Example: *nastaḥ* "nose-cord" or "small nose"].

When the words *tasi* or *kṣudra* follow, the substitute *nas* occurs in place of *nāsikā*. Thus: *nastaḥ*, *naḥkṣudraḥ*. According to Pāṇini 5.2.62 (*yaty avarṇe*), when a suffix beginning with *yat* follows—provided it is not preceded by a vowel—the substitute *nas* occurs in place of *nāsikā*. Thus: *nasyaṃ tailam* ("nose-oil"). Why "not preceded by a vowel" (*avarṇe*)? Consider: *nāsikyo varṇaḥ* ("a nasal sound"). How is it that there is the form *Nāsikyaṃ nagaram* ("the city of Nāsikya")? In this case, the suffix *ṇya* is applied in the sense of the four meanings [of Pāṇini 4.2.67–70].

(5.2.63) *śirasaḥ śīrṣan vā*: When the suffix *yat* follows, the substitute *śīrṣan* optionally occurs in place of *śiras*. Examples: *śīrṣaṇyaḥ*, *śirasyaḥ*. The term *avarṇa* does not carry over [from the previous rule]. (5.2.64) *śīrṣo 'ci*: [The substitute *śīrṣan* occurs] in place of *śiras* when a vowel-initial suffix follows.

In the domain of [patronymic] suffixes beginning with *aja*, the substitution of *śīrṣa* for *śiras* occurs. Examples: *Hāstiśīrṣiḥ*, *Sthaulaśīrṣiḥ*, *Mārgaśīrṣaḥ*. By the indicator (*jñāpaka*) in the rule *adhaḥśirasor* (Pāṇini 6.4.41), this substitution does not occur when a case ending follows. How is it that one says: *ilvalā mṛgaśīrṣasya śirasyās tārakāḥ smṛtāḥ* ("the Ilvalas are known as the stars on the head of Mṛgaśīrṣa")? There exists another base word *śīrṣa*. In the rule *nāmny udakasyodaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.2.65), when a name is intended, the form *uda* replaces *udaka* when it appears as a final member of a compound. Examples: *Udameghaḥ*, *Udapānaḥ*, *Udavāhaḥ*, *udadhiḥ*.

(5.2.66) *uttarasya*: In a compound, when it is a name (*saṃjñā*), the substitution of *uda-* for the final member *udaka-* occurs. For example: the ocean named Kṣīroda ("Milk-Ocean") and the lake named Acchoda ("Clear-Water"). (5.2.67) *vāsavāhane*.
When *vāsa* or *vāhana* follows as a subsequent member (*uttarapada*), the substitution of *uda-* for *udaka-* occurs. For example: *udavāsaḥ*, *udavāhanam*.
Regarding the rule *peṣe piṣau* (Pāṇini 5.4.68):

when *piṣ* follows, the substitution of *uda-* for *udaka-* occurs in that *peṣa* which stands as a subsequent member. For example: *udapeṣaṃ pinaṣṭi*. Why is *piṣau* specified? [To exclude cases like] *udakapeṣaḥ*.

(5.2.69) *ekahalādau bhāṇḍe vā*: When the first member consists of a single consonant (*hal*) and the second member is a word denoting a vessel (*bhāṇḍa*), the substitution of *ud* for *udaka* optionally occurs. Examples: *udakumbhaḥ* or *udakakumbhaḥ*; *udapātram* or *udakapātram*. Why "when consisting of a single consonant"? Consider *udakasthālam*. Why "vessel"? Consider *udakapātaḥ*.

(5.2.70) *manthaudanasaktubinduvajrabhārahāravīvadhagāheṣu*: [The substitution of *ud* for *udaka* occurs] before the words *mantha*, *odana*, *saktu*, *bindu*, *vajra*, *bhāra*, *hāra*, *vīvadha*, and *gāha*.

In the case of *mantha* and other such words, the substitution of *uda-* for *udaka-* optionally occurs. *Udamanthaḥ*, *udakamanthaḥ*; *udaudanaḥ*, *udakaudanaḥ*; *udasaktuḥ*, *udakasaktuḥ*; *udabinduḥ*, *udakabinduḥ*; *udavajraḥ*, *udakavajraḥ*; *udabhāraḥ*, *udakabhāraḥ*; *udahāraḥ*, *udakahāraḥ*; *udavīvadhaḥ*, *udakavīvadhaḥ*; *udagāhaḥ*, *udadagāhaḥ*. Regarding *iko hrasvaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.3.61):
when an *ik*-vowel stands before a following word (*uttarapada*), it is optionally shortened. *Grāmaṇiputraḥ*, *grāmaṇīputraḥ*; *brahmabandhuputraḥ*, *brahmabandhūputraḥ*.

Pāṇini 6.3.43 (*cvau ca*) states: "In the presence of *cvi* and *iṅ*, the short vowel does not occur for an *ik* [vowel] related to a *yaṇ* or to *iy* and *uv*; however, it certainly does occur for *bhrūkuṃsa* and others. Examples: *paṭībhūtās tantavaḥ* ("the threads have become cloth"). *paṭūbhūto 'paṭuḥ* ("one who was not clever has become clever"). *Gārgīputraḥ*, *Gaurīputraḥ*, *Kārīṣagandhīputraḥ*. *Indrahūputraḥ*; *Śrīkulam*, *Bhrūkulam*. Why does the rule specify "not for *bhrūkuṃsa* and others"? Consider *bhrukuṃsaḥ* ("a frown")—[here the shortening occurs]. Another teacher says: "For *bhrūkuṃsa* and others, the vowel becomes *a*: *bhrakuṃsaḥ*, *bhrakuṭiḥ*. How so? [The forms are derived as follows: *bhrukuṃsaḥ* > *bhrakuṃsaḥ*; *bhrukuṭiḥ* > *bhrakuṭiḥ*.

Is it *ekasyā āgatam*, *ekarūpyam*, *ekamayam*; [and] *ekasyāḥ kṣīram*, *ekakṣīram*? This is established precisely because [the word *eka*] belongs to the group beginning with *sarva*. Regarding Pāṇini 5.2.73, *ṅyāpoḥ tv-anāmnor bahulam*: after feminine suffixes ending in *ṅī* or *āp*, the short vowel is optionally applied when followed by the suffix *tva*, provided the word is not a proper name (*anāman*), and also when followed by a subsequent member of a compound (*uttarapada*). Examples: *rohiṇitvam*, *rohiṇītvam*; *ajatvam*, *ajātvam*; *Revatimitram*, *Revatīmitram*; *Śiṃśapasthalam*, *Śiṃśapāsthalam*. In some cases, it does not occur: *nāndīkaraḥ*, *Lomakāṣaṇḍaḥ*.

In the case of *iṣṭakā*, *iṣīkā*, and *mālā* when followed by *cita*, *tūla*, and *bhārin* respectively (Pāṇini 5.2.74), the short vowel is substituted for these words when they precede *cita* and so on. Thus: *iṣṭakacitam*, *iṣīkatūlam*, *mālabhārī*. Since the words *iṣṭakā* and the others occur even at the end of compounds, the shortening indeed takes place: *pakveṣṭakacitam*, *muñjeṣīkatūlam*, *utpalamālabhāriṇī kanyā*.
Furthermore, when the suffix *khit* follows, there is the addition of *mum* after a word accompanied by a numeral (Pāṇini 5.2.75).

When a word ending in *khid* follows as a second member (*uttarapada*), there is shortening of a preceding numeral, and the augment *mum* is also added. Examples: *hariṇimanyā*, *kālimanyā*. Why "of a numeral" (*sasaṃkhyasya*)? Consider: *doṣāmanyam ahaḥ* ("a day considered as evening") and *divāmanyā rātriḥ* ("a night considered as day"). Precisely because of this mention of "numeral," the mention of "ending in *khid*" is understood [to apply here as well]. Regarding *aruṣaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.2.76): the word *arus* takes the augment *mum* when a word ending in *khid* follows as a second member. Example: *aruṃtudaḥ* ("one who pierces a wound").
(5.2.77) *kāre 'stusatyāgadasya*: When the word *kāra* follows, the augment *mum* is applied to *astu*, *satya*, and *agada*. [Examples: *astuṃkāram*, *satyaṃkāram*, *agadaṃkāram*.
(5.2.78) *lokasya pṛṇe*: [The augment *mum* is applied to *loka* when followed by *pṛṇe*.]
The augment *mum* is inserted before the word *lokaṃpṛṇa*.
According to the rule *itye ’nabhyāśasya* (Pāṇini 5.2.79), the augment *mum* is inserted before the word *anabhyāśa* when it follows the word *iti*. [Thus: *anabhyāśamityaḥ*.

(5.2.80) *bhrāṣṭrāgnyor indhe*: after the words *bhrāṣṭra* and *agni*, when followed by the word *indh*, the suffix *mum* is applied. Examples: *bhrāṣṭramindhaḥ*, *agnimindhaḥ*. (5.2.81) *agilasya gile*: [the suffix *mum* is applied] after a word that does not end in the root *gil*, when followed by the word *gila*.

After the word *gila*, when followed by another word beginning with *gila*, the suffix *mum* occurs. For example: *timiṅgilaḥ*. Why does it say "after *agila*" (*agilasya*)? [To exclude cases such as] *gilagilaḥ*. How is this so? [One might ask: "How is this *timiṅgilagilaḥ*? Since the word *gila* exists within the compound *gilagila*, the form is established simply by [the rule for] *gila*.
In the case of *bhadra* and *uṣṇa*, when followed by the word *karaṇa*, the suffix *mum* occurs. For example: *bhadraṃkaraṇam*, *uṣṇaṃkaraṇam*.
In the rule *madhyasya dine* (Pāṇini 5.2.83), the augment *mum* is added after *madhya* when followed by *dine*. Thus: *madhyandinaḥ*.
In the rule *śyenatilayoḥ pāte ñe* (Pāṇini 5.2.84): [The suffix *ñya* is added after *śyena* and *tila* when followed by *pāta*].

The augment *mum* is inserted before a suffix ending in *ñ* when following the words *śyena* and *tila*. Examples: *śyainaṃpātā krīḍā* ("a game of hawk-falling") and *tailaṃpātā* ("an oil-fall"). Why "before *ñ*" (*ña*)? [To exclude cases like] *śyenapātaḥ* ("the flight of a hawk") and *tilapātaḥ* ("the fall of sesame"). Regarding *rātreḥ dhatau vā* (Pāṇini 5.4.85): the augment *mum* optionally occurs after *rātri* when followed by a verbal root as a subsequent member (*uttarapada*). Examples: *rātriṃcaraḥ* or *rātricaraḥ* ("night-walker"); *rātrimaṭaḥ* or *rātryaṭaḥ* ("one who wanders at night"). However, when followed by a suffix beginning with *kh*, it is obligatory: *rātriṃmanyaḥ* ("one who considers it night").
(5.2.86) *dhenor bhavyāyām*:

After the word *dhenu*, the augment *mum* optionally occurs when *bhavyā* is the subsequent member (*uttarapada*). Examples: *dhenuṃbhavyā*, *dhenubhavyā*. It need not be stated that *putraḍ* replaces *duhitṛ* after words such as *sūta* and others, because the word *putra* is already included in the *gaura*-group (Pāṇini 4.1.41). Likewise, forms such as *duhituḥputrī* and even *śailaputrī* are observed. (5.2.87) *māṃsasya paci ghañlyuṭor lopaḥ*: In the case of the root *pac* preceded by *māṃsa*, there is elision [of the final vowel and consonant] when the suffixes *ghañ* or *lyuṭ* follow.

When the suffixes *ghañ* or *lyuṭ* follow the root *pac* preceded by *māṃsa*, the elision (*lopa*) of the final vowel and consonant of the prefix may optionally occur. Thus: *māṃspākaḥ* or *māṃsapākaḥ*; *māṃspacanī* or *māṃsapacanī*. Why "when *pac* [follows]"? [Observe: *māṃsadāhaḥ*, *māṃsadahanī*. Why "when *ghañ* or *lyuṭ* [follow]"? [Observe: *māṃsapaktiḥ*. Regarding the rule *samas tate* (Pāṇini 6.1.143):

when *tata* preceded by *sam* follows, the elision of the final vowel and consonant of the prefix may optionally occur. Thus: *satatam* or *saṃtatam*. How is it that we have *sahitam* and *saṃhitam*? [They result] from the irregular derivation (*nipātana*) in the rule *ūror upamāsaṃhitasahita* (Pāṇini 2.3.79).

*tumaś ca kāmamanasoḥ* (Pāṇini 5.2.89): After *tum*, both *sam* and *tum* undergo elision when *kāma* or *manas* follows as the subsequent member (*uttarapada*). Examples: *bhoktukāmaḥ* (desirous of eating), *bhoktumanāḥ* (intent on eating); *sakāmaḥ* (having desire), *samanāḥ* (having the mind). *avaśyamaḥ tavyādiṣaṭke* (Pāṇini 5.2.90): After *avaśyam*, [the suffix *am*] is elided before the six suffixes beginning with *tavya*.

The elision occurs when the six suffixes beginning with *avaśyamastavya* follow. For example: *avaśyakartavyam*, *avaśyakāryam*. Why "the six"? [To show it does not apply] in *avaśyaṃkārakaḥ*. Regarding *naño naḥ* (Pāṇini 5.2.91):

the *n* of the negative particle *nañ* is elided before a subsequent member of a compound. Examples: *abrāhmaṇaḥ*, *avṛṣalaḥ*. Why the letter *ñ*? So that it does not apply to the simple word *na*: as in *pāmanaputraḥ*.

In the rule *tiṅy avakṣepe* (Pāṇini 5.2.92), when a verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*) follows and contempt is implied, the *n* of the negative particle *nañ* is elided. Examples: *apacasi tvaṃ jālma!* ("You cook poorly, you scoundrel! and *akaroṣi tvaṃ jālma!* ("You do not do [it well], you scoundrel!").
Thereafter, by the rule *ato 'ci nuṭ* (5.2.93), the augment *nuṭ* is added after a short vowel ending in *a*.

Therefore, when the negative particle *nañ* has its *n* elided, the augment *nuṭ* is added before a following word beginning with a vowel. For example: *anaśvaḥ* ("not a horse"), *anuṣṭraḥ* ("not a camel"). Why does the rule say "thereafter" (*tataḥ*)? To prevent [the augment] from applying to the negative particle itself. What is the purpose of the letter *ṭ*? To prevent the doubling of the *ṅ*. Regarding the rule *ekād annādnau saṃkhyāyām* (Pāṇini 5.2.94):

after the word *eka*, the negative particle *nañ* undergoes the substitutions *anna* and *adna* respectively when followed by a numeral as the subsequent member of a compound. For example: *ekena na viṃśatiḥ* becomes *ekānnaviṃśatiḥ* or *ekādnaviṃśatiḥ* ("one less than twenty"); likewise, *ekānnatriṃśat* or *ekādnatriṃśat* ("one less than thirty").

*nakhādayaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.2.95): Words beginning with *nakha* are established as nipātanas (irregular forms) with their nasal *n* not elided. That which has no *kha* is *nakha*; anything else is *akha*. In the case of technical names (*saṃjñāśabda*), etymological derivation should be performed in some way or another merely for the sake of explanation. That which has no *kula* is *nakula*; anything else is *akula*. [The list is: *nakha*, *nakula*, *napuṃsaka*, *nakṣatra*, *nakra*, *nāka*, *nameru*, *Nāsatya*, *Namuci*, *Nabhrāṭ*, *napāt*, *navedāḥ*; here the suffix *asun* is applied according to the *Uṇādi* rules. *nago 'prāṇini vā* (Pāṇini 5.2.96): In the sense of "not moving" (*aprāṇin*), the word *naga* may optionally be used.

The form *naga* is optionally prescribed as a substitute for *agā* when referring to non-living beings. Thus: *nagā vṛkṣāḥ* ("trees are *nagas*") and *nagāḥ parvatāḥ* ("mountains are *nagas*"); likewise, *agā vṛkṣāḥ* and *agāḥ parvatāḥ*. Why "when referring to non-living beings"? Observe: *ago vṛṣalaḥ śītena* ("the low-born man is cold").
[In the following rule: *sahasya so 'nyārthe* (Pāṇini 5.2.97).

When a compound occurs whose referent is something other than its constituent members (*anyapadārthavṛtti*), the word *saha* optionally becomes *sa-* before the final member (*uttarapada*). Examples: *saputraḥ* / *sahaputraḥ*; *sacchāttraḥ* / *sahacchāttraḥ*. Why specify "when the referent is something else"? [Because in these cases it is not so: *sahayudhvā*, *sahakṛtvā*. How then is it that we have *sahakṛtva-priyaḥ* or *priya-sahakṛtvā*? In a compound where the referent is something else, the word *saha* does not stand immediately before the final member; therefore, there is no substitution of *sa-*. By the rule *nāmni* (Pāṇini 5.2.98), when the final member is a proper name (*saṃjñā*), the word *saha* undergoes the substitution of *śa-*. Examples: *sāśvatthaḥ*, *sapalāśaḥ*.

(5.2.99) *anupākhye*: when something imperceptible is understood, the substitution of *sa-* for the word *saha* occurs before a final member of a compound. Examples: *sāgniḥ kapotaḥ* ("a pigeon [seen] together with fire"), *sapiśācā vātyā* ("a whirlwind [accompanied by] a piśāca").
(5.2.100) *akāle svārthe*: [The substitution of *sa-* for *saha* occurs] in the sense of itself [i.e., as an adjective] when not referring to time.

For the word *saha* when it has its own meaning as the primary sense, the substitution of *sa-* occurs before a following nominal stem (*uttarapada*) that does not denote time. Examples: *saṃpannaṃ brahma* (perfected Brahman), *sabrahma Bābhravāṇām* (the Brahman-knowledge of the Bābhravas); *sacakraṃ nidhehi* (place it together with the wheel); *sadhuram*. Why "not denoting time"? As in *sahapūrvāhṇam* (together with the forenoon), *sahāparāhṇam* (together with the afternoon). Regarding the rule *granthāntādhikye* (Pāṇini 5.2.101): the substitution of *sa-* occurs for the word *saha* when it signifies the end of a book (*granthānta*) or an excess (*ādhikya*). Examples: *sakalaṃ jyotiṣam adhīte* (he studies the entire Jyotiṣa); *sajyotiḥ*, *samuhūrtam*. This rule begins for the sake of excluding [the application of] time. Regarding excess: *sadroṇā khārī* (a khārī measure plus one droṇa), *samāṣaḥ kārṣāpaṇaḥ* (a kārṣāpaṇa coin plus one māṣa). This rule begins for the sake of making the substitution obligatory.

(5.2.102) *nāśiṣy agovatsahale*: In the domain of benediction (*āśis*), when the word *saha* is followed by a final member other than *go*, *vatsa*, or *hala*, the substitution of *sa-* for *saha-* does not occur. Example: *svasti devadattāya sahaputrāya sahacchātrāya*. Why "not after *go*, *vatsa*, or *hala*"? Example: *svasti bhavate sagave savatsāya sahalāya*. (5.2.103) *samānasya pakṣādiṣu*: [The substitution of *sa-* occurs] for *samāna-* when followed by words beginning with *pakṣa*.

The substitution of *sa-* for *samāna-* occurs when the words *pakṣa* and others follow as subsequent members (*uttarapada*). Examples: *sapakṣaḥ*, *sajyotiḥ*. Why "when *pakṣa* and others follow"? [Counter-example: *samānaśīlaḥ*. The words are: *pakṣa*, *jyotis*, *janapada*, *rātri*, *nābhi*, *bandhu*, *patnī*, *brahmacārin*. *Brahman* means the Veda; the vow for the purpose of studying it is also called *brahman*; one who practices that is a *brahmacārī*. One who has the same *brahmacarya* is a *sabrahmacārī*. Or, according to Pāṇini 5.2.104: [the suffix *cha* is applied after a word ending in *a*] when followed by *nāman*, *gotra*, *rūpa*, *sthāna*, *varṇa*, *vayas*, *vacana*, *dharma*, or *jātīya*.

In the presence of words beginning with *nāman* and so forth, the substitution of *sa-* optionally occurs for *samāna*. Thus: *sanāmā* or *samānanāmā*; *sagotraḥ* or *samānagotraḥ*; *sarūpaḥ* or *samānarūpaḥ*; *sasthānaḥ* or *samānasthānaḥ*; *savarṇaḥ* or *samānavarṇaḥ*; *savayāḥ* or *samānavayāḥ*; *savacanaḥ* or *samānavacanaḥ*; *sadharmā* or *samānadharmā*; *sajātīyaḥ* or *samānajātīyaḥ*. Regarding the rule *udare ye* (Pāṇini 5.2.105): when followed by a word beginning with *udara* and having the letter *y* as its second member (*yakārapara*), the substitution of *sa-* optionally occurs for *samāna*. Thus: *sodaryaḥ* or *samānodaryaḥ*. Why is it said "when [the following word] begins with *ya*" (*ya iti*)? Consider: *samānodaratā*.
In the presence of *dṛk*, *dṛśa*, and *dṛkṣa* (Pāṇini 5.2.106), the substitution of *sa-* for *samāna-* occurs when these follow. Thus: *sadṛk*, *sadṛśaḥ*, *sadṛkṣaḥ*.
And in the case of the suffix *vat*, as well as after *idam* and *kim*, the substitutions *īś* and *kī* [respectively] occur (Pāṇini 5.2.107).

When the suffix *vat* and the words beginning with *dṛś* follow, the substitutes *īś* and *kī* respectively take the place of *idam*. Thus: *iyān*, *kiyān*; *īdṛk*, *kīdṛk*; *īdṛśaḥ*, *kīdṛśaḥ*; *īdṛkṣaḥ*, *kīdṛkṣaḥ*.

By the rule *āḥ sarvādīnām* (Pāṇini 5.2.108), when *vat* and the words beginning with *dṛś* follow, the vowel *ā* replaces the final letter of the words beginning with *sarva*. Thus: *yāvat*, *tāvat*; *yādṛk*, *tādṛk*; *yādṛśaḥ*, *tādṛśaḥ*; *yādṛkṣaḥ*, *tādṛkṣaḥ*.

(5.2.109) *viṣvag-devayoś ca ḍadrig añcatau vā*: After the words *viṣvak* and *deva*, as well as after the words beginning with *sarva* (i.e., the *sarvādi* group), the augment *ḍadri* is optionally inserted before the suffix *añcu* when it follows [these words]. Examples: *viṣvagañcati* → *viṣvadryaṅ*; *devadryaṅ*; *yadryaṅ*; *tadryaṅ*. Why "optionally" (*vā*)? [Counter-example: *viṣvagañcī*. (5.2.110) *samaḥ samiḥ*: [The substitute] *sami* is used for *sama*.
When the suffix *añc* follows the prefix *sam*, it is replaced by *samyā*. Thus: *samyaṅ*, *samyañcau*, *samyañcaḥ*; *samīcaḥ*, *samīcā*.
According to Pāṇini 5.2.111, when the suffix *añc* follows the prefix *saha*, it is replaced by *sadhrī*. Thus: *sadhryaṅ*, *sadhryañcau*, *sadhryañcaḥ*; *sadhrīcaḥ*, *sadhrīcā*.

*tiras* becomes *tiri* before *añcat*, when followed by a suffix beginning with a vowel other than *a*. Thus: *tiryaṅ*, *tiryañcau*, *tiryañcaḥ*. Why does it say "before a vowel" (*ati*)? [To exclude forms like] *tiraścaḥ* and *tiraścā*. [Furthermore,] for a word ending in *dvi*, *anta*, or *prādi*, the *ap* [of *apa*] becomes *īt* [before a case-ending beginning with a consonant]. (5.2.113)

The substitution of *ī* for the final vowel of the word *āp* occurs after the two words beginning with *anta-* and after those beginning with *pra-*, provided they do not end in the vowel *a*. Examples: *dvīpaḥ*, *antarīpaḥ*; *samīpaḥ*, *nīpaḥ*. Why does it say "not ending in *a*" (*anāt*)? [To exclude cases such as] *prāpam*, *parāpam*.
Regarding the rule *anūpo deśe* (Pāṇini 5.2.114):
when the word *deśa* ("region") is to be expressed, *anūpa* is an irregularly formed (*nipātita*) term. Otherwise, it is *anvīpaḥ*.

(5.2.115) *samāpa* [is formed] when it is a name (*saṃjñā*). *Samāpa* is prescribed as an irregular form (*nipātana*) when it is a name. "Samāpa" is the name of a sacrificial ground (*devayajana*). Any other [form] is *samīpa*.
(5.2.116) When the suffix *cha* is applied, *duK* is substituted for the other [element].
The augment *dug* is added to another [word] when followed by a case-ending (*kāraka*). Examples: *anyadīyaḥ*, *anyatkārakaḥ*.

In the rule *aṣaṣṭhītṛtīyasyāśīrāśāsthāsthitotsukotirāgeṣu* (Pāṇini 5.4.117), the augment *dug* is added to another word that does not end in the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) or the instrumental (*tṛtīyā*), when followed by *āśis*, *āśā*, *sthā*, *sthita*, *utsuka*, *ūti*, or *rāga*. Examples: *anyā āśīḥ* → *anyadāśīḥ*; *anyadāśā*; *anyadāsthā*; *anyadāsthitaḥ*; *anyadutsukaḥ*; *anyadūtiḥ*; *anyadrāgaḥ*. Why specify "not ending in the genitive or instrumental"? Consider: *anyasyāśīḥ* → *anyāśīḥ* (genitive); *anyenāsthitaḥ* → *anyāsthitaḥ* (instrumental).

*Arthe vā* (5.2.118): When *artha* follows, the augment *duk* is optionally inserted before another word. Examples: *anyadarthaḥ* or *anyārthaḥ*. *Koḥ kad acy uttarārthe* (5.2.119): The substitute *kad* is used for *ku* when followed by a vowel (*ac*) in the sense of "other."

When the word *ku* occurs as a prior member (*pūrvapada*) signifying the meaning of the subsequent member (*uttarapadārtha*), it undergoes the substitution of *kad* before a subsequent member beginning with a vowel (*aj-ādi*). Examples: *kad-uṣṭraḥ* ("a bad camel"), *kadaśvaḥ* ("a bad horse"). Why is it specified "before a vowel"? Observe: *kubrāhmaṇaḥ* ("a bad Brahmin"). Why is it said "for the sake of the subsequent rule"? Observe: *kūṣṭro rājā* ("King Kūṣṭra").

Regarding the rule *trirathavadeṣu* (Pāṇini 5.3.120): when *tri* and so forth follow, the substitution of *kad* for *ku* occurs. Examples: *kutsitās trayaḥ* ("three that are contemptible") becomes *kat-trayaḥ*; *kadrathaḥ* ("a bad chariot"); *kadvadaḥ* ("one who speaks badly").

(5.2.121) *tṛṇe jātau*: When *tṛṇa* follows, the substitute *kad* is applied to *ku* when "birth" (*jāti*) is to be expressed. Example: *kattṛṇam*. Why is it said "when [denoting] a genus"? [Consider: *kutṛṇāni*, meaning "wicked grasses. (5.2.122) *kākṣapathoḥ*.
In the words *akṣa* and *pathin*, the substitute *kā* occurs for *ku* when it follows [another word]. Thus: *kākṣaḥ*, *kāpathaḥ*.
Regarding the sense of "slight" (*īṣadartha*), the substitute *kā* occurs for *ku* when it expresses a slight degree. Thus: *kāmadhuram*, *kālavaṇam*, *kāmlam*.

*Puruṣe vā* (5.2.124): When *puruṣa* is the subsequent member [of a compound], the substitution of *kā-* for *ku-* optionally occurs. *Kāpuruṣaḥ*, *kupuruṣaḥ*. This is an optional rule where [otherwise] there would have been no application. However, when used in the sense of "slight," it always occurs by the preceding rule: *īṣatpuruṣaḥ*, *kāpuruṣaḥ*. *Kavaṃ coṣṇe* (5.2.125).

In the word *uṣṇa*, the substitute *kava* occurs after *ku*, and the substitute *kā* optionally occurs as well. Thus: *kavoṣṇam*, *koṣṇam*, *kaduṣṇam*. According to Pāṇini 5.2.126, the substitute *tāra* optionally occurs for *tīra* following a word denoting a direction. Thus: *dakṣiṇatāram*, *dakṣiṇatīram*; *uttaratāram*, *uttaratīram*.

*pṛṣodarādīni* (5.2.127): Words such as *pṛṣodara* and others are correct forms. *pṛṣad udaraṃ asya* [he has speckled bellies], *pṛṣodaraḥ*; *pṛṣad udvānaṃ asya* [he has speckled openings], *pṛṣodvānaḥ*—a cloud; *balāhakaḥ*; *jīvanasya mūtaḥ* [a bundle of life], *jīmūtaḥ*; *śavasya śayanam* [the resting place of the corpse], *śmaśānam*; *ūrdhvaṃ khaṃ asya* [its opening is upward], *udūkhalam* or *ulūkhalaṃ* [a mortar]; *piśitaṃ aśnāti iti piśācaḥ* [he eats flesh, thus a flesh-eater]; *bruvantaḥ asyāṃ sīdanti iti bṛsī* [those speaking sit upon it, thus a seat/mat]; *mahyāṃ rauti iti mayūraḥ* [he cries on the earth, thus a peacock]; *mahyāṃ śete* [he sleeps on the earth], *mahiṣaḥ* [a buffalo]; *ṣaṭ ca daśa* [six and ten].

And: *ṣoḍaśa*—it is offered with difficulty, *dūḍāśaḥ*; it is destroyed with difficulty, *dūṇāśaḥ*; it is deceived with difficulty, *dūḍabhaḥ*; he meditates wickedly, thus *dūḍhyaḥ*; the offspring of *Vāgvāda*, *Vāḍvaliḥ*; heaven is their dwelling, thus *divaukasaḥ*. In this manner, other words such as *kapittha*, *dadhittha*, *aśvattha*, *mahittha*, and so forth, are to be understood from the usage of the learned (*śiṣṭa*).

[The four types of phonetic modification are: the addition of a sound (*varṇāgama*), the transposition of sounds (*varṇaviparyaya*), and two others: the modification of sounds (*varṇavikāra*) and the elision of sounds (*varṇalopa*).
The connection of a nominal stem with a meaning exceeding its own [primary] sense—this is the fivefold etymological derivation (*nirukta*). [Furthermore, there is the rule:
"In place of *ahar-* following a numeral or *vi-* and *sa-* etc., *ahan* optionally replaces it before the locative case-ending *ṅi*. (Pāṇini 5.4.91).

When the word *ahan* follows a numeral, *vi*, *sāya*, or similar [prefix], the substitute *ahan* optionally occurs before the locative case ending *ṅi*. Examples: In the two days (*dvayor ahnoḥ*): *dvyahni*, *dvyahani*, *dvyahne*. In the departed day (*vigata ahani*): *vyahni*, *vyahani*, *vyahne*. *Sāyāhni*, *sāyāhani*, *sāyāhne*. Why "after a numeral, *vi*, *sāya*, or similar"? Observe: *pūrvāhṇe*, *aparāhṇe*. Why "before the locative ending *ṅi*"? Observe: *dvyahnaḥ*, *vyahnaḥ*, *sāyāhnaḥ*. (5.2.129) There is lengthening of the vowel of *viśva* before *vasu* and *rāṭ*.

The long vowel is substituted for *viśva* when it precedes the words *vasu* and *rājan* as final members of a compound. Examples: *viśvāvasuḥ*, *viśvārāṭ*. Because of the specific mention of *rāṭ* [with the short vowel], this substitution does not apply here: *viśvarājau*, *viśvarājaḥ*.

In the case of *nara* when it forms a name (*saṃjñā*), the long vowel is substituted for *viśva* when *nara* follows. Example: *viśvānaraḥ*. Why "when it is a name"? Consider: *viśvanaraḥ* [which is not a proper name].

(5.2.131) *ṛṣau mitre*: When *mitra* follows, the long vowel [is substituted] for the final vowel of *viśva* if it denotes a sage (*ṛṣi*). Example: *Viśvāmitraḥ*. Why "if it denotes a sage"? Example: *Viśvamitro māṇavakaḥ* ("The boy Viśvamitra"). Only when it is a name: *Viśvamitro muniḥ* ("The sage Viśvamitra").

(5.2.132) *vanagiryoḥ koṭarāñjanādīnām*: [The long vowel is substituted for the final vowel of the first member] before *vana* and *giri*, provided they belong to the class beginning with *koṭara* and *añjana*.

In the case of *vana* ("forest") and *giri* ("mountain"), [the final vowel] becomes long when preceded by *koṭara* and so forth, or *añjana* and so forth. Examples: *koṭarāvaṇam*, *miśrakāvaṇam*, *sidhrakāvaṇam*; *añjanāgiriḥ*, *bhañjanāgiriḥ*, *kiṃśukāgiriḥ*. Why "of *koṭara*, *añjana*, and so forth"? [Counter-examples: *kuberavanam*, *asipattravanam*, *kṛṣṇagiriḥ*. Only when it is a name (*nāmni*): *añjanagiriḥ*.
[This applies also to the suffix] *-mat* after words with more than two syllables, excluding *anjira* and so forth (Pāṇini 5.2.137).

In the case of a word ending in *matau* (the suffix *matup*), a long vowel occurs for a stem consisting of more than two syllables, provided it is not one of the *ajira*-group. Examples: *udumbarāvatī*, *vīraṇāvatī*. Why say "consisting of more than two syllables"? [Counter-example: *vrīhimatī*. Why say "not of the *ajira*-group"? [Counter-examples: *ajiravatī*, *khadiravatī*. This applies only when it is a proper name (*nāman*): [Counter-example: *valayavatī*. The *ajira*-group consists of: *ajira*, *khadira*, *pulina*, *malaya*, *kāraṇḍava*, *cakravāka*. [The rule] *śarādīnām* (Pāṇini 5.2.134) [is also relevant].

A long vowel occurs before the suffix *mat* following words such as *śara* and others. For example: *Śarāvatī*, *Vaṃśāvatī*. Only when it is a name [does this apply]; otherwise, it is *śaravatī*. The list includes: *śara*, *vaṃśa*, *dhūma*, *ahi*, *kapi*, *maṇi*, *muni*, *śuci*. This is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open class). Before the suffix *vala* (Pāṇini 5.2.135), a long vowel occurs. For example: *kṛṣīvalaḥ*, *āsutīvalaḥ*, *dantāvalaḥ*.
*ciḥ kapi* (5.2.136): When the suffix *kap* follows, the long vowel [ā] occurs in place of the word *citi*. Examples: *ekacitīkaḥ*, *dvicitīkaḥ*.
*ḍhralope ’ṇaḥ* (5.2.137): [The long vowel occurs] when there is elision of *ḍha* or *ra*, provided that the elided element was not preceded by the suffix *aṇ*.

In a word where there is the elision (*lopa*) of the letters *ḍha* and *ra*, a long vowel takes the place of the preceding *aṇ*. Examples: *līḍham*, *gūḍham*; *nīraktam*, *dūraktam*. Why specify *aṇ*? [Because in] *āvṛḍham*, the rule does not apply. Regarding *sahivahor ot* (Pāṇini 6.3.112): when *ḍha* and *ra* are elided after the roots *sah* and *vah*, the substitution of *o* for the final vowel of the *aṇ* occurs. Examples: *soḍhā*, *voḍhā*; *soḍhum*, *voḍhum*; *udavoḍhām*, *udavoḍham*. How is *ūḍham* explained? It is due to the indicative mark (*liṅga*) found in rules such as *prād ūḍha* (Pāṇini 5.1.89).

(5.2.139) *Karṇe cihnasyāviṣṭāṣṭapañcabhinnacchinnacchidrasruvasvastikasya*: When the word *karṇa* follows, the final vowel of a word denoting a mark (*cihna*) becomes long, provided that the mark is not one of those beginning with *viṣṭa*. Examples: *dātrākarṇaḥ*, *dviguṇākarṇaḥ*, *dvyaṅgulākarṇaḥ*. Why does it say "of a mark"? [Counter-example: *śobhanakarṇaḥ*. Why does it say "excluding those beginning with *viṣṭa*"? [Counter-examples: *viṣṭakarṇaḥ*, *aṣṭakarṇaḥ*, *pañcakarṇaḥ*, *bhinnakarṇaḥ*, *chinnakarṇaḥ*, *chidrakarṇaḥ*, *sruvakarṇaḥ*, *svastikakarṇaḥ*. (5.2.140) *Nahivṛtivṛṣivyadhirucisahitaniṣu kvau*: [The final vowel of the preceding word becomes long] before the suffix *kvip* when it follows the roots *nah*, *vṛt*, *vṛṣ*, *vyadh*, *ruc*, *sah*, and *ni*.

The long vowel does not occur before words ending in *kvip* such as *naha* and others: *upānat*, *nīvṛt*, *prāvṛt*, *marmāvit*, *nīruk*, *ṛṭīṣaṭ*, *parītat*. Regarding the elision of the nasal in *gam* and other roots by the rule *gamādīnāṃ kvau* (Pāṇini 6.4.40), why is *kvau* specified? [Because in other cases, as in] *upanaddham*, the nasal is not elided.
Furthermore, regarding the rule *prādīnāṃ ghañi bahulam* (Pāṇini 6.2.141): [the long vowel is optionally applied].

A long vowel is frequently substituted for the short vowels *i*, *u*, and *ṛ* when followed by a suffix ending in *ghañ*. Because one enters into this, it is *pratīveśaḥ* or *prativeśaḥ*. Awakening is *pratībodhaḥ* or *pratibodhaḥ*. They ward off or make known by means of this, thus it is *pratīhāraḥ* or *pratihāraḥ*. They counteract by means of that, thus it is *pratīkāraḥ* or *pratikāraḥ*. In some cases, there is a difference in meaning: *prakāraḥ* or *prākāraḥ*; *prasādaḥ* or *prāsādaḥ*. In some cases, it does not occur: *niṣādaḥ*, *viṣādaḥ*.
In some cases, it certainly does occur: *nīvāraḥ*, *nīhāraḥ*, *nīśāraḥ*. [The rule] *ikaḥ kāśe* (Pāṇini 6.3.124) [applies].

A long vowel occurs before the suffix *kāśa* when it follows a stem ending in *ik*. Examples: *nīkāśaḥ*, *vīkāśaḥ*, *anūkāśaḥ*, *pratīkāśaḥ*. Why is *ika* specified? [To exclude cases like] *prakāśaḥ*. By the rule *bahulam* ("variously"), we have *nikāśaḥ* and *vikāśaḥ*. This rule is formulated for the sake of the meaning "not old" (*ajara*). By the rule *das ti* (Pāṇini 6.1.143), when the substitute *t* takes the place of the root *dā* (in the sense of giving), a long vowel occurs for prefixes ending in *ik* before that *t*. Examples: *nīttam*, *parīttam*, *vīttam*. Why is *ti* specified? [To exclude cases like] *sudattam*. By the rule *ika* alone, we have *prattam* and *avattam*.

(5.2.144) *vahe*: A long vowel is substituted for a stem ending in an *ik* vowel when followed by the suffix *vaha*. Examples: *ṛṣīvahaḥ*, *kapīvahaḥ*, *kṛṣīvahaḥ*. Only when [the stem ends in] an *ik* vowel: *piṇḍavahaḥ*. Only according to the rule *bahulam* (diversely): *pīluvahaḥ*, *cāruvahaḥ*. (5.2.145) *anyeṣām api*: [A long vowel is substituted] even for others [not mentioned].

The long vowel also frequently occurs in other words when followed by a subsequent member (*uttarapada*). For example: *śvādantaḥ*, *śvādaṃṣṭraḥ*, *śvākarṇaḥ*. In some cases it does not occur: *Śvaphalkaḥ*, *śvamukhaḥ*. In some instances, even when the context is different: *śvapadam*, *śvāpadam*. In some cases, even when not followed by a subsequent member: *puruṣaḥ*, *pūruṣaḥ*. According to Pāṇini 6.3.138 (*cau*), when the suffix *añcu* has its vowel elided (*luptākāra*) and follows [the preceding word], a long vowel occurs. For example: *dadhīcaḥ*, *dadhīcā*; *madhūcaḥ*, *madhūcā*.

*yaṇa ikaḥ* (5.2.147): In place of a *yaṇ*, when an *ik* follows, a long vowel occurs before the second member of the compound (*uttarapada*). Examples: *Kārīṣagandhīputraḥ*, *Kaumudagandhīpatiḥ*. Why "in place of a *yaṇ*" (*yaṇaḥ*)? [Consider: *bhūmipatiḥ*.
The second quarter of the fifth chapter is completed.
Regarding *prakṛteḥ* (5.3.1):
from this point forward, it should be understood that the term *prakṛteḥ* is the governing heading (*adhikṛta*).

A long vowel is substituted for the final *iK* of a base that ends in a *yaṇ* which follows a consonant (*hal*) that is part of the base itself. Examples: *hūtaḥ*, *jīnaḥ*, *saṃvītaḥ*. The phrase "of the base" (*prakṛteḥ*) is specified [in the rule] precisely for this purpose: [otherwise, in cases like] *nirutam*, *durutam*, the substitution would not apply. Why is there a rule regarding the inclusion of what ends in that (*tadantavidhiḥ*)? [To explain: in *viddhaḥ* and *vicitaḥ*, the substitution does not occur. How is *tṛtīyaḥ* formed? It is due to the irregular formation (*nipātana*) in the rule *dvitīyatṛtīyau* (Pāṇini 5.3.59). Regarding the rule *aluki* (5.3.3), it should be understood that whatever is stated [therein] applies when there is no elision (*aluk*).

(5.3.4) *nāmi atisṛcatasroḥ*: When followed by a *nām* [suffix], a long vowel occurs for a base (*prakṛti*), with the exception of *tisṛ* and *catasṛ*. Examples: *vṛkṣāṇām*, *agnīnām*, *vāyūnām*, *kartṝṇām*. Why is there a mention of *nuṭ* [in the rule]? It is for the sake of ensuring the application of the long vowel once *nuṭ* has been applied; otherwise, there would be an absence of *nuṭ*. Why "with the exception of *tisṛ* and *catasṛ*"? [Examples: *tisṛṇām*, *catasṛṇām*. [The phrase] "when there is no elision" (*aluki*) applies as well: *tālavanam*, *pīluvanam*. [The phrase] "for a base" (*prakṛteḥ*) applies as well: *kṛmiṇām paśya*, *pāmanām paśya*. This is not a base when followed by a *nām* suffix. (5.3.5) *nur vā*: [A long vowel optionally occurs] after *nu*.
The vowel of the word *nṛ* becomes long optionally before a *nām* ending. Thus: *nṛṇām* or *nṛṇām*. [Pāṇini 6.4.3] states:

"After a base ending in *n*, a long vowel occurs before a *nām* ending. Thus: *pañcānām*, *saptānām*. Only when it is a *nām* ending [does this apply]; otherwise, as in *carmaṇām*, there is no lengthening.

(5.3.7) *śisuṭi*: When *śi* or *suṭ* follows, a long vowel occurs for a base ending in *n*. Examples: *sāmāni*, *vemāni*; *kuṇḍāni*, *vanāni*. Here, the status of being a base ending in *n* is established even when the *num* augment is present, based on the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in Pāṇini 1.1.35: *sukhādīni*. Examples: *rājānau*, *rājānaḥ*, *rājānam*, *rājānau*. A short vowel occurs as the counterpart to the long vowel, and by the force of the explicit statement (*vacanasāmarthya*), intervention [by an augment] is admitted. Only when there is no elision (*aluki*): *rājaprāptaḥ*. (5.3.8) *smahator numi*: [The rule applies] when *num* follows *sm* or *matup*.

When *num* is inserted after a word ending in *s* and after *mahat* before the nominative plural (*śas*) or before the suffix *su*, a long vowel is substituted for the preceding [vowel] when it is followed by a heavy syllable (*bahrati*). Examples: *śreyāṃsi*, *mahānti*; *śreyāṃsau*, *mahāntau*. Why specify "when *num* is inserted"? Consider *apsarasaḥ*. [This is governed by] Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.4.11: *aptṛsvasṛnaptṛneṣṭṛtvaṣṭṛkṣattṛhotṛpotṛpraśāstṝṇām*.

The long vowel [ā] occurs for the word *āp* ending in *tṛc*, as well as for those ending in *tṛn*, and for *svasṛ* and the others, when followed by the nominative plural (*śas*) or the suffix *suṭ*. Examples: *āpaḥ*; *kartṝṇi*; *kartāraṃ kaṭān*, *vaktāraṃ janāpavādān*; *svasāram*, *naptāram*, *neṣṭāram*, *tvaṣṭāram*, *kṣattāram*, *hotāram*, *potāram*, *praśāstāram*. Because of the specific mention of *naptṛ* and the others, this does not apply to other words ending in *tṛ* that are proper nouns: *mātaram*, *pitaram*, *jāmātaram*, *duhitaram*, *bhrātaram*.
[This rule applies] in the nominative singular (*sāu*), except in the vocative (*asaṃbuddhau*). (Pāṇini 6.4.11–13).

That which is the lengthening [of the vowel] occurs only when there is not a vocative (*asaṃbodhana*). For example: *rājā*, *śreyān*, *mahān*, *kartā*, *svasā*, *naptā*, *neṣṭā*, *tvaṣṭā*, *kṣattā*, *hotā*, *potā*, *praśāstā*. It does not occur in the vocative (*saṃbuddhau*): *he rājan*, *he śreyan*, *he mahan*, *he kartaḥ*. [This is governed by the rule] *atvasoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.11).

The long vowel occurs for a stem ending in *at* and one ending in *as*, before a case-ending with the marker *s*, except in the vocative singular. For example: *bhavān*, *kṛtavān*, *gomān*. The marker *p* attached to the suffix *matup* belongs to that suffix itself, not to the word *atu*; thus, this rule also applies here. Regarding the ending in *as*: *apsarāḥ*, *sumanāḥ*. How is it that *carmavaḥ* (meaning "he who wears leather") is formed? Because of its association with *atus*, only a non-verbal root (*adhātu*) is understood [here]. The restriction "except in the vocative singular" remains in force: *he bhavan*, *he sumanaḥ*. And regarding *in*, *han*, *pūṣan*, and *aryaman*: [the long vowel occurs] also before the nominative plural ending *śas* (Pāṇini 6.4.12).

In the case of *inan* and [stems ending in] *han*, etc., the long vowel occurs only before the suffix *su* when it is not the vocative singular (*asaṃbuddhau*). Examples: *daṇḍīni*, *daṇḍī*; *bhrūṇahāni*, *bhrūṇahā*; *bahupūṣāṇi*, *Pūṣā*; *bahvaryamāṇi*, *Aryamā*. Why is it specified "before *su*"? [Observe: *daṇḍinau*, *daṇḍinaḥ*; *Vṛtrahaṇam*, *Pūṣaṇam*, *Aryamaṇam*. Why "not in the vocative singular" (*asaṃbuddhau*)? [Observe: *he daṇḍin*, *he Vṛtrahan*, *he Pūṣan*, *he Aryaman*. Precisely because of this restrictive rule (*niyama*), there is no lengthening even in subsequent cases: *bhrūṇahani*. Because of the restriction regarding the lengthening of the penultimate vowel: *vṛtrahāyate*. [This is governed by the rule: *ajjhanoḥ sani jhali* (Pāṇini 7.2.13).

A long vowel is substituted for a root ending in *a* and for the root *han*, when followed by the suffix *san* provided it begins with a *jhal* consonant. For example: *cikīrṣati*, *tuṣṭūṣati*, *cicīṣati*; [and] *jighāṃsati*. Why specify "when preceded by a *jhal*"? Consider: *yiyaviṣati*. Why specify "of the base" (*prakṛteḥ*)? Consider: *dadhi sanoti*. [Regarding the rule] *iṅo gamaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.14): a long vowel is substituted for the substitute *gam* of the root *iṅ* when followed by *san* beginning with a *jhal* consonant. For example: *adhijigāṃsate vedam*. Why specify "*iṅo*"? Consider: *saṃjigaṃsate*.

*tano vā* (5.3.15): After the root *tan*, when followed by the suffix *san* beginning with a *jhal* consonant, a long vowel optionally occurs. Thus: *titāṃsati* or *titaṃsati*. Only when a *jhal* follows [is this rule applied]: *titaniṣati*. *kramas tvi* (5.3.16).
However, the vowel following *kram* optionally becomes long. Examples: *krāntvā*, *krantvā*. Only when a *jhal* suffix follows: *kramitvā*, *prakramya*. Regarding *ñamaḥ kiti vau ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.17):

after a stem ending in a *ñ* or *m*, a vowel optionally becomes long before a suffix beginning with a *kit* that has a *jhal* sound, as well as before the suffix *vuṇ*. Examples: *praśān*, *pratān*; *śāntaḥ*, *śāntavān*. Why "ending in *ñ* or *m*"? Consider *odanapak* ("rice-cooker"). Why "before a *kit* suffix"? Consider *gantā* ("one who goes"). Why "and before *vuṇ*"? Consider *gamyate* ("is gone").

*Ñami ca cchavoḥ śūṭh* (Pāṇini 6.4.19): When *ñam* follows, as well as when a suffix beginning with *jhal* follows, the substitution of *ś* occurs for the letter *ch*, and *ūṭh* occurs for the letter *v*. Examples: *viśnaḥ*, *praśnaḥ*; *prāṭ*; *pṛṣṭaḥ*, *praṣṭā*, *praṣṭum*. *syonam*; *akṣadyūḥ*; *dudyūṣati*, *dyūtvā*, *dyūtam*. How is it that [the forms] *dyubhyām* and *dyubhiḥ* occur? Once *ūṭh* has been applied, by the rule *diva ut* (Pāṇini 6.1.131), because of the marker *t* [indicating the short vowel], the duration will be one mātrā. Why say "when *ñam* follows"? [Observe: *devitvā*.
How is it countered? Because the elision (*al-lopa*) is *asiddha* (non-existent for the purposes of subsequent rules), [the substitution] will not occur.

Regarding *jvara-tvara-avaśrava-vamāṃ sopāntasya* (Pāṇini 6.4.20): for the roots *jvara*, *tvara*, *avaśrava*, and *vam*, when the letter *v* together with its preceding vowel is followed by *v* or by an affix beginning with a *jhal* consonant, *ūṭh* is substituted. Examples: *jūḥ*, *jūrau*, *jūrtiḥ*; *tūḥ*, *tūrau*, *tūrtiḥ*, *tūrṇavān*; *ūḥ*, *uvau*, *ūtiḥ*; *śrūḥ*, *śruvau*, *śrūtiḥ*; *mūḥ*, *muvaḥ*, *mūtiḥ*.
*rāl lopaḥ* (5.3.20):

When *jhal*-beginning [suffixes] follow, there is elision (*lopa*) of the *ch* and *v* that follow a *repha* (*r*). Examples: from *mūrchā*, we have *mūḥ*, *murau*, *mūrtiḥ*; from *dhurvī*, we have *dhūḥ*, *dhurau*, *dhūrtiḥ*. [The rule applies] only when *v* follows: *mūrchā*.

*prāg yuvor avugyug asiddhaṃ samānāśraye* (5.3.21): Before the suffixes *yu* and *vu*, the operations involving *avu* and *yuk* are considered non-existent (*asiddha*) when they share the same basis (*samānāśraya*).

Prior to the mention of the suffix *vuñ* (Pāṇini 5.4.1), an operation characterized by *vuk* or *yuk* should be understood as *asiddha* (non-existent) when another operation dependent on the same locus (*samānāśraya*) is to be applied. In *edhi* and *śādhi*: because the substitution of *e* for *i* and the substitution of *śā* for *śās* are *asiddha*, the substitution of *dh* conditioned by a *jhal* consonant takes place. In *jahi*: because the substitution of *ja* for *han* is *asiddha*, the elision (*luk*) of the suffix *hi* does not occur. In these cases, there is a common locus (*samānāśrayatva*) because both operations occur within that same context. Furthermore, the rule here is one characterized by a common locus; it is not a prohibition characterized by different loci (*vyāśraya*).

Why [is it specified] "before *yu*"? [Consider] *abhāji*, *rāgaḥ*. When the substitution of *ā* is to be applied, the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) is already established. Why [is it specified] "*avu* and *yuk*"? [Consider] *babhūvatuḥ*, *upadidīye*. Because the *vuk* and *yuk* augmentations are established, the substitutions of *u* and *vyaṇ* do not occur. Why [is it specified] "having a common locus" (*samānāśraya*)? [Consider] *papuṣaḥ*, *cicyuṣaḥ*, *luluvuṣaḥ*. In the case of *vasuḥ* [ending in *-uṣ-*, the substitution of] *ud* before case-endings, when the elision of *ā*, the substitution of *yaṇ*, and the substitution of *u* are to be applied, [the former] is not considered non-established (*asiddha*). Precisely because of this statement, the paribhāṣā regarding "external" (*bahiraṅga*) operations is not resorted to here, since an external operation has an internal operation as its cause. [The rule] *śnān naḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.30).

The *nakāra* of a subsequent [element] is elided. As in *bhanakti* and *vyanakti*. Why [is it] *śakāra*? [Because in] *prayatnānām* and *praśnānām*, due to being technical (*lākṣaṇika*) and meaningless (*anarthaka*), it does not occur. [This is governed by] Pāṇini 6.4.24: *halo ’niditaḥ kṅity upāntasya*.

When a suffix beginning with *k* or *ṅ* follows, there is elision of the penultimate *n* of a verbal root (*prakṛti*) that ends in a consonant (*halantā*) and does not have an indicatory *i* (*anidita*).
