Examples: *srastaḥ*, *srasyate*; *dhvastaḥ*, *dhvasyate*; *sanīsrasyate*, *danīdhvasyate*. Why say "ending in a consonant" (*hala*)? Observe: *nīyate*. Why say "not having an indicatory *i*" (*anidita*)? Observe: *nandyate*. Why say "when *k* or *ṅ* follows" (*kṅiti*)? Observe: *sraṃsitā*. Why say "penultimate" (*upāntasya*)? Observe: *nahyate*. [This rule applies] except before a suffix marked with *ś* or *ap* (Pāṇini 5.3.24).

The *n* at the penultimate position of a root that does not have an indicatory letter *i* (*anidita*) is elided when followed by an affix marked with *ap*. Examples: *dabhnoti*, *mathnāti*, *śrathnāti*, *grathnāti*. Why "when followed by an affix marked with *ap*"? Consider *sraṃsate* and *dhvaṃsate*. Why "of a root that does not have an indicatory *i*"? Consider *śiñjānaḥ*. Regarding Pāṇini 6.4.125, *liṭīndhiśranthagranthām*:

the *n* of the roots *indh* and others is elided when followed by the *liṭ* suffix. Examples: *samīdhe*; *śrethatuḥ*, *śrethuḥ*; *grethatuḥ*, *grethuḥ*. Why "of these [roots]"? Consider *sasraṃse*. Why "when followed by an affix marked with *ap*"? Consider *śaśrantha*.
*dambheḥ sani ca* (5.3.26):

When *san* beginning with *s*, and when *liṭ* follow, provided they are not marked with *apit*, there is elision of the *n* of the root *dambh*. Examples: *dhīpsati*, *dambhituḥ*, *dambhuḥ*. Why is it specified as having two *s*s (*dvisakāra*)? [To exclude cases like: *didhambiṣati*. *svañjaḥ* (5.3.27).

The elision of *n* occurs when the suffix *liṭ* follows the root *svañj*. [Thus we have] *pariṣasvaje*. By the rule *sadi-svañjer liṭi* (Pāṇini 6.1.98), there is a prohibition of the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*. When the suffix *śap* follows, by the rule *daṃśa-sañjeś ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.28), the elision of *n* occurs after the roots *daṃś*, *sañj*, and *svañj*. [Examples: *daśati*, *sajati*, *pariṣvajate*.

*rañjaḥ* (5.3.29): When *śap* follows, there is elision of the *n* of the root *rañj*. Thus, *rajati*. How is it that [the words] *rajanam*, *rajatam*, and *rajaḥ* [are formed]? These are derived from the *uṇādi* suffixes. For instance: *rajaḥ* is formed with the suffix *kyun*; *rajatam* is formed with the suffix *atac* according to the rule *pṛṣirañjibhyāṃ kit*; and *rajaḥ* is formed with the suffix *asun* according to the rule *uṣirañjibhyāṃ kit*. *ṇau mṛgaramaṇe* (5.3.30).

When the suffix *ṇic* follows, if the sense of "pleasing deer" (*mṛgaramaṇa*) is understood, the *n* of the root *rañj* is elided. Example: *rañjayati mṛgān* ("he pleases the deer"). Here, due to the designation *mit*, the vowel is shortened. Why "if the sense of pleasing deer"? Example: *rañjayati vastrāṇi* ("he dyes the clothes"). How is the form *rāgī* established? It is established by the suffix *ini*. Regarding the rule *ghañi bhāvakaraṇayoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.27):

when the suffix *ghañ* follows in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*) or an instrument (*karaṇa*), the *n* of *rañj* is elided. Examples: *rañjanam* ("the act of pleasing/dyeing"); *rāgaḥ* ("color/attachment"), derived from "that by which one is dyed. Why "in the sense of an abstract state or an instrument"? Example: *raṅgaḥ* ("stage/theater"), derived from "they color themselves therein."

*syada* is a *ghañ*-derived form of the root *syand*, prescribed as a *nipātana* when "speed" (*java*) is to be expressed; otherwise, one has *tailasyandaḥ*. [The rule] *avoda-aidha-udma-praśratha-himaśrathaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.3.33).

*Avoda* is an irregular form (*nipātana*) derived from *und* with the suffix *ghañ*; *edha* is from the root *indh*; *odman* is from *und* with the suffix *manin*; *praśratha* is from *śranth* preceded by *pra* with the suffix *ghañ*; and *himaśratha* is from [the same root] preceded by *hima*.
[The rule] *laṅgikampyor upatāpaśarīravikārayoḥ* (Pāṇini 5.3.34) applies.

The elision of the *n* occurs in the sense of "limping" (*laṅgi*), "trembling" (*kampe*), "affliction" (*upatāpe*), and "bodily transformation" (*śarīravikāra*). Thus, *vilagitaḥ* ("limped") and *vikapitaḥ* ("transformed"). In other cases, it is *vilaṅgitaḥ* ("missed") and *vikampitaḥ* ("shaken"). It should not be stated that [the elision of the nasal] does not occur after the root *vṛh* before a suffix beginning with a vowel (*aci*) that lacks the augment *iṭ*. This is established by the root *vṛh* itself: *nivarhati* ("he uproots") and *nivarhakaḥ* ("one who uproots"). Furthermore, [the form with the nasal] is seen even when an *iṭ*-augment follows a consonant-initial suffix: *nivṛhyate* ("it is uprooted") and *nivarhitā* ("one who has uprooted"). However, from the root *vṛṃh*, we have *nivṛṃhati*, *nivṛṃhakaḥ*, *nivṛṃhyate*, and *nivṛṃhitā*. According to Pāṇini 6.4.24 (*tanādibhyas tathāsoḥ*), for roots beginning with *tan* that lack the augment *iṭ*, the substitution of *ñam* occurs before the suffix *lyap*. (5.3.35)

The *ñam* (the nasal *m*) of the roots beginning with *tan*, as well as of *van*, is elided when followed by the suffix *lyap*, provided they are *aniṭ* (not taking the augment *iṭ*). Examples: *pratatya*, *prakṛtya*; *prahatya*, *pramatya*; *pravatya*. Why "of these"? [Counter-example: *praśasya*. Why "when followed by *lyap*"? [Counter-example: *yamyate*, *ramyate*. *m vā* (Pāṇini 6.4.37): When followed by *lyap*, the *m* of the roots beginning with *tan*, those that are *aniṭ*, and *van*, is optionally elided. Examples: *prayatya*, *prayamya*; *viratya*, *viramya*; *praṇatya*, *praṇamya*; *āgatya*, *āgamya*.

*Jhali tiṅy apiti* (Pāṇini 6.4.103): When a *tiṅ* suffix beginning with a *jhal* consonant follows that is not marked with *p*, there is the elision of the *ñakāra* of roots belonging to the *tanādi* group which lack an *iṭ* augment. Examples: *hataḥ*, *hathaḥ*. Why does it say "when a *jhal* [consonant] follows"? Consider: *ghnanti*. Why does it say "in a *tiṅ* [suffix]"? Consider: *hantā*. Why does it say "not marked with *p*" (*apiti*)? Consider: *hanti*. *Kṅiti* (Pāṇini 6.4.104): [The elision of the *ñakāra* occurs] when a suffix marked with *k* or *ṅ* follows.

When a suffix beginning with a *jhal* consonant follows an affix marked with *ṅ* or *k*, there is the elision (*lopa*) of the *ñam* (the nasal of the *tanādi* group) provided that the root does not take the augment *iṭ*. Thus: *tataḥ*, *tatavān*; *kṣataḥ*, *kṣatavān*; *yataḥ*, *yatavān*; *rataḥ*, *ratavān*. [Note: The suffix *vati* occurs with the suffix *ktin*; however, he will state an exception for *ktic* (Pāṇ. 5.3.43), and elsewhere the augment *iṭ* must apply. Only when a *jhal* consonant follows: *hanyate*, *gamyate*. Only for roots of the *tanādi* group that do not take *iṭ*: *śāntaḥ*, *śāntavān*; *dāntaḥ*, *dāntavān*. Only when *ñam* follows: *pakvaḥ*. [The rule] *janasanakhanām āt* (Pāṇ. 5.3.39) applies.

When a *jhal* consonant or a *kṅit* suffix follows, the letters *ñ*, *m*, or *ṇ* are substituted for the final letter of the roots *jan* and others. Examples: *jātaḥ*, *jātavān*; *sātaḥ*, *sātavān*; *khātaḥ*, *khātavān*. The restriction "when a *kṅit* suffix follows" applies only here: *jantuḥ*. The restriction "when a *jhal* consonant follows" applies only here: *janitvā*. Regarding the *san* affix (Pāṇini 5.3.40): when the *san* affix beginning with a *jhal* consonant follows, the letters *ñ*, *m*, or *ṇ* are substituted for the final letter of *jan* and others. Example: *siṣāsati*. [Note: An augment *iṭ* must be applied to *jan* and *khan*. The restriction "when a *jhal* consonant follows" applies only here: *sisaniṣati*.

*Ye vā* (Pāṇini 6.1.41): When *ya* follows, the vowels of the roots *jan* and others optionally undergo *āt*-vṛddhi. Thus: *jāyate*, *janyate*; *jājāyate*, *jañjanyate*. *Sāyate*, *sanyate*; *sāsāyate*, *saṃsanyate*. *Khāyate*, *khanyate*; *cākhāyate*, *caṅkhanyate*. *Tano yaki* (Pāṇini 6.4.42): [The vowel of the root *tan* undergoes *āt*-vṛddhi] before the suffix *yak*.
The substitution of *ā* for the vowel of the root *tan-* optionally occurs before the suffix *yaK*. Thus, we have *tāyate* or *tanyate*.

Regarding the rule *sanaḥ ktici lopaś ca* (Pāṇini 5.3.43): before the suffix *ktiC*, there is optionally both the elision (*lopa*) of the *san* suffix and the substitution of *ā* for its vowel. Thus, we have *satiḥ*, *sātiḥ*, or *santiḥ*.

(5.3.44) *liṅi taṅi gamaḥ*: When followed by a *liṅ* suffix that is *taṅ*-bhūta, the elision (*lopa*) of the root *gam* optionally occurs. Examples: *saṃgasīṣṭa*, *saṃgaṃsīṣṭa*. Why "when there is *liṅ*"? Example: *saṃjagme*. Why "when it is *taṅ*-bhūta"? Example: *gamyāt*. (5.3.45) *sici*: [The elision of the root *gam* optionally occurs when followed by the *sic* suffix.]
When *sic* follows with *taṅ* suffixes, there is optionally an elision (*lopa*) of the root *gam*. Thus: *samagata*, *samagaṃsta*.
Regarding *hana*: (Pāṇini 5.3.46) after the root *han*, there is an obligatory elision when *sic* follows, due to the separation of the rule (*yogavibhāga*). Thus: *āhata*, *āhasātām*.

*Yamaḥ sūcane* (Pāṇini 5.3.47): When the root *yam* is used in the sense of "hinting" (*sūcana*), its elision occurs before the suffix *sic* when followed by an affix marked with *taṅ*. Examples: *udāyata*, *udāyasātām*. Why "in the sense of hinting"? [Counter-example: *āyaṃsta pādam* ("he stretched out his foot"). Even though the condition *jhali tiṅi api* (before a *jhal*-ending *tiṅ*) would otherwise apply, it does not occur here because of the intervention of *sic*. Only when *taṅ* follows: [Counter-example: *ayaṃsīt*. *Vodvāhe* (Pāṇini 5.3.48).

When the suffix *sic* followed by the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) endings follows the root *yam*, its penultimate vowel is optionally elided when it is in the sense of marriage (*udvāha*). Examples: *upāyata kanyām* or *upāyaṃsta kanyām*.
Regarding the rule *gamādīnāṃ kvau* (Pāṇini 6.4.40):

when the suffix *kvip* follows roots such as *gam* and others, their penultimate vowel is elided. Examples: *janagat*, *saṃyat*, *parītat*. How is the form *agregūḥ* explained? It will be derived from the *uṇādi* suffix *ḍū*.

*nāñcaḥ pūjāyām* (5.3.50): When the sense of "reverence" (*pūjā*) is understood, there is no elision of the *n* of the root *añc*. Example: *añcitam iva śiro vahati* ("he carries his head as if bent in reverence"). Why say "when reverence is expressed"? Observe: *udaktam udakaṃ kūpāt* ("the water has been drawn up from the well"). *ktici dīrghaś ca* (5.3.51).

When *ktic* follows, the elision of *n* and the lengthening [of the vowel] do not occur: *tantiḥ*, *rantiḥ*, *vantiḥ*. Because *ktic* is prescribed for the purpose of forming names (*saṃjñā*), words such as *sañjā* are not employed [with this suffix]. How then are *saktiḥ* and *bhaktiḥ* formed? They are established by means of *ktin*. Or rather, the prohibition of elision applies when there is the possibility of lengthening. Regarding *ktvi* [the rule] "after *skand* and *syand*" (Pāṇini 6.4.31): when *ktvā* follows, the elision of *n* does not occur after *skand* and *syand*. Thus: *skantvā*, *syantvā*.
(5.3.53) *seṭi*: When a suffix marked with *seṭ* follows, the elision of *na* does not take place. Examples: *sraṃsitvā*, *dhvaṃsitvā*, *syanditvā*.
(5.3.54) *vañci-luñci-thapho vā*: [The elision of *na*] is optional when *ktvā* follows the roots *vañci*, *luñci*, and those ending in *tha* or *pha*.

The elision of *n* does not optionally occur before the suffix *seṭ* following roots ending in *vañc*, *luñc*, *śranth*, *granth*, and *gumph*. Thus: *vañcitvā* or *vacitvā*; *luñcitvā* or *lucitvā*; *śranthitvā* or *śrathitvā*; *granthitvā* or *grathitvā*; *gumphitvā* or *guphitvā*.

By the rule *janaśaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.34), the elision of *n* optionally occurs before the suffix *ktvā* following roots ending in *j* and the root *naś*. Thus: *bhaṅktvā* or *bhaktvā*; *naṃṣṭvā* or *naṣṭvā*. The separation of the sūtra (*yogavibhāga*) is for the sake of excluding roots that do not take the augment *iṭ*.
*bhañjeś ciṇi* (5.3.56): When *ciṇ* follows, the elision of the nasal (*n*) of the root *bhañj* is optional. Thus, *abhāji* or *abhañji*.
*śāsaḥ kṅiti śis* (5.3.57): [The substitute *śis* is applied] for *śās* before suffixes marked with *k* or *ṅ*.

The root *śās* undergoes the substitution of *śis* when followed by an affix marked with *k* or *ṅ*. Examples: *śiṣṭaḥ*, *anvaśiṣat*, *śeśiṣyate*, *mitraśīḥ*, *āśīḥ*. Why specify "when followed by an affix marked with *k* or *ṅ*"? [Observe: *śāstā*. When followed by a *tiṅ* affix beginning with a consonant (*hal*) and not having *i* as its *it*, the root *śās* undergoes the substitution of *śis*. Examples: *tau śiṣṭaḥ*, *vayaṃ śiṣmaḥ*. Why specify "when followed by a *tiṅ* affix"? [Observe: *śāstram*. Why specify "beginning with a consonant"? [Observe: *śaśāsatuḥ*. Why specify "not having *i* as its *it*"? [Observe: *śāsti*.
(5.3.59) *śā hau*: The substitution of *śā* occurs for *śās* when followed by *hi*. [Thus: *śādhi*. (5.3.60) *hano jaḥ*: [The substitution of *ja* occurs for *han* when followed by *hi*.]

The substitute *jha* occurs in place of *han* when followed by *parasmaipada*. [The rule] "In the *liṭ*, the *āśīr-liṅ*, and after that which is not a verbal suffix (*atiṅ*) ending in *śit*" (Pāṇini 5.3.61) should be understood as being the governing context (*adhikāra*) for this. *Jahi*.

*bhrasjo bharj vā* (5.3.62): In the *liṅ* and other [suffixes], the substitute *bharj* optionally occurs for the root *bhrasj*. Thus, *babharja* or *babhrajja*; *bharkṣīṣṭa* or *bhrakṣīṣṭa*; *bharṣṭā* or *bhraṣṭā*. How is it that [forms such as] *bhṛjjyāt*, *bhṛṣṭaḥ*, and *barībhṛjjyate* occur? [They occur] by virtue of a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*), or because the form *bhrasj* is taken as the basis [for the rule]. Furthermore, in the case of *pūrva* [in *babharja*], the *yaṇ* replacement takes precedence due to a prior conflict (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*). *lopo 'taḥ* (5.3.63).

The elision of the final *a* of a verbal root (*prakṛti*) occurs when followed by the suffixes beginning with *liṭ*. For example: *cikīrṣāñcakāra*, *lolūyāñcakre*; *cikīrṣyāt*; *cikīrṣitā*. Because the rule for elision is more powerful, the vowel *ā* does not occur [in place of the elided *a*]. Examples: *cikīrṣakaḥ*, *cikīrṣyate*. Only when followed by *liṭ* and so forth: *cikīrṣati*.

Regarding the rule for *yak* (Pāṇini 6.4.64): when *yak* follows, the elision of the final *a* of the root occurs. Examples: *kusubhyati*, *magadhyati*. Why is the letter *k* [in the technical term *yak*] used? [To prevent the rule from applying in cases like: *śyenāyate*.

*yasya halaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.3.65): There is elision of *ya* that follows a consonant (*hal*) when the periphrastic perfect (*liṭ*), etc., occurs. Examples: *bebhidāṃcakre*, *bebhidīṣīṣṭa*, *bebhiditā*. Why [specify] "akāra" (the vowel 'a')? [To exclude cases like] *īrṣyitā*, *madhyitā*. Why [specify] "hal" (consonant)? [To exclude cases like] *lolūyitā*. Alternatively, there is elision of the *ya* prescribed after a verbal root ending in a consonant (*halanta*). Why [specify] "ending in a consonant"? [To exclude cases like] *īrṣyitā*, *madhyitā*. What, then, is the difference between these two interpretations of the sūtra? When the former [interpretation] is adopted, then forms such as *sosūtritā* and *śāśayitā* ought to occur.

When there is another [suffix], then it should be stated as *sosūtritā* or *śāśayyitā*. This applies only in the case of the *liṅ* and other such suffixes: *bebhidyate*. Regarding the rule *kyasya vā* (Pāṇini 6.4.50):

after a consonant (*hal*), the elision (*lopa*) of the *ky* suffix occurs optionally before the *liṅ* and other such suffixes. Examples: *samidhāṃcakāra*, *samidhyāṃcakāra*; *dṛṣadāṃcakre*, *dṛṣadyāṃcakre*; *samidhiṣīṣṭa*, *samidhyiṣīṣṭa*; *samidhitā*, *samidhyitā*. Only when following a consonant (*hal*) does this apply: *paṭīyitā*, *paṭāyitā*. Some desire the optional elision of the *yak* suffix as well: *bhiṣajyitā*, *bhiṣajitā*. That, however, is purposeless, because the form is already established by means of either *kyac* or *kyaṅ*.
*ṇer aniṭi* (Pāṇini 6.4.51):

When an affix beginning with *liṭ* that does not take the augment *iṭ* follows, there is elision (*lopa*) of the *ṇi*-affix. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rules concerning *iyyaṇ*, *adeṅ*, *ādaij*, and lengthening (*dīrgha*). Examples: *atatakṣat*, *āṭīṭat*, *kāraṇā*, *kārakaḥ*, *kāryate*. Why "when it does not take *iṭ*"? Consider *kārayitā*. Only when following *liṭ* etc.: *kārayati*. *tatau ca tasya* (Pāṇini 6.4.52).

The elision of the *ṇi* suffix occurs before the *kta* and *ktavatu* suffixes when they follow a root beginning with *iṭ*. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rules for *iy*, *yaṇ*, *eṅ*, *āT*, *aiC*, and long vowels. Examples: *atatakṣat*, *āṭiṭat*, *kāraṇā*, *kārakaḥ*, *kāryate*. Why specify "when not followed by *iṭ*"? Consider *kārayitā*. The rule applies only in the context of the *liṅ* and other such suffixes: *kārayati*. [The substitution of] *ay* occurs before the suffixes *ām*, *āluc*, *āyya*, *itnu*, and *uṣ*: (Pāṇini 6.1.89).

The suffix *ṇi* is elided when followed by the *kta* and *ktavatu* suffixes provided they begin with the augment *iṭ*. Examples: *kāritam*, *kāritavān*; *hāritam*, *hāritavān*. Why specify "when *iṭ* follows"? [It is] so that the elision of *ṇi* occurs once *iṭ* has been applied. Otherwise, if the elision were to occur first, the rule *ekāca upadeśe 'nudāttāt* (Pāṇini 7.2.10) would prevent the application of *iṭ*. Example: *saṃjñapitaḥ paśuḥ* ("the animal was slaughtered"). By virtue of the inclusion of the term "*iṭ*" [in the rule], the elision does not occur even by the preceding rule (*ṇer aniṭi*). The augment *iṭ* is optional according to the rule *sanīvantardhabhr̥hr̥sramr̥dr̥pr̥kāpājabhLārśubharajñapisanām* (Pāṇini 7.2.49), because of the prohibition in *vibhāṣāpader* (Pāṇini 7.2.61). [Also relevant is the rule] *lyapi laghoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.56).

Furthermore, when *lyap* follows, there is the substitution of *ay* for the *ṇi* suffix that follows a light vowel (*laghu*). Examples: *praśamayya gataḥ*, *prabebhidayya gataḥ*, *pragaṇayya gataḥ*. By the force of the explicit statement [in the rule], separation [by other elements] is admitted. Because the elision of *y* (*yalopa*) and the elision of *a* (*allopa*) depend on different bases, they do not possess the status of being "unestablished" (*asiddhatva*). [Specifically,] the elisions of *y* and *a* occur within the *ṇi* suffix, whereas the substitution of *ay* for *ṇi* occurs when *lyap* follows. Why specify "light" (*laghoḥ*)? Consider: *pratipādya gataḥ*. Or, according to Pāṇini 5.3.71, *āpo vā*: when *lyap* follows, there is optionally the substitution of *ay* for the *ṇi* suffix that follows *āp*. Examples: *prāpayya gataḥ*, *prāpya gataḥ*. The form *adhyāpya* does not occur [with this substitution] because it is derived from a technical grammatical term (*lākṣaṇikatvāt*).
(5.3.72) *kṣeḥ kṣīḥ*: After the root *kṣi*, when the suffix *lyap* follows, the change to *kṣī* occurs. Examples: *prakṣīya*, *upakṣīya*.

(5.3.73) *upadeśe’jjhanagrahadṛgbhyaḥ syasicsīyuṭtāsāṃ bhāvāpyayoś ciṇvad iṭ vā*: In the context of expressing the abstract action (*bhāva*) or the passive (*apya*), after roots taught [in the Dhātupāṭha] that end in vowels other than *a*, or those containing *han*, *grah*, or *dṛś*, the augment *iṭ* is optionally applied like the *ciṇ* augment to the affixes *sya*, *sic*, *sīyuṭ*, and *tās*.

In the *upadeśa* (the original grammatical instruction), the augment *iṭ* optionally applies before the *syādi* suffixes following roots ending in vowels as well as *han* and others, provided they do not have a passive or reflexive sense (*bhāvāpyaviṣaya*). Examples: *cāyiṣyate*, *ceṣyate*; *dāyiṣyate*, *dāsyate*; *śamiṣyate*, *śāmiṣyate*, *śamayiṣyate*; *ghāniṣyate*, *haniṣyate*; *grāhiṣyate*, *grahīṣyate*; *darśiṣyate*, *drakṣyate*. Aorist examples: *acāyiṣātām*, *aceṣātām*; *adāyiṣātām*, *adiṣātām*; *aśamiṣātām*, *aśāmiṣātām*, *aśamayiṣātām*; *aghāniṣātām*, *avadhiṣātām*.

*agrāhiṣātām*, *agrahīṣātām*; *adarśiṣātām*, *adṛkṣātām*. *cāyiṣīṣṭa*, *ceṣīṣṭa*; *dāyiṣīṣṭa*, *dāsīṣṭa*; *śamiṣīṣṭa*, *śāmiṣīṣṭa*, *śamayiṣīṣṭa*; *ghāniṣīṣṭa*, *vadhiṣīṣṭa*; *grāhiṣīṣṭa*, *grahīṣīṣṭa*; *darśiṣīṣṭa*, *dṛkṣīṣṭa*. *cāyitā*, *cetā*; *dāyitā*, *dātā*; *śamitā*, *śāmitā*, *śamayitā*; *ghānitā*, *hantā*; *grāhitā*, *grahītā*; *darśitā*, *draṣṭā*. Why is it said "in the original instruction" (*upadeśe*)? [Because in the case of] *kāriṣyate*, [the substitution does not apply].

What is the purpose of [the rule] "after roots ending in a long vowel, after *grah*, and after those ending in a root with a penultimate *ṛ*"? [The example is: *paṭhiṣyate*. What is the purpose of [the rule] "for *sy*, *sic*, *sīyuṭ*, and *tās*"? [The example is: *cetavyam*. What is the purpose of [the rule] "in the sense of becoming (*bhāva*) and attaining (*āpya*)"? [The example is: *ceṣyati*. Because of the substitution of *ciṇvadi* (as if it were *ciṇ*), the grammatical operations dependent on *ciṇ* take place, but those dependent on *luṅ* do not. Therefore, the substitutes for *han*, *iṇ*, and *ṅi* do not occur: *aghāniṣātām*, *āyiṣātām*, *adhyāyiṣātām*. Regarding [the rule] *dīṅo liṭi yuk* (Pāṇini 6.4.63):
the augment *yuk* is applied to the root *dīṅ* when *liṭ* follows. [Examples: *upadidīye*, *upadidīyāte*. Why specify "when *liṭ* follows"? [Counter-example: *upadedīyate*.
*lopo ’ci kṅiti cātaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.64):

When an affix beginning with a vowel (*aj-ādi*) follows, or when an affix marked with *k* or *ṅ* (*kṅit*) follows, there is elision (*lopa*) of the final *ā* of a verbal base (*prakṛti*). Examples: *godah* ("cow-giver"), *kambaladah* ("blanket-giver"); *saṃsthā* ("standing together"), *avasthā* ("state"). [In the perfect tense: *yayau*, *yayatuḥ*, *yayuḥ*; *yayitha*. Why "when an affix beginning with a vowel"? Witness *dīyate*. Why "when an affix marked with *k* or *ṅ*"? Witness *dānam*. *īd yati* (Pāṇini 6.4.65).

When a suffix beginning with *ya* follows, the substitution of *ī* for the final vowel (*ā*) occurs. Examples: *gleiyam*, *mleiyam*, *deyam*, *dheyam*, *heyam*. Regarding Pāṇini 5.3.77, *mā-sthā-sā-gā-piba-hā-dā-dhām hali*:

when a suffix beginning with a consonant (*hal*) that has the markers *k* or *ṅ* follows, the substitution of *ī* occurs for the vowels *mā* and the others. Examples: *mīyate*, *memīyate*; *sthīyate*, *teṣṭhīyate*; *avasīyate*, *avaseṣīyate*; *gīyate*, *jegīyate*; *pīyate*, *pepīyate*; *hīyate*, *jehīyate*; *dīyate*, *dedīyate*; *dhīyate*, *dedhīyate*. Why is *piba* mentioned? [To exclude forms like] *pāyate*. Why is the letter *k* used [in the rule]? [To exclude forms like] *hāyate*. Why is it said "when a consonant follows" (*hali*)? [To exclude forms like] *godah*. It must be specified "when a suffix marked with *k* or *ṅ* follows" (*kṅiti*): as in *dātā*.

(5.3.78) When *liṅ* follows, *e* is substituted for the initial vowel of roots beginning with *m*. Thus: *meyāt*, *stheyāt*, *avaseyāt*, *geyāt*, *peyāt*, *heyāt*, *deyāt*, *dheyāt*. This applies only when a *kṅit* suffix follows: *dāsīṣṭa*.
(5.3.79) Optionally, [the substitution of *e* occurs] for a root beginning with a conjunct consonant, except for *sthā*.

After a verbal root beginning with a conjunct consonant and ending in /ā/, provided it is not *sthā*, the augment /e/ optionally occurs before the suffix *liṅ*. Examples: *gleyāt* or *glāyāt*; *mleyāt* or *mlāyāt*. Why "beginning with a conjunct" (*saṃyogādeḥ*)? [Counter-example: *yāyāt*. Why "not *sthā*" (*astha*)? [Counter-example: *stheyāt*. The rule applies only when a suffix marked with *k* or *ṅ* follows (*kṅiti*): [Counter-example: *glāsīṣṭa*. The rule applies only in the *āśīr-liṅ* (the benedictive mood): [Counter-example: *mlāyet*. The rule applies only to a "verbal root" (*prakṛteḥ*): [Counter-example: *niryāyāt*. Regarding *na lyapi* (Pāṇini 6.4.69): that which was prescribed for roots beginning with *m* and others does not take place when the suffix *lyap* follows. Examples: *pramāya*, *prasthāya*, *avasāya*, *pragāya*, *prapāya*, *prahāya*, *pradāya*, *pradhāya*.
*meṅa id vā* (5.3.81): When *lyap* follows, the substitution of *it* for *meṅ* optionally occurs. Examples: *apamitya*, *apamāya*.
*luṅlaṅlṛṅkṣv aḍ amāṅyoge* (5.3.82): The augment *aṭ* is applied before the suffixes *luṅ*, *laṅ*, and *lṛṅ*, except when there is connection with *ām* or *mā*.

The augment *aṭ* is added to the root (*prakṛti*) when followed by the suffixes beginning with *luṅ*, provided that there is no connection with the particle *māṅ*. Examples: *akārṣīt*, *akarot*, *akariṣyat*. Why "provided there is no connection with *māṅ*"? [Counter-examples: *mā bhavān kārṣīt*; *mā sma karot*. [Why] "to the root" (*prakṛteḥ*)? [Counter-example: *prākarot*.

[Furthermore, regarding the rule] *aci śnudhātubhruvāṃ yvor iyuvau* (Pāṇini 6.4.77): [the vowels *i* and *u* are substituted for the semivowels *y* and *v* respectively, when they follow the suffixes *śnu*, verbal roots, or the word *bhrū*, before a vowel-initial suffix].

When a vowel (*ac*) follows, *i* and *u* are replaced by *iy* and *uv*, provided that these [vowels] belong to the suffixes *śnu*, verbal roots, or the word *bhrū*. Examples: *āpnuvanti*; *cikṣiyatuḥ*, *cikṣiyuḥ*; *luluvatuḥ*, *luluvuḥ*; *śriyau*, *śriyaḥ*; *bhruvau*, *bhruvaḥ*. Why does it say "when a vowel follows" (*aci*)? Consider *prāpnuyāt*. Why does it say "belonging to *śnu*, verbal roots, or *bhrū*" (*śnudhātubhrūvām*)? Consider *lakṣmyau*, *lakṣmyaḥ*. Why does it say "*y* and *v*" (*yv-*)? Consider *cakratuḥ*, *cakruḥ*. The phrase "of the base" (*prakṛteḥ*) is understood from the previous rule: as in *śryarthaḥ*.
[This applies] when there is reduplication, except for the first [syllable] in the case of *asam* (5.3.84).

When reduplication occurs, *iy* and *uv* are substituted for the *i*-vowel and *u*-vowel of the preceding [syllable] when followed by a non-homogeneous vowel (*aci*). Examples: *iyeṣa*, *uvoṣa*, *iyarti*. Why "non-homogeneous" (*asama*)? [Counter-examples: *ījatuḥ*, *ījuḥ*; *ūṣatuḥ*, *ūṣuḥ*. Only when followed by a vowel (*aci*): *iyāja*, *uvāca*. [From Pāṇini 6.4.79: *striyāḥ*:
The substitution of *iy* occurs for the *i*-vowel of the word *strī* when followed by a vowel (*aci*). Examples: *striyau*, *striyaḥ*. Only when followed by a vowel (*aci*): *strībhiḥ*.
(5.3.86) *vāmśasoḥ*: Before the endings *ām* and *śas*, the substitution of *iy* optionally occurs for the *i*-vowel of a feminine stem. [Examples: *striyam*, *strīm*; *striyaḥ*, *strīḥ*.
(5.3.87) *iṇo yaṇ*: [The substitution of] *yaṇ* occurs [in place of] *iṇ*.

The substitution of *yaṇ* occurs for the root *iṇ* when followed by a vowel (*ac*). [Examples: *yanti*, *yantu*. This is an exception to [the rule for] *i*. (5.3.88) *er asaṃyogād anekācaḥ*: When followed by a vowel, the substitution of *yaṇ* occurs for a root consisting of more than one syllable (*anekāc*) that ends in the vowel *i* (*eṅ*), provided that this *i* is not preceded by a conjunct consonant (*asaṃyoga*). [Examples: *ninyatuḥ*, *ninyuḥ*. Why does it say "ending in *i*" (*er*)? [Counter-example: *luluvatuḥ*, *luluvuḥ*. Why does it say "not preceded by a conjunct consonant" (*asaṃyogāt*)? [Counter-example: *cikriyatuḥ*, *cikriyuḥ*. Why does it say "consisting of more than one syllable" (*anekācaḥ*)? [Counter-example: *adhīyāte*.
Pāṇini 6.1.78 (*kārakāsaṃkhyād oś ca supy asudhiyaḥ*):

After a *kāraka* (agentive case) or after a word that is not a numeral, when followed by a *sup* suffix beginning with a vowel other than *su*, the *yaṇ* substitution occurs for the final *i*-vowel or *u*-vowel of the base, provided the base is not *sudhī*. This applies unless the *i*-vowel or *u*-vowel follows a *saṃyoga* (consonant cluster). Examples: *grāmaṇy-au*, *grāmaṇyaḥ*; *unnya-au*, *unnya-aḥ*; *khalapv-au*, *khalapva-aḥ*; *sakṛllv-au*, *sakṛllva-aḥ*. Why specify "after a *kāraka* or a non-numeral"? Consider: *paramaniy-au*, *paramaniya-aḥ*; *paramaluv-au*, *paramaluva-aḥ*; *niy-au*, *niya-aḥ*; *luv-au*, *luva-aḥ*. (In these cases, the substitution does not apply because the preceding words are not *kārakas*.)

What is the purpose of [specifying] *supi*? [Consider: *upaluluvuḥ*. What is the purpose of [specifying] *asudhiyaḥ*? [Consider: *sudhiyau*, *sudhiyaḥ*. [The rule applies] only when [the stem] does not end in a consonant cluster (*asaṃyogāt*): [consider] *yavakriyau*, *yavakriyaḥ*; *kaṭapruvau*, *kaṭapruvaḥ*. (5.3.90) *varṣādṛnpunaḥkārād bhuvaḥ*: After the word *bhu-* following *varṣa-* and the others, *yaṇ* substitution occurs before a case-ending beginning with a vowel (*aj-ādi*) that follows a nominal suffix (*sup*). [Examples: *varṣābhvau*, *varṣābhvaḥ*; *dṛnbhvau*, *dṛnbhvaḥ*; *punarbhvau*, *punarbhvaḥ*; *kārabhvau*, *kārabhvaḥ*. Why [specify] "after *varṣa-* and the others"? [Consider: *ātmabhuvau*, *ātmabhuvaḥ*; *pratibhuvau*, *pratibhuvaḥ*.

*Huśnuvor aliṭi* (5.3.91): After *hu* and *śnu*, when followed by a vowel beginning with *a*—excluding the *liṭ* (perfect)—the *yaṇ* substitution occurs. Examples: *juhvati*, *juhvatu*, *juhvat*; *sunvanti*, *cinvanti*. Why "after *hu* and *śnu*"? Consider *yuvanti*, *ruvanti*. Why "excluding the *liṭ*"? Consider *juhuvatuḥ*, *juhuvuḥ*. Only if [the root] does not end in a conjunct consonant: *āpnuvanti*, *rādhnuvanti*. *Bhuvo vug luṅliṭoḥ* (5.3.92).

The augment *vuk* is applied before the *luṅ* and *liṭ* suffixes when they begin with a vowel following the root *bhū*. [Examples: *abhūvan*, *babhūva*, *babhūvatuḥ*, *babhūvuḥ*. Regarding *ūṭ* for *guh* before a vowel (Pāṇini 6.4.89): the substitute *ūṭ* is applied to the vowel of the root *guh* (*goher*) when followed by a suffix beginning with a vowel.

[Examples: *nigūhayati*, *nigūhakaḥ*. Why is there a mention of the phoneme *o* (*okāra*)? [To show that it applies] to *nijuguhatuḥ*, *nijuguhuḥ*. Why does it say "of the vowel" (*aca*)? So that it does not apply to the final consonant. It says "before a vowel" (*aci*) specifically: [example] *nigoḍhā*.

When the suffix *ṇi* follows the root *duṣ*, the vowel *a* is replaced by *ū*. Example: *dūṣayati*. Why specify "when *ṇi* follows"? [Because otherwise it would apply to the noun: *doṣaḥ*. *vā citte* (5.3.95): [The substitution of *ū* for the vowel of *duṣ*] is optional when the mind (*citta*) is the object.

In the case of the root *duṣ* when preceded by the word *citta*, the substitution of *ū* for the vowel *a* optionally occurs before the suffix *ṇic*. Thus, one says either *cittaṃ dūṣayati* or *cittaṃ doṣayati*. By the very mention of *citta*, the mental factors (*caitasika*) are also included; therefore, one says *prajñāṃ doṣayati* or *prajñāṃ dūṣayati*.
[Furthermore, regarding the rule] *gamajanakhanaghasāṃ le lopo ’piti* (Pāṇini 6.4.98): [the *n* of these roots is elided before the suffix *liṭ* when it does not have *ap* as its *it*].

When a substitute for *l* (the *liṭ* suffixes) beginning with a vowel follows, there is elision of the vowel of roots such as *gam* and others, provided that the substitute is not marked with *p*. Examples: *jagmatuḥ*, *jagmuḥ*, *jagmivān*; *jajñatuḥ*, *jajñuḥ*, *jajñe*, *jajñāte*, *jajñire*; *cakhnatuḥ*, *cakhnuḥ*; *jakṣatuḥ*, *jakṣuḥ*, *jakṣivān*. Why "when a substitute for *l*" (*la*)? Witness: *agamat*. Why "not marked with *p*" (*apiti*)? Witness: *jagāma*. Regarding the rule *kiti ca hanaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.98): when a substitute for *l* (*liṭ*) marked with *k* follows, or when a substitute for *l* (*luṅ*, *liṭ*, etc. beginning with a vowel and not marked with *p* follows, there is elision of the vowel of the root *han*. Examples: *jāyāghnaḥ*, *nighnaḥ*, *vighnaḥ*; *jaghnatuḥ*, *jaghnuḥ*, *jaghnivān*. The restriction "beginning with a vowel" (*aci*) applies here as well: *hataḥ*, *hathaḥ*.

*hujhalbhyo ’niṭo her dhiḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.101): After the root *hu-* and after a verbal base ending in a *jhal* consonant, the substitute *dhi* occurs in place of the *hi* augment that does not take the *iṭ* augment. Examples: *juhudhi*, *bhinddhi*, *chinddhi*. Why say *hujhalaḥ*? [Consider: *krīṇīhi*. Why say *aniṭaḥ*? [Consider: *rudihi*, *svapihi*. Why say *heḥ*? [Consider: *juhotu*. In *juhutāt* and *bhinttāt*, the substitution *tātaṅ* applies because it is antaranga (internal); furthermore, there is no substitution of *dhi* for that *tātaṅ*, because the rule for *dhi* depends upon the form *hi*. *ato luk* (Pāṇini 6.4.102). [The *hi* suffix is elided after a short *a*.]

Therefore, *her* is elided after [the vowel] *ataḥ*. [Examples: *paca*, *paṭha*. Why say *ataḥ*? [Counter-example: *ehi*. Why say *taparaḥ*? [Counter-example: *yāhi*. (5.3.100) *uto 'saṃyogād adhātoḥ*:

After an *ukāra* (*u*) that is not part of a conjunct consonant and is not a verbal root, *her* is elided. [Examples: *kuru*, *cinu*. Why say *uta*? [Counter-examples: *lunīhi*, *punīhi*. Why say *asaṃyogāt*? [Counter-examples: *āpnuhi*, *śaknuhi*. Why say *adhātoḥ*? [Counter-examples: *yuhi*, *ruhi*.

*vāsya vmoḥ* (Pāṇini 5.3.101): Before the suffixes *vas* and *mas*, there is optionally the elision (*luk*) of the *u* of *as* when it follows a non-conjunct consonant and is not part of a verbal root (*adhātu*). Examples: *tanvaḥ*, *tanuvaḥ*; *tanmaḥ*, *tanumaḥ*. *sunvaḥ*, *sunuvaḥ*; *sunmaḥ*, *sunumaḥ*. The restriction "after a non-conjunct" (*asaṃyogāt*) is necessary: *śaknuvaḥ*, *śaknumaḥ*. The restriction "not part of a verbal root" (*adhātoḥ*) is necessary: *yuvaḥ*, *yumaḥ*. *kṛño ye ca* (Pāṇini 5.3.102).
The *u* of the root *kṛ* is elided when followed by *uta* or *ya*, as well as when followed by *mo*. Thus: *kuryāt*, *kuryātām*; *kurvaḥ*, *kurmaḥ*.

According to Pāṇini 6.4.103 (*ata ut tatrāpi*), the *u* of *kṛ* becomes *ū* before *uta* that is not marked with the *pit* designation; however, it does not become *ū* when the following *uta* is marked with *pit*. Examples: *kurutaḥ*, *kurvanti*, *kurvan*. The vowel *u* in the rule is specified as short (*tapara*) for the purpose of excluding cases where *eṅ* follows. Why is *tatra* used [in the rule]? Consider *kartā*. Why is *apiti* used? Consider *karoti*, *karoṣi*. Regarding the phrase "and when followed by *ya*": consider *kuryāt*. In the forms *kurvaḥ* and *kurmaḥ*, the substitution of *ū* takes place because the elision of *u* is considered non-existent (*asiddha*).

*Śnasor lopaḥ* (5.3.104): When an *apit* suffix follows, there is elision (*lopa*) of the *a* of both the *śnam* augment and the root *as*. [Examples: *runddhaḥ*, *rundhanti*; *staḥ*, *santi*. Only when it is *apit*: *ruṇaddhi*, *asti*. *Śnādviruktayor ātaḥ* (5.3.105).

The *ā* of the verbal root [ending in] *śna* or of a reduplicated stem is elided when followed by the affix *ap*. Examples: *lunate*, *lunatām*; *punate*, *punatām*; *mimate*, *mimatām*; *saṃjihate*, *saṃjihatām*. Why "of *śna* or a reduplicated stem"? Observe: *yānti*, *vānti*. Why "of *ā*" (*ātaḥ*)? Observe: *bibhrati*. Why "only when *ap* follows" (*apiti*)? Observe: *alunām*, *ajahām*.
[Furthermore, the rule] *ī hali tiṅy adādhaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.106) applies.

The vowel *i* is substituted for the long *ā* of a reduplicated root—excluding those belonging to the *dā* and *dhā* groups—when followed by a suffix beginning with a consonant (*hal*) and marked with *ap*. Examples: *lunītaḥ*, *punītaḥ*; *mimīte*, *saṃjihīte*. Why is it said "when a consonant follows" (*halīti*)? Observe: *lunanti*, *punanti*; *mimate*. Why is it said "in a *tiṅ* suffix" (*tiṅīti*)? Observe: *saṃjihāsate*. Why is it said "excluding *dā* and *dhā*" (*adādha iti*)? Observe: *dattaḥ*, *dhattaḥ*. The substitution applies only when the suffix is marked with *ap*: observe *lunāti*, *jahāti*. The vowel *i* is substituted for the final vowel of the root *daridra* before a suffix beginning with a consonant and marked with *ap* (Pāṇini 5.3.107).

When a suffix beginning with a consonant (*hal*) follows the root *daridrā*, and an affix marked with *P* or *K* (*apit*) follows a verbal suffix (*tiṅ*), the vowel *i* is substituted [for the final *ā*]. Examples: *daridritaḥ*, *daridrithaḥ*. Only when a consonant follows: *daridrati*. Only when a verbal suffix follows: *didaridrāsati*. Only when an *apit* affix follows: *daridrāti*. *bhiyo vā* (5.3.108):

When a suffix beginning with a consonant follows the root *bhī* (to fear), and an *apit* affix follows a verbal suffix, the vowel *i* is optionally substituted [for the final *ī*]. Examples: *bibhitaḥ*, *bibhītaḥ*; *bibhithaḥ*, *bibhīthaḥ*. Only when a consonant follows: *bibhyati*. Only when a verbal suffix follows: *bibhīṣati*, *bhītaḥ*. Only when an *apit* affix follows: *bibheti*.

*hākaḥ* (5.3.109): After the root *hā-* (to abandon), when followed by a consonant (*hal*) and an affix beginning with *ap* that is a *tiṅ*, the vowel *i* optionally occurs. Thus: *jahitaḥ* or *jahītaḥ*; *jahithaḥ* or *jahīthaḥ*. Only when followed by a consonant: *jahati*. Only when it is a *tiṅ*: *jihāsati*. Only when the affix begins with *ap*: *jahāti*. *hau vā* (5.3.110).
After the root *jahāti*, the substitution of *it* or *īt* optionally occurs. Thus: *jahihi*, *jahīhi*, *jahāhi*.

By the rule *yi lopaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.111), when a *tiṅ* suffix beginning with *y* follows, the elision (*lopa*) of [the *ā* of] *jahāti* occurs. Thus: *jahyāt*, *jahyātām*. Only when a *tiṅ* follows [does this apply]; otherwise, as in *hīyate*. How is [the form] *heyāt* derived? It is because the rule *liṅy ed* (Pāṇini 6.4.69) takes precedence due to its lack of any other scope (*anavakāśatvāt*).

*daridraḥ kiti* (5.3.112): When a *kit* suffix beginning with the letter *y* follows, there is elision of the root *daridrāti*. Thus: *daridryate*, *daridryāt*. Why "when a *kit* [suffix]"? Consider: *daridrāyāt*. *acy ayuvau* (5.3.113).

The elision of the root *daridrā-* occurs when followed by suffixes beginning with a vowel other than *y* or *v*. Thus: *daridrati*, *adaridran*; *daridritā*, *daridritum*; *didaridriṣati*; *daridraḥ*. Even before the suffix *ṇa* (*ana*), the augment *yuk* does not occur, because the rule for elision is more powerful. Why say "before a vowel" (*aci*)? Consider *didaridrāsati*. Why say "other than *y* or *v*" (*ayuvau*)? Consider *daridrāṇam*, *daridrāyakaḥ*. Only when the suffix is marked as *apit* (not having *p* as an it-marker): *adaridrām*. Regarding the rule *luṅi vā* (Pāṇini 6.4.114): before the *luṅ* (aorist) suffix, the elision of *daridrā-* is optional. Thus: *adaridrīt*, *adaridrāsīt*.

(5.3.115) *aster dādhaś ca hau pare ed bhavati, dviḥprayogaś ca na bhavati.* After the root *as* and after *dadh*, when followed by the suffix *hi*, the vowel *e* occurs, and there is no reduplication. [Examples: *edhi*, *dehi*, *dhehi*.

(5.3.116) *liṭy anādeśāder ekahalmadhye 'taḥ.* In the *liṭ* tense, for a root that does not begin with a substitute [consonant] and which has a single consonant between [the initial and final consonants], the *at* [of the reduplicated syllable] is elided.

When the *liṭ* suffix follows, the substitution of *et* (the change to *e*) occurs for the vowel *a* situated between two single *hal* consonants that do not belong to a verbal root beginning with a substitute [consonant], and there is no doubling [of the following consonant]. Examples: *reṇatuḥ*, *reṇuḥ*; *yematuḥ*, *yemuḥ*. Why "when *liṭ* follows"? [Consider: *yaṃyamyate*. Why "not beginning with a substitute"? [Consider: *babhaṇatuḥ*, *babhaṇuḥ*. Why is this a qualification of the substitute of *liṭ*? [Consider: *nematuḥ*, *nemuḥ*; *sehe*, *sehāte*. Since the changes to *na* and *sa* are not dependent on external conditions (*anaimittika*), this [root] does not begin with a substitute [consonant] in the *liṭ* tense.

What is the purpose of the condition "between two single consonants" (*ekahalmadhya*)? [Consider] *tatakṣatuḥ*, *tatakṣuḥ*. What is the purpose of the condition "after *at*" (*ata*)? [Consider] *didivatuḥ*, *didivuḥ*. What is the purpose of the condition "followed by *tapara*" (*tapara*)? [Consider] *rarāse*, *rarāsāte*. Here, when the root (*prakṛti*) is reduplicated, the substitute for the preceding element is called a "substitute of the root" (*prakṛtyādeśa*), because there is no distinction [between the original and the substitute]; furthermore, due to the prohibition regarding *śas*, *did*, and others, a substitute that has a different form is understood [to be meant]. Only when [the suffix] is not marked with *P* (*apiti*): *ahaṃ papaca*, *ahaṃ papaṭha*. [This applies] before the suffix *thal* with the augment *iṭ* (Pāṇini 5.3.117).

When *iṭ* and so forth follow, and when a suffix beginning with *thal* follows, the substitution of *et* occurs for the vowel *a* situated between two simple consonants (*ekahalmadhya*), provided that the root does not begin with a substitute (*anādeśādi*), and reduplication (*advir*) also takes place. Examples: *pecitha*, *śekitha*. Why say "when *iṭ* [and so forth] follow"? Observe: *papaktha*. Why say "provided that the root does not begin with a substitute"? Observe: *babhartha*. Why say "situated between two simple consonants"? Observe: *tatakṣitha*. Why say "for the vowel *a*"? Observe: *didevitha*. [The rule *tṛphalabhajatrapaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.48) applies here.]

In the case of the roots *tṛ* and others, when followed by a *liṭ* affix that is not marked with *P* (*apit*), as well as after the *thal* affix beginning with *iṭ*, the substitution of *e* for the radical vowel *a* occurs, and there is no reduplication. Examples: *teratuḥ*, *teruḥ*; *teritha*. *phelatuḥ*, *pheluḥ*; *phelitha*. *bhejatuḥ*, *bhejuḥ*; *bhejitha*. *trepe*, *trepāte*, *trepire*. Only when the affix is *apit*: *ahaṃ tatara*.
[The rule] *rādho hiṃsāyām* (Pāṇini 7.1.61) applies.

The vowel *e* is substituted for the vowel *ā* of the root *rādh*, which has the meaning "to injure," when followed by the *liṭ* suffixes *apit* and *thal*, and the augment *iṭ* is also inserted. Examples: *aparedhatuḥ*, *aparedhuḥ*; *aparedhitha*. Why "in the sense of injuring"? [Counter-example: *ārarādhatuḥ*, *ārarādhuḥ*. Why "when followed by *apit*"? [Counter-example: *apararādha*.
[Also, the substitution is optional] for the roots *jṝ*, *bhram*, and *tras* (Pāṇini 6.4.124).

In the case of the roots beginning with *jṝ*, when followed by a *liṭ* suffix that is not marked with *p* (*apit*) or by *thal* with the augment *iṭ*, the vowel *a* optionally becomes *e*, and the reduplication is also applied. Examples: *jeratuḥ*, *jeruḥ*, *jeritha*; *jajaratuḥ*, *jajaruḥ*, *jajaritha*. *bhrematuḥ*, *bhremuḥ*, *bhremitha*; *babhramatuḥ*, *babhramuḥ*, *babhramitha*. *tresatuḥ*, *tresuḥ*, *tresitha*; *tatrasatuḥ*, *tatrasuḥ*, *tatrasitha*. The restriction "when not marked with *p" (*apiti*) applies here as well: *ahaṃ jajara* ("I grew old"). This applies to the seven roots beginning with *phaṇ* (Pāṇini 6.1.121).

In the case of the seven roots beginning with *phaṇ*, when followed by an affix marked with *ṅ* or *k* (apit), or by *thal* beginning with a vowel or *iṭ*, the substitution of *e* for the vowel *a* optionally occurs, and there is also non-duplication (*advirvacana*). Thus: *pheṇatuḥ*, *pheṇuḥ*, *pheṇitha*; or *paphaṇatuḥ*, *paphaṇuḥ*, *paphaṇitha*. The restriction "when followed by an affix marked with *ṅ* or *k*" (*apiti*) is stated because: *ahaṃ paphaṇa*. Why "of the seven"? Because [otherwise] it would apply to *dadhvanatuḥ* and *dadhvanuḥ* (from *dhvan*). [This is governed by] Pāṇini 6.4.122: *dambha-śrantha-granthām*.

In the case of the roots *dambh* and others, when followed by an affix marked with *ṅ* or *k* that is not *pit*, the substitution of *e* for the root-final *a* occurs, and the augment *adviruc* is also applied. Thus: *debhatuḥ*, *debhuḥ*; *śrethatuḥ*, *śrethuḥ*; *grethatuḥ*, *grethuḥ*. The restriction "when not *pit*" (*apiti*) is essential: *dadambha*. This rule is formulated because the elision of the nasal (*na-lopa*) in *dambh* is considered non-existent (*asiddha*), and therefore the rule must be stated. The phrase "when followed by *iṭ* in the *thal* affix" (*thalīṭi*) is no longer applicable here, as there is no elision of the nasal in that context. According to Pāṇini 5.3.123, in the case of *man*, *pac*, and *mac*, the substitution of *e* for the root-final *a* occurs when a name (*saṃjñā*) is formed. Thus: *Menā*, *Menakā*; *pecā*, *pecakā*; *mecā*, *mecakā*.

*naśo ’ṅi* (5.3.124): When *aṅ* follows, the substitution of *e* for the final vowel of the root *naś* occurs. Example: *aneśam*. *na śasadadavādyadeṅām* (5.3.125): [The substitution of *e* for the final vowel does not occur] after the roots *śas*, *sad*, *ad*, *vā* and others, nor after those whose final vowel is *eṅ*.

The substitution of *e* for the final vowel of the roots *śas*, *dada*, and others, as well as for that vowel prescribed by the rule *adeṅ guṇaḥ*, does not take place [in the following forms]: *viśaśasatuḥ*, *viśaśasuḥ*, *viśaśasitha*; *dadade*, *dadadāte*, *dadadire*; *vavamatuḥ*, *vavamuḥ*, *vavamitha*; *viśaśaratuḥ*, *viśaśaruḥ*, *viśaśaritha*; *cicayitha*, *lulavitha*. The forms *arvantam* and *arvantau* are established by means of the suffix *śatṛ*; the forms *arvāṇam* and *arvāṇau* are established by means of the suffix *vanip*.
The forms *Maghavantau* and *Maghavantaḥ* are established by means of the suffix *matup*; however, there exists another base form, *Maghavan*.
[This concludes the section] regarding the rule *yaci bhaṃ aś-isaṭ-suṭ-taddhita-y-eṣu* (Pāṇini 1.4.18).
It should be understood that this [rule] is governed by the condition "beginning with *ya* or beginning with a vowel, excluding *śis*" (*yakārādāv ajādau ca śisuḍvarjite*).

**Pādaḥ pat** (5.3.127): When a suffix beginning with *ya* follows a base ending in *pāda*, provided that *śis* or *suṭ* does not intervene, the word *pāda* is replaced by *pad*. Examples: *Vaiyāghrapadyaḥ* ("descendant of Vyāghrapāt"). *Dvipadaḥ paśya* ("look at the two-footed one"). *Dvipadā kṛtam* ("done by two feet"). *Dvipadikāṃ dadāti* ("he gives two paces"). The rule applies only when a suffix beginning with *ya* follows: *dvipādbhyām* ("by two feet"). The rule applies only when *śis* or *suṭ* do not intervene: *dvipādi kulāni* ("the families have two feet"); *dvipādau*; *dvipādaḥ*. Due to the mention of the *svādi* group [of suffixes], following the logic of the *akiśoradhenu* maxim, we have: *dvipādyati* ("he goes on foot").

*Vasor va ut* (Pāṇini 6.4.132): When a *yac* suffix follows that begins with a vowel and does not have the augment *suṭ*, the *u* of *vas* is replaced by *ū*. Examples: *viduṣaḥ paśya* ("look at the one who knows"), *viduṣā kṛtam* ("done by the one who knows"). *pecuṣaḥ paśya*, *pecuṣā kṛtam*. Only when a *yac* suffix follows: *vidvadbhyām*. Only when there is no *suṭ*: *vidvāṃsau*, *vidvāṃsaḥ*. *Śvayuvanmaghonām anaṇādau* (Pāṇini 6.4.133): In the case of *śvan*, *yuvan*, and *maghavan*, [the final *n* is replaced by *u*] before a suffix beginning with a vowel that is not *aṇ*.

In the case of *śvan* and others, when a suffix beginning with *yaC* and not having *aN* as its first element follows, provided it is not *śi* or *suṬ*, the substitute *uT* is applied in place of the *v*. Thus: *śunaḥ*, *śunā*, *śunī*; *yūnaḥ*, *yūnā*, *yūnī*; *Maghonaḥ*, *Maghonā*, *Maghonī*. Why specify "not having *aN* as its first element"? Consider: *śauvaṃ māṃsam* ("dog's meat"), *yauvanaṃ vartate* ("youth exists"), and *Māghavanaḥ sthālīpākaḥ* ("an offering for Indra"). Why specify the mention of the letter *n*? Because in forms such as *yuvatyā* and *Maghavatyā*, the word is different [and thus the rule does not apply]. By the rule *allopo 'naḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.134), when a suffix beginning with *yaC* and not being *śi* or *suṬ* follows, there is elision (*lopa*) of the *a* of a base that ends in *an*. Thus: *rājñaḥ*, *rājñā*; *takṣṇaḥ*, *takṣṇā*.
(5.3.131) *ṣapūrvahandhṛtarājñām aṇi*:

When the suffix *aṇ* follows, there is elision of the final vowel (*at*) of the root *han* preceded by a *ṣ*-letter, as well as of *dhṛtarājñ*, before that *aṇ*. Examples: *aukṣṇaḥ*, *tākṣṇaḥ*, *bhrauṇaghnaḥ*, *dhārtarājñaḥ*. Why "of these" (*eṣām*)? [To exclude cases like] *sāmanaḥ*, *vaimanaḥ*. Why "before *aṇ*" (*aṇi*)? [To exclude] *tākṣaṇyaḥ*, where the suffix *ṇya* is applied because he is a craftsman (*kāru*). (5.3.132) *ṅiśyor vā*: [The elision of the final vowel of *dhṛtarājñ*] is optional when the suffixes *ṅi* or *śya* follow.

The elision of the final *a* of the stem *ananta-* occurs when followed by the two suffixes *ṅi* and *śī*. Thus: *sāmni*, *sāmani*; *sāmnī*, *sāmanī*. According to Pāṇini 6.4.137 (*na saṃyogād vamaḥ*), the elision of the final *a* of *ananta-* does not occur when it follows a consonant cluster (*saṃyoga*) ending in *v* or *m*. Thus: *carmaṇā*, *carmaṇe*; *parvaṇā*, *parvaṇe*. Why "after a cluster" (*saṃyogāt*)? Consider: *pratidīvnā*, *sāmnā*. Why "ending in *v* or *m*" (*vamaḥ*)? Consider: *takṣṇā*.

When *yaC* follows *añc*, with the exception of *si* and *suṬ*, there is elision of the *a* [at the end] of the verbal root *añc*. For example: *dadhīcaḥ*, *dadhīcā*; *madhūcaḥ*, *madhūcā*. Since there is no possibility [of the elision applying here], the prohibition does not apply. *uda īt* (5.3.135).
When *yac* follows *añc*, provided that *si* or *suṭ* does not intervene, the substitution of *īt* occurs for the final vowel *at* of the word *udaḥ*. Thus: *udīcaḥ*, *udīcā*.

By rule 5.3.136 (*ātaḥ*), when *yac* follows, provided that *si* or *suṭ* does not intervene, there is elision (*lopa*) of the final vowel *ākāra* (*ā*) of a stem. Thus: *kīlālapaḥ*, *kīlālapā*; *śubhaṃyaḥ*, *śubhaṃyā*. The condition "when *yac* follows" (*yaci*) applies here as well: *kīlālapābhyām*. The condition "provided that *si* or *suṭ* does not intervene" (*aśisuṭi*) also applies here: *kīlālapāṃ paśya*. How is it that [the forms] *khaṭvāḥ paśya* and *khaṭvayā kṛtam* are formed? This is due to the *jñāpaka* (indicative evidence) of rules such as 6.2.43 (*ṭi cāpaḥ*) and 2.4.57 (*kulaṭāyā vā*).

(5.3.137) *viṃśater ḍiti teḥ*: When followed by an affix beginning with the letter *ḍ*, there is elision of the word *ti* in *viṃśati*. [Examples: *viṃśatyā krītaḥ* ("bought for twenty"), *viṃśakaḥ*; *viṃśaṃ śatam* ("one hundred less twenty"). (5.3.138) *antyājādeḥ*: [The elision occurs] of the final [letter] when the affix begins with a vowel (*ac*).

The final vowel, beginning with *a*, of that which is a constituent part of a base (*prakṛti*) is elided when followed by a suffix marked with the marker *ḍ*. Examples: *triṃśakaḥ* (consisting of thirty), *kumudvān* (abounding in water-lilies), *naḍvān* (abounding in reeds), *upasarajaḥ* (produced from a secondary cause). By virtue of the inclusion of the marker *ḍ*, this elision occurs even after bases ending in *as* when followed by *ayaC* (the suffix *ya*), though it does not begin with a vowel. Regarding the rule *no ’ṇādau* (Pāṇini 5.3.139): when followed by a suffix beginning with *yaC* that does not begin with *aṆ*, there is elision of the final vowel, beginning with *a*, of a base ending in *n*. Examples: *Āgniśarmiḥ*, *Auḍulomiḥ*. Why is it said "ending in *n*"? Consider *Sātvataḥ*. Why is it said "beginning with *aṆ*"? Consider *śarmaṇā*, *śarmaṇe*.

*Kalāpyādīnām* (Pāṇini 5.3.140): For *kalāpin* and the others in this group, when a suffix beginning with *yaC* follows an *aṇ* suffix and so forth, there is elision of the final vowel and the following consonant (*jādi*). Those who know or study the Veda taught by Kalāpin are called *Kālāpāḥ*. [Similarly,] *Kauthumāḥ*. There were two teachers, Taitala and Jājali; the work composed by them is referred to by those names. Those who study that [work] are *Taitalāḥ* and *Jājalāḥ*. Likewise, *Lāṅgalāḥ*.

*Kalāpin*, *Kuthumin*, *Taitalin*, *Jājalin*, *Lāṅgalin*, *Brahmacārin*, *Pīṭhamardin*, *Sūkaramardin*, *Suparvan*. In the sense of "a modification of stone" (*aśman*): *āśmaḥ*; but something other than stone: *carmaṇaḥ kośe*: *cārmaḥ* (made of leather). Why say "in the sense of a sheath" (*kośe*)? [To exclude: *cārmaṇaḥ* (the leather itself). In the sense of "a part of a dog" (*śvan*) or "contraction": *śauvaṃ māṃsam* (dog-meat), *śauvaḥ saṃkocaḥ* (contraction of a dog); but something other than these: *śauvanaḥ*. In the sense of "not infrequent" (*anārācchaśvataḥ*) and "continual" (*śaśvataḥ*), provided it does not end in *-as* (*asiti*): *sāyaṃprātikaḥ* (occurring every evening and morning), *paunaḥpunikaḥ* (repeated). Why say "not infrequent and continual"? [To exclude: *ārātīyaḥ* (coming from afar), *śāśvatikaḥ* (eternal). Why say "provided it does not end in *-as"*? [To exclude: *śaṃyuḥ*, *kaṃyuḥ*.

(5.3.141) *ahnaḥ khe*: When the suffix *kha* follows *ahan*, there is elision of the final vowel and the following consonant (*jādi*). For example: *dve ahnī bhūtaḥ* → *dvyahīnaḥ*; *tryahīnaḥ*. Why "when *kha* follows"? [Observe: *āhnikaḥ*.
(5.3.142) *asarvāsaṃkhyaikadeśāt ṭeḥ*: [The suffix *kha* is applied] after a word that is not *sarva*, not a numeral, and not a part-whole expression, provided it ends in the suffix *ṭi*.

The elision of the final vowel and following consonant (*ṭi*) occurs after [the word] *ahan* when it follows another word, provided that it does not follow the word *sarva*, nor a numeral, nor a term denoting a single part. Examples: *paramāhaḥ*, *uttamāhaḥ*, *puṇyāhaḥ*, *saṃkhyātāhaḥ*. Why is there an exclusion of the words beginning with *sarva*? [Examples: *sarvāhnaḥ*; *pratyahnaḥ*, *nirahnaḥ*; *pūrvāhṇaḥ*, *aparāhṇaḥ*.

Regarding the compound of aggregation (*samāhāra*): when *ahan* is used in the sense of an aggregate, the elision of the final vowel and following consonant (*ṭi*) occurs before [the suffix] *ṭac*. Two days combined: *dvyahaḥ*. Three days: *tryahaḥ*.
(5.3.144) After *eka*, when followed by *ahnaḥ* with the suffix *ṭa*, there is elision of the final vowel and the following consonant (*jādi*). Example: *ekāhaḥ*.
(5.3.145) For *antika*, when followed by a suffix beginning with *ta* and having *tamap* as its initial element, [the final syllable is elided].
When the suffix *tama* follows the word *antika*, there is elision (*lopa*) of the initial portion beginning with *ta*. Thus: *antamaḥ*.
Regarding the rule *kāder bahulam* (Pāṇini 5.3.146):

when *tama* or other suffixes follow the word *antika*, there is optionally (*bahulam*) elision of the initial portion beginning with the letter *ka*. Thus: *antikātamaḥ* or *antitamaḥ*; *antitaḥ* or *antikataḥ*. In the sense of "sitting near," one forms *antikasad* or *antiṣad*.

*Or ot* (5.3.147): For a base ending in *u*, *o* is substituted for *u* diversely (*bahulam*) when followed by a suffix beginning with *yaṇ*. Examples: *Bābhravyaḥ*, *Māṇḍavyaḥ*; *Aupagavaḥ*, *Kāpaṭavaḥ*. Only because it says "diversely" (*bahulam*): *Svāyaṃbhuvaḥ*. *Ḍhe* (5.3.148).

In these cases, there is frequently (*bahulam*) elision of a base ending in *u*. Examples: *kāmaṇḍaleyaḥ*, *śaitibāheyaḥ*, *mādrabāheyaḥ*. Because of the word "frequently," [we have] *kādraveyaḥ*. By the rule *yasya* (Pāṇini 6.4.149), there is frequently elision of the final vowel and the preceding consonant of a base ending in *i* or *u* when followed by the suffix *yañ* or any suffix beginning with *aṇ*. Examples: *sāṃkṛtyaḥ*, *gārgyaḥ*, *aitikāyanaḥ*, *kāleyaḥ*, *dauleyaḥ*, *dākṣiḥ*, *plākṣiḥ*. Because of the word "frequently," [we have] *ūrṇāyuḥ*.

(5.3.150) *ṅyām*: Elision occurs when followed by a feminine suffix (*ṅī*). Examples: *Dākṣī*, *Plākṣī*, *kumārī*, *kiśorī*, *gaurī*. (5.3.151) *matsyasya yaḥ*: [The elision of] the *ya* of *matsya* [occurs].

The *y* following [the final consonant] of *matsya* is elided when followed by a *ṅī*. Thus, *matsī*. According to Pāṇini 5.3.152 (*halo yañādeḥ*), the *y* at the beginning of an affix beginning with *yañ* that follows a consonant is elided when followed by a *ṅī*. Thus, *Gārgī*, *Saumī*. Why is it said "following a consonant" (*halaḥ*)? Consider *Kārikeyī*. Why is it said "beginning with *yañ*" (*yañādeḥ*)? Consider the wife of a physician (*vaidya*), who is called *Vaidyī*.

(5.3.153) *sauryāgastyayoś che ca*: After the words *sauriya-* and *āgastya-*, when the suffix *cha* or the feminine suffix *ṅī* follows, there is elision of the letter *y*. Thus: *saurīyaḥ*, *saurī*; *āgastīyaḥ*, *āgastī*. Because the letter *y* is specified as being modified by the suffixes *cha* and *ṅī*, the elision does not occur here: *āgastyacarī*. (5.3.154) *tiṣyapuṣyayor nakṣatre ’ṇi*: [The elision of *y* occurs] after *tiṣya* and *puṣya* when the suffix *aṇ* follows, provided they denote a lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*).

When the asterisms Tiṣya and Puṣya are present [as the first members], there is elision of the final vowel and consonant (*aṇ*) when a suffix follows. *Taiṣī rātriḥ* (the night of Tiṣya), *taiṣam ahaḥ* (the day of Tiṣya); *pauṣī rātriḥ* (the night of Puṣya), *pauṣam ahaḥ* (the day of Puṣya). Why "asterism"? [Consider: *puṣyasya māṇavakasyedaṃ pauṣyam* (this belongs to the boy Puṣya)—here it is not so. [This is governed by] *apatyasyānārṣasyāṇādau* (Pāṇini 5.3.155).

The *y* that is prescribed after a consonant (*hal*) for the formation of a descendant (*apatya*), is elided when followed by a suffix beginning with *yaC* (any vowel except *a*) provided it does not begin with *ā*. Examples: *gārgyāṇām samūhaḥ* (a collection of the descendants of Garga) becomes *gārgakam*; *vātsakam*. Why "of a descendant" (*āpatyasya*)? [To exclude cases like] *sāṃkāśyakaḥ*, *kāmpilyakaḥ* (which are derived from place names). Why "not beginning with *ā*" (*anāti*)? [To exclude] *gārgyāyaṇaḥ*. Why "beginning with [a suffix] other than *aṆ*" (*aṇādau*)? [To exclude] *gārgye*. Why "after a consonant" (*halaḥ*)? [To exclude] *kārikeyiḥ*. [This rule applies] to the suffixes *kyac* and *kyaN* (Pāṇini 5.3.156).

The *yakāra* of a patronymic (*apatya*) following a consonant is elided when followed by the suffixes *kyac* or *kyaṅ*. Examples: *gārgīyati*, *gārgīyate*; *gārgībhūtaḥ*. The restriction "of a patronymic" (*āpatyasya*) applies here as well: *sāṃkāśyīyati*, *sāṃkāśyībhūtaḥ*. The restriction "following a consonant" (*halaḥ*) also applies: *kārikeyīyati*.
[This refers to] the *īya* suffix in *bilvakīya* and others, according to Pāṇini 5.3.157.

When suffixes such as *aṇ* follow, the word *īya* is elided in the case of *bilvakīya* and others. [For example: "In this place there are *bilva* trees" → *bilvakīyā*; "those who live in it" → *bailvakāḥ*. Likewise, *vaiṇukāḥ*. [The forms are: *bilvakīya*, *veṇukīya*, *vetasakīya*, *vetrakīya*, *ikṣukīya*, *kāṣṭhakīya*, *kapotakīya*, *kruñcakīya*. [This is governed by] Pāṇini 5.3.158: *iṣṭhemeyassvantyājādeḥ* ("In the case of the suffixes *iṣṭhan*, *imanic*, and *īyasun*, the initial portion following the final vowel is replaced").

In the case of suffixes beginning with *iṣṭha* and others, there is the elision of the final vowel and following consonant of the base. Thus: *paṭiṣṭhaḥ*, *paṭīyān*, *paṭimā*; *laghiṣṭhaḥ*, *laghīyān*, *laghimā*. Because of the application of the rules as if they were *iṣṭhan*, the same occurs before the suffix *ṇa*: *paṭayati*, *laghayati*.
[Furthermore,] for the words *sthūla*, *dūra*, *yuvan*, *kṣipra*, and *kṣudra*, there is the substitution of *eṅ* for the *y* and *v* when followed by a *yaṇ*. (Pāṇini 5.3.159)

In the case of *sthūla* and other such words when followed by suffixes beginning with *iṣṭhan* and so on, there is the elision (*lopa*) of the *yaṇ*-substitute and other such constituent parts as applicable; furthermore, the vowels *i* and *u* become *eṅ* (i.e., *e* and *o*). Thus: *sthaviṣṭhaḥ*, *sthavīyān*, *sthavimā*; *daviṣṭhaḥ*, *davīyān*, *davimā*; *yaviṣṭhaḥ*, *yavīyān*, *yavimā*; *kṣepiṣṭhaḥ*, *kṣepīyān*, *kṣepimā*; *kṣodiṣṭhaḥ*, *kṣodīyān*, *kṣodimā*. Because of the application of the *iṣṭhavadbhāva* (the treatment as if it were *iṣṭhan*), [the suffix *ṇic*] does not apply: *sthavayati*, *davayati*, *yavayati*, *kṣepayati*, *kṣodayati*. [Regarding *bahu*: according to Pāṇini 5.3.160, *bahor er bhū ca*.]
The *i*-vowel of the word *bahu* is elided when followed by suffixes such as *iṣṭha*, and *bahu* undergoes the substitution of *bhū*. Thus: *bhūyān* and *bhūmā*.

By the rule *iṣṭhe yik ca* (Pāṇini 5.3.161), when *iṣṭha* follows, *bahu* undergoes the substitution of *bhū*, and the augment *yik* is added. Thus: *bhūyiṣṭhaḥ*. Due to the treatment as if it were *iṣṭha* (*iṣṭhavadbhāva*), [the denominative] *bhūyayati* is formed with the suffix *ṇic*.
The substitution of *ā* for the *ī* of the suffix *īyasun* following the word *jya* is prescribed as an irregularity (*nipātana*).

*priyasthirasphirorugurubahulatṛpradīrghahrasvavṛddhavṛndārakāṇāṃ prasthasphavaragarabaṃhatrapadrāghahrasvarṣavṛndāḥ* (5.3.163): For the words *priya*, *sthira*, *sphira*, *uru*, *guru*, *bahula*, *tṛpra*, *dīrgha*, *hrasva*, *vṛddha*, and *vṛndāraka*, there are the substitutions *pra*, *stha*, *spha*, *vara*, *gara*, *baṃha*, *tra*, *dra*, *ghra*, *sra*, *vṛnda*, and *araka* respectively [when followed by the superlative suffix *iṣṭhan*].

In the formation of the superlative (*iṣṭha*) and comparative (*īyasun*) suffixes, the *pra*-class of prefixes undergo substitution according to their respective possibilities. Thus: *preṣṭhaḥ*, *preyān*, *premā*; *stheṣṭhaḥ*, *stheyān*, *sthemā*; *spheṣṭhaḥ*, *spheyān*, *sphemā*; *variṣṭhaḥ*, *varīyān*, *varimā*; *gariṣṭhaḥ*, *garīyān*, *garimā*; *baṃhiṣṭhaḥ*, *baṃhīyān*, *baṃhimā*; *trapiṣṭhaḥ*, *trapīyān*, *trapimā*; *drāghiṣṭhaḥ*, *drāghīyān*, *drāghimā*; *hrasiṣṭhaḥ*, *hrasīyān*, *hrasimā*.

*varṣiṣṭhaḥ*, *varṣīyān*, *varṣimā*; *vṛndiṣṭhaḥ*, *vṛndīyān*, *vṛndimā*. Due to the application of the rules governing the superlative suffix (*iṣṭhan*), [the following forms are derived]: *prāpayati*, *sthāpayati*, *sphāpayati*, *varayati*, *garayati*, *baṃhayati*, *trapayati*, *drāghayati*, *hrasayati*, *varṣayati*, *vṛndayati*. [The substitution of] *ra* for *ṛt* occurs in the case of *pṛthu*, *mṛdu*, *kṛśa*, *bhṛśa*, *dṛḍha*, and *parivṛḍha* (Pāṇini 5.3.164).

In the case of the roots beginning with *pṛthū*, when *iṣṭha* and other suffixes follow, the vowel *ṛ* is replaced by *r*. Examples: *prathiṣṭhaḥ*, *prathīyān*, *prathimā*; *mradiṣṭhaḥ*, *mradīyān*, *mradimā*; *kraśiṣṭhaḥ*, *kraśīyān*, *kraśimā*; *bhraśiṣṭhaḥ*, *bhraśīyān*, *bhraśimā*; *draḍhiṣṭhaḥ*, *draḍhīyān*, *draḍhimā*; *parivraḍhiṣṭhaḥ*, *parivraḍhīyān*, *parivraḍhimā*. This occurs because of the application of the *iṣṭhavadbhāva* (the treatment as if it were *iṣṭha*) in the case of the suffix *ṇa*.

[The suffixes] *prathayati*, *mradayati*, *kraśayati*, *bhraśayati*, *draḍhayati*, and *parivraḍhayati* [are formed]. Why specify "of the *pṛthu*-class and others"? [Consider: *ṛjiṣṭhaḥ*, *ṛjīyān*; *kṛcchrayati*, *kṛtayati*. (5.3.165) That which is prescribed when the suffixes beginning with *iṣṭha* follow does not apply to a monosyllabic base (*ekāc*). [Examples: *srajiṣṭhaḥ*, *srajīyān*, *srajayati*; *sruciṣṭhaḥ*, *srucīyān*, *srucayati*. Why specify "monosyllabic" (*ekāc*)? [Consider: *vasumattamaḥ*, *vasiṣṭhaḥ*.

(5.3.166) *ake rājanyamanuṣyayūnām*: When the suffix *aka* follows, that which has been prescribed for the words *rājanya* and others does not take place. Thus: *rājanyakam*, *mānuṣyakam*. By virtue of belonging to the *manojñādi* group (4.1.149), the suffix *vuñ* is applied: *yauvanikā*. (5.3.167) *ātmādhvanoḥ khe*: [The suffix *kha* is applied after *ātman* and *adhvan* when followed by *aka*].

That which was prescribed after the suffix *ātmanīna* and *adhvanīna*, when followed by *khe*, does not take place. Examples: *ātmanīnaḥ*, *adhvanīnaḥ*. Why [is] *khe* [specified]? [Counter-examples: *pratyātmam*, *prādhvam*.

Regarding the rule 5.3.168, "after [a stem ending in] *ana*, when [the suffix] *ya* follows, provided it is not prescribed for the sense of an abstract quality (*bhāva*) or an action (*karman*)," that which was prescribed after the suffix *an* does not take place if [the suffix *ya*] is not prescribed for the sense of an abstract quality or an action. Examples: *sāmasu sādhuḥ* → *sāmanyaḥ*; *brahmaṇyaḥ*. Why [is] "not for the sense of an abstract quality or an action" [specified]? [Counter-example: *rājño bhāvaḥ karma vā* → *rājyam*. Why [is] "the suffix *ya*" [specified]? [Counter-example: *mahārājaḥ*.
Aṇi (Pāṇini 5.3.169): When *aṇ* follows, that which was prescribed for an infinite [base] does not take place. Examples: *sāmanaḥ*, *vaimanaḥ*. Karmaṇo ’śīle (Pāṇini 5.3.170).

That which was prescribed [by rule 4.2.60] after the suffix *aṇ* does not take place when it follows *kārmaṇa*, provided that it is not a name (*śīla*). [Example: *kārmaṇaḥ*. Why say "not a name"? [Counter-example: *kārmaḥ*. [The word] *aṇi* [from the previous rule] is still understood: [example: *kārmukam*. [Rule 5.3.171: *mād varmaṇo 'patye*: After *mat* [denoting a patronymic], and only after such a *mat*, when the suffix *aṇ* follows in the sense of "descendant" (*apatya*) for the word *varman* itself, that which was prescribed [by 4.2.60] does not take place. [Example: *Cākravarmaṇaḥ*. Why say "after *mat*"? [Counter-example: *Sautvanaḥ*. Why say "*varmaṇaḥ*"? [Counter-example: *Sauṣāmaḥ*.

(5.3.172) *hitanāmno vā*: Regarding the descendant of one whose name contains the word *hita*, that which was prescribed [by 4.1.95] does not necessarily apply; it is optional. Thus, *haitanāmanaḥ* or *haitanāmaḥ*. (5.3.173) *brahmaṇo jātau*: [The suffix *aṇ* is applied after *brahman* when referring to a class or caste.]

When the suffix *aṇ* is applied to *brahman* to denote a descendant (*apatya*) in the sense of a genus (*jāti*), that which was previously stated [regarding the elision of the final vowel] does not occur. Thus: *brāhmaṇaḥ*. Why "in the sense of a genus"? Consider: *brāhmaḥ manuḥ* ("Manu, the son of Brahmā"). Why "descendant"? Consider: *brāhmī oṣadhīḥ* ("the herb belonging to Brahmā"). Regarding *ukṣan* (Pāṇini 5.3.174): when the suffix *aṇ* is applied to the word *ukṣan* to denote a descendant, that which was previously stated [regarding the elision of the final *n*] does not occur. Thus: *aukṣṇaḥ*. Because of this re-statement, there is no elision [of the *n*]. Why "descendant"? Consider: *aukṣaṃ padam* ("a footprint of a bull").

"From a conjunct consonant, [the suffix] *in* [is applied], provided it does not denote a collection" (5.3.175). When *in* follows a word ending in a conjunct consonant, that which was prescribed for the suffix *aṇ* does not apply when the meaning is not a collection (*asamūha*). Examples: *Śāṅkhinaḥ*, *Vājriṇaḥ*. Why "not a collection"? Because the collection of *daṇḍins* is called *dāṇḍam*.
"Of *gāthika*, *vidathika*, *keśin*, *gaṇin*, and *paṇin*" (5.3.176).

That which was prescribed for the suffix *aṇ* after [words ending in] *gāthin*, etc., does not apply when there is no collective sense (*asamūha*). Examples: *gāthinaḥ*, *vaidathinaḥ*, *kaiśinaḥ*, *gāṇinaḥ*, *pāṇinaḥ*. Only when it is "not a collective" (*asamūha*): a collection of *gaṇins* is *gāṇam*. And by the rule *anapatye ca* (Pāṇini 5.3.177), that which was prescribed for a word ending in *in*—provided it is a "remainder" (*śeṣa*)—does not apply when the meaning is neither a descendant (*apatya*) nor a collective (*asamūha*). Examples: *sāṃkūṭinam*, *sāṃrāviṇam*; this belonging to *sragvins* is *srāgviṇam*. However, in the case of a descendant, it certainly does apply: the descendant of *medhāvin* is *maidhāvaḥ*. Only when it is "not a collective" (*asamūha*): a collection of *rathins* is *rātham*.
The forms *dāṇḍināyana*, *hāstināyana*, *jaihmāśineya*, *vāsināyani*, *bhrauṇahatya*, *dhāivátya*, *sāravaikṣvāka*, and *hiraṇmaya* [are formed with the suffix *yañ*]. (Pāṇini 5.3.118)

The word-forms *Dāṇḍināyana* and so forth are formed as irregular derivations (*nipāta*) according to their respective applications. From *daṇḍin* and *hastin*, the suffix *phañ* is applied due to their inclusion in the *Naḍādi* group; there is no elision [of the final *in*], resulting in *Dāṇḍināyanaḥ* and *Hāstināyanaḥ*. From *jihmāśin*, the suffix *ḍhak* is applied because it belongs to the *Śubhrādi* group, resulting in *Jaihmāśineyaḥ*. From *vāsin*, the suffix *phiñ* is applied according to Pāṇini 4.1.157 (*vāsino ’gotrād ādaijādyaca*), resulting in *Vāsināyaniḥ*. From *bhrūṇahan* and *dhīvnan*, the suffix *ṣyañ* is applied in the sense of abstract action (*bhāva*), resulting in the substitution of *t* for *n*: *bhrauṇahatyam* and *dhaivatyam*. When the suffix *aṇ* is applied in the sense of "occurring on the Sarayū," there is the elision of *y*, resulting in *Sāravaḥ*.

In the word *Ikṣvāku*, there is the elision of the vowel *u* after the suffixes *aṇ* or *añ*: [the form] *Aikṣvākaḥ* means "this belongs to Ikṣvāku" or "he is the offspring of Ikṣvāku. In the word *hiraṇmaya*, when the suffix *mayaṭ* is applied to denote a modification of gold (*hiraṇya*), there is the elision of *y*.
The third quarter of the fifth chapter is completed. [The rule:
*yuvo ranākāv asaḥ* (5.4.1).

In place of *yu* and *vu*, when they follow a suffix that does not have the augment *it*, the substitutes *an* and *āk* respectively occur. Examples: *nandanaḥ*, *gamanam*; *kārakaḥ*, *Kācchakaḥ*. Why "not having the augment *it*" (*asa*)? [Consider] *kaṃyuḥ*, *śaṃyuḥ*. In the rule *yuvor* (Pāṇini 7.1.1), the singular number is used because the compound *yu-vu* is a collective singular. Because the option (*vikalpa*) from the previous rule continues to apply, there is no neuter gender. The substitution does not occur for roots such as *yudh* and *budh* because they lack meaning [in this context], as indicated by the rule *yavayavaka* (Pāṇini 4.2.3) following the root *yauti*, and because *bhujyuḥ* is derived from the *uṇādi* suffixes (Uṇādisūtra 1.34).
[The suffixes] *āyan*, *eyin*, *īy*, and *īya* are applied in place of *pha*, *ḍha*, *kha*, *cha*, and *gha* respectively, according to the rule *ṣphādyādīnām* (Pāṇini 5.4.2).

For those sounds beginning with *ph* that occur at the beginning of the group starting with *ṣpha*, the substitutes *āyan* and so forth are applied. *Ṣpha*: *Gārgyāyaṇī*. *Ḍhak*: *Sauparṇeyī*. *Kha*: *kulīnaḥ*. *Cha*: *svasrīyaḥ*. *Gha*: *kṣatriyaḥ*. Why is the mention of *ṣpha*-beginning words used? [To exclude cases such as: *phakkati*, *ḍhaukate*. Why is the mention of "beginning" (*ādi*) used? [To exclude cases such as: *jānudaghnam*. By the rule *ṭhasyekaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.4.3), for the *ṭha* of words beginning with *ṣpha*, the substitute *ik* is applied. Example: *ākṣikaḥ*. Why is it said "of words beginning with *ṣpha*" (*ṣphādīnām*)? [To exclude cases such as: *kaṇṭhaḥ*. Why is it said "of those beginning with" (*ādīnām*)? [To exclude cases such as: *karmaṭhaḥ*.

*Isusugdobhyaḥ kaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.4.4): For a base ending in *is*, *us*, or *uk*, as well as for the word *doh*, the substitution of *ka* occurs in place of the suffix *ṭha*. Examples: *sārpiṣkaḥ* (one who deals with clarified butter), *dhānuṣkaḥ* (an archer), *śābarajambukaḥ* (a jackal-like follower of Śabara), *mātṛkaḥ* (relating to a mother), *paitṛkaḥ* (relating to a father). From *dorbhyāṃ carati* ("he moves by means of his arms"), we get *dauṣkaḥ*. [The forms] *āśiṣikaḥ* and *auṣikaḥ* do not occur because [the suffixes involved] are either meaningless (*anarthaka*) or merely derivative (*lākṣaṇika*). Furthermore, these [suffixes] such as *āyana* and others occur precisely at the stage of the original instruction (*upadeśāvasthā*), because they lack a specific cause [for their application later], and because the *ca* in the rule *yuc-ṭhaj-ca* (Pāṇini 3.2.150) serves the purpose of making the final syllable accented (*antodātta*). *Tosśvaśvataḥ* (Pāṇini 5.4.5): [The suffix *kan* is added after a word ending in *taddhita* suffix *ta*] except when it refers to something eternal (*aśvaśvataḥ*).

The substitution of *kā* occurs for the suffix *ṭha*, which is prescribed after a base ending in *t* that does not denote something eternal (*aśaśvat*). Examples: *audaśvitkaḥ*, *bhāvatkaḥ*. Why "not denoting something eternal"? Consider *śāśvatikaḥ*. Why is it specified that [the suffix] is "prescribed"? Consider *māthitikaḥ*.
[In the case of the suffix *ṭhañ*,] *lyap* replaces *ktvā* when there is no negative compound (*anañ-samāsa*). (Pāṇini 5.4.6)

In a compound with a word ending in *ktvā*, provided it is not preceded by the negative particle *nañ*, the suffix *lyap* replaces *ktvā*. Examples: *prakṛtya*, *prastutya*, *prahṛtya*. Why "not preceded by *nañ*"? Example: *akṛtvā*. Why "in a compound"? Examples: *pṛthak kṛtvā*, *hiruk kṛtvā*. Because the term "not *nañ*" includes words similar to *nañ* that do not denote a number, *lyap* does not apply here: *paramakṛtvā*; and because in compounds such as *pītvābhuktaka*, *snātvākālaka*, etc., there is no application due to their not being [simple] compounds.

*Lyap* occurs precisely in the state of the original grammatical instruction (*upadeśāvasthā*), because although the rule *ti kiti* (5.4.85) would have already established it, the specific mention of *lyap* in the rule for *jagdhi* (5.4.86) indicates this.
[This applies to the substitution of *i* for *ṛ*] according to *ṝta id dhātoḥ* (5.4.7).

The substitution of *id* occurs for the final *ṛ* of a verbal root (*dhātu*). For example: *kirati*, *girati*; *cikīrṣati*, *jihīrṣati*. Why specify "of a verbal root"? [To exclude cases such as] *mātṝṇām*. Furthermore, this serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that even derivative forms (*lākṣaṇika*) are to be included. By the rule *upāntasya* (Pāṇini 6.4.8), the substitution of *id* occurs for an *ṛ* that is near the end (*upānta*). For example: *kīrtayati*, *kīrtakaḥ*. Why specify "near the end"? [To exclude cases such as] *ṝkārīyati*.
(5.4.9) *ud oṣṭhyāt*:

In place of the vowel *ṛ* following a labial (*oṣṭhya*), the substitute *u* occurs. Examples: *prapūrtāḥ piṇḍāḥ*; *pūḥ*, *purau*, *puraḥ*. Why is the marker *t* used [in *tapara*]? So that a long vowel might not replace a long vowel, as in *amū* and *amī*.
(5.4.10) *idito num*: [The augment *num* is added] after a verbal root ending in the marker *it*.

The augment *num* is applied to a verbal root (*dhātu*) ending in *i*. For example: *kuṇḍā*, *huṇḍā*, *kuṇḍitā*. The *num* occurs precisely in the state of the original instruction (*upadeśāvasthā*), because there is no other cause for it and because the context is that of verbal roots. [The rule applies] only to a verbal root: *acaīṣīt*. Regarding *śe mucādīnām* (Pāṇini 7.1.59): the *num* is applied to the group of roots beginning with *muc* when followed by the suffix *śa*. Examples: *muñcati*, *lumpati*. How is it that we have *tṛpati* and *tṛmpati*, as well as *dṛpati* and *dṛmpati*? This is because these roots are indeed listed in two ways within the list of verbal roots (*dhātu*).

*naśo jhali* (5.4.12): The augment *num* is added after the root *naś* when followed by an affix beginning with a *jhal* consonant. Example: *naṃṣṭā*. Why specify "when followed by a *jhal* consonant"? [Counter-example: *naśanam*. *masjo 'ntyāt pūrvaḥ* (5.4.13).

Before the final letter, when followed by a *jhal* consonant, the augment *num* occurs. [Example: *maṅktā*. Why "before the final"? So that the elision of the first member of a conjunct (*saṃyogādilopa*) may take place. Only when a *jhal* follows: [in *majjanam*, it does not occur]. Regarding *jabha* before a vowel: by *jabho 'ci* (Pāṇini 6.1.14), *num* occurs after the root *jabh* when followed by a vowel-initial suffix. [Examples: *jambhayati*, *jambhakaḥ*.
(5.4.15) *radha*: the augment *num* occurs before suffixes beginning with a vowel that start with a non-*j* letter. Thus: *randhayati*, *randhakaḥ*.
(5.4.16) Before the *liṭ* [perfect] tense, [the augment *iṭ* is applied].

The augment *num* occurs after the root *radh* only when followed by the *liṭ* [perfect] suffixes. [Examples: *rarandhiva*, *rarandhima*. Why specify "in the *liṭ*"? [Counter-example: *radhitā*. *rabho ’śapliṭoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.63):

The augment *num* occurs after the root *rabh* when followed by a suffix beginning with a vowel, provided it is not the *śap* [present stem marker] or the *liṭ* [perfect]. [Examples: *ārambhaḥ*, *ārambhakaḥ*. Why specify "not the *śap* or *liṭ*"? [Counter-examples: *ārabhate*, *ārebhe*.

*Labhaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.4.18): After the root *labh*, the augment *num* occurs before an affix beginning with a vowel, provided it is not *śap* or *liṭ*. Examples: *ālambhaḥ*, *ālambhakaḥ*. Only when it is not *śap* or *liṭ*: *ālabhate*, *ālebhe*. *Āṅo yi* (5.4.19).

The augment *num* is inserted before a suffix beginning with *ya* after the root *labh* when preceded by the prefix *ā*. Example: *ālambhyā gauḥ* ("the cow to be sacrificed"). (5.4.20) *upāt stutau*: When the sense of praise (*stuti*) is understood, the augment *num* is inserted before a suffix beginning with *ya* after the root *labh* when preceded by the prefix *upa*. Example: *upalambhyā bhavatā vidyā* ("knowledge is to be acquired by you with praise"). Why say "when praise is understood"? Consider: *upalabhyam asmād vṛṣalāt kiṃcit* ("something is obtainable from this low-born man"). Here, it refers to mere acquisition, not praise.

*Prādibhyaḥ khalghañoh* (5.4.21): The augment *num* is applied to the root *labh* when it follows prefixes (*prādi*) and is followed by the suffixes *khal* or *ghan*. Examples: *īṣatpralambhaḥ kaṭo bhavatā* ("the mat is easily obtained by you"), *upalambhaḥ*. Why "after prefixes"? [Counter-examples: *īṣallabhaḥ*, *lābhaḥ*. *Na suduraḥ kevalāt* (5.4.22): [The augment *num* is not applied] to *labh* when preceded by *su* or *dura* alone.

The augment *num* does not occur after the root *labh* when it follows *su-* or *dur-* alone. Examples: *sulabhaḥ*, *durlabhaḥ*. Why "alone"? [To exclude cases such as] *atisulambhaḥ*, *atidurlabhaḥ*. (5.4.23) *ciṇṇamor aprāder vā*: After the root *labh* that is not preceded by a preverb (*prādi*), the augment *num* optionally occurs before the suffixes *ciṇ* and *ṇamul*. Examples: *alambhi*, *alābhi*; *lambhaṃ lambham*, *lābhaṃ lābham*. Why "not preceded by a preverb"? [To exclude cases such as] *prālambhi*, *pralambhaṃ pralambham*.

(5.4.24) *puṃsi ugitaḥ*: after a base ending in an *ugit* vowel, *num* is inserted when the masculine marker *suṭ* follows. Examples: *śreyān*, *śreyāṃsau*, *śreyāṃsaḥ*; *śreyāṃsam*, *śreyāṃsau*. Why "in the masculine"? Consider *śreyasī kule* ("an excellent woman in the family"). Why "when *suṭ* follows"? Consider *śreyasaḥ paśya* ("look at the excellent one"). (5.4.25) *añcaḥ*.

The augment *num* occurs after the root *añc*, provided it ends in *u* or *g*, when the suffix *suṭ* follows. [Examples: *prāṅ*, *prāñcau*, *prāñcaḥ*, *prāñcam*, *prāñcau*. Why "after *añc*"? [Counter-examples: *ukhāsrat*, *parṇadhvat*. How is it that *gomān* is formed from *gomatyati* with the suffix *kvip*? Because the restriction applies to roots beginning with *bhū* and others; therefore, *num* will occur here. Regarding *yuj* not in a compound (*asamāse*, Pāṇini 5.4.26):

the augment *num* occurs after the root *yuj* when *suṭ* follows, provided it is not in a compound. [Examples: *yuṅ*, *yuñjau*, *yuñjaḥ*, *yuñjam*, *yuñjau*. Why "not in a compound"? [Counter-example: *aśvayuk*.

*Śāv ayamah* (5.4.27): After a stem ending in *yam*, the augment *num* is inserted before the nominative plural suffix *śi*. Examples: *śreyāṃsi*, *mahānti*, *udaśvinti*, *kuṇḍāni*, *vanāni*. Why specify "before *śi*"? Consider: *śreyasī kule* ("two superior things in the family"). Why specify "after *yam*"? Consider: *catvāri*, *ahāni*. *bahūrji bahūrñji* (5.4.28): [The forms] *bahūrji* and *bahūrñji* [are established].
