Before a *śas* ending that begins with a vowel, the augment *num* optionally occurs before the final vowel of the word *bahūrj*. Thus, one forms either *bahūrji* or *bahūrñji*. [This is governed by] Pāṇini 6.4.81: *iko 'ci supi*.

The augment *num* occurs after a stem ending in an *ik* vowel when followed by a case-ending (*sup*) beginning with a vowel. For example: *dadhini*, *dadhinī*; *madhuni*, *madhūni*. This rule applies only to the neuter gender, because it is introduced in that context and because there is an option for stems that have a corresponding masculine form (*bhāṣitapuṃska*). This is indicated by the rule *tasmād dīrghībhūtāc chaso naḥ puṃsi* (Pāṇini 7.1.110), and by the fact that the term "in the masculine" (*puṃsi*) serves as a qualifier for the substitution of *na* [for *śas*]. Therefore, since the long vowel would also apply to the feminine, this rule must apply to the neuter alone by process of elimination. Why specify "after an *ik* vowel"? Consider *kuṇḍe*.

What is the purpose of *aci*? [In the example] *he trapo*, because of this very rule, the prohibition [of *eṅ*] stated in [Pāṇini 6.1.69] *aluki* does not apply; thus, *eṅ* occurs. What is the purpose of *supi*? [In the example] *taumburavaṃ cūrṇam*, [the substitution does not occur]. [Now for Pāṇini 7.1.93: After a neuter-stem ending in *i* or *u* that has a corresponding masculine form (*uktapuṃska*), the augment *num* optionally occurs before case-endings beginning with a vowel starting from the third case (*ṭādi*) onward. [Examples: *kartṛṇā kulena* or *kartrā*; *śucine kulāya* or *śucaye*. Why "that which has a corresponding masculine form" (*uktapuṃskasya*)? [In the examples] *vāriṇā*, *vāriṇe*, [the *num* does not occur because *vārin* has no corresponding masculine form]. Why "before endings beginning with *ṭā*" (*ṭādau*)? [In the example] *grāmaṇinī kule*, [the *num* does not occur because the following suffix begins with *n*, not *ṭ*].

*asthi-dadhi-sakthi-akṣṇām anaṅ* (Pāṇini 5.4.31): When a *sup* suffix beginning with a vowel follows, the substitute *anaṅ* is applied to *asthi* and the others. [Examples: *asthnā*, *dadhnā*, *sakthnā*, *akṣṇā*.
*nājjheḥ śatuḥ* (Pāṇini 5.4.32).

The augment *num* does not occur after the suffix *śatṛ* when it follows a verbal root ending in *aj* (*ac*) that has lost its *hi*. Examples: *dadat*, *dadhat*, *jakṣat*, *jāgrat*. Why say "after [a root] other than *lih*"? Consider: *lihan*. Regarding Pāṇini 5.4.33, *śau vā*:

the augment *num* optionally occurs after the suffix *śatṛ* ending in *aj* when followed by the nominative-accusative plural ending *śas* (*śi*). Examples: *dadanti kulāni*, *jāgranti kulāni*, *jāgrati kulāni*.

(5.4.34) After a word ending in *a*, the augment *num* is optionally inserted before the suffixes *śī* and *ṅī* that follow the present participle suffix *śatṛ*. [Examples: *tudantī kule* or *tudatī kule*; *tudantī brāhmaṇī* or *tudatī brāhmaṇī*. (5.4.35) [The augment *num* is also applied] after the suffixes *śap* and *śyan*.

The augment *num* is inserted before the suffixes *śap* and *śyan*, as well as before the suffix *śatṛ* when followed by *śīṅ*; this is because of its constant re-mention [in subsequent rules]. Examples: *pacantī kule* ("the cooking woman in the family"), *dīvyantī kule* ("the playing woman in the family"); *pacantī brāhmaṇī* ("the cooking Brahmin woman"), *dīvyantī brāhmaṇī* ("the playing Brahmin woman"). Regarding the rule *sāv anaḍuhaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.92):

the augment *num* is inserted after *anaḍuh* when the nominative singular suffix *su* (*s*) follows. Example: *anaḍvān*. Why specify "when *su* follows"? Consider: *anaḍvāhau* (nominative dual), *anaḍvāhaḥ* (nominative plural).
(5.4.37) *diva aut*: After the word *div*, when followed by the nominative singular suffix *su*, the substitution *aut* occurs. [Thus: *dyauḥ*.
(5.4.38) *pathimathyṛbhukṣām āt*: [The substitution *āt* occurs] for the final vowel of *pathin*, *mathin*, and *ṛbhukṣin*.

In the case of *pathin* and others, *āt* is substituted [for the final vowel] when *śas* and *suṭ* follow. *panthāḥ*, *manthāḥ*, *ṛbhukṣāḥ*. Regarding *śis* and *suṭ*: according to Pāṇini 5.4.39, *āt* is substituted for the *ik* vowel of *pathin* and others when *śas* and *suṭ* follow. *bahupanthāni*, *panthānau*, *panthānaḥ*. *bahumanthāni*, *manthānau*, *manthānaḥ*. *bahvṛbhukṣāṇi*, *ṛbhukṣāṇau*, *ṛbhukṣāṇaḥ*.
(5.4.40) *tho nthaḥ*: When a suffix beginning with *śi* follows, the substitute *nth* occurs for the *th* of words such as *panthān*. Examples: *bahupanthāni*, *panthāḥ*; *bahumanthāni*, *manthāḥ*.
(5.4.41) *ino ’ci lopaḥ*: The suffix *in* is elided before a vowel-initial suffix.

The *in* of *pathin* and other such stems is elided when followed by a case ending (*sup*) beginning with a vowel, provided it is other than the *śi* and *suṭ* augments, due to the requirement of the rule's applicability. Thus: *pathaḥ*, *pathā*; *mathaḥ*, *mathā*; *ṛbhukṣaḥ*, *ṛbhukṣā*. Regarding the rule *puṃso 'suṅ* (Pāṇini 7.1.89): the substitution *asuṅ* occurs for the stem *pums* when followed by the *śi* ending or the *suṭ* augment. Thus: *bahupumāṃsi*; *pumān*, *pumāṃsau*, *pumāṃsaḥ*, *pumāṃsam*, *pumāṃsau*. Only when followed by *śi* or *suṭ*: *puṃsaḥ*, *puṃsā*.

*gor auḥ svārthe* (5.4.43): When the word *go* occurs in its own sense (*svārthe*), the vowel *au* is substituted for it when followed by the augment *suṭ*. Examples: *gauḥ*, *gāvau*, *gāvaḥ*. Why "in its own sense"? [Consider: *he citrago*, *he citragavaḥ*. [The rule applies] only when *suṭ* follows: *gavā*. *sakhyur aśāv ait* (5.4.44).

When the suffix *suṭ* follows, the word *sakhi* becomes *aid* [i.e., *sakhāy-*] except when followed by *śi*. [Examples: *sakhāyau*, *sakhāyaḥ*. Why "except when followed by *śi*"? [Counter-example: *atisakhīni*. Why "when *suṭ* follows"? [Counter-example: *sakhīn*. (5.4.45) After the vowel *ṛ*, as well as for *uśanas*, *purudaṃśas*, *anehas*, and the word *sakhi*, the substitute *anaṅ* occurs before the nominative singular suffix *su*. [Examples: *kartā*; *uśanā*, *purudaṃśā*, *anehā*; *sakhā*.

In the vocative singular, the substitution of *anaṅ* for the final vowel and following consonant of words beginning with *ṛt* does not occur when they are used in the vocative case. Examples: *he pitaḥ*, *he purudaṃśaḥ*, *he anehaḥ*, *he sakhe*.
[The rule] *vośanasaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.4.47) applies.
In the vocative case, the suffix *sa* of *uśanas* optionally becomes *anaṅ*. Thus: *he uśanaḥ*, *he uśanan*.

Regarding the rule *kruśas tunas tṛc* (Pāṇini 5.4.48): after the root *kruś*, the substitute *tṛc* occurs in place of *tun* when a *śi* suffix follows. Examples: *bahukroṣṭṝṇi*; *kroṣṭā*, *kroṣṭārau*, *kroṣṭāraḥ*. Only when a *śi* suffix follows: *kroṣṭūn*.

(5.4.49) *striyām*: For the word *kruś*, when it occurs in the feminine, the substitute *tṛc* is applied in place of the suffix *tun*. [Examples: *kroṣṭrī*. With chariots purchased for five *kroṣṭrīs*: *pañcakroṣṭṛbhiḥ rathaiḥ*. In the case of the third case (*tṛtīyā*) and subsequent cases, there will be the usage of both the form ending in *tun* and the form ending in *tṛc*: *kroṣṭunā* and *kroṣṭrā*. (5.4.50) *catur-anaḍuhor ām*: [The suffix] *ām* is applied after the words *catur* and *anaḍuh*.

The augment *ām* is inserted after the words *catur* and *anaḍuh* when the suffixes *śi* or *suṭ* follow. [Examples: *catvāri*, *catvāraḥ*; *priyacatvāḥ*, *priyacatvārau*. *anaḍvān*, *anaḍvāhau*; *bahvanaḍvāṃhi kulāni*. Only when *śi* or *suṭ* follows: *caturaḥ*, *anaḍuḥ*. (5.4.51) *am sau saṃbuddhau*: The augment *am* is inserted after *catur* and *anaḍuh* when the vocative singular suffix *su* follows. [Examples: *he priyacatvaḥ*, *he anaḍvan*. Why "when *su* follows"? [Counter-example: *he anaḍvāhau*, *he anaḍvāhaḥ*. Why "in the vocative"? [Counter-example: *anaḍvān*.

(5.4.52) *aṣṭano vā supy āt*: After *aṣṭan*, when followed by a case-ending (*sup*), the augment *āt* optionally occurs. [Examples: *aṣṭābhiḥ*, *aṣṭabhiḥ*. Why "when followed by a case-ending"? [Counter-example: *aṣṭakaḥ saṃghaḥ* ("a group of eight"). Only when there is no elision (*aluki*) [of the case-ending]: *aṣṭa*. (5.4.53) *rāyo hali*: [The substitute *ai* is applied] for *rāyaḥ* before a consonant (*hal*).

The substitution of *ā* occurs for the word *rāi* when followed by a case ending (*sup*) beginning with a consonant (*hal*). Examples: *rābhyām*, *rābhiḥ*. Why specify "when beginning with a consonant"? [Because otherwise it would apply to] *rāyau*, *rāyaḥ*. Why specify "a case ending" (*sup*)? [Because otherwise it would apply to] *raitvam*, *raitā*. (5.4.54) When followed by a case ending (*sup*) that is not a substitute (*anādeśa*), the substitution of *ā* occurs for *yuṣmad* and *asmad*. Examples: *yuvābhyām*, *āvābhyām*; *yuṣmābhiḥ*, *asmābhiḥ*; *yuṣmāsu*, *asmāsu*. Why specify "not a substitute" (*anādeśa*)? [Because otherwise it would apply to the substitutes] *yuṣmat*, *asmat*.

*Auśasam* (Pāṇini 5.4.55): When *au* (the long vowel *au*) follows, as well as when *śas* or *am* follow, the initial *ā* is substituted for *yuṣmad* and *asmad*. Examples: *yuvāṃ tiṣṭhathaḥ*, *āvāṃ tiṣṭhāvaḥ*; *yuvāṃ paśya*, *āvāṃ paśya*; *yuṣmān*, *asmān*; *tvām*, *mām*.
*Yo 'ci* (Pāṇini 5.4.56).

When a case ending (*sup*) beginning with a vowel follows *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, the substitution of *ya* occurs for the final syllable of these two words. Thus: *tvayā*, *mayā*; *tvayi*, *mayi*; *yuvayoḥ*, *āvayoḥ*. Only when there is no substitution [of *tva* and *ma*] does this apply; thus: *tvat*, *mat*. Regarding the rule *śeṣe lopo ’daḥ* (Pāṇini 5.4.57): where neither the substitution of *āt* nor the substitution of *ya* occurs, when such a case ending (*sup*) follows, the *ac* portion of *yuṣmad* and *asmad* is elided. Thus: *tvam*, *aham*; *yūyam*, *vayam*; *tubhyam*, *mahyam*; *yuṣmabhyam*, *asmabhyam*; *tvat*, *mat*; *yuṣmat*, *asmat*; *tava*, *mama*; *yuṣmākam*, *asmākam*.

(5.4.58) *māntasya yuvāvau dvivacane*: When occurring in the dual number, the forms *yuṣmad* and *asmad* ending in *-m* undergo the substitutions *yuvā-* and *āvā-*. [Examples: *yuvām*, *āvām*; *yuvābhyām*, *āvābhyām*; *yuvayoḥ*, *āvayoḥ*. The rule "ending in *-m*" (*māntasya*) is a governing heading (*adhikāra*).
(5.4.59) *yūyavayau jasi*: [The substitutes *yūya-* and *vaya-* apply] when the suffix *jas* follows.
When *jas* follows *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, those ending in *m* become *yūya* and *vaya*. [Thus: *yūyam*, *vayam*.
When *su* follows *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, the substitutes *tva* and *aha* respectively occur. [Thus: *tvam*, *aham*.

(5.4.61) *tubhyamahyau ṅayi*: when the suffix *ṅe* follows, *yuṣmad* and *asmad* become *tubhya* and *mahya*. (5.4.62) *tavamamau ṅasi*: when the suffix *ṅasi* follows, [the forms] *tava* and *mama* occur. Thus: *tava*, *mama*.
When followed by the suffix *ṅasi*, *yuṣmad* and *asmad* become *tava* and *mama* respectively: *tava*, *mama*.

When referring to a single entity (*ekasminnarthe*), *yuṣmad* and *asmad* become *tvam* and *mam* (Pāṇini 5.4.63): *tvām*, *mām*; *tvayā*, *mayā*; *tvat*, *mat*; *tvayi*, *mayi*; *tvadīyaḥ*, *madīyaḥ*; *tvatputraḥ*, *matputraḥ*.
Pāṇini 5.4.64: *tricaturor striyāṃ tisṛcatasṛ*.
When the words *tri* and *catur* occur in the feminine and are followed by a case-ending (*sup*), they undergo the substitutions *tisṛ* and *catasṛ*, respectively. Examples: *tisṛbhiḥ*, *catasṛbhiḥ*.
Pāṇini 5.4.65: *tisṛkā*. [The suffix *kan* is applied after these words.]
The form *tiṣṛkā* is an irregularly formed (*nipātita*) term used as a proper name. *Tiṣṛkā* is the name of a village.
According to the rule *ṛto ro 'ci* (Pāṇini 5.4.66), the vowel *ṛ* of the words *tri* and *catur* becomes *r* when followed by a case-ending beginning with a vowel. Thus: *tisraḥ*, *catasraḥ*.

*jarāyā jaras vā* (5.4.67): When followed by a case-ending (*sup*) beginning with a vowel, the substitution *jaras* optionally occurs for the word *jarā*. Thus, one says either *jarasā dantāḥ śīryante* ("the teeth decay through old age") or *jarayā*. *tyadāṃ tasādiṣu cā dver aḥ* (5.4.68): In the case of the pronouns beginning with *tyad*, when followed by the suffixes *tas* and so forth, as well as the dual endings, the substitution *a* occurs [for the final vowel].

The vowel *a* is substituted for the words beginning with *tyad* (the pronouns *tyad*, *tad*, *yad*, etc. ending in the dual number, when followed by a case-ending (*sup*) or by the suffixes beginning with *tas*. Examples: *syaḥ*, *tyau*, *tye*; *saḥ*, *tau*, *te*; *tataḥ*, *tatra*, *tadā*, *tathā*. Why is it said "up to the dual" (*ā dver*)? [To exclude forms like] *bhavān*. Why is it said "when followed by *tas* and so on"? [To exclude forms like] *tyadīyaḥ*. It is understood as "provided there is no elision" (*aluki*); thus: *tat*, *yat*. *kimaḥ kaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.3.12): For the word *kim*, the substitution of *ka* occurs when followed by the suffixes beginning with *tas* or by a case-ending (*sup*). Examples: *kaḥ*, *kau*, *ke*; *kadā*, *kathā*, *karhi*.

*taḥ saḥ sau* (Pāṇini 5.4.70): When *su* follows, the *t* of the pronouns beginning with *tyad* is replaced by *s*. Thus: *syaḥ*, *saḥ*, *eṣaḥ*. Why say *sau* (in the locative case)? [To exclude examples like] *tau*. *asāv asuko 'sakau* (Pāṇini 5.4.71).
These words are irregularly formed (*nipātita*) from *adas* with the nominative singular suffix *su* when it ends in that [suffix]. *Asau*. When accompanied by the *kāc* augment: *asukaḥ*, *asakau*.
*Idam ayam iyam* (Pāṇini 5.4.72):
These words are irregularly formed from *idam* with the nominative singular suffix *su* in all three genders. *Ayam*, *iyam*, *idam*.
*do maḥ* (Pāṇini 5.4.73): When *sup* follows, the *d* of *idam* becomes *m*. [Thus: *imau*, *ime*.
*ṭausy ako 'naḥ* (Pāṇini 5.4.74).
When *osi* follows the syllable *ṭā*, the substitute *an* occurs for the *a* of *idam*. [Examples: *anena*, *anayoḥ*. Why say "*aka*" (the letter *a*)? [Counter-example: *imakena*.

When a *sup* suffix beginning with a consonant (*hal*) follows, the substitute *aś* occurs for *idam*. [Examples: *ebhiḥ*, *ābhyām*. Only if it is the letter *a* [as specified by "aka"] does it apply: [Counter-example: *imakaiḥ*.

Regarding the subsequent mention (*anvādeśa*) of this [pronoun], Pāṇini 5.4.76 states: *enaḥ* [is substituted] for the word *etad* when it is in the second case (*dvitīyā*), provided that the mention follows what has already been stated (*kathitānukathana-viṣaye*).

When the second case ending or the dual endings *ṭā* and *osi* follow, the substitution of *ena-* occurs for the form *eta-* of the word *etad*. Examples: *Etaṃ chātraṃ vedam adhyāpaya, atho enaṃ vyākaraṇam adhyāpaya.* "Teach this student the Veda; and then teach him grammar. *Etat kuṇḍam ānaya, atho enat parivartaya.* "Bring this bowl; and then turn it over. *Etau chātrau vedam adhyāpaya, atho enau vyākaraṇam adhyāpaya.* "Teach these two students the Veda; and then teach them grammar. *Etāñ chātrān vedam adhyāpaya, atho enān vyākaraṇam adhyāpaya.* "Teach these students the Veda; and then teach them grammar."

"By this student the night was studied; moreover, by him it was studied thoroughly. "Of these two students the conduct is excellent; moreover, of these two there is abundant wealth. "In these two villages we dwelt happily; moreover, in these two we sacrifice correctly. In this same way, *idam* is also to be applied, but with this distinction: "Bring this bowl; moreover, turn it over"—here it remains ending in *m*.

In the case of the third case and those following, if *tra* and *tas* are used, this very form will also occur even when there is a subsequent reference (*anvādeśa*). This is established by the specific rule (*nipātana*) [Pāṇini 4.3.8] "kuto 'taḥ" and [4.3.11] "atra. Regarding the rule *panniśamāshṛdyūṣandoṣañ śasādau vā* (5.4.77): when a case ending beginning with *śas* follows, the substitutes *pada*, etc., optionally take the place of *pāda*, etc. Thus: *padbhyām* or *pādābhyām*; *niśi* or *niśāyām*; *māsi* or *māse*; *hṛdi* or *hṛdaye*; *yuṣṇā* or *yūṣeṇa*; *doṣṇā* or *doṣā*. Why specify "beginning with *śas*" (*śasādau*)? [To exclude forms such as: *pādaḥ*, *niśā*, *māsaḥ*, *hṛdayam*, *yūṣaḥ*, *doḥ*.
Regarding *liṭ*, *āśīr-liṅ*, *atiṅ*, and *aśit* (Pāṇini 5.4.78): it should be understood that this governs [the subsequent rules] prior to the mention of *tiṅ* (5.4.173).
For the root *as*, there is *bhū* (5.4.79).

In the place of *as* (the root *as-*) before the *liṭ* and other [affixes], the substitute *bhū* occurs: *babhūva*, *bhūyāt*, *bhavitā*. Why is there a mention by means of *luk* (elision)? So that it does not apply to *as-* [in the sense of "to throw"]: *asitā*. How is it that we have *kārayāmāsa*? Because of the rule stating that the *liṭ* is used after *kṛ*, *bhū*, and *as* (Pāṇini 3.1.40). Only in the case of the *liṭ* and others: *syāt*, *asti*, *san*. Regarding *bruvo vac* (Pāṇini 2.4.53): after *brū*, the substitute *vac* occurs when the *liṭ* and other [affixes] follow: *uvāca*, *ūce*, *ucyāt*, *vaktā*. Only in the case of the *liṭ* and others: *brūyāt*, *bravīti*, *bruvan*.

*cakṣaḥ khyāñ* (Pāṇini 5.4.81): In place of the root *cakṣ*, the substitute *khyāñ* occurs before the *liṅ* and other [suffixes]. Examples: *khyāyāt*, *khyātā*. Only before the *liṅ* and others: *ācakṣīta*, *ācaṣṭe*, *ācakṣāṇaḥ*.
*vā liṭi* (Pāṇini 5.4.82).

When the *liṭ* affix follows, the substitute *khyāñ* optionally occurs for the root *cakṣ*. Thus: *ācakhyau*, *ācakhye*; [and in the alternative,] *ācacakṣe*. According to Pāṇini 5.4.83, when the suffixes *asun* and *ana* follow, or when the sense of "excluding" (*varjana*) is intended, the substitute *khyāñ* does not occur for *cakṣ*. Examples: *nṛcakṣāḥ*, *vicakṣaṇaḥ*, *parisaṃcakṣyaḥ*. How is the form *vyākhyānam* derived? It will be from the root *khyāti* (*khyā*).

*ajer vy ayughañapkyeṣu* (5.4.84): In place of the root *aj*, the substitution *vī* occurs before the *liṭ* and other affixes, with the exception of *yu*, *ghañ*, *ap*, and *kyap*. Examples: *vivāya*, *vīyāt*, *pravetā*, *vītaḥ*, *vītavān*. Why specify "except for *yu*, *ghañ*, *ap*, and *kyap*"? [Consider: *prājanam*, *samājaḥ*, *udajaḥ*, *samajyā*. How is *pravayaṇam* formed? [Answer: *vī* is a different root. *ti kity ado jagdhaḥ* (5.4.85).

When a *kit* suffix beginning with the letter *t* follows, the substitute *jagdha* occurs in place of *ad*. Examples: *jagdhaḥ*, *jagdhvā*. Why "beginning with *t*" (*ti*)? [Counter-example: *adyate*. Why "*kit*" (*kiti*)? [Counter-example: *attā*. [This rule also applies] before the suffix *lyap* (Pāṇini 5.4.86).

Even when *lyap* follows, the substitution of *jagdha* occurs. Although [the rule] is established by the condition "before *kṛt* suffixes marked with *k* or *ṅ*" (*ti-kitī*), the fact that it is stated again here as a rule for *lyap* indicates, by way of a grammatical hint (*liṅga*), that *lyap* occurs precisely in the state of the original verbal root (*upadeśāvasthā*). Consequently, the following operations do not take place: the doubling of a consonant (*hitva*), the substitution of *da* for *dā* (*dattva*), the substitution of *i* for *ī* (*ittva*), the lengthening of a vowel (*dīrghatva*), and the substitution of *śūṣ* for *siv*. Examples: *hitvā*, *pradhāya*; *dattvā*, *pradāya*; *khātvā*, *prakhanya*; *sthitvā*, *prasthāya*; *śāntvā*, *praśamya*; *pṛṣṭvā*, *āpṛcchya*; *dyūtvā*, *pradīvya*; *devitvā*, *pradīvya*. [The rule] *luṅ-san-ja-ghañ-ap-su ghaslḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.37) applies.

In the *luṅ* (aorist), *san* (desiderative), *aci* (beginning with a vowel), and also after *ghañ*, the substitute *ghas* occurs in place of *ad*. Examples: *aghāsat*, *jighatsati*, *praghasaḥ*, *ghāsaḥ*, *vighasaḥ*. Although this is established by means of another verbal root (*ad*), this specific rule is stated to exclude [the substitution of] *at*. However, in the *liṭ* (perfect), both forms occur: *āda* and *jaghāsa*. Regarding *veñ*: "In the *liṭ*, *vay* optionally replaces *veñ*" (Pāṇini 6.1.48). In the *liṭ* following *veñ*, the substitute *vay* optionally occurs. Examples: *uvāya* and *vavau*.

*Hano vadha liṅi* (5.4.89): When *liṅ* follows, the substitute *vadha* occurs for the root *han*. Example: *vadhyāt*. This applies only in the sense of benediction (*āśis*); [otherwise] one says *hanyāt*. *Luṅi* (5.4.90).

In the *luṅ* [aorist] tense, when followed by an affix other than *taṅ*, the substitute *vadh* occurs for the root *han*. Thus: *avadhīt*. Because the root *vadhi* ends in a short vowel (*adanta*), the augment *āṭ* does not occur.
When followed by an affix belonging to *taṅ* in the *luṅ* tense, the substitute *vadh* optionally occurs for the root *han*. Thus: *āvadhiṣṭa* or *āhata*.
*eter gāḥ* (Pāṇini 5.4.92): When *luṅ* follows, the substitute *gā* occurs for both the root *iṇ* and the suffix *ik*. Examples: *agāt*, *adhyagāt*.
*ṇau gam abodhe* (Pāṇini 5.4.93).

For the roots *iṇ* and *ik*, when followed by the suffix *ṇic*, the substitution of *gam* occurs provided they do not mean "to understand. Examples: *gamayati grāmam* ("he causes [him] to go to the village"); *adhigamayati priyām* ("he causes [her] to understand the beloved"). Why say "provided they do not mean to understand"? Observe: *arthān saṃpratyāpayati* ("he makes [him] comprehend the meanings"). Regarding the rule *sani* (Pāṇini 7.2.49):

for the roots *iṇ* and *ik*, when followed by the suffix *san*, the substitution of *gam* occurs. Examples: *jigamiṣati grāmam* ("he desires to go to the village"); *adhijigamiṣati priyām* ("he desires to understand the beloved"). With the same restriction "provided they do not mean to understand," observe: *arthān saṃpratīṣiṣati* ("he desires to comprehend the meanings").
*iṅaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.4.95): When *san* follows, the substitute *gam* occurs for the root *iṅ*. Example: *adhijigāṃsate vidyām* ("he desires to learn the science").
*gāṅ liṭi* (Pāṇini 5.4.96).
When the *liṭ* suffix follows, the substitute *gāṅ* is applied to the root *iṅ*. Example: *adhijage*.
(5.4.97) When the *luṅ* or *lṛṅ* suffixes follow, the substitute *gāṅ* is optionally applied to the root *iṅ*. Examples: *adhyagīṣṭa*, *adhyaiṣṭa*; *adhyagīṣyata*, *adhyaiṣyata*.
*ṇau saṃścaṅoḥ* (5.4.98):

When followed by a *ṇi*-affix, as well as when followed by a desiderative (*san*) or a reduplicated aorist (*caṅ*), the substitution of *gāṅ* for *iṅ* is optional. Examples: *adhijigāpayiṣati*, *adhyāpipayiṣati*; *adhyajīgapat*, *adhyāpipat*. Why "when followed by *saṃ* or *caṅ*"? [Counter-example: *adhyāpayati*. *valāder iṭ* (5.4.99): [The augment] *iṭ* is added after [a root ending in a consonant] when followed by an affix beginning with a consonant other than *y*.

The augment *iṭ* is added after roots beginning with *val* in the *liṭ*, the benedictive (*āśīrliṅ*), and after [suffixes] other than *tiṅ* and *śit*. Thus: *lulavitha*, *laviṣīṣṭa*, *lavitā*. Because the rule refers to that which resembles a *tiṅ* suffix, it does not apply to the *svādi* group: *lūbhyām*, *lūbhiḥ*. Regarding *graho ’syāliṭi* (Pāṇini 6.1.16):

after the root *grah*, the *i* of the augment *as* becomes *ī* when followed by anything other than the *liṭ*. Thus: *grahītā*. Why "of this" (*asya*)? To prevent the application to the *iṭ* of the *ciṇvat* substitute (Pāṇini 6.1.41): *grāhiṣyate*. Why "not in the *liṭ*" (*aliṭi*)? To exclude cases such as *jagṛhiva*, *jagṛhima*.

For the augment *iṭ* following the roots *vṛṅ* and *vṛñ*, as well as those ending in the vowel *ṝ*, the substitution of *ī* optionally takes place. Thus: *varītā*, *varitā*; *prāvarītā*, *prāvaritā*; *āstarītā*, *āstaritā*. (5.4.102) *na liṅi*: [This substitution does not occur] in the *liṅ* (optative).

When the *liṅ* affix follows, the substitution of *ī* for the subsequent *iṭ* after the root *vṛ* does not take place. Examples: *variṣīṣṭa*, *prāvariṣīṣṭa*, *āstariṣīṣṭa*. Regarding the rule *sicy ataṅi* (Pāṇini 7.2.43): when the *sic* affix follows that is not followed by a *taṅ* (ātmanepada) affix, the substitution of *ī* for the subsequent *iṭ* after the root *vṛ* does not take place. Examples: *prāvāriṣṭām*, *āstāriṣṭām*. Why is it said "not followed by a *taṅ*"? Consider: *avarīṣṭa*, *avariṣṭa*.

(5.4.104) *iṭ sano vā*: The augment *iṭ* optionally occurs after the root *vṛ* before the suffix *san*. Examples: *vivariṣate*, *vuvūrṣate*; *prāvivariṣati*, *prāvuvūrṣati*; *nipipariṣati*, *nipupūrṣati*.
(5.4.105) *liṅsicāv ātmanepadeṣu*: [The augment *iṭ* is applied] to the roots *liṅ* and *sic* when followed by the suffixes of the middle voice (*taṅ*).

The augment *iṭ* is optionally applied after a root ending in *ṛ*, as well as after the suffixes *liṅ* (optative) and *sic* (aorist), when they occur in the domain of *taṅ* (the middle voice endings). Examples: *variṣīṣṭa* / *vṛṣīṣṭa* (from √*vṛ*) *āstariṣīṣṭa* / *āstīrṣīṣṭa* (from √*stṛ*) *avariṣṭa* / *avṛta* (from √*vṛ*) *āstariṣātām* / *āstīrṣātām* (from √*stṛ*) By the rule *ṛtaḥ saṃyogādeḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.43), the augment *iṭ* is optionally applied after roots ending in *ṛ* that begin with a consonant cluster (*saṃyoga*), when followed by *liṅ* or *sic* in the *taṅ* domain.

Examples: *smariṣīṣṭa* / *smṛṣīṣṭa* (from √*smṛ*) *asmariṣātām* / *asmṛṣātām* (from √*smṛ*) Because the term "consonant cluster" (*saṃyoga*) refers here to a cluster present in the original instruction (*aupadeśika*), the augment does not apply in the following cases: *saṃskṛṣīṣṭa* (from *sam* + √*kṛ*) *samaskṛta* (from *sam* + √*kṛ*)

Pāṇini 5.4.107: *svṛ-sū-ūditaḥ*. After the roots *svar*, *sū* (meaning "to bring forth"), *sūyati*, and those marked with the indicatory vowel *ū*, the augment *iṭ* optionally occurs before an affix beginning with a consonant (*val*). Examples: *svaritā*, *svartā*; *savitā*, *sotā*; *mārjitā*, *mārṣṭā*. Why is the indicatory letter [ū] necessary? [To distinguish them from] *suvati*, which has [the form] *savitā*. How is it that [the forms] *vidhotā* and *vidhavita* are established? They are established by means of the roots *dhū* and *dhūñ*. Pāṇini 5.4.108: *radhādibhyaḥ*. [The augment *iṭ* is optional after the roots beginning with *radh*.]

The augment *iṭ* optionally occurs after roots beginning with *radh* followed by a consonant (*val*) in the *liṭ* and other such suffixes. [Examples: *radhitā*, *raddhā*; *naśitā*, *naṃṣṭā*; *tarpitā*, *traptā*; *darpitā*, *draptā*; *drohitā*, *drogdhā*; *mohitā*, *mogdhā*; *snohitā*, *snogdhā*; *snehitā*, *snegdhā*. In the case of *liṭ*, because of the restriction regarding *srādi* (Pāṇini 5.4.158), *iṭ* applies due to its higher priority: *rarandhiva*, *rarandhima*.
After the root *niṣkuṣ*, the augment *iṭ* optionally occurs before a consonant-initial suffix marked with *kṛt* (Pāṇini 5.4.109). [Examples: *niṣkoṣitā*, *niṣkoṣṭā*.

The augment *iṭ* occurs after the root *niṣ-kuṣ* before the suffixes *kta* and *ktavatu*, because it is prescribed as a mandatory rule (*nityam*) by the subsequent injunction [Pāṇini 7.2.49], since that [rule] does not mention the optionality [of *iṭ*] for *niṣ-kuṣ* in the case of *apatiniṣkuṣo vā* (5.4.140). Examples: *niṣkuṣitaḥ*, *niṣkuṣitavān*. Furthermore, [the augment *iṭ* occurs] after *pū* and *kliś*, and there is also the substitution of *a* for the root vowel (5.4.111).

The augment *iṭ* is optionally applied after the roots *pū* and *kliś* when followed by the suffixes *kta*, *ktavatu*, and *ktvā*. The subsequent rule is for the sake of making it obligatory; because of this specific statement, *iṭ* is applied. Examples: *pavitvā*, *pūtvā*; *kliśitvā*, *kliṣṭvā*; *pavitaḥ*, *pavitavān*; *pūtaḥ*, *pūtavān*; *kliśitaḥ*, *kliśitavān*; *kliṣṭaḥ*, *kliṣṭavān*. Regarding the rule *vasakṣudha iṭ* (Pāṇini 7.2.52):

the augment *iṭ* is applied after the roots *vas* and *kṣudh* when followed by the suffixes *kta*, *ktavatu*, and *ktvā*. Examples: *uṣitvā*, *uṣitaḥ*, *uṣitavān*; *kṣudhitvā*, *kṣudhitaḥ*, *kṣudhitavān*. For the root *vas*, the *iṭ* augment is indeed mandatory.

When the letter *n* follows, the augment *iṭ* occurs after the suffix *ktvā* and the suffixes *kta* and *ktavatu* of the root *añc*. Examples: *añcitvā jānu juhoti* ("having bent the knee, he offers"); *añcitam iva śiro vahati* ("he carries his head as if bent"); *añcitavān*. There is no elision of the nasal [of the prefix] due to the rule *na añcaḥ pūjāyām* (Pāṇini 5.4.118). Why "when *n* follows"? Consider *udaktam udakaṃ kūpāt* ("the water drawn from the well"). [The rule] *lubha ākule* (Pāṇini 5.4.114) [is also mentioned].

The augment *iṭ* is applied after the roots *lubh* followed by the suffixes *kta*, *ktavatu*, and *ktvā*, when the sense of "being agitated" (*ākula*) is conveyed. Examples: *vilubhitāḥ keśāḥ* ("the hair is disheveled"); *vilubhitavān* ("he has disheveled [the hair]"). Why specify "when agitated"? [Consider: *lubdho vṛṣalaḥ* ("the low-born man is greedy"). Regarding the rule *jṝṣas tvaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.56):
the augment *iṭ* is applied after the root *jṝṣ* before the suffix *ktvā*. Examples: *jaritvā*, *jarītvā*.
*vraścitvā* (5.4.116):
this word *vraścitvā* is established as an irregular form (*nipātana*).
The augment *iṭ* optionally occurs after the root *śam* when followed by the suffix *ktvā*. Thus: *śamitvā*, *śāntvā*. Regarding *tīṣusahalubharuṣariṣaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.48):

the augment *iṭ* optionally occurs after the roots *iṣu* and others when followed by a suffix beginning with *t* that requires *valādi* strengthening. Thus: *eṣitā*, *eṣṭā*; *sahitā*, *soḍhā*; *lobhitā*, *lobdhā*; *roṣitā*, *roṣṭā*; *reṣitā*, *reṣṭā*. Why is *tī* mentioned? [To exclude cases where *t* is not present. For example: *sahiṣyate*. Because of the specific mention of *iṣu* (as *iṣu* and not *iṣ*), the augment does not apply to the roots *iṣyati* and *iṣṇāti*: *preṣitā*. In the rule, the ablative case (*pañcamī*) in *tī* functions as a genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) due to the principle that a subsequent rule (*para*) takes precedence over a preceding one.
The suffix *ni* is applied after the verbal roots *san*, *iṇ*, *vanta*, *ṛdh*, *bhrasj*, *dambh*, *śri*, *svṛ*, *ūrṇu*, *bhṛ*, *jñapi*, *san*, *tan*, *nipati*, and *daridra*. (Pāṇini 5.4.119)

The augment *iṭ* is optionally applied after the suffix *san* following roots ending in *iv*, as well as after *ṛdh* and others. *dideviṣati*, *dudyūṣati*. *ardidhiṣati*, *īrtsati*. *bibhrajjiṣati*, *bibhrakṣati*. *didambhiṣati*, *dhīpsati*. *śiśrayiṣati*, *śiśrīṣati*. *sisvariṣati*, *susvūrṣati*. *yiyaviṣati*, *yuyūṣati*. *proṛṇunaviṣati*, *proṛṇunūṣati*. *bibhariṣati*, *bubhūrṣati*. Because of the specific mention [of the root] with the suffix *śap*, it does not occur for another: *bubhūrṣati*. *jñīpsati*, *jijñapayiṣati*.

*sisaniṣati*, *siṣāsati*; *titaniṣati*, *titaṃsati*; *pipatiṣati*, *pitsati*; *didaridriṣati*, *didaridrāsati*. Pāṇini 5.4.120: *sya-sici-kṛta-cṛta-chṛda-tṛda-nṛtaḥ*. After the roots *kṛt* and others, an augment *iṭ* is optionally applied before a suffix beginning with *s* that is not *sic*. Examples: *kart-i-ṣyati*, *kartsyati*; *cart-i-ṣyati*, *cartsyati*; *chard-i-ṣyati*, *chartsyati*; *tard-i-ṣyati*, *tartsyati*; *nard-i-ṣyati*, *nartsyati*. Why [the condition] "before *si*" (*sīti*)? Consider: *kartitā*. Why [the condition] "not *sic*" (*asici*)? Consider: *akartiṣṭām*.

*aniṅgameḥ iṭ* (5.4.121): After the substitute *iṅ* for the root *gam*, an augment *iṭ* is added to a following suffix beginning with *s*. Examples: *gamiṣyati*, *jigamiṣati*, *jigamiṣitā*, *saṃjigamiṣitā*. Why "after the substitute *iṅ* for *gam*"? Consider: *adhijigāṃsitā*. *na taṅānaiḥ* (5.4.122): [The augment *iṭ* is not applied] after [the roots *gam* and *han*] when followed by the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) or *āna* (periphrastic future) affixes.

When used in conjunction with *taṅ* affixes, the augment *iṭ* does not occur after the root *gam* followed by a suffix beginning with *s*. Examples: *saṃjigaṃsate*, *saṃjigaṃsamānaḥ*. The *taṅ* affixes are applied here according to Pāṇini 1.4.71 (*samo gamṛchi...*). Further examples: *saṃgaṃsyate*, *saṃgaṃsyamānaḥ*, *saṃgaṃsīṣṭa*.
[The rule] *vṛdbhya iṭ* (5.4.123) applies.

The augment *iṭ* is applied after roots beginning with *vṛt* when followed by suffixes beginning with *s* that are used exclusively with the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) endings and the *āna* (present middle participle suffix). For example: *vartiṣyate*, *vartiṣyamāṇaḥ*; *vivartiṣate*, *vivartiṣamāṇaḥ*. Likewise, *vardhiṣyate*, *vardhiṣyamāṇaḥ*; *vivardhiṣate*, *vivardhiṣamāṇaḥ*. This applies only when used with the *taṅ* and *āna* suffixes; otherwise: *vartsyati*, *vivṛtsati*, *vivṛtsitā*.
[Also, the augment *iṭ* is applied] after the root *kḷp* when followed by the suffix *tās* (Pāṇini 5.4.124).

The augment *iṭ* occurs after the root *kḷp* when followed by the suffix *tās* and the initial *s* of the suffixes beginning with *taṅ* and *āna*. Examples: *kalpitāse*, *kalpiṣyate*, *cikalpiṣate*. Only when combined with *taṅ* and *āna*: *kalptā*, *kalpsyati*, *cikḷpsati*, *cikḷpsitā*. Regarding *snu*: (Pāṇini 7.2.125), when combined with *taṅ* and *āna*, the augment *iṭ* does not occur after the suffix *tās* or the initial *s* of the suffixes beginning with *taṅ* and *āna* following *snu*. Examples: *prasnoṣyate*, *prasnoṣyamāṇaḥ*, *prasnotāse*. Only when combined with *taṅ* and *āna*: *prasnavitā*.

When used in conjunction with the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) endings or the *āna* suffix (*śānac*), the augment *iṭ* does not occur after the root *kram* followed by the suffix *tās* or a suffix beginning with *s*. Examples: *prakramiṣyate*, *prakramyamāṇaḥ*, *prakrantāse*. Only when used with *taṅ* and *āna*: *kramitā*.
[This rule applies] to the agent (*kartṛ*) when the suffix is other than *tiṅ* and falls within the domain of *taṅ*. (5.4.127)

After a root belonging to the *taṅ* domain (*ātmanepada*), the augment *iṭ* does not occur before a suffix beginning with *vaś* that follows a verbal stem functioning as an agent (*kartṛvṛtti*), provided it is not an *iṅ* suffix. Examples: *prakrāntā*. Why "belonging to the *taṅ* domain"? Consider: *kramitā*. Why "functioning as an agent"? Consider: *prakramitum*, *prakramitavyam*. Why "not an *iṅ* suffix"? Consider: *pracakramiṣe*. Regarding the rule *vaśi* (Pāṇini 6.1.20):

after a verbal stem beginning with *vaś* that is not an *iṅ* suffix, the augment *iṭ* does not occur. Examples: *īśvaraḥ*, *bhāsvaraḥ*; *dīpraḥ*; *bhasma*; *rakṣṇaḥ*, *yācñā*; *khaṇḍaḥ*, *daṇḍaḥ*. Only "not an *iṅ* suffix" applies here: *jagmiva*.

Regarding *ter agrahādibhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.4.129): the augment *iṭ* does not occur after the suffix *ti* when it follows roots other than those beginning with *grah*. Examples: *tantiḥ*, *rantiḥ*, *vantiḥ*. How is it that words such as *saktuḥ*, *pattram*, *hastaḥ*, *kāṣṭham*, *kukṣiḥ*, *ikṣuḥ*, *tasaraḥ*, *śalkaḥ*, and *vatsaḥ* are formed? These belong to the *auṇādika* (Uṇādi) group, just like *garbhaḥ*, *darbhaḥ*, *gulphaḥ*, *śarkarā*, and so forth. Why exclude the *grahādi* group? [Because otherwise we would have] *nigṛhītiḥ*, *upasnihitiḥ*, *nikucitiḥ*, *nipaṭitiḥ*. Since it is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open-ended class), forms such as *prabhaṇitiḥ* are also included. Regarding *ekāco 'śviśriḍīśīṅūyvādiṣaṭkāt* (Pāṇini 5.4.130): [the augment *iṭ* is not applied to the suffix *ti* after a root consisting of a single vowel, except for the six roots *aś*, *śri*, *ḍī*, *śī*, *ūy*, and others].

The augment *iṭ* does not occur after a monosyllabic root that is excluded from the six beginning with *yu*, as well as from the roots ending in *ū*—namely *śvi*, *śri*, *ḍī*, and *śī*—and *īṅ*. Examples: *yātā*, *cetā*, *netā*, *stotā*, *kartā*. Why specify "monosyllabic"? Consider: *daridritā*, *ādīdhitā*, *vevitā*, *prorṇavitā*, *jāgaritā*. Why exclude *śvayati* and the others? Consider: *śvayitā*, *śrayitā*, *ḍayitā*, *śayitā*; *lavitā*; *yavitā*, *navitā*, *kṣṇavitā*, *prasnavitā*, *kṣavitā*, *ravitā*. Why specify "from the group of six"? Consider: *kotā*.

This [augment *iṭ*] does not occur here because of the exclusion of roots such as *śvi* and others, and because of the subsequent mention of "roots ending in a consonant" (*halanta*). For example: *paṭhitā*. How then is it that forms such as *varitā*, *prāvaritā*, and *āstaritā* are possible? This is due to the rule: "The augment *iṭ* is optional after the root *vṛ*, but not in the *liṅ* [optative]" (Pāṇini 7.2.39–40). Regarding the rule "After the roots *sidh*, *budh*, *svid*, *man*, *puṣ*, and *śliṣ*, when followed by the suffix *śyan*, there is no *iṭ* before a suffix beginning with a consonant and having an indicatory *v*" (Pāṇini 7.2.13):

this means that after roots such as *sidh* and others characterized by the suffix *śyan*, there is no *iṭ* before a suffix beginning with a consonant (*valādi*). Examples: *seddhā*, *boddhā*, *svettā*, *mantā*, *poṣṭā*, *śleṣṭā*. Why is "when followed by *śyan*" specified? [To exclude cases where other suffixes follow: *sedhitā*, *bodhitā*, *sveditā*, *manitā*, *poṣitā*, *śleṣitā*.

*vider alukaḥ* (5.4.132): After the root *vid* when its *aluk* [augment] is present, the augment *iṭ* does not occur before an affix beginning with a consonant (*valādi*). Example: *vettā*. Why "when *aluk* is present"? Consider: *veditā śāstrāṇām*.
*yaralād bhaḥ* (5.4.133).

The augment *iṭ* does not occur after a root ending in *bha* that follows *ya*, *ra*, or *la*. Examples: *yabdha*, *rabdha*, *labdha*. Why "after *ya*, *ra*, or *la*"? Consider *umbhitā*. Why "after *bha*"? Consider *lagitā*. (5.4.134) *yaranagān maḥ*:
The augment *iṭ* does not occur after a root ending in *ma* that follows *ya*, *ra*, *na*, or *ga*. Examples: *yantā*, *rantā*, *praṇantā*, *gantā*.

Regarding *śakādibhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.4.135): the augment *iṭ* does not occur after roots such as *śak* and others when followed by an affix beginning with a consonant (*valādi*). For example: *śaktā*, *ghastā*, *vastā*. However, the augment *iṭ* certainly does occur after the roots *śak* and *vas* when followed by an affix beginning with a vowel: *śakitā*, *vasitā*.

[The suffix *kvip* is applied] after the roots *śakl*, *ghasl*, *vas*, *tan*, and *han*; after *pac*, *vac*, *ric*, *vic*, *vic*, *sic*, *muc*, and *prach*; after *diś*, *dṛś*, *viś*, *liś*, *riś*, *ruś*, *mṛś*, and *spṛś*; after *kruś* and *daṃś*; after *tyaj*, *yaj*, *yuj*, *ruj*, *nij*, *vij*, *bhuj*, *bhaj*, *sṛj*, *sañj*, *rañj*, and *bhañj*; after *svañj*, *masj*, and *bhrasj*; after *ruh*, *duh*, *diha*, *liha*, *mih*, *nah*, *dah*, and *vah*; after *ad*, *hi*, *diś*, *dis*, *sad*, *tud*, *nud*, *bhid*, *chid*, *kṣud*, *pad*, *khid*, and *skand*; and after *tap*, *paś*, *pav*, *vap*, *lip*, *lip*, *sṛp*, *svap*, *āp*, *kṣip*, and *chup*.

[The suffix *ktvā*] is added after the roots *śuṣ*, *kṛṣ*, *piṣ*, *viṣ*, *śiṣ*; after *tuṣ*, *tviṣ*, *duṣ*, *dviṣ*; after *vyadh*, *yudh*, *rudh*, *śudh*, *bandh*, *krudh*, *kṣudh*; and after *rādh* and *sādh*. (5.4.136) After the root *śri*, after a one-syllable root ending in a long vowel (*ū*), and after *ūrṇu*, the augment *iṭ* does not occur before a suffix beginning with a consonant (*valādi*) that has the marker *k*. Examples: *śritvā*, *śritaḥ*; *yutvā*, *yutaḥ*; *lūtvā*, *lūnaḥ*; *vṛtvā*, *vṛtaḥ*; *tīrtvā*, *tīrṇaḥ*; *ūrṇutvā*, *ūrṇutaḥ*. The rule applies only to one-syllable roots: *jāgaritaḥ*. Why say "before a suffix marked *k*"? Observe: *lavitā*.

Regarding *sano grahaguhaś ca* (Pāṇini 5.4.137): the augment *iṭ* does not occur after the suffix *san* following the roots *grah* and *guh*, nor after a root ending in long *ū*. Thus: *jighṛkṣati*, *jughuksati*; *lulūṣati*, *pupūṣati*. Regarding the roots *śvi*, *ūrṇu*, *yu*, and those ending in long *ṝ*, it is stated that the augment *iṭ* after *san* is optional (Pāṇini 5.4.119, 101).
Regarding the sense of the same meaning (*svārthe*) [Pāṇini 5.4.138].

The augment *iṭ* does not occur after a *san* that has a privative meaning (*svārthika*). [Examples: *titikṣate*, *cikitsati*, *jugupsate*. Regarding Pāṇini 6.1.139, *śvīdito niṣṭhāyām*: the augment *iṭ* does not occur after the root *śvi* or after roots marked with *īt* when followed by the past participial suffixes *kta* or *ktavat*. [Examples: from *śvi*: *śūnaḥ*, *śūnavān*; from *lasj* (with *o*): *lagnaḥ*, *lagnavān*.

After a root from which *iṭ* is optionally prescribed by [Pāṇini 7.2.45] *yato ’pateḥ*, provided that the root does not contain the element *pati*, the augment *iṭ* does not occur before the suffixes *-ta* and *-tavat*. Examples: *sūtaḥ*, *sūtavān*. Why say "after one other than *pati*"? Observe: *patitaḥ*, *patitavān*. The rule applies only when the root has a single vowel: *daridritaḥ*. How is *viditaḥ* formed? Because of the inclusion of *vid* as associated with *viś* in [Pāṇini 7.2.16] *vidi-viśibhyāṃ ca*. Also, [the rule] *āditaḥ* [applies].
The augment *iṭ* does not occur after roots beginning with the vowel *a*, whether they are marked with the suffix *kta* or *ktavat*. Examples: *minnaḥ*, *minnavān*.
According to Pāṇini 5.4.142, *iṭ* is optionally absent after such roots when used in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāva*) or when denoting the commencement of that action.
Examples: *minnam* or *meditam*; *praminnaḥ* or *prameditaḥ*. The restriction "beginning with *a*" (*āditaḥ*) applies here as well: *gatam*.

*Japivamaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.4.143): The augment *iṭ* is optionally absent after the suffixes *-tata-* and *-tavat-* when they follow the roots *japi-* and *vami-*. Thus: *japtaḥ* or *japitaḥ*; *vāntaḥ* or *vamitaḥ*. *Vyāṅaḥ śvasaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.4.144).

The augment *iṭ* is optionally absent after the roots *śvas* preceded by *vi-* and *ā-* when followed by the suffixes *-ta* and *-tavat*. Thus: *viśvastaḥ*, *viśvasitaḥ*; *āśvastaḥ*, *āśvasitaḥ*. Why "after *vi-* and *ā-*"? [Observe: *niḥśvasitaḥ*, *ucchvasitaḥ*. *kṣubdha-svānta-dhvāntam* (Pāṇini 5.4.145):

The words *kṣubdha* and others are irregularly formed (*nipātita*) in the senses of "churning-stick" (*mantha*) and so forth. *Kṣubdhaḥ* means a churning-stick; *svāntam* means the mind (*manas*); *dhvāntam* means darkness (*tamas*). Why "in apposition" (*samānādhikaraṇam*)? [Observe: *kṣubhitam manthena* (agitated by the churning-stick), *svanitam manasā* (resounded by the mind), *dhvanitam tamasā* (resounded by darkness).

*Viribdha*, *phāṇṭa*, *bāḍha*, and *mliṣṭa* are irregularly formed (*nipātita*) when they signify, respectively, *svara* (tone), *anāyāsa* (effortlessness), *bhṛśa* (intensity), and *aviśpaṣṭa* (indistinctness). (Pāṇini 5.4.146) The words *viribdha* and so forth are prescribed as irregular forms when the meanings of *svara* and the others are intended. If it refers to a tone, it is *viribdha*; otherwise, it is *virebhita*. If it refers to something produced without effort, it is *phāṇṭa*; this term specifically denotes a liquid substance consisting of medicinal herbs that have been freshly pressed and extracted. Otherwise, it is *phāṇita* (molasses). If it means intense, it is *bāḍha*; otherwise, it is *bāhita*. If it means indistinct, it is *mliṣṭa*; otherwise, it is *mlechita*. *Dhṛṣa* and *śasa* [are used] in the sense of boldness (*prāgalbhya*). (Pāṇini 5.4.147)

The augment *iṭ* does not occur after the roots *dhṛṣ* and *śas* when followed by the suffixes *kta* and *tavat*, provided they denote "boldness" (*prāgalbhya*). Thus, *dhṛṣṭaḥ* and *viśastaḥ*. Why "boldness"? [To show: *dharṣitaḥ* and *viśasitaḥ*.
*dṛḍhaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.4.148): The form *dṛḍha* is an irregularly formed (*nipātita*) word meaning "thick" (*sthūla*) and "strong" (*balavat*). Thus, *dṛḍhaḥ*. Other forms are *dṛhitaṃ* and *dṛṃhitaṃ*.
*parivṛḍhaḥ* in the sense of "lord" (5.4.149):
the word *parivṛḍha* is irregularly formed (*nipātita*) in the sense of a lord; otherwise, it means "strengthened.
*Kaṣaḥ* [takes the suffix *kha*] in the senses of "difficulty" and "thicket" (5.4.150).

The augment *iṭ* does not occur after the roots *kaṣ* when followed by the suffixes *kta* and *tavat* in the senses of "difficult" (*kṛcchra*) and "impenetrable" (*gahana*). For example: *kaṣṭo 'gniḥ* ("the fire is difficult [to approach]") and *kaṣṭāḥ parvatāḥ* ("the mountains are impenetrable"). In other senses, the form is *kaṣitam*. Regarding the rule *ghuṣer aviśabdane* (Pāṇini 7.2.23): the augment *iṭ* does not occur after the root *ghuṣ* when followed by the suffixes *kta* and *tavat*, except in the sense of "making a sound" (*viśabdana*). For example: *ghuṣṭā rajjuḥ* ("the rope has been made to resound"). Why say "except in the sense of making a sound"? Consider: *avaghuṣitaṃ vākyam āha* ("he spoke a sentence that was already proclaimed"). From this indicative mark (*liṅga*), it follows that the causative suffix *ṇic* is optionally present; thus, forms such as *jughuṣuḥ Puṣyamāṇavāḥ* ("the Puṣyamāṇavas shouted") are established.

*saṃniver ardaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.4.152): The augment *iṭ* does not occur after the root *ard* preceded by *sam-* and others when followed by the suffixes *-tṛc* and *-tavat*. Examples: *samarṇaḥ*, *nyarṇaḥ*, *vyarṇaḥ*. Why "after *sam-* and others"? [Counter-example: *arditaḥ*.
*abher avidūre* (Pāṇini 5.4.153).

The suffix *iḍ* does not occur after the roots *ṛd* ("to go") preceded by *abhi*, or *tṛ* and *stṛ* preceded by *pari*, when the sense is "near. For example: *abhyarṇā śarat* ("the autumn is near"). Why say "when meaning 'near'"? Consider: *abhyarditaḥ* ("tormented").

Regarding the rule *ṇer vṛttaṃ granthe* (Pāṇini 6.4.154): the form *vṛttam* is prescribed as a substitute for the root *vṛt* ending in *ṇi* (*varti*) followed by the suffix *kta*, specifically when the subject matter is a book (*grantha*). Examples: *vṛttaṃ pārāyaṇaṃ Devadattena* ("Devadatta has completed the recitation"); *vṛttaṃ pārāyaṇe* ("the recitation is finished"). Any other usage is *vartitam*.

The forms *dānta*, *śānta*, *pūrṇa*, *dasta*, *spaṣṭa*, *channa*, and *jñapta* are optionally substituted for the causative (*ṇyanta*) roots when the suffix *kta* follows. Thus: *dāntaḥ* or *damitaḥ*; *śāntaḥ* or *śamitaḥ*; *pūrṇaḥ* or *pūritaḥ*; *dastaḥ* or *dāsitaḥ*; *spaṣṭaḥ* or *spāśitaḥ*; *channaḥ* or *chāditaḥ*; *jñaptaḥ* or *jñapitaḥ*.
[Also, the substitution of *na* for the final consonant occurs] after the roots *ruṣ*, *hṛṣ*, *atvar*, *saṃghuṣ*, and *asvan*. (Pāṇini 5.4.156)

The augment *iṭ* is optionally not applied after the roots *ruṣ* and others when followed by the suffixes *-ta* and *-tavat*. Thus: *ruṣṭaḥ*, *ruṣitaḥ*; *hṛṣṭaḥ*, *hṛṣitaḥ*. It need not be stated that for the root *hṛṣ* [the option applies] regarding body hair, or in the senses of "astonishment" and "resistance," because it is observed elsewhere as well, even when the meaning differs; or rather, it is due to the rule of restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*). Examples: *hṛṣṭāḥ keśāḥ*, *hṛṣitāḥ keśāḥ*; *hṛṣṭā dantāḥ*, *hṛṣitā dantāḥ*; *hṛṣṭaṃ lomabhiḥ*, *hṛṣitaṃ lomabhiḥ*. Also: *abhyāntaḥ*, *abhyamitaḥ*; *tūrṇaḥ*, *tvaritaḥ*.

*saṃghuṣṭaḥ*, *saṃghuṣitaḥ*; *āsvāntaḥ*, *āsvanitaḥ*. Since [the roots] do not denote sound (*aviśabdane*) and refer to the mind (*manasi*), this very rule must apply by virtue of its subsequent position. *Apacitaḥ* will be derived from the root *ci* (to gather/heap); from that alone, honor (*pūjā*) is understood. *Apacāyitaḥ* will be derived from the root *cāy* (to honor). Regarding *apacitiḥ* (Pāṇini 5.4.157): when the suffix *ktin* follows the root *cāy* preceded by *apa*, the substitution of *ci* is prescribed as an irregularity (*nipātyate*). Thus, *apacitiḥ*. This statement is for the purpose of excluding the root *cāyṛ*.

(5.4.158) *sṛ-bhṛ-vṛ-stu-dru-sru-śruvo liṭaḥ*: The augment *iṭ* does not occur after the *liṭ* affixes beginning with a consonant (*valādi*) following the roots *sṛ* and the others. Thus: *sasṛva*, *sasṛma*; *babhṛva*, *babhṛma*, *babhṛvahe*, *babhṛmahe*; *vavṛva*, *vavṛma*, *vavṛvahe*, *vavṛmahe*. For the roots *vṛṅ* and *vṛñ*, the prohibition applies specifically to that which is characterized by beginning with a consonant (*valādi*). Thus: *tuṣṭuva*, *tuṣṭuma*; *dudruva*, *dudruma*; *susruva*, *susruma*; *śuśruva*, *śuśruma*. Why "after *sṛ* and the others"? Observe: *peciva*, *pecima*; *śekiva*, *śekima*. (5.4.159) *kṛño 'suṭaḥ*: [The same rule applies] to the root *kṛ* when it is not preceded by the augment *suṭ*.

The augment *iṭ* does not occur after the root *kṛ* when it is followed by the suffix *liṭ* and is not accompanied by the augment *suṭ*. Examples: *cakṛva*, *cakṛma*. This is a prohibition of the *iṭ* that would otherwise have been required by the rule concerning roots ending in *sṛ* and others (*sṛdiniyama*). Why specify "not accompanied by *suṭ"*? Consider: *saṃcaskariva*, *saṃcaskarima*. [This concludes the discussion of] Pāṇini 7.2.13. Now, Pāṇini 7.2.65: *ṛtaḥ tāsi nityāniṭaḥ thalaḥ*. [The augment *iṭ* is not applied to the suffix *thala* after a root ending in *ṛ* which is invariably without *iṭ* before the suffix *tās*.]

The augment *iṭ* does not occur after a root ending in *ṛ* that is invariably without *iṭ* (*nityāniṭ*) when followed by the suffix *thāl*. Examples: *hartā*, *jahartha*. Why "ending in *ṛ*" (*ṛtaḥ*)? Consider *bhettā*, *bibheditha*. Why "after [a root] with *tāsī*" (*tāsīti*)? Consider *vṛtaḥ*, *vavaritha*. Why "invariably" (*nityam*)? Consider *svarṭā*, *svaritā*; *sasvaritha*. Why "without *iṭ*" (*aniṭaḥ*)? Consider *jāgaritā*, *jajāgaritha*. Why "*thāl*" (*thalaḥ*)? Consider *jahriva*, *jahrima*. This is a prohibition of what would otherwise be obtained by the rule *aco vā* (Pāṇini 7.2.61). *Aco vā* (7.2.61).

The augment *iṭ* is optionally not applied after a root ending in a vowel that is invariably without *iṭ* before the suffix *tās*, when followed by the suffix *thāl*. Examples: *yātā*: *yayātha*, *yayitha*; *cetā*: *cicetha*, *cicayitha*; *hotā*: *juhotha*, *juhavitha*. Only when *tās* follows: *yutaḥ*, *yuyavitha*. Only when [the root] is invariably [without *iṭ*]: *sotā*, *savitā*, *susavitha*. Only when [the root] is without *iṭ*: *lavitā*, *lulavitha*. Only when *thāl* follows: *yayiva*, *yayima*. [This applies to roots] other than those ending in *a* in the root list (*pāṭha*), according to Pāṇini 7.2.162.

In the *upadeśa* (original grammatical instruction), the suffix *thala* following a root that ends in the vowel *a*, and which is invariably without the augment *iṭ* in the *tās* (future participle), optionally does not take the augment *iṭ*. Examples: *paktā*: *papaktha*, *pecitha*; *śaktā*: *śaśaktha*, *śekitha*. Why say "in the *upadeśa*"? Consider *karṣṭā*: *cakarṣitha*. Why say "ending in *a*"? Consider *bhettā*: *bibheditha*. Why say "the *t* is for the sake of brevity" (*tapara*)? Consider *rāddhā*: *rarādhitha*. The rule applies only when there is the suffix *tāsī* (the future participle): e.g., *śāntaḥ*, *śemitha*. The rule applies only when [the root] is "invariably" (*nitya*) without *iṭ*: e.g., *raddhā*, *radhitā*, *rarandhitha*. The rule applies only when [the root] is "without *iṭ*" (*aniṭ*): e.g., *phaṇitā*, *pheṇitha*. The rule applies only when the suffix is *thala*: e.g., *peciva*, *pecima*. [Roots ending in] *sṛj* and *dṛś* [take *iṭ* before *thali*] (Pāṇini 7.2.59).
The augment *iṭ* is optionally not applied after the suffix *thala* following the roots *sṛj* and *dṛś*. Thus: *sasraṣṭha*, *sasarjitha*; *dadraṣṭha*, *dadarśitha*.

Regarding the rule *ṛvṛvyeñadaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.164): the augment *iṭ* is necessarily applied after the suffix *thala* following the roots *ṛ*, *vṛñ*, *vyeñ*, and *ad*. This is because the option (*vikalpa*) from the preceding rule continues to apply, while the mention of *vyeñ* and *ad* would otherwise be redundant. Thus: *āritha*, *vavaritha*, *saṃvivyayitha*, *āditha*.

Pāṇini 5.4.165: *kvasor ekājādghasaḥ*. The augment *iṭ* is applied after the suffix *kvasu* when it follows a monosyllabic root ending in long *ā*, as well as after the root *ghas*. Examples: *pecivān*, *yayivān*, *jakṣivān*. Why specify "after a monosyllabic root ending in *ā* or *ghas*"? Consider: *babhūvān*. Pāṇini 5.4.166: *vā hanagamavidaviśadṛśaḥ*. [The augment *iṭ* is optional after the suffix *kvasu* following the roots *han*, *gam*, *vid*, *viś*, and *dṛś*.]

The augment *iṭ* optionally occurs after the suffix *kvasu* following roots such as *han* and others. Thus: *jaghnivān*, *jaghanvān*; *jagmivān*, *jaganvān*; *vividivān*, *vividvān*; *viviśivān*, *viviśvān*; *dadṛśivān*, *dadṛśvān*.
According to Pāṇini 5.4.167 (*ṛhanaḥ sye*), the augment *iṭ* occurs before the suffix *aya* when it follows a root ending in *ṛ* or the root *han*. Thus: *kariṣyati*, *haniṣyati*.
(5.4.168) *añjeḥ sicaḥ*: The augment *iṭ* is added after the *sic* affix following the root *añj*. Example: *āñjīt*.
(5.4.169) *stusuño 'taṅi*: [The augment *iṭ* is added after the *sic* affix] following the roots *stu* and *suñ*, except when the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) endings are used.

The augment *iṭ* is applied after the *sic* suffix following the roots *stu* and *su*, provided that a non-*taṅ* (non-ātmanepada) affix follows. Examples: *astāvīt*, *asāvīt*. Why specify "provided that a non-*taṅ* affix follows"? Observe: *astoṣṭa*. The form *adhāvīt* is established by the root *dhūñ*; however, for the root *dhū*, the form should be *adhauṣīt*. Regarding the rule *yamaramanamātāṃ sak ca* (Pāṇini 5.4.170):

the augment *iṭ* is applied after the *sic* suffix immediately following the roots *yam*, etc., as well as those ending in long *ā*, and the augment *sak* is also added to these. Examples: *ayaṃsiṣṭām*, *araṃsiṣṭām*, *anaṃsiṣṭām*; *ayāsiṣṭām*. Why specify "provided that a non-*taṅ* affix follows"? Observe: *āyaṃsta pādam* (he stepped with his foot).

Pāṇini 5.4.171: *ṛsmipūṅañjaśaḥ sanaḥ*. The augment *iṭ* is added after the suffix *san* following roots beginning with *ṛ*, as well as *smi*, *pū*, *ūṅ*, *añj*, and *aś*. Examples: *aririṣati*, *sismayiṣate*, *pipaviṣate*, *añjijiṣati*, *aśiśiṣate*. Pāṇini 5.4.172: *kṝbhyaḥ pañcabhyaḥ*. [The augment *iṭ* is added after the suffix *san* following the five roots beginning with *kṝ*.]

The augment *iṭ* is applied after the suffix *san* following these five roots beginning with *kṝ*: *cikariṣati*, *jigariṣati*, *didariṣate*, *didhariṣate*, *pipṛcchiṣati*. Why "after five"? [Observe: *sisṛkṣati*. *Rudbhyaḥ tiṅaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.76): The augment *iṭ* is applied after the suffixes beginning with a consonant (*valādi*) that follow these five roots beginning with *rud*: *roditi*, *svapiti*, *prāṇiti*, *śvasiti*, *jakṣiti*. Why "after a *tiṅ* suffix"? [Observe: *svaptā*. Only "after five" applies here: *jāgarti*.

(5.4.174) *janī-īś-īḍaḥ sdhve*: After the roots *jan*, *īś*, and *īḍ*, the augment *iṭ* is added before the suffix *dhve* when it begins with *s*. Examples: *vyatijajñiṣe*, *vyatijajñidhve*; *vyatijajñiṣva*, *vyatijajñidhvam*. [In these forms,] reduplication occurs because they belong to the *juhotyādi* class. Examples: *īśiṣe*, *īśidhve*; *īśiṣva*, *īśidhvam*. Examples: *īḍiṣe*, *īḍidhve*; *īḍiṣva*, *īḍidhvam*. (5.4.175) *āne mug ataḥ*: The augment *muk* is added after the final vowel of a verbal stem ending in *a* when followed by the suffix *āna*.

The augment *muk* is added after a verbal stem ending in *a* when followed by the suffix *āna*. Examples: *pacamānaḥ*, *yajamānaḥ*. Why "after [a stem] ending in *a*"? Consider *kurvāṇaḥ*. Why "followed by *ta*" (*tapara*)? Consider *dadānaḥ*. Only when referring to the base form (*prakṛti*): *prāṇaḥ*. Regarding *āsīnaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.4.176):
the substitution of *ī* for the final vowel of the root *ās* before the suffix *āna* is prescribed as a nipātana (irregular formation). Example: *āsīnaḥ*.

The fifth chapter is completed. [Pāṇini 6.1.1] *mṛjer āt*: for the root *mṛj*, the vowel *a* becomes *ā*. [Examples: *mārṣṭi*, *mārṣṭā*. Only because of the rule "for *a*" [does this apply]: *mṛṣṭaḥ*.
(6.1.2) *ṛta aci vā*:

After the root *mṛj*, the vowel *ṛ* may optionally become *āt* before a following vowel-initial suffix. Examples: *mārjanti* / *mṛjanti*; *mārjan* / *mṛjan*. Why is it said "after *ṛ*" (*ṛta*)? Consider *saṃmārjanam*. Why is it said "before a vowel" (*aci*)? Consider *mṛṣṭaḥ*. (6.1.3) *ajāgṛṇiśvīnāṃ sicy ataṅy ādaic*: After the roots *aj*, *gṛ*, *ṇi*, and *śvi*, the vowels *ā*, *ai*, and *au* (*ādaic*) are substituted for the *iṭ* augment when followed by the *sic* suffix, provided it does not belong to the *ātmanepada* (*ataṅ*).

When *sica* follows, provided it is not preceded by a *taṅ* (ātmanepada) affix, the *āṬ* augment (*āṬ*) is applied to the initial vowel of a verbal root ending in *i*, *u*, or *ṛ*, excluding *jāgṛ*, *niś*, and *śvi*. Examples: *akārṣīt*, *acaiṣīt*. Here, due to proximity (*pratyāsatti*), *āṬ* is applied after the vowel *i* as *ai*, after *u* as *au*, and by elimination, after *ṛ* as *ā*. It will not apply to the remaining vowels because they are impossible [in this context]; for instance, in *udavoḍhām*, it does not apply because the elision of *ḍh* is considered non-existent (*asiddha*). Why say "not preceded by *taṅ*"? Consider *acyoṣṭa*. Why exclude *jāgṛ*, *niś*, and *śvi*? Consider *ajāgarīt*, *aunayīt*, *aśvayīt*.

How is it that [the forms] *nyanuvīt* and *nyadhuvīt* are formed? Because the substitution of *u* (*uvi*) is internal (*antaraṅga*), once it has been applied, the [substitution of *ī* for *u*] will not occur due to the intervention of the letter *v*. Furthermore, there is a prohibition by the rule *neṭi* (Pāṇini 6.1.5), which states that the [substitution of *ī* for *u*] characterized by a final consonant does not apply when *iṭ* follows. [Objection: In that case, even in the form *alāvīt*, after the substitution of *o* (*okāra*) and the subsequent substitution of *av* (*avādeśa*), the [substitution of *ī* for *u*] would likewise not apply. [Response: No; the rule for the substitution of *āT* and *eṅ* (*adeṅ*) is initiated precisely when *āT* and *aij* (*ādaij*) have not yet applied. However, the substitution of *u* (*uvi*) applies both when [the conditions for *āT*/*aij*] have applied and when they have not. Nor is the mention of the roots *ṇi* and *śvi* an indicator (*jñāpaka*) of the absence of internal operations (*antaraṅga*) in the case of the *sic* suffix, because the substitution of *āT* and *eṅ* is an exception (*apavāda*) to the substitution of *āT* and *aij*.

And there is no purpose [for this rule]. As for the one who says: "In *acecāyīt*, *anenāyīt*, *acirāyīt*, and *ajirāyīt*, there would be a prohibition based on the characteristic of having a *y*-augment (*yānta*)," even in that case, there is no possibility of *āt* or *eṅ* [being applied], because they have been superseded by *ādaic*.

According to *halo 'caḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.4), when *sic* follows that is not followed by a *taṅ* suffix, *ādaic* replaces the *ā* or *eṅ* that belongs to a verbal root ending in a consonant. Examples: *apākṣīt*, *abhaitsīt*, *arautsīt*, *atāpsīt*, *arāṅkṣīt*, *asāṅkṣīt*.
When *sic* with an initial *iṭ* follows, the *āṭ* augment does not occur after a verbal root ending in a consonant. Example: *akoṣīt*.
The substitution of *aij* (i.e., *ai* or *au*) optionally occurs for the root *ūrṇu* when followed by a *sic* suffix beginning with *iṭ*. Thus: *praurṇāvīt*, *praurṇavīt*, or *praurṇuvīt*.

[This is governed by] Pāṇini 6.1.7: "In place of the *at* (the penultimate vowel) of a root beginning with a consonant, having a single consonant as its penultimate (*upadhā*), and ending in *ś*, *v*, *s*, *kṣa*, *ṇa*, *ha*, *m*, *y*, or *v*, [there is the substitution of *vṛddhi*]."

For a root beginning with a consonant and ending in a consonant—other than those ending in *h*, *kṣaṇ*, or *ṇi*, and other than those ending in a vowel (*e*, *o*, or *ai*)—if its penultimate vowel is *a*, then that *a* optionally becomes *āt* before the *sic* suffix when it begins with a vowel (*iṭ*) and is followed by a non-*taṅ* (non-ātmanepada) affix. Examples: *arāṇīt*, *araṇīt*. Why "beginning with a consonant" (*halādeḥ*)? Consider: *mā bhavān aṭīt* ("may you not perish"). Why "penultimate" (*upāntasya*)? Consider: *arakṣīt* ("he protected"). Why "other than those ending in *h*, *kṣaṇ*, *ṇi*, or a vowel" (*aśvas-kṣaṇa-hmy-editaḥ*)? Consider: *aśvasīt* ("he breathed"), *akṣaṇīt* ("he sacrificed"); *agrahīt* ("he seized"), *avamīt* ("he vomited"), *avyayīt* ("he covered"); *aragīt* ("he sang"). Why "of the *a*" (*ataḥ*)? Consider: *akoṣīt* ("he was angry"). The rule applies only to roots ending in a consonant (*halaḥ*): consider *avadhīt* ("he killed"). [This concludes the rule] *vadavrajalraḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.8).

In the case of roots ending in *v* or *d*, and those ending in *r* that begin with a consonant, the vowel *a* is replaced by *āt* when followed by the suffix *sic* beginning with *iṭ* and so forth, because this is a mandatory (*nitya*) rule. Examples: *avādīt*, *avrājīt*; *acālīt*, *akṣārīt*. Only for those ending in *upadhā* [the penultimate vowel] does this apply: *aśvallīt*, *avabhrīt*.

By the rule *ñṇiti* (Pāṇini 6.1.9), when a suffix marked with *ñ* or *ṇ* follows, the vowel *a* of the penultimate syllable is replaced by *āt*. Examples: *pākaḥ*, *pācakaḥ*. Only for those ending in *upadhā* does this apply: *bhaṅgaḥ*, *bhañjakaḥ*.

*acaḥ* (6.1.10): When followed by an affix marked with *ñ* or *ṇ*, the *āṬ* augment is applied to the vowel immediately following the *ac*. Examples: *kārakaḥ*, *nāyakaḥ*, *lāvakaḥ*. As for the form *babhṛvā*, since the suffix *akac* is added invariably, the *āṬ* will not apply because it is separated from the root by the letter *v*. And in the case of a *kit* affix, when it does not denote descent (*apatya*), the *āṬ* augment is applied to the first of the vowels. (6.1.11)

When suffixes marked with *ṇ*, *ṇit*, or *kit* are applied in the sense of "offspring" (*apatya*) and so forth, the *āṭ* augment is added to the first vowel (*ac*) among those vowels of the base (*prakṛti*). Examples: *Dākṣiḥ*, *Plākṣiḥ*, *Aupagavaḥ*, *Aitikāyanaḥ*. Why specify "in the sense of offspring and so forth"? [Observe: *kaṇḍūyati*, *śithilayati*. Why specify "among the vowels" (*acām*)? So that it may apply even when the base begins with a consonant (*hal*). [Rule 6.1.12 applies: *devikā-śiṃśapā-dīrghasattra-śreyasām āt*.

When suffixes marked with *ñ*, *ṇ*, or *k* are applied in the sense of "offspring" (*apatya*) and so forth, the first vowel (*ac*) of the base words beginning with *devikā* becomes long (*āt*). Examples: *dāvikam udakam* ("water from the Devikā river"); *dāvikākūlāḥ śālayaḥ* ("rice growing on the banks of the Devikā"). *Pūrvadevikā* is the name of a village in the East; that which originates there is *pūrvaśāṃśapaḥ*. That which exists in a long sacrificial session (*dīrghasattra*) is *dārghasattram*. That which exists in what is excellent (*śreyasi*) is *śrāyasam*. The restriction "in the sense of offspring and so forth" is stated [in the rule] because: *devikīyati* ("he acts like the Devikā river"). How is it that the offspring of *Vahīnara* is *Vaihīnariḥ*? There is another base word, *vihīnara*. [Furthermore: For *kekaya*, *mitrayu*, and *pralaya*, the *iy* replaces the portion beginning with *y*. (Pāṇini 6.1.13)

In the case of *Kekaya* and others, when followed by an affix marked with *ṇ*, *ṇit*, or *kit*, the substitution of *ai* for the initial vowel (*ac*) is already established; however, for the constituent part beginning with *y*, the substitution of *iy* occurs. Thus we have *Kaikeyaḥ* and *Maitreyaḥ*. That which has come from the melting [of snow] is *prāleyaṃ* snow. Regarding the rule "before a suffix containing *aij*, *aic* is substituted for *y* and *v* at the end of a word" (Pāṇini 6.1.14): *Note:* This passage explains the application of Pāṇini’s rules concerning the formation of patronymics and derivatives from place names, specifically addressing the treatment of the initial vowels and the subsequent semi-vowels (*y* and *v*) when specific suffixes follow. It clarifies that while the general rule for the initial vowel replacement is already established, a specific modification applies to the *y* following the vowel. The example *prāleyam* illustrates the derivation from *pralaya* ("melting"), where the *y* is replaced by *iy*. The final sentence provides a reference to a grammatical rule governing the insertion of diphthongs (*aic*) before certain suffixes containing *aij*.

When suffixes marked with *ñ*, *ṇ*, or *k* are prescribed in the sense of "offspring" (*apatya*) and so forth, the vowels *ai* and *au* (*aic*) that precede the semivowels *y* and *v*—which arise from the substitution of *aij* for a vowel (*ac*)—become the forms *ai* and *au* when those semivowels stand at the end of a word. For example: *vaiyākaraṇaḥ* and *sauvaśvaḥ*. Why specify "arising from the substitution of *aij*"? Consider *dvyāśītikaḥ*. Here, because the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) is stated not to contain *aij* (by Pāṇini 6.1.26), the preceding member (*pūrvapada*) likewise lacks *aij*. Thus, the rule does not apply.

How is it that *pūrvatryalinde* becomes *pūrvatraiyalindaḥ*? Here too, because this *y*—standing in the final syllable of the compound—is a *y* substituted in place of the first vowel of the following member (*acām ādeḥ*) which is subject to the change into *aij*, the form indeed arises. Why [is the rule] "after *y* or *v*" (*yvoḥ*) stated? [Consider: *dvaimāturaḥ*. Why [is the rule] "from the end of a word" (*padāntāt*) stated? [Consider: *yataś chāttrāḥ* ("the students from where"), *yātāḥ* ("those who have gone"). [This applies to] *dvārādīnām* (Pāṇini 6.1.15).

Before suffixes marked with *ñ* or *ṇ* as indicatory letters (*it*), and before *k*-suffixes (*kit*), the vowels *ai* and *au* that precede *y* and *v* respectively undergo *vṛddhi*. Examples: *dvāre niyuktaḥ* (appointed at the gate) → *dauvārikaḥ*; *svaram adhikṛtya kṛto granthaḥ* (a treatise composed concerning accentuation) → *sauvaraḥ*; *vyalikaśe bhavaḥ* (existing in a thicket) → *vaiyalkaśaḥ*—this is established by the preceding rule itself [since it involves *vy-*, which begins with *v*]; *svastīty āha* (he says "may it be well") → *sauvastikaḥ*; *svarbhavam* (produced from accentuation) → *sauvam*.

By the rule *asaṃkhyānārācchaśvatositi* (Pāṇini 5.3.140, Gaṇapāṭha), there is elision of the final vowel and following consonants: *sauvargagamanikaḥ* means "one who speaks of going to heaven"; *sphaiyakṛtaḥ* is the descendant of *Sphyakṛt*; *sauvādumṛdavaḥ* is the descendant of *Svādumṛdu*; *śauvanam* means "belonging to a dog" (*śunaḥ*), where there is no elision when the suffix *aṇ* is applied. *Śauvam māṃsam* ("dog meat") is a modification (*vikāra*) of a dog, where elision occurs when the suffix *añ* is applied. *Śauvādaṃṣṭro maṇiḥ* ("a jewel found on a dog's fang") means "that which exists in a dog's fang" (*śvādaṃṣṭrāyām bhavaḥ*).

The lengthening of the vowel occurs by the rule *anyeṣām api* (Pāṇini 6.3.137): *śvaḥ-bhavaḥ* becomes *śauvastikaḥ* ("belonging to tomorrow"); *svasyedam* becomes *sauvam* ("belonging to one's own [village]"); *svagrāme bhavaḥ* becomes *sauvagrāmikaḥ* ("born in one's own village"). By the addition of the suffix *ṭhañ* according to the group beginning with *adhyātma* (Pāṇini 4.3.60), we have *svādhyāyena jayati* becoming *sauvādhyāyikaḥ* ("one who excels through his own study"). Although this would be established by the inclusion of the word *sva*, it does not apply here because of the specific listing of "one's own village" (*svagrāma*) and so on: thus, *svāpateyam* ("wealth") is formed. [Also, regarding the rule *nyagrodhasya kevalasya* (Pāṇini 6.1.16):]

When the uncompounded word *nyagrodha* is followed by an affix marked with *ñ*, *ṇ*, or *k*, the diphthongs *ai* and *au* (*aij*) are substituted for the vowel preceding the *y* before that affix. For example: *naiyagrodhaś camasaḥ* ("a ladle made from a banyan tree"). Why specify "of the [word] alone"? Consider: *nyāgrodhamūlāḥ śālayaḥ* ("rice growing at the roots of banyan trees"). This [sūtra] serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the rule of extension to the beginning of a compound (*tadādividhi*). On the view that words are derived (*vyutpattipakṣa*), it serves as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*); on the view that words are underived (*avyutpattipakṣa*), it serves as an original injunction (*vidhyartha*). [The sūtra] *na vyatihāre* (6.1.17) states:

when there is a mutual exchange of actions, the diphthongs *ai* and *au* (*aij*) are not substituted for the vowels preceding the *y* when that *y* is at the end of a word. Examples: *vyāvakrośī* ("mutual reviling"), *vyāvacarcī* ("mutual discussion"). [In these cases, the suffix] *ṇac* is applied according to 1.3.76, and from that, the suffix *aṇ* is applied according to 4.4.21.

Regarding *svāgatādīnām* (Pāṇini 6.1.18): for words beginning with *svāgata*, when followed by a suffix marked with *ñ* or *ṇ* or a *k*-suffix, the *aij* (the diphthongs *ai* and *au*) does not occur before the final syllable of the word. Examples: from *svāgatam ity āha* (he says "welcome"), we get *svāgatikaḥ*; from *svadhvareṇa carati* (he performs [the rite] well), we get *svādhvarikaḥ*; from *Svaṅgasyāpatyam* (the offspring of Svaṅga), we get *Svāṅgiḥ*; *Vyāṅgiḥ*; *Vyāḍiḥ*; and from *vyavahāreṇa carati* (he conducts business), we get *vyāvahārikaḥ*. Regarding *śvāder iti* (Pāṇini 6.1.19).

Before an affix beginning with *ñ*, *ṇ*, or *k* that has an indicatory *i* (*ñṇit*, *kit*), the substitution of *aij* (*ai* or *au*) does not occur for the *y* or *v* that precedes [the vowel] in the word *śvan* and others. For example: the descendant of *Śvabhastra* is *Śvābhastriḥ*; one who moves with a pack of dogs is *śvāgaṇikaḥ*. How is it that we have *Śvābhastram* meaning "belonging to Śvābhastrin"? Even though the *iñ* suffix has been elided, the prohibition caused by it still remains in effect. Why specify "before an affix" (*iti*)? Consider *śauvādaṃṣṭro maṇiḥ* ("a gem from a dog's fang"). Alternatively, by rule 6.1.20 (*padasya vā*), the substitution of *aij* does not optionally occur for the *y* or *v* preceding [the vowel] at the end of a word in *śvan* and others when followed by an affix having *ñ*, *ṇ*, or *k* as an indicatory letter. Thus: *śvāpadam* or *śauvāpadam*.

(6.1.21) *uttarasya*: When a suffix marked with Ñ or Ṇ follows, or when a suffix beginning with K or T follows, the first vowel (*ac*) among the vowels of the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) undergoes *vṛddhi*. This is also a governing rule (*adhikāra*). (6.1.22) *aṃśād ṛtoḥ*.

When a suffix beginning with *ñ*, *ṇ*, or a *k* follows a word denoting a part (*avayava*), which itself is followed by a word expressing the whole (*uttarapada*), the first vowel among the vowels of that [whole] undergoes *ādaic* substitution. Example: *pūrvavārṣikaḥ*. Here, the word *pūrva-* refers to the first part of the rainy season (*varṣāṇām*). Since a part may also be designated by the name of the whole, the term *pūrva-* is used for that portion. Thus, "those which are both *pūrva-* and *varṣāḥ*" forms a descriptive compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsaḥ*). Why is it said "from a part" (*aṃśāt*)? Consider: one who exists during the "former rains" (*pūrvavarṣāḥ*) when they are separated from other seasons; this is *paurvavarṣikaḥ*. Another example: *sauvarṣikaḥ*. [The rule continues:
"After *su-*, *sarva-*, and *ardha-*, [the final vowel of] a country name (*janapada*) [undergoes *ādaic* substitution]. (Pāṇini 6.1.23)

After the words *su*, *sarva*, and *ardha*, when followed by an affix marked with *ñ* or *ṇ* or by a *kṛt* affix, the initial vowel of the first syllable of a word denoting a country (*janapada*) is replaced by *ādaic*. Examples: *supāñcālakaḥ*, *sarvapāñcālakaḥ*, *ardhapāñcālakaḥ*.

Regarding the rule *amadrāṇāṃ diśaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.24): When followed by an affix marked with *ñ* or *ṇ* or by a *kṛt* affix, the initial vowel of the first syllable of a word denoting a country other than *Madra*—provided it follows a word denoting a direction (*dik*) as its prior member—is replaced by *ādaic*. Examples: *pūrvapāñcālakaḥ*, *uttarapāñcālakaḥ*. Why does the rule specify "not *Madra*" (*amadrāṇām*)? Consider: *paurvamadraḥ*.

(6.1.25) *prācāṃ grāmāṇām*: When followed by a suffix marked with *ñ* or *ṇ*, or by a *kit* suffix, the initial vowel of those words denoting eastern villages that follow words for directions undergoes *vṛddhi*. For example: *pūrvakārṣṇamṛttikaḥ*. Even though the whole compound *pūrvakṛṣṇamṛttika* denotes a village, its constituent part (*kṛṣṇamṛttika*) also denotes a village. Since cities are a specific type of village, the rule applies there as well: *pūrvapāṭaliputrakaḥ*. (6.1.26) *saṃkhyāyāḥ saṃvatsaraparimāṇasyāsaṃjñāśāṇakulijasya*: [The same applies] after a numeral denoting a measure of years, provided it is not a technical name (*saṃjñā*), nor is it *śāṇa* or *kulija*.

When a suffix beginning with *ñ* or *ṇ*, or one that is *kit*, follows, the *ādi-ādeśa* (the substitution of *ā*) occurs for the first vowel among the vowels of a word denoting a number, followed by a word for a year (*saṃvatsara*) or a measure (*parimāṇa*), provided it is not a technical name (*asaṃjñā*) and does not contain the elements *śāṇa* or *kulija*. Examples: *dvisāṃvatsarikaḥ* (lasting two years), *dvisauvarṇikaḥ* (weighing two *suvarṇas*), *dvisāptatikaḥ* (consisting of two groups of seventy), *dvināvatikaḥ* (consisting of two groups of ninety). Why say "not a technical name (*asaṃjñā*) and not containing *śāṇa* or *kulija*"? Consider: *pāñcalohitikam* (a field bought for five red cows—a technical name), *dvaiśāṇaḥ* (worth two *śāṇas*), *dvaikulijikaḥ* (worth two *kulijas*). [Note: This rule applies] except in the case of the word *varṣa* when used in the sense of "future" (*abhāvini*). (Pāṇini 6.1.27)

When a suffix marked with Ñ or Ṇ, or a KṬ suffix, follows a numeral and denotes something that is not yet to come (*abhāvin*), the *āṬ* augment is applied to the first vowel among the vowels of the word. For example: *dvābhyāṃ varṣābhyāṃ bhṛtaḥ adhīṣṭo vā* ("hired or commissioned for two years") becomes *dvivārṣikaḥ*. Why "not yet to come"? Consider: *trīṇi varṣāṇi bhāvi dhānyam* ("grain that will be produced in three years") becomes *traivarṣikam*. [Also, regarding the rule] *jāte proṣṭhabhadrāt padasya* (Pāṇini 6.1.28).

When the word *pada* follows the words *proṣṭha* or *bhadrā*, provided that a suffix with the markers *ñ*, *ṇ*, or *k* is applied in the sense of "born there" (*jāta*), the initial vowel among the vowels of the preceding word is replaced by *ādaic*. Examples: *Proṣṭhapadāsu jātaḥ* → *proṣṭhapādo brāhmaṇaḥ* ("A Brahmin born under the Proṣṭhapadā asterism"). *Bhadrapadāsu jātaḥ* → *bhadrapādaḥ*. Why is it said "born" (*jāta*)? [Counter-example: *Proṣṭhapadāsu bhavaḥ* → *prauṣṭhapado meghaḥ* ("A cloud existing under the Proṣṭhapadā asterism"). *Bhādrapadaḥ*. [Note: By Pāṇini 6.1.29, *hṛdbhagasindhoḥ pūrvasya ca*, the *vṛddhi* substitution also applies to the preceding vowel.]

When a suffix beginning with *ñ* or *ṇ*, or having *k* or *ṭ* as its marker (*ñṇit*, *kit*, *ṭit*), follows, the initial vowel of the first member and of the subsequent members such as *hṛd* and others undergoes *vṛddhi*. Examples: *sauhārdaṃ*, *saubhāgyaṃ*, *sāktusaindhavaḥ*. [In the last case], the suffix *aṇ* is applied because it belongs to the *kacchādi* group (Pāṇini 4.2.134). In the case of *sauhṛdaṃ*, the substitution of *hṛd* for *hṛdaya* occurs when the suffix *aṇ* follows (cf. Pāṇini 5.2.55); here, *hṛd* is not the subsequent member. This is according to the rule for the *anuśatikādi* group (Pāṇini 7.3.20).

In the *anuśatikādi* group, when a suffix beginning with *ñ*, *ṇ*, or *k* follows, the first vowel (*ac*) of both words is replaced by *ādaic*. Examples: *ānuśātikam* ("belonging to this *anuśatika*")—from *anuhoḍena carati* ("he acts according to the *anuhoḍa*"), [we derive] *ānuhauḍikaḥ*; *ānusāṃvatsarikaḥ* ("given every year")—from *anusaṃvatsare dīyate*; *āgāradhainavam* ("the offspring of a domestic cow")—from *agāradhenor apatyam*; *āsihātyam* ("produced by a sword-strike")—from *asihatyāyāṃ bhavam*; *āsyahātyaḥ* ("one who has a weapon-strike")—[this is derived] from *vimuktādibhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.2.155) with the suffix *aṇ*, because the word *asyahatya* does not exist [as a compound]; *āsyahātyaḥ* ("one for whom a weapon-strike is the purpose").

The suffix *haitika* is applied to this [word]; from this very statement, the suffix *ṭhañ* is added to the collection of words (*padasamudāya*), and there is elision (*aluk*) of the case-ending. Thus: the descendant of Vadhryoga is *Vādhryogaḥ*, by virtue of belonging to the *bidādi* group (Pāṇini 4.1.104); the descendant of Puṣkarasat is *Pauṣkarasādiḥ*; and the descendant of Anurāhata is *Ānurāhatiḥ*, by virtue of belonging to the *bāhvādi* group (Pāṇini 4.1.96)—namely, *Kaurukātyaḥ*.

By virtue of being included in the *gargādi* group (Pāṇini 4.1.105), the suffix *yañ* is applied: "born among the Kurus and Pañcālas" is *Kaurupāñcālaḥ*; "the offspring of Udakaśuddha" is *Audakaśauddhiḥ*; "existing in this world" is *aihaukikaḥ*; and "pertaining to the other world" is *pāralaukikaḥ*. By virtue of ending in *loka* (Pāṇini 4.3.26), the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied: "belonging to all men" is *sārvapauruṣam*; "the cause, conjunction, or portent relating to the whole earth" is *sārvabhaumaḥ*; and "existing in usage" is *prāyaugikaḥ*.

By [the rule] *adhyātmāditvāt* (Pāṇini 4.3.60), the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied: the offspring of another’s wife (*parastriyāḥ*) is *pārastraiṇeyaḥ*. By [the rule] *kalyāṇyāditvāt* (Pāṇini 4.1.126), the suffix *ḍhak* is replaced by *īnaṅ*: from *rājapuruṣa*, with the suffix *ṣyañ*, we have *rājapauruṣyam*. Why mention *ṣyañ*? [To show that it does not apply here: *rājapuruṣāyaṇiḥ*. By [the rule] *agotrād ādaijādyacaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.78), the suffix *phiñ* is applied: the offspring of Sūtranaḍa is *Sautranāḍiḥ*. And this is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open class).

The qualities [denoted by the suffix] are those worthy of being approached (*abhigamārhā guṇāḥ*); they are "approaching" (*ābhigāmikāḥ*). Regarding the divine (*adhideve bhavaḥ*), there is the *ādhidevika*; likewise, the *ādhibhautika*. There are exactly four sciences (*vidyāḥ*), which is *cāturvaidya*. In this way, *śātakaumbha* and so forth are also established. (6.1.31) *devatānāṃ cārthe sūktahaviṣoḥ*: When words denoting deities (*devatāśabda*) function as the meaning [of a compound], and when the meanings are a hymn (*sūkta*) or an oblation (*havis*), then before a suffix marked with *ñ*, *ṇ*, or *k*, the *āṭ* augment is applied to the first vowel of both members of the compound. For example: *āgnivāruṇaṃ havir vā* ("an oblation for Agni and Varuṇa"). Why specify "when the meanings are a hymn or an oblation"? [Consider: *skāndaviśākham* ("the section concerning Skanda and Viśākha").

*nendrasya parasya* (6.1.32): When the word *indra* occurs as a subsequent member [of a compound], the substitution of *aij* for the initial vowel of the preceding members does not take place before a suffix marked with *ñ*, *ṇ*, or *k*. Example: *āgnīndram*. Why "as a subsequent member"? Observe: *aindrāgnam*. *dīrghād varuṇasya* (6.1.33): [The substitution of *aij* for the initial vowel of the first member does not take place] when *varuṇa* follows a long vowel.

When followed by a *ñit*, a *ṇit*, or a *kit* suffix, the initial vowel (*ac*) of the word *Varuṇa* that follows a long vowel does not undergo substitution with *āT-aiC*. Example: *Maitrāvaruṇam*. Why say "after a long vowel"? Consider: *Āgnivāruṇam*.

Regarding the rule *prācāṃ nagarasya* (Pāṇini 6.1.34): when followed by a *ñit*, a *ṇit*, or a *kit* suffix, the initial vowel of the word *nagara* ("city") denoting a city located in the eastern region (*prāc*) undergoes substitution with *āT-aiC*, and the preceding vowel also undergoes such substitution.
