Examples: *Sauhmanāgaraḥ*, *Pauṇḍranāgaraḥ*. Why say "of the easterners" (*prācām*)? Consider: one born in the northern village of *Mādranagara* is called *Mādranagaraḥ*.

(6.1.35) *jaṅgaladhenubalajasya vā*: When *ñ*, *ṇit*, or *kit* suffixes follow, the first vowel among the vowels of the words beginning with *jaṅgala*, *dhenū*, and *balaja* optionally becomes *ādaic* (i.e., *ā*, *ai*, or *au*), while for the preceding [vowel], it is obligatory. Examples: *Kaurujāṅgalam* / *Kaurujaṅgalam*; *Vaiśvadhainavam* / *Vaiśvadhenavam*; *Sauvarṇabālajam* / *Sauvarṇabalajam*. (6.1.36) *ardhāt parimāṇasya pūrvasya tu vā*: When a measure (*parimāṇa*) follows the word *ardha*, the first vowel among the vowels of that [measure] optionally becomes *ādaic*. (The rule regarding the preceding vowel remains as before. Examples: *Ardhakhārīkam* / *Ardhakhārikam*. (Note: *Khārī* is a measure.)

When a suffix beginning with *ñ* or *ṇ* followed by *it*, or a suffix beginning with *k* or *t* follows, the vowels *ā*, *ai*, and *au* (*ādaic*) replace the first vowel of a word denoting a measure that follows after the word *ardha*; however, for the preceding [vowel], the replacement is optional. Examples: *ārdhadrauṇikaḥ* (half-a-droṇa), *ardhadrauṇikaḥ*.

By the rule *nātaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.37), when a suffix beginning with *ñ* or *ṇ* followed by *it*, or a suffix beginning with *k* or *t* follows, the augment *ān* is not added to the final *a* of a word denoting a measure that follows after the word *ardha*; however, for the preceding [vowel], the addition is optional. Examples: *ārdhaprasthikaḥ*, *ardhaprasthikaḥ*. Why is the phrase *taparaḥ* ("followed by *t*") used [in the sūtra]? Consider: *ardhakhāryāṃ bhavā* = *Ardhakhārī* (one who exists in half a khārī). If she is his wife, we have *Ardhakhārībhāryaḥ*. Here, by the rule *ādaij-hetur* (Pāṇini 5.2.36), the prohibition of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva-pratiṣedhaḥ*) applies.

*Prād vāhanasya ḍhe* (6.1.38): When the suffix *ḍha* follows, the vowel *ā* is substituted for the initial vowel of the word *vāhana* when it follows the word *pra*; however, for the preceding vowel, the substitution is optional. The offspring of *Pravāhaṇa* is *Prāvāhaṇeyaḥ* or *Pravāhaṇeyaḥ*. The suffix *ḍhak* is applied here because [the stem] belongs to the *śubhra* group (2.4.53). In the case of *pravāhaṇeyī bhāryā asya* ("one whose wife is a woman of the Pravāhaṇeya clan"), the form becomes *pravāhaṇeyībhāryaḥ*; this is so that the prohibition of the masculine treatment (*puṃvadbhāva*) may apply by the rule *ādaij jheḥ* (5.2.36). In the case of *pravāhaṇeyasya bhāvaḥ*, the form is *pravāhaṇeyakam*; here too, since the suffix *ḍha* follows, the option applies.

Pāṇini 6.1.39: *naño śucīśvarakṣetrajñakuśalanipuṇānām*. When *nañ* (the negative particle *a-*) precedes the words *śuci*, *īśvara*, *kṣetrajña*, *kuśala*, and *nipuṇa*, and when followed by an affix marked with *ñ* or *ṇ* or a *kit* affix, the first vowel among the vowels [of these words] becomes *ādic* (i.e., *ā*, *ai*, or *au*), while the preceding [vowel] optionally remains as it was. Examples: From *aśuci*: *āśaucam* (impurity), *aśaucam* (impurity). From *anīśvara*: *ānaiśvaryam*, *anaiśvaryam* (lack of sovereignty). From *akṣetrajña*: *ākṣaitrajñyam*, *akṣaitrajñyam* (lack of self-knowledge). Here, the suffix *ṣyañ* is applied in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*) because the word is listed in the *brāhmaṇādi* group (Pāṇini 4.1.141). From *akuśala*: *ākauśalam*, *akauśalam* (inability). From *anipuṇa*: *ānaipuṇam*, *anaipuṇam*, *anaipuṇyam* (lack of skill). In these cases, the suffixes *ṣyañ* and others are applied according to the rules in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*) derived from the meaning of the other member of the compound (*anyapadārtha*).

What is "not according to reality" (*ayāthātathyam*), [meaning] "unreality" (*āyathātathyam*)? That which is not as it truly is (*yathātatham*) is "not as it truly is" (*ayathātatham*). The state of being "not as it truly is" is "unreality" (*āyathātathyam*). The state of being "as it truly is" is "reality" (*yāthātathyam*). That which is not reality is "unreality" (*ayāthātathyam*). In the same way, there is "unfoundedness" (*āyathāpuryam*), [meaning] "unfoundedness" (*ayāthāpuryam*). [The rule *hanas to 'ciṇṇaloḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.40) applies.]

In place of the final letter of the root *han*, there is the substitution of *t* when followed by any suffix beginning with a *ñ* or *ṇ* consonant, provided that it is not the *ciṇ* or *ṇal* affixes. Examples: *ghātayati*, *ghātakaḥ*, *sādhughātī*, *ghātaṃ ghātam*, *ghāto vartate*. Why specify "not *ciṇ* or *ṇal*"? Observe: *aghāni*, *jaghāna*. Regarding the rule *āto yug aṇali* (Pāṇini 6.1.41): after a verbal root ending in long *ā*, the augment *yuk* is inserted before the *ṇal* affix and any other suffix beginning with a *ñ* or *ṇ* consonant. Examples: *dāyaḥ*, *dhāyaḥ*; *dāyakaḥ*, *dhāyakaḥ*. [Note: Regarding *adāyi*, the author will state the *puk* augment later (6.1.45). Why specify "not *ṇal*"? Observe: *dadau*, *dadhau*.

Pāṇini 6.1.42: *maḥ seṭo 'nāvamyamikāmacāma-viśramāṇām*. When a suffix beginning with *ñ* or *ṇ* follows, that which has been prescribed for a root ending in *m* does not apply if the root is *seṭ* (having an indicatory *iṭ*) and excludes *vām*, *amik*, *āmac*, and *viśram*. Examples: *śamaḥ*, *damaḥ*; *śamakaḥ*, *damakaḥ*; *aśami*, *adami*. Why "ending in *m*" (*maḥ*)? Consider *pāṭhaḥ*, *pāṭhakaḥ*. Why "having an indicatory *iṭ*" (*seṭaḥ*)? Consider *yāmaḥ*, *yāmakaḥ*, *rāmakaḥ*. Why exclude *vām*, *amik*, *āmac*, and *viśram*? Consider: *vāmaḥ*, *vāmakaḥ*, *avāmi*; *āmaḥ*, *āmakaḥ*, *āmi*; *kāmaḥ*, *kāmakaḥ*, *akāmi*; *ācāmaḥ*, *ācāmakaḥ*, *ācāmi*; *viśrāmaḥ*, *viśrāmakaḥ*, *vyaśrāmi*.

The rule *aṇ al* applies here: [the suffix] *aṇ* is elided. How is it established that *udyamaḥ* and *uparamaḥ* are formed? They are established by means of a specific grammatical injunction (*nipātana*), based on the roots *aḍ* in the sense of "exertion" (*udyama*) and *yam* in the sense of "cessation" (*uparama*) (Dhātupāṭha 1.131, 296).

Regarding the rule *janivadhor ñṇiti* (Pāṇini 6.1.43), that which was prescribed for the roots *jan* and *vadh* when followed by a suffix marked with *ñ* or *ṇ* does not apply here. Thus: *janaḥ*, *janakaḥ*, *ajani*; *vadhaḥ*, *vadhakaḥ*, *avadhi*. The rule *aṇ al* applies here as well: *jajāna*, *vavādha*.
*mer ṇali vā* (Pāṇini 6.1.44):

*svikā*, *svakā*; *asvikā*, *asvakā*. (6.1.78) *Āśiṣi*: When a benediction (*āśis*) is implied, the substitution of *it* does not take place. For example: *jīvatāt*, *jīvakā*; *nandatāt*, *nandakā*.
(6.1.79) *Kṣipakādīnām*: [The feminine suffix *ṭāp* is applied after these words].
The substitution of *it* does not occur for *kṣipakā* and others: *kṣipakā*, *dhuvakā*, *eḍakā*, *caṭakā*, *devakā*.
Regarding *tārakā* when it denotes a star (*jyotis*): the form *tārakā* is prescribed as an irregularity (*nipātana*) when a star is to be expressed. Any other [meaning] is *tārikā*.

*varṇaka* [is used] in the sense of *tāntava* (6.1.81): *varṇaka* is an irregularly formed word (*nipātita*) when a woven textile (*tāntava*) is to be expressed; otherwise it is *varṇikā*. *aṣṭakā* [is used] in the sense of the ancestors (*pitṛṇām*) (6.1.82).

The form *aṣṭakā* is an irregularly formed (*nipātita*) word when it refers to that which is related to the ancestors (*pitṛ-sambandhinī*). In other cases, it is *aṣṭikā khārī*. Regarding the rule *cajoḥ ku ghiṇnyatoḥ* (6.1.83): when a suffix beginning with *ghi* or *ṇyat* follows, the substitute *kavarga* (the guttural series) takes the place of the sounds *c* and *j*. Thus: *pākaḥ*, *rāgaḥ*, *tyāgaḥ*; and *pākyam*, *vākyam*, *vyaṅgyam*.

*nyaṅkvādayaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.84): Words such as *nyaṅku* and others are established as irregular forms (*nipātana*) with the substitution of *kutva* (the change of *s* to *ṣ*). These are: *nyaṅku*, *madgu*, *bhṛgu*, *takram*, *vakram*, *okas*, *dṛk*, *meghaḥ*, *arghaḥ*, *nidāghaḥ*, *avadāghaḥ*. [In the case of] *vyatiṣaṅgaḥ*, *avasargaḥ*, *vyatibhaṅgaḥ*, and *anuṣaṅgaḥ*, they will end in the suffix *gha*, because the rule of "diversity" (*bahulādhikāra*) permits it even when the agent (*kartṛ*) is expressed.

For this very reason, the suffix *añ* will not be applied after these words: *śvapākaḥ*, *māṃsapākaḥ*, *ulūkapākaḥ*, and *kapotapākaḥ*; rather, there will be a compound with the word *pāka*. Regarding *dūrepākuḥ*, *kṣaṇepākuḥ*, and *phalepākuḥ*, these are correctly formed because they belong to the *auṇādika* group. [The word] *nyagrodhaḥ* is derived from the sense "it grows downwards" (*nyag ruṇaddhi*); it is a plant (*vīrut*), and its long vowel is established by Pāṇini 6.3.137 (*anyeṣām api*). Therefore, the substitution of *dha* for *ha* in these two cases need not be explicitly stated. By Pāṇini 6.1.85 (*ñṇinni hano haḥ*), the substitution of *gh* for the *h* of the root *han* occurs when followed by an affix marked with *ñ*, *ṇ*, or the letter *n*. Thus we have *ghātaḥ*, *ghātakaḥ*, and *ghnanti*. However, the form *hananīyakaḥ* does not occur because of the intervention [of other elements].

(6.1.86) *dvitvahetau*: When a cause for reduplication follows, the substitution of *k* occurs for the *h* of the root *han*. Examples: *jaṅghanyate*, *jighāṃsati*. The form *jihananīyiṣati* does not occur because of the intervention [of other elements]. (6.1.87) *her acaṅi*: [The substitution of *k* occurs for the *h* of *hi* when followed by a cause for reduplication], except when *caṅ* follows.

When a cause for reduplication follows, provided that *acaṅ* does not intervene, the substitution of *ku* occurs for the root *hi*. Examples: *prajighāya*, *prajighīṣati*. Why "provided that *acaṅ* does not intervene"? Consider *prājīhayat*. Since the rule would have been established even when *ṇi* intervenes, the prohibition by the phrase "provided that *acaṅ* does not intervene" indicates that the substitution of *ku* occurs elsewhere even when *ṇi* intervenes, provided it is a cause for reduplication:
*prajighāyayiṣati*. [Also applies] *jeḥ sani liṭi ca* (Pāṇini 6.1.88).

The substitution of *k* for the *j* of the root *ji* occurs when the suffixes *san* or *liṭ* follow. Examples: *jigīṣati*, *jigāya*. Why is it specified "when *san* or *liṭ* follow"? [Consider: *jejīyate*. Why does this not occur here in *jijyatuḥ* and *jijyuḥ*? Because they are derived forms (*lākṣaṇikatvāt*). For these forms arise from the root *jināti* when the semivowel *y* has been replaced by *i*. Or, according to 6.1.89, the substitution of *k* optionally occurs for the *c* of the root *ci* when *san* or *liṭ* follow. Examples: *cikīṣati*, *cicīṣati*; *cikāya*, *cicāya*. Only when *san* or *liṭ* follow: *ceccīyate*.
(6.1.90) *na kvādeḥ*:
The substitution of *k* for *g* does not occur after a verbal root beginning with the *ka*-group (the gutturals). For example: *kūjaḥ*, *kūjyam*; *kharjaḥ*, *kharjyam*.
(6.1.91) *ajivrajoḥ*.

The substitution of *ku* for *j* does not occur after the roots *aj*, *vraj*, *samāja*, *udāja*, *parivrāj*, and *parivrājya*. How is the form *bhuja* derived? It will be formed from the root *bhuj* with the suffix *ka*. An instrument (*karaṇa*) may also be intended as the agent (*kartṛ*). How is *nyubja* derived? It will be formed with the suffix *ac* when denoting the agent. *Bhoga* is formed with the suffix *ghañ*; *abhyudga* and *samudga* will be formed from the root *gam* with the suffix *ḍa*. Regarding *vañc* in the sense of "going" (Pāṇini 6.1.92): when the sense of "going" is understood, the substitution of *ku* for *j* does not occur. For example: *vañcyam vañcanti vaṇijaḥ* ("the merchants go by the way they should avoid"). Why specify "in the sense of going"? [Consider: *vaṅkaṃ kāṣṭham* ("crooked wood"); the meaning here is "curved."

Regarding the rule *ṇya āvaśyake* (Pāṇini 6.1.93): when the suffix *ṇya* follows, the substitution of *ku* (i.e., *k*) for the palatal does not occur if the meaning is "necessary" (*āvaśyaka*). For example: *pācyam* (to be cooked), *avaśyapācyam* (necessarily to be cooked); *mocyam* (to be released), *avaśyamocyam* (necessarily to be released). Why specify "when necessary"? Consider *pākyam* (to be cooked [as a possibility]). Regarding the rule *ṛcarucayācatyajām* (Pāṇini 6.1.94): [the substitution of *ku* does not occur] after roots ending in *ṛ*, or after *ruca*, *yāca*, and *tyaja*.

The substitution of *k* for the semivowel (*ṛ*) in the roots *ṛc* and others does not occur when the suffix *ṇya* follows. For example: *arcyam*, *rocyam*, *yācyam*, *tyājyam*. It is precisely because of this [rule] that the suffix *ṇya* is applied after the root *ṛc*.
Regarding *vaco ’śabdākhyāyām* (Pāṇini 6.1.95):

when the suffix *ṇya* follows the root *vac*, the substitution of *k* does not occur provided that "not being a name" (*aśabdākhyā*) is understood. For example: *vācyam*, *pravācyam*. Why is it said "not being a name"? Consider: *vākyam*.

*prayojya-niyojyau śakye* (Pāṇini 6.1.96): These two words, *prayojya* and *niyojya*, are irregularly formed (*nipātita*) when they have the sense of "capable" (*śakya*). [Examples: *prayoktuṃ śakyaḥ* = *prayojyaḥ*; *niyoktuṃ śakyaḥ* = *niyojyaḥ*. Why "capable"? [Counter-examples: *prayogyaḥ*, *niyogyaḥ*. *bhojyam anne* (Pāṇini 6.1.97).

The word *bhojya* is an irregularly formed term (*nipātana*) when the object to be expressed is food. Examples: *bhojya odanaḥ* (food that is to be eaten), *bhojyā yavāgūḥ* (gruel that is to be eaten). Why "food"? [Counter-example: *bhogyaḥ kambalaḥ* (a woolen blanket to be used/enjoyed). Regarding *yaj* [in Pāṇini 6.1.98]: the substitution of *k* for *j* in the root *yaj* does not occur diversely (*bahulam*). Examples: *yājyam*, *prayājyam*, *patnīsaṃyājaḥ*, *upāṃśuyājaḥ*, *ṛtuyājaḥ*; [with the regular form: *yāgaḥ*, *prayāgaḥ*, *anuyāgaḥ*.
*Olopaḥ śye* (Pāṇini 6.1.99):
When *śya* follows, the elision (*lopa*) of the vowel *o* occurs. Example: from *do*, *avadyati*; from *so*, *avasyati*. *Kṣasyāci* (Pāṇini 6.1.100).

When a *kṣa* sound follows a vowel (*aj*), the final [consonant] of the root is elided. Examples: *adhukṣātām*, *adhukṣi*. Why does it say "when a vowel follows" (*aci*)? Consider: *adhukṣat*. Alternatively, there is elision (*lug*) of the final consonant of the roots *duh*, *diha*, *liha*, and *guh* before an affix marked with *taṅ* that begins with a dental (*dantya*). (Pāṇini 6.1.101)

When the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) endings follow the roots *duh* and others, there is optionally the elision (*luk*) of the suffix *kṣa*. The mention of *luk* is for the purpose of total elision [of the suffix]. Examples: *adugdha*, *adhukṣata*; *adugdhāḥ*, *adhukṣathāḥ*; *adugdhvam*, *adhukṣadhvam*; *aduhvahi*, *adhukṣāvahi*; *adigdha*, *adhikṣata*; *alīḍha*, *alikṣata*; *nyagūḍha*, *nyaghukṣata*. Why "of *duh* and others"? Consider: *vyatyamukṣata*. Why "when *taṅ* follows"? Consider: *adhukṣat*. Why "dental" (*dantya*)? Consider: *adhukṣāmahi*. (Regarding Pāṇini 6.1.102:
"In the case of the eight roots beginning with *śam*, there is lengthening of the vowel before the suffix *śya*."

In the case of the eight roots beginning with *śam*, a long vowel occurs before the suffix *śya*. [Examples: *śāmyati*, *dāmyati*, *tāmyati*, *śrāmyati*, *bhrāmyati*, *kṣāmyati*, *klāmyati*, *mādyati*. Why "of the eight"? [Counter-example: *asyati*. Why "before *śya*"? [Counter-example: *bhramati*.

Regarding the rule *ṣṭhivuklamācamāṃ śiti* (Pāṇini 6.1.103): a long vowel occurs before a *śit* suffix after the roots *ṣṭhivu*, *klam*, and *ācam*. [Examples: *ṣṭhīvati*, *klāmati*, *ācāmati*. Why is the inclusion of the prefix *āṅ* mentioned? [Counter-example: *camati*.

*ataṅāne* (Pāṇini 6.1.104): When *śit* affixes follow the root *kram*, a long vowel occurs [in place of the radical vowel] provided that it is not in the *ātmanepada*. Examples: *krāmati*, *krāman*. Why "not in the *ātmanepada*"? [Consider: *ākramate sūryaḥ*; *ākramamāṇaḥ sūryaḥ*. [The rule] *iṣugamiyamāṃ chaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.105) [applies].

After the roots *iṣu* and others, when followed by a suffix beginning with *ś*, the substitution of *ch* occurs: *icchati*, *gacchati*, *yacchati*. Why is the mention of the vowel *u* included [in the rule]? [To exclude cases such as] *iṣyate* and *iṣṇāti*. Furthermore, this substitution does not occur after the root *paryeṣ* (*pari-iṣ*). [The following rule applies:

For the roots *pā*, *ghrā*, *dhmā*, *sthā*, *mnā*, *dāṇ*, *dṛś*, *śas*, and *sad*, there are the substitutions *piba*, *jighra*, *dhama*, *tiṣṭha*, *mana*, *yaccha*, *paśya*, *śīya*, and *sīda* respectively. (Pāṇini 6.1.106)

When a *śit* affix follows, the substitutes *piba-* and so forth occur in place of [the roots] *pā-* and the rest. Because *pib-* ends in an *ad-* vowel, the substitution of *adeṅ* does not take place. Thus: *pibati*, *jighrati*, *dhamati*, *tiṣṭhati*, *manati*, *yacchati*, *paśyati*, *śīyate*, *śīdati*. How is it that [the forms] *ṛcchati* and *dhāvati* are formed? Because they belong to different verbal roots (*prakṛtyantara*). There will be no usage of the root *ṛ* with a *śit* affix, because, like *gharati* and others, its scope is restricted. As for the root *sṛ*, [the forms] *visarati* and *prasaratī* are established by the absence of such a substitute. [The rule] *jñājanor jāḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.107) [applies].
The substitution of *jā* occurs for the roots *jñā* and *jan* when followed by a *śit* affix. Thus: *jānāti*, *jāyate*.

By the rule *pvādīnāṃ hrasvaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.108), a short vowel is substituted for the roots beginning with *pū* when followed by a *śit* affix. Thus: *punāti*, *lunāti*. The roots beginning with *pū* extend up to the end of the *gaṇa*. How is it that [the form] *jānāti* is derived? It is because of the explicit mention of the long vowel in the rule *jñājanor jā* (Pāṇini 6.1.107).

In the case of the root *mid*, the vowel *i* is replaced by *e* when followed by an affix beginning with a *śit* letter. Thus: *medyati*, *pramedyati*. This rule is formulated to set aside the prohibition [of *e* for *i*].
The first quarter (*pāda*) of the sixth chapter is completed.

*iko ‘deṅ kriyārthāyāḥ* (Pāṇini 6.2.1): For a verbal root ending in *ik* that has another action as its purpose (*kriyārthā*), the vowels *a*, *e*, and *o* (*adeṅ*) are substituted [for the final *ik*]. Examples: *kartā*, *cetā*, *stotā*. Here, by proximity (*pratyāsatti*), the substitution of *ai* occurs for the vowel *i*, the substitution of *au* for the vowel *u*, and, by elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), the substitution of *ā* for the vowel *ṛ*. Why does the rule specify *ika*? Consider: *yānam*, *mlāyati*, *umbhitā*. Why does the rule specify *kriyārthāyāḥ*? Consider: *vāyubhiḥ*, *paṭutaraḥ*, *agnikāmyati*. *uśnoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.2.2).

The *eṅ* vowels (*e* and *o*) are substituted for the *u* prescribed by *prakṛti*, as well as for the *śnu* suffix. Thus: *karoti*, *cinoti*. How then [is it explained] in the case of *taruḥ* and *madguḥ*? Because of their association with *śnu*, only the *vikaraṇa* suffix is understood here. Regarding *juspukoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.59): when *jus* or a *pu*-ending suffix follows, *eṅ* vowels are substituted for *ik* vowels. Thus: *abibhayuḥ*, *abibharuḥ*, *ajuhavuḥ*; *hrepayati*, *knopayati*. Only when referring to *ik* vowels: *anenijuḥ*, *yāpayati*. How then [is it explained] in the case of *cinuyuḥ*? Here there are two prohibitions: one based on the *apit* [suffix] and one based on the *yāsuṭ* [augment].

(6.2.4) *laghor upāntasya*: For a light penultimate vowel that is an *adeṅ* (a, e, o), the substitutes [of the third person singular] occur. Examples: *vartitā*, *bhettā*, *boddhā*, *yoddhā*. Why "for a light [penultimate]"? [Counter-example: *dhūpitā*. Why "for a penultimate"? [Counter-example: *ruṇaddhi*. Only when there is a sense of purpose (*kriyārthāya*) [does the rule apply]: [in the absence thereof, as in] *kāṣṭhabhidbhyām*. (6.2.5) *sṛjidṛśor jhaly am*: For the roots *sṛj* and *dṛś*, the augment *am* is inserted before a suffix beginning with *jhali*.

The augment *am* is inserted after the roots *sṛj* and *dṛś* when followed by an affix beginning with a consonant (*jhal*). Thus: *sraṣṭā*, *sraṣṭum*; *draṣṭum*. How is it that [the forms] *asrākṣīt* and *adrākṣīt* occur? This rule is an exception to the substitution of *adeṅ* (P. 1.1.2); however, the substitution of *ādaic* does indeed take place. Why say "when followed by a consonant" (*jhal*)? [Because otherwise] *sarjanam* and *darśanam* would result. Due to the prohibition regarding *kṅit* affixes (P. 1.1.5), we have *sṛṣṭam* and *dṛṣṭam*. The condition "for the sake of an action" (*kriyārthāyāḥ*) applies here as well: thus, *rajjusṛḍbhyām*.
Regarding the roots *spṛś*, *mṛś*, *kṛṣ*, *tṛp*, *dṛp*, and *sṛp*, the augment is optional (P. 6.2.6).

The augment *am* optionally occurs before an affix beginning with a *jhal* consonant after the roots *spr̥ś* and others. Thus: *spraṣṭā*, *sparṣṭā*; *mraṣṭā*, *marṣṭā*; *kraṣṭā*, *karṣṭā*; *traptā*, *tarptā*; *draptā*, *darptā*; *sraptā*, *sarptā*. [The rule applies] only when a *jhal* follows: *sparśanam*. [The rule applies] only when the root expresses an action (*kriyārtha*): *ghr̥taspr̥gbhyām*.
[The augment does not occur] after a reduplicated root, except in the *aliṭ* (non-aorist) tense: (Pāṇini 6.1.8).

That which has been prescribed for a reduplicated root with a light penultimate vowel when followed by an affix beginning with a vowel, excluding the *liṭ* (perfect), does not take place. For example: *nenijāni*, *anenijam*. Why "of a reduplicated [root]" (*dviruktasya*)? Observe: *vedāni*, *avedam*. Why "beginning with a vowel" (*aci*)? Observe: *nenekti*. Why "excluding the *liṭ*" (*aliṭi*)? Observe: *nineja*. Only when it is "penultimate" (*upāntasya*): observe *juhavāni*.
[This rule applies] even before a *tiṅ* or a *śit* affix, including the *āśīr-liṅ* (precative). (Pāṇini 6.1.8)

When a *tiṅ* or a *śit* affix—excluding the *liṅ* used for benediction (*āśīrliṅ*)—follows, an *ik* vowel that is not *eṅ* does not undergo substitution. Examples: *cinutaḥ*, *cinvanti*, *bibhidatuḥ*, *bibhiduḥ*; *tudati*, *nudati*; *cinvīta*. Why specify "when a *tiṅ* or a *śit* follows"? Consider *kartā*. Why specify "excluding the *liṅ* used for benediction"? Consider *tarati*, *bibheda*, *ceṣīṣṭa*. How is it that [the rule] does not apply in *babhūva* and *babhūvitha*? Because the *vuK* augment is obligatory, once it has been applied, the presence of the letter *v* acts as an intervention, and thus the rule will not apply. [This is governed by] *jāgur aliṭi* (Pāṇini 6.2.9).

When a *tiṅ* or a *śit* affix follows, except for the *aliṭ*, the vowels *e*, *ai*, and *o* do not occur in place of *ā*. Examples: *jāgṛtaḥ*, *jāgṛthaḥ*; *jāgrat*. Why "except for the *aliṭ*"? [Consider: *jajāgaratuḥ*, *jajāgaruḥ*. Why "when a *tiṅ* or a *śit* affix follows"? [Consider: *jāgaritā*. Why "except for the *āśīrliṅ* (optative)"? [Consider: *jāgarti*, *jāgariṣīṣṭa*. [This rule applies] when *ciṇ*, *ṇal*, or *ṅit* affixes follow (Pāṇini 6.4.63).

In the domain of *ciṇ* and *ṇal*, and in the domain of *aṅ* as well as in the domain of the prohibitive *kṅit*, the substitutes *at*, *eṅ*, and *oṅ* do not occur for the root *jāgarti*. Thus: *ajāgāri*, *jajāgāra*, *jāgṛyāt*. How is *jāgṛviḥ* formed? It will not [be subject to this rule] because it is derived from the *uṇādi* suffixes (*auṇādika*). Why "in these"? [Consider: *jāgarayati*, *jāgarakaḥ*, *jāgaraḥ*, *jāgaritaḥ*, *jāgaryāt*. Regarding the rule *kṅiti* (Pāṇini 6.4.11):

when *kit* or *ṅit* affixes follow, the *ik* vowels of the base (*prakṛti*) do not undergo the substitutions *at*, *eṅ*, and *oṅ*. Examples: *kṛtam*, *jitam*, *śuddham*, *buddham*. [Examples with *ṅit* affixes: *narīnṛtyate*, *cecīyate*, *toṣṭūyate*, *lolūyate*.

(6.2.12) *Atiṅy āc ca tallope*: When there is the elision of *ta* following an affix that is not a verbal root (*atiṅ*), and when there is the elision of *iK* or *ṅit*, the substitutions for *eC* do not occur, nor does [the substitution] for *aC*. In the case of the elision of *yaK*: *kusubhitā*, *magadhakaḥ*. In the case of the elision of *kyac*: *samidhitā*. In the case of the elision of *yaṄ*: *loluvaḥ*, *popuvaḥ*, *cecyah*, *dedyah*, *nenyah*, *marīmṛjah*, *bebhiditā*. Why say "not after a verbal root" (*atiṅi*)? [Consider: *roravīti*. [Note: In the case of *nikucitam*, there is a prohibition based on the fact that the suffix is *kit*. (6.2.13) *Kuṭādīnām añṇiti*: For the roots beginning with *kuṭ*, [the substitution of *guṇa* occurs] except before an affix marked with *Ṇ* or *ṆIT*.

When followed by another suffix marked with *ñ* or *ṇ*, the vowels *a*, *e*, and *o* (*adeṅ*) do not occur for roots beginning with *kuṭ*. For example: *utkuṭitā*, *utkuṭitum*, *utkuṭitavyam*; *utpuṭitā*, *utpuṭitavyam*. Why does the rule specify "not when marked with *ñ* or *ṇ*" (*añṇiti*)? Consider: *utkoṭaḥ*, *utpoṭakaḥ*. Regarding the rule *vija iṭi* (Pāṇini 6.1.19): when followed by a suffix beginning with *iṭ*, the vowels *a*, *e*, and *o* do not occur for the root *vij*. For example: *udvijitā*, *udvijitum*, *udvijitavyam*. Why does the rule specify "when *iṭ* follows" (*iṭi*)? Consider: *udvejanam*.
(6.2.15) *vorṇoḥ*: After the root *ūrṇu*, when followed by an affix beginning with *iṭ*, the substitution of *adeṅ* does not optionally take place. Examples: *prorṇavitā*, *prorṇuvitā*.

(6.2.16) *tatanator apūśīsvidimidikṣvididhṛṣaḥ*: [The substitution of *adeṅ* does not take place] after the roots *tan*, *tan*, *pū*, *śī*, *svid*, *mid*, *kṣvid*, *dhṛṣ*, when followed by an affix beginning with *iṭ*.

The substitution of *e* and *o* (*adeṅ*) does not occur for roots beginning with *pū* and others—excluding those starting with *pū*—when followed by the augment *iṭ* and the suffixes *ktvā* and *kta*. For example: *tṛṣitaḥ*, *tṛṣitavān*; *ruṣitaḥ*, *ruṣitavān*. Why is there an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of the group beginning with *pvā*? [Examples: *pavitaḥ*, *pavitavān*; *śayitaḥ*, *śayitavān*; *prasveditaḥ*, *prasveditavān*; *prameditaḥ*, *prameditavān*; *prakṣveditaḥ*, *prakṣveditavān*; *dharṣitaḥ*, *dharṣitavān*. The rule applies only when the augment *iṭ* is present: *pūtaḥ*, *prasvinnaḥ*. [Note: Pāṇini 6.2.17 states that the substitution of *e* and *o* occurs for the root *mṛṣ* when it means "not enduring" (*akṣāntau*).]

The vowels *a* and *eṅ* do not occur after the roots *kṣam*, *mṛṣ*, and *tṛ* when followed by the suffixes *iṭ* and others (*ktvā*, *kta*, etc.). [Examples: He spoke words that were not forgotten (*apamṛṣitam*). Why say "except in the sense of forbearance" (*akṣāntau*)? [Counter-examples: Forborne (*marṣitaḥ*), he has forborne (*marṣitavān*). [Vārttika 6.2.18: The vowel *u* is substituted for the penultimate vowel of the root *śvi* when it denotes a state or an action, optionally.

In the case of a verbal root ending in *u* or *ū*, when the suffixes *ta* and *tavat* follow—whether they begin with the augment *iṭ* or not—the vowels *a*, *e*, or *o* (*adeṅ*) do not optionally occur [in place of the radical vowel] before the past passive participle (*kta*) or the active past participle (*ktavat*), provided that the root ends in a consonant (*śabvat*). Examples: *dyutitam* anena, *dyotitam* anena. *pradyutitaḥ*, *pradyotitaḥ*. Why "ending in *u* or *ū*" (*udupāntasya*)? *sveditam* anena, *prasveditaḥ*. Why "ending in a consonant" (*śabvataḥ*)? *gudhitam* anena, *pragudhitaḥ*. Why "in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*) or the beginning of an action" (*bhāvārambhayoḥ*)? *rucitā* kanyā ("the girl has been pleased"). [The substitution occurs] only before the augment *iṭ*: *rūḍham* anena, *prarūḍhaḥ*. [Note: Pāṇini 6.2.19 states: "In the case of the roots *mṛḍ*, *mṛd*, *gudh*, *kuṣ*, *kliś*, *vad*, *vas*, *luc*, and *grah*, [the long vowel is substituted] before the suffix *ktvā*."

In the case of the roots *mṛḍ* and others, when the suffix *ktvā* follows with the augment *iṭ*, the vowels *a* and *eṅ* do not occur. Examples: *mṛḍitvā*, *mṛditvā*, *gudhitvā*, *kuṣitvā*, *kliśitvā*, *uditvā*, *uṣitvā*, *lucitvā*, *gṛhītvā*. Why specify "of *mṛḍ* and others"? [To exclude: *devitvā*, *pavitvā*. Why specify "with the augment *iṭ*"? [To exclude: *pūtvā*. (6.2.20) *ṛta-tṛṣa-mṛṣa-kṛśāṃ vā*:

For the roots *ṛt* and others, when the suffix *ktvā* follows with the augment *iṭ*, the vowels *a* and *eṅ* optionally do not occur. Examples: *ṛtitvā* or *artitvā*; *tṛṣitvā* or *tarṣitvā*; *mṛṣitvā* or *marṣitvā*; *kṛśitvā* or *karśitvā*.

Pāṇini 6.2.21: *ralo halāder idutoḥ sani ca* (After a verbal root ending in *ra* or *la*, beginning with a consonant, the vowels *i* and *u* do not optionally undergo the substitution of *e* and *o* [the *adeṅ* rule] before the suffix *ktvā* when it begins with *iṭ*, nor before the desiderative suffix *san*. Examples: *likhitvā*, *lekhitvā*; *lilikhiṣati*, *lilekhiṣati*. *dyutitvā*, *dyotitvā*; *didyutiṣate*, *didyotiṣate*. Why "ending in *ra* or *la*" (*rala*)? Consider *devitvā*, *dideviṣati* (where the root ends in a vowel). Why "beginning with a consonant" (*halādeḥ*)? Consider *eṣitvā*, *eṣiṣiṣati* (where the root begins with a vowel). Why "of *i* and *u*" (*idutoḥ*)? Consider *vartitvā*, *vivartiṣate* (where the vowel is *ṛ*). The restriction "before *iṭ*" (*iṭi*) applies as well: *bhuktvā*, *bubhukṣate*. Pāṇini 6.2.22: *rudavidamuṣagrahām* (The substitution of *e* and *o* for *i* and *u* does not occur after the roots *rud*, *vid*, *muṣ*, and *grah* before the suffix *ktvā* when it begins with *iṭ*, nor before the desiderative suffix *san*.)

In the case of roots beginning with *rud*, when a suffix beginning with *iṭ* follows, as well as the suffix *san* or *ktvā*, the vowels *a* and *eṅ* do not undergo substitution. Examples: *ruditvā*, *rurudiṣati*; *viditvā*, *vividiṣati*; *muṣitvā*, *mumuṣiṣati*; *gṛhītvā*. Regarding the suffix *san*, there is no example [of this rule applying] because of the absence of *iṭ*.

By the rule *iko 'niṭi* (Pāṇini 6.1.23), when a suffix beginning with *san* that does not take *iṭ* follows, the vowels *a* and *eṅ* do not undergo substitution for a root ending in an *ik* vowel. Examples: *cicīṣati*, *tuṣṭūṣati*, *cikīrṣati*. Why "when it does not take *iṭ*" (*aniṭi*)? Consider *śiśayiṣate*.

(6.2.24) *Upāntasya*: When followed by a *san* suffix that begins with a consonant other than *n*, the *i* and *u* vowels (*adeṅ*) at the end of a root that is near the final syllable do not undergo *vṛddhi*. Examples: *bibhitsati*, *bubhutsate*, *vivṛtsati*, *dhitsati*, *jighṛkṣati*. Only when the *san* is *aniṭ* [does this apply]: *vivartiṣate*. (6.2.25) *Liṅsicos taṅi*: [The same rule applies] to the *liṅ* and *sic* suffixes when they take the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) endings.

In the *liṅ* and *sic* [augment], when followed by *taṅ* [the ātmanepada endings], the penultimate *ik* vowels that are not *eṅ* do not undergo [guṇa substitution]. Examples: *bhitsīṣṭa*, *bhutsīṣṭa*; *abhitta*, *abuddha*. Why "when followed by *taṅ*"? Consider: *abhaitsīt*. Why "not being *aniṭ*"? Consider: *vardhiṣīṣṭa*, *avardhiṣṭa*. Why "penultimate"? Consider: *ceṣīṣṭa*, *aceṣṭa*. [The rule] *uḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.26): In the *liṅ* and *sic* [augment], when followed by *taṅ*, the penultimate *ṛ*-vowel (*ṛvarṇa*) that is not *eṅ* does not undergo [guṇa substitution]. Examples: *kṛṣīṣṭa*, *akṛta*. Why "when followed by *taṅ*"? Consider: *akārṣīt*, *jāgaryāt*. Why "not being *aniṭ*"? Consider: *variṣīṣṭa*, *avariṣṭa*.

*sici dādhāsthām ic ca* (Pāṇini 6.1.27): When *sic* follows these roots—*dā*, *dhā*, and *sthā*—and is followed by a *taṅ* affix, the substitution of *i* occurs, and the *adeṅ* substitution does not take place. Examples: *ādita*, *ādhita*, *upāsthita*. Only when a *taṅ* affix follows: *adāt*, *adhāt*, *asthāt*. *gāṅa īt sye ca* (Pāṇini 6.1.28): [The substitution of *gāṅ* for the root *iṅ* "to study" occurs] before the suffix *sya* as well as before *sic*.

Before the suffix *sya* and before the *sic* augment, the vowel *ī* occurs [in place of the root vowel], and *adeṅ* does not occur. Examples: *adhyagīṣyata*, *adhyagīṣṭa*. Only when not in the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) system: *agāt*.

Regarding *bhūsuvor adve stiṅi* (Pāṇini 6.2.29): after the roots *bhū* and *sū* when they are not reduplicated (*adviruktau*), *adeṅ* does not occur before a *tiṅ* suffix. Examples: *abhūt*, *abhūḥ*; *suvai*, *suvāvahai*, *suvāmahai*. Why "when not reduplicated" (*adver*)? Consider *bobhavīti*. Why "before a *tiṅ* suffix" (*stiṅi*)? Consider *bhavitā*.

*hali pity uta* (Pāṇini 6.2.30): When a *tiṅ* suffix beginning with a consonant (*hal*) follows a *pit* suffix, the substitute *aud* is applied for a stem ending in *ut*. [The rule applies] only after a root other than *ad* (*adver*); thus, *juhoti*. *vorṇoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.2.31): [The substitute *aud* is applied] for the root *ūrṇu* when followed by a *tiṅ* suffix beginning with a consonant and having a *pit* marker. In place of *ū* in the root *ūrṇu*, when followed by a *tiṅ* suffix beginning with a consonant (*hal*) that has the marker *p*, there is optionally the substitution of *au*. Thus: *prorṇauti* or *prorṇoti*. Only when a consonant follows: *prorṇavāni*. Only when the suffix has the marker *p*: *prorṇutaḥ*. By rule 6.4.107 (*nāli*), when a *tiṅ* suffix beginning with a single consonant (*ekāl*) and having the marker *p* follows, there is no substitution of *au* for *ū* in *ūrṇu*. Thus: *praurṇot*, *praurṇoḥ*.

*tṛṇaha im* (Pāṇini 6.2.33): After the root *tṛh*, when followed by the suffix *śnam*, the augment *im* is inserted before a *tiṅ* ending that begins with a consonant (*hal*) and has an indicatory *p*. Examples: *tṛṇeḍhi*, *tṛṇekṣi*, *tṛṇehmi*, *atṛṇeṭ*. The rule applies only when the suffix begins with a consonant: *tṛṇahāni*. It applies only when the suffix has an indicatory *p*: *tṛṇḍhaḥ*. *bruva īṭ* (Pāṇini 6.2.34).

The augment *īṭ* is added to a following *tiṅ* suffix that begins with a consonant and ends in *p* after the root *brū*. Thus: *bravīti*, *abravīt*. Only when a consonant follows (*halīti*): *bravāṇi*. Only when it ends in *p* (*pitīti*): *brūtaḥ*. (6.2.35) *yaṅo vā*:

After a *tiṅ* suffix beginning with a consonant and ending in *p* that follows a reduplicated stem (*yaṅanta*), the augment *īṭ* is optionally applied. Thus: *bobhavīti*, *bobhoti*. By means of a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*), it is necessarily applied in some cases: *vāvadīti*, *lālapīti*. In other cases it is not applied: *narnartti*. Only when a consonant follows (*halīti*): *bobhavāni*. Only when it ends in *p* (*pitīti*): *bobhūtaḥ*.

*astisico 'laḥ* (6.2.36): After the root *as-* and after the suffix *sic*, the augment *īṭ* is applied to a following *tiṅ* ending that consists of a single consonant (*ekāl*). Examples: *āsīt*; *akārṣīt*. Why does the rule specify *alaḥ* ("a single consonant")? [Observe: *āstām*. [The rule applies] only when a consonant (*hal*) follows: [e.g.,] *kārayāmāsa*. *rudbhyaḥ pañcabhyo 'ṭ ca* (6.2.37): After the five roots beginning with *rud*, the augment *aṭ* is also applied [to the same endings].

The augment *īṭ* is applied after the singular endings of the *tiṅ* suffixes following the five roots beginning with *rud*, and the augment *aṭ* is also applied. Examples: *arodīt*, *arodat*; *asvapīt*, *asvapat*; *aprāṇīt*, *aprāṇat*; *aśvasīt*, *aśvasat*; *ajakṣīt*, *ajakṣat*. Why "after the five"? Observe: *ajāgaḥ*. Why "after the singular ending" (*ala*)? Observe: *roditi*. Why "when a consonant follows" (*halī*)? Observe: *ruroda*. After the root *ad*, the augment *aṭ* is applied to the singular *tiṅ* suffixes. Example: *ādat*. Why "after the singular ending" (*ala*)? Observe: *atti*.

Therefore, by *ata ā dyañi* (Pāṇini 6.2.39), the substitution of *āt* occurs for that which ends in *at* when followed by a *tiṅ* suffix beginning with *yañ*. Examples: *pacāmi*, *kariṣyāmi*. [Objection: It will not apply because it is impossible for such a base (*prakṛti*) to exist. [Question: Why say "for that which ends in *at*" (*ataḥ*)? [Answer: [Otherwise, the rule would apply to] *ruvaḥ*, *rumaḥ*. [Question: Why say "when followed by *yañ*" (*yañi*)? [Answer: [Otherwise, it would apply to] *bhavati*. [The rule applies only] when a *tiṅ* suffix follows: [as in] *keśavaḥ*, *ūṣaraḥ*. By *supi* (Pāṇini 6.2.40): [the substitution of *āt* occurs for that which ends in *at* when followed by a case-ending (*sup*)].

When a case ending (*sup*) beginning with *yañ* follows, *āt* is substituted for the final *at*. Examples: *vṛkṣābhyām*, *plakṣābhyām*. Only when preceded by *at*: *vāyubhyām*. Only when followed by *yañ*: *vṛkṣasya*. Regarding [Pāṇini 7.3.103]: *bahusu jhaly et*. When a case ending (*sup*) beginning with a *jhal* consonant follows a stem expressing plurality, *et* is substituted for the final *at*. Examples: *vṛkṣebhyaḥ*, *plakṣebhyaḥ*; *vṛkṣeṣu*. Why "in the plural" (*bahuṣu*)? Consider: *vṛkṣābhyām*. Why "beginning with a *jhal*" (*jhali*)? Consider: *vṛkṣāṇām*. Only when followed by a case ending (*sup*): consider *yajadhvam*. Only when preceded by *at*: consider *khaṭvābhyaḥ*.
*osi* (6.2.42): When *osi* follows, the substitution of *et* occurs for the final vowel *at*. For example:

*vṛkṣayoḥ svam* ("your own [property] of the two trees"), *vṛkṣayor nidhehi* ("place [it] in the two trees"). Only when it is *at* does this apply; thus, *vāyvoḥ* ("of the two winds" [does not change]). *ṭi cāpaḥ* (6.2.43): [The substitution of *et* occurs] also for the final *ṭi* sound of the word *āp*.

When *osi* follows, *āp* becomes *et*. [Examples: *khaṭvayā*, *khaṭvayoḥ*; *bahurājayā*, *bahurājayoḥ*. Why is the letter *p* mentioned? [Counter-example: *kīlālapā brāhmaṇena* ("by the milk-drinking Brahmin"). How is it that [the form] *atikhaṭvena* occurs? It will not occur because of the reliance on the long vowel form (*dīrgharūpa*).
In the case of the vocative singular (*sau*), when the vocative singular follows, *āp* becomes *et*.
[Examples: *he khaṭve*, *he bahurāje*. Why "in the vocative" (*saṃbodhane*)? [Counter-example: *khaṭvā*. Why "in the singular" (*sāv*)? [Counter-example: *he khaṭvāḥ*.

*ambārthānām aḍalekānām hrasvaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.2.45): For words synonymous with *amba* that do not contain the phonemes *ḍa*, *la*, or *ka*, a short vowel is substituted when followed by the nominative singular suffix *su* used in address. Examples: *he amba*, *he akka*, *he alla*. Why does it say "not containing *ḍa*, *la*, or *ka*"? Observe: *he ambāḍe*, *he ambāle*, *he ambike*. *ṅy-ūṅaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.2.46).

When *su* follows in the vocative case, a short vowel is substituted for a stem ending in *ṅī* or *ūṅ*. Examples: *he kumāri*, *he gauri*, *he brahmabandhu*. It should not be stated that the substitution of a short vowel occurs optionally before the genitive suffix *ṭā* and the vocative suffix *ṅi* (Pāṇini 1.4.8), as in: *devate devatāyāṃ nidhehi*, *he devata*, *he devate*; this is due to the Vedic character (*chāndasatvāt*) of the usage.
Regarding the rule *mātur mātac putre ślāghye* (Pāṇini 6.2.47): [the suffix *mātac* is added after *mātṛ* when the son is praiseworthy].

When the vocative singular suffix *su* follows a word ending in *mātṛ*, provided that it refers to a son who is praiseworthy and capable of representing his mother, the substitute *māt* occurs in place of *mātṛ*. Example: *he gārgīmāta*. The inclusion of the letter *c* in the rule is for the sake of the accent (*svarārtha*). This rule is an exception to [the suffix] *kap*. Why is "son" specified? [Counter-example: *he mātaḥ*. Why is "praiseworthy" specified? [Counter-example: *he gārgīmātṛka*. Regarding the vowels *i* and *u*: when the vocative singular suffix *su* follows, the substitutes *e* and *o* (*eṅ*) occur in place of *ik* (i.e., *i* and *u*). Examples: *he agne*, *he vāyo*. Due to the force of the specific prescription of short vowels, this does not apply here: *he kumāri*, *he gauri*, *he brahmabandhu*.

When *jas* follows, *i* and *u* are replaced by *eṅ* (*e* and *o*). [Examples: *agnayaḥ*, *vāyavaḥ*. When a *ṅit* suffix follows, except for those belonging to *sakhi*, [the final vowel of the stem is replaced by *eṅ*]. (Pāṇini 6.2.50)

When a *sup* suffix beginning with a *ṅ* follows, the vowels *e* and *o* (*eṅ*) replace the final *i* or *u* (*idut*) of a word, provided it is not the word *sakhi*. For example: *agnaye*, *agneḥ*; *vāyave*, *vāyoḥ*. Why does the rule specify "not *sakhi*"? [Because for that word, it remains: *sakhye*, *sakhyuḥ*.

Regarding the rule *patiḥ samāse* (Pāṇini 6.2.51), the vowels *e* and *o* (*eṅ*) replace the final vowel of the word *pati* only when it occurs in a compound (*samāsa*) followed by a *sup* suffix beginning with a *ṅ*. For example: *bṛhaspataye*, *bṛhaspateḥ*. Why does the rule specify "in a compound"? [Because outside of a compound, it remains: *patye*, *patyuḥ*.

(6.2.52) Before a feminine *ṅit* case-ending (*sup*), the vowels *e* and *o* optionally take the place of the final *i* and *u* of a feminine stem ending in those vowels. Thus: *mataye*, *matyai*; *dhenave*, *dhenvai*.
(6.2.53) And before the dual endings *bhyām* and *bhyas*, the augment *āt* is added.

The augment *āṭ* is added to a *sup* case-ending that begins with a *ṅit* suffix following a feminine stem ending in the vowels *ī* or *ū*, as well as those ending in *i* or *u*. Examples: *kumāryai*, *kumāryāḥ*; *gauryai*, *gauryāḥ*; *brahmabandhvai*, *brahmabandhvāḥ*; *lakṣmyai*, *lakṣmyāḥ*; *matyai*, *matyāḥ*; *dhenvai*, *dhenvāḥ*. It does not apply here: *mataye*, *dhenavaḥ*, because once the substitution of *eṅ* (*ay* or *av*) has occurred, the form is different. The rule applies only when the word is feminine: *grāmaṇye*, *grāmaṇyaḥ*; *khalapve*, *khalapvaḥ*; *agnaye*, *agneḥ*; *vāyave*, *vāyoḥ*. [The following rule applies: "After a stem ending in *s* or *yu*, [the *ṅit* suffixes of the dative and ablative singular] optionally [take the augment *āṭ*]. (Pāṇini 6.2.54)

The augment *āṭ* optionally occurs before a case-ending (*sup*) that begins with a *ṅit* consonant following a word that contains either *i* or *u*. Thus: *śriyai*, *śriye*; *śriyāḥ*, *śriyaḥ*; *bhruvai*, *bhruve*;
*bhruvāḥ*, *bhruvaḥ*. Regarding *striyāḥ* (Pāṇini 6.2.55):

the augment *āṭ* necessarily occurs before a case-ending beginning with a *ṅit* consonant following the word *strī*, because it is prescribed again here as an obligatory rule. Thus: *striyai*, *striyāḥ*.

*yāḍ āpaḥ* (6.2.56): The augment *yāṭ* is added to a case-ending (*sup*) that begins with a *ṅit* suffix following a stem ending in *āp*. For example: *khaṭvāyai*, *khaṭvāyāḥ*; *bahurājāyai*, *bahurājāyāḥ*. The rule applies only when [the feminine] is expressed as such (*striyām*): thus, *atikhaṭvāya* [is formed from *atikhaṭvā-ī*]. *smaivataḥ syāḍ ac ca* (6.2.57): [The augment *syāṭ* is added to a case-ending beginning with a vowel after a feminine stem ending in *smāt* or *vat*], and the preceding vowel is replaced by *ā*.

The augment *syāṭ* is applied after a *ṅit* case-ending (*sup*) following a feminine stem ending in *smāt* (i.e., *sarva*, etc. that ends in long *ā*; furthermore, the substitution of *āp* occurs for [the final vowel of the stem]. Thus: *sarvasyai*, *sarvasyāḥ*; *viśvasyai*, *viśvasyāḥ*. Why "after *smāt*"? [Consider: *sarvāyai*, *atisarvāyai*. Regarding Pāṇini 6.2.58, *dvitīyātṛtīyād vā*:

after the case-endings *ṅi* and *ṅasi* following the words *dvitīyā* and *tṛtīyā*, the augment *syāṭ* optionally occurs, and the substitution of *āp* also takes place. Thus: *dvitīyasyai*, *dvitīyāyai*; *dvitīyasyāḥ*, *dvitīyāyāḥ*. *tṛtīyasyai*, *tṛtīyāyai*; *tṛtīyasyāḥ*, *tṛtīyāyāḥ*.

*ṅer ām tatra* (Pāṇini 6.2.59): When these [suffixes] beginning with *āṭ* have been applied, the substitution of *ām* occurs for the locative case ending (*ṅi*). Examples: *kumāryām*, *gauryām*, *brahmabandhvām*, *lakṣmyām*; *matyām*, *dhenvām*; *śriyām*, *bhruvām*, *striyām*; *khaṭvāyām*, *bahurājāyām*; *sarvasyām*, *viśvasyām*, *dvitīyasyām*, *tṛtīyasyām*. Why does the rule specify *tatra* ("there")? [To exclude cases where the suffix is not preceded by *āṭ*: as in *śriyi*, *bhuvi*. *niyaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.2.60).
The suffix *ṅi* of another [stem] becomes *ām*. [Example: *grāmaṇyām*.
From the two vowels *i* and *u*, *aut* (6.2.61):
after the two vowels *i* and *u*, the substitute *aut* occurs for the suffix *ṅi*. [Examples: *sakhyau*, *patyau*. This is an example here for the non-feminine gender.

*eṅo 'cca* (Pāṇini 6.2.62): After a word ending in *i* or *u* that has been formed with the suffix *kṛt* *eṅ*, the substitution of *au* occurs for the locative singular (*ṅi*), and *eṅ* is also substituted for the initial [of the case-ending]. Examples: *agnau*, *vāyau*, *matau*, *dhenau*. Why is *eṅ* specified? [To exclude cases like] *matyām*, *dhenvām*. *ṭo 'striyāṃ nā* (Pāṇini 6.2.63).

In a word that is not feminine, the substitution of *nā* occurs for the suffix *ṭā* following a stem ending in *i* or *u*. Because this is the subject under discussion, the substitution of *nā* applies only to those stems ending in *eṅ* (*e*, *o*) or *at* (*a*). Examples: *agninā*, *vāyunā*. Why "not feminine"? Consider *matyā*, *dhenvā*. Regarding the rule *ṛto ṅisuṭy at* (Pāṇini 6.1.64):

when the locative singular suffix *ṅi* or the augment *suṭ* follows, the substitution of *ad* occurs for a stem ending in *ṛ*. Examples: *mātari*; *mātarau*, *mātaraḥ*, *mātaram*, *mātarau*. *pitari*; *pitarau*, *pitaraḥ*, *pitaram*, *pitarau*. Why "when *ṅi* or *suṭ* follow"? Consider *mātrā*, *pitrā*.

(6.2.65) *saṃyogāder liṭi*: After a root beginning with a conjunct consonant and ending in the vowel *ṛ*, the substitution of *at* occurs when the suffix *liṭ* follows. Examples: *sasvaratuḥ*, *sasvaruḥ*; *sasmaratuḥ*, *sasmaruḥ*. This is a re-exception (*punaḥ-prasava*) regarding the scope of the prohibition, not a new injunction. Otherwise, however, it is *sasvāra*, *sasmāra*. (6.2.66) *skṛñaḥ*.

The substitution of *at* occurs for the root *kṛ*, when it begins with a conjunct consonant and is accompanied by the augment *suṭ*, followed by the suffixes of the perfect tense (*liṭ*). Examples: *saṃcaskaratuḥ*, *saṃcaskaruḥ*. Why is *suṭ* mentioned? [To show that the rule does not apply otherwise: *cakratuḥ*, *cakruḥ*. This rule is formulated to indicate that in rules concerning the beginning of a conjunct, the conjunct must be one that is present from the outset (*aupadeśika*). [This refers to the rule: *ṛdṛchṛṇām* (Pāṇini 6.1.67).

In the *liṭ* [perfect] tense, the substitution of *at* occurs for verbal roots ending in *ṛ*, as well as for the root *ṛch*. Thus: *vicakaratuḥ*, *vicakaruḥ*; *ānarchatuḥ*, *ānarchuḥ*; *āratuḥ*, *āruḥ*; and *viśaśratuḥ*, *viśaśruḥ*—this is established by the rule for the root *śrā*. *Vidadratuḥ*, *vidadrur*—this is established by the rule for the root *drā*. *Nipapratuḥ*, *nipaprur*—this is established by the rule for the root *prā*. Regarding the rule *ṛśvidṛśo ’ṅi* (Pāṇini 6.1.68): the substitution of *at* occurs for roots ending in an *ṛ*-vowel, as well as for the roots *śvi* and *dṛś*, when followed by the *aṅ* [aorist] suffix. Thus: *ārat*, *samārata*; *asarat*, *ajarat*; *aśvat*, *adarśat*.

*asu-pata-vaca-thuk-pum-um-aṅi* (Pāṇini 6.2.69): After the verbal roots *asu*, *pata*, and *vac*, when followed by the suffix *aṅ*, the augmentments *thuk*, *pum*, and *um* respectively are applied. [Examples: *āsthat*, *āsthatām*; *apaptat*, *apaptatām*; *avocat*, *avocatām*. *ke ’ṇo hrasvaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.2.70): When the suffix *ka* follows, a short vowel is substituted for the final vowel of a stem ending in *aṇ*.

The *aṇ* [suffix] becomes short before a feminine suffix marked with *ṅ*. Examples: *khaṭvikā*, *kumārikā*, *brahmabandhukā*. Why specify *aṇ*? [Because in these cases the suffix is not *aṇ*: *gokā*, *naukā*. [The rule applies] only when referring to the original base (*prakṛti*): *kumārīkaḥ* [is derived from] "one who behaves like a maiden" (*kumārīṃ kāyati*).
Before the suffix *kap*, the *aṇ* does not become short (Pāṇini 6.2.71). Example: *bahukumāriko deśaḥ* ("a country with many maidens").
*Āpo vā* (Pāṇini 6.2.72): The vowel *ā* of the word *āp* becomes optionally short (*hrasva*) when followed by the suffix *kap*. Examples: *bahukhaṭvikā*, *bahukhaṭvākā*.
*Śīṅa ed aliṭi* (Pāṇini 6.2.73): [The substitution of] *e* for the final vowel of the root *śīṅ* occurs before any suffix other than *aliṭ*.

Before an affix beginning with *liṭ* other than *liṭ*, the root *śīṅ* becomes *ed*. Examples: *śete*, *śayāte*, *śayānaḥ*. Why "before an affix other than *liṭ*"? [Counter-example: *śiśye*. In the rule *yi kṅity ayaṅ* (Pāṇini 6.1.74), before an affix beginning with *y* that is marked with *k* or *ṅ*, the substitute *ayaṅ* is applied for the vowel *a* of the root *śī*. Examples: *śayyate*, *śāśayyate*, *adhiśayya gataḥ*. Why "before an affix marked with *k* or *ṅ*"? [Counter-example: *śeyam*.

*prādibhya ūho hrasvaḥ* (6.2.75): When a suffix beginning with *y* that is marked with *k* or *ṅ* follows, the root *ūh-* undergoes shortening after prefixes (*prādi*). Examples: *samuhyate*, *samuhyāt*, *samuhya gataḥ*. Why "after prefixes"? Witness: *ūhyate*. Why "beginning with *y*" (*yīti*)? Witness: *samūhitaḥ*. Why "marked with *k* or *ṅ*" (*kṅitīti*)? Witness: this meaning is *abhyūhyaḥ*. Why "of *aṇ*" (*aṇa iti*)? Witness: *ā ūhyate*, *ohyate*, *samohyate*. *liṅīṇaḥ* (6.2.76): [The substitution of *ī* for *a* occurs] before the optative (*liṅ*) suffix following the root *iṇ-*.

When *liṅ* follows a prefix (*prādi*) and is characterized by *ya*-initial *kṅit* suffixes, the vowel of the root *iṇ* becomes short. Examples: *udiyāt*, *samiyāt*. Why specify "in *liṅ*"? Observe: *udīyate*, *samīyate*. Why specify "after prefixes"? Observe: *īyāt*. Why specify "of *iṇ*"? Observe: *ā īyāt*, *eyāt*, *sameyāt*. Regarding [Pāṇini 6.4.68]: "In the benedictive (*āśis*), there is lengthening" (6.2.77). When *liṅ* follows a prefix and is characterized by *ya*-initial suffixes, the vowel of the root *iṇ* becomes long in the sense of a benediction. Examples: *cīyāt*, *stūyāt*, *īyāt*. Why specify "in the benedictive"? Observe: *cinuyāt*, *stuyāt*, *iyāt*.

*cviyaṅyakkyeṣu* (6.2.78): When *cv*, *yaṅ*, *yak*, or *ky* follows, the long vowel is substituted for the *aṇ* [vowel] of the base. For example: *paṭūkaroti*, *paṭūbhavati*, *paṭūsyāt*; *cecīyate*; *cīyate*; *mantūyate*; *bhṛśāyate*; *lohitāyati*, *lohitāyate*. *rīṅ ṛto ye ca* (6.2.79): When *ya* follows, *rīṅ* is substituted for the *ṛ* of the base.

For a word ending in *ṛ*, the substitution of *rīṅ* occurs when followed by suffixes such as *ya* and *cvī*. Examples: *pitryaḥ sthālīpākaḥ* ("an offering to the ancestors"); *pitrībhavati* ("he becomes a father"); *pitrīyati* ("he treats like a father"); *pitrīyate* ("he behaves like a father"); *cekrīyate* ("he repeats"). The rule *riṅ śayagāśīrliṅi* (Pāṇini 6.4.80) states that for a word ending in *ṛ*, the substitution of *riṅ* occurs when followed by the suffix *śe*, the suffix *yak*, or the optative (*liṅ*) used in the sense of benediction (*āśis*). Examples: *ādriyate* ("he respects"); *kriyate* ("it is done"); *kriyāt* ("may he do"). Why specify "in the sense of benediction"? [Because it does not apply otherwise: *bibhṛyāt* ("he should support"). Why specify "when followed by *yī*" (the suffix *ya* and *yak*)? [Because it does not apply otherwise: *kṛṣīṣṭa* ("may he draw").

*ṛsaṃyogādyor at* (Pāṇini 6.2.81): After the roots *ṛ*, those beginning with a consonant cluster (*saṃyoga*), and those ending in *ṛ*, the substitution of *at* occurs before the suffixes of the benedictive (*āśīr-liṅ*) and before the suffix *yak*; however, it does not occur before *śe* because that is impossible. Examples: *aryate*, *aryāt*; *smaryate*, *smaryāt*. The rule applies only when *y* follows: *smṛṣīṣṭa*. It applies only in the benedictive: *iyṛyāt*. How is it that we have *saṃskriyate* and *saṃskriyāt*? Because the term "consonant cluster" (*saṃyoga*) refers here to what is taught in the original grammatical instruction (*aupadeśika*). [The following rule applies] before *yaṅ*: (6.2.82).

When *yaṅ* follows, *at* is substituted for [the final vowel] of a root that begins with a consonant cluster (*saṃyoga*) and contains *ṛ*. Thus, *arāryate*, *sāsmaryate*. Regarding *hano ghnī hiṃsāyām* (Pāṇini 6.4.98): when the sense of "injury" (*hiṃsā*) is understood, the substitution of *ghnī* occurs for the root *han* when *yaṅ* follows. Thus, *jeghnīyate*. Why is "long" (*dīrghaḥ*) specified? [To show it does not apply in cases like] *jeghnītaḥ*. Why "when injury is meant" (*hiṃsāyām*)? [Otherwise, it would apply in cases like] *jaṅghanyate*.
Pāṇini 6.2.84: *ī ghrā-dhmoḥ*.

When the suffix *yaṅ* follows, the vowel *ī* is substituted for the roots *ghrā* and *dhmā*. Thus: *jeghrīyate*, *dedhmīyate*. Why is the long vowel [prescribed]? [To show that it does not apply] in forms such as *jeghrītaḥ*.
Pāṇini 6.2.85: *asya cvau*. [The long vowel is substituted] for the final vowel of this [stem] when the suffix *cv-* follows.

The vowel *ī* is substituted for a word ending in a non-vowel (*avarṇa*) when followed by the suffix *cv-* [in the sense of becoming that]. Examples: *śuklīkaroti*, *śuklībhavati*, *śuklīsyāt*; *khaṭvīkaroti*, *khaṭvībhavati*, *khaṭvīsyāt*.
Regarding *kyac*: [Pāṇini 6.2.86] the vowel *ī* is substituted for a word ending in a non-vowel when followed by the suffix *kyac*. Examples: *putrīyati*, *vastrīyati*, *mālīyati*.

(6.2.87) *na kṣudhi aśanasya*: When *kṣudh* is understood, the substitution of *ī* for the final vowel of *aśana* does not occur before a suffix beginning with *kyac*. Example: *aśanāyati*. Why say "when *kṣudh* [is understood]"? [Counter-example: *aśanīyati dānāya* ("he desires food for the sake of giving"). (6.2.88) *dhanasya tṛṣṇāyām*: [The substitution of *ī* for the final vowel of *dhana* does not occur] when *tṛṣṇā* (thirst/desire) is understood.

When the word *dhana* is understood in the sense of "thirst" (*tṛṣṇā*), the substitution of *ī* does not occur before the suffix *kyac*. Thus: *dhanāyati*. Why "in the sense of thirst"? [Consider: *dhanīyati dānāya* ("he desires wealth for the sake of giving"). Regarding *udanyaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.89): when *kyac* follows *udaka* and "thirst" is understood, the form *udana-* is prescribed as a substitute. Thus: *udanyati*. Only the thirst for water (*udakatṛṣṇā*) is intended here, because that is what is perceived; otherwise, one says *udakīyati*.

*vṛṣāśvayor maithune suk* (Pāṇini 6.2.90): When the desire for sexual intercourse is implied, the augment *suk* is added to *vṛṣan* and *aśva* when followed by the suffix *kyac*. Thus: *vṛṣasyati gauḥ* ("the cow desires [to mate with] a bull"); *aśvasyati vaḍavā* ("the mare desires [to mate with] a horse"). Why "in the context of sexual intercourse"? [Observe: *vṛṣīyati*, *aśvīyati* ("he desires like a bull," "he desires like a horse"). *asuk cāttum* (Pāṇini 6.2.91): [The augment *suk* is added] and it is also *asuk* (i.e., *su* with the vowel *a*) when the root *ad* follows.

When the suffix *kyac* follows the verb root *aś* (to eat) in the sense of "desiring to eat," the augment *asuk* is added after the base, and *suk* is also substituted [for the final *a*]. Thus: *dadhyasyati*, *dadhisyati*; *madhvasyati*, *madhusyati*; *kṣīrasyati*; *lavaṇasyati*. Why say "in the sense of eating"? [Consider: *kṣīrīyati* [meaning] "he desires milk for the sake of giving. [This is governed by the rule: *do-so-mā-sth-ām iti kiti* (Pāṇini 6.4.112).

In the case of these roots—*do*, *sthā*, and *mā*—when followed by a *kit* suffix beginning with *t*, the substitution of *i* occurs. Examples: *avaditaḥ*, *avaditavān*; *avasitaḥ*, *avasitavān*; *mitam*, *mitavān*; *sthitam*, *sthitavān*. Why "beginning with *t*" (*ti*)? Consider *avadāya*. Why "*kit*" (*kiti*)? Consider *avadātā*. Regarding *cho vā* (Pāṇini 6.1.93): for the root *chā*, when followed by a *kit* suffix beginning with *t*, the substitution of *i* optionally occurs. Examples: *avacchitam*, *avacchātam*. How is it that we have the forms *śitam* and *śātam*? They are forms derived from the roots *śinoti* and *śyati* respectively.

*dhāño hiḥ* (Pāṇini 6.2.94): The substitution of *hi* occurs for the root *dadhāti* (*dhā*) when followed by a *kit* suffix beginning with the letter *t*. Examples: *vihitam*, *vihitavān*. Why is the letter *ñ* [in *dhāñ*] specified? [To exclude other roots, such as] *dhītam*, *dhītavān*. *hākas tvi* (Pāṇini 6.2.95).

The substitution of *hi* occurs for the root *ohā* when followed by the suffix *ktvā*. Thus: *hitvā*. Why [is there] the letter *k* [in the suffix]? [To show that the substitution does not apply to other forms: *hātvā*. Only when [the suffix begins with] *t*: *prahāya*. Regarding *do dat* (Pāṇini 6.2.96): for the roots *dāṇ*, *deṅ*, and *dadāti*, the substitute *dad* occurs before a *kit* suffix beginning with *t*. Thus: *dattaḥ*, *dattavān*.

*prāder acas taḥ* (6.2.97): When a *kit* suffix beginning with *t* follows, the *t* is substituted for the final vowel of the prefix *pra-* and others that end in a vowel, provided that the word governed by these prefixes ends in the root *dā*. Examples: *prattam*, *avattam*. How is it that forms such as *pradattam*, *sudattam*, *vidattam*, and *anudattam* are accounted for? They will be explained through the formation of *prādi-samāsa* compounds with the word *datta*. *apo bhi* (6.2.98).

The letter *t* replaces the [final] *s* of the word *ap-* when followed by a word beginning with *bh*. Examples: *adbhiḥ*, *adbhyaḥ*. Why say "when followed by *bh*" (*bhīti*)? Observe: *apsu*. The rule applies only to the original form (*prakṛteḥ*): *abbhakṣaḥ*. *S si liṅatiṅi* (Pāṇini 6.1.99):

When followed by a word beginning with *s* that is either a *liṅ* suffix or not a *tiṅ* suffix, the *s* is replaced by *t*. Examples: *vatsīṣṭa*, *vatsyati*, *vivatsati*. Why say "when followed by a *liṅ* or not a *tiṅ*" (*liṅatiṅi*)? Observe: *āsse*, *vasse*.

*tāsaso ri ca lopaḥ* (6.2.100): When *ri* (the letter *r*) follows, as well as when a *s*-beginning suffix follows, there is elision (*lopa*) of the *s* belonging to both *tās* and *as* (the root *as*). [Examples: *kartārau*, *kartāraḥ*; *kartāsi*, *kartāse*. [Also in the case of *as*: *asi*, *vyatise*. *ha eti* (6.2.101): [The *s* of *tās* and *as* is elided] before the particle *ha* and before the suffix *eti*.
The letter *h* replaces [the final *s*] of the suffixes *tās* and *as* when followed by another element. For example: *kartāhe*, *vyatihe*.
Regarding the rule *kyaṅi vā* (Pāṇini 6.2.102):
when *kyaṅ* follows, the elision (*lopa*) of the *s* may optionally occur. For example: *payāyate*, *payasyate*.
(6.2.103) *ojas* and *apsaras*: When *kyaṅ* follows, the *s* of *ojas* and *apsaras* is elided, because it is prescribed as an obligatory rule. Examples: *ojāyate*, *apsarāyate*.
(6.2.104) *yi* and *varṇa* [are substituted] for *dīdhī* and *vevī*.

When *yakāra* (the letter *y*) or an *ivarna* (the vowels *i* or *ī*) follows, there is elision of the final [vowel] of the roots *dīdhī* and *vevī*. Thus: *ādīdhyate*, *āvevyate*; *ādīdhitā*, *āvevitā*; *ādīdhitaḥ*, *āvevitaḥ*. Why "when *y* or an *ivarna* follows"? [Observe: *ādīdhyanaṃ*, *āvevyanaṃ*. By Pāṇini 6.1.77 (*yaṇ aci*), when an *ac*-beginning suffix follows *dīdhī* and *vevī*, a *yaṇ* substitute occurs. Thus: *ādīdhyanaṃ*, *āvevyanaṃ*; *ādīdhyakaḥ*, *āvevyakaḥ*. How is it that we have *ādīdhet* and *ādīdhayuḥ*? Because they belong to the Vedic language (*chāndasatvāt*), there is the substitution of *adeṅ* and the absence of the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) endings.
The suffix *san* is applied after [roots ending in] *mimī*, *ārabh*, *labh*, *śak*, *pat*, *pad*, *dā*, *dhā*, and *mac*. (Pāṇini 3.1.6)

When the suffix *san* beginning with *sa-* follows, the vowel of roots such as *mī* is replaced by *i*. *ḍu-mīñ*: *pramitsati*. *mīṅ*: *mitsate*. *māṅ*: *mitsate*. *rabha*: *āripsate*. *labha*: *ālipsate*. *śakḷ*: *śikṣati*. *patḷ*: *pitsati*. *pada*: *pitsate*. *dāṇ*: *ditsati*. *do*: *avaditsati*. *deṅ*: *avaditsate*. *ḍudā*: *ditsati*. *ḍudhāñ*: *dhitsati*. *dheṭ*: *dhitsati*. Why say "before *si*" (*sīti*)? [Consider: *pipatiṣati*. Here, the augment *iṭ* is optional according to Pāṇini 6.1.119 (*sanīvantardha...*). Why say "before *san*" (*sanīti*)? [Consider: *dāsyati*. [The rule] *rādho hiṃsāyām* (Pāṇini 6.2.107) applies when the sense is injury.

When the sense of injury (*hiṃsā*) is understood, the vowel *a* of the root *rādh* is replaced by *is* before the suffix *san*. Example: *pratiritsati*. Why "when injury is understood"? [Counter-example: *ārirātsati*. Regarding Pāṇini 6.4.108, *jñapy-āp-ṛdhām īt*: when *san* follows, the vowel *i* of these roots—*jñapi*, *āp*, and *ṛdh*—is replaced by *ī*. Examples: *jñīpsati*, *īpsati*, *īrtsati*. Only when the suffix begins with *s* does this apply; [otherwise: *jijñapayiṣati*, *ardidhiṣati*.

*dambha ic ca* (6.2.109): When the suffix *san* with an initial *s* follows the root *dambh*, the vowel *a* is replaced by *i* and *ī*. Thus: *dhīpsati* or *dhīpsati*. Only when [the suffix] begins with *s*: *didambhiṣati*. *avyāpyasya mucer od vā* (6.2.110): For the root *muc* not having an object, the vowel *o* is optionally substituted [for the radical *u*].

For the root *muc*, when it is devoid of an object (*avyāpya*) and followed by the suffix *san*, the vowel *a* optionally becomes *u*. Thus: *mokṣate vatsaḥ svayam eva* ("the calf releases itself") or *mumukṣate vatsaḥ svayam eva* ("the calf desires to release itself"). Why "when it is devoid of an object"? Observe: *mumukṣati vatsaṃ Devadattaḥ* ("Devadatta desires to release the calf").

Regarding the rule *dvitve pūrvasyātra lopaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.111): "In this [section], when there is reduplication, there is elision of the preceding [element]. This refers to what has been discussed previously concerning the substitution of *sani* and so forth; in those cases, when reduplication occurs, the elision of the preceding element takes place. And thus it has been illustrated. Why "in reduplication"? So that it does not apply to a single phoneme. Why "in this [section]" (*atra*)? To exclude forms such as *amīmapat* and *adīdapat*. Furthermore, this phrase *dvitve pūrvasya* is a governing heading (*adhikāra*).
*halo 'nādeḥ* (6.2.112):

When a reduplication occurs, there is elision of the initial *hal* (consonant) that is not the first [of the root]. Examples: *jaglau*, *mamlau*; *āṭatuḥ*, *āṭuḥ*. Why "not the first"? [Consider: *papāca*.
*khayi kharaḥ* (6.2.113).

In the case of a reduplicated form, when a *khay* sound follows, there is elision (*lopa*) of a preceding *khar* sound. Examples: *tiṣṭhāsati*, *pispandiṣate*, *ucicchiṣati*. Because the *khay* sounds serve as the cause for elision, there is no elision of a consonant (*hal*) that is not initial. Why specify "*khayi*" [as the condition]? Consider *sasnau*. Why specify "*khara*" [as the sound to be elided]? Consider *aujiḍhat* and *yayāce*. This objection does not hold; the term *hal* will be understood as carrying over from the previous rule, and since that too is separated by the vowel *ā*, the elision will not occur. If so, the term *khar* will be used for the sake of the subsequent rule. [The next rule is: *car* (Pāṇini 6.2.114).

In a reduplicated form (*dvirukti*), the *khar* (voiceless unaspirated consonant) of the first [element] becomes *car* (the corresponding voiced unaspirated consonant) for the remainder. Examples: *paphāla*, *ciccheda*, *tasthau*, *ṭiṭhakārayiṣati*. By Pāṇini 6.1.115 (*jhaṣo jaś*), in a reduplicated form, the *jhaṣ* (voiced aspirated consonant) of the first element becomes *jaś* (the corresponding voiced unaspirated consonant). Examples: *jijhakārayiṣati*, *babhūva*, *ḍuḍhauke*, *dadhyau*. Due to the established reading in the *Siddhakāṇḍa*, in forms such as *babhaṇatuḥ* and *babhaṇuḥ*, the substitution of *e* does not occur because they begin with an *ādeśa* (substitute). In the case of *ucicchiṣati*, because the change to *car* is already established, the augment *tuK* prescribed by Pāṇini 5.1.70 (*che*) does not apply.

*kuhoś cuḥ* (6.2.116): In a reduplication, the *ca*-class (*cavarga*) replaces the *ka*-class (*kavarga*) and the letter *ha* of the preceding syllable. Examples: *cakāra*, *cakhāda*, *jagāda*, *jaghāsa*, *ñuṅuve*, *jahāra*.
*na kuṅo yaṅi* (6.2.117): [The substitution does not occur] for the root *kuṅ* in the *yaṅ* intensive.

In the reduplication of the *yaṅ* [intensive] suffix, the change of *kuṅ* to *cut* does not occur for the preceding element. *Kokūyate*. Why is the letter *ṅ* [in *kuṅ*] specified? [To exclude cases like: *cokūyate*. Why is it said "in *yaṅ*" (*yaṅi*)? [To exclude cases like: *cukūṣate*. Regarding the rule *ur at* (Pāṇini 6.2.118):
in the reduplication of a root containing an *ṛ*-vowel, the vowel *a* is substituted for the preceding [element]. *Vavṛdhe*, *cakratuḥ*, *cakruḥ*.
*hrasvaḥ* (6.2.119): In a reduplicated form, the first member becomes short. Examples: *ḍuḍhaukiṣate*, *tutraukiṣate*, *siṣeviṣate*.
*dyutisvāpyor yaṇa ik* (6.2.120): [The short vowel substitute applies] for the semivowel (*yaṇ*) of the roots *dyuti* and *svāpi*.

When there is reduplication of *dyuti* and *svāpi*, the semivowel (*yaṇ*) of the first member becomes a vowel (*ig*). Thus: *didyutiṣate*, *suṣvāpayiṣati*. This is desired only when the cause for reduplication is immediate; here it does not apply: *siṣvāpakīyiṣati*. Regarding *vyatha* in the *liṭ* [perfect] (Pāṇini 6.1.121): when there is reduplication of *vyatha* in the *liṭ*, the semivowel (*yaṇ*) of the first member becomes a vowel (*ig*). Thus: *vivyathe*, *vivyathāte*. Why "in the *liṭ*"? Observe: *vāvyathyate*.

*dīrgho ‘piti* (Pāṇini 6.2.122): When *liṭ* follows, provided it does not have the augment *apit*, the long vowel is substituted for the first member of the reduplicated form of the root *iṇ*. Examples: *īyatuḥ*, *īyuḥ*. Why specify "provided it does not have the augment *apit*"? [Observe: *iyāya*, *iyayitha*. *ata ādeḥ* (Pāṇini 6.2.123).

In the case of reduplication, the first vowel *ā* becomes long. *āṭatuḥ*, *āṭuḥ*. Why "of the first"? [Observe: *papāca*. And for a root consisting of more than one consonant (*anekahal*), when followed by the *liṭ* suffix, there is lengthening of the first vowel in the reduplicated form, and the augment *nuK* is added. *ānañjatuḥ*, *ānañjuḥ*; *ānṛdhatuḥ*, *ānṛdhuḥ*; *ānarchatuḥ*, *ānarchuḥ*. Why "more than one consonant"? [Observe: *āṭatuḥ*, *āṭuḥ*.

(6.2.125) *aśnoteḥ*: When the suffix *liṭ* follows the root *aś*, after reduplication, the augment *nuk* is added to the initial *a* of the first member which has undergone lengthening. Examples: *ānaśe*, *ānaśāte*. Why is *śnu* mentioned [in the rule]? To prevent it from applying to the root *aś* (of the sixth class): as in *āśatuḥ*, *āśuḥ*. (6.2.126) *bhuvo ’t*: [The augment *at* is added to the root *bhū* when followed by *liṭ*.]

In the case of the root *bhū* when followed by the *liṭ* suffix, after reduplication, the substitute *ed* occurs for the first part. Thus: *babhūva*, *babhūvatuḥ*, *babhūvuḥ*. Regarding the rule *nijāṃ luky et* (Pāṇini 6.1.127): when there is reduplication of roots beginning with *niJ*, and the *śap* suffix is elided (*luk*), the substitute *ed* occurs for the first part. For example: from *niJ*: *nenekti*; from *viJ*: *vevekti*; from *viṣḷ*: *veveṣṭi*. The roots *niJ* and others are understood here specifically because they are included in the *vṛt* group. Why does the rule specify "when there is elision" (*luki*)? Consider: *nineja* (where the *śap* is not elided).

*ṛpṝbhṛmāhāṅām it* (Pāṇini 6.1.128): When there is elision of *śap* following these roots—*ṛ*, *pṝ*, *bhṛ*, *mā*, and *hāṅ*—and when reduplication occurs, the vowel *i* is substituted for the first syllable. Thus: *iyarti*, *piparti*, *bibharti*, *mimīte*, *jihīte*. Why is the marker *ṅ* used [in *hāṅ*]? [To distinguish it from *jahāti*, which does not undergo this change]. *sany ataḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.129).

When *san* follows, the substitution of *it* for the preceding *a* occurs. For example: *pipakṣati*, *yiyakṣati*. Why is it said "when *san* follows"? [Observe: *papāca*. Why is it said "for *a*"? [Observe: *cukūṣati*.
[This is governed by] Pāṇini 6.1.130: *oḥ puyaṇjyapare*.

When a root ending in *u* undergoes reduplication before the suffix *san*, the vowel *i* is substituted for the first syllable if it is followed by a labial (*pavarga*), a semi-vowel (*yaṇ*), or the letter *j*, provided that an *a*-vowel follows these sounds. Examples: *pipaviṣate*, *pipāvayiṣati*; *bibhāvayiṣati*; *yiyaviṣati*, *yiyāvayiṣati*; *rirāvayiṣati*; *lilāvayiṣati*; *jijāvayiṣati* (the root *ju* is a Vedic [sautra] root). Why is it said "ending in *u*" (*or*)? Consider *pāpacyate*; with *san*: *pāpaciṣate*. Why is it said "labial, semi-vowel, or *j*" (*puyaṇji*)? Consider *nunāvayiṣati*, *juhāvayiṣati*. Why is it said "followed by an *a*-vowel" (*avarṇapare*)? Consider *bubhūṣati*.
The substitution of *i* for the roots *sru*, *śru*, *dru*, *pru*, *plu*, and *cyu* is optional (Pāṇini 6.2.131).

When the desiderative suffix *san* follows roots such as *srav*, there is optionally the substitution of *it* for the first vowel of the reduplicated syllable when a semivowel (*yaṇ*) preceded by *a* (or *ā*) follows. Thus: *sisrāvayiṣati*, *susrāvayiṣati*; *śiśrāvayiṣati*, *śuśrāvayiṣati*; *didrāvayiṣati*, *dudrāvayiṣati*; *piprāvayiṣati*, *puprāvayiṣati*; *piplāvayiṣati*, *puplāvayiṣati*; *cicyāvayiṣati*, *cucyāvayiṣati*. The intervention [of the reduplicated syllable] is accepted here due to the force of the explicit statement. This applies only to those [roots] where *a* or *ā* precedes the semivowel, as in: *susrūṣati*. [The rule] *ādeṅ yaṅi* (Pāṇini 6.1.45) applies.

In the case of a reduplication (*yaṅ*), the *ā*, *e*, and *o* vowels (*ādeṅ*) of the preceding syllable occur. Thus: *pāpacyate*, *lolūyate*, *cecīyate*. This *ādeṅ* substitution is not caused by the *yaṅ* suffix itself; therefore, it occurs even when the *yaṅ* is elided (*luk*): *pāpacaḥ*, *dedyaḥ*, *nenyaḥ*, *loluvaḥ*, *popuvaḥ*. In the case of the elision of *yaṅ* from the root *jahāti*, the substitution of *ā* for *ha* (*nāttvam*) does not take place because of the rule of diversity (*bahulavacanāt*). The *nīg* augment is applied to the roots *vañc*, *sraṃs*, *dhvaṃs*, *bhraṃś*, *kas*, *pat*, *pad*, and *skand* [in the feminine]. (Pāṇini 6.4.133)

When there is reduplication in the *yaṅ* [intensive] suffix, the augment *nīg* is added to the first member of the roots *vañc* and others: *vanīvacyate*, *sanīsrasyate*, *danīdhvasyate*, *banībhraśyate*, *canīkasyate*, *panīpatyate*, *panīpadyate*, *canīskadyate*. By the rule *ñamo 'to nuk* (Pāṇini 6.4.134), when there is reduplication in the *yaṅ* suffix, the augment *nuk* is added to the first member ending in *a* of roots ending in a *ñam* consonant: *tantanyate*, *jaṅgamyate*, *bambhaṇyate*, *jañjanyate*, *tantamyate*. Why does the rule specify "ending in *a*" (*ataḥ*)? Consider: *tetimyate*.

*Japajabhadahadaśabhañjapaśām* (Pāṇini 6.1.135): After the reduplication of *yaṅ*, the augment *nuṭ* is added to the first syllable of the roots *jap*, *jabh*, *dah*, *daś*, *bhañj*, and *paś*. Thus: *jañjapyate*, *jañjabhyate*, *dandahyate*, *dandaśyate*, *bambhajyate*, *pampaśyate*. *Paś* is a root found in the Vedic (Sūtra) lexicon. *Caraphaloḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.136).
When the suffix *yaṅ* follows the roots *car* and *phal*, after reduplication, the augment *nuk* is added to the initial vowel of the former member. Thus: *cañcūryate*, *pamphulyate*.

Furthermore, by the rule *ti co 'dataḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.137), when *yaṅ* beginning with *t* follows, the vowel *u* replaces the *a* of *car* and *phal*. Thus: *caraṇam* becomes *cūrtiḥ*; *praphullāḥ sumanasaḥ*. [Examples: *cañcūryate*, *pamphulyate*.

*rīg ṛtvataḥ* (Pāṇini 6.2.138): When a root containing the vowel *ṛ* undergoes reduplication in the *yaṅ* formation, the augment *rīg* is added to the first member. Examples: *narīnṛtyate*, *darīdṛśyate*, *parīpṛcchyate*, *varīvṛścyate*. *rugrikau ca luki* (Pāṇini 6.2.139).

When there is elision of *yaṅ*, and when a reduplication occurs for a root containing the vowel *ṛ*, the substitutes *ruṭ* and *riṭ* are applied to the preceding [portion], as well as *rīṭ*. Thus: *marmṛjaḥ*, *marimṛjaḥ*, *marīmṛjaḥ*.
[This is governed by] Pāṇini 6.1.9: "In the case of *caṅ*, before a light syllable and before a *ṇi*-affix, the operations are like those of *san*, provided there is no elision of *a*."

When a light vowel (*laghu*) is followed by a *ṇi* suffix that is itself followed by *caṅ*, provided there is no elision of *na*, the operation of *sanvadbhāva* applies to the preceding [reduplicated] syllable after reduplication has occurred. It was stated [in Pāṇini 6.1.9] that *sany ata* [the shortening of *a* occurs in *san*]; here too it is the same: *apīpacat*. It was stated [in Pāṇini 6.1.11] that *oḥ puyaṇjy apara*; here too it is the same: *apīpavat*, *alīlavat*. It was stated [in Pāṇini 6.1.12] that *sravatyādīnām*; here too it is the same: *asisravat*, *asusravat*; *aśiśravat*, *aśuśravat*; *adidravat*, *adudravat*; *apipravat*, *apupravat*.

*apiplavat*, *apuplavat*. *acicyavat*, *acucyavat*. It does not occur for another [root]: *anūnavat*, *ajūhavat*. Why [is it specified] "when light"? [As in: *atatakṣat*, *ararakṣat*. Why [is it specified] "in the case of the causative suffix" (*ṇau*)? [As in: *acakamata*. Why [is it specified] "when there is no elision of a semivowel" (*anaglope*)? [As in: *ajagadat*, *aśaśaṭhat*, *atastanat*. Why [is it specified] "in the context of *caṅ*" (*caṅi*)? [As in: *riramayiṣati*. The mention of *caṅ* is for the sake of what follows. [The rule continues: "A long vowel replaces a light vowel" (*dīrgho laghoḥ*).

When there is reduplication, the vowel of the first syllable becomes long if that vowel is light (*laghu*) and the following syllable is also light, provided that the suffix *ṇi* is present and the elision (*alopa*) of the penultimate vowel has not occurred in the *caṅ* formation. Examples: *apīpacat*, *abībhavat*, *alīlavat*, *anūnavat*, *ajūhavat*. The rule applies only when the vowels are light: *atatakṣat*. Why "of a light vowel"? Consider: *asisravat*. Why "when *ṇi* is present"? Consider: *acakamata*. Why "in the *caṅ* formation"? Consider: *riramayiṣati*. Why "provided there is no elision (*alopa*)"? Consider: *ajagadat*, *aśaśaṭhat*. [Also, for the roots] *smṛ*, *dṝ*, *tvara*, *pratha*, *mrad*, *stṝ*, and *spaś*, the substitute *at* [is applied in place of the reduplicated syllable]. (Pāṇini 6.1.42)

In the case of roots such as *smṛ* and others, when followed by the causative suffix *ṇiC* and the *caṅ* substitute, after reduplication, the vowel *aT* is substituted for the preceding light vowel. Thus: *asasmarat*, *adadarat*. Because of the inclusion of the long vowel *taP* (indicating length), this substitution does not apply to a long vowel either. Examples: *atatvarat*, *apaprathat*, *amamradat*, *atastarat*, *apaspaśat*. Regarding *veṣṭ* and *ceṣṭ*: "Optionally [aT is substituted] for the root *veṣṭ* and *ceṣṭ* when followed by the causative suffix *ṇiC* and the *caṅ* substitute, after reduplication" (Pāṇini 6.1.43). Thus: *avaveṣṭat* or *aviveṣṭat*; *acaceṣṭat* or *aciceṣṭat*.

*Īt ca gaṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.144): When *gaṇ* is followed by a *ṇi* that is itself followed by *caṅ*, the substitution of *īt* occurs for the first syllable of the reduplicated form, as well as the substitution of *ac*. Examples: *ajīgaṇad gāḥ* and *ajagaṇad gāḥ*. This rule is formulated because [the root *gaṇ*] ends in *a*, making it *aglopi* (having lost its penultimate vowel). By this rule, the elision of the non-initial consonant (*halanādilopa*) is not superseded, because there is no conflict and because the rules belong to different syntactic units (*anekavākyatva*). In cases such as *apīpacat*, the substitution of *īt* is not superseded by the lengthening of the vowel (*dīrghatva*). However, where there is a single syntactic unit (*ekavākyatva*), supersession would indeed occur; for example, the substitution of *āt* supersedes the substitutions of *nīg* and so forth. The second quarter of the sixth chapter is completed.

(6.3.1) *vīpsābhīkṣṇyayor dve*: for that which expresses distributive repetition (*vīpsā*) or frequency (*ābhīkṣṇya*), two forms occur. Distributive repetition (*vīpsā*) is the desire to pervade distinct objects—whether actions, qualities, or substances. Examples: *vṛkṣaṃ vṛkṣaṃ siñcati* ("he waters tree after tree"); *grāmo grāmo ramaṇīyaḥ* ("every village is beautiful"); *grāme grāme pānīyam* ("there is water in every village"); *gṛhe gṛhe svāmī* ("there is a master in every house"); *rasaṃ rasaṃ bhakṣayati* ("he eats juice after juice"); *kriyāṃ kriyām ārabhate* ("he undertakes action after action"). Distributive repetition certainly exists even in the case of sequential order (*ānupūrvya*): *mūle mūle sthūlāḥ, agre 'gre sūkṣmāḥ* ("they are thick at the root after root, and fine at the tip after tip").

For if there were no distinction between the root and the tip here, there would be no sequence either. In the expression "Give one *māṣa* after another from this *kārṣāpaṇa*, sirs," the repetition (*vīpsā*) of "one *māṣa* after another" is understood; however, by the different word "from this *kārṣāpaṇa*," a restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) is established. In the cases "They flower one after another" and "They ripen one after another," there too it is simply a repetition.

"Both of these are wealthy; which one of these two is wealthy? "All of these are wealthy; which one among them is wealthy?"—here too, there is only repetition (*vīpsā*). *Ābhīkṣṇya* means frequency or repetition. He cooks again and again (*pacati pacati*). He cooks thoroughly again and again (*prapacati prapacati*). He cuts, indeed he cuts (*lunīhi lunīhīty evāyaṃ lunāti*). Having eaten repeatedly, he goes away (*bhuktvā bhuktvā vrajati*). He makes a *paṭapaṭa* sound; he acts with a *paṭapaṭa* sound; he behaves with a *paṭapaṭa* sound.
According to Pāṇini 6.3.2, when *pari* is used in the sense of exclusion (*varjana*) in a sentence, [the following rule applies].

When *pari* is used in the sense of exclusion (*varjana*) and occurs in a sentence construction, two forms [of the word] may optionally occur: *pari pari Trigartebhyaḥ vṛṣṭo devaḥ* or *pari Trigartebhyaḥ vṛṣṭo devaḥ*. Why "in the sense of exclusion"? [Consider: *odanaṃ pari siñcati* ("he sprinkles around the rice"). Why "in a sentence construction"? [Consider: *paritrigartaṃ vṛṣṭo devaḥ* ("the god has rained all around Trigarta"). (Pāṇini 6.3.3): *adhi*, *upari*, and *adhas* [take the genitive case when expressing proximity].

When proximity (*sāmīpya*) is understood, two forms occur for the words *adhi*, *upari*, and *adhas*. *adhyadhiṣṭhāpayati* ("he places [it] right upon"). *uparyupari brāhmaṇān udīkṣate* ("he looks at the Brahmins one after another"). *vyasany adho'dho vrajati* ("in his distress, he goes lower and lower"). Why "when proximity" (*sāmīpya*)? [Consider: *adhikaroti* ("he appoints"). [Also: *vākya-āder āmantritasyāsūyā-saṃmatyoḥ* (Pāṇini 8.1.8).

That which is addressed is called *āmantrita* (vocative); it refers to that which is being called upon. Regarding such a word at the beginning of a sentence, two forms occur in cases of censure (*asūyā*) and in cases of approval (*saṃmati*). In censure: *avinītaka3 avinītaka*, "O ill-behaved one! Ill-behaved one! Now you shall know, you rogue! Since censure is indeed present even in anger, contempt, and threats, anger and the others are not mentioned separately.
