In approval: *abhirūpaka3 abhirūpaka*, "O handsome one! You are truly beautiful. Why does it say "at the beginning of a sentence"? [Consider: "You are noble, Devadatta" (*udāro 'si, Devadatta*). Why does it say "in cases of censure and approval"? [Consider: "Devadatta, drive the cow hither, the white one" (*Devadatta, gām abhyāja śuklām*). [The rule] *ekasya supluk* (Pāṇini 6.1.69) applies.

When the word *eka* is doubled in the sense of distributive repetition (*vīpsā*), there is elision of the initial case-ending (*sup*). Example: *ekaikaḥ*. Regarding the rule *ābādhe puṃvac ca* (Pāṇini 6.1.129): "In the sense of distress" (*ābādha*)—that is, when the speaker’s mind is in a state of agitation—two forms occur for the word; there is elision of the case-ending and the application of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) to the initial member. Examples: *gatagataḥ*, *naṣṭanaṣṭaḥ*; *gatagatā*, *naṣṭanaṣṭā*.

(6.3.7) *prakāre guṇasya*: When "manner" (*prakāra*) is implied, a word expressing a quality (*guṇavacana*) takes two forms. There is elision of the case-ending (*sup-luk*) and the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) for the initial [of the second member]. Examples: *paṭupaṭuḥ* ("moderately clever") and *paṭupatvī* ("moderately clever"). Why "manner"? [Answer: *paṭuḥ* ("clever"). Why "quality"? [Answer: *agnir māṇavakaḥ* ("the boy is fire-like"; here *agni* is a substance, not a quality). Because it does not function as a manner, this does not apply to words such as *rūpa* ("form"), etc. (6.3.8) *akṛcchre priyasukhayor vā*: Optionally, when "not with difficulty" (*akṛcchra*) is implied, the words *priya* ("dear") and *sukha* ("pleasant") take two forms.

In the sense of "without difficulty" (*akṛcchra*) or "pleasure" (*priya*), the words *priya* and *sukha* optionally appear doubled, with the elision of the case-ending (*sup-luk*) and the substitution of the masculine form for the first member (*pūṃvad-bhāva*). Thus: *priyapriyeṇa dadāti*, *priyeṇa dadāti*; *sukhasukhena dadāti*, *sukhena dadāti*. Why say "without difficulty"? [Consider: *priyaḥ putraḥ* ("a beloved son"), *sukho rathaḥ* ("a comfortable chariot"). Regarding the rule *vyatihāre sarvādīnāṃ sur bahulam* (Pāṇini 8.1.12):

when reciprocity (*vyatihāra*) is implied, words beginning with *sarva-* take a double form; furthermore, the nominative singular ending (*su*) of the first member is frequently elided (*sup-luk*). Examples: *anyo'nyaṃ bhojayanti* ("they feed one another"), *itaretaraṃ bhojayanti* ("they feed one another").

(6.3.10) *parasyāpumsy ām*: After the words beginning with *sarva* (*sarvādi*), when followed by the feminine suffix *ām*, the form *ām* optionally occurs in the feminine and neuter genders. *anyo'nyām ime brāhmaṇyau bhojayataḥ*, *anyo'nyam*. *anyo'nyām ime brāhmaṇakule bhojayataḥ*, *anyo'nyam*. *itaretarām*, *itaretaram*. Why does the rule specify "not in the masculine" (*apumsi*)? Consider: *anyo'nyaṃ brāhmaṇau bhojayataḥ*. (6.3.11) *yathāsve yathāyatham*: [The word *yathāyatham* is formed from *yathāsvam* according to this rule.]
The term *yathāyatham* is an irregular formation (*nipātana*) in the sense of *yathāsvam* ("according to each [its own]").

Regarding the rule *dvandvaṃ rahasyamaryādāvyutkrāntiyajñapātraprayogeṣu* (Pāṇini 6.3.12): the word *dvi* is irregularly formed as *dvandvam* when used in the senses of "secret," "limit," "transgression," and "employment of sacrificial vessels. Examples: *dvandvaṃ mantrayante* ("they consult in secret"). *ācaturaṃ hīme paśavo dvandvam* ("for these animals pair up even unto the fourth generation"). *dvandvaṃ vyutkrāntāḥ* ("they have transgressed in pairs"). *dvandvaṃ yajñapātrāṇi prayunakti* ("he employs the sacrificial vessels in pairs"). Why specify "in the sense of secret and so forth"? Consider: *dvau dvau* ("two by two"). Here, the form *dvandvam* does not apply.

(6.3.13) *dvandvam* is an irregularly formed (*nipātana*) term for a pair (*yugma*) that is universally known in the world as being in constant association (*atyanta-sahacarita*), characterized by non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*). Examples: *sūryācandramasau dvandvam* (the sun and the moon as a pair); *Nāradaparvatau dvandvam* (Nārada and Parvata as a pair). Why "in constant association"? [Counter-example: *dvau Yudhiṣṭhirārjunau* (Yudhiṣṭhira and Arjuna—these two are brothers but not inseparable companions). Why "universally known in the world"? [Counter-example: *dvau Devadattayajñadattau* (Devadatta and Yajñadatta—these two are known only to specific individuals). (6.3.14) In cases of agitation (*saṃbhrama*), up to the point of comprehension (*yāvadbodham*).

When there is agitation on the part of the speaker, as many words as are necessary for that meaning to be understood should be employed: *ahir ahir ahiḥ!* (*snake, snake, snake!*); *budhyasva budhyasva budhyasva!* (*awake, awake, awake!*). It should be understood that this [rule] is governed by the sūtra *apādādau padād ekavākye* (Pāṇini 8.1.18), which states: "Except at the beginning of a foot [of a verse], [a word] following a word within a single sentence [is not pluta]. A *pada* is that by which a meaning is reached or understood; it consists of both a nominal form ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*) and a verbal form ending in a personal suffix (*tiṅanta*). A *vākya* (sentence) is a collection of *padas*.

(6.3.16) *yuṣmadasmadoḥ ṣaṣṭhīcaturthīdvitīyāntayor vāṃnau vā*: In a single sentence, when *yuṣmad* and *asmad* ending in the sixth, fourth, or second case occur after a word (*padāt*) and do not begin a sentence (*apādādau*), the substitutes *vām* and *nau* optionally take their place. Examples: *grāmo vāṃ svam*, *janapado nau svam* (The village is yours; the country is ours). [Alternatively: *grāmo yuvayoḥ svam*, *janapada āvayoḥ svam*. *grāmo vāṃ dīyate*, *janapado nau dīyate* (The village is given to you; the country is given to us). [Alternatively: *grāmo yuvābhyāṃ dīyate*, *janapada āvābhyāṃ dīyate*. *grāmo vāṃ paśyati*, *janapado nau paśyati* (He sees the village; he sees the country). [Alternatively: *grāmo yuvāṃ paśyati*, *janapada āvāṃ paśyati*.

"The village sees you two; the countryside sees us two. Why is there the mention of "the sixth case" (*ṣaṣṭhī*) and so forth? [To exclude cases such as: "It was done by you two in the village; it was done by us two in the countryside. Since the rule would be established even by the principle of "specifying what ends in that" (*tadantavidhi*), the explicit mention of the word "end" (*anta*) is for the sake of the actually heard form: "The village of your son; the countryside of our son. Only when not at the beginning of a *pāda* [is the substitution applied]:
"Rudra, the Lord of the Universe, the God, is the family deity of you all."

The Blessed One, the Buddha, the Conqueror of Māra, is the delighter of our family. By the rule *padāt* alone: *yuvayoḥ svam* ("your own") and *āvayoḥ svam* ("our own"). By the rule *ekavākya* alone: *Devadattas tiṣṭhati grāme, yuvayoḥ svaṃ nagaram* ("Devadatta stands in the village; the city is yours [two]"). For the plural, the substitutes are *vas* and *nas* (Pāṇini 6.3.17).

When the plural forms of *yuṣmad* and *asmad* occur after a word (*padāt*) within a single sentence (*ekavākye*), provided they do not occur at the beginning of a verse-quarter (*apādādau*), they optionally take the substitutes *vas* and *nas*, respectively. Examples: *grāmo vaḥ svam*, *janapado naḥ svam* [or] *grāmo yuṣmākaṃ svam*, *janapado 'smākaṃ svam*. *grāmo vo dīyate*, *janapado no dīyate* [or] *grāmo yuṣmabhyaṃ dīyate*, *janapado 'smabhyaṃ dīyate*. *grāmo vaḥ paśyati*, *janapado naḥ paśyati* [or] *grāmo yuṣmān paśyati*, *janapado 'smān paśyati*. In the case of the singular forms, *te* and *me* are substituted [according to Pāṇini 6.3.18].

In the singular, for the two [pronouns] *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, the substitutes *te* and *me* respectively optionally occur. *Grāmas te svam*, *janapado me svam*; *grāmas tava svam*, *janapado mama svam*; *grāmas te dīyate*, *janapado me dīyate*; *grāmas tubhyam dīyate*, *janapado mahyam dīyate*. By the rule *tvā-mau dvitīyāyāḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.94), for the two [pronouns] *yuṣmad* and *asmad* ending in the second case singular, the substitutes *tvā* and *mā* respectively optionally occur. *Grāmas tvā paśyati*, *janapado mā paśyati*; *grāmas tvām paśyati*, *janapado mām paśyati*.

(6.3.20) *Anvādeśe*: In the context of restating what has already been mentioned, the substitutes for *yuṣmad* and *asmad* occur by virtue of this mandatory re-statement. For example: "The village is yours two; moreover, the country is yours two. This applies everywhere.
(6.3.21) *Sapūrvāt prathamāntād vā*: [The substitutes occur] optionally when [the pronouns] are preceded by another word and end in the nominative case.

The substitutes for *yuṣmad* and *asmad* optionally occur even in subsequent reference (*anvādeśa*) after a word ending in the nominative case that is preceded by another word. For example: *grāme paṭo yuṣmākaṃ svam, atho janapade kambalo vaḥ svam*; or *atho janapade kambalo yuṣmākaṃ svam*. Likewise: *grāme kambalo 'smākaṃ svam, atho nagare kambalo naḥ svam*; or *atho nagare kambalo 'smākaṃ svam*. Why is it said "preceded by another word" (*sapūrvāt*)? [Consider: *paṭo yuṣmākaṃ svam, atho kambalo vaḥ svam*. (In this case, the option does not apply.)

Why [is it specified] "from that which ends in the first case"? [Consider: *paṭo nagare yuṣmākaṃ svam*, "the cloth in the city is yours," and *atho kambalo grāme vaḥ svam*, "and the blanket in the village is yours.
[This is because of the rule: *na cavāhāhaivayoge* (Pāṇini 6.3.22).

When used in conjunction with *ca* and other such particles, the substitutes for *yuṣmad* and *asmad* do not occur. For example: "The village is yours and my own; the country is mine and yours. "The village is given to you and to me; the country is given to me and to you. "The village sees you and me; the country sees me and you. "The village is perhaps yours and perhaps my own; the country is perhaps mine and perhaps yours. "The village is perhaps given to you and perhaps to me; the country is perhaps given to me and perhaps to you. "The village perhaps sees you and perhaps me; the country perhaps sees me and perhaps you."

The village is indeed yours; the countryside is indeed mine. The village is given to you; the countryside is given to me. The village sees you; the countryside sees me. The village is indeed your own; the countryside is indeed my own. The village is indeed given to you; the countryside is indeed given to me. The village indeed sees you; the countryside indeed sees me. The village belongs only to you; the countryside belongs only to me.

"The village is given to you alone; the country is given to me alone. The village sees only you; the country sees only me. In this manner, examples for the dual and plural numbers should be cited. Why [is it specified] "in the sense of *yoga*"? [Consider: "The village is yours, and the city is mine.
[This refers to the rule] 6.3.23: *dṛśyarthe ’nālocane*.

When objects of sight are present, but devoid of visual perception (*ālocana*), the substitutes for *yuṣmad* and *asmad* do not occur. For example: *grāmas tvāṃ saṃdṛśyāgataḥ*, "The village has come after seeing you"; *janapado māṃ saṃprekṣyāgataḥ*, "The country has come after seeing me. *grāmas tava svaṃ saṃdṛśyāgataḥ*, "The village has come after seeing your property"; *janapado mama svaṃ saṃprekṣyāgataḥ*, "The country has come after seeing my property. Why say "not visual perception"? [Observe: *grāmas tvālocayati*, "The village looks at you"; *janapado mām ālocayati*, "The country looks at me. A vocative that precedes [another word] is treated as non-existent (*asadvat*). (Pāṇini 6.3.24)

When *yuṣmad* and *asmad* are subject to substitution [by the case-endings], a preceding vocative (*āmantrita*) is treated as if it were non-existent. *Devadatta tava svam* ("O Devadatta, this is your property"). *Yajñadatta mama svam* ("O Yajñadatta, this is my property"). This applies in all such cases. Why specify "vocative"? Consider: *kambalas te svam*, *paṭo me svam* ("A woolen blanket is your property; a cloth is my property"). Why specify "preceding"? Consider: *mayaitat sarvam ākhyātaṃ yuṣmākaṃ dvijapuṅgavāḥ* ("All this has been told by me to you, O best of the twice-born"). For if the subsequent element were treated as non-existent, the prohibition *apādādau* ("not at the beginning of a verse-quarter") would not apply. What is the purpose of using the term *-vat* ("as if")? It is so that the original form may still be heard. [This is because of the rule: *na sāmānyavacanam ekārthe* (Pāṇini 6.3.25).

When a general term (*sāmānyavacana*) follows another word in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*), it does not behave as if non-existent (*asadvat*) when it is in the vocative (*āmantrita*). For example: *māṇavaka jaṭilaka te svam* ("O matted-haired boy, this is your own"). When the subsequent word behaves as if non-existent, the grammatical operations (*ādeśa*) depend on the preceding word. Why is it specified "a general term"? Consider: *Devadatta māṇavaka tava svam* ("O Devadatta, boy, this is yours"). Why is it specified "having a single referent" (*ekārtha*)? Consider: *Devadatta Yajñadatta yuvayoḥ svam* ("O Devadatta and Yajñadatta, this is yours both"). Or, according to rule 6.3.26, [the vocative] may optionally behave as if non-existent when there is plurality.

A vocative in the plural number, being a general term (*sāmānyavacana*), is optionally treated as non-existent (*asat*) when followed by a word in the same grammatical relation (*samānādhikaraṇa*). Examples: *brāhmaṇāḥ śaraṇyā yuṣmākaṃ svam* ("O Brahmins who are protectors, yours is the property") or *brāhmaṇāḥ śaraṇyā vaḥ svam*.
[The rule] "that which precedes is not established" (Pāṇini 6.3.27).

In the preceding section where *lakṣaṇas* (grammatical operations) are to be performed, that which follows is to be understood as *asiddha* (non-existent). Furthermore, from this point onward, each subsequent rule is *asiddha* with respect to each preceding one. In the examples *asmā uddharati*, *dvā atra*, *dvā ānaya*, and *asā ādityaḥ*, vocalic sandhi (*svarasandhi*) does not occur because the elision of the semivowel (*vyalopa*) is *asiddha*. In the examples *amuṣmai*, *amuṣmāt*, *amuṣya*, and *amuṣmin*, the suffixes *smāy* and so forth occur because the substitution of *u* (*utva*) is *asiddha*; thus, by the rule *ataḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.2), the forms are established.

In *śuṣkikā*, because the substitution of *k* is not established (*asiddha*), the optional substitution of *i* does not occur. In *kṣāmimān*, because the substitution of *m* is not established, the substitution of *v* for the suffix *mat* does not occur. In *guḍaliḍmān*, because the substitutions of *ḍh* and *j* are not established, the substitution of *v* for *mat* by rule 6.3.36 (*jhayaḥ*) does not occur. In *aujiḍhat*, because the substitution of *ḍh* and so forth are not established, the letter *j* remains when there is reduplication. [This applies also to] *supi nalopaḥ* (6.3.28).

The elision of *n* (*nalopa*) is indeed treated as non-existent (*asiddha*) when a case ending (*sup*) follows. Thus, in *rājabhyām*, *rājabhiḥ*, and *rājabhyaḥ*, because the elision of *n* is non-existent, the substitution of *āt* (*āttvam*), *ai* (*aistvam*), and *et* (*ettvam*) do not take place. In *vṛtrahabhyām* and *vṛtrahabhiḥ*, the augment *tuk* does not occur. Why is it said "when a case ending (*sup*) follows"? [Consider] *vṛtrahacchāyā*; here, the elision of *n* does not occur before a case ending. In *pañca brāhmaṇyaḥ*, the elision of *n* does not occur because the elision (*luk*) has not yet taken place, and furthermore, the suffix *ḍāp* does not apply due to the absence of a gender marker (*liṅga*).
[This is governed by] *na ni muḥ* (Pāṇini 6.3.29).

When a subsequent operation is to be applied that does not involve the sound *ś*, the substitution of *m* (*mubhāva*) is not considered non-existent (*asiddha*). Thus, in *amunā*, the substitution of *ā* (*āttva*) prescribed by Pāṇini 6.2.39 and 40 (*yañi supi*) does not take place. From this very statement, it is understood that even when the substitution of *na* (*nābhāva*) is to be applied, the substitution of *m* is not considered non-existent. Regarding the elision of *sij* (*sijlopa*), as stated in Pāṇini 6.3.30, when a single-substitute replacement (*ekādeśa*) is to be applied, the elision of *sij* is not considered non-existent. For example: *alāvīt*.

*ṣaṭhani ktādeśaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.3.31): When the substitution of *ṣatva* and the suffix *ṭhan* are to be applied, the substitution of *t* for *th* is not considered *asiddha*. [Example: *vṛkṇaḥ*. Because of the rule *jhali* (6.3.55), the substitution of *ṣatva* does not occur. [Example: *kṣībikaḥ*, meaning "one who behaves like a drunkard" (*kṣībeṇa carati*). The suffix *ṭhan* is applied by the rule *dvyajnaubhyāṃ ṭhan* (3.4.6). *plutas tuki* (6.3.32).

When a *tuṅ* (the augment *t*) is to be applied, a *pluta* vowel is not considered *asiddha*. In the example *agnā3i chattram*, the *tuṅ* is applied by [Pāṇini 6.1.70]. Once the *tuṅ* has been applied to form *agnici3t*, the *pluta* remains. When a *dhuṭ* (a consonant of the *jhal* class) is to be applied, the *ścutva* (the substitution of *ś* for *s*) is not considered *asiddha*. In the example *bhavāñ ścyotati*, the *dhuṭ* does not occur because of [Pāṇini 6.4.14], which states "not when *na*" follows.

(6.3.34) *dvitve parasavarṇaḥ*: In the case of doubling (*dvitva*), a subsequent homogeneous sound (*parasavarṇa*) is not considered non-existent (*asiddha*). [In *sayyaṇyanta*] doubling occurs by [Pāṇini 6.1.2] *yara*. (6.3.35) *mād upāntāc ca mator vaḥ*: After the letter *m*, and also after a penultimate [vowel], the suffix *matup* is replaced by *vaḥ*.

The substitution of *vat* occurs for the suffix *matup* after a word ending in *m*, ending in the vowel *a*, having *m* as its penultimate letter, or having *a* as its penultimate letter. Examples: *idaṃvān*, *kiṃvān*; *dāḍimīvān*; *vṛkṣavān*, *mālāvān*; *aharvān*, *bhāsvān*.

According to Pāṇini 6.3.36 (*jhayaḥ*), the substitution of *vat* occurs for *matup* following a word ending in a *jhay* consonant. Examples: *agnicitvān grāmaḥ* (a village possessing fire-altars); *vidyutvān balāhakaḥ* (a cloud possessing lightning).
In the sense of a name (*saṃjñā*), the substitution of *vat* for the suffix *matup* occurs [after a word ending in *a*]. Examples: *Kapīvatī*, *Maṇīvatī*.
[However,] this does not apply after words such as *yava* and others. (Pāṇini 6.3.37–38)

The substitution of *v* for *m* does not occur after [the words] beginning with *yava* when followed by the suffix *matup*. Examples: *yavamān*, *ūrmimān*, *bhūmimān*, *kṛmimān*. This is a prohibition where the rule *mād upāntāt* (Pāṇini 6.3.35) would otherwise have applied: *vaśāmān*, *śimbimān*; and where the rule *nāmni* (Pāṇini 6.3.37) would have applied: *kakudmān*; and where the rule *jhaya* (Pāṇini 6.3.36) would have applied. The group beginning with *yava* is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open class): *ikṣumatī*, *drumatī*, *kāntimatī*, *bandhumān* (name of a mountain), *bindumatī*, *cārumatī*—these are used as proper names (*saṃjñāyām*). Also: *aṣṭhīvaccakrīvatkakṣīvadudanvadrumaṇvaccarmaṇvatī* (Pāṇini 6.3.39).

These words are irregularly formed (*nipātita*) as proper names (*saṃjñā*). *Aṣṭhīvān* ("knee-jointed"), *cakrīvān* ("donkey"; *gardabhaḥ*), *Kakṣīvān* (the name of a seer), *udanvān* ("ocean"; *udadhiḥ*), *Rumaṇvān* (the name of a mountain), and *Carmaṇvatī* (the name of a river). When not used as a proper name: *asthimān*, *cakravān*, *kakṣāvān*, *udakavān*, *lavaṇavān*, *carmavān*. How is it that *Āsandīvān* is the name of a village? There exists another root-form for the word *āsandī*; thus, by the rule for proper names, the substitution of *vat* occurs for the suffix *mat*. [The rule] *rājanvān saurājye* (Pāṇini 6.3.40) [applies].

The form *rājanvān* is a nipātana (irregular formation) when it signifies good governance (*saurājya*). For example: *rājanvān deśaḥ* ("a country possessing good kings"). Why "when signifying good governance"? [Otherwise: *rājavān* ("possessing a king"). Regarding *kṛpo ro la akṛpaṇādīnām* (Pāṇini 6.3.41): the substitution of *l* for the *r* of the root *kṛp-* occurs, but not for those words beginning with *kṛpaṇa*. Examples: *kḷptam*, *kḷptavān*, *kalptā*, *kalpakaḥ*. Why "not for those beginning with *kṛpaṇa*"? [Counter-examples: *kṛpaṇaḥ*, *kṛpāṇaḥ*, *kṛpīṭam*, *karpaṭaḥ*.

(6.3.42) *prādīnām ayatau*: When *aya* follows *pra* and other such prefixes, the letter *r* is replaced by *l*. Examples: *palyayate*, *palāyate*. (6.3.43) *gro yaṅi*: [The substitution applies] when *yaṅ* follows *gṛ*.
The substitution of *l* for the *r* of the root *gṛ* occurs when followed by the intensive suffix (*yaṅ*). Thus: *nijegilyate*.

By the rule *aci vā* (Pāṇini 6.1.44), the substitution of *l* for the *r* of *gṛ* optionally occurs when a suffix beginning with a vowel follows. Thus: *nigalanam* or *nigaraṇam*; *nigālakaḥ* or *nigārakaḥ*; *nigālyate* or *nigāryate*. The substitution of *l* occurs [for the *r*] precisely before the causative suffix (*ṇic*). Why is it necessary to specify the condition "when prescribed" (*vihitaviśeṣaṇam*)? [To exclude cases such as: *girau*, *giraḥ*.

In the case of *pari* followed by words beginning with *gha*, etc., the substitution of *la* for the *ra* occurs optionally. Thus: *palighaḥ* or *parighaḥ*; *palyaṅkaḥ* or *paryaṅkaḥ*; *paliyogaḥ* or *pariyogaḥ*.
[The substitution of *la* for *ra* also occurs] in the case of *kapirika*, etc. (Pāṇini 6.3.46).

In the case of *kapirikā* and others, the substitution of *l* for the letter *r* optionally occurs. Thus: *kapilikā*, *kapirikā*; *talpilikā*, *tarpirikā*; *tilpirikā*, *tirpirikā*; *tilpilikaḥ*, *tirpilīkaḥ*; *lomāni*, *romāṇi*; *aṅguliḥ*, *aṅguriḥ*; *galaḥ*, *garaḥ*; *alam*, *aram*; *laghuḥ*, *raghuḥ*; *mūradevaḥ*, *mūladevaḥ*; *vālaḥ*, *vāraḥ*. This is an optionality restricted by specific conditions (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*). By rule 6.3.47, the substitution of *l* for the letter *ḍ* optionally occurs. Thus: *valabhī*, *vaḍabhī*; *nālaḥ*, *nāḍaḥ*.

*supaḥ prakṛter no lopaḥ* (6.3.48): The *n* at the end of a base that ends in a *sup* suffix is elided. Examples: *rājā*, *rājīyati*, *rājāyate*, *rājapuruṣaḥ*; *pañca*, *sapta*. Why "after a *sup* suffix"? [Counter-example: *ahan*. Why "of the base (*prakṛti*)"? [Counter-example: *tasmin*, *vṛkṣān*. *na saṃbuddhau* (6.3.49).
The elision of *n* does not occur in the vocative. *He rājan*; *he takṣan*.
In the neuter, optionally (*napuṃsake vā*, 6.3.50): for that which stands in the neuter gender in the vocative, the elision of *n* occurs optionally. *He varman*; *he varma*.

*Supi vali tadvat* (6.3.51): When a suffix beginning with a *val* sound follows a nominal stem (*sup*), the grammatical operation is the same as if it followed a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*). For example: *pañcānām*, *pañcakaḥ*, *rājabhyām*, *rājavat*. Why does the rule specify "when a case-suffix follows" (*supi*)? Consider *hanti*. Why does it specify "beginning with a *val* sound" (*vali*)? Consider *rājānau*, *rājānaḥ*. *Saṃyogasya padasya* (6.3.52): [The elision of a final *y* or *v* occurs] when the *saṃyoga* (consonant cluster) belongs to a complete word (*pada*).

The elision of the final consonant of a word occurs when it follows a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*). For example: *apacan*, *gomān*, *śreyān*. By extension (*atideśa*) from that [rule], the form is treated as masculine (*puṃvat*). According to *rāt saḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.53), the elision applies only to the *s* that follows the letter *r*. Examples: *kartuḥ*, *kartuḥ*, *dhātuḥ*. Why does the rule specify *sa* ("the *s*")? Consider: *ūrk*, *ūrgbhyām*.
*dhi saṅi* (Pāṇini 6.3.54): When *saṅ* follows a root ending in *dh*, the elision of the *s* occurs before an affix beginning with *dh*. Example: *cakādhi*. Why specify *saṅi*? Consider: *payodhiḥ*.
[The next rule is: *jhalo jhali* (Pāṇini 6.3.55).

The *sakāra* (*s*) following a *jhala* [consonant] is elided when followed by a *saṅ* [suffix] beginning with a *jhala*. Examples: *abhitta*, *abuddha*. Why "after a *jhala*"? Observe: *āstām*. Why "when followed by a *jhala*"? Observe: *abhitsvahi*. Only when followed by a *saṅ* suffix: *dṛṣatsthānam*.

By rule 6.3.56, the *sakāra* following a short vowel is elided when followed by a *jhala*. Examples: *akṛta*, *akṛthāḥ*. Only when followed by a *jhala*: observe *akṛṣātām*. Only when followed by a *saṅ* suffix: observe *dviṣṭarām*. [Objection: Since there is the indicator (*liṅga*) in rule 5.4.79 stating "of the root *as*," does this not mean the elision does not apply to verbal roots? [Response: How then do we explain *alaviṣṭa*? It does not occur because of the indicator in rule 6.3.57, "before *īṭ*."

*iṭa īṭi* (6.3.57): When *iṭ* follows, there is elision of a *s* that follows an *iṭ*, provided another *iṭ* follows. Example: *alāvīt*. Why does it say "after *iṭ*"? Observe: *ayākṣīt*. Why does it say "when *iṭ* [follows]"? Observe: *alaviṣṭa*. *skoḥ saṃyogādyor ante ca* (6.3.58): There is elision of the first element of a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*) consisting of *s* or *k*, whether at the end of a word or before a suffix beginning with *iṭ*.

The *saṃyoga* (consonant cluster) beginning with *s* or *k*, when followed by a *jhal* consonant or at the end of a word (*padānta*), undergoes elision (*lopa*). Examples: *laghuḥ*, *taṣṭaḥ*; *mak*, *taṭ*. By extension (*atideśa*) of that same rule: *magbhyām*. Only when *saṅi* follows: *śaksthātā*.

By the rule *coḥ kuḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.59), the *cavarga* (the group of palatal consonants) becomes the *kavarga* (the group of velar consonants) before a *jhal* consonant or at the end of a word. Examples: *paktā*, *pak*, *pagbhyām*. Only when *saṅi* follows: *kruñcaḥ*.

*kvinaḥ* (6.3.60): For a stem ending in *kvip*, there is the substitution of *ku* [for the final consonant] before a *jhal* sound and at the end of a word. Examples: *ghṛtaspṛk*, *tādṛk*, *tādṛgbhyām*.
The substitution of *k* for the final letter of the root *naś*, when it ends in *kvip*, is optionally prescribed as a *nipātana*. Thus: *jīvanak*, *jīvanaṭ*; *jīvanagbhyām*, *jīvanaḍbhyām*.
By the rule *ho ḍhaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.3.62), the letter *ḍh* is substituted for *h* when followed by a *jhal* consonant or at the end of a word. Thus: *soḍhā*, *voḍhā*; *madhuliṭ*, *madhuliḍbhyām*.

*dāder dhātor ghaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.3.63): For a root beginning with *d*, the *h* [at the end] becomes *gh* before an affix beginning with a *jhal* consonant or at the end of a word. Examples: *dagdhā*; *dhak*, *dhagbhyām*. Why "beginning with *d*" (*dādeḥ*)? [Consider] *soḍhā*, *voḍhā*. Why "of a root" (*dhātoḥ*)? [Consider] *dāmaliṭ*.
*vā druhamuhasnuhasnihām* (Pāṇini 6.3.64).

In the case of *druh* and other roots, the letter *gh* optionally replaces the letter *h* before a *jhal* consonant or at the end of a word. Thus: *drogdhā*, *droḍhā*; *mitradhruk*, *mitradhruṭ*; *mitradhrugbhyām*, *mitradhruḍbhyām*. *unmogdhā*, *unmoḍhā*; *unmuk*, *unmuṭ*; *unmugbhyām*, *unmuḍbhyām*. *utsnogdhā*, *utsnoḍhā*; *utsnuk*, *utsnuṭ*; *utsnugbhyām*, *utsnuḍbhyām*. *celasnegdhā*, *celasneḍhā*; *celasnik*, *celasniṭ*; *celasnigbhyām*, *celasniḍbhyām*. [The rule] *nahāho dhaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.3.65) applies.
*Na* becomes *dha* before a *jhal* consonant and at the end of a word. Examples: *naddhā*; *upānat*, *upānadbhyām*. [The root] *āh* [becomes *āth*]: *āttha*.
*vraśca-bhrasja-sṛja-mṛja-yaja-rāja-bhrāja-śāṃ ṣaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.15):

For the roots beginning with *vraśca*, the substitution of *ṣ* occurs before a *jhal* consonant and at the end of a word. Examples: *vraṣṭā*, *mūlavṛṭ*; *bhraṣṭā*, *dhānābhṛṭ*; *sraṣṭā*, *rajjusṛṭ*; *mārṣṭā*, *kaṃsaparimṛṭ*; *yaṣṭā*, *upayaṭ*, *virāṭ*, *vibhrāṭ*; *veṣṭā*, *viṭ*; *praṣṭā*, *prāṭ*, *pṛṭ*.
*jhalo jaś* (Pāṇini 6.1.67):

*jaś* substitution occurs for *jhal* sounds [at the end of a word] before a *jhali* sound or at the end of a word. Examples: *labdhā*; *triṣṭub atra*. [The author] will state *khari caraṃ* (6.4.148) and *jhayo hasya pūrvasavarṇam* (6.4.156).
*taso matvarthe* (6.3.68): [The suffix] *tas* is substituted for *tasi* when it has the sense of the possessive suffix *matup*.

When a suffix expressing possession (*matvarthīya*) follows, the substitutes *ta* and *sa* replace the letters *t* and *s*, respectively. This statement is made for the purpose of overriding the rules of *jaś*-substitution and *rut*-substitution. Examples: *vidyutvān balāhakaḥ* ("the cloud possessing lightning") and *yaśasvī* ("possessing fame"). (6.3.69) *jhaṣa ekācaḥ sdhvor baśo bhaṣ*:

When a suffix beginning with *s* or *dhv* follows, or at the end of a word (*padānte*), the *baś* sounds of a one-syllable root ending in a *jhaṣ* sound are replaced by *bhaṣ* sounds. Examples: *bhotsyate*, *abhuddhvam*, *bhut*. Why "ending in a *jhaṣ* sound" (*jhaṣaḥ*)? [Counter-example: *dāsyati*. Why "one-syllable" (*ekācaḥ*)? [Counter-example: *dāmaliṭ*. Why "beginning with *s* or *dhv*" (*sdhvoḥ*)? [Counter-example: *boddhā*. Why "a *baś* sound" (*baśaḥ*)? [Counter-example: *krotsyati*, *krut*.

*dhas tathoś ca* (Pāṇini 6.3.70): When *t* or *th* follow, as well as when *s* or *dhv* follow, the *baś* sounds of the root *dadhāti* become *bhaṣ*. Thus: *dhattaḥ*, *dhatthaḥ*, *dhatse*, *dhaddhve*. Why does the rule specify "when *t* or *th* follow"? Consider: *abhidadhmahe*. [The substitution applies] only after a *jhaṣ* sound: *dadhāti*, *dadhāsi*. *tathor dho 'dhaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.3.71).

In place of the *t* and *th* of the roots *labh* and *dadh*, there occurs *dh* when they end in a *jhaṣ* consonant. Examples: *alabdha*, *alabdhāḥ*. Why "of *dadh*" (*adha*)? [To exclude cases like] *dhattaḥ*, *dhatthaḥ*. Precisely because of this statement, the substitution of *jaś* does not apply first.
According to *si ṣaḍhoḥ kaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.41), when a suffix beginning with *s* follows, *k* is substituted for *ṣ* and *ḍh*. Examples: from *piṣ*—*pekṣyati*; from *vah*—*vakṣyati*.

*mo no mvoś ca* (Pāṇini 6.3.73): When a root ending in *m* is followed by a *jhal* consonant or a word-final position, and when *m* or *v* follows, the *m* is replaced by *n*. Examples: *śāntaḥ*, *śāntavān*; *praśān*; *jaṅganmi*, *jaganvān*. The rule applies only when following a root: [as in *praśān*, but not in] *agnim*. *radāt tatavator daś ca* (Pāṇini 6.3.74): When *t* or *tavant* follows a root ending in *r* or *d*, the *m* is replaced by *n*, and the *r* or *d* is also replaced by *n*.

When the suffixes *kta* and *ktavat* follow the letters *r* or *d*, the initial letter of those suffixes becomes *n*, and the preceding vowel becomes long (*da*), because it is heard [as the result] of the preceding element. Examples: *pūrṇaḥ*, *pūrṇavān*; *bhinnaḥ*, *bhinnavān*. In the form *bhinnavadbhyām*, [the substitution] will not occur because the following [element] is not heard. Why "after *r* or *d*" (*radāt*)? Consider *kṛtam*, *kṛtavān*. Why "of *kta* and *ktavat*" (*taktavatoḥ*)? Consider *bhettā*. Only when a *jhal* consonant follows: consider *muditam*. How about *Kārtiḥ*? The *repha* is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) due to its being extrinsic (*bahiraṅga*). [This is governed by] Pāṇini 6.3.75: *yaṇ-saṃyogād ātaḥ*.

The letter *n* occurs in place of the *t* or *tavant* suffixes following a word ending in the vowel *ā*, provided that this *ā* is preceded by a consonant cluster (*saṃyoga*). Examples: *glānaḥ*, *glānavān*; *mlānaḥ*, *mlānavān*. Why "after a semi-vowel" (*yaṇ*)? Consider: *āmnātaḥ*. Why "after a consonant cluster" (*saṃyogāt*)? Consider: *yātaḥ*. Why "ending in *ā*" (*ātaḥ*)? Consider: *cyutaḥ*. The rule applies only when [the root] is a verbal root (*dhātu*): consider *niryātaḥ*. [Rule 6.3.76:

After roots ending in *ṛ* and after roots beginning with *lū*, the *n* is substituted for the *t* or *tavant* suffixes and for the suffix *ktin*. Examples: *kīrṇaḥ*, *kīrṇavān*; *lūnaḥ*, *lūnavān*; *līnaḥ*, *līnavān*; *kīrṇiḥ*, *lūniḥ*, *līniḥ*.
In the case of the root *pūñ* meaning "to destroy," the substitution of *na* occurs for the suffixes *t* and *tavat* following it. For example:
*pūnā yavāḥ* ("the barley grains have been destroyed"). Why specify "in the sense of destroying"? [Because otherwise: *pūtaḥ*, *pūtavān*. [Next rule:
*dugvor ū ca* (Pāṇini 6.3.78).

After the two [roots] *du* and *gu*, when followed immediately by the suffixes *t* or *tavant*, the substitution of *n* occurs; furthermore, the *u* of *du* and *gu* is replaced by *ū*. Thus: *ādūnaḥ*, *ādūnavān*; *vigūnaḥ*, *vigūnavān*.

According to Pāṇini 6.3.79 (*ser grāse*), after the root *si* (*sinoti*), when followed by the suffixes *t* or *tavant*, the substitution of *n* occurs provided that "swallowing" (*grāsa*) is expressed. Example: *sino grāsaḥ* ("a swallowed morsel"). Why specify "swallowing"? [Counter-example: *sitā pāśena sūkarī* ("the sow is bound by a snare").

*oditaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.24): After a root marked with the *odit* designation, the *ta* and *tavat* suffixes undergo the substitution of *na*. Examples: *lagnaḥ*, *lagnavān*. This is because of the rule *svādaya oditaḥ* (Dhātupāṭha 4.91): *prasūnaḥ*, *prasūnavān*; *ḍīnaḥ*, *ḍīnavān*. The absence of the augment *iṭ* occurs precisely due to this *odit* marker as an indicator (*liṅga*). *kṣeḥ kṣī ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.25): [After the root *kṣi*, there is the substitution of *kṣī* for *kṣi*].

The substitution of *na* for the final vowel and consonant of the root *kṣi* before the suffixes *tata* and *tavat* does not occur; furthermore, there is the change to *kṣī*. [Examples: *kṣīṇaḥ*, *kṣīṇavān*. Pāṇini 6.3.82: "Optionally before suffixes expressing state (*bhāva*), abuse, or wretchedness. When the meanings of state and so forth are intended, the substitution of *na* for the final vowel and consonant of *kṣi* before *tata* and *tavat* optionally occurs; furthermore, there is the change to *kṣī*. [Examples: *kṣībhāvaḥ* ("the state of being wasted") and *kṣībhūtaḥ* ("become wasted"). *kṣīṇam anena*, *kṣitam anena* ("this has been wasted by him"). *kṣīṇāyuḥ*, *kṣitāyuḥ* ("one whose life is exhausted"). *kṣīṇakas tapasvī*, *kṣitakas tapasvī* ("a wretched ascetic").

In the rule *śyo 'sparśe* (Pāṇini 6.3.83), the substitution of *n* for the *t* and *tavat* suffixes following the root *śyai* does not occur when it signifies anything other than touch. Example: *śīnaṃ ghṛtam* ("the clarified butter has congealed"). Why "other than touch"? Example: *śīto vāyuḥ* ("the wind is cold").
In the rule *añco 'navadhau* (Pāṇini 6.3.84): [The substitution of *n* for the *t* and *tavat* suffixes following the root *añc* does not occur when it does not signify a limit.]

The suffix *na* does not occur after the roots *añc* and *śak*, followed by the suffixes *-tata* and *-tavat*, when they refer to an object that lacks a limit (*anavadhi*). For example: *samaknau śaknuneḥ pakṣau* ("the two wings are capable of reaching as far as the ears"). Why "when there is no limit"? Consider: *udaktam udakaṃ kūpāt* ("water drawn from a well").

Regarding *adyūte divaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.3.85): the suffix *na* does not occur after the root *div*, followed by the suffixes *-tata* and *-tavat*, except in the sense of gambling (*dyūta*). For example: *ādyūnaḥ*, *ādyūnavān*. Why "except in the sense of gambling"? Consider: *dyūtaṃ vartate* ("gambling is taking place").

*Avāte nirvāṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.3.86): The form *nirvāṇa* is prescribed [as a substitute for *ni-vṛt*] except when preceded by *vāta*. Examples: *nirvāṇo bhikṣuḥ* ("the monk has attained extinction"); *vātena nirvāṇaḥ pradīpaḥ* ("the lamp is extinguished by the wind"). Why say "except when preceded by *vāta*" (*avāte*)? [Observe: *nirvāto vātaḥ* ("the wind has ceased"). *Ghrātrārtihrīnudondavido vā* (Pāṇini 6.3.87): [The substitution of *na* for the final vowel of the prefix] is optional after the verbal roots *ghrā*, *ṛ*, *hī*, *nud*, *und*, and *vid*.

After the roots *ghrā* and others, the substitution of *na* for the suffixes *kta* and *ktavatu* is optional. Thus: *ghrāṇaḥ*, *ghrātaḥ*; *trāṇaḥ*, *trātaḥ*. By virtue of the rule of fixed optionality (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*), we have *Devatrātaḥ*. *Ṛṇam* means "that which is to be cleared" (*śodhyam*); *ṛtam* means "truth" (*satyam*). *Hrīṇaḥ*, *hrītaḥ*; *nunnaḥ*, *nuttaḥ*; *samunnaḥ*, *samuttaḥ*; *vinnaḥ*, *vittaḥ*. Because of its association with the root *undi*, the term *vittaḥ* here refers to the root *vid* (to find), not *vid* (to know). Regarding *prastyo maḥ* (Pāṇini 6.3.88): after the root *styai* preceded by *pra*, the substitution of *ma* for the suffixes *kta* and *ktavatu* is optional. Thus: *prastīmaḥ*, *prastīmavān*; *prastītaḥ*, *prastītavān*.

*kṣaḥ* (6.3.89): For the root *kṣai*, the final *m* occurs in place of [the suffixes] *tata* and *vatu*. Examples: *kṣāmaḥ*, *kṣāmavān*. The separation of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) is for the sake of making it obligatory. *śuṣaḥ kaḥ* (6.3.90).
The suffix *ka* occurs after the root *śuṣ* when followed by the participial suffixes *t* and *tavat*. [Examples: *śuṣkaḥ*, *śuṣkavān*.
By rule 6.3.91, the suffix *va* occurs after the root *pac* when followed by the participial suffixes *t* and *tavat*. [Examples: *pakvaḥ*, *pakvavān*.

*hlāda-hlad- (6.3.92): When the suffixes *tā* and *tavant* follow, the substitution of *hlad* occurs for *hlād*. Examples: *prahlannaḥ*, *prahlannavān*. In the case of the causative (*ṇyanta*), it is *prahlāditaḥ*. [The rule] *ktini* (6.3.93) [follows].

When the suffix *ktin* follows, *hlāda* is substituted for *hlād*. [Examples: *prahlattiḥ*. The words *phulla*, *kṣība*, *kṛśa*, and *ullāgha* are irregularly formed (*nipātyante*). [Examples: *phullaḥ*, *kṣībaḥ*, *kṛśaḥ*, *ullāghaḥ*. Because these are irregular formations (*nipātana*) when devoid of prefixes (*prādi*), this substitution does not occur here: *praphullāḥ*. How then are *utphullaḥ*, *saṃphullaḥ*, and *parikṛśaḥ* explained? They will be derived from *prādi* compounds.

*na dhyākhyāpṝmūrchimadām* (Pāṇini 6.3.95): That which has been prescribed [by the substitution of *kta* for *niṣṭhā*] after the roots *dhyai*, *khyā*, *pṝ*, *mūrch*, and *mad* does not take place. *dhyātam*, *dhyātavān*; *khyātam*, *khyātavān*; *pūrtaḥ*, *pūrtavān*; *mūrtaḥ*, *mūrtavān*; *mattaḥ*, *mattavān*.
*vittaḥ* [is used] in the senses of "known" (*pratīta*) and "possessed" (*bhoga*). (6.3.96)

In the case of the root *vid* ending in the suffix *kta*, when the meaning is "known" (*pratīta*) or "wealth" (*artha*), the absence of the change to *n* is prescribed as a nipātana. Thus: *vittaḥ* (known), *vittam* (wealth). Any other [meaning] is *vinnam*.

Regarding *bhittam* in the sense of a "fragment" (*śakala*) [Pāṇini 6.3.97]: in the case of the root *bhid* ending in the suffix *kta*, when the word to be expressed is a fragment, the absence of the change to *n* is prescribed as a nipātana. Thus: *bhittam*, meaning a fragment. Why "fragment"? [To show: *bhinnam* (split). How is it that *bhittabhinnam* occurs? It means fragments.

*Sasajuṣo ruḥ* (6.3.98): For a word ending in *s*, and for the word *juṣ* preceded by *sa*, the substitute *ru* occurs. Examples: *agniḥ*, *sajūḥ*. By extension of that same rule, [the forms] *payobhyām* and *sajūrbhyām* are formed.

The word *ahan* undergoes the substitution of *ru*. [Examples: *ahaḥ*, *ahobhyām*, *ahaḥsu*. When there is elision (*luk*) [of the case-ending], *ra* is substituted for the *n* of *ahan* before a word beginning with a vowel that does not contain *r* (Pāṇini 6.3.100). [Examples: *ahar dadāti*; *ahar bhuṅkte*. Why is it said "before a vowel not containing *r*" (*arī*)? [Counter-examples: *ahorūpam*; *ahorātram*. [In these cases, the *n* remains because the following words begin with *r* or *l*. *Kṛtsnam aho rathantaram sāma gāyati*. *Sarvam aho ramasva*. *Yātaḥ śanaiḥ sarvam aho rathena*. Why is it said "when there is elision" (*lukī*)? [Counter-example: *dīrghāhā nidāghaḥ* (where the *n* is retained because the case-ending is not elided).
In the case of *pracetas* before the word *rājan*, a *repha* (visarga) optionally occurs when *rājan* follows.
Thus: *praceto rājan* or *pracetā rājan*. In the case of words beginning with *pati*, [the final vowel] of words beginning with *ahar* undergoes substitution [with *a*]. (Pāṇini 6.3.102)

The letter *r* optionally occurs after words such as *ahar-* when followed by words beginning with *pati-*. Thus: *aharpatiḥ*, *ahaḥpatiḥ*, *ahanpatiḥ*; *gīrpatiḥ*, *gīṣpatiḥ*, *gīḥpatiḥ*; *dhūrpatiḥ*, *dhūṣpatiḥ*, *dhūḥpatiḥ*.

Regarding the rule *do 'naḍuhaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.3.103): the letter *d* is substituted for the final letter of the word *anaḍuh-* [when followed by a case ending]. Thus: *bahvanaḍut kulam* (a family with many oxen), *anaḍudbhyām*. [Question: How is it that [the form] *anaḍvān* is formed? [Answer: It will not occur [as a substitute], due to the force of the prescription of the augment *num* [in Pāṇini 5.4.36].

(6.3.104) *vasusraṃsudhvaṃsāṃ saḥ*: For the *s* of a word ending in *vas*, and for the *s* of *sraṃsu* and *dhvaṃsu*, the substitution of *d* occurs. Examples: *vidvat-kulam*, *vidvadbhyām*; *ukhā-srat*, *ukhāsradbhyām*; *parṇa-dhvat*, *parṇadhvadbhyām*. Why "of that [word]" (*saḥ*)? Consider *papivān* (in the nominative singular). (6.3.105) *ti-pi*: [The substitution of *d* occurs] when the suffix *tip* follows.

In certain cases, the letter *d* replaces the final *s* of a word ending in *s* when followed by [the suffix] *si*. For example: *anvaśāt*. Only when it follows *sa-* [as part of the root]: *anvahan*. Only when it is a word (*pada*): *śāsti*. Regarding Pāṇini 6.3.106, *sipi rur vā*:

When followed by the suffix *si*, the substitute *ru* optionally occurs for the final *s* of a word ending in *s*, or the letter *d* may occur. For example: *acakās tvam*, *acakāt tvam*. Why specify "when followed by *si*" (*sipi*)? Consider: *acakād bhavān*.
(6.3.107) *daḥ*: When *sip* follows, a word ending in *d* optionally takes *ru*. Thus, *abhinas tvam* or *abhinat tvam*.

(6.3.108) *dhātor vor anaci ko dīrghaḥ*: A long vowel is substituted for *u* or *ū* of a verbal root (*dhātu*) when followed by a consonant (*k*), provided that the following syllable does not begin with a vowel (*anaci*).

When the letters *r* or *v*, not followed by a vowel (*anac*), follow a verbal root (*dhātu*), a long vowel (*dīrgha*) is substituted for the *ik* vowels (*i, u, ṛ, lṛ*) that precede them. Examples: *gīḥ*, *dhūḥ*, *pūḥ*, *āstīrṇaḥ*, *kīrtayati*, *dīvyati*, *sīvyati*, *pratidīvnā*. Why specify "of a verbal root"? [To exclude cases like: *sarpiḥ*, *vāyuḥ*, *kurkuraḥ*, *kurkurīyati*, *caturbhyaḥ*, *caturyati*. For it is a conventional rule (*rūḍhi*) that only those forms which are explicitly taught as such are considered verbal roots. Why specify "of *r* and *v*"? *samaḥ suṭi saḥ* (6.4.1): When *suṭ* follows, the *s* of *sam* becomes *ṣ*. *saṃsskartā*, *saṃskartā*, *saṃskartā*.

When a vowel follows a word ending in *ṅ*, *m*, or *s* that is preceded by a short vowel, doubling occurs before that vowel. For example: *pratyaṅṅ āste*, *vaṇṇ āste*, *pacann āste*. The *visarjanīya* replaces the *repha* (*r*) when it occurs at the end of a word (*virāma*). For example: *vṛkṣaḥ*, *agniḥ*. By rule 6.4.21, *khari*:
the *visarjanīya* replaces the *repha* when followed by a *khar* (voiceless consonant). For example: *vṛkṣaḥ khanati*, *vṛkṣaḥ pacati*.

The *visarjanīya* is substituted for the *ru* [the substitute for *r*] when followed by a *sup* [case-ending]. As in: *payaḥsu*, *sarpiḥṣu*. Why "for *ru*"? [Consider: *gīrṣu*, *dhūrṣu*. Why the letter *p* [in *supi*]? [Consider: *gīḥ*.

there is elision (*lopa*) of *ru* following a vowel (*avarṇa*) before a vowel (*aś*). For example: *ka āste* ("Who sits? and *brāhmaṇā hasanti* ("The Brahmins laugh").

When followed by a vowel (*aci*), the *v* and *y* sounds become slightly more constricted (*īṣatspṛṣṭatara*), and their elision (*lopa*) may optionally occur. Regarding the rule *chavi raḥ saḥ* (Pāṇini 8.3.28): when a *repha* (*r*) is followed by a *chavi* (a voiceless consonant), since the substitution of *visarjanīya* would otherwise apply, the substitution of *sakāra* (*s*) is prescribed here. Examples: *punar chādayati*, *rathaś carati*. Why "after *chavi*"? Consider: *ākhur yāti*, *vāyur bhramati*.

*vā śari* (Pāṇini 6.4.29): When followed by a *śar* sound, the letter *r* optionally becomes *s*. Examples: *gauḥ śete*, *gauḥ śete*; *vṛkṣaḥ sāye*, *vṛkṣaḥ sāye*; *vṛkṣaṣ ṣaṇḍe*, *vṛkṣaḥ ṣaṇḍe*. *khari lopaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.30): Before a *khar* sound, [the *r*] is elided.
The elision of the letter *r* optionally occurs before a sibilant (*śar*) when it follows a hard consonant (*kharpare*). Examples: *vṛkṣāḥ sthātāraḥ*, *vṛkṣās sthātāraḥ*, *vṛkṣāḥ sthātāraḥ*.

According to *kupvoḥ xkafpau* (Pāṇini 8.3.37), when the guttural class (*kavarga*) or the labial class (*pavarga*) follows, the substitutes *jihvāmūlīya* (*x*) and *upadhmānīya* (*f*) optionally take the place of the letter *r*. Examples: *vṛkṣax karoti*, *vṛkṣaḥ karoti*; *vṛkṣax khanati*, *vṛkṣaḥ khanati*; *vṛkṣaf patati*, *vṛkṣaḥ patati*; *vṛkṣaf phalati*, *vṛkṣaḥ phalati*. The rule applies only when a hard consonant (*khari*) follows: *bhānur gacchati*, *vāyur bhramati*.

(6.4.32) *sasaṃkhyasyānādau saḥ*: In place of the *repha* (*r*) belonging to a word that includes a numeral, a *sakāra* (*s*) is substituted when followed by *k* or *p*, provided these sounds do not occur at the beginning of a word. The *sakāra* (*s*) replaces the *repha* (*r*) of *ror* itself when followed by a form of the suffix *kāmya*. Example: *payaskāmyati*. Why specify *ror*? The restriction "when followed by *kāmya*" (*kāmye*) also applies: *gīḥkāmyati*. From this point onward, both the rules *saḥ* and *iṇaḥ ṣaḥ* remain in force.

The letter *s* replaces the *r* of a word accompanied by a numeral when it follows the vowel *a* and occurs before roots such as *kṛ* ("to do") and others. Examples: *ayaskāraḥ*, *ayaskāmaḥ*, *ayaskaṃsaḥ*, *ayaskumbhaḥ*, *ayaspātram*, *ayaskuśā*, *ayaskarṇī*. Why is it said "after *a*" (*ataḥ*)? Consider *gīḥkāraḥ*. Why is it said "followed by *t*" (*taparaḥ*)? Consider *bhāḥkaraṇam*. Why is it said "before *kṛ* and others" (*kṛñādiṣu*)? Consider *ayaḥkīlaḥ*. Why is it said "accompanied by a numeral" (*sasaṃkhyasya*)? Consider *śvaḥkāraḥ*. This applies only within a compound (*samāse*): *payaḥ karoti*. This applies only when the preceding word is not a subordinate member (*anuttarasya*): *paramapayaḥkāraḥ*. [Also see] *adhaḥśirasoḥ pade* (Pāṇini 6.4.41).

In the words *adhas* and *śiras*, the letter *r* becomes *s* when followed by the word *pada*. Examples: *adhaspadam*, *śiraspadam*. This applies only within a compound (*samāsa*); otherwise: *adhaḥ padam*. This applies only when [the preceding word] is not part of a further compound (*anuttara*); otherwise: *paramaśiraḥpadam*. (6.4.42) In the word *namas*, the letter *r* becomes *s* when followed by the letters *k* or *p* (or their voiced counterparts). Examples: *namaskṛtya*, *namaskartā*. This applies only within a compound; otherwise: *namaḥ kṛtvā*.
When *kṛ* follows, the *r* of *namas* optionally becomes *s*. Thus, *namaskaroti* or *namaḥ karoti*. This rule is commenced for the sake of the *tiṅ* suffixes. *tirasaḥ* (6.4.44).

The letter *s* optionally replaces the *r* of *tiras* when followed by the root *kṛñ*. Thus: *tiraskṛtya*; *tiraskaroti*, *tiraḥ karoti*. By virtue of the rule of restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*), the form *tiraḥ kṛtvā* does not occur.
[The group beginning with] *kaska-* [is treated as a *kṛt-gati* compound]. (Pāṇini 6.4.45)

The words beginning with *kaska-* are correct forms. *Kas*, *kaḥ*—*kautaskutaḥ*—*bhrātuṣputraḥ*—*śunaskarṇaḥ*—*sadyaskālaḥ*—*sadyaskrīḥ*; [the latter] from the root *krī* with the suffix *kvip*: "a sacrifice performed at that very time" (*sādyaskraḥ*). As for *kāṃ* and *kām*, they are established by the preceding rule (6.4.4). Regarding *sarpiṣkuṇḍikā*, *dhanuṣkapālam*, and *yajuṣpātram*, although these are already established by the preceding rule (6.4.39), this statement is made for the sake of the meaning of the subsequent word.

*paramasarpiṣkuṇḍikā*, *paramadhanuṣkapālam*, *paramayajuṣpātram*; for others it does not occur: *paramasarpiḥkumbhaḥ*—this refers to a magnet. This is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open class); therefore, *bhāskara* and others should also be understood as belonging here.
And [the rule] "for *ādeśa*, *sanādi*, *śās*, *vasi*, and *ghas*, there is *sa*" (Pāṇini 6.4.46).

The *ṣ* is substituted for the *s* of an affix following a guttural (*kavarga*) or the vowel *iṇ*, provided that the affix is related to the desiderative suffix (*san*) and so forth, as well as for the *s* of the roots *śās*, *vas*, and *ghas*. Examples: *siṣeca*, *suṣvāpa*; *pipakṣati*, *cikīrṣati*, *tuṣṭūṣati*; *vṛkṣeṣu*, *dhātuṣu*, *goṣu*, *kartṛṣu*; *acaiṣīt*; *śiṣṭaḥ*, *uṣitaḥ*, *jakṣuḥ*. Why does it say "and after *ka*" (*koś ca*)? [Observe: *svapiti*, *yiyāsati*. Why does it say "of the substitutes and so forth" (*ādeśādīnām*)? [Observe: *visismiye*. Why does it say "*sa*" (the letter *s*)? [Observe: *kurutaḥ*.
[This rule applies] even when there is an intervention by *num*, *visarjanīya*, or *śar* sounds (Pāṇini 6.4.47).

When there is an intervention by nasal sounds (*num*) and so forth, the substitution of *ṣ* occurs for an initial *s* that follows a guttural (*kavarga*) or a vowel (*iṇ*). Examples: *sarpīṃṣi*, *yajūṃṣi*; *sarpiḥṣu*, *yajuḥṣu*; *sarpiṣṣu*, *yajuṣṣu*. [Question: How is it that we have *niṃsse* and *niṃssu* (with *kvip* and *su* suffixes)? When the desiderative suffix *san* becomes *ṣan*, the change to *ṣ* occurs for the letter *iṇ* that follows it. Thus, *tuṣṭūṣati*. Because the restriction applies only to letters of the same class (*samānajātīya*), there is no substitution here in *pratīṣiṣati*. The restriction "only when *ṣan*" does not apply here, because of the repeated mention of *ṇi*. Why [is the suffix] specified as *ṣanī*? [Consider] *siṣeca*. Why is the specific mention of *ṣ* used? *ṇer asvidisvadisahasaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.49): When a *ṣaṇ* affix follows a causative (*ṇyanta*) root that excludes *svid*, *svad*, and *sah*, the substitution of *ṣ* occurs for the letter *iṇ* (the letter *s*) that follows it. Example: *siṣecayiṣati*. Why is there an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of *svid* and the others? [To show: *sisvedayiṣati*, *sisvādayiṣati*, *sisāhayiṣati*. Because the exclusion of *svid* and the others implies the inclusion of those similar roots that are taught with an initial *ṣ* (*ṣopadeśa*), this is a re-activation (*punar-prasava*) of a rule, not an original injunction (*vidhi*). Example: *sismārayiṣati*. *prādīnāṃ susūsostustubhasthāsenisedhasicasañjasvañjām* (Pāṇini 6.4.50).
