Examples: *vadhāluḥ*, *ghātāluḥ*, *hantāluḥ*. (6.4.104) *apādāne striyām ktin* [The suffix *ktin* is applied after a verbal root to form a feminine noun denoting the point of departure (*apādāna*). Example: *āgamanaṃ vatsyānām* ("the arrival of the Vatsyas"). (6.4.105) *striyāṃ ktin* [The suffix *ktin* is applied after a verbal root to form a feminine noun. Example: *kṛtiḥ*. (6.4.106) *er ac* [The suffix *ac* is applied after a verbal root ending in *i* or *ī* to form a feminine noun. Example: *citiḥ*. (6.4.107) *ṇyāsaśrantho yuc* [The suffix *yuc* is applied after roots ending in *ṇi*, as well as after *ās*, *śranth*, and *granth* to form a feminine noun. Examples: *kāraṇā*, *pāraṇā*, *āsanā*, *śranthanā*, *grathanā*. (6.4.108) *upasargasya ghañyamanuṣye bahulam* [In a word formed with the suffix *ghañ*, the initial letter of a prefix is often replaced by its corresponding aspirate mute (*ru*) when followed by a consonant, provided the word does not denote a human being. Example: *praghaṇaḥ*, *praghāṇaḥ*. Why "when followed by a consonant"? [Observe: *prasevaḥ*. Why "not denoting a human being"? [Observe: *prakhyaḥ*. (6.4.109) *ieghaḥ* [In a word formed with the suffix *ghañ*, the initial letter of the prefix *ā* is replaced by its corresponding aspirate mute when followed by the root *ghas*. Example: *āghāṭaḥ*. (6.4.110) *vibhāṣābhyavapūrvasya* [In a word formed with the suffix *ghañ*, the initial letter of the prefix *abhi* or *ava* is optionally replaced by its corresponding aspirate mute when followed by the root *ghas*. Examples: *abhyāghātaḥ*, *abhighātaḥ*; *avāghātaḥ*, *avaghātaḥ*. (6.4.111) *hanaś ca vadhaḥ* [When the suffix *ghañ* is applied after the root *han*, the resulting word is *vadhaḥ*. Example: *vadhaḥ*. (6.4.112) *mūrtī ghanaḥ* [The word *ghanaḥ* is formed from the root *han* with the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of a solid mass (*mūrti*). Example: *ghanam jñānam*. (6.4.113) *abhranirghātau* [The words *abhraghanaḥ* and *nirghātaḥ* are formed from the root *han* with the suffix *ghañ* in these specific senses. Examples: *abhraghanaḥ*, *nirghātaḥ*. (6.4.114) *udghano 'striyām* [The word *udghanaḥ* is formed from the root *han* with the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of a solid mass, provided it is not feminine. Example: *udghanaḥ*. Why "not feminine"? [Observe: *udghanī*. (6.4.115) *avadātaṃ śuddhe* [The word *avadātam* is formed from the root *do* with the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of purity (*śuddha*). Example: *avadātaṃ vastram*. (6.4.116) *avadātaḥ site 'pi* [The word *avadātaḥ* is also used in the sense of white (*sita*). Example: *avadāto brāhmaṇaḥ*. (6.4.117) *praṇāma prahvatve* [The word *praṇāmaḥ* is formed from the root *nam* with the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of bowing down (*prahvatva*). Example: *praṇāmo devānām*. (6.4.118) *upasthānam* [The word *upasthānam* is formed from the root *sthā* with the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of attendance (*sevā*). Example: *upasthānaṃ rājñaḥ*. (6.4.119) *pratiṣṭhānam* [The word *prati

The substitution of *ṣ* for the *s* of the root *sah* does not occur when it takes the form *soḍ*. For example: *nisoḍhā*, *nisoḍhum*. Why is there the mention of the change to *o* (*otva*) and the substitution of *ḍ* (*ḍhatva*)? [To show that it does not apply here: *niṣahate*. According to Pāṇini 6.4.96, *prādibhyaḥ stambhusivusahāṃ caṅi*: when *caṅ* follows after prefixes such as *pra-* and the roots *stambh*, *siv*, and *sah*, the substitution of *ṣ* does not occur. For example: *abhyatastambhat*, *paryasīṣivat*, *paryasīṣahat*. Because of the inclusion of the term "prefixes" (*prādi*), the substitution of *ṣ* certainly does occur when the cause is reduplication (*dvirukta*). This has been illustrated accordingly.

*soḥ syasanoḥ* (6.4.97): The substitution of *ṣ* for the *s* of the root *su* (*sunoti*) does not occur when followed by the suffixes *sy* or *san*. Thus, *abhisoṣyati* and *paryasoṣyat*. In the case of *susūṣati*, [the substitution] will not occur due to the restriction *stoḥ ṣaṇi* (6.4.48). In the case of *abhisusūṣati*, it will not occur due to the restriction *stautiṇyor eva ṣaṇi* (6.4.58). If that is so, then [consider] *abhisusūṣateḥ* with the suffix *kvip*: *abhisusūḥ*. Why specify "when followed by *sy* or *san*"? [Observe] *suṣāva*. [Also, the rule] *sadisvañjer liṭi* (6.4.98) [applies].

The substitution of *ṣ* for *s* does not occur for the roots *sad* and *svañj* when followed by the suffix *liṭ*. For example: *niṣasāda*. However, in the case of the former (*sad*), the substitution does indeed occur because it is separated from the preceding [root] by another element: *pariṣasvaje*. Pāṇini 6.4.99 states: *dhātoḥ sīluṅoś ca dho ḍhaḥ*. The substitution of *ḍh* for *dh* occurs for the *dh* belonging to the suffixes *sī*, *luṅ*, and *liṭ* when they follow a root ending in *iṇ*. Examples: *cyoṣīḍhvam*, *acyoḍhvam*, *cakṛḍhve*. Why is "of a root" (*dhātoḥ*) specified? Consider: *āsiṣīdhvam* (where the *dh* belongs to the desiderative suffix *san*, not a root). Why is "for *sī* and *luṅ*" (*sīluṅoś ca*) specified? Consider: *studhve* (where the *dh* belongs to the suffix *dhve*, not *sī* or *luṅ*). Why is "ending in *iṇ*" (*iṇaḥ*) specified? Consider: *pakṣīdhvam* (where the root ends in *kṣ*, not *iṇ*).

After the augment *iṭ*, the *ḍha* of the suffixes *sī*, *luṅ*, and *liṭ* optionally becomes *ḍha*. [Examples: *laviṣīḍhvam*, *laviṣīdhvam*; *alaviḍhvam*, *alavidhvam*; *luluviḍhve*, *luluvidhve*; *upadidīyiḍhve*, *upadidīyidhve*. Only after *iṇ* [does this apply]: *āsiṣīdhvam*. *Rṣān no ṇa ekapade* (6.4.101): Within a single word, *ṇa* replaces *na* following *ra* or *ṣa*.

The substitution of *ṇ* occurs for a following [nasal] when it stands within a single word after the letters *repha* (*r*) or *ṣakāra* (*ṣ*). Examples: *āstīrṇam*, *muṣṇāti*, *mātṝṇām*. Because the *repha* that occurs before a vowel (*ṛ-varṇa*) is taken as the basis [for this rule], the substitution of *ṇ* indeed takes place. Why does the rule specify "within a single word"? [Observe: *Agnir nayati*.
[Also, the rule] *pūrvapadān nāmni* (Pāṇini 6.4.102) [is relevant here].

The substitution of *ṇ* for a *n* situated in the second member (*uttarapada*) occurs only when it follows a *r* or *ṣ* situated in the first member (*pūrvapada*), provided that this refers to a proper name (*saṃjñā*). Examples: *druṇasaḥ*, *kharaṇasaḥ*. Why is it specified "in a proper name"? [Answer: As in *carmanāsikaḥ*. Since the first member depends upon the second member, the restriction [of the rule] excludes only those cases where the *n* is situated in the second member; however, in the following cases, the substitution does indeed occur: *khārapāyaṇaḥ*, *mātṛbhogīṇaḥ*. By the indicator (*jñāpaka*) in the rule *ṛgayanādibhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.3.73), the form *ṛghayanaḥ* does not occur. [Also]: *vanaṃ puragāmiśrakāsidhrakāśārikāgrekoṭarāt* (Pāṇini 6.2.85).

The substitution of *ṇ* for the letter *n* occurs only when it follows [the final vowel] of words such as *puraga*, etc., provided that the word forms a proper name (*nāman*). Examples: *puragāvaṇam*, *miśrakāvaṇam*, *sidhrakāvaṇam*, *śārikāvaṇam*; *agrevaṇam*—here the change to *e* occurs by way of a formal rule (*nipātana*); *koṭarāvaṇam*. Why "after *puraga* and so forth"? [Counter-examples: *kuberavanam*, *asipattravanam*. [Also, the substitution of *ṇ* occurs after the following: *pra*, *niḥ*, *antar*, *śara*, *ikṣu*, *plakṣa*, *āmra*, *kārṣya*, *pīyūkṣā*, and *khadira* [when followed by *vana*]. (Pāṇini 6.4.104)

The substitution of *ṇ* for the *n* of the word *vana* occurs when it follows prefixes such as *pra*, etc. Examples: *pravaṇam*, *nirvaṇam*, *antarvaṇam*, *śaravaṇam*, *ikṣuvaṇam*, *plakṣavaṇam*, *āmravaṇam*, *kārṣyavaṇam*, *pīyūkṣāvaṇam*, *khadiravaṇam*. According to Pāṇini 6.4.105 (*vauṣadhivṛkṣād dvitryaco'nirikādeḥ*), the substitution of *ṇ* for the *n* of *vana* optionally occurs when it follows a word denoting a medicinal herb or a tree that consists of two or three syllables, provided it does not begin with *irikā* and contains the letters *r* or *ṣ*. Examples: *dūrvāvaṇam* / *dūrvāvanam*; *śirīṣavaṇam* / *śirīṣavanam*.

Herbs (*oṣadhi*) are those that end with the ripening of their fruit; creepers (*latā*), shrubs (*gulma*), and climbing plants (*vīrudh*) are also included. A fruit-bearing tree is to be known as a *vanaspati*, while trees that bear both flowers and fruit are called *vṛkṣa*. Why [is it said] "after *oṣadhi* and *vṛkṣa*"? [Consider] *vidārīvana* ("a forest of *vidārī* herbs"). Why [is it said] "having two or three syllables"? [Consider] *devadāruvana* ("a forest of *devadāru* trees"). Why [is it said] "not beginning with *irikā* etc."? [Consider] *irikāvana* ("a forest of *irikā* trees") and *timiravana* ("a forest of *timira* trees"). [The rule] *ahno 'taḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.106) [applies].

The substitution of *ṇ* occurs for the *n* of the word *ahan* ("day") when it follows a word ending in *repha* (*r*) or *ṣakāra* (*ṣ*), provided that [the preceding word] ends in a vowel other than *a*. Examples: *pūrvāhṇaḥ*, *aparāhṇaḥ*. Why "other than *a*" (*ataḥ*)? [Counter-examples: *nirahnaḥ*, *durahnaḥ*. Why the specification of the vowel *a* (*akāranirdeśaḥ*)? [Counter-example: *dīrghāhnī śarat* ("an autumn with long days"). Regarding Pāṇini 6.4.107, *tricaturbhyāṃ hāyano vayasi*:

the substitution of *ṇ* occurs for the *n* of the word *hāyana* when it follows *tri* or *catur*, provided that age is being expressed. Examples: *trihāyaṇo vatsaḥ* ("a three-year-old calf"), *caturhāyaṇaḥ*. Why "age" (*vayasi*)? [Counter-example: *trihāyanā śālā* ("a three-year-old house").

*vāhanaṃ vāhyāt* (Pāṇini 6.4.108): The substitution of *ṇ* occurs for the *n* of the word *vāhana* when it follows a word denoting that which is to be carried (*vāhya*), provided that [the preceding word] contains either *r* or *ṣ*. Examples: *ikṣuvāhaṇam*, *śaravāhaṇam*. Why "when following a word denoting that which is to be carried"? [Counter-example: *Dākṣivāhanam*.
*pānaṃ deśe* (Pāṇini 6.4.109).

The substitution of *ṇ* occurs for the *n* of the word *pāna* when it follows *r* or *ṣ* situated in a preceding member (*pūrvapada*), provided that a specific region (*deśa*) is being indicated. "Pāna" means "that which is drunk" (*pīyate iti pānam*). Those for whom milk is their drink are the *kṣīrapāṇā* Uśīnaras; those who drink liquor are the *surāpāṇāḥ* Easterners (*prācyāḥ*); those who drink sour gruel are the *sauvīrapāṇāḥ* Bāhlīkas; and those who drink astringent decoctions are the *kaṣāyapāṇāḥ* Gāndhāras. Why is "region" specified? [To exclude cases such as: a vessel for drinking milk (*kṣīrapānaṃ bhājanam*).
[The rule] "optionally (*vā*) when denoting an abstract state (*bhāva*) or an instrument (*karaṇa*)" (Pāṇini 6.4.110).

When the word *pāna* occurs in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*) or an instrument (*karaṇa*), the substitution of *ṇ* optionally takes place for the *n* that follows the *r* or *ṣ* situated in the preceding member. For example: *kṣīrapāṇaṃ vartate* / *kṣīrapānam*; *kaṣāyapāṇaṃ vartate* / *kaṣāyapānam*. Likewise: *kṣīrapāṇaṃ bhājanam* / *kṣīrapānam*; *kaṣāyapāṇaṃ bhājanam* / *kaṣāyapānam*. Regarding the rule *girinadyādīnām* (Pāṇini 8.4.111):
the substitution of *ṇ* optionally takes place for the *n* in words such as *giri-nadī*. Examples include: *giriṇadī* / *girinadī*; *cakraṇitambā* / *cakranitambā*; *vakraṇadī* / *vakranadī*.

(6.4.112) *samastāntasamīpayor ayuvādīnām*: When the letter *n* occurs at the end of a compound or in proximity to it, its change to *ṇ* optionally takes place—provided it is preceded by a cause consisting of *r* or *ṣ*—if the word does not belong to the *ayuvādi* group. Examples: *māṣavāpiṇau*, *māṣavāpinau*; *māṣavāpiṇī*, *māṣavāpinī*; *māṣavāpāṇi*, *māṣavāpāni*; *māṣavāpeṇa*, *māṣavāpena*. Why is the mention of "end of a compound" (*samastānta*) included? Consider *Gargabhaginī*. However, when it is analyzed as *Gargāṇāṃ bhagaḥ* = *Gargabhagaḥ*, and [the suffix *ini*] is added in the sense that she possesses that, resulting in *Gargabhagiṇī*, the change to *ṇ* certainly occurs.

What is the purpose of [the restriction] "not after *ayu* and so forth"? [Examples: *āryayūnā* ("by a noble youth"), *kṣatriyayūnā* ("by a Kṣatriya youth"), *prapakvāni* ("half-ripened"), *paripakvāni* ("fully ripened"), *prapakvena* ("by one who is half-ripened"), *paripakvena* ("by one who is fully ripened"). This is a re-introduction of that which was excluded by the rule *pūrvapadāt* (Pāṇini 8.4.102), not an original injunction. Therefore, in *māṣavāpān* ("rice-fields sown with beans") and *vrīhivāpān* ("rice-fields sown with rice"), the substitution of *ṇ* does not occur. [The following applies: *kumader ekācaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.4.113).

When the final member of a compound ends in a monosyllabic word containing a guttural (*kavarga*), the *ṇ*-substitution occurs for the *n* that stands either at the end of that compound or in its vicinity; this is because the rule is prescribed as being obligatory (*nitya*). Examples: *vastrayugiṇau*, *vastrayugiṇaḥ*, *vastrayugāṇi*, *vastrayugeṇa*. *Vṛtrahaṇau*, *Vṛtrahaṇi*; *kṣīrapāṇi*, *kṣīrapeṇa*. The form *brahmaghnī* does not occur because of the prohibition [stated] in Pāṇini 6.4.134: *ghā ha*. [Also, the substitution applies] according to 6.4.114: *prādyantaro 'duro ṇaḥ*.

The substitution of *ṇ* for the initial *n* of a suffix occurs after the words *pra*, *pari*, and others, as well as after the word *antar*, provided it is not preceded by *duḥ*. For example: *praṇamati*, *pariṇamati*; *praṇāyakaḥ*, *pariṇāyakaḥ*; *antarṇayati*, *antarṇītaḥ*. By virtue of the sense and proximity, only those prefixes (*prādayaḥ*) that are connected with the action [of the verb] are understood here; therefore, the substitution does not occur in the following cases: *pragatā nāyakā asmād deśāt* ("the leaders have departed from this region"), resulting in *pranāyako deśaḥ*. Why say "not preceded by *duḥ*" (*adura*)? Consider *durnayaḥ*. Why say "*ṇ*" (referring to the substitute)? Consider *pranardati*. [This concludes the rule regarding] *hi*, *nu*, and *mī* (Pāṇini 6.4.115).

The substitution of *ṇ* occurs for the initial *n* of these roots when preceded by prepositions (*prādi*): *hinu*, *mīnā*, and so forth. Examples: *prahiṇoti*, *prahiṇutaḥ*; *pramīṇāti*, *pramīṇītaḥ*; *pravapāṇi*, *parivapāṇi*. The form *pravapāni* [with dental *n*] does not occur in the sense "I shall cut the meat," because that meaning is not applicable here. Furthermore, according to Pāṇini 6.4.116: *ner gadanadapatapadadādhāmāvādihavahaśamahanayāsādrāpsācivapiṣu* ("the *n* of the prefix *ni-* is replaced by *ṇ* before the roots *gad*, *nad*, *pat*, *pad*, *dā*, *dhā*, *mā*, *vā*, *ihi*, *vah*, *śam*, *han*, *yā*, *sā*, *drā*, *pā*, *sā*, and *ci-vap*").

The substitution of *ṇ* occurs for the *n* of the root *ni* when it follows prefixes such as *pra-* and so forth, provided that it is followed by roots beginning with *gad-* and others. Thus: *praṇigadati*, *praṇinadati*, *praṇipatati*, *praṇipadyate*; *praṇiyacchati*, *praṇidadāti*, *praṇidayate*, *praṇidyati*; *praṇidhayati*, *praṇidadhāti*; *praṇimimīte*, *praṇimayate*, *praṇimāti*.

*praṇiyāti*, *praṇidegdhi*, *praṇivahati*, *praṇiśāmyati*, *praṇihanti*, *praṇiyāyi*, *praṇiṣyati*, *praṇidrāti*, *praṇipsāti*, *praṇicinoti*, *praṇivapati*. Because the prefix *pra-* is separated from roots such as *gad-* by the augment *aṭ*, the rule applies even when there is an intervening element: *praṇyagadat*. [This occurs] when the root begins with a letter other than *k* or *kh* and ends in a letter other than *ṣ* or *s*, according to Pāṇini 6.4.117.

The substitution of *ṇ* for *n* optionally occurs after the prefix *pra-* and others, provided that the following root does not begin with *k* or *kh*, nor end in *ṣ*. For example: *praṇibhinatti* or *pranibhinatti*. Why is it said "not beginning with *k* or *kh*" (*akakhādau*)? Consider: *pranikaroti*, *pranikhādati*. Why is it said "not ending in *ṣ*" (*aṣānta*)? Consider: *pranipinaṣṭi*, *pranipinaṣṭi*. Why is it said "in the original recitation" (*pāṭhe*)? This is so that the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) applies even in cases such as *pranicakāra*, *pranicakhāda*, and *pranipekṣyati*, but it should not apply in a case like *praṇiveṣṭā*. [Also, the rule] *ano 'nte ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.118) [applies].

The substitution of *ṇ* for the *n* of the root *an* occurs when it follows prefixes (*prādi*), whether that *n* stands at the end of a word (*padānta*) or not. Thus: *prāṇiti*, *parāṇiti*; and [the vocative] *he prāṇ*. Alternatively, the substitution of *ṇ* for *an* occurs after a *repha* (*r*) that is in proximity to *an*. Therefore, it does not occur here: *paryaniti*. Regarding *prāṇiṇiṣati* and *prāṇiṇat*: once the substitution of *ṇ* has been made, reduplication (*dvirvacana*) will take place. [This is because of the rule: "That which is treated as non-existent (*asiddha*) in a preceding operation is not considered so for the purpose of reduplication. [Next is the rule: *hanaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.119).

The substitution of *ṇ* for the *n* of the root *han* occurs when it follows prefixes such as *pra*. Thus, we have *prahaṇyate* and *parihaṇanam*. However, forms such as *praghnanti* and *parighnantī* do not occur, due to the prohibition stated in *ghā ha* (Pāṇini 6.4.134).

According to *vmor vā* (Pāṇini 6.4.120), the substitution of *ṇ* for the *n* of *han* following prefixes may optionally occur when followed by the vowels *v* or *m*. Thus, we have *prahaṇvaḥ* or *prahanvaḥ*, and *prahaṇmaḥ* or *prahanmaḥ*.

*Antaro ’yanasya cādeśe* (Pāṇini 6.4.121): When the word *antar-* precedes, the substitution of *ṇ* occurs for the *n* of the root *han* and for the suffix *-ana*, provided that these refer to an *ādeśa* (substitute). Examples: *antarhaṇanam*, *antarayaṇam*. Why "when it is an *ādeśa*"? [Counter-examples: *anterhanano deśaḥ* ("a place where killing occurs within"), *antarayanaḥ*. *Supy acaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.122): [The substitution of *ṇ* occurs] when a verbal root beginning with a vowel follows the prefix *antar-*.

When a *su*-prefix is present, the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* occurs for that *n* which follows a vowel (*ac*) and is preceded by a cause such as *pra* and so forth. Examples: *prayāṇam*, *prayāyamāṇam*, *prayāṇīyam*, *aprayāṇiḥ*, *prayāyiṇau*, *prahāṇaḥ*. Why is it said "when *su* is present"? [Observe: *prabhinatti*, *prapunāti*. Why is it said "after a vowel" (*aca*)? [Observe: *prabhugnaḥ*. Regarding *nirviṇṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.123):

the form *nirviṇṇa* is established as an irregularity (*nipātana*) for the root *vid* ending in the suffix *kta* when preceded by *nis*. Precisely because of this statement, the substitution does not occur in forms such as *nirbhinna*.

*ṇer vā* (Pāṇini 6.4.124): When a vowel (*ac*) is prescribed after a causative suffix (*ṇic*) in the domain of *sub*-suffixes, the *ṇatva* (the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*) optionally occurs for the *n* that follows it, provided it is caused by a prefix (*prādi*). Examples: *prayāpaṇam*, *prayāpanam*; *prayāpyamāṇam*, *prayāpyamānam*; *prayāpaṇīyam*, *prayāpanīyam*; *aprayāpaṇiḥ*, *aprayāpaniḥ*; *prayāpiṇau*, *prayāpinau*. *halāder ijupāntāt* (Pāṇini 6.4.125): [The rule applies] when the word begins with a consonant (*hal*), ends in a consonant, and has *i* or *u* as its penultimate letter (*upāntya*).

When a vowel follows a consonant beginning with *ij* or *up*, and a *nakāra* follows that vowel, the substitution of *ṇ* for that *nakāra* optionally occurs, provided it is caused by a prefix (*prādi*). Examples: *prakopaṇam* or *prakopanam*. Why "beginning with a consonant" (*halādeḥ*)? [Counter-examples: *prehaṇam*, *prohaṇam*. Why "ending in *ij* or *up*" (*ijupāntāt*)? [Counter-example: *pravapaṇam*. The rule applies only when there is a vowel (*acaḥ*): [counter-example] *prabhugnaḥ*. [This is governed by] Pāṇini 6.4.126: *numījāder halaḥ*.

The substitution of *ṇ* for *n* occurs for a *n* following an *ac* that stands after a verbal root ending in a consonant which begins with a vowel having *num*, provided that the cause (*nimitta*) is a prefix such as *pra*. Examples: *preṅkhaṇam*, *preṅgaṇam*. Why say "after *num*"? Because if the restriction were "only after a root beginning with a vowel and ending in a consonant," then in the case of *prāpaṇa*, the substitution would not occur. Why say "beginning with a vowel" (*ijādi*)? Because if the restriction were "only after a consonant ending in *num*," then in the case of *pravapaṇa*, the substitution would not occur. Why say "consonant" (*hal*)? Otherwise, the substitution would apply even after a root ending in a *ṇ* by virtue of being a causative (*ṇyanta*). [The rule] *vā nikṣaniṃsanindām* (Pāṇini 6.4.127) [applies].

For the words *nikṣ* and others, when preceded by *pra* and other such particles acting as causes, the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* optionally occurs. Examples: *praṇikṣaṇam*, *pranikṣaṇam*; *praṇiṃsanam*, *praniṃsanam*; *praṇindanam*, *pranindanam*. Since these roots are taught with an initial *ṇ* (*ṇopadeśa*), the substitution would have been obligatory; this rule provides an option. However, it does not apply to the roots *bhā*, *bhū*, *pū*, *kram*, *gam*, *pi*, *āyī*, or *vep* (Pāṇini 6.4.128).

When *bhā* and the other roots are employed, the substitution of *ṇ* for the following [nasal] does not occur when preceded by *pra* and the like, which serve as the cause. Thus: *prabhānam*, *prabhavanam*, *prapavanam*, *prakamanam*, *pragamanam*, *prapyāyanam*, *pravepanam*. Since the employment of *bhā* and the others also occurs with the causative suffix (*ṇic*), there is likewise no substitution of *ṇ*: *prabhāpanam*. Because of the specific mention of *pūñ*, it does not apply to *pūṅ*: *prapavaṇam*. [This is governed by the rule] *ṣaḥ pade* (Pāṇini 8.3.129).

The substitution of *ṇ* does not occur for a letter following a *ṣ* that stands at the end of a word (*pada*). Examples: *niṣpānam*, *sarpiṣpānam*. Why "after *ṣ*" (*ṣa*)? Consider *niryāṇam*. Why "at the end of a word" (*pada*)? Consider *susarpiṣkeṇa*.

Regarding the rule *naśeḥ ṣkaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.4.36): the substitution of *ṇ* does not occur for the root *naś-* when it ends in *ṣ* or *k*. Examples: *pranaṣṭaḥ*, *pranaṃkṣyati*. Why "*ṣka*" (*ṣka*)? Consider *praṇaśyati*.
The substitution of *ṇ* for *n* does not occur when *n* stands at the end of a word (*padānte*). For example: *vṛkṣān*. [This is further specified by:
"When there is an intervention (*vyavāye*) by *c*, *ṭ*, *t*, *p*, *ś*, *ṣ*, or *s*... (Pāṇini 6.4.132).

The substitution of *ṇ* for *n* does not occur when there is an intervention by the *ca*-group (*ca*, *cha*, *ja*, *jha*, *ña*), the *ṭa*-group (*ṭa*, *ṭha*, *ḍa*, *ḍha*, *ṇa*), the *ta*-group (*ta*, *tha*, *da*, *dha*, *na*), the letter *l*, or the sibilants (*ś*, *ṣ*, *s*). Examples: *arcanam*, *mūrchanam*, *sarjanam*; *Kirāṭena*, *karmaṭhena*, *dṛḍhena*, *karaṇena*; *kīrtanam*, *caturthena*, *mardanam*, *ārādhanam*; *prenvanam*—this is the form of the root *iv*, *div*, or *dhiv* (Dhātupāṭha 1.202, 204); *viralena*; *raśanā*, *rasanā*. Why "by these"? [Counter-examples: *karaṇam*, *giriṇā*; *mūrkheṇa*, *argeṇa*; *darpeṇa*, *repheṇa*.

*pūrveṇa*; *vṛṃhaṇam*; *uraḥkeṇa*, *uraḥkeṇa*; *urafpeṇa*, *uraḥpeṇa*. According to Pāṇini 6.4.133, the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* does not occur when there is an intervention by a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*), with the exception of the prefix *āṅ* and the suffix *mayaṭ*. Examples: *māṣakumbhavāpena*, *caturaṅgayogena*. Why does it say "not [intervened by] *āṅ* or *mayaṭ*"? Consider: *paryāṇaddham*, *ārdragomayeṇa*.

*Ghā haḥ* (6.4.134): When there is an intervention by the letter *gha* or by the substitute *ha*, the substitution of *ṇa* does not occur. Examples: *srughnaḥ*, *śatrughnaḥ*. This is a prohibition of what would otherwise have been required by *pūrvapadāt nāmni* (6.4.102). Example: *prāghāni*, which would otherwise have been required by *hanaḥ* (6.4.119). Why say *ha*? [Counter-example: *argheṇa*. *Kṣubhnādīnām* (6.4.135).

In the case of *kṣubhna* and similar forms, the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* does not occur. Regarding *kṣubhnāti*, *tṛpnoti*, and *Nṛnamanaḥ*: although the rule *pūrvapadāt saṃjñāyām am-n-iti* (Pāṇini 8.4.3) would have required the change, it is blocked. Examples include: *Harinandī* (from *nandin*), *Harinandanam* (from *nandana*), and *Harinagaram* (from *nagara*), where the rule *pūrvapadāt saṃjñāyām* (6.4.102) would otherwise apply. Regarding *narīnṛtyate* (from the intensive *yaṅ* of *nṛt*) and *nartanam*, as well as *parinartanam*, *gahanam*, and *parigahanam*, the rule *pūrvapadāt saṃjñāyām* (6.4.102) would have applied, but it is blocked. The form *nandanam* is also an example where the same rule would have applied.

When *parinandaṇam* is expected by [Pāṇini 8.4.14] (*ṇopadeśasya*), we have *nivāsaḥ*: *parinivāsaḥ*; *niveśaḥ*: *pariniveśaḥ*; *agniḥ*: *haryagniḥ*, *śarabhāgniḥ*; *anūpaḥ*: *darbhānūpaḥ*—this being expected by [Pāṇini 6.4.102] (*nāmni*). [Examples of] *ācāryabhogīnaḥ* and *ācāryānī*. The *kṣubhna*-group is an *ākṛtigaṇa*.
[Regarding the rule] *stoḥ ścuṣṭubhyāṃ ścuṣṭavaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.4.40): [the examples are as follows].

When *s* and the *ta*-group come into contact with *ś* and the *ca*-group, or with *ṣ* and the *ṭa*-group, those *ś* and *ca*-groups and those *ṣ* and *ṭa*-groups respectively take their place. The *s* [is replaced] by *ś*: *vṛkṣaś śete*. By the *ca*-group: *vṛkṣaś cinoti*, *vṛkṣaś chādayati*. The *ta*-group [is replaced] by *ś*: *agnicic chete*. By the *ca*-group: *agnicic cinoti*, *somasuc chādayati*, *agnicij jayati*, *somasuj jhaṣati*, *agniciññakāraḥ*.

In *majjati*, the *s* becomes *d* by the rule of *jaś*-ness (*jaśtva*), and the *j* becomes *g* by the rule of *cut*-ness (*cutva*). [Examples: *yajñaḥ*, *yācñā*. With the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*: *vṛkṣaṣ ṣaṇḍe*. With the *ṭa*-group (*ṭavarga*): *vṛkṣaṣ ṭīkate*, *vṛkṣaṣ ṭhakāraḥ*. With the substitution of *ṣ* for the *ta*-group (*tavarga*): *peṣṭā*. With the *ṭa*-group: *agniciṭ ṭīkate*, *somasuṭ ṭhakāraḥ*, *agniciḍ ḍīnaḥ*, *somasuḍ ḍhaukate*, *agniciṇ ṇakāraḥ*. With *adṭ* (the *ṭa*-group): *aṭṭate*. With *adḍ* (the *ḍa*-group): *aḍḍati*.

In the case of the original signs (*nimitteṣu*), [the substitution] does not occur, because of the prohibitions in Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.4.138 and 6.4.139. However, it certainly occurs in the case of the substitute (*ādeśe*). Regarding Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.4.137, *na ṭor anavatinagaryor ādeḥ*:

that which was prescribed for the beginning of a word following a *ṭa*-class consonant does not take place, except in the case of *navati* and *nagarī*. Examples: *śvaliṭ sāye*, *śvaliṭ tarati*. Why "after a *ṭa*-class consonant" (*ṭoḥ*)? Consider *yajuṣṭvam*. Why "except in the case of *navati* and *nagarī*" (*anavatinagaryoḥ*)? Consider *ṣaṇṇavatiḥ*, *ṣaṇṇagarī*. Why "of the beginning" (*ādeḥ*)? Consider *īḍaḥ*, *īṭṭe*, *ṣaṇṇām*.

*Toḥ ṣi* (6.4.138): That which was prescribed [regarding the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*] does not occur when a palatal sibilant (*ṣ*) follows a dental stop (*tavarga*). For example: *agnicit ṣaṇḍe*; *bhavān ṣaṇḍe*.
*Śāt* (6.4.139): [The rule regarding the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*] does not occur when the dental stop follows a *ś*.

That which was prescribed for the *tavarga* following the letter *ś* does not occur: *viśnaḥ*, *praśnaḥ*. Regarding Pāṇini 6.4.140, *yaro ñami ñam vā*: when a *yar* (any consonant except *ha*) is followed by a *ñam* (a nasal), the substitution of a *ñam* is optionally applied as the closest substitute. Examples: *vāṅ ñakāraḥ* / *vāg ñakāraḥ*; *vāṅ madhurā* / *vāg madhurā*; *tvaṅ nayati* / *tvag nayati*. In the case of *vāṅmaya-* and *tvaṅmaya-*, the substitution occurs invariably due to the rule of fixed optionality (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*). In some cases it does not occur: *yatnaḥ*, *yajñaḥ*, *yācñā*.

*aco rahābhyāṃ dve* (6.4.141): After a vowel (*ac*), the *yaraḥ* (consonants other than semivowels and nasals) following the letters *ra* and *ha* may optionally be doubled. Examples: *arkkaḥ* / *arkaḥ*; *brahmmā* / *brahmā*. Why "after a vowel" (*aca*)? [Consider: *hnute*. *anaci* (6.4.142).

A *yar* (any consonant except *h*) following an *ac* (vowel) may optionally be doubled, provided that it is not followed by another *ac*. Examples: *daddhy atra*, *dadhy atra*; *maddhv atra*, *madhv atra*; *vākk*, *vāk*. However, doubling does not occur when an *ac* follows: *dadhi*, *madhu*. Regarding *yaṇo mayaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.143):

A *khay* (any consonant except *h*, *y*, *v*, and *r*) following a *yaṇ* (semivowel) may optionally be doubled. Examples: *ulkkā*, *ulkā*; *Vālmmīkaḥ*, *Vālmīkaḥ*. Alternatively, according to this rule, a *yaṇ* following a *may* (the semivowels *y*, *v*, *r*, *l*) may optionally be doubled: *dadhyy atra*, *dadhy atra*; *madhvv atra*, *madhv atra*.

*Śaraḥ khayaḥ* (6.4.144): A *śara* consonant following a *khaya* consonant may optionally undergo doubling. For example: *sththānam*, *sthānam*. Alternatively, a *śara* consonant preceding a *khaya* consonant may optionally undergo doubling: *vatssaḥ*, *vatsaḥ*; *kṣṣīram*, *kṣīram*.
However, this does not apply when the word *putra* is used in an abusive sense (*ākrośe*), nor when it is followed by *ādi* or *tat*. (6.4.145)

When a term of abuse (*ākrośa*) is being expressed, there is no doubling (*dvitva*) of the consonant following *ādin* when it follows *putra*, etc. Examples: *putrādinī*, *putraputrādinī*. Why "in a term of abuse"? [Counter-example: *puttrādinī śiśumārī* ("a female crocodile who devours her own offspring"), *puttraputtrādinī*. Why "after *ādin*"? [Counter-example: *puttrahatī*, *puttrajagdhī*. Regarding Pāṇini 6.4.146, *śaro 'ci rāt*: there is no doubling of a consonant (*śara*) following a *repha* (*r*) when an *ac* vowel follows. Examples: *vimarṣaḥ*, *ādarśaḥ*. Why "consonant" (*śara*)? [Counter-example: *arkkaḥ*. Why "vowel" (*aci*)? [Counter-example: *kārśśyam*. Why "following *repha*" (*rāt*)? [Counter-example: *vatssaḥ*.

(6.4.147) After a long vowel, the following [consonant] does not become doubled. For example: *dātram*, *sūtram*. (6.4.148) Before a *khari* [stop or sibilant], a *jhali* [consonant] becomes a *cari* [corresponding voiceless stop or sibilant].

A *jhala* consonant becomes a *car* [unaspirated stop or sibilant] when followed by a *khar* [voiceless consonant]. Examples: *bhettā*, *lipsā*. Why does it say "followed by a *khar*"? Observe: *bhidyate*. Why does it say "*jhala*"? Observe: *kaṇṭhaḥ*. (Pāṇini 6.4.149) *vā virāme*:
A *jhala* consonant standing at the end of a word (*virāma*) optionally becomes a *car*. Examples: *vāk*, *vāg*; *śvaliṭ*, *śvaliḍ*.

Aṇo ’nunāsikaḥ (Pāṇini 6.4.150): For an *aṇ* vowel occurring at a pause (*virāma*), the state of being nasalized (*anunāsikatva*) optionally occurs. *dadhī̇*, *dadhi*; *madhū̇*, *madhu*. By means of a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*), it does not occur in some cases: *agnī*, *vāyū*; *amū*, *amī*. Anusvārasya yayi yam (Pāṇini 6.4.151).

When followed by a *yay* sound (any consonant except *h*), the *anusvāra* is replaced by a nasal (*yam*) that is phonetically similar to the following sound. For example: *śaṅkitā*, *unchitā*, *kaṇṭhitā*, *nanditā*, *kampitā*. Why "when followed by a *yay* sound"? Consider *kaṃsaḥ*. Why "nasal" (*anunāsika*)? Consider *yaṃyamyate*, *raṃramyate*.
[Also,] optionally at the beginning of a word: (Pāṇini 6.4.152).

When followed by a *yay* (any consonant except *h*, *r*, or *v*) at the beginning of a word, the *anusvāra* optionally undergoes substitution by a nasalized *yama*. Examples: *say̆̇yattā*, *saṃyattā*; *sav̆̇vatsaraḥ*, *saṃvatsaraḥ*; *tal̆̇ lokaḥ*, *taṃ lokaḥ*; *divyañ cakṣuḥ*, *ivyaṃ cakṣuḥ*; *sukham puṇyaḥ*, *sukhaṃ puṇyaḥ*. Only when followed by a *yay* does this apply; otherwise: *paraṃ śreyaḥ*. Only for a nasalized substitute does this apply; otherwise: *balaṃ rājā*. By the rule *tor li* (Pāṇini 8.4.62), when a letter of the *tavarga* (the dental class) is followed by *l*, a *yama* similar to it is substituted. Examples: *dṛṣal lunāti*, *bhaval̆̇ lunāti*.

*udaḥ sthāstambhos taḥ* (6.4.154): After the word *ud*, the substitute *t* occurs for the initial sounds of the roots *sthā* and *stambh*. Examples: *utthātā*, *uttambhitā*. Why specify *sthāstambhoḥ*? [Counter-example: *utsnātā*. How is it that *utkandaka* is a disease? It will come from the root *kandi*.
*halo jharāṃ jhari sa-sthāne lopo vā* (6.4.155): When a *jhara* sound follows a consonant (*hal*), its elision may optionally occur before another *jhara* sound that stands in the same position.

When *jhar* sounds follow a *hal* (consonant), their elision (*lopa*) may optionally occur before another *jhar* sound that shares the same place of articulation (*samānasthāna*). In *prattta*, there are three *t* sounds; the fourth arises from doubling. Among these, the elision of the two middle ones may optionally occur. In *maruttta*, there are four *t* sounds; the fifth arises from doubling. Here, the elision of the middle ones may optionally occur. Why "after a *hal*" (*halaḥ*)? [Consider] *dattam*. Regarding the word *śayyā*, since the doubling [of the *y*] is optional, the elision need not be stated. A *jhay* [consonant] optionally undergoes the substitution of another *jhay* before the letter *ha*. The lips [are the place of articulation] for the *upadhmānīya* and the *upū* (the labial vowels). 11.
The teeth and lips [are the place of articulation] for the letter *va*. 12.
The root of the tongue [is the place of articulation] for the *jihvāmūlīya*. 13.
The organ of articulation: 14. The tip of the tongue for the dentals. 15. The middle of the tongue for the cerebrals.
16. The root of the tongue for the palatals.

The middle of the tongue is the place of articulation for the palatals (tālavya). 17. The remaining [consonants] have their own respective places and organs of articulation. 18. Effort (prayatna) is of two kinds: internal (ābhyantara) and external (bāhya). 19.
Among those, the internal [articulation] consists of: 20.
closure (saṃvṛtatva), openness (vivṛtatva), contact (spṛṣṭatva), and slight contact (īṣatspṛṣṭatva). 21. Closure belongs to the vowel *a*. 22.

The vowels and the sibilants (ūṣman) possess an open articulation (vivṛtatva). 23. The vowels e and o possess an even more open articulation than those. 24. The diphthongs ai and au possess an even more open articulation than those two; and the vowel ā possesses an even more open articulation than those two as well. 25.
26. Contact is the quality of the *sparśa* (contact) consonants.
27. Slight contact is the quality of the semivowels (*antaḥstha*).
28. External [articulation].

The first and second letters of the classes, as well as *ś*, *ṣ*, *s*, *visarjanīya*, *jihvāmūlīya*, and *upadhmānīya*, have an open throat (*vivṛtakaṇṭha*), are produced with the emission of breath (*śvāsānupradāna*), and are voiceless (*aghoṣa*). 29.
The first, third, and fifth letters of the classes, along with the semivowels (*antaḥstha*), are weakly aspirated (*alpaprāṇa*). 30.
The others are strongly aspirated (*mahāprāṇa*). 31.

The third, fourth, and fifth [consonants] of each class, along with the anusvāra, the semi-vowels (*antaḥstha*), and the letter *ha*, have the throat constricted (*saṃvṛtakaṇṭha*), possess nasal resonance as their secondary emission (*nādānupradāna*), and are voiced (*ghoṣavat*). 32. The second and fourth [consonants] of each class, as well as *śa*, *ṣa*, *sa*, and *ha*, are sibilants (*ūṣman*). 33.
The consonants beginning with *ka* and ending with *ma* are the stops (*sparśa*). 34.

The semivowels *ya*, *ra*, *la*, and *va* are internal [articulators]; this constitutes the external effort (*bāhyaprayatna*). 35. Here, the vowel *a* is divided into three types: short, long, and protracted. 36.

Each of these is further divided eighteenfold by the distinctions of acute (*udātta*), grave (*anudātta*), and circumflex (*svarita* accents), as well as by the distinctions of nasalized (*sānunāsika*) and non-nasalized (*niranunāsika*). 37.
In this way, the *ivarṇa* and *uvarṇa* vowels, as well as the *ṛvarṇa*, [each have twelve varieties]. 38.
Since there are no long forms for the *ḷvarṇa*, it consists of twelve types. 39.
Because the diphthongs (*sandhyakṣara*) lack short forms, they too consist of twelve types. 40.
A short vowel consists of one mātrā. 41.
A long vowel consists of two mātrās. 42. A protracted vowel consists of three mātrās. 43.
44. A high pitch is udātta. 45. A low pitch is anudātta.
46. A combination [of the two] is svarita.
The vowels are both nasalized (*sānunāsika*) and non-nasalized (*niranunāsika*). 47.
The semivowels (*antaḥstha*), excluding the letter *r*, are of two types: nasalized and non-nasalized. 48.
Thus ends the *Varṇasūtra* composed by Candragomin.
